I tried to give this game a chance, I understand how daunting it is to create a game as an independant developer. But there's no excuse for this. Anodyne is an Action-Adventure game that draws heavy influence from the Legend of Zelda series, along with Yume Nikki (a surreal, horrorfying exploration game). Unlike LoZ, almost everything is amateurish in this game; the animations, the sprites, level design - it just all seems really poor. Unlike Yume Nikki, the atmosphere that the game presents is cheesy and trite. I never got that "dreamlike" vibe from the game just because of how clumsily it presented itself.  Many of the enemies you encounter don't even look like they belong in the area they reside in. The soundtrack can be hit-or-miss but is mediocre for the most part.
After defeating 3 ridiculously easy bosses, I lost interest and motivation to continue trying to make sense of the cryptic plot  - which was the only thing keeping me from quitting the game earlier.

The game draws heavily from the top down Zeldas in terms of puzzles, combat, and dungeon design which is why I'm surprised that I didn't like the game more.  It kept me entertained, but I think the major difference between it and Zelda resulted in repetitive combat, that distinction being there are only a handful of secondary items you earn in the game so most enemies are killed by just slashing over and over.  Story wise, the game has some very insightful moments, but, if there was a coherent subtext in the game, then I did not get it.  If there is a deeper narrative that the designers had in mind, then it is buried deep.  Other individuals might be able to relate to the story more and understand the intention of the creator, but because I never got into the story, I never really understood what was going on.  I don't think it is a bad game, just one I was hoping to like more.

A lot of people are comparing this game to 2D Zeldas, and while there are a lot of similar elements and it's obvious that there was some inspiration drawn from it (there's even a few Zelda jokes), to me this game was more akin to Earthbound or Yume Nikki, at least in terms of atmosphere. The game comes off as a fairly basic "save the world from evil" but takes a more eerie turn as you play through it. Even more so if you're going for 100% of the cards and you start exploring with swap tool post-endgame.
It was an entertaining game, and kept me busy for 7 hours (one playthough to experience the whole game and get all the items, and another to get the 3 hour achievement). I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants to get lost in a surreal world while solving some puzzles as you go. Though some of the puzzles can be bypassed entirely at times by finding a way to cheat the system.

This is a beautiful sandbox game in that it is literally like playing in the sand. I bought it on sale, and for whatever it cost me (maybe $10) it is one of by happiest gaming hours/$ spent. I got about 10 hours out of it at this point and am very satisfied.
Visuals:
Totally great. Sure, they could be better, but I loved getting down to the tribe's viewpoint and watching the tidal waves come, or the water rise. So neet.
Challenge:
Not too hard, but kept me on my toes even on low difficulty on the later levels. YMMV.
Replay:
The game is really attractive, and the challenges of each level ensured that I played each level through at least twice. However, beyond this once-or-twice level replay I did not feel the urge to replay. Partilly this is because on many levels while there are multiple ways to get through the challenges, but usually there is a clear optimal one. I know I'll pick it up in a few months and enjoy it again, once I have forgotten some of the tricks though.
Imagination inspiring:
Just amazing. If you ever played in the sandbox as a kid, or built sand castles on the beach, check this out. Some of the less obvious strategies can be fun to at least try!
Uplay/copy protect:
Whatever system other people have their legitimate complaints about... it didn't effect me. Maybe there was an overhaul of the system? It did not affect me in the slightest, so I consider this issue resolved. Note, I played on steam/pc.

There’s a simplicity about Welkin Road that works in its favor. Set in first-person, The graphics looks nice, but there isn’t a ton of detail. The sound is mostly ambient wind and your own footsteps. The only things to focus on are the geometric sections in front of you and how you aren’t going to fall to your death.
From the get go, almost every step of the way each platform is a new way to get from point A to point B. By level 5 I felt like I was still playing a tutorial despite each level taking me thirty plus minutes each to get through. Some of my stats said I had fallen 100 or more times before reaching the end.
I’m not suggesting that “the game’s no good because I suck.” Far from it. The trouble I had with Welkin Road is that it’s going to test the patience of a lot of gamers that could really love it.
In Welkin’s Road, trial and error along with overcoming physics give you a real reward to successes. The game is in early access, though, and the only way to go from here is up (or down, if you lose your balance). While the game definitely has some pace issues, and a lot of frustration, if you’re willing to practice and want a new type of platforming experience, players will definitely want to try Welkin Road.

If someone came up to me and told me I got one chance to rename this game, it would be:
Welkin: Road to frustration
If you like games such as Mirror's Edge and DeadCore, there's a chance that you will resort to these again after playing just a few levels of Welkin Road, because this game is currently not worth it. Why? Because:
- All the puzzles are designed to the maximum pixel limit. Pixel perfect precision is still, and will never be something that is enjoyable in puzzle games. HOWEVER, this is OK if this only happens a few times towards the latter levels of a puzzle game. Here, it's almost every single puzzle that feels like an unbeatable obstacle. The problem is that the level were designed from the developer's point of view, who has so much more knowledge of the most finicky bits of the movements, and not from a player's POV that will take a considerable amount of time to perfect some of the hardest moves. Instead, you're faced with seemingly impossible obstacles as early as level 3...
- The targetting system of the orbs is completely unpredictable, and there are definitly problems with distance measuring where sometimes you can clearly see your grappling beam actually hit the orb but it will simly not grapple whatsoever.
- The movements, in particular jumping, are incredibly finicky and feel very unstable. You feel as if you could just fumble down anytime even when just running (it hobbles from left to right way too much). This can, however, be disabled, so it's advised you do so.
- Finally, there are clearly optimisation problems on the grappling walls who just feel incredibly akward and jumping off of them is a nightmare.
The truth is that this game has a ton of potential, but currently reaches no pinnacles anywhere. Here are some of the things it does very good:
+ The visuals are great. Simple, but great. Mostly cubic and one prominent color mixed with white. The phong shading on them gives more life to the overall picture and the clouds are among the best I've seen so far.
+ There is one thing that carries the game, and that's the checkpoint system. It's so good it actually makes me wonder whether the developer himself was clearly aware of just how mundanously difficult the game is.
+ The music of the menu is great. Now add music in-game while we're playing and it's perfect.
+ The physical movement of swinging around does feel realistic (but as mentioned, the controls are completey hampering this).
For now, I cannot recommend it because the negatives outweigh the positives by a longshot. What I think is most keenly felt is how there is just no story whatsoever. There are supposedly secrets in the levels, but they are nothing more than just 'trophies' to say you were able to get on spot X or Y. How amazing would it have been if this game had a story that elaborated on how this world got created, what it's purpose it, what the orbs are and where your powers come from. Combine this with ambient music that stages the atmosphere and this game would be a masterpiece.
If that could be implemented, along with some obvious bugfixes and optimisations, I would immediatly change my rating to a high thumbs up. But for now, I can't. Don't get me wrong however, I think that for the amount of playtime you would actually set in the game, this price is worth it. They're not charging too much, which is a step in the right direction. Just wait for some patches that make this game just a little more forgiving, and we're in for a great score.

One of the weirdest games i've played so far. Deadly Premonition is an action adventure with mysterious/weird characters and an interesting story about the "Red Seed Killers".
It's touched by series like "Twin Peaks".
You are investigating about the murders, talking to people, doing (optional Sidequests) and driving through the town (which has no useful map!) mostly. That's the "fun" and interesting part about the game.
The other, not so "fun" part: From time to time you have to fight against zombie-like enemies. The controls are... "not good". You'll get used to it, but it's something worth mentioning. Also the "Quick Time Events" can be a pain the a**.
Both, the "gun gameplay" and the QTE's are feeling forced in the game. I believe, i read an article where the developer mentioned, they planed the game without this, but the Publisher wanted them to be in, because of the Call of Duty-trend.
Also the graphics are very outdatet. It looks and feels technically like an old PS2-Game.
I only can recommend this game to gamers, who like "weird and trashy" games with a bigger focus on the Story than the gameplay. You also should be able to bear the technical problems the game has.

I will start out by saying this game is terrible. The gameplay, the graphics, and almost every single facet of this game is so poorly done to the point where every frame of this game is questionable. And yet, this game is one of the most memorable and enjoyable experiences I have ever had in the medium of video games. I sit alone in my bed some nights desperately searching for the answer of "Why did I have so much damn fun with this game, and why am I spending $30 on this awful game I already beat in 2010?". I can never truly come up with a definitive answer.
The gameplay is awful. There is no other way to put it. The gameplay consists of the third-person, survival horror-action gameplay popurized and prototyped by the fantastic Resident Evil 4. The gunplay of this game is anything but fantastic though. The aiming is awful and sluggish, enemies are bullet sponges, and the boss fights are devoid of fun.
However, the gameplay is kind of serviceable outside of the action aspects. The game is an open-world (not exactly world, more like small town? open-hamlet?) game. There are plenty of side missions to keep you busy for up to 20+ hours. However, you may have guessed these side missions are some of the most menial and uninspired tasks in any video game ever. You also have a vehicle to get you from one objective to the next, and boy oh boy... You will learn to dread the cars in this game. Trying to tame these cars is like holding a rabid dog on a molasses soaked leash. In other words, Forza has nothing on this game.
Despite all these gripes with the gameplay, I enjoyed playing this game. The menial tasks were fun in a mindless way. The gunplay was truly awful, yet I found myself having fun with it near the end. And the driving? Well, that was just bad.
Furthermore, the graphics are just atrocious. I remember playing this back in 2010 and being absolutely floored. I could not believe video games could look this awful in 2010. The graphics were decent for a game released in the middle years of the PS2's life span. The graphics in this game truly shock the senses, and yet, I find something charming about them. When the main character makes his awkward, constipated grin, the game seemingly pauses on this face for a second, so the player can soak the glory all up.
What exactly redeems this game? I suppose it is the humor of it all. The story is a cobbled, convoluted mess of tropes, yet there is something undeniably interesting to it. The essential premise is you play as an FBI detective exploring a murder mystery in a small town. Along the way, you meet a wide assortment of characters. The characters are so oddball and off-their-rocker to the point of being instantly memorable. The crux of the humor comes from the interaction with these characters, where the gameplay, plot, and graphics collide into a beautiful mess. The "F.K. in the Coffee" scene succintly sums up this unholy union in one absolutely, show-stoppingly funny scene.
This game truly revels in its absurdity. Deadly Premonition is not a good game by any means. The plot has more holes than a nice wheel of swiss cheese, the graphics are indescribably bad, and the gameplay is appalling. Yet, those three facets were truly memorable, and even outright hilarous. Deadly Premonition is quite possibly the first "so bad, it's good" video game. There are many that would claim that title; Earth Defense Force is one that comes to mind. Yet, even that game is pretty decent on a pure gameplay standpoint. Deadly Premonition is a game that should not work, but it does in some kind of magical way. You may not like this game, but you will remember it
On a side note: The music in this game is absolutely stellar. Try listening to the Whistle Theme, and see if you can ever get it out of your head... I dare you.

Why this game hasn't received the same level of attention as others in the swath of roguelikes over recent years is beyond me. It controls smoothly, it introduces new elements at just the moment you've mastered the old, unlocks occur at a decent click for completing challenges, and most importantly, it gets the difficulty just right - it doesn't start♥♥♥♥♥♥hard and get harder; it starts easy, and gives you generous checkpoints so you can practice just the section that's giving you grief without going through the motions for five minutes beforehand. Then, after it's given you room to practice and learn its mechanics - that's when it gets♥♥♥♥♥♥hard. It never feels cheap or unfair because of the breathing room it gives to beginners. Additionally, because you are DEscending a tower, there is always a strong sense of momentum, so the 30 second time limit doesn't feel punitive, but rather acts as a mechanical reinforcement of the play style most people will gravitate towards anyway. In short it's a well programmed, thoughtfully designed game that's a great deal of fun to play. Easy to learn, hard to master, I recommend SHODN strongly.

Did you love Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm?  Were you one of the few who played and loved Vietcong?  Then you'll love this game!
It's a little rough around the edges and a little short on maps right now but when it all comes together and you're on a team that communicates with explosions all around you and helos flying overhead there's no better multiplayer shooter out there.
If you're new to the series then expect to die a LOT at the beginning from people you never see.   If you push through and take the time to learn the game while not handicapping your team by taking an important role without understanding what to do then you will be rewarded with one of the best simulations of the Vietnam war ever released.

Although I own the first rising storm, I do not have alot of time spent on it. So I will not be comparing RS2 with RS1. Gunplay feels great in my opinion, they could do with some more guns and maps definitely. Overall the game is extremely fun. Even after reaching over 130 hours, I still have fun playing it. I would say it is worth the full price. The gameplay does feel a tad clunky, but it is very easy to get used to. The game stutters like crazy at random points, but usually only once per time I play it. It is very annoying, but the game is so fun I learn to ignore it. If you have a full squad of friends or just a squad that is really into the game, you will have a fantastic time. It is a team effort, so at times you will be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off if you have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ team. This game always has me so focused, trying to spot movement and muzzle flashes from the enemy. Running from artillery, napalm, gunships, helicopters. Listening for any footsteps, taking cover, moving up to take objective, lobbing grenades into a group of enemies. Getting a kill is so satisfying in this game. Learning the roles of the game is fairly simple if you watch the tutorials and play a few games. It can use some work definitely, but It is a fantastic game either way in my opinion.

Very original and highly addictive. An RPG-solitaire mashup that works surprisingly well. The game is split up into a series of story chapters, each of which is divided into a number of "hands" of solitaire. There are two types of hand, regular ones, and duels. The regular ones play out more like a regular game of solitaire, although you have a number of equippable special abilities and skills which give you some tactical flexibility. However, it's the duels where the game really shines! During these you have to charge your attacks by playing consecutive cards. You have all the same tactics available to you during the normal hands to eke out longer combos but you also have an RPG layer added on top. You'll have to choose your equipment depending on the enemy you're fighting, some have high armour so you'll want to equip "pierce" weapons, some have a chance to deflect pistols and muskets, so you'll want to go melee. These bouts can often be quite tense and close right up to the last card if you play on hard mode (recommended!) and are very satisfying when you pull them off. But do these duels make all the other hands feel lame in comparison? Well actually no, I must admit, it's really nice to relax and play some normal solitaire after a tough fight, and they are interspersed well so there's a nice mix. Overall highly recommended!

I've been following this game since its debut at EGX in 2015 (the badges are still on my bag!!). After eagerly anticipating the release for two years, I was hoping I hadn't gotten myself too hyped and set myself up for disappointment.
Thankfully, I was not disappointed in the slighest. Shadowhand is a near-perfect card game. The blend of RPG elements really help to set it apart from other bog standard card games.
The story is slightly lacklustre, though the gameplay is so brilliantly solid that the story was the least of my concerns. It's still a decent story, though the game would still be just as good without it, in my opinion.
The art is extremely well polished and I enjoy actually being able to see my selected gear on Shadowhand, something that I feel is missing from so many RPGs these days.
The luck aspect can be slightly frustrating at times, though with any card game a high element of luck is going to be present as that's just the nature of the genre. Passive and active abilities are well-thought out and can really help to get Lady Luck on your side.
Shadowhand does a brilliant job at combining some of my favourite genres together to create something that is incredibly addictive, if not a little niche (don't get me wrong though - I live for niche games!).

I liked Regency Solitaire so I was eager to see what this new game would be like. So far (about ten "chapters" into the story) I am enjoying it and having fun. More mechanics have been added to the solitaire aspects of the game, and the osscasional "duel" segments against opponents are a fun addition. The difficulty level has increased steadily as the story progresses (I am playing on normal mode, have not tried hard yet) and it can sometimes be frustrating if you get a poor start to a tough segment; sometimes there is no option but to restart a hand as certain deals are just impossible to beat even with careful use of special abilities. (Suit locks with sizable numbers are the biggest problem, usually.)
Being able to customize the character with different weapons, gear, special abilities, etc. works well and lets you customize your play style a bit more. Don't get too fond of any piece of gear, though, as the difficulty scales so rapidly that an item which was excellent when you found it is average to useless two chapters later. Constant replacement with the new thing is necessary.
There is some heavy suspension of disbelief required with the duel opponents, as they auto-level worse than Elder Scrolls Oblivion did. Seemingly every random thug, brawler, or drunk in a bar has more health, better weapons, and better gear than our poor heroine does. A thug's bare fist or a beggar's dirty fingernails are deadlier weapons than the best sword or pistol you will possess. I understand the game has to throw ever-increasing challenges at you, but the repetition of "random nobody is three times stronger than the previous chapter's final boss, and his toenails/beard stubble/body odor are the deadliest weapons so far seen" really strains my acceptance of the story.
Still, if you can suspend your disbelief the  game mechanics are fun and challenging, the story is servicable and amusing in places, and the whole experience is well presented with nice art and music. I am enjoying the game and having fun. But maybe they can adjust the enemies' weapons to be a bit more believable?

The above however has zero influence on my following review.
RFLEX is a spiritual successor to Super Hexagon, utilizing the same style of 2D twitch reflex mechanics to dodge obstacles for a nearly impossible 60 seconds. However, I felt while playing this game that it had on edge on Super Hexagon due to more random obstacles than the same 7 memorizable patterns. Lets head to the pros and cons.
Pros:
Amazing sound design, with a unique song for each level, made by brilliant electronic composers.
Simple yet deceivingly difficult gameplay that successfully fulfills the neo-arcade design, complete with customizable screen curving!
Minimalist graphics that focus back on to the gameplay rather than distracting you.
Extra modes that affect the regular levels for more fun!
Cons:
Controls were a teensy bit weird to understand at the start. Instead of permanent twitch moves you use the arrow keys to hold the hexagon in place and then release to bring it back to the center. Ultimately not a problem but it takes time to get used to. Would love to see an extra mode without it though ;)
Overall, RFLEX is a really fun and addicting twitch-reflex-neo-arcade-minimalist-psychedelic experience. Like Super Hexagon I will spend quite a bit of time getting used to the controls and tricks required to survive. Have fun!

An alright Zelda clone that has a very wistful, dreamy feeling to it. The entire game pushes that sort of aimless, wandering quality while dropping hints of what's at the heart of the game on a deeper philosophical level. Ultimately though, I found it a bit too aimless, and got bored a little over halfway through, when I discovered the only way to the end of the game was finishing a collection of cards, and relentlessly screen-hunting through a game that doesn't have any tracking system for if you've been to a place or not. While I have no issue doing it myself, the game wasn't compelling or entertaining enough to make me want to do it. The only puzzle mechanic was Roc's Feather style jumping, button pushing, and pushing dust around with a broom. No other puzzle, items, or anything to use. Bosses were unimaginative and felt like slogs, and even with the portals and jumping around, a great deal of the maps felt like empty needless filler, walking from place to place in what is, admittedly, a chamring, quirky (and sometimes fairly dark and entirely unsettling) little world, but filled with very little actual substance.
I think that's what the game was trying to do, though, which means I can't really fault it for being exactly that. The game would get a neutral rating from me if I could give it one, so I'll recommend it and give it a positiv erevie wbecause I think the game is well done, it's just not a game for me.

The Steam version of From Dust runs just fine without Uplay. If that's the only thing preventing you from buying it, then don't let it keep you from experiencing what is a very unique and enjoyable strategy game.
It will only take you 5 minutes, at most, to create a firewall rule so that From Dust will run just like any other non-Uplay Steam game. You don't need a Ubisoft account either, and you can play in offline mode.
After downloading From Dust, but before starting it for the first time, install Ubisoft Game Launcher from the From Dust\Support\Ubisoft directory. Then use Windows Firewall to block the Ubisoft launcher from using the internet, which will prevent it from updating to Uplay when you start the game.

Strike Team Hydra is the debut title from indie developers, Wave Light Games, beginning its life on mobile and now available on Steam.
In Strike Team Hydra you play the role of a commander in charge of a six-man strike team sent aboard the SS TALWAR, a stricken battleship on patrol in system NS-14. After heavy fighting the TALWAR has been boarded by enemy aliens, the Sethari, and it's your job to get on board, rescue the survivors, and wipe out any Sethari you find.
Kick some Sethari butt, commander!
The game is in 3D, with all levels taking place inside the TALWAR. Stages are well made, though rather small, with cover and interesting gadgets and scenery to look at. Some appear to be multi-levelled, but you'll find you can't use the stairs; they're only for show.
Enemy and character graphics are also good, with lifelike animations. Animations on prefabs are synchronised, though, meaning that enemies all check their guns at the same time, which is a bit dodgy. Weapon and special ability effects look good, with glowing force fields, bright lasers, explosions, and other cool stuff going on.
The interface doesn't quite work. Sometimes you'll have to move the pointer back and forth over target hexes multiple times to get the interface to show the terrain/cover modifiers or allow targeting, or change to a different character and then back again. This seems to happen more when zoomed in, but it's not consistent. It's also more fiddly than it should be; in the lobby you can't look at characters' abilities without loading up the swap screen. And on the swap screen you can only swap one at a time. The lack of tooltips for any in-game items -- and for some of the UI overlay -- is frustrating, too, as is having to right-click to find out information; why not just hover like a normal tooltip?
Sound and music are mostly well produced and functional. Weapon and effect sounds are appropriate, though teleporting is a bit too loud. Music is typical science-fiction-actiony fare, electronic with some dramatic bits, but there are too few tracks and it gets repetitive quickly. There are voices for character actions, too. These range from outright terrible to not too bad, but even the bad ones are mostly amusing so I'm glad they're included.
The Unity launcher provides the standard options: resolution selection, full-screen / windowed mode, and one graphics detail selector from Fastest through to Excellent. An in-game menu includes independent voice, sound effect, and music volume sliders, as well as some PC-only graphical toggles. These add some great shadows, fancy-looking effects, and other assorted coolness. All up the game looks rather good.
Strike Team Hydra first appeared on Android and iOS before coming to Steam, with the magic of Unity allowing for deployment to multiple platforms. It's unfortunate that its heritage shows, with the tutorial still describing touch-screen controls and on-screen buttons that don't exist in the PC version. With a bit of playing around you can find out that WASD pans, Q/E rotates, and mouse wheel zooms the camera; I'm not sure if you can tilt up/down. There's also no way to remap controls; the standard Unity launcher's 'input' tab doesn't provide anything obviously useful in this regard and there's no in-game menu providing the functionality either. And there's no Steam integration yet, either: no achievements, cloud saving, or trading cards.
The game is a squad-based, turn-based strategy game, played over a series of campaign missions (28, by the look of it, plus a similar number of 'extra missions') on the besieged SS TALWAR. You control six soldiers from a selection of 12, each of whom gains experience and levels, unlocking new abilities. You can also buy and sell armour and weapons, as well as receiving them as rewards for missions, but many seem to only be for flavour, having no obvious effect on a soldier's stats. The game plays a lot like the combat part of the original XCOM / UFO: Enemy Unknown from the 1990s. You can swap out characters between missions, which is excellent, allowing you to pick and choose as you like, or even double-up on some character types. There's no character customisation, but there is a good range of abilities across the 12 characters, so you can try a few different play styles.
Most of the game rules are explained via a Rules tab, but anyone familiar with turn-based squad games should find them relatively straightforward. For some reason you can't check the rules in-mission, either; you can only do it from the lobby. There's no overwatch, which is a bit of a shame; the counterattack feature that replaces it works well enough in response to enemies that directly attack a unit, but movement through fire zones or attacking other soldiers will not trigger a counterattack. There are a few other silly game mechanics, too, such as the 15-85% range for attacks and criticals, and the undo movement feature, which is great, but lets you move to collect power-up items and then undo your movement.
Other than that, it's typical turn-based combat, and it's mostly very well done. Each character has an Action Point (AP) pool and a number of actions or abilities to use, each of which uses a certain number of APs. Movement costs differ between characters, too, allowing your faster and lighter soldiers to move further and do more than your slower and heavier ones. There are no restrictions on ordering of moving and shooting; as long as you have the APs you can do what you want. Once you've moved all your soldiers it's the aliens' turn, and so on until you've met the mission objectives (usually kill everything that moves) or died.
There's no manual saving in missions, but the game does have an auto-save feature that seems to save at the beginning of each turn.
Unfortunately there are a number of gameplay issues that detract from what would otherwise be an excellent game. First, it's one of the most unstable non-EA games I've played in the last few years. It's crashed on me about once an hour, which is bad enough, but all but one of those crashes has been when I've just finished a mission. And that lovely auto-save feature I just mentioned? It doesn't work; the game deletes the auto-save when this happens and I'm left having to redo the mission again, losing the progression and item I just received.
Less important, but still annoying, are the weird interface issues mentioned earlier, line of sight that doesn't quite make sense, weird pathing stuff-ups on one mission that made characters walk around the whole map to cover two hexes, and the numerous grammar errors throughout. It's the crashing issue that drove me to give up, though.
Pros:
+ Core gameplay is great fun, with plenty of tactical options
+ A range of well-balanced characters
Cons:
- Horribly unstable, no manual saves to cope with it
- Glitchy and frustrating interface
- Mobile heritage is evident
Strike Team Hydra ended up disappointing me for all the wrong reasons. Presentation is good, there's a lot to do, and the core gameplay is great fun. But the game interface is glitchy and fiddly, and the game is often unstable, crashing at the worst possible times. This would be excusable to a degree if you could save mid-mission, but the auto-save system doesn't cope and all too often I've lost whole missions. It's got to the point now that I just can't be bothered trying anymore.
If you're a fan of turn-based strategy and don't mind a few rough edges then Strike Team Hydra is definitely one to watch, and pick up once the stability issues have been fixed. I would love to recommend it, but until the developers fix the crashing I'm not going to.

I'm an old Julian Gollop fan from ZX Spectrum days and enjoy this style of TRPG a lot.  Strike Team Hydra is a very accessible 3D hex-based (if that makes sense.. units stand in a hex but the view can be zoomed and rotated) tactical squad shooter.  Kind of a simpler/more arcadey XCOM.  Quite a lot of use of terrain and ranged attacks vs direct scrapping, plus use of return/suppressing fire.  If you dont play the tutorial first time (I admit it, I skipped it as I'd played this already on IOS but forgot a few things...) it doesnt pop up again but can be started from Missions/Training.
Runs smoothly on my Surface Pro 2017 (i5/8GB RAM/Intel HD 620 integrated graphics) at 2736x1824 on "Good" mode with extra effects turned off (transparency/dynamic shadows/post-processing effects) as I'm more interested in the mechanics not the visuals; I should probably just play in a much lower res.  Install was fast but you have to pick your graphic preferences on first startup and I intially chose the top settings and even the main menu screen struggled a bit..
Basic Touch funtionality is ok (ie mouse-click-as-finger), but I didnt get a right-click for a touch-and-hold when wanting to look at a unit/terrain detail.  And two-finger pinch or rotate didnt control the zoom/angle for me even in tablet mode.
A few interface glitches; some of the UI/menus are a little inconsistent - eg some screens have a red "Leave" button, others expect you to press ESC - and at the resolution I play the scrollbars are so tiny i have use scrollwheel/two fingers to move down menus.  And if you arent paying attention you'll start relying on the End Turn button to find your units that still have action points left..
The game mechanics are easy to pick up and the missions/specials are compact enough to have a quick game as and when.
Overall - great graphics and mechanics, decent amount of content, a few UI blemishes.  Fresh, faster-paced take on the genre.

Ah, Rising Storm 2: VIETNAM, where we shoot the Gooks and the GI go home! The game essentially captures the essence of the Vietnam War. Anything from napalm to punji traps, you name it, it's probably in the game.
When the game was first announced it was a mere unexaggeration to say that I was highly anticipating this game to come out. I must say that they did a good job in getting everyone hyped about the game. One thing that you may notice on the store page is that the game only costs twenty dollars or so. This is because the game is ran on an old enjin from 2010. Don't worry, the graphics are honestly pretty decent, and the napalm explosions are cinematic. However, the main issue was that the release dates kept getting pushed farther back. Originally it was set to release at the end of 2016, but then it was moved to "Early 2017" although the game actually released in late May. Early 2017 people am I right?
After purchasing the game on the day of release, I began playing the sh*t out of it. What can I say? I don't have a job and it was in the middle of the summer. My first impressions were amazing. The weapons, the helicopters, the main menu music, this game seemed to have it all!
Though the game seemed great and all, it did have its cons. As I played it more and more, in attempt to get to the top as fast as I could, I slowly noticed that there was no point in the leveling system. All it really allowed you to do was unlock new cosmetics. Don't get me wrong, this certaintly gave me motivation to level up during the first few weeks of the game. The primary issue with this however is that all of the really cool cosmetics required you to be level eighty or more. This normally wouldn't be a problem but once the first update of the game came around they removed the double experience. With the new update, it became incredably time consuming to level up. With every game roughly taking you thirty minutes to complete at minimum, I saw that grinding just wasn't worth my time.
Gameplay wise, my main complaints are the sound and spawning. Whenever I'm on the map Cu Chi and I'm crawling through the tunnels I somehow hear bullets whisking past my head and my vision is being distorted even though there is no enemy in sight. Logic right? Another flaw is that both sides should be able to spawn on their squad leaders. I see how you want the Vietnamese to utilize the tunnel system but in all honesty the US has a mass advantage when it comes to respawning. Especially when you have a bad squad leader on the NLF or PAVN, it can be a pain in the a*s when you have to run all the way to the point from main.
I've pointed out some flaws in the game, but I believe that they can be easily fixed within an update. If they've somehow convinced you into not buying the game then I highly advise against your decision. Although the game has its issues, it's still a fecking blast to play with a group of friends.

Let me start off by saying that i love the Vietnam War and anything about it. History never really gets too deep into this war and not a lot of Vets talk about it for obvious reasons which leads to my fascination about the Vietnam War. I want to love this game i really do and Tripwire did a good job on RO2/RS1 as far as i am concerned (coming from someone who has played it more receently within the last year) its not really the final product. That said, I give it a thumbs down (for now) and i will be explaining in more detail about why i love/hate this game.
As i explained in the first paragraph I love Vietnam War for what it was. America wanting to stop the spread of Communism do to the Dominoe Effect that might take place should Vietnam be lost. Also, it was in a time when culture and revolutionary change where a thing thus the music and psychological mindset of people in that time are truly immitated in this game to a certain degree (not much you can do in a war game, trust me, I'm aware). The environments and immersion are there. The weapons are there and feel authentic. The chaos and mayehm definitely are there. Seeing and hearing your teammates characters and watching them burn due to a misplaced napalm or seeing there bits on the ground from a explosion are definitely there (this is Rising Storm 2 after all) making the experience a real and fun experience. I say this because, no matter how i feel about the game, I feel Tripwire nailed this perfectly. I'm very happy to finally experience the true nature of Vietnam even if I wasnt there for it. I also like the teamwork play when it works as well as you really have to push those Obj as an American or NVA since its so hectic. But that is where this gets out of pros for me and straight into the cons which is next.
Now im a firm believer that any game that requires shooting should never have lag issues or Desync and in this day and age of gaming it seems developers have forgotten how to optimize their games in general when it comes to shooters and Tripwire is no exception to this rule. I feel like my bullets are paper airplanes that go around my target even when im ADSing (aim down sight) someone thats right in front of me. There is a litany of problems with this game, though to say the following is an exhaustive list would be inaccurate:
-It's a shoddy port that doesn't appear to render properly, nor hide the mouse cursor (that's okay though, you can just push the cursor off to the side and ignore it, I suppose).
-Its narrative is shallow and horrifyingly pretentious; being populated by insufferably stupid characters who are either boring, annoying, or both.
-The game’s limited number of environments are populated with bland art assets that in some cases don’t look suitable for a modern game.
-Excessive is a good descriptor for the game’s length.  The story is not compelling enough to justify the amount of time it takes to unfold, particularly when one considers the amount of filler you’re forced to go through as well.
-The side quests do very little to support or expand upon the story, and are instead mostly drudge work collecting stuff for people, punctated by transit between areas.
My recommendation is you don't spend money on this game, or at least don't pay full price for it.  Check out some of the other stuff PlatinumGames has worked on instead.

Cute little A-RPG obviously inspired by 2D Zelda games.
Everything about it is very dream-like, from the environment to the soundtrack. Some of it made me feel a bit nostalgic and sad while sometimes it was just eerie.
It's difficult to make sense of the story but you do kind of get the idea. Do keep in mind that this is supposed to be your character's subconscious. It will make allusions to real life and how your character, Young, is just trying to stay out of it.
Even though it's left to interpretation quite a bit, it doesn't feel like one of these very artsy games that makes no sense no matter how you look at it and that any vague interpretation could somewhat match. It's dreamy but still fairly obvious.
The game never feels exceptional but it's fun to go through. It shows multiple good example of game design where the game will
you that something is possible rather than tell you. You learn from doing and looking rather than reading.
Puzzles were never overly elaborate or complicated but required enough thinking that it felt satisfying to solve them most of the time. Some enemies were difficult enough to be challenging without being frustrating.
The only thing I liked less of the game is the lack of "tracking". The lack of direction it has is perfectly fine as it just reinforces the exploration and adventure part. But there are some stuff that you will need to go back to later on in the game and the only thing the game tracks is where you've been. It would have been cool to see how many chests/cards you've obtained in each area. I found myself 2 or 3 cards short from being able to access the last area and just looked them up since I didn't feel like exploring every area I've been to another time.
Otherwise, it was a really mysterious and cool experience. Although it borrows a lot from Zelda, don't expect this game to be one, just similar in some regards.
Takes about 6 hours or so to finish, without skipping anything before the end of the game (there are some extra stuff once you're done). Considering this, 11$ might be a tad expensive but definitely get it if it's on sales.

Anodyne is a proud, blatant Zelda-like, but it doesn't feel like a ripoff.  Its world is uniquely both off-the-wall and melancholic.  The atmosphere is what stands out most to me--the overworld is serene and mesmerizing to explore, the dungeons vary in tone, and the game in general has sort of paradigm shifts that caught me off-guard in a way I very much appreciated.  The gameplay is very reminiscent of Link's Awakening, while subverting many of its key elements, and virtually eliminating item management by having the puzzles revolve less around items and more around how Young's broom interacts with the environment.  As a result, the puzzles tend to be simpler and easier than those in Zelda dungeons, but they are also quite imaginative and manage to stay fresh.
If I had anything negative to say about this game, it's that the hitboxes are a bit too big, which gets frustrating on any screen with holes or big rolling spike columns.  I also think that while it isn't necessary, it would have been nice if there were indicators on the map of where things like unopened treasure chests and boss rooms are, and more guidance for where to find the post-game items.
For anyone looking for the gameplay of Zelda, combined with Metroid's attention to atmosphere, in a package that's more than the sum of its parts, Anodyne is a fine experience.

Only real RS2 players will understand what I mean here:
Gạo là một sản phẩm lương thực thu từ cây lúa. Hạt gạo thường có màu trắng, nâu hoặc đỏ thẫm, chứa nhiều dinh dưỡng. Hạt gạo chính là nhân của thóc sau khi xay để tách bỏ vỏ trấu. Hạt gạo sau khi xay được gọi là gạo lứt hay gạo lật, nếu tiếp tục xát để tách cám thì gọi là gạo xát hay gạo trắng. Gạo là lương thực phổ biển của gần một nửa dân số thế giới.
Cây lúa hiện nay được nông dân gieo trồng là kết quả xử lý trong phòng thí nghiệm và lai tạo tự nhiên cũng như nhân tạo của nhiều thế kỷ từ cây lúa dại.
Vì quỹ đất có giới hạn, các nhà khoa học đang nghiên cứu biến đổi gien của cây lúa để tạo ra giống lúa mới có năng suất cao, chống được bệnh tật và thời tiết khắc nghiệt, đồng thời rút ngắn thời gian chăm bón và sớm cho thu hoạch. Những thành công ban đầu của lúa biến đổi gien đã được ghi nhận, song hiện các nhà khoa học vẫn chưa thống nhất được liệu loại lúa này có tác động xấu đến sức khỏe con người hay không.
Gạo là sản phẩm từ cây lúa và nằm trong một quá trình sản xuất nông nghiệp, thường bao gồm những khâu chính sau: làm đất, chọn thóc giống, gieo hạt, ươm mạ, cấy, chăm bón (bón phân, đổ nước), gặt và xay xát.
Gạo là nguồn thu nhập và cuộc sống của hàng triệu nông dân trên toàn thế giới. Họ dùng khoảng 150 triệu hecta hàng năm để trồng lúa, với sản lượng khoảng 600 triệu tấn.
Châu Á là nơi sản xuất và cũng là nơi tiêu thụ khoảng 90% lượng gạo toàn thế giới.
Ở châu Phi, gần như toàn bộ 38 nước đều trồng lúa trong tổng số 54 quốc gia, song diện tích lúa ở Madagascar và Nigeria chiếm 60% tổng diện tích lúa tương đương 8,5 triệu hecta của châu lục này. Năng suất lúa của châu Phi thấp, khoảng 1,5 tấn/ha và chỉ bằng 40% năng suất của châu Á.
Phần lớn cây lúa nói đến trong sản xuất là lúa nước (tức ruộng lúa phải ngập nước theo một tiêu chuẩn khắt khe), song cũng có những loài lúa mọc trên ở vùng đồi núi mà ít cần đến công tác thủy lợi.
Việt Nam có hai vùng trồng lúa chính là đồng bằng sông Hồng ở phía Bắc và đồng bằng sông Cửu Long ở miền Nam. Vào thời điểm năm 1922 thời Pháp thuộc toàn cõi Việt Nam tức cả ba kỳ: Bắc, Trung, Nam diện tích canh tác là 4.640.000 hecta lúa với sản lượng 7.200.000 tấn thóc.[6] Năng suất ở mỗi miền khác nhau. Tính đến thập niên 1930 một hecta ở Bắc Kỳ thu hoạch được 1.470 kg thóc; Trung Kỳ đạt 1.370 kg/ha; và Nam Kỳ là 1.340 kg/ha.[7] Tuy nhiên vì diện tích trồng trọt ở Nam Kỳ rộng lớn hơn nên miền Nam đã là vựa thóc, cung cấp phần thặng dư lớn nhất của cả sáu xứ Liên bang Đông Dương.[8]
Sang thế kỷ 21 hàng năm sản lượng của cả nước đạt 33-34 triệu tấn thóc, trong đó chỉ sử dụng khoảng 8 triệu tấn (tương đương 4 triệu tấn gạo sau khi xay xát) cho xuất khẩu, còn lại là tiêu thụ trong nước và bổ sung dự trữ quốc gia.
Ở miền Bắc Việt Nam một năm có hai vụ lúa chính: vụ chiêm và vụ mùa.
Ở miền Nam Việt Nam, nông dân trồng ba vụ một năm: vụ đông xuân (có sản lượng cao nhất và thóc cũng đạt chất lượng tốt nhất cho xuất khẩu), vụ hè thu và vụ ba. Do lũ hàng năm ở đồng bằng sông Cửu Long trong những năm gần đây ảnh hưởng đến sản xuất, một phần nữa người dân có thể kiếm lời ổn định hơn từ việc nuôi thủy sản (tôm) hay trồng cây ăn quả, chính quyền đã khuyến cáo nông dân giảm và chuyển đổi một phần đất trồng lúa vụ ba.
Bộ Nông nghiệp và Phát triển Nông thôn là bộ chủ quản, quản lý việc sản xuất lúa gạo của Việt Nam.

Finally got my hands on this game as I'm a big fan of the TV Show.
So, here's my review for it so far (reaching 6 hours into it)
Final Score - 7 out of 10
Storyline ; ( 6/10 )
The storyline doesn't follow Game Of Thrones stories but it has some parts that will remind you of the TV Show.
So you play as 2 different characters, one is a survivor and leader of the Night's Watch.
The other one is an old priest that returns to his city and tries to bring justice into it.
So as for the story goes you will get yourself into the character's head, it's pretty fun.
Dialogs are general I skip the conversations sometimes but I like the variety of ways you can play this game.
Gameplay ; (7/10)
1) Quests -
After you create your character and give him his attributes,stats and class you follow the story that the game has given to you and move along the maps to complete the quests.
You can do some side quests that will not take long and kill extra enemies.
Nothing to explore really besides finding more quests/enemy and items.
As for the equipment you have you can trade it (sell/buy) in merchants in each map.
So, there's nothing much to do in this game.
2) Combat -
As for the combat goes, if you played Of Orcs and Men and enjoy it you will enjoy the combat in this game as well.
You have pause menu where you can choose which abilities to do with each character and then execute it on the enemy.
The enemy A.I have different types of weapons/armor so it is challenging.
RPG Elements ; (8.5/10)
1) Skills - Skill Trees with upgrades for each character, and also to the character A.I assistant.
2) Items - variety of weapons to use, and in differnet types as well. Ranged/Closed , Blunt/Cutting , Short blades etc.
3) Equipment - You have 2 weapon sets in this game so you can switch from 1 set to another anytime.
Example: [Set One] can be crossbow or heavy axe and [Set Two] can be 2 weapons in hand or sword+shield.
You also have body armor (helmet etc) flasks (potions etc) and rings.
4) Character Build - in 4 phases.
[Phase 1] Class [Phase 2] Stats [Phase 3] Skill Tree [Phase 4] Strength and Weakness attributes
So combine all of this in this game and you will enjoy your time playing as a badass ruthless warrior with strong weapons and heavy damage, or as the protector of the city with health and dodging abilities, or as a scouting rouge that has stealth moves. (yes, stealth is also a mechanic in this game).
A.I ; ( 6/10 )
1) Enemy A.I - They are challenging because each has different type of armor and weapon.
The come in groups so you will have to combine strategy and tactics to defeat them.
2) Character A.I - You control your A.I (ofcourse because it's a rpg fantasy game) just like in Of Orcs And Men.
Each character has different abilities and different tasks. (control the dog of Mors or the soldier of The Priest).
Overall ;
If you enjoyed games like Of Orcs and Men and Divinity you will find common combat system like in Orcs and Men and similiar rpg elements like in Divinity.
You will enjoy the gameplay, cuz it's also repetetive as you can play in different classes, different builds/skills and making your character be a ruthless heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or a good "governor" for the people of Riverspring.
But if you've watched the show and expect the characters from the show and storylines from the show, you are to be mistaken.
You should give this game a try cuz it's unique and good as it is.
Thanks for watching this review.

Game of Thrones: the RPG is overall a well-done game that I recommend.
The universe is - of course - extremely well-done. All those now famous locations or characters, the plots, the lands...
The RPG part is there, and while the game isn't the most stunning visually speaking, it's not bad.
But for me, there was one problem: right from the beginning, I found the combat system absolutely awful. I would personally have loved a more dynamic system, maybe less strategy-focusing and more graphical, even with comobos or stuff like that... But that's the devs choice.
Anyway, despite the fighting system, I recommend it to anyone in love with the Game of Trones serie or the ASOIAF universe in general, or to all RPG fans who wouldn't mind the change of pace when fighting. The devs focused really hard on the story, giving us a believable plot, with no "right" choices but instead "less-worse" choices that do have consequences on the future, and I simply loved the main characters.

As someone who played this game after it was promoted on TPB and who had followed and speedran it for a long time since, I would say that I had fun with this.
As a first attempt at a full on big project like this it makes me optimistic for Sean and Jon's other projects. Now, with that there are some pros and cons.
Pros
-Good soundtrack. I particularly love the Fields and Windmill themes as well as the final boss theme, "Understanding". I personally enjoy listening to OSTs outside of the context of the game and while you can do that easily with this OST and enjoy it in it's own right, the environments blend very, very well with the score here.
-Interesting area layouts. During the post-game exploration there are a lot of new places to go to add some challange and lore to the game world.
-Good dialogue. There are a few nice EarthBound-esque  moments in the dialogue.
-Interesting boss ideas. Yes, all of them come down to hit it 4-12 (respectively) until die, the ideas behind the bosses were at least neat.
-If you're like me and like non-standard, more surreal elements in level design then this has it in terms of the level concepts. This does, admittedly, take some inspiration from Link's Awakening (I also, litterally, see some Binding of Isaac in there as well) but never so much that I get "rip off" vibes ever.
Cons
-While the dialogue is good at points the story loses focus, especially when it comes to the post-game exploration. Once you've gone everywhere in search of every item and new area it leaves you with a sense of "was that it?", sadly. There's definitely some good ideas here, but with the somewhat oblique storyline - that addmittedly does add to the surreal aspects of the game - coupled with the overarching goal of the game being vauge even to the credits I can't help but feel there could be more done with it.
-This is a slightly personal thing but I really wish there were more achivements in the game to further reward replays. Not a big deal, but it's a minor nitpick. For a game where there's so many easter eggs and weird things to see (Elk) there could've been more unique achivements.
I will give one neutral remark: like I said I speedran this game for nearly 2 years and while I do know of more than a dozen huge glitches in this game, rest assured that you'll never run into them in this game. They're the type of glitches that you have to be purposfully trying to achive.

Anodyne is basically Link's Awakening meets Yume Nikki. You play as a kid named Young, who has to explore The Land in order to save The Briar from the Darkness... yeah, Anodyne's pretty tongue-in-cheek about its Chosen One schtick.
You spend the game exploring strange, eerie environments, fighting monsters, and solving puzzles. These range from a highway, to a classic Zelda-style temple, to an apartment complex, to an 8-bit maze full of zombies. The devs definitely didn't skimp on the environmental diversity.
Like Yume Nikki, Anodyne's heavy on symbolism and light on explanations. (Why is the boss of the caves talking to you about video games? What's the deal with the Red Sea, and what are the things living in it?) The ending, as you'd expect, answers none of these questions and leaves the player even more confused. Maybe the postgame sheds some more light on things, but I doubt it.
There are a couple things I disliked, though. You can't get to the final dungeon unless you collect all 36 cards hidden around the world- there are markers telling you which area's you haven't cleared out, but it's still a pain going through the whole game trying to find the things you missed. The combat is pretty bleh- unlike Zelda, there aren't any special weapons, so bosses boil down to "dodge their attacks and hit them until they die", except the final boss, which is more of a puzzle than anything. There are some pretty brutal jumping puzzles toward the end of the game. And it's short: I beat it in about 5 hours.
Despite these flaws, Anodyne is still worth checking out- I had fun with most of the puzzles, and enjoyed exploring all the weird locales (the game's oppressive ambient soundtrack helped). Play the demo on Newgrounds, and if you like what you see, pick up the full game.

Every kill counts—as long as the Blutonium vial gets picked up. Picking up the red vials dropped by dead opponents scores your team points. Deny the other team from scoring by grabbing the green vials dropped by dead allies. It’s vital to stick together in Death Snatch so that there’s someone left alive to grab the vials and score points. Here's a video showing how to play
Forget capturing flags. Capture the enemy’s hammer and take it back to your base while protecting your own to score. Oh, and the hammer is a brutal melee weapon. Smashing enemies with it nets more points on a successful capture. Steal the hammer -> smash people -> profit. Here's a video on how to play
Grab the unrefined Blutonium scattered over the map and take it to the grinder bins for processing—and points. Stop the other team from scoring by killing their collector. When a collector dies, another player on the team is randomly chosen. Unrefined Blutonium is incredibly volatile when shot or thrown—watch out! Watch the tutorial on how to play
Capture the active control point to score. The more players in proximity to the control point the faster it captures. Taunting in the capture zone also speeds up the process—but makes the capping team an easier target. The closer a team gets to capturing, the longer it will take the other team to capture the point. Watch this video that shows you how to play
For serious competitors we have Annihilation, which combines elements from Blitz, Death Snatch, and Jackhammer into one humungous pot of hardcore: cap the points, cap the vials, and cap the hammer! Win Annihilation by racking up ten thousand Team Points, thereby lowering the enemy shields so you can blow up their dropship. Boom! Watch this video that shows you how to play

Summary: Surreal Zelda-lite
Multiplayer: No
Completion: 6 hrs
Cards: Yes
Cloud: Yes
The first thing you'll notice about Anodyne is how it is inspired from Zelda... in a strange surreal sort of way. You play as the silent protagonist Young in a real-time top-down action RPG. Armed with his trusty broom, Young sets out to battle the forces of... his mind? The game is curiously unclear about this. Going by in-game text only, it's anyone's guess where you are - Limbo? Someone's dream? Tartarus? A video game?
The first thing you are told is that you must reach something known as the Briar before darkness does. Young thus sets out on his journey to collect keys and cards in order to unlock gates in order to enter the next area. While keys make sense, it's peculiar that many gates require a certain number of cards to access. This wouldn't be a problem if it wasn't for the fact that the last gate requires obtaining nearly all the cards, and so you must do a lot of backtracking to find what you were missing.
The game plays out in a number of different, often disjointed areas, notably modern ones. They range from streets, to caves, to suburbs, to hotels. It's cool, and it's well-drawn, but there's seemingly no coherence. Even if it's a dream world, there's no rhyme or reason ever given for why you may suddenly find yourself in an 8-bit dungeon. There's a town where you can go around stabbing npcs with a sword. It's creepy and unsettling, much like the music in the game, but you just accept it and move on. I feel there were some missed opportunities to expand upon these mysterious worlds.
If there's one thing I want in the game, it's more items. Early on you are given your trusty broom, which is a fair enough starter weapon. But throughout the entire game you never get anything different. You can obtain alternative attack patterns, but in the end it's still a broom. The only other power you obtain is jumping (and eventually another late-game power). You don't even learn to dash. I would have liked ranged attacks, learn to set fire to things, communicate with the strange walkers, etc.
Anodyne boasts a remarkable large world map and a half a dozen moderately sized dungeons. While it can get a little confusing where to go sometimes, merely heading for parts of the map you haven't explored often sets you on the right path. The maps are fairly well constructed and have a nice open feel to them. I like that switches to open doors will often keep the door open so you don't have to repeat most difficult rooms you come across. There's some good enemy variety too, with unique AI patterns for each type of enemy you face. The boss battles are appropriately intense and often involved some gimmick. They have many varied attack patterns and genuinely feel like bosses, so good marks on that.
The game runs pretty well overall. I did occasionally clip into terrain, but other than that, there were no major bugs I found. I give Anodyine a 7/10. It doesn't quite live up to the legacy of Zelda, but it does manage to hold its own. Anodyone is a very commendable game to be accomplished with such a small team. I would have liked a more fleshed out story but I understand that's not what they were going for.
I've played many Zelda-games, and this just felt too much like a cheap version of Link's adventures.

Verdict: I got Anodyne as a gift and it's been a game I've always been curious about. I had that GBC throughout my teen years and I finished both Pokémon and TLoZ: OoA way too many times to count. Later when I was 18-19 I had the opportunity (after all those years) to play TLoZ: Orace of Seasons, a game I've always wanted to try out (and actually the one I wanted instead of OoA). I'm quite certain that Anodyne pays tribute to the GB-GBC TLoZ era, including Link's Awakening. Walking around some areas, I even felt like I was back at Labrynna due to how similar that particular spot was to another one in OoA. It's actually the first tribute game to make me nostalgic and if I used scores on my reviews, it would get a 10/10 just because of that.

Update 11/19/17: After viewing content from other community members and my own friends; I can say that the Synthetic Dawn DLC was not as I had feared, and is a decent addition to the game and fairly priced as well; good on Paradox. As for the recently announced changes to FTL; while I'm primarly a Hyperlane player, I'm not thrilled by the loss of the other two types as they have added diversity to play as well as (at least in terms of warp civs) added extra danger in times of war. Hopefully; our modding community will be able to at least restore or even expand upon the soon-to-be-lost FTL types moving forward. While I still have little care for supporting the Utopia DLC, it looks more and more like I'll be forced to bite the bullet at some point as the traditions/ascension system is expanded & improved upon by both the devs and the modding community. Hopefully; the upcomming Black Friday or Winter Sales on Steam will provide a much needed discount but for now, I have galaxy to conquer...
First off; I'm going to talk a lot; so there's a TL:DR at the bottom for those who don't have the time for my long-winded approach. For those that do read it all; thanks for reading; hope it helps. :)
I bought this game shortly after it's launch; and now with over 300 hours of playtime, I think I can give a fair review of what I've experienced with it. Starting off; Stellaris can be a little overwhelming to new players; what with all the content that is offered. Between managing your individual planets and fleets to managing your empire and it's overall growth, things can start to get quite involved and you'll find the hours ticking away as if they were minutes as you delve into a playthru. While the vanillia game is great by itself; Stellaris really shines with the plethora of content mods that have been created by the community and distributed via the Workshop and you'll likely find yourself quickly adding mods that both enhance and further complicate (in terms of micromanagement or difficulty) things. With this in mind however, the game itself has included things like sectors and such that help to aleviate some of the tedium of mircromanaging everything, but you'll still spend a lot of time focusing on little things as you also work on the bigger glactic picture, which for someone like me, who enjoys the micromanaging; will make this game one you keep comming back to again and again.
At it's core; Stellaris is your typical 4x game; you build up planetary infarstructure; gather resources, build orbital stations for more resources; build a fleet to protect/attack and expand your territory. But it goes far beyond something like Sins of a Solar Empire does by adding politics and factions to the player's country that can have both positive and negative effects, it throws in random events that can be both a boon and a curse to your people, the interplay of your nation and the other nations around you can lead to great alliances and federations; it can also lead to great wars and total anniliation. Also; endgame events like the scourge; they can wipe the entire galaxy if not focused on early upon their arrival, seriously; these things add a sense of urgency to the endgame, have you been wiping out everything and taking the galaxy for yourself? Well better get ready to fight alone, have you been forming small alliances and are on the cusp of a fully-fledged federation? Time to get that set in stone and get your allies ready for the endtimes.
Looking back at factions for a second, you might for instance have a starting civ that has the religous and militaristic traits; eventually a religous and militaristic faction forms within the government, being somebody who favors combat and expansion yourself; you embrace the militaristic faction, angering the religious faction to the point that they rebel, and now you have a civil war on your hands, in the middle of an expansionist war against a federation of 4 other civs around you. It's storys and elements like these that make Stellaris such a great 4x game; because it adds so much more to the equasion than just the basic build up -> fight -> build up or build up -> diplomacy -> build up cycle of most 4x titles.
Now praise aside for a moment; lets look at my one major con to this title; Paradox's DLC for this title; or rather their DLC pricing.  The first DLC for Stellaris was the 'Plantoids' Pack; this minor content pack added a new species, new ship design and a few new random events. For $7.99 USD you get this pack....the problem is, community modders have been adding new species, ship designs and random event mods on the Workshop since launch....FOR FREE. Now I understand that Paradox is a game company and they should be paid for their work; but this DLC was, is and will always be worth nothing more than $2.50 tops. The $8 price tag on it is a money grab; plain and simple. 'Levithians' was the second DLC pack and it was fairly priced at $9.99; it added new content and was (to me) the first 'Actual' DLC, no complaints about that one; today's Synthetic Dawn is priced the same; and while I cant say whether or not it's fairly priced at the moment, I'll touch on it some in a moment.
The third DLC to Stellaris, the 'Utopia' DLC, is just plain mod theft. (and yes I understand that most if not all modding EULAs let game devs use mod content w/o the need to credit or pay modders, but while they made the software the modder did the work but I digress...) Lets look a little bit at Utopia, first off it added traditions and Unity/Unity Perks. These are new content and prior to Utopia there had been no (to my knowledge) mods that added this kind of mechanic; that adds another level of customization to your empire during gameplay, so Good on Paradox there for something new. Then it added megastructures and Advanced Governments. These catagories had been covered by several workshop mods long prior to Utopia, namily 'Megastructures' by TTFTCUTS & Nutsoman and 'Ethic&Government Rebuild' by petruxa. (and yes; there were many others that added or built off of or onto these mods as well; but these two were (at least to me) the most refined.) While Paradox did make various tweaks and little changes to Utopia's megastructures and governments, its clear that in regards to these major changes for the vanilia game; that mods were used as the backbone. Oh and Utopia is priced at $20 US...so I'm paying at least $10 for free mod content and another $10 for the Unity Tradition system...actually no I'm not; ever. Maybe I dont get that system but I get a plethora of other things for free from the Workshop by modders who create works for free; for the love of the game. I'f I'm going to pay anyone, it will be them.
Now I said that I'd touch on today's release of Synthetic Dawn, and while I've not played it, on the surface it seems like a mix of the already, readily available AI civ mods on the workshop. I can't say for sure that it is; but it seems like they've just cobbled AI civ mods together and added in a few new random events; in which case, if that IS the case; stay away from it, you can get all the AI civ mods you need/want from the workshop; FOR FREE.
So in closing, Stellaris is a great game and with mods you'll keep coming back for more. But stay away from Utopia and Plantoids, they are money grabs for little content. Paradox has historically been bad on it's DLC pricing schemes, and sadly; stellaris is no exception. But Levithians is worth the cash, especially if you can get it on discount (like I did).
TL:DR
Stellaris is a great game worth the buy/play, but stay away from the overpriced DLC that is Utopia and Plantoids since they add little actual content that isn't readily available on the workshop for free.

The story will take such a grasp of you that you'll find yourself trying to keep your eyes open at 8am to play just a little bit more. The story saves it all. It's one of the best experiences I've had in singleplayer games this millennia. Buy it. Show those critics they're wrong.

This game was tragically under estimated from the moment it was released. Once you get through the introduction and preface scenes in the beginning of the game you are no longer playing as a character in some game but you feel as if you are transformed into the main characters and you forget that you are playing a video game.
Someone obviously ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the cornflakes of all of the major game reviewers right before they gave their opinions of this game. It was blantantly obvious they did not play more than 30 minutes of the actual game and the rest of the drivel they wrote came from the pamphlet that was inserted into the box. The little bit of the game they did play, it was quite clear that they were not paying attention to the story being unfolded or the characters they were playing because all they could do was complain about the graphics art not being up to their "standards" and how the combat system took actual strategy and forethought in order to win a battle.
The story line itself was captivating and full of constant twists and turns. Nothing was as it appeared to be throughout the entire gaming experience and by the time you reach the end you are blown away because NO ONE saw that ending coming. Unlike many rpgs out there that try to create the illusion that you are making the decisions for your character that matter in the world around you, this game actually does make all of your choices have consequences. Sometimes they are immediately revealed and other decisions that you thought were trivial end up drastically changing major plot lines throughout the game. While it is a colossal cliche it applies to this game whole-heartedly, "I laughed, I cried, it became a part of me."
I highly recommend this game to anyone that deeply enjoys real rpgs and is starving for orginality and complete immersion into the rpgs they play. While this game was not on the same financial budget as say Skyrim, it is a testament to the developers of this game that they spent all of their energy and money into making a quality game that surpasses any of the blockbuster games that have been released in the last couple of years.

This game is for you if you like Solitaire style card games, obviously, and can deal with a substantial amount of RNG. If you insist on having perfect score in every chapter (which you really don't), then expect to do many, many retries.
Like Hand of Fate, the general approach is to add RPG-style elements to a card playing game with straightforward rules. While Hand of Fate is more action oriented, this game uses the additional gameplay concepts to add depth to the simple Solitaire rule set.
Individually, the implementation of the two underlying concepts of the gameplay - card game and RPG - maybe wouldn't hold up as no particularly new concepts are introduced. Together however, they offer a very compelling and addictive mix with a surprising amount of strategic possibilities.

It's solitaire with a story!  And loot!  Your character gets different weapons (dagger, sword, gun), clothing/armor, and usable items (Grog Bomb!). You can decide what you want to use. That's when it gets interesting and you need to use strategy.  Each card match you make charges up your weapons and abilities until you can use them.

A compelling idea let down through a shallow combination of gameplay mechanics resulting in a massive reliance on luck.
I've been into the pseudo-solitaire approach of casual games like this ever since I tried out Fairway Solitaire on iOS, and find it rather fun when casual games  in this vein put some kind of contextual twist on things. And this game felt like it was going in the right direction with a post-medieval highwaywoman setting with a very nicely-done art style reminiscent of the developer's last game, Regency Solitaire, with added mechanics involving duels, loot and RPG elements. I was all on board with this.
It's such a shame that it didn't hold up in the end.
Have you ever been worried about coming across the kind of puzzle game (or really any game in any genre) where the difference between winning and losing very transparently comes down to luck? Well, Shadowhand is probably the worst example of this I've seen in a long while. It starts off fair enough with an optional star rating system that grades you based on how far you get through the hand. So far so standard. I can live with that.
But when it gets to the dueling segments dotted throughout the chapters, it completely collapses. It can boast all the stat modifiers and RPG elements all it pleases, but more often than not, I found myself in the situation where the opponent instantly spotted cards that could rack up a lengthy combo, and dealt the kind of cheap damage I've not seen in a CPU opponent since Puzzle Quest. Except at least that game had a lot more complexity to its puzzle mechanics to the degree where getting locked into a bad situation was more the exception than the rule.
Shadowhand, meanwhile, seems content to shunt you and your opponent into a constant situation of flipping over cards until one of you gets to continue the combo, and the opponent often finds a way to catch up regardless of how far ahead in health you are. There was always the lingering possibility of your opponent making a massive comeback, be it through both massive combos and healing items. And I get that such a possibility works in favour of some games, but this is not what I bought a game like this for.
I came across this combat scenario multiple times in a row to the point I had not one but *two* occasions where I was thinking to myself, "If I lose this one more time, I'm refunding". And a game that's testing my patience this intensely, especially this early on, is not looking at a good writeup from me. This was on the lower difficulty setting, incidentally. I dread to think what the higher one would have been like.
Sorry, but I cannot, in all good faith, recommend this game. The art style is nice and the story and setting are both as compelling as it looks to you. But the colossal overreliance on luck puts this firmly lower in my estimation than other games of its ilk. If you must play a solitaire-style RPG on steam, stick with Solitairica - the roguelite unlocks at least give some motivation in the face of failure, and there's more the player can do to tilt the situation in their favour. This is just a weaksauce shambles of an idea that really needed some serious fleshing out before being announced.
Oh, but it's supposed to be based around luck, I envision some people saying? Ok, fair enough. That doesn't make this game particularly fun, I'm afraid.
