Let me tell you a story...
It was back in 1968. Me and my squad were to go in behind emy lines, and stab the Charlies in the back. But that failed miserably, as we encountered resistance from two enemy squads heading back to their base. A fierce firefight broke out, and I took down 2 of 'em. But it was no good. My squad got mowed down by an enemy machine gun. I threw a frag at him, and he didn't hear it landing behind him.
When the bomb went off, I had no idea what the hell I should do.
Should I fight my way out? Or sneak past. I chose the latter.
I crawled throught the foliage of the jungle, with distant gunfire echoing throught the trees constantly reminding me of the danger I was in.
After crawling for a couple of minutes, I decided I should go through a narrow passage between two rocks, instead of crossing the open ricefields. Only problem was, there was an enemy in that passage. Luckily, his back was turned against me. I decided a quick bash to the head would best, not making any noise. I snuck up on him, and right when I redied the butt of my rifle, he turned around, froze for a split second, and fired his rifle in panic.
But I was faster.
The hard stock hit his forehead, spilling blood everywhere. I smiled to myself, only to realize that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ DIDN'T miss his mark. I looked down to my chest, seeing two bloody marks there. They didn't hurt, but the area just felt... dead.
I took my bandage, and patched myself up as best I could, while cursing the war, the Charlies, the Us, my fellow soldiers, and myself.
After I healed myself it was time to move on. I had to be quicker now, since my compadres were losing ground. I ran to the edge of the treeline, and looked over the ricefields. I could see my friends in the distance. I had to make it now, or I would die.
I took a deep breath.
"Alright" I said. "here we go".
I screamed to my friends: I'M COMING OVER TO YOU, COVER ME!
Without waiting for a response, I darted out of my cover. Bullets whizzed by my ears.
"F*ck" I thought. "I'm going to die".
But then I realized they were OUR bullets. My allies were covering me. I grinned like an idiot.
I ran like the devil himself was after me. A chopper swooped down right above my head, causing me to lose my footing, and I fell down face-first into the muddy water. I rolled over on my back and saw the helicopter obliterating the jungle I had emerged from, pounding the ground with rockets, and cutting down trees and enemy aliek with a hail of bullets.
"Good effect, coming in for another run, over" I heard the pilot say over the radio.
"Negative, Napalm strike inbound on that area in 10 seconds, danger close!" It was the commander. My whole team were helping me!
"GET OFF YOUR FEET SOLDIER" I heard a familiar voice shout. So that's what I did. I ran like there was no tomorrow, because I knew there wouldn't be, if the Charlies hit me. I was already hit. I couldn't take more.
I heard the roar of jet engines closing in, closing in fast. A salvo of bullets struck down on the ground in front of me, causing me to fall down yet again, just in time for the show. The jungle was engulfed in fire, like it was the playground of Satan himself. The screams were gut-wrenching. But that couldn't stop me.
"THIS IS NO SPA, GET THE F*CK UP" I heard the familiar voice shouting.
Once again, I got up, all while cursing the war. I was going home after this.
I barely had enough strenght to carry on. But I had no choice. I threw my M16 aside, I din't care about the cost. I had to make it to my allies.
Last 30 metres, come on!
25 metres left...
20 metres, COME ON GODDAMMIT!
15 metres, RUN, F*CKING RUN!
10 metres...
That's when I felt a sharp pain in my back. I had been hit. I fell down for the third time, but this time I had no strenght to get up.
"NOOOOOOOO!!!" I heard people scream in unison. "MAKE THOS F*CKERS PAY FOR WHAT THEY'VE DONE".
I heard a distant scream of pain.
"THAT'S FOR OUR FRIENDS, YOU LINE-EYED F*CKERS!"

To start off, this is the first game I have ever tried to get a refund on... EVER... Everything about this game is just bad and is not something I expect out of an FPS that releases today.  This game plays much similar to the game preceding it Rising Storm: Red Orchestra 2.  Had this game been set in WWII, I would have thought I was playing Red Orchestra 2.  There is nothing new or innovative about this game.  It carries all the same problems that the previous game had and more.  The graphics optimization is bad, the server optimization is bad, the controls are overcomplicated, and in my experience with the game I had several occassions where I saw that I had hit my target in the back and then had them turn around and headshot me almost instantly in instances similar to that of BF4 on launch.
On top of this, there are no tutorials on how to play this game.  For a game that advertises as a tactical 'realism" game that requires a lot of teamwork, the best it does on how to play the game is to read/watch these tutorials and figure it out.  When you have a game as seamingly complicated as this, having a bunch of noobs just jump into a multiplayer match with no hands-on, closed experience with any of the mechanics such as commanding, flying, and playing a radio operator, you have doomed your game to turn into nothing but a cluster♥♥♥♥ of people trying to figure out what the hell they are supposed to do.
And last, but not least, there is no Singleplayer experience.  I know Singleplayer experiences are not really relevent in games like these, but with a setting like Vietnam it would have been perfect as the Vietnam war is not a popular war to visit in video game and it would have been nice to actually play a story in this era.  But for $22 I think its ok to overlook this spot a little.
In conclusion, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!!! Do not let the developers think that selling a reskin of a game they have already made without fixing any of the issues is an acceptable business practice.

This is going to sound like an exageration, but I think this is an example of a perfect game. 10/10.
It does everything right! The gameplay is tight, the graphics are intresting and it's easy to quickly determine what's quickly coming towards you. Every single element that is in this game pushes forward a single theme for being an awesome extremely fast-paced action arcade game.
Basically the gyst is you endlessly drop down and down through randomly generated enviromnents. The goal is to get as deep into the game as you can get. But to do that you have to slice the blood out of everything that moves. It even has freaking boss battles! Love it.
It's got a really good sense of action. First of all the controls are tight, and that's the most important thing really. And then they also have really cool combo systems where you can become invincible and just wreck everything all day. There's lots of differnet weapons too add to replayablility. and just slicing enemies feels really good. It's just the way the game feels, the particles, the sound, and the animations. The way that all meshes makes slicing dudes feel slick. Really slick.
And personally I like that the game is really forgiving. In a lot of these types of games you get 1 life and then have to restart, but in this game you can die multiple times. You get like 15 lives right off the bat or something crazy like that. I really like that, it helps keep the action going.
It's one of those games that you'll lose, and then be like.... ok just 1 last run... i mean this time is the last time for sure.... oh but that run was crappy so it doesn't count... I get to keep playing until I get at least 1 good run....
that sort of game.
Also this game feels pulled out of time almost. It feels like and old classic arcade game from another universe that everybody knows and loves, like pacman... only for some reason our universe didnt get that game... it's perfectly retro.
I wouldnt reccomend this game to people who won't be able to keep up with all the action. It's a hard game and it move FAST, and it can be really overwhelming really quickly. So I reccomend checking out some gameplay vids first to see if the pace is too fast for your taste.
However, if you can handle the difficulty and speed of this game please go buy it. I'm not sure if Its gonna be like my personal favorite game ever or anything like that, but it's definitly a perfect game by all standards.
OH, and you'll probably want to use a controller for this. If you don't have one I think that not having a controller WOULD stop me from ever wanting to play this. So keep that in mind if you don't have one.

I rarely find a game that I just refuse to finish. Usually when I find something bad, I just go through it for the laughs: this is not one of those bad-but-f#cking-hilarious games. Not a piece of sh#t, just a whole sh#t. Doesn't mean that it doesn't have any redeeming qualities, but that the negatives far outweight the positives, one to ten. As I usually do I'm gonna start with the negative stuff, and I feel like I've got plenty to talk about.
First and foremost, this is a horrible port. Now, I'm pretty sure there are fan-made fixes and all of that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but just bother to read the title. "The Director's Cut", right? Director's Cut my #ss, this is broken as all hell. If you release a game with that in the title, it has to mean it's the definitive edition, however what you get is a lazily put together port that becomes a nightmare. This ain't like the Dark Souls 1 port to PC (at least not the Games For Windows Live one), mainly because Dark Souls 1 was a good game beyond the sh#t quality port that was eventually somewhat fixed. Keyboard controls suck, the fps rarely either stay consistent or beyond 18, can't lower the sound of cutscenes (which might blast your ears off), there's only one bad resolution available by default, it even dares to have quick time events on scenes that barely run at all. The game is a technical mess.
Second is the sound department. This game has one of the weirdest and most awkward voice acting I've heard in a looooong time. They don't feel at all like they're in the same conversation, or even living in the same damn universe. The main character has to be the biggest example, as he has some of the most unnatural reactions to things while also casually talking to what probably is his imaginary friend. And I'm still totally convinced that the zombies scream "Welcome to die" when killed, and for some reasons the squirrels sound like monkeys, something that had me confused for a while.
Some of the animations also kinda bugged me out the completely wrong way, for one specific reason: they don't seem consistent. You have the main character who has good facial animations (but stupidly creepy and unnatural smiles), then you have characters that neither move their mouths, move their eyes or even blink during conversations. They look like motherf#cking Garry's Mod ragdolls, for f#ck sake.
Also, I feel obligated to comment on how so many elements from Resident Evil are in here, feels like they went wild with "taking inspiration" and just copied elements as they went on. I'm honest, the first 20 or so minutes of the game feel like a poorly done Resident Evil 4 clone.
Last thing is the story, however as you might remember, I haven't complete it. So I'll just talk about the story as far as I got: It was a clusterf#ck of awkward crap that didn't make any sense with a weird mix between comically upbeat moments and mediocre to decent horror elements. It was way too hard to take seriously, specially when the cutscenes are so loud I decided to just skip them entirely for the safety of my ears and I don't even think that would've helped much when the characters themselves act in such unnatural and robotic ways, as if they're not even in the same game.
Now, does the game have good things? Yeah, plenty.
First of all, the atmosphere of the game was quite well done. The forest at the beginning? Quite well done. Sure the sh#t dialogue kinda took me out of the moment, but I do see that good effort was put on it. The town itself was also alright, way more open that I would've expected.
The game also mixes both a horror-like story with an open-world setup, which is... Creative, actually. I feel like it could've made the game amazing if it wasn't made by actual
monkeys. Sure I didn't get a look at it for too long but I do see that there was an effort to make the town your hub, to call it something meaningful, where you would be between the main story missions. Kind of a shame that many horror games just go the linear-dull way.
The story itself is actually alright. I bothered to look it up in wikies and♥♥♥♥♥♥ and it ain't too bad, however the sh#tty dialogue, the bugs and the poor state of this port will give you the wrong idea. I'll probably never touch this game ever again, but the story was at least enjoyable to read (specially as it didn't have those horribly acted voices behind it).
Lastly, the car and other minigames the game has are kinda fun. I sure as f#ck wasn't expecting the game to have a God-damn fishing minigame, but hey. It is confusing though that the game puts those dumb medals that work as currency behind things to break but other times it randomly takes money away from you for "vandalism". Dude, you either reward me for driving like a jack#ss or you don't, there's no gray area.
In the end, do I recommend this game? Ultimately, yes. But not on PC. No way, not here. I don't care if there's mod that fix it, the devs don't deserve to get paid for such a poorly put together port that seems like it's on the verge of crashing your whole computer at any moment. Instead, try to play it in any other platform the game came out. And maybe play it on it's original dub with subtitles instead of hearing the sh#t english voices, holy mother of f#ck they suck nuclear #ss.
TL;DR Edition: The f#ck did I just play. This is a really bad port of a game with some of the worst dubs I've had the displeasure of hearing. However, I think the game itself is average, so playing it on a platform where the port ain't a horrible piece of crap might actually be worth it. On PC though? Just no.
Also, I kinda made a video about my first impressions of the game. You're free to watch it if you feel like it, though be aware that it might spoil parts of the first act of the game.

This is the review I thought longest and hardest about writing because I really want to be fair to both the game devs and potential purchasers of this game.
This is a diamond-in-the-rough, game. Personally? I enjoyed it. Immensely in fact.
Let me caveat that, first.
It was crashy during the first few hours. I nearly quit several times. The combat system is annoying, mainly because every time the player gains a new skill, when using a controller, the old skills shifts slots on the dial thus meaning that combat can never be played with muscle memory. That may be less of a problem when using k/m. The combat was no great shakes due to that time-slowing mechanism [geez if yer gonna have pause-based, have pause-based, going half-azzed is just silly] but this game, like Torment, isn't so much about combat as it is about what that combat reveals about the story.
A common complaint was the graphics. Okay, I get that...this game is not $60 however and I really have no problem with dated graphics so if you are expecting Skyrim you will hate it. If you like older games played for their plots and characters the graphics probably won't bother you.
I don't understand the complaints about the voice acting. I thought the two main protagonists fit the story very well. Other than the odd unimportant NPC--it was adequet to decent voice acting all the way through. I've played games with far worse vocals, for sure.
While the villains of the tale are rather generic, the main characters [you, as the player, play two of them] were deep, inspired characters with flaws, vulnerabilities and strengths.
It has replayablity from the perspective not so much of outcome but of revealing more story. If that's what you're into--then it provides that experience. It also provides the choices of changing the skill sets of the main characters if desired.
The Writing:
That's where this game shines all the way. It's deep, complex, dark and compelling. I was driven to finish it because that story drove me on from start to finish. It opens up questions on the nature of responsibility and making difficult choices, honor, family, committment, etc.
I am going to recommend it because at this price point--it IS an enjoyable game to play for a couple of days and while many of the complaints about it are valid--it is far more interesting than many AAA titles with better graphics and bigger budgets. Remember, when this was made, nobody was quite sure that GoT was going to be the huge hit that it became so this was farmed out to a smaller, less expensive developer. It feels to me as if the devs were cut off what they really wanted to do with this game due to budgetary constraints and as such, did the best they could under the circumstances.
And for all that--it IS worth playing and I would recommend it.

First off; I'm going to talk a lot; so there's a TL:DR at the bottom for those who don't have the time for my long-winded approach. For those that do read it all; thanks for reading; hope it helps. :)
I bought this game shortly after it's launch; and now with over 300 hours of playtime, I think I can give a fair review of what I've experienced with it. Starting off; Stellaris can be a little overwhelming to new players; what with all the content that is offered. Between managing your individual planets and fleets to managing your empire and it's overall growth, things can start to get quite involved and you'll find the hours ticking away as if they were minutes as you delve into a playthru. While the vanillia game is great by itself; Stellaris really shines with the plethora of content mods that have been created by the community and distributed via the Workshop and you'll likely find yourself quickly adding mods that both enhance and further complicate (in terms of micromanagement or difficulty) things. With this in mind however, the game itself has included things like sectors and such that help to aleviate some of the tedium of mircromanaging everything, but you'll still spend a lot of time focusing on little things as you also work on the bigger glactic picture, which for someone like me, who enjoys the micromanaging; will make this game one you keep comming back to again and again.
At it's core; Stellaris is your typical 4x game; you build up planetary infarstructure; gather resources, build orbital stations for more resources; build a fleet to protect/attack and expand your territory. But it goes far beyond something like Sins of a Solar Empire does by adding politics and factions to the player's country that can have both positive and negative effects, it throws in random events that can be both a boon and a curse to your people, the interplay of your nation and the other nations around you can lead to great alliances and federations; it can also lead to great wars and total anniliation. Also; endgame events like the scourge; they can wipe the entire galaxy if not focused on early upon their arrival, seriously; these things add a sense of urgency to the endgame, have you been wiping out everything and taking the galaxy for yourself? Well better get ready to fight alone, have you been forming small alliances and are on the cusp of a fully-fledged federation? Time to get that set in stone and get your allies ready for the endtimes.
Looking back at factions for a second, you might for instance have a starting civ that has the religous and militaristic traits; eventually a religous and militaristic faction forms within the government, being somebody who favors combat and expansion yourself; you embrace the militaristic faction, angering the religious faction to the point that they rebel, and now you have a civil war on your hands, in the middle of an expansionist war against a federation of 4 other civs around you. It's storys and elements like these that make Stellaris such a great 4x game; because it adds so much more to the equasion than just the basic build up -> fight -> build up or build up -> diplomacy -> build up cycle of most 4x titles.
Now praise aside for a moment; lets look at my one major con to this title; Paradox's DLC for this title; or rather their DLC pricing.  The first DLC for Stellaris was the 'Plantoids' Pack; this minor content pack added a new species, new ship design and a few new random events. For $7.99 USD you get this pack....the problem is, community modders have been adding new species, ship designs and random event mods on the Workshop since launch....FOR FREE. Now I understand that Paradox is a game company and they should be paid for their work; but this DLC was, is and will always be worth nothing more than $2.50 tops. The $8 price tag on it is a money grab; plain and simple. 'Levithians' was the second DLC pack and it was fairly priced at $9.99; it added new content and was (to me) the first 'Actual' DLC, no complaints about that one; today's Synthetic Dawn is priced the same; and while I cant say whether or not it's fairly priced at the moment, I'll touch on it some in a moment.
The third DLC to Stellaris, the 'Utopia' DLC, is just plain mod theft. (and yes I understand that most if not all modding EULAs let game devs use mod content w/o the need to credit or pay modders, but while they made the software the modder did the work but I digress...) Lets look a little bit at Utopia, first off it added traditions and Unity/Unity Perks. These are new content and prior to Utopia there had been no (to my knowledge) mods that added this kind of mechanic; that adds another level of customization to your empire during gameplay, so Good on Paradox there for something new. Then it added megastructures and Advanced Governments. These catagories had been covered by several workshop mods long prior to Utopia, namily 'Megastructures' by TTFTCUTS & Nutsoman and 'Ethic&Government Rebuild' by petruxa. (and yes; there were many others that added or built off of or onto these mods as well; but these two were (at least to me) the most refined.) While Paradox did make various tweaks and little changes to Utopia's megastructures and governments, its clear that in regards to these major changes for the vanilia game; that mods were used as the backbone. Oh and Utopia is priced at $20 US...so I'm paying at least $10 for free mod content and another $10 for the Unity Tradition system...actually no I'm not; ever. Maybe I dont get that system but I get a plethora of other things for free from the Workshop by modders who create works for free; for the love of the game. I'f I'm going to pay anyone, it will be them.
Now I said that I'd touch on today's release of Synthetic Dawn, and while I've not played it, on the surface it seems like a mix of the already, readily available AI civ mods on the workshop. I can't say for sure that it is; but it seems like they've just cobbled AI civ mods together and added in a few new random events; in which case, if that IS the case; stay away from it, you can get all the AI civ mods you need/want from the workshop; FOR FREE.
So in closing, Stellaris is a great game and with mods you'll keep coming back for more. But stay away from Utopia and Plantoids, they are money grabs for little content. Paradox has historically been bad on it's DLC pricing schemes, and sadly; stellaris is no exception. But Levithians is worth the cash, especially if you can get it on discount (like I did).
TL:DR
Stellaris is a great game worth the buy/play, but stay away from the overpriced DLC that is Utopia and Plantoids since they add little actual content that isn't readily available on the workshop for free.

I have played Stellaris for a while now, and I feel that the best way to describe it is as a pausable real time 4x game.
The graphics are pretty, especially when zoomed in a lot, but that is not practical, so mostly all the time you're staring at the star map.
The main reason I'm not recommending it is that somewhat counter intuitively the game design punishes you for not going with the cookie cutter way the designers imagined, and I feel there isn't all that much strategic freedom.
You're in space and can expand in any direction, so the direction you expand in doesn't matter much. You have to find planets you can colonize, but they can't be in the territory of aliens. The planets have to be big, because you are only allowed to have so many planets, and the planet size affects how much population and buildings they can host. The planets shouldn't be too far away from your other planets though, because colonizing planets further away is more expensive. Eventually a bunch of aliens end up walling you in, and you can then go to war with them (and spend ages sieging planets, much like forts in EU 4), or just sit around doing not much of anything while hoping that you can eventually win the game. All the while you have to keep pumping out fleets that become obsolete 5 minutes later to keep up with the joneses, but you're of course not allowed to have too many ships, because they, just like pretty much everything in the game, cost energy, and for the limited size your empire is allowed to be energy is pretty much constantly low. There is also no real freedom in research: For each of the three research fields you're given the choice of 3 technologies to research when a technology is completed that are the next steps for where you happen to be in the game, so every game you pretty much end up researching the same things in the same order, and you're not even allowed to decide in which order research of the same tier should be taken.
So, my main complaint, and the reason I'm thumbing Stellaris down is that in the beginning you don't have a lot of interesting choises to make, and later on you get even less. The game makes up for lack of choises with a lot of micro management though, you have to manually tell each space port what to build, and you have to manually tell your explores where to go exploring next. It's definitely not my cup of tea, and unlike EU4 I don't even sense the potential for greatness, Stellaris is just bland.

After 100+ hours of playtime, what can I say about Stellaris? I will be brief.
Sure, the game has lovely visuals and an exceptionnal soundtrack. Being able to genetically alter your species or fully customize every single ship of your fleet, every space station of your empire, was really interesting. Nevertheless, I can't give to this game a positive review, and here is why.
-There is a cruel lack of micromanagement concerning colonies/planets. I'll explain. Every liveable planet is divided into a certain amount of squares. On each square, the player can chose to build a single building and allow a single unit of population to exploit said building. That's it : there is not much else that you can do. To be honest, I was expecting a bit more from a 4x revolving around galactical colonization...
-Diplomacy with the AI is extremely flawed, not to say absent in the game. Apart from declaring a rivalry or war to another empire, interactions are scarce. Sure, you can, theoretically, trade ressources, science or informations with the neighborhood... but it is really unlikely to happen, since their acceptance of any treaty is determined by how much they like you. Since the most trifling action from your part (i.e. : refusing an offer) will seriously and often irreversibly anger them forever, non aggressive diplomacy is pointless. It was lacking features anyway...
-The AI. The AI is overall unspeakably broken. Most of the time, your allies will build ships one after another and ... send them on by one against large ennemy fleets, untill complete destruction of their own fleet and exhaustion of their ressources. Do not waste time building alliances... You don't trust me? Just browse the Steam workshop and look for every mod that consists in a fix for the AI!
-Combat. As soon as your fleet enters Combat mode, your admirals developp a "brain" of their own. Indeed, you can't give orders to your ships anymore : everything is administered by the AI until complete anihilation of one fleet or emergency FTL. For instance, you can't tell your fleet to focus down a particular ennemy ship (meaning that your fleet can just tickle an ennemy ship's shield a bit and then switch to another ship without dealing a single point of hull damage to the first one, and repeat, etc.). You can't order your fleet to back off a bit either (meaning that, if your high ranged ships get in range of low range ennemy artillery, your admiral will vaillantly (allbeit very recklessly) refuse to get out of ennemy's range. Thus, you cannot possibly take benefit from your fleet's high range weaponry). Such issues could be easily solved if Paradox was actually concerned about something else than DLCs...
-General lack of content. Although military aspects are quite detailed, there's not much to do in the other domains. My friends and I, indeed, felt the need to deeply mod the game as soon as we finished our second playthrough. That's speaking by itself.
-This emphasizes an other important problem : repetitiveness. After the first couple of hours, once you are in front of your opponents regarding technology and economy, every hour is pretty much the same as the last or the next one, every war is pretty much the same war. The "endgame crisis" fail to solve that problem. The Prethoryns often feel a bit weak and the Unbidden will simply erase you if they spawn near your imperial capital (yes, that can happen). Regarding the Awakened Fallen Empires, there is nothing a player or a coalition of players can do. Indeed, Paradox offset the flaws of their AI by absurdly buffin it. So, even if you manage to destroy the Awakened Empire's fleets (and that will take you some time), their civilization will remain a threat solely thanks to its bonuses.
-More or less gamebreaking bugs. When (and I underline the "when") these issues are addressed, the fix is often put behind the paywall of the habitual absurdly costly Paradox's DLC. The list is far too big after 100+ hours to be developped here, but I will nevertheless take an example. If you take a planet located in a system where another empire (even if it is allied to tou) already owns a planet, the ressources of this system won't be exploitable, by neither of you. Let's say that you want to build a mine on a random asteroid to gain the minerals ? Ok : you'll have to declare war on your ally and conquer every other planet in this solar system. Pretty dumb, isn't it? And it's far from being the worst...
All in all, I was really hyped for Stellaris, and I still think that the game has great potential. Although, it is far too flawed in my eyes to be recommended in this state and at full price. It can get quite interesting once modded, but mods won't solve everything, and by the way they don't have to ! Finally, I firmly oppose Paradox's policy. Many of the abovementioned issues were indeed addressed in some of the DLC (i.e. : Leviathans). But here is the problem : it's a DLC. Seriously, someone who already paid for the game shouldn't have to pay again for basic updates addressing the major flaws of the game...

At the time of this review, I'm 6 hours into game play and have gotten to chapter 10 (out of 22 chapters), so I figure I'm about a 3rd in on Normal mode.  Yes, this game is very much like Regenency Solitaire (RS) with the same style of card play and progression system.  BUT it is quickly left behind as the game has so so much more to it than RS.  Don't let the fact this is a card game hide the true nature of this fun game.
Here are the features of the game I like:
* Easy to play -- You can quickly jump in and start playing the game.  Instructions are clear and the base game play is simple.  The user interface is the right balance between clean clear design and yet provides for some of the crunchy bits you'll need later.
* Dueling Enemies -- You will start with the same style as RS by clearing boards of cards.  But don't let that fool you'll.
Soon after you'll have enemies that you'll play against.  When doing a dule, you take turns playing against an AI who is trying to steal all the cards.  When you have an opponent, the strategy is flipped on its head and you'll find the need to lay traps for your opponent instead of just being greedy with the longest run.
* Story -- The story presents the enemies and provides continuity using concise cut scenes that is worth reading.  In addition, it provides intresting twists on your character's items and abilities that challenge you from time to time and keeps gameplay interesting.  If story isn't your thing, no problem, click the Skip button and go direct to the action.
* Weapons & Abilities -- When dueling, you work by charging up your weapons and abilities.  The RPG element really kicsk in here as you start having to choose which weapons to use and whether or not to overcharge your weapon or risk your opponent getting a card ladden turn.
* Potions & Items -- and just like any good RPG, there are consumables you can earn (loot) or buy (store).  The game is fair with the number you find and buy, but just limited enough you don't get overly powerful.  Being limited to 3 on your character at any one time is a great idea.
* Balanced -- Although I've only been to level 10, gameplay has been very balanced.  Enemies feel right and typically will challenge you down to your last hit points.  With a game like this, you'll lose a few battles, but it is fairly painless to retry the level (regaining all lost items before the loss).  And if you do come across a powerful enemy, you need only re-equip your items to counter that enemy's type of attacks.
* Casual-ish -- The difficulty is ramping up on me and pushing me harder, so it is getting harder to call this a casual game.  This may turn off truly casual players at times, but there are places where you can push through with fewer stars instead of replaying for a perfect win.  And yes, if you get stuck, you can go back to previous chapters and replay them to build up the gold you need to buy the better items -- but so far this has not been necessary.
* Variety -- Each chapter has been unlocking new enemies, weapons, buff/debuff types, and new strategies.  So far, the game play has not gotten stale and I've enjoyed the constant flow of new ideas.
* Quality -- Like all Grey Alien games, the quality is outstanding and the download is small.  I have had no crashes or any of the weird problems you see in other games.  The user interface is super polished and graphics nicely done.  The story is interesting and the dialog is clear.
Grey Alien Games have truly outdone themselves this time.  I think this is their best game to date!  Two thumbs up.

This is a very slick just-one-more-round kind of game.
There's a surprising amount of depth here for something that looks like basic solitaire on its face. A good game is full of interesting decisions, and Shadowhand keeps offering you difficult choices. Not just high-level choices about how to allocate your skill points each chapter, or mid-level choices over gearing up and how to spend your money. Even at the card-by-card level, you're forced to make much more interesting decisions than a normal game of solitaire.
Do you take the 7 of cups to free up the key below it and unlock another bundle of cards, maybe extending your combo - or do you take the 7 of swords, sitting on its own, to charge your melee attack faster and rush down your opponent? Do you use one of your slowly-charging special skills to reshuffle the board, or burn a joker from your hand to keep the combo going and get a massive multiplier on your earnings? Do you use your piercing attack to maybe inflict more damage, or do you eschew attacking to stick a poultice on that bleed before it wears you down?
These mechanics are introduced steadily throughout the game, pacing the escalation of difficulty and complexity just well enough to keep you on your toes. You never go into a duel feeling confident of your chances, but once you've figured out the opponent's strengths & weaknesses and geared up appropriately, you can tip the balance enough in your favour to make each card-turn a genuinely nerve-wracking moment.
Mix all that skillful mechanical ingenuity up with a fun tale of skullduggery & class conflict, and some utterly gorgeous artwork, and you have a game that is really well balanced to keep you playing for Just One More Round. Damn, where did my afternoon go...?
If only all "casual games" had this quality and cleverness, I'd have gotten into them much sooner.

I'm enjoying this game even more than Regency Solitaire, and that's saying something. The back-and-forth combat in the duels is a great mix of luck and using skills to get the advantage. It's really great

The mechanics of this game are fun as heck, the art is gorgeous, the themes are really interesting, and yet again I'm totally hooked. Even if you've never played a solitaire game, play this one. The gear, skill, item, and leveling mechanics add so much to the concept! I can't recommend it enough.

<EDIT> I see negative reviews criticising the game for being random. This IS a solitaire-type game (with a nice strategy wrapper around it) and if it wasn't random it wouldn't be solitaire. This is like criticising COD for having too many guns; just what were people expecting? Also I've not seen any evidence of the game cheating so far which is refreshing.
Further, people saying it lacks depth clearly aren't playing it long enough. There is a steady drip drip of features which leaves you with multiple options strategy wise in later rounds. Obviously the first few rounds are simplistic... 4+ hours in and I'm still finding new strategies and new unlocks </EDIT>
If you can live with the RNG screwing you over occasionally (which you can definitely influence by careful strategy) then it's a fun game and great to drop into for ten minutes here and there. It's solitaire at it's heart, so wouldn't be the same game without the RNG aspect.
Music, art and general visual design are excellent and show a love for the story background.
The developer is very visible on the forums which is always a good thing as it shows a belief in their product.
My only complaint so far is I'd like to see the stats visible as a history so I can see what levels I need to go back to, but the developer is aware of this need already I believe so I expect something will get patched in later.
I'm happy to recommend it as a game which uses RNG in a fair and expected way, which is how it should always be used.

To start off, this is the first game I have ever tried to get a refund on... EVER... Everything about this game is just bad and is not something I expect out of an FPS that releases today.  This game plays much similar to the game preceding it Rising Storm: Red Orchestra 2.  Had this game been set in WWII, I would have thought I was playing Red Orchestra 2.  There is nothing new or innovative about this game.  It carries all the same problems that the previous game had and more.  The graphics optimization is bad, the server optimization is bad, the controls are overcomplicated, and in my experience with the game I had several occassions where I saw that I had hit my target in the back and then had them turn around and headshot me almost instantly in instances similar to that of BF4 on launch.
On top of this, there are no tutorials on how to play this game.  For a game that advertises as a tactical 'realism" game that requires a lot of teamwork, the best it does on how to play the game is to read/watch these tutorials and figure it out.  When you have a game as seamingly complicated as this, having a bunch of noobs just jump into a multiplayer match with no hands-on, closed experience with any of the mechanics such as commanding, flying, and playing a radio operator, you have doomed your game to turn into nothing but a cluster♥♥♥♥ of people trying to figure out what the hell they are supposed to do.
And last, but not least, there is no Singleplayer experience.  I know Singleplayer experiences are not really relevent in games like these, but with a setting like Vietnam it would have been perfect as the Vietnam war is not a popular war to visit in video game and it would have been nice to actually play a story in this era.  But for $22 I think its ok to overlook this spot a little.
In conclusion, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!!! Do not let the developers think that selling a reskin of a game they have already made without fixing any of the issues is an acceptable business practice.

A resident evil set in an abandon curise liner...sign me up. Is resident evil revelations a good game? I will review the game in a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.
Pro:
The game looks pretty good graphics wise in the world. I certainly do enjoy how the ship was visually designed, the place looks well abandoned which is what makes any real resident evil game shine. Much like how the mansion in the very first game was well designed with tight corners that puts the fear of something right around the corner.
The 3rd person camera is always welcomed in my book. This camera view first was implemented back in resident evil 4 which was not entirely a horror game but a super great action game. This camera angle here helps to view and aim for those tense action segments. Now the game further improves the overall aiming that resident evil 4 might have suffered from. Rather than looking for a small red dot that is coming from the gun, you have a targeting reticle which makes getting those very important shots on critical locations much more easier.
The game has a wide array of characters that are well played. Each character except maybe a few are very interesting characters with good dialogue. They can be funny if need be or serious depending on what character that is being played.
Guns pack a punch with weapon parts. New to the game is a unique upgrade system using weapon parts found through out the game. They apply boost to the gun only if it has any avalible slots to add said upgrades. Some guns have 5 slots while others may have 3 or 6. Each part has a number tied to it, the higher the number the more boost the gun gets.
A new mode called raid mode. Raid mode plays like a basic kill all enemies and get to the finish line game mode. It is available in co-op and has rpg mechanics. Through playing the player gets exp that levels up their level rank. The higher level the player is the higher level weapons they will find in the stores or better chance of beating a stage. This mode is not entirely stressing survival since guns can be bought from the in game store with BP, resident evil currency gain through gameplay of either raid or the campaign. Not to mention the player can always restock on ammo and herbs from the store between selected missions.
Con:
The story teeters between boring and being a chore. The story is boring because of how uninteresting the plot is and at the end there is no real conclusion. It is not nearly as in depth as other resident evil games like the original where the motives of the main villian is clear at the end. The story also becomes a chore when playing as a totally new character without any equipment or ability to upgrade their guns makes playing these segments a pain to deal with. Especially when something really interesting happens to one set of characters and when this rising action of the plot is here it takes a long time to get back to it because it is time to play as another set of characters you dont want to play as. Not because they are bad characters but because I rather be playing as Jill than those two dudes in the snow storm. They are great characters with loads of good communication but being locked in these segments with no choice of my arsenal really bogs down the pacing and the thrill.
Enemies are a huge disappointment. The enemies look really interesting and borderline cool but the issue is their weakpoints are visually hidden. The early enmies you face apparently the weak point for them is its arm. Shooting them with enough damage in the arm will cause them to be stunned so the player can perform a melee attack. Basic knowledge of how enemies work from other games like resident evil 4 or 1 is always aim for the head. Basic weak point but never in this game.
Wow a new mechanic lets force it down the players throats. The new mechanic is the ability to dodge an incomming enemy attack. That is really cool but it is technically very flawed. The main issue is the way to dodge is not entirely clear as to how to preform it. There is a tutorial early on in the game but what is the issue is that the dodge sometimes works when it wants to. Many times I tried to dodge either for practice or survival in a tense situation and it would refuse to give me any leway in unfortunantly I end up taking the hit. The mechanic is very flawed and yet they focus the whole game around it. They intentally limit the ammo that can be found throughout the game to make the player focus on using the dodging which was a horrible move on the developers part. None of the other games had dodging other than resident evil 4 with it's button prompts mainly on boss related enemies. I understand that resident evil is very much a survival horror game but revolving the game over a mechanic that is very fickle is lazy and all around bad game design.
Previously on revelations. Get use to that small sentece there because the game very much enjoys saying it and recaping the story even though you did not turn off the game and just experienced said moments. I get the idea that they were trying to go for but ultimately an odd design choice. If it exist to recap moments for a player that turned off the game then it makes sense but the recap happens after every chapter.
infernal mode is awful. What infernal mode does is that it adds more enemies and changes the damage modifies. Lazy work there developers and again it is designed to focus on the mechanic of dodging so you know that this is going to be a huge flawed design for a difficulty. It would help in the the secret unlockables ment much in making the harder difficulties more reasonable but that is not the case. What is the main focus is on weapon parts and how well one can dodge.
Conclusion:
This game was very interesting at first glimps. It had very nice close quarter combat on the ship and an interesting plot but then shifts focus. It is like trying to teach a child with ADD. Not to mention the bs designs like invisible laser trap maze because that is fair or how about hunters that are invisible and are very good at dodging. It is not fair designs in the game and breaks the game's flow. There is so much bad with the game but the one part that really connects it all together is the horrible dodge mechanic. It is way to unpredictable to be remotely a reliable thing to do in the game let alone make it the main focus of how the game is going to be structured around. Needless to say if those who read the review and are not sure what i think about the game, let me say I think this game is bad and dont reccomend it at all.

Loadout probably is one of the most generous free-to-play games on the market right now.
Except from the costumes, everything in this game can be bought and achieved without spending any real money whatsoever. While there are "Boosts" you can buy to accelerate your progress, you never feel like a second class player, if you choose to not spend money on this game. And even if you come across an enemy with a weapon feeling surperior to yours, you actually can use his weapon if you manage to kill him - even if that may involve a bit of teamplay.
The gun-building aspect of the game itself is very satisfying. What game besides Loadout allows you to build a healing shotgun or a hexapod-rocketlauncher? Even though not all choices might be feasible I still had a blast trying out the sheer unlimited amount of different guns.
The 4on4 match-up however didn't quite hit the spot on my end. While it should encourage players to work together as a team, it in most of the cases does not do the job, while playing with random allies. And this - like say in MOBAs like DOTA 2 - can get very frustrating.
But still - since it is such a generous free-to-play game - there is no way I would not recommend it to everybody who has only the slightest interest in a a teambased third-person shooter. Just give it a try!

Given the game's competitive nature, and the fact that your team is more tightly bound together than most other team-based competitive games, Guns of Icarus Online puts a lot of pressure on you as a player. As a beginner in any such game, feelings of inadequacy are to be expected, but having each member of your team knowing almost second-by-second just how inept I am at this game, whether they're nice about it or not, makes me feel uncomfortable the entire time I play. Since you need other players on the other team to play against, I could either take on other people by myself with a crew of AI, which wouldn't help me at all because I'd have no one to learn from on my team.
If this game had a complete offline campaign with a little plot, characters, learning the gameplay elements, and playing the different roles on the ship, that could be totally awesome, but as it is, I have a tough time getting behind games that are entirely multiplayer versus, and that feeling of being scrutinized in a game at every moment is too unnerving for me to feel comfy playing this title. If these aren't issues for you, you might enjoy this game, because it's not a terrible product or anything. If you have ever had similar feelings or prefer offline means of really training to be ready for the online component like me, then I'd suggest avoiding the game.

There's lots to like about this game, and I hope the devs apply the same solitaire/RPG model to start a series, but...
It would have benefited HUGELY from progression without the steep & constant escalation:
1. Armour (damage reduction) level with/outstripping weapon damage while health climbs & climbs - it makes the duels get ever-longer and weapon acquisition disappointing (since chance of penetration is the only meaningful increase), though the star rating system doesn't take this into account.
2. Giving every NPC a full stock of consumables (3) amplifies this, often effectively increasing their health by 50% or stretching the match with debuffs & stuns.
3. The 50/50 prospect of them picking up the consumables on the board amplifies further, and on the most awkward layouts can mean you have to attack 5+ times each board refresh just to break even with their alcohol fuelled health gain.
4. The fact that the cards aren't based on a deck - while freeing - can make for some un-fun experiences where both sides are passing turn after turn waiting to see who draws the right number to start an enormous cascade.
So it is a tricky beast to rate; would very much like to see & try more such games, but on the other-hand I just ragequit after 40 minutes of retrying a tediously prolonged boss fight - don't honestly know if I'll persevere.
P.S. Devs: being able to choose between a female & male protagonist would be great next time!

I really wish there was a neutral option for reviews, but since this game at least bring what it describes to the table, I'll recommend it with the caveat that it might not appeal to everyone.
This game is similar to solitaire games like Fairway Solitaire - it's solitaire, but with the added twist of an inventory, attributes that can affect gameplay, and other RPG-ish systems. It also suffers from the problem that games with a shared play area generally share: it feels like the RNG is constantly against you.
This comes up in the "fighting" portion of the solitaire game, where you and an opponent take turns matching cards. Sometimes, after a pretty sparse hand, your opponent just goes on to clear the board for no other reason than your poor luck. Although yes, you do get your own amazing runs as well, it can feel pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for the same reason missing a 95% chance shot in XCOM feels bad.
Sometimes your enemy doesn't even have to work against you. It's possible to have such a bad board--maybe everything is just one number--that your opponent and yourself have nothing to do but mash the "end turn" key.
Some of the skills also work against you. The "luck" attribute will sometimes randomly drop an extra card from the board when you match a card, bringing you one step closer to finishing the level. However, since it does this randomly, it sometimes screws up your combo. Imagine you have a nice match incoming--you'll just match the 9, 8, 7, and then 6! Well, imagine your anger if you matched the 9, and then it randomly dropped the 8, leaving no way for you to complete your combo. The longer you play, the more likely this situation is to happen.
All in all, it's a flawed work that would have benefitted from a "bad luck" mechanism in order to round off the rough edges of the RNG. The story is nothing to write home about, but let's be honest, you're probably just here to play solitaire, and this game does that decently enough.

I can't get enough of this game.
This game is a beautifully fast-paced action game. You play as a ninja warrior who wants to kill things. I'm totally 300% sure that's the story. You can read the story in comic book form in-game. I couldn't pull myself away from the actual gameplay for long enough to see that option in the main menu, though.
This game moves so fast (or, at least, you can move so fast). You just run through the tower killing anything that gets in your way and go for the boss. Simple, but very addictive.
I should mention it's really easy to die in the game. Well, more accurately, it's really easy for me to get too complacent and reckless in the game. I died. A lot. I got the bonus lives perks really quickly (you can unlock them for dying a certain number of times in excess of 100) because I just died so much. I died because the game is incredibly fun to try and move through as fast as possible.
The game has a good way of knowing where you're going to do something silly too. The game really discourages you from moving quickly without knowing what certain enemies do. Man, what do those fast spiney things do? Oh, they kill you and kill you and kill you. There's good news. Since you lose a life in one hit, it becomes of paramount importance to avoid as many enemies as you can... while still trying to build rage.
Rage builds up by killing a certain amount of enemies while not dying. When the rage meter is fully charged, you are invulnerable until the meter depleats. This gives the player the ability to make a decision about moving quickly vs killing things to build up rage.
After all the stuff I said about dying, I should mention that the game does deaths in a perfect way for this type of game: you regenerate where you are. While it might seem pretty obvious that that would be the case, it's important to distinguish this game from Mario type games. There are no checkpoints, but instead you can insantly revive where you died and even if you spend all your lives and get a game over, you can still rejoin the game where you are.
The soundtrack is nice too. It's certainly no Bit.Trip Runner, but it's still pretty thematic and well done.
The visuals are done in a retro-esque style which is a good design choice; it allows the whole game to be loaded all at once taking nothing away from gametime and player tempo.
Overall, this game was an extremely fun expense of time. I cannot get over how well it was designed and just how fun it is.

RFLEX at first glance looks like a simple game (in some ways it's like frogger, you have to dodge oncoming traffic) but eventually you'll come to realise it's tough. If you're a fan of super hard games like Super Hexagon you'll definitely enjoy the challenge but for some it might not be your cup of tea (sadly wasn't mine).
You have 5 different levels (+5 Drunk level modes) and each one is more challenging than the last, timing is crucial as one slip up can result in having to start the level again. All you have to do to pass a level is let your little pentagon survive for 60 seconds, which may or may not be easy depending on your reaction speed.
The sound design and music is fantastic though and is probably one of the high points I found in the game, if you can get the soundtrack I would recommend it.
Is the game worth the price? I'd say yes, despite the fact I wasn't any good at it doesn't mean everyone is going to be as bad as me.
In future I'd like to see more levels added or different challenges though!

Some complaints about RS2 and explanations (How I make sense of it):
"There are no land vehicles!"
Many players returning from RO2/RS games complained of how RS2 lacks tanks which previous games had.  Although land vehicles played a role in the Vietnam War, they seem to be lacking ingame.  With the current maps, rich with dense forests and mountaineous terrain, land vehicles wouldn't fit well in the game.  The reason the previous games had tanks was because the maps that allowed tanks were relatively flat and were clear of dense foilage which allowed tanks to maximize their usefulness in the battlefield.  Adding tanks to RS2 at this time would challenge tankers in being able to maneuver around the map rather than fighting.  Perhaps when flatter maps are introduced will tankers be an appropriate option.
"What about boats in RS2?"
Similar to the tanker issue, the current maps don't have much room for boats.  The only bodies of water seen in the game are rivers and streams, but are too shallow for any boats to physically pass through (shallow enough for soldiers to wade through).  Until maps with deeper bodies of water are introduced, boats won't be an appropriate option.
The developers have to take into account balancing issues as well.  During the Vietnam War, only the Americans had boats designed to withstand combat situations and were fitted with armaments.  The Northern forces did have boats available, but they were mostly used for transporting supplies.  Very few were used specifically for combat purposes and those few were outclassed by the US patrol boats.
On top of that, boats weren't primarily used for situations encountered in the game currently.  American boats were deployed for reconnaissance and to disrupt enemy weapon shipments.  They were never deployed specifically for combat purposes and only saw combat when they were being ambushed.  Although this may make a nice gamemode (escort the boats or something like that) boats won't fit well into the current maps.
"There's too many explosions!  What is this, a Micheal Bay movie?"
A lot of RO2/RS returning players seem to complain about this.  Of course there's going to be more explosions in RS2 than the previous installments.  Afterall, the Vietnam War took place a decade after World War II.  The technology and support armaments available during the Vietnam War exist in much larger numbers and were far deadlier than those available during World War II.  Not only is artillery improved, but planes specializing in ground support is now available to the American forces.  There are more explosions in the game because there is a wider variety of support options available to the players.
"It's turning to an arcade shooter."
This is a very broad statement with many factors, but it all boils down to two points: its weapons and the flow of each game.
One of the largest weapon traits that sets RS2 from its predecessors is the availability of automatic weapons.  Now that nearly every class has the option of using an automatic weapon, players no longer need to be as careful and precise about their movement and decisions as was required in RO2/RS.  Before, concentration was crucial when firing since bolt-action rifles had such a low firerate; missing the first shot could cost you your life.  Battles were fought at distances and progress was slow as players moved very little to be as indistinct as possible and to ensure accuracy and precision when firing.  With automatic weapons, players are encouraged to fight in closer quarters as they now possess the power of a high rate of fire.  Follow-up shots are easy and the accuracy and precision of RO2/RS now only apply to the marksman class.
In contrast of the slow movement of the previous installments, RS2 encourages faster paced action and getting close and personal with the opponent.  With Americans being able to spawn in hueys and get transported behind enemy lines and Vietnamese squad leaders being able to dig tunnels that serve as spawn points, players are pretty much guarenteed to get into a firefight just seconds into spawning.  In terms of the layout of the maps, almost all parts of the maps are covered in dense foilage and trees.  This limits possibilities for long range engagements and forces players to close their distances if they want to make any progress.
Both of these factors can be justified using the game's historical context.  Automatic weapons became available to both sides and seeing how it prevails as combat is modernizing, of course both factions will adopt automatic weapons as their standard arms.  During the Vietnam War, the Americans were known to use helicopters to get right into the fight and the Vietnamese were notorious for their intricate tunnel systems that allowed infantry transport to the battlefield.  As stated earlier, the natural terrain and locations battles took place during the Vietnam War just made long distant combat an uncommon sight.
"FPS problems"
Vietnam is known for its dense jungle and this detail is shown in great detail in RS2.  Using the same Unreal Engine 3 as RO2/RS, optimization would be much more difficult as computers have to render the large amounts of leaves and foilage.  On top of that, there are much more particle effects as RS2 heavily emphasizes the usage of weaponized fire (flamethrower, napalm, and already burnt down areas).  In other words, RS2 has more particles and details to take into account which takes a toll in its performance.
==========================================================================
These are all how I justify the issues many players complain about in RS2.  There are still many other issues about the game which can't be justified with historical relevance (i.e. buggy hit registration), but hey nothing is perfect.

I have played Stellaris for a while now, and I feel that the best way to describe it is as a pausable real time 4x game.
The graphics are pretty, especially when zoomed in a lot, but that is not practical, so mostly all the time you're staring at the star map.
The main reason I'm not recommending it is that somewhat counter intuitively the game design punishes you for not going with the cookie cutter way the designers imagined, and I feel there isn't all that much strategic freedom.
You're in space and can expand in any direction, so the direction you expand in doesn't matter much. You have to find planets you can colonize, but they can't be in the territory of aliens. The planets have to be big, because you are only allowed to have so many planets, and the planet size affects how much population and buildings they can host. The planets shouldn't be too far away from your other planets though, because colonizing planets further away is more expensive. Eventually a bunch of aliens end up walling you in, and you can then go to war with them (and spend ages sieging planets, much like forts in EU 4), or just sit around doing not much of anything while hoping that you can eventually win the game. All the while you have to keep pumping out fleets that become obsolete 5 minutes later to keep up with the joneses, but you're of course not allowed to have too many ships, because they, just like pretty much everything in the game, cost energy, and for the limited size your empire is allowed to be energy is pretty much constantly low. There is also no real freedom in research: For each of the three research fields you're given the choice of 3 technologies to research when a technology is completed that are the next steps for where you happen to be in the game, so every game you pretty much end up researching the same things in the same order, and you're not even allowed to decide in which order research of the same tier should be taken.
So, my main complaint, and the reason I'm thumbing Stellaris down is that in the beginning you don't have a lot of interesting choises to make, and later on you get even less. The game makes up for lack of choises with a lot of micro management though, you have to manually tell each space port what to build, and you have to manually tell your explores where to go exploring next. It's definitely not my cup of tea, and unlike EU4 I don't even sense the potential for greatness, Stellaris is just bland.

After 100+ hours of playtime, what can I say about Stellaris? I will be brief.
Sure, the game has lovely visuals and an exceptionnal soundtrack. Being able to genetically alter your species or fully customize every single ship of your fleet, every space station of your empire, was really interesting. Nevertheless, I can't give to this game a positive review, and here is why.
-There is a cruel lack of micromanagement concerning colonies/planets. I'll explain. Every liveable planet is divided into a certain amount of squares. On each square, the player can chose to build a single building and allow a single unit of population to exploit said building. That's it : there is not much else that you can do. To be honest, I was expecting a bit more from a 4x revolving around galactical colonization...
-Diplomacy with the AI is extremely flawed, not to say absent in the game. Apart from declaring a rivalry or war to another empire, interactions are scarce. Sure, you can, theoretically, trade ressources, science or informations with the neighborhood... but it is really unlikely to happen, since their acceptance of any treaty is determined by how much they like you. Since the most trifling action from your part (i.e. : refusing an offer) will seriously and often irreversibly anger them forever, non aggressive diplomacy is pointless. It was lacking features anyway...
-The AI. The AI is overall unspeakably broken. Most of the time, your allies will build ships one after another and ... send them on by one against large ennemy fleets, untill complete destruction of their own fleet and exhaustion of their ressources. Do not waste time building alliances... You don't trust me? Just browse the Steam workshop and look for every mod that consists in a fix for the AI!
-Combat. As soon as your fleet enters Combat mode, your admirals developp a "brain" of their own. Indeed, you can't give orders to your ships anymore : everything is administered by the AI until complete anihilation of one fleet or emergency FTL. For instance, you can't tell your fleet to focus down a particular ennemy ship (meaning that your fleet can just tickle an ennemy ship's shield a bit and then switch to another ship without dealing a single point of hull damage to the first one, and repeat, etc.). You can't order your fleet to back off a bit either (meaning that, if your high ranged ships get in range of low range ennemy artillery, your admiral will vaillantly (allbeit very recklessly) refuse to get out of ennemy's range. Thus, you cannot possibly take benefit from your fleet's high range weaponry). Such issues could be easily solved if Paradox was actually concerned about something else than DLCs...
-General lack of content. Although military aspects are quite detailed, there's not much to do in the other domains. My friends and I, indeed, felt the need to deeply mod the game as soon as we finished our second playthrough. That's speaking by itself.
-This emphasizes an other important problem : repetitiveness. After the first couple of hours, once you are in front of your opponents regarding technology and economy, every hour is pretty much the same as the last or the next one, every war is pretty much the same war. The "endgame crisis" fail to solve that problem. The Prethoryns often feel a bit weak and the Unbidden will simply erase you if they spawn near your imperial capital (yes, that can happen). Regarding the Awakened Fallen Empires, there is nothing a player or a coalition of players can do. Indeed, Paradox offset the flaws of their AI by absurdly buffin it. So, even if you manage to destroy the Awakened Empire's fleets (and that will take you some time), their civilization will remain a threat solely thanks to its bonuses.
-More or less gamebreaking bugs. When (and I underline the "when") these issues are addressed, the fix is often put behind the paywall of the habitual absurdly costly Paradox's DLC. The list is far too big after 100+ hours to be developped here, but I will nevertheless take an example. If you take a planet located in a system where another empire (even if it is allied to tou) already owns a planet, the ressources of this system won't be exploitable, by neither of you. Let's say that you want to build a mine on a random asteroid to gain the minerals ? Ok : you'll have to declare war on your ally and conquer every other planet in this solar system. Pretty dumb, isn't it? And it's far from being the worst...
All in all, I was really hyped for Stellaris, and I still think that the game has great potential. Although, it is far too flawed in my eyes to be recommended in this state and at full price. It can get quite interesting once modded, but mods won't solve everything, and by the way they don't have to ! Finally, I firmly oppose Paradox's policy. Many of the abovementioned issues were indeed addressed in some of the DLC (i.e. : Leviathans). But here is the problem : it's a DLC. Seriously, someone who already paid for the game shouldn't have to pay again for basic updates addressing the major flaws of the game...

SPOILER FREE REVIEW
The Game of Thrones RPG isn't the perfect game, but it does have a perfect story. George R.R Martin helped write it and you can tell, especially with all the intrigue and twists and turns. The game suffers from annoying combat mechanics and there isn't that much to do besides the main quest and one or two side quests, but it is a perfect game for any hardcore ASOIAF fans.
The story is great and you play as two main characters, and you visit many places throughout the game. The iconic locations are in such as Castle Black and King's Landing, you can go to Mole's Town as well. But most of the NPC in the game just stand around and offer nothing to the story but to make the locations look full of life. You can also hear the authentic voices of Joer Mormont and Varys, and the voice acting of the two main characters is great also.
The combat is a good system, but the annoyance is being ganged on upon by 5-6 enemies at a time. Even on the easiest difficulty the combat was annoying, not hard, just a pain. Many times I just wanted to skip the combat and advance throughout the story. Levelling up is cool, and there are alot of cool items in the game. My character for example was weilding Ser Duncan's sheid, and you can even use The Red Viper's spear. Those items are included with the Weapon Pack DLC though.
Each "Chapter" in the game has the main quest and 1-2 side quests you can do. Side quests usually help you out later with the main quest if you accomplish them. But once you complete the quests there is nothing to do in the game but maybe fight in the arenas to get more cash. Making cash is easy, just sell all the stuff you don't have. No need to really fight for it.
The game is great for all ASOIAF and GOT fans to enjoy. The story is great and you will feel for the characters, but just remember in GOT their is no such thing as a happy ending.

I tried hard to enjoy the game, to me this felt more like a $5 game not a $20 game.  The game has some good ideas and potential but if felt like once everything started to come together it just ended.  Now I have never watched the game of thrones so my review is going to be purely based off of the game play.  I got over small things like the camera angle being horrible and your actions not really effecting the outcome of anything.  The game is very restrictive and you will follow a  certain path no matter how you choose to play your character.
Combat:
The combat is a turn based/real time format.  It was very fun and I would recommend watching a youtube video to get an idea of what I mean.
Skills:
The game does a good job of explaining these but you will learn that if you spend your skill points on certain skills you have wasted them.  The biggest of these being the one that effects your buying/selling skill. I invested most of my skill points on this skill and then a few hours in I realized there was no way I would ever be able to buy any of the gear so I would never use this skill. (at least not until the end of the game, and at that point you'll start to get so much money you could buy everything twice)
Economy/Gear:
Do not plan on doing anything with buying/selling.  You will never have enough money to buy better gear until the very end of the game.  At that point it becomes completely rediculas and money is basically being thrown at you.  Just plan on looting and wearing that gear.
Why I'm NOT recommending:
The biggest things that made me decide to not recommend the game is that you put all this time into developing your characters skills, finally get enough money to buy some decent equipment, and then the game just ends.  I was left going why did I waste all that time planning and training up?  I should have just sprinted through the game play and listened to the story.  Also once the story ends your done, there is no going back and replaying things your just finished.
Conclusion:
If you just want a story this might be your game.  Do not spend to much time planning out your skill tree's or traits or anything else about your character because in the end you will never get to use your thought out plan.  Play this game to just hear the story and nothing more.  I personally didn't find the story all that amazing but that does not mean you wont.  If you buy this game set the difficulty to easy and just sit back and enjoy the story.
Thank you for reading my post, I hope this helps you to decide if this game is worth it for you.  Either way enjoy your gaming.

I have played exactly 88 minutes of this game. I've done the tutorials, played a couple matches, and browsed through the customization. My time is valuable; this game needed to convince me that it's worth the chance, instead of the other million or so games in Steam I could be playing. It failed spectacularly.
Guns of Icarus is a game that caters to the elite. It has been built to exclude casual players, so that the people that have put 500+ hours into the game can dominate everyone else. The game mechanics, while polished and with lots of potential, are as unintuitive as the developers can get away with.
For instance, the airships players are in have giant balloons. In any other game, an airship's balloon is a weak spot. Not in Guns of Icarus! Sure, sometimes you should shoot the balloon. But sometimes you should be shooting the hull, or the engine. It depends on your weapon, your ammo, where your teammates are shooting, etc. If this was Pokemon, I'd love to sort through all these buffs and modifiers. But this game is in real-time; if you don't know exactly what to do every second of the game, you're at a disadvantage. And trust me, your instincts will be wrong.
Your equipment is equally complex. For instance, the repair specialist has not one, not two, but three tools that repair your airship. They're all common repair tools, used in exactly the same way, without anything differentiating them visually. What's the difference between repairing with a screwdriver and a wrench? Why, one has a different recharge time, of course! That's intuitive, right? Oh, and good luck figuring out which is better without a guide.
Speaking of the repair tools, the very mechanics seem to make as little sense as possible. To repair your ship, you hit a part of the ship with your tool. Fair enough. But if your tool is recharging, you can still swing your tool. It just won't do anything. If the tool is useless, then why does the game let you use it? You'd think that, because you can swing the tool, you're still able to repair. Have fun figuring out why your ship isn't repairing.
I could go on, but you get the picture. This kind of elite-pandering design is in every detail of the game. You'll need to invest dozens of hours before you start having fun. When you have to waste all that time, why not just play something else that's fun from the start?

1- GENERAL
The Binding of Isaac is a roguelike shooter run in a dungeon environment.
McMillen made a game inspired in religious beliefs that is at the same time funny, hard and sarcastic. It was one of the most discussed games of 2011, when it was launched. In fact, is not a common plot to a game having mother that wants to kill her son after God told her to.
Designwise it’s a simply top down cartoon style game, nothing fancy, but it does the trick quite good tbh. The game is full of usual stuff, like demoniac children, bombs, decapitated children, poop, several monsters... everything that we have done in our childhood. Who has not faced a monster covered in blood.
2- GAMEPLAY
It's a very hard roguelike game. Death is permanent, but you can see what you have already found in the current save. You use WASD to move and the arrows to fire, so this can be a little tricky to the brain at first, but in a short time you get the hang of it.
It has a dungeon system and it has a random generation system, so you'll never play the same level twice. So you can go through it in a hour, or you can take ages to reach the ending.
You can unlock some different characters, which one with different perks.
At the end of each level we face a random boss and only then we go through the next level. Some levels have some hard characters to face during the dungeon exploration. Each level is progressively harder to play with harder opponents. With some luck we can face the hardest ones at first, when they are easier to kill, or the game is almost impossible to finish.
3- CONCLUSION
For me this game is incredibly fun. It's insanely hard, but with lot's of replay ability. It's hours of fun. Ok, it's a bit creepy, but that is part of it's charm.
