An exceptionally charming solitaire/rpg hybrid complete with dress-up! The first few rounds of Shadowhand make you think you're playing Regency Solitaire again - it's classic up/down solitaire where your goal is to clear the board and collect gold, with all the twists that come along with the genre - locked off stacks of cards, powers that let you shuffle the board, etc. Then you hit your first duel, and the game dials the difficulty right up.
Let me take a step back before I describe duels, however. The structure of this game involves twenty or so chapters, each one containing at least five different matches - a mix of solitaire hands and these duels. Loot and powers are persistent through the rounds, adding an element of strategy as you consider using a special power to completely clear the board in a match, but...what if that power could win you the duel later on? Those powers do recharge, but not that quickly. Every chapter ends in a climactic duel with an enemy - a pirate, a robber, worse.
So, duels! The highlight of this game, and the reason I threw down my money instead of waiting for a steeper sale or a bundle. Duels are essentially co-op solitaire - you and the AI take turns clearing the board and chaining combos. The duel aspect comes in how every card cleared from the board charges up your weapons, making the co-op tense as you try not to leave the board ripe for a combo on the AI's turn - because oh, they will seize any opportunity to take a ten card combo and destroy you.
Details: instead of the duel ending when the board is cleared, a new board is provided. What determines the winner of a duel is (usually) who's alive at the end. Your weapons do set damage, theirs do set damage, and while it initially seems straightforward, there's a huge variety of twists to this basic premise: different enemise have different clothes which give them armor values, which means your five damage sword may do only three damage. The damage race between the two of you depends on how well you can play, what weapons you brought - some can pierce armor or add status effects like bleeding - and the RNG.
Mark my words, the RNG is going to get you in this game. Like all solitaire games, sometimes you just get a lousy board, and keep drawing the wrong cards. It's just part and parcel of the game, so go in expecting to retry rounds or duels when the RNG decides you have to lose. But! As you proceed in the game, you unlock more and more ways to tilt the RNG in your favor - those aforementioned special powers, you'll find wildcards, etc. You even have stats to level up so good things happen to you more often.
Another piece to mention, because oh my goodness there's a lot in this game. Items! Consumables also join the mix, because what's a duel without throwing diseased rats at each other? There are the standard healing items and recovery from status effects, along with the ones that give status effects, or buff you for your next attacks. Good stuff!
The main gameplay loop are those rounds, prepping for the duels, and enjoying the charming story. It's similar to Regency Solitaire - nothing to write home about, alas, but it's charming. You're a noble lady who gets thrust into becoming an outlaw, murdering thugs and trying to find out what some scheming nobles are up to. You'll get thrown into prison, rob nobles yourself, and so on - exciting fluff that lends fun themes to the gameplay as you proceed through the chapters.
Final bits and bobs: gosh, the artwork is good. Gosh, the sound design is good. The polish on this title is ridiculous, complete with your lady getting brand new art whenever you swap her costume around. ... Oops, forgot equipment! You find equipment as you go along, new weapons, new masks - they all influence gameplay by giving you armor or resistances or other fun effects, and best of all they all have art! I spent a chapter in an appalling combination of yellow scarf with purple domino, but the stat boosts were crucial... Fortunately I was soon given a faux-beard and a better looking domino, as well as other accessories.
In conclusion, this game is a feast. It's casual enough that I can chill and play cards, but has enough complexity that I have to form strategies for certain duels, and it's just plain fun. You already know if you're in or not, but if my opinion counts for anything - check it out!

I loved Black & White, and that is what I wanted From Dust to be. That was sort of how I interpreted the game's marketing. Instead of being like Black & White, this game felt flat. First and foremost, as of this review I had no issue installing or playing this game on PC. I played the game on Xbox 360 prior to purchasing on PC.
The engine behind this game is something spectacular. The ability to manipulate sand, water, and lava is definitely a really fun mechanic. Rivers will flow dynamically in sand, creating their own path and carving their way into the world (with or without your help). Lava will flow and harden into rock which allows for various other uses throughout the game. Sand will spread out over the terrain in a natural soft and smooth manner.
The game is pretty simple, your ultimate goal on each level is to move to the next level. In order to move on, you need to unlock totems. The totems grant additional powers as well as more villages and people. Of course, each totem may have their own challenge to obtain, such as raising the land out of water or using lava to help secure it from threats. There are side objectives to the game, such as collection these minor totems and filling the land completely with vegetation.
Although manipulating the elements is fun, it leaves a strong desire for more. Thinking back to games such as Populous: The Beginning, this engine could be so much more in the right hands and it's sad that it's not being used for something greater. Ultimately, expect to get several fun hours of this game, but if you're like me, you'll thirst for something more. If you haven't played Populous, it's over on GOG for $6, which may give you many more hours of a God game experience for less dollars spent.

I seldom bother to write reviews for games, but felt that this one warranted one because of its conflicting nature of pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Best thing about this game is the storyline. It has one of the more detailed, involved and believable stories among games of its level. It starts off slowly, but gets really gripping towards the end. The way they took the stories of two different characters and meshed them together really works. The game's story runs concurrent to events in the main GoT storyline, which is also great if you're a fan.
+ They didn't bill this game as one that provides many decision choices, yet there are a surprisingly decent amount of dialogue and character choices. It doesn't change the main story outcome very much, but definitely changes some side quests etc, as well as the feel of the story.
+ Lots of GoT lore throughout the game (optional for you to read), and I love that they include weapons and armor of famous characters from the main GoT story.
Cons:
- Biggest flaw is a graphic bug that I could not find a fix to. All suggestions I came across did not solve the bug. Very often (in 'walled' surroundings) when panning the camera, it skips madly, making it impossible to face / run in the right direction, and causing a huge amount of nausea. Its the main reason why it took me so long to finish the game. Granted, this bug does not occur for everyone, so it's just a risk you have to take if you decide to get the game.
- Voice acting could have been better. Most of the time the characters (aside from Mors) sound either flat or fake. Better voice acting would really have helped make the story so much better, given the already good storyline. Alester also sounds a bit flat at points, which a main character really shouldn't.
- Combat is also very cumbersome. You have to 'pause' the game to use abilities, which makes combat rather slow, and constant toggling between characters to use their skills is a bit of a pain.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend the game, unless you're the kind that absolutely hates graphic bugs and will trash the com in a rage. Given the price, and how good the story is, I'd say go for it if you like detailed stories, or if you're a GoT fan. If you're not so much of a fan of GoT / RPGs, or are hesitant to risk getting the bug, then wait for it to go on sale and then get it. Because it'll certainly be worth it on sale.

Known as one of the most polarizing games of all time, it can be hard to know what you should do if you're thinking about getting Deadly Premonition, and my review (although positive since I liked it) will be one that I hope will help you figure out if this game is for you or not.
What does the game have (speaking positively)?  It's got a great horror/murder mystery storyline with 3-dimensional characters.  If you're a gamer who loves good stories, a fan of crime drama/murder mysteries, and/or you enjoy the more psychological, atmospheric horror of games like Silent Hill, then you're in the right place.  If you liked David Lynch's short TV series, "Twin Peaks," then you'll probably like this game, altough there are some fans of Twin Peaks who felt like this game was ripping it off and didn't appreciate that (personally, I found it to be more along the lines of a loving tribute to Twin Peaks, however, I'll admit that, with all the similarities, I can understand where those that called it a rip-off were coming from).
That said, what is the game lacking?  For the most part, I'd say the game is weak in it's main gameplay mechanics, but I didn't find it to be TERRIBLE.  It's a fairly simple 3rd-person action/shooter style game that implements elements of realism (eating when you are hungry, sleeping when you've been up for a certain amount of time, ect.).  The control scheme is somewhat clunky and not as polished as it should be, but once you get used to it, it doesn't take too much away from the overall experience.
Gameplay isn't all a big negative either - there was a pretty big positive element having nothing to do with the main gameplay mechanics: the game's open-world with lots of optional sidequests.  Some people don't like it as much, but I had tremendous fun collecting weapons, cash, and other helpful items for the main game by doing the errands, jobs, and other plentiful optional tasks that are available to you throughout the game.  If you're a sidequest lover (especially of the open-world/sandbox variety), then getting enjoyment from playing the game shouldn't be a problem for you as you are enjoying the storyline (and it makes for lots of extra gameplay hours, making the game feel more like it earned your money).
Overall, I loved this game, but I will say this: if you're not easily gripped by a game's storyline and/or you absolutely NEED a 3rd-person action/adventure/sandbox game to have well-honed controls and an intuitive, unique style of gameplay that stays fresh and exciting at every turn, then you might want to look elsewhere.
My Over Rating:  9.0 / 10.0

"At times we must purge things from this world because they should not exist. Even if it means losing someone that you love."
According to this quote taken directly from the game itself, Deadly Premonition probably shouldn't exist either. The graphics are horrible, the sounds are cheap, the controls are clunky and you'll encounter lots of crashes and freezes along the way... yet it still manages to be one of my favourite games of all time!
So I'd rather say "If you really, truly love something, you'll stick with it - no matter what!"
Plot
FBI agent Francis York Morgan (just call him York, everyone does that!) is sent to the small town of Greenvale to investigate a murder case.
It doesn't take long until strange things start to happen and more people are getting killed. Who or what is responsible and who is "Zach" York keeps talking to? An imaginary friend? You, the player?
If you've ever watched Twin Peaks, you'll feel right at home with lots of similarities, especially a huge number of eccentric characters.
Graphics
Well, it doesn't look too bad for a Dreamcast title, does it? Except that it isn't a Dreamcast title...
Originally the resolution is fixed to 720p, but just google "DPfix" for that. This mod allows you to raise the resolution and add a few improvements, but it will still look like a PS2 title. The textures are rather simplistic, the animations are stiff and sometimes hilariously bad, especially some face animations, objects tend to pop up right in front of you and sometimes shadows will be displayed wrong or might be missing alltogether. Well, it just looks horrible.
But you will get used to it and even consider it as one of the game's charming features, I kid you not! In fact, you will start to notice that indeed a lot of detail and effort have been put into the visual presentation - at times, at least. The environments are diverse and plentyful and there certainly is a high level of detail considering the insides of rooms etc. Small things like different posters, objects etc. make every place look and feel different and unique.
It's just that it never really looks convincing from a technical standpoint. In fact, Deadly Premonition is an ugly game, but you won't mind that anymore after a while, right, Zach?
Music & Sound
The music is really weird. Some tracks feel completely out of place, sometimes the music might even drown out the dialogue during cutscenes and sometimes it will be annoying to have to listen to the same short track loop over and over again... but you'll start to love and appreciate that! It's almost like hypnosis and the tracks tend to become real earworms over time. A couple of hours in, you'll be humming and whistling along the melodies and be purchasing the game's soundtrack too, if you haven't already. I know it sounds weird, but you'll end up loving the game's music and it really fits the title's quirky mood.
The sound effects are... well... pretty bare bones, actually. It's like only the most important events actually even have sound. And there's not much variety. A steel door opening will sound just the same like a wooden door opening, the gunshots are more like "pew pew" and the car sounds are laughably cheap. If you've never had to laugh simply because how things sounded or didn't make sound at all... Deadly Premonition will change that!
Gameplay
Basically, Deadly Premonition is an open world 3rd person adventure with a lot of driving. You'll talk to people, collect evidence, investigate, navigate through the town, solve a few (simple) riddles here and there and when you don't want to progress further with the main story, you can roam around freely, go fishing, play darts, have a few drinks, go shopping, shave, or start doing some of the numerous sidequests, which happen to be interesting short stories with sometimes great rewards.
At certain points, the game will transport you to the "Otherworld" where everything is dark and gloomy and you'll be fighting some strange zombie-like creatures. Think about a cheap version of silent hill which still manages to feel scary and foreboding at times. Luckily, those segments aren't really very hard, which makes up for the overall clunky controls. You even have unlimited ammo for your pistol and most enemies will go down after 1-2 hits with melee weapons as well. The latter ones will break and become unable to use after a couple of strikes, but you'll find plenty of them lying around anyways. While there hardly is any real sense of dread during those segments, at least there's also no frustration and even people inexpierienced with combat mechanics in games should be able to finish the title. Ironically, those passages still manage to convey a dreadful and creepy atmosphere and absolutely justify calling Deadly Premonition a horror game.
There are even some quick time events and hide-and-seek segments in the game, but those are few and far between, plus there's usually a checkpoint right in front of them, keeping frustration from failing those to a minimum.
Controls
Imagine performing a heart surgery with a spoon... while wearing winter gloves! The controls feel awkward and unprecise most of the time, but then again, the game doesn't even need you to be precise most of the time. So you'll somewhat get used to it. It certainly doesn't feel as natural and smooth as other 3rd person games, the driving physics are hilarious and you'll be fumbling around a lot, but it's actually more awkward in a funny way than frustrating.
Bugs
Yes, this has to be adressed. The game is definitely prone to crashes and freezes, and you will have to play around a little with DPfix, the 4GB Patch (google this one as well!) and compatibility modes. Once you've figured out a setup which works for you, you should be able to play the game pretty much without any crashes and freezes. But consider saving a lot, just to be safe.
There will also be a lot of non-gamebreaking bugs, but those are actually fun and will even add to the overall enjoyment. Let's just say that you'll probably encounter lots of crazy and unexpected things during your playthrough... One might even assume that some of those bugs would have been added on purpose!
This sounds quite horrible so far! Then why do I even like the game, let alone consider it one of my favourite games of all times?
First, it's really unique and feels extremely "honest". It doesn't even try to cover its technical flaws.
Then there's lots of of extremely likeable and weird characters. The game will surprise you by throwing weird stuff and memorable dialogues at you all the time. Even the lesser important characters are created with lots of detail, unique backstorys, daily routines, etc. which makes Greenvale really come to life and feel like a real (albeit weird) place.
York himself is probably one of the greatest videogame characters of all time. He's eccentric, weird and you never know how even the seemingly most mundane dialogues will play out and in what direction he will take them, making each and every interaction quite memorable.
The story itself is also great and intriguing. Without spoiling anything, what starts out as a simple murder mystery starts to get more and more complex and interesting. You'll be starting to make your own assumptions, have your own suspects and will want to see everything unfold.
And that's the most important thing about Deadly Premonition and why people who like it actually like it: The way the story progresses, the quirky, loveable and memorable characters, the whole weird and sometimes even meditation-like feel of the game and the true and honest emotions it triggers in the player. Over the course of the game, you will laugh, cringe, even cry, be shocked, be on the edge of your seat, feel relaxed...
Despite all the technical flaws, Deadly Premonition is one of the few games that will keep you emotionally engaged during the whole time and stick with you long after playing - if you give it the chance to do so!

1- GENERAL
The Binding of Isaac is a roguelike shooter run in a dungeon environment.
McMillen made a game inspired in religious beliefs that is at the same time funny, hard and sarcastic. It was one of the most discussed games of 2011, when it was launched. In fact, is not a common plot to a game having mother that wants to kill her son after God told her to.
Designwise it’s a simply top down cartoon style game, nothing fancy, but it does the trick quite good tbh. The game is full of usual stuff, like demoniac children, bombs, decapitated children, poop, several monsters... everything that we have done in our childhood. Who has not faced a monster covered in blood.
2- GAMEPLAY
It's a very hard roguelike game. Death is permanent, but you can see what you have already found in the current save. You use WASD to move and the arrows to fire, so this can be a little tricky to the brain at first, but in a short time you get the hang of it.
It has a dungeon system and it has a random generation system, so you'll never play the same level twice. So you can go through it in a hour, or you can take ages to reach the ending.
You can unlock some different characters, which one with different perks.
At the end of each level we face a random boss and only then we go through the next level. Some levels have some hard characters to face during the dungeon exploration. Each level is progressively harder to play with harder opponents. With some luck we can face the hardest ones at first, when they are easier to kill, or the game is almost impossible to finish.
3- CONCLUSION
For me this game is incredibly fun. It's insanely hard, but with lot's of replay ability. It's hours of fun. Ok, it's a bit creepy, but that is part of it's charm.

I got this off the Humble Bundle. At the price point I paid for the bundle of games ($5), this game is well worth it.
I want to point out that this game is exactly like the description - a mix between Dr. Mario and Ikagura. It's quick, colorful, and extremely arcade-like. You'd think this game was not made for the colorblind, but there actually is a setting just for that.
It's one of those games that's all about your driving your physical and mental reflexes to their limits. Like an old-school arcade game, you play with simple game mechanics and for the sole reason of how far can you get and how many points you can score. Shoot the right colored pills, keep the combos running to boost your score, and most of all, avoid losing the few lives granted. You can also purchase more music, more powerups, more lives, more colors, and so much more with your... um... "drug money?". These will help you accomplish so much more in the game, but they can also be turned off if you don't like the option, or if you really wanted to test yourself. Great game for picking up, playing a few times, and then getting off. Just remember that with the exception of THIS game, "Winners don't use drugs".

I love Intake.  I grabbed it awhile back before it was on Steam and loved it - how excited was I when a few months later I noticed I could activate it in my library!
It's a sleeper hit, unknown gem, whatever adjective pair you want to use to describe it is applicable.  It's well polished, addictive, and fast paced - like the best Shmups (might be why I'm so drawn to it).
The premise is simple: click on pills to make them explode.  Two colors come down at once, right click to swap between colors, build combos, and set high scores.
In execution, it gets tricky: the music is blaring, your palms are sweating, and the pills keep coming.  You click and click and click but the waves keep coming down.
It's intensely fun with superb sound design.  Speaking of which, make sure you have some solid headphones.  You'd be doing yourself a disservice if you had little cheapo earbuds in while you played this.  The best experience is engrossed with your nose an inch from the monitor and the EDM soundtrack and high-quality sound effects bursting your eardrums.
The visuals are really nice too.  Nothing too complex, a few particle effects and some color shadings but the game pulls it together into a great, color popping aesthetic.
As for settings options, for an indie game this guy is packed full of them.  Full featured color-blind modes, "gartnervision", which gives background to the landscape mode the game is set in, a full suite of upgrades to unlock and turn on and master, even different game modes and challenges including a "No Nonsense" mode which cuts out bonus levels and keeps you in the heat of things longer and at a faster pace.  You can really tell with the available settings, options, and unlocks that the developers really cared about this game and took the time to polish all the edges - even the flavor text for your power ups has funny little quips that fit the theme of the game.
Don't miss this one.  I'd recommend it for just about any gamer with a love for pulse-pounding action, especially if you want something to pick up for short period of time play...if you can put it down.
-Be Aggressive.

(Hint: if you like the music, you'll love the game - the songs are even better with explosions)

This game is an underknown little gem of minimalist gameplay.
It asks you to click some falling pills to explode them before they hit the lower part of the screen. There is a color switch system.
- Pills come in two colors, shoot the pills of the same color or switch colors anytime)
- Black flashbang pills to avoid
The gameplay has a few more subtle points: explosions push away nearby pills, pills can collide together, etc.
After every short level, you get rewarded with a circle of bonus coins you have to hit quickly. CLICK CLICK CLICK CLICK !
To break the monotony every once in a while,, you get a special level with one difficulty setting pushed much higher, like much more pills onscreen ("flood" levels), or less pills onscreen with a much faster falling speed.
This is 100% skill based and feels like a nice mouse aiming / reaction time skill test.
I think the game is entirely procedural/randomized. It just gets harder until you eventually lose.
There are some bonuses here and them (items, unlockable) which you should have all unlocked in a few hours hours. Hopefully they do not distract too much from the gameplay (just like the special levels, they help break the monotony).
About the graphics: they do their job. Pretty but the readibility is good, which is absolutely necessary for a fast-paced game like this. There are some nice hommages to arcade some will catch :) With some tweaks to difficulty and items, this would sure make an excellent arcade game. If arcades still existed. Whatever.
Last but not least, the game comes with a huge amount of achievements and ... leaderboards =)
Highly recommended.

Great solitaire game, very fun to play.  You have a mix of two types of games - standard remove cards game with usual small extras like find keys to open locked cards - also a few special abilities such as shuffling the cards that are out.  Then there are duals where the cards you (or your opponent) click out charge up your weapons and then you select a weapon to attack with.
Then in between you have the story and upgrades screens.  Upgrades takes the form of new weapons, new wearables and dual consumables.
The intro at the top of the store page currently says "Build mini-decks".  This is not accurate - it gives the impression of deck-building mechanic in the game, and there is no deck building in this game.  The "mini-deck" is simply the weapons and wearables which are those objects placed on playing cards.  Placing objects on playing cards does not make it a "deck".  There is no drawing cards from a deck you have built.
I am having a lot of fun, but it does seems to have a limited lifespan by the end of the plot - unless something surprising happens between now (4-5 hours in, about halfway through the plot) and the end.  There is always 'hard' mode I suppose, but not sure I will be motivated to play that.
So the question is:  Will this be a "living" game that gets content upgrades.  The previous game Regency Solitaire seems to have no updates after launch, but then that was a couple of years ago and this game is 50% more expensive.  The trend towards people preferring living games is very strong, so let's see if the developer responds to trends and adds more content.
If no new content gets added do I recommend this game?  Well, yes just about.  I am not particularly price sensitive myself and this is better than other solitaire games.
If the game will be getting updates then I would strongly recommend it.
Would be good if the developer can give a reply to my review to say if it will be a living game with content updates or not.

Like all other "tie in" games I've ever played, this suffers from being a rushed budget effort, borrowing much from other games, presenting nothing new of its own (it's built on UnrealEngine3, like many, many other almost identical games).  The release in 2012 would imply a better package of graphics and combat smoothness than we get here, both these elements are around 4 years behind the times (as you'd only expect with UE3-made titles).  For comparative purposes, this should be viewed as a peer of games like Gothic 4, Witcher 1 (also built on UE3) and Risen 1, they have a lot of dubious qualities in common, such as slow, affected dialogue to expand apparent game time, NPCs drawn from a limited stock of character skins, and more.  You can get through it by plodding carefully and muzzing through early quests and objectives which are just a bit dull, like chores, and winning valueless "achievements" which you'd get by playing the game normally anyway.  The combat can be clumsy and frustrating unless you painstakingly control every single blow, but this becomes a nonsense when selected team-mates can't reach selected targets due to obstruction by other team-mates and overcrowding.  This just smacks of an ill-considered game, where certain shortcomings weren't ironed out during beta testing -- if indeed it was ever beta tested.
Some characters are made to look like the actors in the TV series, and like-soiunding voices are used, but that's where the similarities end -- on the voice subject, you'll quickly realise the dialogue was recorded at many different sessions, and not sequentially, making it sound like bits cut out of radio pla\ys and pasted in, with mis-matched environmental reverb and rather disgruntling emphasis-flow.  Plotlines have little bearing on either the books or the TV series, its just an adventure game set in the Westeros world; this will either disappoint you or delight you, depending on how you see these things.  We must remember this is a game, and games have a very different set of rules, especially RPGs, where options are granted and choices can be made -- often not the choices we're pushed into making, or the choices made on TV.  I just think it's a cheap shot at a tie-in, with below par graphics and a very "generic" feel to it (there we go, UE3 again).  Even in 2012, the industry could have turned out something much better, and certainly the "franchise" as it has become, deserves only the best.  Experienced gamers will quickly feel they've played this game before, those new to the genre will no doubt be awed by the next title you play, which will seem so much better.

Oh and the graphics were considered ugly even when it was released. Also the driving is bad, and gunplay bugged (use alt tab to get your crosshair working).
So why do I like it?
Well apart from the obvious 'Twin peaks' homage, the game tries to do a lot, has a great story and good characters. The voice acting is top notch and the atmosphere is excellent. The map is large and nice to explore and the games pacing is great, with plenty of little side missions to achieve outside of the main story.

This is really something special. Take a mix of B-Horror films, mix in a bit of comedy, creative writing, survival horror, life simulation, life management and open world and  you have  Deadly Premonition: The Director's Cut.
You play as autastic FBI agent Morgan as he wanders around, makes weird comments and observations, while talking to his imaginary friend "Zack" (I assume that's the player). While exploring the town of Greenvale, you'll need to keep Morgan well fed, make sure he sleeps enough, makes it on time to his appointments and more. Things like having to shave, clean his clothes or buy new outfits adds just enough depth to make the game even more intresting.
I have no problems with the controls. Others may be playing with a keyboard and mouse, but the game was clearly designed to be played with a controller, which I have been using myself. It's pretty much your run of the mill tank controls ala Resident Evil, with an auto-aim assist that comes in handy at times.
I think my biggest complaint with the game so far is the driving segments. Driving in this game tends to be clunky at best and eventually because tedious and frustrating. Some sort of quick travel feature would have been *really* nice for this game.
The game is clearly showing it's age, it doesn't look nearly as good as modern day games, but what do you expect for a port of a 7th generation console game?
On a side note, I guess lots of people are having issues with the performance of the game. Since I am all too aware of how problematic PC games can be when running on different hardware, I am not discounting other users' problems. But, I must be lucky, because this game installed and ran just fine without any major issues or difficulties. I am unsure if the poor reviews for this game are based around technical problems other users are having, but I simply don't see why it is being judged so poorly.
In the end, this is a unique, quirky game that has done a fine job at entertaining me and making me laugh and that's all that matters. Play this game, it's a blast.

If you like Red Orchestra in general, this game is pretty much a must have.
The game itself provides somewhat more grounded combat in a Vietnam setting and sure delivers an authentic experience. The gameplay is a bit smoother compared to Red Orchestra 2, it's a bit swifter and overall much more enjoyable. The guns are absolutely lethal and this game is pretty much a death simulator. Beware of a somewhat high difficulty curve, this game can be quite unforgiving. The graphics themselves are on par with Red Orchestra 2, a tad outdated but still quite solid. The sound assets are quite great except for the voice acting which is a bit weak compared to the previous entries that had quite unique and authentic voice acting. But for the rest, it just suits the setting so much.
The gameplay itself is challenging and somewhat slow paced but still quite intense. Firefights are all about situational awareness and knowing when to strike at your enemy. As of now the map variety is a bit limited and most servers play the same kind of maps but they are overal great and very enjoyable.
Most mechanics are straight taken out of the previous game and it fits the game well. There is truly nothing to complain about except the lack of maps. Also at times the game tends to bug out when it comes to navigating around while prone but most of the time it plays flawlessly.
I definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoyed Red Orchestra or likes the Vietnam setting in a more grounded multiplayer shooter. Teamwork and skill are definitely required to play this game.

The Binding Of Isaac delves deeply into the mind of Indie Gamers and Developers alike. The game is very religion based, but made like a Zelda game, such as A Link To The Past or The Phantom Hourglass.
Isaac's mother is a strong Christian who constantly watches Christian Television Programming. One day she gets a message from God, who tells her to remove everything from Isaac so he may be pure and not sinful, for so told he has supposedly been corrupted by sin.
After everything is lost, evn Isaac's clothes on his own back, his mother is satisfied. But then she gets another message from God, telling her to kill Isaac for the greater good.
So as she agrees and takes a kitchen knife as she chases Isaac, Isaac manages to escape through a trap door under the rug in his room. As he hops into the trap door, he goes through cellars, sewage tunnels and caves (caverns) to find his way through a safer place.
While exploring these places, he can grab special items to help him along his journey to uncover the game's multiple endings as he fights enemies along the way with his own tears.
You can also unlock multiple characters based off of Christian descendants such as Cain, Magdalene and Lazarus.
This game is recommended to those interested in exploration and the multiple bosses in the game such as the Duke of Flies and Monstro, or just interested in the game's straight premise.

This definitely is a great game and also a good modern RE. Capcom did an amazing job with this port considering that the original system is the 3DS
8.5/10
Good things
-Good story that involves the classic duo of RE (Jill and Chris), with a lot of secrets and a persistent touch of mystery that keeps going and going until the end.
-A "Ghost Ship", the perfect place for a horror game, a ship full of monster in the middle of the ocean and the characters go inside to resolve a mystery.
-Most of the places reminds to the olds RE, there are dark corridors, dark rooms and fancy places. In the dark places the lightning effect is also good, so the enemies have a cool shade effect that combines well with the concept of the game
-In some part of the campaign, the enemies appear from places you will never expected.
-60FPS with no drops even in old computers.
-The graphics are nice considering this is a port of a portable console.
-Great control, feels and respond very well with mouse+keyboard or a controller.
-Great soundtrack.
-Perfect combination of the amount of ammo you can find and number enemies. In your first game you will never feel overpower with a lot of ammo unless you scan a lot.
-Some of the weapons are not in the main route of the campaign so are easy to miss if you don't explore.
-Water system, well considering that the story of the game is developed in a ship is good that the game allows swim or dive.
-The game have options for multi audios, which is cool.
-Infernal difficulty: this is perfect for this kind of game, in this difficulty everything is different. More enemies appear, strong enemies appear way early, they take less damage and the items (ammo) have changed locations. (There is a trailer for this mode).
-The raid mode: in this mode you pick a character, the weapons you want to use and select a stage. Basically you have to reach the destination point and kill, plus not die, the enemies to keep advancing. While you play in this mode you level up the character, you can find new weapons during the stages and also you can buy weapons in the shop. You can customize the weapons with perks.
Finally, you can play this mode in co-op. The level is universal meaning that all characters share the same level and there are three specific conditions/bonus for all the stages. If you do it, you gain more points (experience and money for the shop), also unlock some achievements.
Bad things:
I honestly can think in three negative things this game have.
-The design of the enemies is really not scary. For me there are only 3 enemies with cool design, one is a sub-boss the others two are bosses. That can give you an idea of how the design of the enemies is.
-"Do not get hit": I said there are three specific conditions/bonus for the stages in raid more, well one of those is do not get hit. In the first difficulty this can be achieved with practice and a lot of ammo but in the high difficulties is just ridiculous. If you really want to do it then you have to memorize the stage, like what enemy appears, how many appears, kill them all as fast as possible and of course, do not get hit. In Revelations 2 Capcom "fix" this.
-The side history in the campaign, I will prefer this be optional because is really not good. One moment you are in the ship, then a movie starts and you are move to another location with a couple of nobodies. Same happens after but this time at least one of the two characters is memorable, I talking of the lady of course.
At the end Resident Evil Revelations is a safe buy even for full price because is a good Resident Evil game.

There is a litany of problems with this game, though to say the following is an exhaustive list would be inaccurate:
-It's a shoddy port that doesn't appear to render properly, nor hide the mouse cursor (that's okay though, you can just push the cursor off to the side and ignore it, I suppose).
-Its narrative is shallow and horrifyingly pretentious; being populated by insufferably stupid characters who are either boring, annoying, or both.
-The game’s limited number of environments are populated with bland art assets that in some cases don’t look suitable for a modern game.
-Excessive is a good descriptor for the game’s length.  The story is not compelling enough to justify the amount of time it takes to unfold, particularly when one considers the amount of filler you’re forced to go through as well.
-The side quests do very little to support or expand upon the story, and are instead mostly drudge work collecting stuff for people, punctated by transit between areas.
My recommendation is you don't spend money on this game, or at least don't pay full price for it.  Check out some of the other stuff PlatinumGames has worked on instead.

Im going to preface this review by saying that words cannot possibly do NieR: Automata justice, but im going to try to tell you how much of a masterpiece this game is, and how it made me feel anyway.
Every element of this game melds together to create a damn near flawless experience.  Everything falls into place so seamlessly.  The meticulous attention to detail is evident in the characters, the combat system, the environment, the story etc.
The gameplay is so diverse.  The game frequently switches from an open world 3D hack and slash to a 2D sidescroller, a top down style, and an 80's style arcade bullet hell.  The hack and slash gameplay is the real star, however, with its lenience in terms of how you want to take the enemies down.  This is due to the many different combinations of enemies the game throuws at you, the several different weapons you can use, and the chips you can customize to suit your playstyle.  The boss fights, especially, feel intimidating, urgent, scary even, and are always challenging, not brainlessly easy, nor rage-inducingly hard.  Be it dodging and running around and using well-placed counterattacks, running in gung-ho into a group of enemies and spamming evade and light attacks, hell, even button mashing, every form and style of combat feels so exciting and intense.
The reuse of several parts of the in-game world/environment make you feel a form of attachment to them.  Instead of a stale linear progression through areas you will most likely never see again, you develop a familiarity towards the areas you go through.  As they change, crumble, or reveal other parts of the environment as a consequence of the story, they make you feel as if the events are actually unfolding around you with an intensity and urgency I have never seen before in a video game.
The game touches on many deep themes, like life and death, free will, love, loss, betrayal, good vs bad, identity, purpose, existentialism, sentience, etc.  Each of these themes blend so perfectly with the masterfully written and designed story and characters, and they pop out at you while playing and almost force you to think about them.  "Who is the real villain here?"  These serve to strengthen the plot of the game.
The soundtrack is one of the strongest points of this game.  In my opinion, there is not a single weak track on this game's OST.  Each track is placed perfectly, doing wonders to enhance the atmosphere, allowing for a more immersive experience.
The characters feel so real, human and bright, each with their own quirks.  The English voice actors, especially 9S', create a dynamic and real feeling.  Their moods change in response to the events happening in the story; instead of being stale, distant protagonists in a superhero film, they feel close, and their emotions feel genuine.  You can't help but feel attached to them as you progress.  You can't help but feel as they do, even if it is just a fictitious video game.
And finally, the plot.  The strongest point of NieR: Automata.  It blends flawlessly with every element of the game, but most of all, the authentic and real characters to create a fantastic story and atmosphere you immediately feel an extremely strong connection to.  NieR: Automata's story is so beautifully crafted and perfectly put together, that even if you feel the gameplay is boring and repetitive, you feel the need to continue, to progress, to learn more.  As the story unfolded, as truths were uncovered and lies exposed, I felt shock, anger, sadness, relief, etc. just as 2B, 9S and A2 did.  With every character death, I felt more and more hopeless.  When the characters pushed through despite the pointlessness of the situation, despite the bleak future, it reignited some of that hope within me.  While playing, I did not find any plot holes, because in actuality, each part of the plot raised questions that I desperately wanted the answer to while answering others in a way that surprised and evoked emotion within me every time.  The story progresses as fast as you want it to, giving you the freedom to explore the world, to do various sidequests that reveal small details and backstories that further explain other major details, plot points, and character motives.  No sidequest feels tedious or boring.  There are 26 total endings for this game, 5 of them being canon.  These 5 endings provide perfect conclusions to the buildup of the story, and make you feel so intensely and vividly when looking back.  They make you feel as if you played a part in completing the story, as if you were in the world.
My only (very minor) complaint with this game is the hacking.  There is an excessive amount of it at times, and some of the minigames can be annoying.
Yoko Taro is a ♥♥♥♥ing genius.  This game had me ♥♥♥♥ed up for a week.  NieR: Automata is one of the very few games that has made me feel such an intense rollercoaster of emotions.
Is it a stretch to say that i will remember this game for the rest of my life?  Sure, and it's also corny as ♥♥♥♥.  To be honest, I feel like a huge chunk of this review is corny as ♥♥♥♥.  But that is honestly how I feel right now.  This game gave me the worst case of post-game depression I have ever had in my life.
This game is breathtaking.  Sure, it has its shortcomings, but the sheer brilliance and quality of this game just eclipse them.
Beats out MGS: Peacewalker for the best game I have ever played.  10/10.

It's been out for less that 24 hours, and I've spent nearly four hours on it... and I don't much care for fighting card games like Magic: The Gathering and such.
The general card play mechanic is solid and fun, and the different dynamics that progressive chapters add on top of that help to keep things fresh. Skills, abilities, gear and weapons progress along with the story. Thus far I've found the player challenge level ramping up with the power level of opponents nicely, with strategic thought going into how you choose to develop your play style and tactics.
There are no "experience points" with your levels. Story progress is linked to skill progress, so you can't just grind away forever in the early chapters until you can win effortlessly. Conversely, if the challenge at the head of the story is currently too high, feel free to drop back a chapter, gather money and items and steel yourself for the fight ahead.
I'm enjoying the story elements thus far, and not just as a theme to the duels. I'm keen to see where this goes.

After loving Regency Solitaire, I have been looking forward to Shadowhand's release for some time, to the extent that it has been one of my very few day one purchases.
I have not been disappointed. Shadowhand builds on, and alters, the solitaire mechanics of Regency Solitaire. So far, all of the additions and changes that I have seen have been positive.
The first obvious difference is the addition of more detailed RPG-like equipment and abilities that alter the solitaire mechanics (usually a chance to cheat in your favour in certain circumstances). The effects are varied and I am finding that changing my equipped gear to meet a particular need is worthwhile and interesting.
The new duel games are the second major addition. I was unsure how these would work, but I am enjoying the variation in gameplay that they offer, and the new avenues for interaction between game elements. In particular, the varying abilities of different opponents can force a change in your playstyle to deal with. Having to think, adapt, and not simply steamroller through things is a very positive piece of game design.
The other changes (reduction of decks from A-K to 0-9, new in-hand unlocking/design, and so on) have also enhanced the game.
Altogether, combined with the lovely aesthetic, care and detail in both game and visual design, and entertaining writing make this a great game that I am happy to have bought and thoroughly recommend.
Essentially Regency Romance themed SolitareQuest.

Shadowhand's pretty great. It's a lovely collection of art, card based animations, and a mix of mechanics that steadily increases complexity as you learn the rules.
It has a fairly smooth ramp up in difficulty, with you always feeling challenged enough as you move from boss to boss. The mix of randomized board states and player choice in gear, attributes, and various active and passive skills means that even if you hit a wall you have quite a bit of room to change up your strategy, whether it's going straight to the face, slotting appropriate consumables, or denying your opponent combo opportunities.
One thing I do very much appreciate is that once you're in the game proper, outside equipping your character, the majority of the board complexity is in card positioning/rank/suit and turn order. There's not a lot of fiddling with stuff like multiplying numbers, it's primarily counting for combos and weighing the risks of targeting this card for a guarantee or taking a risk on flipping this other face down card. There are also "environmental" considerations, like revealing piles of cards, exploding barrels to shake up the top cards, key/lock mechanisms, et cetera, and these meld into the core mechanics very smoothly.
I played on Hard (there's a normal difficulty option as well) and was more than pleasantly surprised with the experience. I would add: I likely have, on average, suboptimal play on Chapter 9, Section 3/8.

Anodyne bleeds it's influences in the most charming and effective way, and it will be hard to play this Zelda-like game without being reminded (oddly enough, more-so than Zelda) of Earthbound and Yume Nikki, from the gorgeous music that nearly sounds like it was lifted from Yume NIkki to the beautiful environments that shift through conciousness and time. And like these games, Anodyne can be poignantly creepy, with sporadic shifts between the sublime lakes and cliffsides to the stoicly maccabre cities and apartment complexes. The vague story can leave a lot to be desired at it's conclusion, but there is more than enough substance throughout that will leave you trying to pull together some kind of larger, overarching meaning, of which it definitely seems to have earned, setting itself apart from many indie RPG-like games that overvalue their use of subtlty. The writing is casual and full of humor, reminding me of Stephen Murphy's absurd Space Funeral with it's occasional, nearly fourth wall breaking vulgarity, which like Space Funeral seems more true to life than awkwardly transgressive. But it's smart, and full of substantial moments that will both stir your emotions and fill you with curiosity.
If I could come up with any faults, I could say that near the end of the game the enemy types start to wear a little thin on you, possibly because there are some very backtrack heavy moments. And that overall, particularly where bosses are concerned, the game is very easy and will rarely give you any challenges, unlike Cave Story, which it seemed very akin to me all though they are of completely different genres.
This is to say nothing about the lasting appeal of Anodyne, I haven't had as satisfying of a gameplay experience with as much charm and surprising moments of wonder in a very, very long time, and if you are a fan of games like the afformentioned Yume Nikki and Earthbound, this is absolutely a mandotory play.

If you just want to play the main game and stop there and ignore the postgame, then it's okay, I guess. Nothing special though, but decent fun. Some good atmosphere, some decent puzzles, a pretty decent-sized world to explore.
The post-game, though, feels like something that was thrown together in a few hours and they didn't bother to test it or fine-tune it at all. It's easy to get stuck and have to warp back to the nexus, the challenges tend to be tedious and unfun without being really hard in a legitimate way, and the world loses a lot of its charm when you just want to friggin' be done already. I went from "meh" to "despise" on this game pretty quickly and I can't say I'd recommend it for a good gaming experience.
Oh yeah, AND. The game is really pretentious and tries to be super creepy but it ends up trying way too hard and I'm so done with the "spookiness" pretty quickly into it. Gag me.

Whole bunch of caveats --
First, this is a remarkably unstable / poor port - you will run into a lot of issues getting it to run at all (due to a variety of compatibility issues), and even past that getting it to be stable, sporting a memory leak that will cause crashes after every 1-2 hours of play (unless corrected through some settings).
There's also an aiming issue with controllers that makes aiming up and down beyond a certain range impossible (this gets in the way of playing in only a couple of spots, most notably in the coup-de-grace at the final boss).
All of that can be worked around (PC Gaming Wiki outlines all of the issues and workarounds in good detail:
but is not super acceptable.
Second, the game itself is not exactly _good_. It's extremely rough around the edges - combat is both annoying and boring, driving is a chore, the enviornments and characters don't look very good (even with some of the fixes/tweaks available), the world is way too spread out for its own good, the 'other world' (combat) sections are over-long for what they bring to the table. There are good quality of life upgrades you can unlock (the radio, infinite weapons, etc) that are a chore to unlock, espccially without a walkthrough, I could go on and on with complaints like that.
With all of that said... I love Deadly Premonition. If you can look past the (myriad) problems, you get bizarre and really endearing characters (especcially your player-character, Agent Francis York Morgan), a sense of style (borrowed VERY liberally from Twin Peaks), a compelling plot full of bonkers twists, charming and dumb cutscenes, and a very unique and interesting open world mechanics.
If you're willing to put up with a lot to get at something really one-of-a-kind and weird, it's well worth it.
(Probably easier to recommend the PS3/360 versions, as they avoid many of the technical issues present in the PC release -- although the 360 release lacks the control upgrades present here or in the PS3 versions).

Steam is bursting with card solitaire games, and a lot of them are disappointingly soulless  - they function on a purely technical level, but have no atmosphere and tend to have horrible balancing problems.
Shadowhand shows you how it should be done. Grey Alien's previous solitaire game, Regency Solitaire, was already brimming with personality, and the levels had a real sense of handcraftedness. Shadowhand takes that as its startingpoint, and adds a wonderful layer of strategy through use of RPG elements.
I actually was surprised how granular the RPGness of the game gets - there are stats (the stats have an effect on the card game) and there is leveling (with points to be distributed), there are skills (recharging 'powers'), there are lots of equipable clothing items that change stats or provide buffs (your character does visibly wear the items) and there are useable items that provide buffs. If that makes it sound complicated, it's really not - the game straddles a perfect middleground between the casual roots of solitaire games and the light complexity of its RPG layers.
As with all solitaire games, the inherent randomness can still turn against you - but you now at least have ways to combat bad luck. On top of this, there is a light story, with some suprisingly deft writing.
If you hadn't guessed, I can't recommend this game enough!

But it's still a solitaire game, so if you hate the idea of using that game as the core mechanic for everything else you won't like this.

This game is everything I had hoped it would be.
Regency Solitaire is the game that made me discover Grey Alien Games. It had spit-polished, elegant and addictive gameplay, which was unfortunately hidden behind a story that I was glad I could skip through as it did not hold my interest in the least. Nevertheless, it captured my heart and I heartily recommended it to everyone I knew.
ShadowHand not only brings back an even more polished version of that gameplay but the story is also genuinely engaging and feels much more integral to the game now. It brings context to the Soltaire sections and drives the addictiveness of the whole experience to dangerous levels.
The Solitaire gameplay has also been upgraded with RPG flavors, where you can equip your character with various pieces of armor and weapons that will significantly change your gameplay experience.
The level of polish that can be found in this game astounds me. Everything is silky smooth, the User interface responds well and satisfyingly, making it an absolute joy to play.
All in all, ShadowHand was precisely what I expected yet I am still surprised at how solid of a game it is.
Must-buy.

So this game is fun. Which surprised me initially, as i'm not someone that normally enjoys these more casual / card based games. And yet... here I am, telling you its a fantastically enjoyable title.
Video:
Text:
While the game starts you of with simple "clear the field" challenges, it quickly adds more mechanical complexity and secondary mechanics to keep you going. Including various cool extras that spice up gameplay during a fight.
Yes, Fights.
This is a interesting switch where you gather charges for your weapons to use on your opponent, which has  a whole other layer to the game. Where progression, skills, gear and equipment upgrades also join in. It truly feels like an RPG was built around the idea of solitaire... and it was done REALLY well.
That isn't say there isn't some stuff that they could do better: The options menu is inadequate, missing even resolution options, and while the visuals of the title are stylistically fitting, i dislike the character models the game went with, as they seem jarring... that said, that is a personal preference and they do fit well thematically.
Audio though... just doesn't fit. I dislike the combat music immensely as i feel it doesn't fit with the theme of the game overall. Especially in a card game, having music that i expect in something like DOOM.
That all said though. I've immensely enjoyed my time with the title and its a great game to pick up for 30 minutes of fun in a quick session, which to often games don't offer these days.

If you like Red Orchestra in general, this game is pretty much a must have.

The gameplay is a bit smoother compared to Red Orchestra 2, it's a bit swifter and overall much more enjoyable. The guns are absolutely lethal and this game is pretty much a death simulator. Beware of a somewhat high difficulty curve, this game can be quite unforgiving. The graphics themselves are on par with Red Orchestra 2, a tad outdated but still quite solid. The sound assets are quite great except for the voice acting which is a bit weak compared to the previous entries that had quite unique and authentic voice acting. But for the rest, it just suits the setting so much.
The gameplay itself is challenging and somewhat slow paced but still quite intense. Firefights are all about situational awareness and knowing when to strike at your enemy. As of now the map variety is a bit limited and most servers play the same kind of maps but they are overal great and very enjoyable.
Most mechanics are straight taken out of the previous game and it fits the game well. There is truly nothing to complain about except the lack of maps. Also at times the game tends to bug out when it comes to navigating around while prone but most of the time it plays flawlessly.
I definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoyed Red Orchestra or likes the Vietnam setting in a more grounded multiplayer shooter. Teamwork and skill are definitely required to play this game.

Let me preface by stating that I've never played the original Rising Storm or the vanilla Rising Storm 2 for that matter, so all of my opinions are based soley off this game and nothing from the predecessors.
I personally really enjoy this game. My friends first showed it to me by explaining it as a fairly difficult tactical shooter where you die in a couple hits. As a casual gamer, this had me worried. I am not very good at games like CS:GO or Rainbow Six, so I was expecting to get bashed online because I sucked. Though my K/D currently sits at an wobbly 0.5, I can tell you that the experience was nothing of that sort.
This needs to be said: IF YOU PLAY A LOT OF TACTICAL SHOOTERS, YOU WILL PROBABLY NOT LIKE THIS GAME. In my opinion, this game is a perfect mix of a casual shooter game (like Battlefield) and a tactical shooter game. Sure, you and your squad / team can totally create strategies and whatnot to take over the enemy base. However, most players will not follow this plan. It's completely possible to just Rambo a place and kill everyone. While this sounds aggravating on the surface (and I won't lie, it can be if ou're on the opposing team), the system backs it up with the fact that you kill others in 1-2 shots. This creates a fair situation, where some smaller strategies will be necessary before you can go full Rambo. As a more casual gamer, I love this! More games should have a more realistic 1-2 shot kill system. It makes the playing field so much more fair. Plus, the game does make you feel like a total badass at points. Always a plus.
To conclude, most people will enjoy this game. Those who won't would probably include: newer gamers and fans of full-on tactical shooters. Those who are more middle of the road, like me, will most likely enjoy the experience! Hopefully I can help some!

So, the one thing that SquareEnix is known for is amazing ambience and story telling. This game is
for the person who enjoys a game driven by the story. The replayability of the game is not limitless, however. Yet, do not give up on the game if you've only completed a single runthrough of the very first or second character endings (A and B). Trust me when I say that it is worth hanging in there for each runthrough of the game. The sotryline continues to evolve, the characters and gameplay style continues to evolve, and even the levels and challenges continue to change and evolve. There are multiple paths to multiple endings!
Now, for some of the things that are "meh" - take-it-or-leave-it. Although questing is interesting in the sense that some good side storylines and dialog are revealed, the actual quests themselves don't have a ton of variety to them. This is understood, given the environment you have to work in. Plus, it is nice that there are a variety of swords to collect and upgrade; however, upgrading your actual POD unit can be teadious and pointless. It would've been nice if there were a way to change armor and clothing customization built into the default gameplay, as well. The game plays fairly smoothly on ultra settings with an Gigabyte Nvidia 1080 Geforce Extreme and 64 GB of RAM. Yet, the cutscenes can still be a bit choppy and stuttery at times.
In general, if you love Japanese Action-RPG games, this one will certainly not disappoint. You can overlook the minor flaws and anoyances to experience a truly beautifully told story.

So. Stellaris.
The first thing I think needs to be said about this game is if you go in and try to min/max it, you won't get the full experience. Sure, you might have some fun, as the game alone is amazingly well done. But treating Stellaris as a way to create the perfect Empire, and then only playing that against the hardest AI you can find, will not gain the full experience.
Stellaris, as with many other Paradox games, is about the story. But Stellaris does this even more so than any game in the past, because the entire game is about YOUR story.
At the very beginning, you create your race. You choose their appearance, name lists, government setup, ethics, weapon and FTL type. You can, and most certainly should, write a backstory, coming up with what got your people to this point. Let your imagination run wild. Got into a war with a neighboring species? Come up with why. BECOME your species.
The true fun of Stellaris comes when you make decisions cause they feel right. Colonizing that planet might not seem smart; its small, irrelevent, and will♥♥♥♥♥♥off your neighbor. But maybe, as a spiritualist, a Gaia world is a gift from the gods. Do it. Make sense of it for YOUR empire. Maybe you'll lose, maybe it hurts you. But it MADE SENSE to your empire, so do it. Once you play stellaris to create a story in your head, a novel about your species rise from a single planet to an intergalactic empire, and possibly their fall, you will find this game to be one of the greatest ever created.
Get this game. Try it. Create your own story.

Started playing Stellaris recently, Paradox's most recent grand strategy game (something they do a lot of). I almost always really really love the idea of Paradox's games, but don't actually enjoy playing them. As cool as I think strategy games are, I rarely have the attention span to get into them or find them satisfying. A paper description of Crusader Kings II is like the coolest concept for a game I've ever heard, but I just can't commit to playing it.
Stellaris however seems pretty different, so far. I pirated it first to get a feel for it, and it didn't take me long to commit to buying it. I'm having a great time.
The essential premise is that you play a civilisation just as they acquire FTL interstellar travel, and you begin as a single planet to expand and establish a massive interstellar empire. Along the way you'll meet other empires, aliens, the remnants of long-dead precursor civilizations, dangerous void-faring wildlife, pirates, and all kinds of stuff. There's a huge amount of customization room for you to run exactly the kind of empire you want - you can be the Federation from Star Trek, peacefully exploring the galaxy in the name of science and inviting any and all races, species, and creeds into your ranks; or you can be the Imperium of Man from WH40k, sweeping through the galaxy in a blaze of xenos purges and zealotry. You can be classic individualist humans, a collectivist hive-mind of insectoids, pacifist fungal hippies, all kinds of stuff.
The mechanics of the game are sort of a combo of a bunch of concepts - when it comes to managing planets and your economy, they borrowed heavily from the civ series, planting workers on plots with certain resources to add those to your income. Where you see the classic Paradox style is in the diplomacy, combat, and certain niche aspects of empire management. There are a huge amount of mechanics at play here, which is parr for the course for Paradox grand strategy games, but unlike their previous games, Stellaris does a good job of only bringing them up when they're relevant. If you just pick the classic Federation-style human civ, all you have to worry about is defending yourself, managing your economy, and expanding. But if you want to go crazy, you can create a fanatically religious empire, convinced that they must enslave all other races as sentient cattle; juggle warring internal political factions; carefully tip-toe around ancient declining empires with far superior armies and technology; or form galaxy-wide federations with combined arms and mingling populations.
It definitely feels like Paradox have done the best job they ever have of balancing a complex and deep strategy game, with the accessibility that's so necessary for somebody like me to enjoy it. It has a very good tutorial to start with, and unlike Crusader Kings II where you start essentially in medias res, every game of Stellaris starts with you and most other empires having only a single planet under your control.
Overall, it's definitely a recommendation from me, especially if you're like me: you've always wanted to play strategy games, but never found one you could really sink your teeth into. Plus, like all Paradox games, there's amazing potential for roleplaying and creating your own stories.
10/10 Must buy.

This game was a wild ride.
The controls are better than some say, though driving can turn very awkward at times and sometimes helicopter controls downright ignored my inputs and crashed it even if I kept hitting the ‘up’ button. The enemy IA is mediocre at best. Most of them just stand around without covering and shooting at you, though they make up for it by having insane accuracy that makes you yell ‘not fair’ if you’re suddenly surrounded. There’s an absurd amount of exploring available in Stillwater as it’s a huge city with spots where you have to graffiti on, CDs to collect and many kinds of shops sch as restaurants, clothing stores and drive-bys to take out your notoriety. hen, to diversions, those minigames you play for ‘respect’ in order to be allowed to do the main missions. Most of them are fun, others turn horrible. The escort, snatch and insurance fraud are bugged and bothering. Mostly because of the screwed up vehicle collisions and driving and how the game fails to add score if you get hit by a car without having pressed the pratfall button first. Still, the FUZZ and the septic avenger missions were insanely fun (you go around in a truck throwing poop at buildings and people), a shame they were removed in the next games. Last but not least, the main missions: most of them were fun, but involve advancing and killing people through some bosses were interesting, such as the sword battles and the monster truck rally. Still, reminding me of the two generations ago games, this game had THAT mission, insanelty hard to get through that I won't talk about.
The graphics? Eh. This game hasn’t aged well. The textures are off, the character creation would have been a lot better if the faces didn’t all look horrible (reminds me of Oblivion). Then, we hit the meat of the problem: wonky animations. They’re not exaggerated, but ridiculous to look at. The sprint animation is just like the normal running but sped up, which only makes it look weird as if you feet could take little steps very fast. The position while holding guns is the same you would take while holding a book away from you to look at the cover. Surprisingly, the facial expressions are fine and the animation suddenly improves in the cutscenes, which makes me think they mo-caped these to improve the quality.
And lastly, we get to optimization! I played the game in Windows 7, where I ran into no problems mostly because I was lucky enough to have a processor that ran exactly at Xbox360 speed, if not it'd have gotten it weirdly sped up as others have reported. Now, I have been doomed to Windows 8 and this problem curiously doesn't appear even if I'm running now at 3,6gH. Instead, I get constant, unexplainable crashing that renders me unable to play the game because I'm risking it to suddenly close in middle of a mission and you just get angry. A pity, but oh well.
It's still a recommended game if you like sandboxes or just like Saints Row.

3rd person, action, adventure, RPG that follows closely to the storyline of George R. R. Martin's - "Game of Thrones" books. If you read the books or watched the TV series of "Game of Thrones", then you might enjoy it more than those who will go into it blindly, because you will miss the whole story surrounding this fantasy world. Story takes place in the timeline of 1st "Game of Thrones" book.
To not spoil the story, I will only state that characters you play as are not in the books, nor TV show and are made up, but game itself follows the books. You will also hear about and meet many well known characters that appear in the books / TV show.
Moving forward on to the actual game, story is strong, with A LOT of dialogues and choices that will reward or punish you, depending on what you chose. Voice acting is great and includes some voices from the TV show, but not many. You can chose character stats, skills and preferred fighting style, be it shield and 1 hand, two 1 hand, 2 hand or ranged weapons, basically your generic yet somewhat limited RPG.

A great mature RPG.
+ Very good, tight, quite lengthy and powerful story (with a fair amount of twists and multiple endings)
+ Interesting main and side characters
+ Good (sometimes perhaps a little too strict) to very good voice acting (and plenty at that)
+ Nicely written, believable dialogues (there are light dialogue trees too)
+ Thick character and world lore (accessible to people new to GOT by codex/encyclopedia pages ingame)
+ Nice music (composed by the TV show composer, it seems)
+ For fans: Familiar places (King's Landing, The Wall, ...) and cameos (Joer Mormont and Varys have their looks and voices from the TV show)
~ Combat can feel easy/underwhelming for perhaps 1/3 of the game. For some time I was wondering why I should care about what abilities to use even if it's always been fun to do so. Your character automatically attacks a random target or one you choose, with you moving him around if you will or by using active skills that use stamina or have a fixed cooldown. Sometimes my foes stood no chance even if I let my characters just do basic attacks. A few parts aren't winnable for story-reasons. I don't know anymore if you select a difficulty and which one I might have chosen. It got more interesting halfway through when I was able to utilize different skill sets and characters (usually two at a time) at a regular rate (it changes for many parts for story-reasons, which I am welcoming, it shouldn't subjugate to the gameplay mechanics, this game should be mainly about it's characters and the story and it is).
~ Character development/gear usage seems a little strict. Depending on your very first choices in the game your character is set on a rather narrow path regarding the weapons and armor he should use. This can be important later on because there is a "rock, paper, scissors" system in place that encourages you to use specific armor to counter specific enemies and, on the other hand, use specific gear to fight specific enemies. Upon leveling up you can put skill points in other, "unusal" weapon/armor areas but that's not very wise since it requires more points to get those up and you cannot use any skills for weapon sets unfamiliar to your class. So, for example if you choose a class using two-handed weapons and heavy armor in the beginning you will want to stick with just two-handed weapons and heavy armor for many parts even if you should loot or want to buy one-handed and lightly armored gear, and even if you should encounter enemies that use equipment that literally works like scissors to your paper-based gear. You can use everything at any time - but you won't be very effective. Around halfway through you can select a secondary class where things get truly interestings and where you can actually mix things up without feeling like being on a disadvantage.
~ Should you get ideas to fight random mobs to level up unusual/inexperienced areas to redeem for the lacking bonuses/skills: That won't work. Because enemies aren't randomized. Cleared areas won't have enemies spawn unless the story wants to. Not even random brigands or wildlife or something. This can add to the immersion in some ways, for the very least makes post-combat exploration easier (the two main characters have special skills to find hidden objects) and there are plenty of enemies to fight and good numbers of quests to do before you reach the end of the game, and if you stick to the class and thus weapon/armor selections you made early on you'll probably have no serious problems getting through this game. But straying off from these pre-defined leveling paths may leave you very vulnerable later on with no other way to deal with it but bite yourself through it.
~ Combat can be a little mess at times, particularily indoors with the camera not getting a good look on things. Not too dramatic since you have a pause button that almost freezes time when issuing commands, but still. The straightforward/head-on mechanics don't work well if you for example try to shoot someone with a bow from an elevated position as I tried in King's Landing. It would trigger a mass rush of all allied and hostile characters to clash into each other around several corners with my bowman having struggles to follow after.

- Some more face models and clothing may not have hurt. The main and some special side characters aside most other characters can look a little generic, even if they are never really unfitting by looks or voice. It's not too dramatic but more often than not you'll see the pretty much same gown or rags on female characters, at times same faces even, and would have hard times to differ between some side characters if not for their varying names and voice actors.
+ That being said, those characters for which the devs had more love/time for really look nice and impressive, with scars and veins and freckles and such. Overall the game is nicely-looking and very immersive even if it won't sate the high-res texture junkies. And it has a clear and nice interface and runs very stable (thanks to the Unreal Engine, I guess) even if I had some odd mini-freezing when turning the camera around some places but that might be my relatively old system and not the game.

(-) The technical realisation is awful. The fighting system is interesting but gets pretty boring after a few fights. But only in the very late game you have enough gold (and the chance to visit a trader) to buy some legendary stuff.
All in all there are some heavy issues with how the epic story is implemented and it's really sad, because with a little more budget and a little more time this game could have been awesome.
(->) Anyway: I liked the game because of it's great story which made up for all the pain I suffered while playing. I think I won't play it again even if i want to check out some different classes (haven't played the archer yet), but it's just too boring if you know whats going on.
