Without viewing any sort significant gameplay or information before starting the Game of Thrones it became quite an unexpected surprise. If you have a soft spot for these sort of games then I believe this one deserve a humble chance. You will play as two very different characters in different time frames until you reach a point where they will meet in the story. The game offers you a lot of content to read and if you are a fan of the Books or the TV show this will be something you will simply should keep on your radar. There is a vast amount of Lore regarding the cities and the people who live in them, the religion or their beliefs as well, the characters and the different house banners and so on.
There is a lot of talk so I found this game to be very relaxing to play in a nice session after a long, tiresome day. You answer the questions by choosing one of the possible outcomes and they are written in first person. From the main quests to the secondary ones you will be faced with some choices to be made. Some will decide the faith of people, others will let you seek revenge or prove that you are merciful and fair. Expect to be a lot of political games where even when trust is earned you should always suspect everyone, after all, everyone wants their share of wealth. I did some of the secondary quests but not all them. They are mostly focused in side stories and are not boring at all as opposed to those fetch quests where you need to gather ingredients or something similar. Usually, it’s about someone needing help, recruiting members to the Wall, see why someone did something or seek more information that can be useful for you in the future.
The main story is divided in Chapters which offers a great time frame if you just want to play bit here and there. You can start a chapter and be done with it, get some rest and on the next day advance a bit more. I admit that as I was advancing in the game I got surprised more than once for the outcomes I was facing. This is Game of Thrones so you should always expecting deaths from those you love or care while playing the game. Trust no one and remember to not follow only your heart as you might be betrayed for being too gentle.
The combat is slower than any other similar RPG but it can be tactic as well during combat you can open your Abilities wheel and select what moves or skills you want to do. The game won’t fully stop but you will enter in a very slow motion giving you time to make the best strategy for your enemies. Different weapons are good or bad depending on what sort of armor your enemy is wearing. A heavy armor is resistant to swords since it can’t be pierced but are weaker to blunt weapons so pay attention to this in order to end the combat quicker.
The way healing works is also very creative in my opinion. You can get some flasks but they will be empty. Then, you will have to go to a store who sell potions in order to fill them with what you desire. You can fill them with poison, oil in order to burn your enemies and other healing herbs and medicine like the famous milk of the poppy. You can replace already filled bottles with other things if you desire. This is crucial for some harder fights and will help you in the long run.
The voice acting however is very poor, especially in the sad or dramatic scenes. During certain critical events I really tried to let myself get immersed by the things that were happening but the poor voice acting broke the immersion I was trying to achieve. That often used moment of “Noooooo!” is rather embarrassing and anger, sadness or fury moments are not strong enough to make some scenes more believable. It’s a shame because a game with such emphasis on story elements you really want to feel the tension you witness when watching the TV series or when reading the books but I’m afraid that sometimes this simply won’t do. You will notice some voices from the show like Varys the Spider but even with familiar voices, as soon other characters start to talk in a more emotional sense it won’t feel immersive. As for the normal and non-emotional conversations I believe it’s more than doable.
The visuals are also nothing to be amazed but this did not bother me at all. I played the game at 1080p and while it’s nothing to be stunned about I noticed some really nice details like when you are carrying a shield in your back and you see the scratches in it or the reflections of the sun in that golden lion shield from the Lannisters. While this is not a game to be played for the visuals I also saw my fair share of people trespassing doors, my dog getting his head between the iron of gates and other small glitches. Nothing game breaking, you just see that it’s something that could have been more polished. Because it’s in the deep of the lore that you will find the bigger satisfaction I ended up ignoring these small technical issues and I focused on my decisions, the stories and most of all, the outcomes based on what I said or done.
If you are a fan of the theme then I believe this game deservers a fair chance. It took me around 20 hours to finish (one of) the endings and I know there’s some replay value if you wish to see a different ending in the last couple of chapters.

Despite that, with a lot of patience, trial and error and tweaking I finally made it work and I have to recognize it is a great game. Besides that the game has a great variety of units, decent graphics, most of the important historical figures and many character skills that give more depth to the grand strategy aspect of the game (just don't expect it to be like Hearts of Iron or any of the other hardcore strategy games).

In a nutshell: it is a fun "Total War" style game set between WW1-WW2, definitely worth the buy.

I'm really divided on this game. Deadly Premonition stars you as an FBI agent investigating a murder in a countryside town. It is intriguing, cheesy and witty all at the same time. An amusing storyline that is quite easy to get into, and is certainly worth playing through.
However, there are so many things wrong with the game; Technical issues are paramount. Enemy hitboxes don't seem to align very well, making combat sluggish. Aiming with weapons is slow and clunky, driving is tedious, with NPCs driving about 15mph even on main roads!
But the main problem with the game, is even with fanpatches, it just simply isn't stable enough. The game crashes relentlessly, sometimes because it screws up loading an area, sometimes because it decides cutscenes are too much hassle, other times because it just doesn't want to work anymore.
You need to save religiously just to get through the story alone. I've clocked 25ish hours on Steam, however my in-game save file is a mere 11hours at time of writing. That's 14 hours of progress lost from crashes, requiring me to re-load a save and go through it again.
Worth it? Absolutely not. Not even on sale. You need to be a die hard for cheesy detective stories to even bother with this, and I admit, it is a fun and cute story, but you need to put in a hell of a lot of work just to get through it, and for most people, that simply isn't worthwhile.

This is the only game I have ever reviewed but holy hell this game is amazing. This review is current up to the v1.6.2 patch and is subject to lots of change and improvement. It has its weak points so I'll just shoot off that small list first.
Ground combat - It’s pretty bland and has no interaction outside of army set up.
Diplomacy - Cut and dry with very few options outside of your standard 4x games, Federation system needs major improvement outside of “Has a big military”.
Espionage - There is none. The major flaw with Ethics being such a huge part of the game; having nearly no way for less militant empires to directly change Ethics in a rival or neighboring country.
Now with that being said this game’s shine vastly outweighs its current flaws.  If you consider yourself a world builder, or someone who loves to become immersed and encounter almost endless replayability this is nothing short of a treasure trove for you to have hours of your life sucked into. This game really gives you the ability to play out any sci-fi fantasy story you may have thought of. The ability to customize a vast amount of variables; Ranging from the genetic traits of your species to what type of FTL travel physics will allow for in this galaxy. All of this before you even begin the game. Once you begin the game the entire galaxy is procedurally generated with the parameters you defined and fills in ones you didn’t. It allows for endless stories to be formed around when, how, and who you are when you react to a situation.
The best part of this game is the community, both the players, modders, and developers are quite invested. Patches coming in often to respond to community request, a massive modding community (With overhaul mods for Star Wars, Star Trek, and more), and a large player base full of discussion about the game. We all know paradox has a history with DLC content...but I have been pleasantly surprised by this game. Almost every DLC pack has been well worth the money. The story packs such as leviathan and utopia are an immediate buy. They add so much content. All in all 9.9/10
TLDR: Buy this game...just...do it.

Stellaris is an amazing grand strategy game set in space that you can get a lot of enjoyment out of. From wiping out entire civilizations, to making large federtions to quell a dangerous foe, and even conquering the world through vassalizations.
The first time I played this war around may of last year. I chose to be a fanatic materialist and individualist human science directorate. I was quite well of by 2400, I had 25% of the galaxy under me. I had the cutting edge technology and a fleet to rival a fallen empire and then some. Unbenownst to me (since I didn't care to explore the area for a long time) there was a xenophobic fallen empire along one of my expanding borders. They told me that I wasn't welcome to colonize near their borders, but I shrugged it off. After all, I had a fleet that was roughly their strength. Twenty years later, I started to colonize close to their border --  ignoring their request --  and they demanded that I leave my colony at once. I was outraged! No alien could tell me what to do! So I refused their offer and sixth months later they finally declared war upon me. It raged on for five years, with me only taking one planet. While sieging their capital, the unbidden (who I didn't know a wealth about) event started. I didn't think anything of it, but a while later I recieved a transmission stating they sensed food, and that I was it. I moved my main fleets to take out the unbidden who were on the other side of my empire, and had my small vassal patrol the Fallen Empire. The unbidden sent wave after wave of fleets at me, utterly killing my fleets. I was facing a battle on two fronts, with no hope of victory. Much to my suprise the Fallen Empire started to battle to unbidden after a whole sector of mine was wiped out. The fallen took severe losses, but managed to kill the majority, leaving only a few scattered ships. A couple years later, I finally won the war against the Fallen Empire, taking a planet in the process.
I've had many more exciting games of Stellaris, but this is just a taste of what can happen in one game.

My favourite new release game in 2017. The gameplay is varied, consisting mostly of third person behind the character dodge/combo based action, often switching to a 2D plane, and has occasional 2D shoot 'em up sections. The melee combat is phenomenal; slick, fluid, and skilful. The visuals and design of everything is excellent. The soundtrack is inspired, probably one of the best soundtracks that'll come out this year. The characters are endearing and the story is impactful. I don't want to give anything away, but the story frequently surprises you in its execution and presentation. Some of the plot threads are never resolved, unfortunately. However it does explore some interesting themes, using its medium uniquely to convey its story and a philosophy that is endearingly optimistic.
It does have some minor issues. It could have used larger or more environments as the mid to late game spreads its content over previously explored areas. Difficulty could use some tweaking; normal difficulty rarely feels like a challenge, yet hard is incredibly punishing. Sidequest design is bland, with numerous fetch quests that make you return to previously explored areas. The 2D shoot 'em up parts feel slightly anaemic, with few enemy types and overly simple bullet patterns and enemy placement. From the midgame, the melee combat often takes a backseat to a hacking mechanic, which isn't as fun. However these flaws stick out in an otherwise excellent game.
Unfortunately, I can't not mention the technical issues. This is a terrible port. It runs at subnative resolution in fullscreen, various graphical settings such as antialiasing are broken by graphical settings such as ambient occlusion, cutscenes and user interface elements are stretched on anything other than a 16:9 monitor, the game often stutters and pauses for a second, and the game commonly crashes. The publisher seems to be disinterested in fixing these issues; despite the game being on sale for months, no patch has been released. Thankfully, most of these issues can be fixed using third party tools like the FAR mod and Vidsquish. But it's shameful that these tools, which were released within a very short period post release are necessary. There's a great game here and it's a waste to have it let down by shoddy porting and a complete lack of post release support.

Anodyne is small indie game that will no doubt, and rightfully so, draw comparisons to the age old classic The Legend of Zelda. The gameplay is virtually identical featuring 2D graphics, similar combat, and puzzles. All that makes you wonder if you should actually play Anodyne instead of just playing Zelda, and frankly the answer to that is yes. While Anodyne is very similar gameplay wise, it really shines in aesthetic and the weird world it creates. The setting is one entirely of its own and it does surreal in a skillful way not often seen in video games. The story is also better than anything a Zelda game could ever offer by benefit of having an actual writer, though it can tend to wax philosophically which may not be everyone's cup of tea. It's not a long game so if you're fan of the original Zeldas, I'd wholeheartedly reccomend it.

Saint's Row 2 is an exciting, hilarious over-the-top crime simulator set in the fictional city of Stilwater.  You play as the boss of the gang, the Third Street Saints.  Following the explosive events in the previous game, you awake in a prison hospital.  Eventually you escape, and set about rebuilding your tattered gang.  Your objective is to eliminate the competing gangs that have moved in in your absense.  You'll also gring with Ultor, a mega corporation that has major gentrification plans for the city.
Before you can make moves on the various story missions, you need to build up respect by partaking in various activities around the city, such as insurance fraud (play in traffic!), mayhem (blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up!) or heli assault (blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up in the air!).  As you complete activities you gain respect 'levels' which act as sort of currency.  Playing a story mission costs a level of respect.    Many of the activities are a lot of fun, and there are more than enough that you can generally focus on the ones you enjoy most.  Plus, you get upgrades for completing all the levels of each activity, such as unlimited stamina, damage reduction, or unlimited ammo for various weapon types.
Unfortunately, the PC port of Saint's Row 2 is sloppy.  You may need some third party tools to help reign in some of the shoddy issues that plague it.  I suggest looking up the PC Gaming Wiki for support for various issues.
If you can get past the sloppy porting, you'll find taking over Stilwater to be a good time.  Thanks to mouse aiming in the PC version, the combat is fairly easy.  You'll probably find yourself dying more often to glitches or getting run down by gang cars that spawn nearby.  Mission variety is decent, including various on-rails shooting sections, vehicle chases, protection jobs and good old fashioned shooting dudes in the face.
The graphics generally don't hold up well but they're passable.  You'll see quite a bit of pop-in as you travel around the city.  I suggest turning off HDR lighting, it adds ridiculous amounts of bloom and makes it look like someone smeared your screen with vasoline.  Despite middling graphics, there are some intense, over-the-top cutscene events throughout the game.  The writing is witty and the voice acting is excellent.  Sound effects are generally boring, but adequate.  The soundtrack is hit or miss, depending on your tastes.

I'm a little thick sometimes.  When I first bought SHoDN during the summer sale, I played it about three times and I didn't get it.  There wasn't a lot of explanation to the game and with the over stimulation that the summer sale brings, I didn't have the attention span to sit down and give it a chance.  I wound up shutting the game down, vaguely wondering if I wasted $3 and proceeded to waste my time in other things.
Cut to three weeks later, I see people talking about SHoDN on the forums a lot and I figure I paid $3 for it; I might as well give it a shot.  The first time through, I thought the keyboard controls were a little cumbersome but I was starting to understand the game concept; score points, extend your time, get us far down the tower as you can. Seemed solid, it was starting to sink its claws in.
Later that morning, I was messaged by someone on my friends list, urging me to submit my scores so they had somebody to compete against on the leader boards.  I hadn't even realized there were leaderboards, so I played through again and submitted.  That's when the claws sunk in even deeper; competing against your friend’s high scores is super addictive.  I figured I was in there, so I started clicking around in the menus and that's when I discovered that there's controller support in SHoDN!  Around this time, a game I thought I might have wasted my money on turned into a full on addiction.
SHoDN is dead simple in concept, but with challenging maps and tight controls it turns into a great little time attack platformer.  It's difficult in all the right ways and its design of getting ever farther down the tower, combined with trying to outscore your friends list makes it a game you'll return to.  It’s simple nature makes it a perfect fit for those times when you want 10 minutes of distraction instead of 3 hours of character development, but there's a strong chance it's going to suck you into that dreaded, "just one more try" state of mind.

Concerning the crashing.
Bugs are one thing, but crashes are an entirely more disgusting beast. The game routinely crashes anywhere from 20-40 minutes of play, which means that in my 20 hours so far it has crashed upwards of 40 times. It can crash at any point completely randomly, so you cannot mitigate this in any way.
Crucially, the game will not let you save during chapter replays, which are needed to complete several side quests, so you will undoubtedly have to redo large sections of the game many, many times to progress.
The DPFix mod you can download online cleans up the graphics and seems to reduce the amount of crashes, but does not completely eliminate them.
Add to this a known game-breaking bug concerning item disappearances that forces you to restart the entire game from the beginning, a wealth of technical issues, long loading times, and poor PC optimization means you should stay far away from this port.
I will say this though: if you aren't much of a completionist and just wish to experience the main story, you can save regularly throughout the campaign and mostly ignore the open world, which will mean that the crashes will affect you a bit less. Having said that, some of the most useful items in the game (including the entire fast travel system) are unlocked through side quests, so they are pretty essential for anyone not wanting to spend too much time wrestling with the game's atrocious driving physics. I would suggest using a guide to seek these few items out early on in the campaign and then ignoring the rest of the filler material. (The side quests are mostly awful anyway: incidental to the plot, hard to find without a guide, and requiring lots of wasted time manipulating the game's time passage and weather mechanics to make certain NPCs appear.)
If you have a PS3, I would still recommend checking the game out on a more stable platform. Or hell, just watch a cutscene compilation online and save yourself the hassle of actually playing the damn thing. It would be disingenuous to call this a "good" game, but no one is expecting that at this point. We all know it's a quirky B-game that is borderline unplayable. My standards aren't high, and I'm willing to forgive how bad the foundation is because the world, story, and characters are pretty interesting.
But the game needs to run. This port, unfortunately, is in a completely unacceptable state and should frankly be pulled from the Steam store.
But as we all know, Steam Quality Control isn't a thing that exists.
*******************************************************************************************************
ADDENDUM: Concerning the story.
Usually when I neg a game, my review gets negged in turn, so thank you for all of the positive feedback.
When I wrote my initial review, it was strictly to call out the technical issues. However, if any of you are still on the fence because you feel like you still may get a decent story experience despite the technical apocalypse, I thought I would write a quick spoiler-free addendum about the plot and give you further reason to avoid the game. This is at the risk of contradicting my earlier statement that the story is interesting, but what we have here is an example of a well-written journey with a flat payoff.
There are many examples in modern fiction where the plot twists can be unpredictable because they are poorly crafted. Deadly Premonition is one such example. You are very unlikely to construct the game's full plot in your mind before the final act's sequence of revelations lays it bare, but this doesn't mean that the game was smarter than you.
Whodunnits are tough to write, since any astute gamer will have processed every character at least once as a potential suspect, and thus actual surprise needs to be very clever. The way this game deflects suspicion is by essentially creating two different culprits: the one you interact with, and the true self.
This is immediately apparent in the voice acting: the pre- and post-twist voices are delivered completely differently, as if the actor had been hired for two separate games. This is problematic because deranged sociopaths and serial killers will usually exhibit some form of their identity when interacting with other people, but Deadly Premonition is straight out of the 90s Scream-style horror playbook - you cannot begin to suspect anybody because the liars so perfectly masquerade as normal people.
Although most characterization is shallow, there is still some really good writing here...for a video game. But dialogue and plot are two different things, and it's in the plot where the game flounders.
It's frustrating because there is no cathartic wide-eyed moment where you realize you've been hoodwinked by clever plot construction. Instead, it's as if characters you scratched off your suspect list long ago suddenly become different people, and the resulting reaction is something along the lines of, "Oh, I guess this person is a bad guy now." In fact, you may wind up crafting more elaborate theories about what's going on due to the sheer amount of mysteries involved, whereas the truth is much less exciting.
It doesn't help that the plot winds up having holes you could fly a 747 through. There are several discrepancies between the evidence you collect and the end result, and many of the clues remain unexplained at the end. Furthermore, there are many tenuous backstory elements that just don't make any sense - unrelated characters portrayed together in scenes without any context to explain their proximity, and a macguffin that serves two discrepant functions.
Psychological thrillers are at their best when examining the characters' mindstates and developing them as complex individuals. Deadly Premonition's one saving grace is that your player character is very interesting, almost to the point where he is able to carry the entire game and lift it from the dregs of pulp fiction. The game's final act incorporates his own backstory and psyche into the plot in an organic way, and it's safe to say that the moments where we are exploring him are where the storytelling is at its best. Unfortunately, it's not enough to hang a 20-40 hour bad game on (depending on the number of side quests and crashes you experience, of course), and the supporting cast of characters do nothing to deepen the plot's complexity. It's a shame - had every character been as well developed as the lead, we might have had something truly special here.
I feel like I could only recommend a playthrough to those who study games as an artform, rather than those seeking to be entertained (i.e. most of us). And even then, I would strongly encourage those few to seek out the PS3 version and avoid the incessant crashes.

Anodyne is a very fun, and sufficiently lengthy Legend of Zelda-like fantasy adventure game.  However, don't expect an ending that explains anything of the story nor wraps up tight very many loose ends. I'm sure, however, there are plenty of fans out there who will attempt to defend the game by claiming that this unfinished ending is meant to be cryptic somehow and you make of it what you will.  I simply say to that, were that the case, I still consider it a lazy way to not finish what you started.  So then, fun gameplay and lots of interesting secrets to find if you like Zelda clones, well-made and great story up to a point just when it begins to feel unfinished.  Real stinker of an ending when it could have easily been very epic.  I still recommend it to play through once and only once for anyone.

This game is a slightly terrifying and realistic representation of war. Hearing the screams of your squadmates as they die of napalm, throwing my hands off the keyboard and mouse after the first time getting shot in the head and suddenly all is black, trying in general not to die while still being useful and then you just end up being a lowly body just to take a point that seconds later gets blasted by artillery. All of this makes a shooter that I feel represents how terrifying war can really be. As for the game itself, it is fairly balenced, runs well, controls well, looks beautiful, and though you might die a lot the game is never unfair and even the least skilled of players can serve as bodies on points that make them useful. The game is in its infancy and has many glitches, and unlike similar games like Battlefield and CoD the team is smaller making those glitches far more likely to stick around for a bit, expect the game to crash every now and then. Even with the crashes though it is worth the play in my opinion. Rising Storm 1 was great, and Rising Storm 2 just improved on it. 9/10 Easily my favorite FPS.

When call of duty and battlefield strayed from their path - the rising storm series takes a turn for realism. I just hope they don't stray as well in the future. If someone would ask me why I prefer this game to most multiplayer fps out there like counter-strike global offensive (mind you I was an LEM once I was actually good at fps) or the aforementioned franchises above, it's because this game, Rising Storm 2: Vietnam actually requires team work. People actually lead and follow in this game. And with that context it amazes me how people with so much diversity due to the difference in country, faith, culture and language among the sorts come into one and work together to win and say "GO HOME GI".
More Battlefield than Red Orchestra, this game is a step in the wrong direction.

I liked this game at first. I think it had great potential. But I can't give this a recommendation. Here is why:
The pros:
1) It can be quite fun watching your empire of lemonade stands grow. The game has some nice moments like when your lemonade stands suddenly become more profitable than your oil rigs and you start shifting your investments.
2) The game actually tells you when you are about to over spend on angels (the currency that stays after resetting the game) which I haven't seen in other clicker games. That means you don't have to look up guides or anything to play this game.
The cons:
1) Inconsistency between mobile and PC versions. In the beginning this was my biggest gripe with the game. On mobile you get a 2x boost on all your profits for watching an ad (or rather setting the phone down for 25 seconds until the awful ad is done plaing). There is no such thing on the PC version. This makes playing on PC incredibly slower. Like by a mile slower. Like I started on pc and mobile at the same time but on PC I'm not even close to where I was weeks ago with the mobile version. Thats how much of a difference it makes. But don't even bother playing on mobile. The performance of the mobile app is abysmal. It runs so poorly that it will often not count your idle profits, leaving you with nothing after days of waiting.
2) Greed. This wasn't so apparent at first but it became pretty clear after the moon was introduced. This game is not like other idle clicker games where you may have slow progress but progress none the less. Adventure Capitalist will slow to a halt if you don't decide to pay money for boosts. You will go weeks on the moon without ANY progress. There is no way of aquiring the in game gold currency needed to buy these boosts without paying money or attending events that only happen for a limited time period and after that are not open for play anymore. The developer really wants you to pay money for this.

Given that I've been able to beat this game on Normal and a Hard run encompasses beating the whole thing without losing all your lives once (Normal supplies continues) I can safely say that I've played enough of SHDN to give it a recommendation.
You're a ninja. Your mission is to make it to the bottom of a monstrous tower owned by the local demon lord. You heard me right, the bottom. You move very quickly, you attack very quickly, you die very quickly. The game also ends very quickly and can be finished within six or seven minutes if you really practice and speedrun the hell out of it. Every time you take a hit, you lose a life but instantly respawn where you were smacked. Run out of lives and you can continue, on normal. On hard if you run out of lives the game's over. But thankfully after beating a boss a third of the way down the tower, you have a continue point if you wish to play again, making a whole tower (~350 floors, that's actually not as bad as that sounds) run optional.
If you've noticed the awesomely outragous title yet, you'd be reminded of older games, maybe for the SNES. That's where the charm jumps in. Super House of Dead Ninjas is a side scroller platforming game with an emphasis on speed and difficulty, very much from older games. The game even comes with a handy dandy hint comic book which you can read if you feel like the game needs some story. You should also read it because it'll teach you some tricks that will allow you to actually survive your decent. And give you a free unlockable item. I usually don't like retro-esque games, but Super House of Dead Ninjas not only has a lot of charm, but uses the retro feel for more of an atmospheric effect rather than making it its main feature (see: Evoland) and it truly benefits from it (the game even slows down when a lot of action happens at once, a quick breather for us normal folk but if it's truly obnoxious you can turn it off in the options menu).
For $7 the game offers a ton of replayability and is perfect for those who desire something incredibly challenging in their gaming experience. Even if you finish the tower on Hard, there are still two randomly generated inifite towers to explore if you really feel like you have to show off. For those who would like to try before buying it, you can play the original version on Adult Swim's website. If you're still on the edge, wait for a sale. You won't be disappointed.

Do you want to manage surprisingly-sparse resources with unfriendly and broken menus over a time period that covers 2 world wars? If yes, you might enjoy this game. I've heard a great deal about Aggression's depth, and even with my limited playtime I managed to experience some of it.
However, to say Aggression is an unfriendly game is an understatement. While not the buggiest game I've played, Aggression is prone to crashes. The tutorial is easily broken, but this is actually due to poor design rather than poor code. Multitudes of information windows are lacking important information or hold no information at all. In game objectives suffer from the same bad design as the tutorial, ensuring they are far too easy to fail (if you don't have, say, an exact number of troops exactly close enough to reach an out of the way area of the map by a very short deadline).
I don't usually play large-scale strategy games, so perhaps when I say resources were uncomfortably limited I mean that it would take an expert or a person willing to fail over and over to really learn the ins and outs. I never had enough resources to feel comfortable with the economy, and I set all of my cities to auto-construct to compensate. Unfortunately, if your not invading or managing your cities, you really don't have much to do beside moving your ministers around (your ministers effectively being agents of your will). The most interesting part of the game is therefore management, but as I said many features and windows are either poorly explained or missing information completely, so you really have to research outside the game to figure out what it all means.
Combat is the weakest point of Aggression. The AI is some of the worst I've ever seen, and while the enemy can usually figure out how to kill you, your own units will struggle simply to follow your orders without getting slaughtered or running in front of tanks. This means that the second game mode, "Missions," which consists only of combat, is entirely a waste of time. the campaign mode, the only real mode, features an auto-resolve button that should be used unless you're confident of overwhelming superiority or have put in the time to figure out how to abuse the system.

what is the game about?
you play as one of 4 countries (russia, france, germany, britain) in europe between 1910-1945. You play on a strategic map, where you can build units and buildings, manage your cities and population and explore technologies, which range from the first to the end of the second world war.

Surprisingly it's not as bad as people make it out to be but I do understand what people mean when they mock certain features of this game. I also do agree the price is a bit high but it does include DLC so at least when it goes on sale I highly recommend grabbing it (as I did).
There are some generally fine features in the game such as the actual RPG elements (you even get the feel your choices matter), the story is interesting and gives that whole Game of Thrones vibe many seek from this game (also I think even people who have not read any books or watch the series can play and enjoy this) and voice acting is overall very good but some characters do seem to suffer from the monotone book reader syndrome. What comes to graphics they're pretty decent but just like any good features mentioned above they do lose to many other games if you start to compare.
I also do think some of the features are quite unique such as your characters special skills (hard to explain but you can use a dog for tracking for example). I haven't completed the game and I'm writing this review after 3 hours (2 chapters) so I'm not sure what to say to the claims on the game being too short but I personally like how you switch between main characters every now and then.
Now like said, I also do understand why some people don't like the game much: it's whole battle system is quite flawed and very tedious especially for the veteran players who can compared it to better systems. It's mediocre and typical skill system (minus the mentioned special skills) doesn't seem to help the situation much either. You do get a lot of choice in weapon types but it can be more confusing than fun as many weapons are not labeled as they should be (this is merely my personal opinion). I also think how you select your attacks in battle feel very much like if you're playing a online flash game of sorts and that cheapens it a lot. I can tell they did try think out of the box but instead of getting out of the box they just jumped into anothert one.
But like mentioned above, I do recommend this game (especially for GoT fans and others who love a good story) if you can grab it from a sale because while many including myself enjoy the game... it IS very mediocre in this sea of modern RPG games you can pick from and the chance you can't overcome it's tedious system is quite high.

Revelations is a great mix of classic survival horror atmosphere and modern third-person shooter gunplay, combining the best of both worlds with only a handful of the drawbacks. As a bonus, it also has a strangely addictive additional looter game mode.
Resident Evil: Revelations was the game many older RE fans dreamed of, where the classic survival horror aspects of the early games meet the modern, user-friendly mechanics of the later ones.
The level design is an obvious callback to the early Resident Evils. Not only this is the third RE game placed on a ship, but also it manages to evoke the old RE1 atmosphere with some posh, spacious rooms and many narrow corridors with their infinite possibilities of running into a blind corner.
The controls are a variation of the third-person shooter style from RE5, but simplified to fit Revelation’s handheld roots. On PC, it is fast, responsive, and easy to learn, but it has some tricky mechanics (like dodges), which may be difficult to master.
The quintessential RE experience is not complete without some low-grade writing, and this is where RER1 went all-out. The conspiracy-ridden plot, goofy characters, and especially the cheesy dialogue and hammy acting create a perfect B-movie feeling, even if some may feel it too stupid sometimes.
Like in most old RE games, the campaign is short (3-7 hours), even if it offers some good replay value with a challenging difficulty option and a nice weapon upgrade system (where you have to search for additional parts instead of using a store).
Still, this would have not been enough for that final score, and this is where Raid mode comes up. It is an additional game mode, replacing Mercenaries, where the goal is to complete small combat stages for experience, money, and random loot drops. It is practically a Diablo/Borderlands style looter minigame with some addictive mechanics, offering dozens/hundreds of hours of additional fun (and quite some mindless grinding towards the end).

Concerning the crashing.
Bugs are one thing, but crashes are an entirely more disgusting beast. The game routinely crashes anywhere from 20-40 minutes of play, which means that in my 20 hours so far it has crashed upwards of 40 times. It can crash at any point completely randomly, so you cannot mitigate this in any way.
Crucially, the game will not let you save during chapter replays, which are needed to complete several side quests, so you will undoubtedly have to redo large sections of the game many, many times to progress.
The DPFix mod you can download online cleans up the graphics and seems to reduce the amount of crashes, but does not completely eliminate them.
Add to this a known game-breaking bug concerning item disappearances that forces you to restart the entire game from the beginning, a wealth of technical issues, long loading times, and poor PC optimization means you should stay far away from this port.
I will say this though: if you aren't much of a completionist and just wish to experience the main story, you can save regularly throughout the campaign and mostly ignore the open world, which will mean that the crashes will affect you a bit less. Having said that, some of the most useful items in the game (including the entire fast travel system) are unlocked through side quests, so they are pretty essential for anyone not wanting to spend too much time wrestling with the game's atrocious driving physics. I would suggest using a guide to seek these few items out early on in the campaign and then ignoring the rest of the filler material. (The side quests are mostly awful anyway: incidental to the plot, hard to find without a guide, and requiring lots of wasted time manipulating the game's time passage and weather mechanics to make certain NPCs appear.)
If you have a PS3, I would still recommend checking the game out on a more stable platform. Or hell, just watch a cutscene compilation online and save yourself the hassle of actually playing the damn thing. It would be disingenuous to call this a "good" game, but no one is expecting that at this point. We all know it's a quirky B-game that is borderline unplayable. My standards aren't high, and I'm willing to forgive how bad the foundation is because the world, story, and characters are pretty interesting.
But the game needs to run. This port, unfortunately, is in a completely unacceptable state and should frankly be pulled from the Steam store.
But as we all know, Steam Quality Control isn't a thing that exists.
*******************************************************************************************************
ADDENDUM: Concerning the story.
Usually when I neg a game, my review gets negged in turn, so thank you for all of the positive feedback.
When I wrote my initial review, it was strictly to call out the technical issues. However, if any of you are still on the fence because you feel like you still may get a decent story experience despite the technical apocalypse, I thought I would write a quick spoiler-free addendum about the plot and give you further reason to avoid the game. This is at the risk of contradicting my earlier statement that the story is interesting, but what we have here is an example of a well-written journey with a flat payoff.
There are many examples in modern fiction where the plot twists can be unpredictable because they are poorly crafted. Deadly Premonition is one such example. You are very unlikely to construct the game's full plot in your mind before the final act's sequence of revelations lays it bare, but this doesn't mean that the game was smarter than you.
Whodunnits are tough to write, since any astute gamer will have processed every character at least once as a potential suspect, and thus actual surprise needs to be very clever. The way this game deflects suspicion is by essentially creating two different culprits: the one you interact with, and the true self.
This is immediately apparent in the voice acting: the pre- and post-twist voices are delivered completely differently, as if the actor had been hired for two separate games. This is problematic because deranged sociopaths and serial killers will usually exhibit some form of their identity when interacting with other people, but Deadly Premonition is straight out of the 90s Scream-style horror playbook - you cannot begin to suspect anybody because the liars so perfectly masquerade as normal people.
Although most characterization is shallow, there is still some really good writing here...for a video game. But dialogue and plot are two different things, and it's in the plot where the game flounders.
It's frustrating because there is no cathartic wide-eyed moment where you realize you've been hoodwinked by clever plot construction. Instead, it's as if characters you scratched off your suspect list long ago suddenly become different people, and the resulting reaction is something along the lines of, "Oh, I guess this person is a bad guy now." In fact, you may wind up crafting more elaborate theories about what's going on due to the sheer amount of mysteries involved, whereas the truth is much less exciting.
It doesn't help that the plot winds up having holes you could fly a 747 through. There are several discrepancies between the evidence you collect and the end result, and many of the clues remain unexplained at the end. Furthermore, there are many tenuous backstory elements that just don't make any sense - unrelated characters portrayed together in scenes without any context to explain their proximity, and a macguffin that serves two discrepant functions.
Psychological thrillers are at their best when examining the characters' mindstates and developing them as complex individuals. Deadly Premonition's one saving grace is that your player character is very interesting, almost to the point where he is able to carry the entire game and lift it from the dregs of pulp fiction. The game's final act incorporates his own backstory and psyche into the plot in an organic way, and it's safe to say that the moments where we are exploring him are where the storytelling is at its best. Unfortunately, it's not enough to hang a 20-40 hour bad game on (depending on the number of side quests and crashes you experience, of course), and the supporting cast of characters do nothing to deepen the plot's complexity. It's a shame - had every character been as well developed as the lead, we might have had something truly special here.
I feel like I could only recommend a playthrough to those who study games as an artform, rather than those seeking to be entertained (i.e. most of us). And even then, I would strongly encourage those few to seek out the PS3 version and avoid the incessant crashes.

Stellaris is an amazing grand strategy game set in space that you can get a lot of enjoyment out of. From wiping out entire civilizations, to making large federtions to quell a dangerous foe, and even conquering the world through vassalizations.
The first time I played this war around may of last year. I chose to be a fanatic materialist and individualist human science directorate. I was quite well of by 2400, I had 25% of the galaxy under me. I had the cutting edge technology and a fleet to rival a fallen empire and then some. Unbenownst to me (since I didn't care to explore the area for a long time) there was a xenophobic fallen empire along one of my expanding borders. They told me that I wasn't welcome to colonize near their borders, but I shrugged it off. After all, I had a fleet that was roughly their strength. Twenty years later, I started to colonize close to their border --  ignoring their request --  and they demanded that I leave my colony at once. I was outraged! No alien could tell me what to do! So I refused their offer and sixth months later they finally declared war upon me. It raged on for five years, with me only taking one planet. While sieging their capital, the unbidden (who I didn't know a wealth about) event started. I didn't think anything of it, but a while later I recieved a transmission stating they sensed food, and that I was it. I moved my main fleets to take out the unbidden who were on the other side of my empire, and had my small vassal patrol the Fallen Empire. The unbidden sent wave after wave of fleets at me, utterly killing my fleets. I was facing a battle on two fronts, with no hope of victory. Much to my suprise the Fallen Empire started to battle to unbidden after a whole sector of mine was wiped out. The fallen took severe losses, but managed to kill the majority, leaving only a few scattered ships. A couple years later, I finally won the war against the Fallen Empire, taking a planet in the process.
I've had many more exciting games of Stellaris, but this is just a taste of what can happen in one game.

cons - combat is tedious (like CK2) you click on their ships and whoever has the biggest number GENERALLY wins. Not always but about 95% the time. For a while I've been looking for good grand strategy game since I sort of fell out with the Total War series. I loved that serie when it was sandbox rather than a lineair open world so my fav Total War game is Medieval 2.
After a bunch of reviews and youtube videos I settled on Stellaris and I'm honestly not disappointed. Being an avid gamer I would say that the game values between €35 and €45. it just misses the mark to be an AAA title. Overall it's a good game and I'm happy that I bought it.
Graphics
+ there's alot of detail and given the different varieties and combat looks great.
- Since they want to render every little bit as is, with the current optimization, a fleet of over 200 ships stutters here and there and 500+ fleet almost completely freeze up when entering combat. I'm not sure this is a graphics rendering issue it could be they're doing to many calculations for each individual ship to fire at who with what and so on but the FPS just drops badly. Especially since the game is now over a year old this should have really been adressed.
Feel
+ The game feels great to play the controls are easy and the learning curve is fine. The tutorial is very total war like (i.e. no training just a sodding msword paperclip like thingy that tries to explain stuff) which is ok. I have no real need for it personally and building an extensive tutorial would not be the focus I want to the developers to have. I experienced no problems in navigating through the various menus at all and the feel of it is one of the best features imho.
Combat
+ for a passive combat setup it's ok
- It's way too passive for my taste. I don't think it's necessary to give it the influence that you have in total war combat, but it needs some of it. I take that back it needs alot of it. You don't even see what range your ships have, no formations, no tactics NOTHING. you just dump your fleet on the other and then you wait until all the pretty lasers stop shooting.
- You can't ask allied fleets for help, steer them in any way so aside from what you do there's no tactics surrounding the direct combat either.
Politics
+- Are strange at best. It works fine but there are some stupid mechanics and some omissions so it misses both finesse and detail. However it's on par with most grand strategy games so it's not really a letdown in that sense.
Ships
+ There's only 4 combat ships but they're customizable. There is a good variety of weapons you can fit to each ship and in the end you can probably use every weapon in game because you looted parts of enemy detroyed ships. There a good rock paper scissors goin on with range, tracking, good/bad vs shields armor etc. Every ship has 3 customizable sets offense, defense and utility. The utility groups lineair upgradable but still selectable. The offense slots have prearranged ships sections (bow, stern etc) and you select the layout of those so this is pretty well done.
- Small let down is that the defenseive slot config comes with the offensive slot config and thus has no variation whatsoever.
Replayability / Longevity
There comes a point in these type of games where, while far from victory, it's no longer a matter of 'if' but 'when' due to superior resources etc. After that the game is more of a chore since you have to use 0 effort to win. Annoyingly, you cannot take more than about 12 systems per war since there's a set cap on warscore rather than a dynamic cap, I can't really be arsed to finish a single campaign. takes maybe 50+ hours to get to that point and more on the first attempt, but that's about it. PLEASE note that this is a generic problem with grand strategy games in general, i.e. it's not a negative point but also not something this game fixed or so.
AI
Is pretty dimwitted. Not completely clueless but that's about it. It should be alot better to make the game difficult as it really is too easy. (NB: If you are now thinking I should increase the difficulty that you misunderstand; any difficulty setting would just increase enemy aggresiveness and fleet numbers, not wit or tactics)
Bugs:
Not sure if I should mention these...... there aren't any really game breaking bugs or crashes nor any of the sort which makes you want to brick your PC, but it's also far from bug free, expeically for a game that is 15+ months old.

I can't recommend this experience enough. It started as average and organically built itself up into something special. If you are going to play this game though, be prepared to give it at least three full playthroughs (which shouldn't take more than 20 hours for someone taking their time) to see at least Ending E. Each one builds up a foundation for the next and it pays off to make you feel much more than the satisfaction of just beating a great game. There's also a hefty number of side quests which establish lore and make connections to the previous game (which isn't necessary to understand the plot for this one, but will make you appreciate a lot of the lore and some of the side characters more).
On the flip side, this game has a LOT of technical issues on PC and there have yet to be any performance patches from the dev (as of 7/7/2017). The biggest ones are poor fps, lack of true fullscreen resolutions, and a white screen softlock. There is an easy to install fan made mod to address a lot of the issues, but it shouldn't fall on the community to fix actual technical issues. That said, I didn't use the mod personally since I have a high tolerance for subpar game performance in general and played the vanilla version dealing with a non-fullscreen. Here's to hoping a patch eventually comes to streamline the process of enjoying this game.
Also, a less popular opinion, the combat is one of Platinum's weaker systems. It's very level/number dependant and the combat itself doesn't have the depth of other action games like DmC or Bayonetta. It can be flashy, but a lot of the game's encounters can be trivialized by circle strafing and holding down the pod fire button or hacking (in game). But I will commend them for including an easy difficulty that lets the game essentially play itself if you want, so everyone can experience the game. It's always nice to see devs offer options to accomodate all skill levels. The combat isn't terrible, it just isn't the draw of the game (for me personally).
The draw of this game lies primarily in the story, characters, soundtrack, and game design. To say what makes the story and characters special would enter spoiler territory, but it all grows throughout the three playthroughs. Even if you don't like some aspects or characters, the transitions feel justified (empathy goes a long way). I can't say anything bad about the soundtrack, following in the footsteps of the first game, it's top notch with appropriate vocals and very unique sounds and compositions. Many tracks capture the feeling of the areas and scenes perfectly. The game design has lots of meta moments and the UI/gameplay is often shifted to serve the narrative in a unique way. And a review wouldn't be complete without a mention of Yoko Taro and the insanity that he adds to every aspect of this game.

TL;DR: This is hardly a game at all, allowing for very little combat choices and even less exploration.  The story is good, though, and ties into the franchise quite well.  Music is straight out of the show, and some memorable characters came from the show to appear in this game.  However, it is not fun; it is tedious.
Full review:
For starters, you choose dialogue options in a similar fashion to Mass Effect but rarely see an actual difference in the responses from the other characters.  This illusion of interactivity works against the game because I would most likely be more immersed in the story if I could turn off the captions and watch everything like a movie.
If you manage to ignore the gigantic captions at the bottom of the screen, the characters are bland and unexciting.  This is a problem I have with The Elder Scrolls games, too.  Characters are unappealing and uninteresting.  They rarely do anything other than move their lips and maybe wail their arms about them in random directions.  Most of the time, they don't even move their heads!  The lack of animation leads to some major cinematic flaws which make this a hard story to follow, but in general, lack of animation would be OK if the gameplay could make up for it.
The gameplay consists of mostly menus, going from one place to another, and watching characters move in slow motion.  The combat is as unexciting as can be, yet you may find it frustrating due to the lack of a good user interface design.  I chose the normal difficulty level and could not get past the first non-tutorial fight without choosing the damage sponge class.  Did I mention the class system?  Yes, there's a class system, a damn good one!  Unfortunately, it goes to waste due to the horrible way it was implemented in combat.  Basically, the combat consists of pressing space to go into slomo mode, choosing a couple actions for your character(s), and then proceeding to watch those actions unfold.  It may sound like a decent strategy system, but it doesn't work.  The first battle was so difficult I had to do it four times, switching classes on the fourth try, requiring me to sit through a bunch of boring loading screens due to skipped cinematics replaying everything all over again.  A retry button would have been nice there.  Hell, an auto-save would have been nice there!
The overall presentation of this game's story is a mixed bag of awesomeness and futility.  The entire game is voiced, but the characters aren't animated very well.  The combat system makes me want to avoid combat rather than look forward to it.  The menu is poorly implemented but has a nice visual appeal.  The control scheme is horrible both in the combat and in explorable areas, requiring you to use the numpad and the mouse at the same time for example just to do a simple task like change your target.  The music was straight out of the show, so it was awesome, but come on, we can just listen to the music elsewhere.
I do not recommend this game, because it is absurdly frustrating to play and offers little in the form of entertainment.  Fans of the show may find some redeemable value in the character appearances or the backstory of The Wall, but nothing justifies playing through the entirety of this game in my opinion.  My patience wears thin after just one hour.

Anodyne is small, 2d-Zelda-like game. It remindes me a lot of Links Awakening, with the world being a dream and the jumping-puzzles, although the latter being much more present in this game.
It is quiet simple, your only weapon is a broom. Enemies have a good variety and the levels are very well designed, especially the dungeons. They require some thinking to solve the puzzles and the game does not hold your hand, which I think is good. Reminded me of the old times and the feeling figuring out on yourself is very rewarding. Half-way through the game you get jumping boots and thats where the game got frustrating for me. The controls are very spongy and the jumps require pixel-perfect jumps, sometimes under pressure: jumping on one-tile-platforms with rolling bars of death? So much fun, especially when you realize that you get knocked back every time you get hit.
The story is very confusing and the writing keeps it that way. I'm not sure if I get it at all or it was deliberate that way, since it all happens in a dream and dreams don't always make sense. Still it reminds me somewhat of the story of Links Awakening, the bosses seem to warn you that be beating them, you will eventually destroy the whole world - at least thats what I got from it.
If you like the old, 2d-Zelda games, Anodyne is very well done spin on it. Especially the dungeons are very well designed, but the jumping puzzles can get frustating.

This game stands as one of my very favorite space 4x games, a genre that I wish was larger.  Adapting Paradox's ambitious grand strategy model to space opera results in an intricate empire management game, focusing primarily on exploration and internal politics of the empire you run.  There are hundreds of permutations of possible species/empire combinations, and massive replayability thanks to both this and the randomly-generated galaxy, plus multiple potential late-game "Crisis" events designed to shake up the status quo once empires have fully colonized the galaxy and possibly ossified into opposing power blocs.
For anyone who likes space 4x, and doubly especially if they already enjoy the Paradox grand strategy genre, I cannot recommend this game highly enough.  Being a Paradox game, it will likely continue to recieve gameplay updates and DLC for quite a while, adding additional content to the game.  I've put a couple hundred hours into the game already, and I will likely double that once Synthetic Dawn comes out, as I have been wanting to play a machine empire since the game came out.

Background: On my first playthrough, I set the game up so that my Omnpotent Alfaekan Imperium would be the first to evolve into space. No Fallen Empires or AI Empires on the biggest galaxy size (not spiral). Authoritarian, Materialist, and Militarist. Hyperlanes and Energy Weapons.
The homeworld, Celestial Jewel, was on the westernmost edge of the galaxy. Our emperor Lucius Windsor, on the same day our first ships, declared that one day, all would kneel before the banner of the Imperium. After around 20 years, planet of Nafflthi was discovered, which had industrial age bird people, was discovered. We welcomed them into our empire with Titanic Beasts and vicious Slave Armies. Within two days, we had our first xeno slaves (and free xenos, since we were a caste system). Soon after, our top scientists perfected cybernetics, and all our subjects took the first step in leaving our filthy organic husks with cybernetic parts.
A few decades, with the whole galactic west under our control, we met the other alien empires: the authoritarian Autocracy of Pithaj Mog, which ruled the galactic south, the spiritual, pacifist, and egalitarian Zimmerpuk Consortium, which controlled the east, and their vassals the Screk Alliance. Within a century, our technological supremacy wiped out the Autocracy, won the race to colonize the north, and freed ourselves from organic filth into cold synthetic bodies With three fourths of the galaxy under our control, we geared up for war against the Zimmerpuks, who had assimilated the Screk. Before we could declare said war however, a strange hive-mind of vast, living ships called the Prethoryn Scourge appeared, in the northeastern fringe of Zimmerpuk territory. They devoured a third of the Zimmerpuk colonies, including their homeworld, before we they turned their ravenous gaze to us.
But we were ready.
The first system they attacked was a fortress. 12 space stations, a spaceport, and a large army of synths, xenomorphs, and older robots, all supplemented with xenomorph cavalry awaited them. 2 of their fleets were annihilated before our specialized task fleet, battleships armed to the teeth with strike-craft, tachyon lances, lasers, and plasma cannons attacked the remaining Prethoryn fleet, obliterating them before bombarding their worlds into oblivion. In the end, the Prethoryn were destroyed, and their worlds terraformed. The Zimmerpuks were ours, and purged as our ethics switched from authoritarian to xenophobe. Lucius' decree was fulfilled, and all the galaxy belonged to the Steel Galactic Imperium, ruling from the ringworld formerly known as Cybrex Prime.

Summary: Deeply recommended. It is a full game stated 'early access' presumably because some features are still not yet 100% finished (eg localization, language translations, and finishing end-game content), however there is more than a full day's worth of content within! 24 hours+ of content, a fully fleshed out storyline, every detail and graphics done in hand-drawn pixels, and the free demo was first seen on Newgrounds in 2015 and was a hit ever since.
While my playtime may look little, as I've only played it online to be able to write a review for it, I've had my eye on this ever since it appeared as a 'free flash game' on Newgrounds back in 2015 (It is still up there for anyone who wonders), a long time before anything about it on steam occurred--it was a hit back then, and I am very happy to see the consistency that stuck carry over until now. Back then, CrossCode was swamped with high rating reviews focused on the effort and detail thrown into it, as all its art is done by hand (by the mouse), inasmuch as everything else (writing, characterization, concept), and all that time in creating this reflects in its quality. One personal sticking factor is its smoothness even on low-end or 'old' computers (like mine); it runs with visuals as smooth as videos running on 1080 HD; videos that struggle to play with stutter or lag at the same quality in many other games of that graphics. This smoothness follows in your playstyle and gameplay too--when you get hit, the responsibility is onto yourself, rather than anything with the controls (although one can blame the bullets because they are speedy too :P). And with these graphics, it avoids the annoying 'garish' levels of 'too much' graphics that would cause eyestrain or irritation after a long while too. The NPCs and characters are similar to many RPGs; some have lines that repeat or are linear to repeat after it gets exhausted, but a difference is they live with the world rather than act as static characters at different times.
The game comes with subtitles for everything, and even its art has been updated time and time again (from the generic shaded NPC, to a personalized grayscale NPC for more characterization--the developer team didn't need to do that, but they did, and this is the point of quality which drew me back over the years, pining to save up money to buy this when I could.)
The developers are responsive to the community too, and overall decent people. Aside from that, even at the time of writing this, the game is in 'early access', much of the news has clearly stated the goals and present/future content (although there are gift codes that anyone can get online by search engine, these aren't noticeable with the game unless people search for it), and it is technically a finished product at this point with its potential being unravelled as it goes. This was also a factor way back when all everyone knew about CrossCode was 'flash game on this website'; this attitude of consistency remarks a lot about both this game, and the ones developing it.
This is pretty much staying within my favorites as far as I'm reading (and having finished as much content as released at the moment), and has filled my nostalgia back to older games where pixels were done piece by piece, and thoughtfulness was placed in the framework of the whole set. And the good thing is, there is still a lot of space for growth.
Overall, I'd recommend it, even if it says it is "Early Access". It has hours of fun stacked inside it, with a deep story and characterization, also somewhat humoring classic MMO games. Personally--this "Early Access" means you get to see it grow.

My main issue with this game is match making. It's no surprise that there's no real good science behind match making but it's also a bit ridiculous when you're a casual player and you end up playing against people who abuse the movement system of certain characters and probably have hundreds of hours in the game.
Some characters feel over powered due to their movement system and you can never bloody hit them. Then some characters feel entirely useless because they don't have a movement system.
It's frustrating to come across some experienced flanker who's spamming all their movement dashes and double jumps, while you're just trying to hit them. You can't out-run them and you can't hit them so what the hell are you supposed to do?!
I feel the game needs some more tweaks to maintain some sort of fairness between characters and classes. Flankers are supposed to be glass cannons. But when they're moving faster than you can snap your fingers, it's annoying, aggrivating and at times impossible to do anything against them.
I don't care about the competitive side of the game, I just want a fun little team-based game and play against people who are at least close to my skill level. Not players who spend their whole day playing this game mastering their characters.
The other thing that I do have to mention is that I can't tell whether they're hacking or not and frankly I don't care. I gave this game a chance, I've played it for as long as I have because it was fair at first. They continue adding more and more characters that continue to break the game itself.

Take away the fact this game is tied into the intellectual property of
, and you will be left with a pretty damn good RPG.  If you like good RPGs, you will want to consider playing this, regardless of if you care about the
franchise or not.  That said, this game does a pretty good job of tying into the first book/season; so if you are a fan, it certainly adds to the experience and helps you appreciate the rich story in the game.
There are several mechanics that contribute to the high quality of the game as an RPG.  You play as two characters, back and forth, each with separate stories that inevitably collide later in the game.  The game is very heavy on cutscenes and plot development, but it is done well and is generally pretty enjoyable.  There are dialogue trees you will explore during the many conversations in the game, being thorough and inquisitive will often reward you with items or little permanent trait boosts.  There are decisions to be made, which will have minor consequences (like extra rewards for quests from NPCs); there is also a major decision late-game and a few different endings.   There are active abilities you can use while exploring out of combat to discover secrets in the world.  The combat is active, but has a tactical-pause which can be utilized to issue specific commands and tactics to your character(s).  There are a handful of fighting styles you can pick from for each character, and you also get other party members that will have various styles which will spice up combat here and there.  There is definitely a good amount of substance, and it makes for a very enjoyable RPG experience.
The story is enjoyable.  And for a game so story-driven it better be.  The plot of the game is a “sidequel” to the first book/season— that is to say: it takes place during the same time and in the same place, but follows a different set of characters/events.  I think the writers did a good job of creating an atmosphere pretty true to
If you are a fan of the books/show you will probably be intrigued by the story in this game.
The game does have some flaws.  The graphics are not as great as they could have been.  The voice acting is mostly solid, but at times feels forced.  There is limited variety to gear/weapons, and the combat does get repetitive even though the fights are distanced with cutscenes.
In summary,
is a very enjoyable RPG.  It does have some flaws, and may drag at times, but seems to be well made (no bugs/crashing) and tells a good story.   It has plenty to offer for fans of RPGs, and if you are a fan of the books/shows you will enjoy that added bonus.

If you like action, if you like skill trees, if you like immersive worlds with challenging enemies CrossCode if for you.  This game elegantly replicates all of the fast pased hack and slash action of your favorite action RPGs like Tales of Symphonia or Kingdom Hearts and combines it with some of the the patience and que-reading required for Games like Dark Souls; all presented in a gorgeous 16-bit style.  The controls take a little getting used to due to the nontraditional configuration but  feel tight and responsive after a bit of practice.  Level progression as you move from area to area is right up there with Golden Sun.  Enemies are challenging but teach you to use different skills as you get them.  Bosses are pretty difficult and will probably beat you the first time you face them, but it never feels cheap.  It never feel like the game cheated you out of a win.  More like shows you that your skills can improve which just drives you to focus a little harder and be more patient.  You rarely feel underleveled when going to a new area if you fight most of what you come across as you backtrack or explore.  And OMFG is there exploration.  There are enough treasures and pathways between area hidden throughout each land to give you that metroidvania fix!  Seariously folks I can't recomend this game enough.
TL;DR: Tight controls, ♥♥♥♥♥in gameplay, Kindom Hearts+Golden Sun+Metroidvania with a side of Dark Souls. Don't miss out.

A much more accessible 4X game by Paradox, I would say that it fits neatly between Civilization V and Crusader Kings II in terms of learning curve (and share mechanics of both those games).  It is quite a solid game, with a lot of content and unique events from beginning stages to endgame.  There is really no wrong way to play — you can strike out on your own or join a Federation, customize the disposition and ideology of your spacefaring civilization, and decide the path of advancement (military fleets, the various branches of science, what to build on colonized planets, etc).
The customization in this game is great.  This, along with the emergent gameplay that comes with the procedurally generated galactic neighbors and scripted events, helps to make a unique story for every playthrough.  I have no real complaints about this game — the developers are tweaking the combat and a few small mechanics, but it is definitely a solid purchase, especially if you are only starting out with the grand strategy genre and find other titles daunting.

This is the most important game nobody played. It's true, virtually nobody played it...and it's also important.
Nobody played it because it has little more than cult status in the world of gaming and in keeping with the tradition of Japanese game development from the mid to late 90s and early 2000s (it actually looks like a game from that time period), it has interesting gameplay mechanics, a bizarre storyline and quirky character presentation, so it's easy to see why SWERY's game ranks right up there with the likes of Suda51 games, such as Lollipop Chainsaw and Shadows of the Damned (please Steam, add these games to your store) or lesser known games like Mr. Mosquito, Incredible Crisis, the Siren series (arguably much more popular but still a series largely forgotten or that nobody really cared about), the Choaniki series, etc.
It's important because of the aforementioned cult status and Japanese quirkiness - they simply don't make games like this anymore, or at least nowhere near as often as they used to. It's also important because it pays homage to Twin Peaks and because it was actually awarded a Guinness record for most polarizing game, meaning that gamer reviews, and especially critical reviews, held it in either very high esteem, praising it for what it was, or utterly trashing it for what it wasn't (a good game) - there was absolutely no gray area by which to even things out.
I believe this was a budget game at the time of its release back on Xbox 360 and then again on PS3 with the exclusive director's cut (so it was $20 or thereabouts) and it's regularly the same price on Steam, except when it goes on sale for 90% off (which frequently happens). If you can look past its many bugs/flaws and very much dated graphical appearance, you're in for an interesting gaming experience that you won't soon forget.

Known as the most critically polarizing game in video game history, Deadly Premonition is definitely a game that stands out from the crowd and establishes itself as a unique and bizarre specimen. Borrowing heavily from David Lynch's phenomenal television show, Twin Peaks, Deadly Premonition tells the story of FBI Agent Francis York Morgan who is called in to investigate the murder of a young woman in the sleepy mountain town of Greenvale. Along the way he meets various colorful and unique characters that add more to the allure and mystery of his investigation.
PROS:
Fantastic story - A very deep and amazing story with many shocking developments and plot twists. One of the best written and presented stories I have ever seen in a video game.
Unique characters - Every character in Deadly Premonition is different and bursting with personality. A lot of care was put into every person's back story and quirks to make each one stand out.
Plenty to do - There are points in the story where you can go fully open world. Inside Greenvale are plenty of side quests and activities to take part in. Some activities you can only do at certain times of the day or before or after particular story events.
Genuinely creepy - The game starts off like a typical horror game, but slowly begins to twist and contort into a more unsettling and disturbing tale.
CONS:
Odd controls - Some of the games controls are a bit sluggish, especially the driving controls. Every car feels like a tank and will randomly spin off the road for no reason.
PC Version plagued with technical issues - If you play Deadly Premonition on PC, be prepared to fight with it. The game has loads of technical problems from random crashing and freezing, to frame rate and graphical errors. It's a miracle if you can get the game to run for more than 10 minutes without it crashing. There are workarounds, but it's upsetting to see how little care went into the PC port.
Maybe a little too weird - Deadly Premonitions charm lies in it's quirky characters and twisting story. A lot of crazy things happen throughout and the narrative can be a little weird for some. Not a game for people who like a more straightforward story.
If you can see past all the technicaly problems with the PC port, Deadly Premonition is a superb action/horror game with one of the best stories I have ever witnessed. If you can, I highly recommend getting the PS3 version since it is more stable and less likely to give you problems.
