After years of getting disappointed by games from big publishers; I've become extremely reluctant to buy any games over 30 euros. As a result, it took me months (until the summer sale) to finally convince myself to get Nier: Automata.
The day I finally got it, I played it for 10 hours straight; the second day for another 8 hours and by the end of the week, I had 100% cleared everything. It has been years since a singleplayer game had me so hooked that I forgot to eat or sleep until suddenly the sun came up. I usually don't play singleplayer games anymore, because without an online aspect, I find it impossible to stay interested for long enough to see where the story goes. In this game however, I replayed the game several times without getting bored for a second, and even though I 100% cleared the game now; I'm planning on playing through the endings A to E on hard mode now, because the game is simply that good.
I don't want to get into the story too much out of fear of spoiling an amazing story that should be experienced going in completely blind. Just know that it's a really gripping story that deals with existentialism in machines and references many great thinkers from the past and their points of view as shown in the character design of certain machines and the quests they give you.
The customization options for your chipsets (basically your passive skills) are so expansive that you can really build the character that fits your playstyle. Want a super flimsy high damage glass cannon-type build? no problem; want your character to regenerate hp on every hit, be super tanky in general and shoot out shockwaves at your enemies with every swing of your blade? no problem. Do you want to go for the realistic approach? no problem, just chuck out any chip that makes up your UI, and fill that space with more damage... because why not? Maybe you're even too lazy to fight at all, and just want to enjoy the amazing story, in which case you can just turn on easy mode and equip chips that do the fighting for you.
Sadly no game is perfect. I was fortunate enough to only get one problem, which I was able to circumvent (at a certain point in the game, I was unable to pass by a certain monster in the game without my game crashing over and over, but for some reason, staring at the floor and walking in a big circle around that area prevented it from crashing... (maybe something that was corrupted that crashed the game when it got rendered?))
I've heard many reports from people even being unable to start the game at all, or getting crashes constantly, which is probably why the community reviews score this game relatively low... I am fairly certain that the bad reviews are not because they think the game is bad, but because of the technical difficulties you can have with it.
Luckily, we have steam refunds for that though, so if you are one of the unlucky ones with issues, you can just refund the game if you haven't played it for over 2 hours and the game hasn't been in your library for over two weeks!
I guess many people might consider the fanservice as a positive thing; but to me it just gets cringy if the game even forces you to indulge in it to get all achievements. (can't be more specific because of spoilers)
Finally, the game is obviously made for a controller; the hacking minigames (little shoot-em-up sections) feel very clunky with mouse and keyboard, and since hacking is such a strong tool in your arsenal later on, I definitely regretted not having a controller.
Of course, these negatives are not bad enough to take away the enjoyment of this amazing game, so aslong as you simply look past that, this game is definitely worth trying, even at full price.

+ Amazing Story
+ Great Customization options
+ Responsive Combat
- Possible Technical Difficulties (if so -> get refund)
- Fanservice can be Cringy at times
- Controller is strongly advised

If there is one thing you can expect of Anodyne, it's a superb sense of atmosphere. Every zone you explore oozes feeling, whether that feeling may be lonliness, wide-eyed exploration, or even general strangeness. This is thanks to quality atmospheric music and some above-average artwork. Each zone has their own feeling, and that helped greatly with the enjoyment of exploring them and finding new zones.
Gameplay wise, the game is alright. You have a broom weapon you hit dudes with, and you can pick up dust from the ground. You can use said dust to do things like wade across water (you cannot swim) and activate switches. Although simple, it makes the broom feel like an actual broom instead of a sword-that-isn't-a-sword. Combat wise, if you've ever played a top-down Zelda game (Link to the Past, Zelda 1), you will probably feel right at home with the combat. It lacks depth beyond dodging projectiles and hitting things, but it's definitely not unenjoyable.
On a combat note, the enemies of the game felt quite varied, and the bosses moreso. Each enemy has unique behavior and tactics on how to damage you, and always feel suited to the zone you find them in. The bosses of each zone test one's skills in a way that really impressed me, and they did kill me a few times in my playthrough.
I do have a few gripes with the game that hampered my enjoyment, which I will list in order of lowest-to-highest severity:
1) Although the music definitely builds atmosphere, this strangly also applied to boss battle music. I didn't expect the game to jump straight for atmospheric to Japanese shred metal when a boss fight occured, but the low-key tunes of the boss battles clashed with the threatening feeling of the bosses. The bosses definitely were challenging, and unfortunately the music does not reflect that.
2) I got lost many times, and felt that some "ease-of-life" features would be nice. I am not someone who needs handholding in a game, and I can respect a game that requires some do-it-yourself thinking to progress. However, I could have saved a lot of time hunting down collectables and figuring out where to go if, for example, the map included icons for locked doors I've run into, or chests I hadn't opened yet. Furthermore, many times I found tiles where one part of the screen I could pass through, but another I did not. It was very difficult to realize (without going back to said tile) that I hadn't fully explored that part of the zone yet.
3) The story, even after seeing all the plot pieces and zones, felt utterly incomprehensible. I understand that the game is supposed to (or at least implied to) take place in a dream-like world. While the dream theme really helped make the game feel varied and enjoyable to explore, the interactions with NPCs and how the plot turns out didn't feel cohesive to me. Again, I get that dreams don't usually feel cohesive, and that the game is not supposed to feed you the story on a silver spoon, but many games with a non-direct story typically leave many bits and pieces that fit together after inspection. After thinking about the story for a while, I still can't understand what it's about or what the journey was meant to symbolize. If someone can clue me in, I would greatly appreciate it.
Don't let my negativity get to you though. Overall, Anodyne is a fine game and probably one of the better indie games I've played. I would definitely give it a look.

An RPG light strategy tower defense game? Yes, yes, and yes. This is a massive game with outstanding replayability, hundreds of achievements, and many choices. You will lose over and over again until you master it.
This is an incredibly deep and addictive game and it gives you new items and abilities slowly. You receive shadow cores to spend on abilities, but spend too many shadow cores and your starting mana is lower, making it harder to start each level. The gems you use can either be used by themselves and upgraded or can be combined with any type and number of other gems. The gems are all different, like poison, increased hit or critical hit chance, decreased armour, decreased healing, etc. You can also build walls and use gems in traps. One main strategy is to build fewer towers with stronger gems and traps with gems. Use your bolts and beams wisely as they take time to recharge. You can throw gem bombs.
Seeing fast enemies and giants can make you panic. You don't want them to reach your orb. Just build a combination of towers and traps and make sure you use poison a lot. Keep upgrading gems as you go and make sure you put them at strategic points. Walls can also help a lot if you make your enemies travel as far as possible so the gems can do their damage.
I keep coming back to play more of this game because it is such a fun, challenging, and massive game. Achievement hunters will love it. If you like tower defense games or just a good challenge, play this game. It is one of the few best of its type.

Meh. I like the GoT universe, and it was cool to sort of be "in" it, but...I'm not sure who the target audience of the game is. It seems like it might be people who know *of* GoT, but don't actually have any familiarity with it, other than "hey, isn't that the theme music?" I say that because characters spout exposition constantly (the voice acting is almost universally monotone), and someone like myself who's read the books will probably find it profoundly boring.
Bottom line:
- If you're intimately familiar with GoT, you'll probably find the story elements of the game incredibly dull. Unless you just absolutely-cannot-get-enough-of-Westeros...in which case, just find a Skyrim mod or something.
- If you've played an RPG before, you will find the game mechanics boring and unoriginal. Especially if you've played a PC RPG before (again, Elder Scrolls, I'm lookin' at you)
- The UI seems like it was designed for the lowest common denominator, I.E. - consoles, which means that on PC there are several aspects that are really unintuitive if you have, say, a keyboard and mouse attached. Like PC users tend to have. (Of course, it's possible that this was released PC-only--I haven't checked--in which case, shame on the developers for a UI that's atrocious for no good reason)
Okay, so...my bottom line is longer than the rest of the review, but my point is this: do NOT waste your money on this game, even it's on sale...unless you know nothing of Game of Thrones--other than that it's "a thing"--AND have never played an RPG videogame before.

A much more accessible 4X game by Paradox, I would say that it fits neatly between Civilization V and Crusader Kings II in terms of learning curve (and share mechanics of both those games).  It is quite a solid game, with a lot of content and unique events from beginning stages to endgame.  There is really no wrong way to play — you can strike out on your own or join a Federation, customize the disposition and ideology of your spacefaring civilization, and decide the path of advancement (military fleets, the various branches of science, what to build on colonized planets, etc).
The customization in this game is great.  This, along with the emergent gameplay that comes with the procedurally generated galactic neighbors and scripted events, helps to make a unique story for every playthrough.  I have no real complaints about this game — the developers are tweaking the combat and a few small mechanics, but it is definitely a solid purchase, especially if you are only starting out with the grand strategy genre and find other titles daunting.

Super House of Dead Ninjas feels like a cross between NInja Gaiden and Spelunky with the twitchiness of Super Meat Boy. The pacing is super fast as you work your way down the hundreds of floors that make up this enemy- and trap-infested tower. The mechanics are simple to get a hang of yet can be difficult to master and will test your reflexes constantly. Thankfully the game controls nicely with a 360 pad because I couldn't imagine executing some of these precise maneuvers on a keyboard. A strong variety of weapons/explosives/powerups at your disposal will aid you on your trek downward. Floors are randomly-generated, but for the most part each section feels mostly the same from one playthrough to the next. This could result in some repetitiveness over time. In spite of that, SHODN has a very addictive feel to it thanks to the overall pacing and arcade-style gameplay. Strikes me as a great "Pick up and play" type game for short 30-minute bursts in the same vein as The Binding Of Isaac.
In all, this is a highly enjoyable rogue-like that features some frantic action, crisp controls, and fun/satisfying combat. A nice throwback to the old-school hack-and-slash days that's well worth the bargain basement price.

This game is awsome. I've been with this back in early 2016 and I've been hooked since.
The style is amazing, the controls are intuitive, game mechanics are smooth, dialogue is honestly quite funny (coupled with character reactions), and you aren't locked down in the abilities you choose to get - leading to a very expansive way to play the game.
If you think this is a game where you could f-stuff up, your gonna die. Each species of enemies brings there own challenges to the table and every boss forces you to up your game - if you want any hope of defeating them.
The description of the game says, "engaging puzzle"(s). That is a huge understatement. Everything is a puzzle. No, I'm not saying that to get from one side of the map to the other is not a clear cut path, but CrossCode rewards players who explore and discovers it's secrets. You are a pathfinder. Traversing through a dungeon will stretch your imagination, and even if you figure out how to get past a certain part, you'll still need the ability to back it up. No talk the talk here.

OVERALL:
I would reccomend this game to retro, and modern gamers alike. Am I saying this game is for everyone? No. But I would reccommened everyone at least TRIES the demo, cause there is a lil something for a lot of different people.

Deadly Premonition is one of the most unique and memorable games I have ever played. I could leave the review at that because really, that's all it is, at the end of the day. But, there's more to it, than that. This game pits you as Special Agent Francis 'York' Morgan, an FBI agent traveling to a small town to investigate a serial killer murder mystery. In this small town exists a special and unheard-of cast of characters, 50 side missions, collectibles, and a gruesome murder mystery story that was able to keep me interested the entire ride. Greenvale has such an off-air around it, I can't imagine these characters existing and interacting anywhere else. The dialogue/interactions between York and others is very entertaining. Though it's not the part of the game you should be focusing on, the combat is standard Resident Evil 4 over-the-shoulder style with some action buttons every now and again. From the town citizen's quarrels you help solve along side an intense investigation, to the very strange and touching character and character developments of York, to the troubleshooting; this game is unique and interesting. But, there is something to be said about the troubleshooting, as it will be a very core part of your experience.
The games cons come in usually right from the start; you have to be able to get this game to work before you enjoy any of it (read the Discussions and Guides sections for this game, they can usually get you on the right path to getting it running and give you a good idea of what settings you can change around to get it to work, as there is no one set solution to getting it to work for everyone). The horrendous optimisation has made for some very unique bugs, such as crashing after chapter end scenes (turning autosave on can alleviate any progress lost, as it always crashes after it autosaves, for me), graphics going to absolute garbage during one type of weather (true clear), having to choose between running the game on Windows 98 compatibility mode and having almost no crashes but dealing with the game losing framerate over time and not being able to aim up or turning off compatibility mode completely letting you aim up and no lag over time but dealing with random crashes (chapter ends, looking up in the morning, general random (by the way, you can totally beat the game without ever aiming up, does make you have to get creative with some puzzles)) There's an area on the map that makes the screen do random white flashes and it hurts your eyes but its ONLY that area (you only get this issue if you don't run on Windows 98 compat mode, another trade off between compat and no compat mode). There's a game breaking bug on Chapter 9 where if you happen to decide you want to replay a chapter while on chapter 9, you will lose a key object you need to progress the story (simple fix is to back up your game save when you get to chap 9 and not replay any chapters during it).
This game has a lot of technical issues, some I didn't think I would ever encounter, as a gamer. So, with that; it's hard to casually recommend this game. But, there's only one word that describes this game; unique. And I think that cult classic vibe uniqueness alone is well worth any amount of troubleshooting you have to go through to get it running. From start to finish, from every single side mission, I enjoyed it and highly recommend anyone into niche games, mystery games, comedy games, or anyone wanting something different, pick it up. If you can't get it running, you can always return it.
NOTE: DON'T READ THE ACHIEVEMENTS IF YOU DON'T WANT THE STORY SPOILED FOR YOU.

As a devoted fan of the books and the TV series, I'm trying very hard to view this game in a positive light, but the blemishes just won't go away, no matter how hard I squint.
It does have many positive aspects. Just being in Westeros is a big deal and it's nice to meet characters that you already know. The story has the right feel. The graphics, while not spectacular by current standards, are enough to convey the required look and mood.
Unfortunately, the game play is abysmal. The combat mechanics, in particular, are downright painful and completely break the immersion in the battle as you have to fight more with the UI to do anything meaningful than you do with your opponent. I do like the "active pause" mechanism, where action (and even speech) continues in slow motion rather than stopping completely, but that's part of what breaks the immersion. If you want any chance to win your fight, you can't do it in adrenaline-pumping real time. As an option, "active pause" would be phenomenal. As an obligation, it sucks. And once you're in combat, you're locked in place with your opponent. You can't back down, move sideways, or go to a tactically better location. The only thing you can do is to change target. This  is even worse as an archer. Once you start shooting, the game decides where you stand. You can't seek cover, even partial cover. You just stand there in the middle of the combat field like a big idiot while enemies either shoot at you or charge you, at which point you can switch to a melee weapon.
And then, there are cut scenes. Billions and billions and billions of cut scenes! While the cut scenes are interesting, they're too long and too frequent. If they wanted to make a movie, I would have gladly bought the DVD, but what I wanted here was a game.
Interaction with the world is also painful. You can't interact with most things and the only way to know that you can interact with something is when you're nearly on top of it and an obnoxious glowing icon suddenly appears over it. You can't talk to most NPCs, either. Unless they're a merchant or a quest giver, they're basically just mindless decorations. Even the ones you can talk to have no variety. They will repeat the exact same phrases over and over and over. You can't get into most buildings. You can't pick up objects that are on the ground. That beautiful sword on the ground? Forget it. It's just part of the backdrop. It might as well be a painting.
Basic movement is also incredibly primitive. We're talking Doom grade primitive. You can't jump and every drop is protected by a forcefield that prevents you from falling, even if it's only a couple of feet. You can't crouch or change speed either.
This final point bothers me personally, but some people might like it, though I can't begin to understand why they would. If you chose to play with the controller, the controller becomes the only thing you can use. The keyboard and mouse seem to be completely deactivated, except for the arrow keys when navigating a menu. Maybe they just wanted it to
feel like a console port.
So, if you're a Game of Thrones fan, you're kind of in a bind because you will want to play this, if only for the story and the chance to meet some of your favorite characters or to visit some of the locations. But if you're not a GoT fan and are just looking for a good RPG, walk past this one.

I know I have not played much of this game, 2.4 hours as I'm writing this, but I still must say that it is one of the best third person rpg games I've ever played. I say this because there is extensive amounts of dialogue, which I happen to enjoy, as it conveys story, as well as it's strategic combat system and it's lore. When I say lore, I mean that  it's a game about game of thrones, which is my second favorite show of all time. It's combat system is hard to get the hang of at first, unless you've played Of Orcs and Men, because it's quite a lot like that.
It's also nice to know that If you don't like one storyline that you're playing in the game, there's always the other to look forward to. One storyline is about a Night's Watch Veteran, Mors, and the other is about the eldest son of the Lord of a town he deserted 15 years prior, and his name is Alester. I personally prefer Alester, because he's a more interesting character in a more interesting plot line, wereas Mors is fairly interesting in a storyline that is difficult and honestly somewhat boring. But any reader of this review should still recognize that I've not played much of the game, so I can't truthfully describe each of the storylines and what they are like.
Alester's storyline, so far, is that he left his town 15 years ago because he didn't want to keep being reminded by the past, but leaving emotionally destroyed his father and sister, throwing the town into turmoil. He returns after his fathers death and that's where the player starts, so i won't reveal any more about it.
Mors storyline is that he is part of the night's watch, and has been for about 15 years, when his friend he's been with for those fifteen years attempts to desert the Watch, resulting in the consequences that any fan of the show or books will already know. Mors is then put in command of 4 new recruits, who he must take to track down a Watchmen who has broken one of his vows. That's where the player must continue from.
So far my pros and cons are:
Pros:
+lots of dialogue with mass effect like choices
+varying storylines
+interesting strategic combat
+fairly good visuals
+moral choices that affect the future
+cutscenes are skippable
Cons:
-Cutscenes around every corner
-High prices at merchants
-Dialogue is a bit wordy
-Camera mostly restricted
Misc:
*Doesn't remind you to check character screen when you level up
*Rarely autosaves- remember to manually save periodically

Surprisingly deep 2D tower defense game, heavily favoring strategy and core gamers.
Really, it's quite deep. There's a lot of different ways to kill the monsters, and so much strategy you will learn and develop. It can be easy to get started, but you will eventually reach a point where you need to understand what's happening, strategize more deeply, and think hard about what to place where, when to enter certain levels, and what skills to have active for which field.
I'm not sure I will ever reach the higher levels, and instead I tend to play the same few fields that I enjoy over and over. For the casual gamer, this might be a compromise if you're bogged down in the strategy overload.
I especially appreciate the ability to build walls to redirect monsters - in a way I end up designing my own field, if I really use a lot of them.
Overall really excellent, and will give you anything you'd want in a tower defense game.

Puzzle: 5/5
It has well build structure. They first give you easy basic ones with one idea, then develops on that idea - evolving into challenging yet very doable puzzles. It's very polished and it's clear they put a lot of care into their puzzles.
Combat: 5/5
Aside from the feeling I got that melee build is lot more powerful than ranged, it's pretty good. The combination of butter-smooth movement and satisfying hitting sounds make a great combat system. Every enemy has their unique attack you should watch out for, and weakness you can exploit.
Story: ???/5
It's not particularly good, but not bad either so far. I mean, the storyline isn't even released fully in this early acess version. I personally hope they could tone down the "Ancient" lores and "Master Sensei" vibes a bit.
Visuals: 4/5
The pixel art part is absolutely beautiful. characters, worlds, enemies... the illustrations are bit plain. Their faces are in good balance between being cute and realistic, but the attire designs show the limits of concep artist(Sorry devs!). The armors are depicted as more or less square/sphere shapes, without any sort of filler details. I suspect that's the artist's weakness...
Playtime: about 32 hours as of 0.97 early access. Not bad at all!
However I feel like they sort of overdid it with the first dungeon, it's crazy long! Thankfully I didn't have much problem due to me enjoying it a lot, but that dungeon really should've been split into two sections or somthing.
I'm not sure if they're planning to add cosmetics(items with different looks). It's probably not gonna happen due to the amount of work required while having no impact in gameplay, but I just want to play dress up on my Lea...it would be so much fun...

It isn't a stretch to say that this is the best ARPG I have ever played. The unique gameplay of CrossCode integrates itself into  the puzzles and the combat in more than just a few ways and does so wonderfully. The bosses are well thought out and very fun to fight. The world is built around the progression of your character, and even uses backtracking in a way that isn't annoying or tedious to deal with due to easy fast travel. The game lets you take everything at your pace, which not only adds a personalized player experience, but also adds a bit of replay value. The game is not done yet, so if you really want the full story and full expanse of the world I would hold off on buying, put it on the wishlist and wait until the full release. However, if you are into fast-paced, timing heavy combat with interesting and involving puzzles, then this game is absolutely for you, do not hesistate in buying this like I did.

Where do I even begin? First things first I'd be one of the first to say that this game is absolutly fantastic
Crosscode is a homage to the old style Legend of Zelda type puzzle games originally released for the SNES and anything of its ilk. The most significant dfference between Crosscode and its predecessors is that it also takes on an open world (Think World of Warcraft) that encourages the player to persue quests to upgrade stats and gear rather than simply finding or upgrading what you have. The world is large and divided into multple areas with various difficulties that increase as you advance. Simply traversing the terrain at times can be a puzzle but that's not to imply that its neccesary to do so.
Crosscode also exceeds gameplay wise. Cross code has a level based system that gives you points to upgrade various skill trees as you advance. This encourages multple styles of gameplay and doesn't restrict you to simple button mashing (should you not prefer it).
The music is beautiful, the artwork is highly detailed and enchanting to look at, the story is intriguing and the characters are fun.
Normally I would not condone buying a game that isn't finished but the developers are wonderful at maintaing consistent updates and they even allow you to keep up with their progress live at their discord/twitch channel
TL;DR
A wonderful and content packed game that fufills the desires of the RPG and fast paced fighting communities alike. Do yourself a favour and buy it

TL;DR, I highly, highly recommend playing this game, but I do not recommend buying it. This is one of the coolest concepts I have ever seen destroyed by an unusable DRM scheme.
From Dust is a work of art. Watching the form of the earth change and mould as the player manipulates it brings back memories of Black and White, but with a sense of visual awe that comes from being a much more recent game. It is something that I feel any gamer owes it to themselves to experience at least once. Sadly, I can't recommend buying the game, as I have an ethical objection to UPlay. The alternative, a Chrome app that is free in the Chrome Store, is okay, but ultimately Ubisoft's disingenuity has ruined, or at least limited access to, what I consider to be an actual art piece.
Fun fact: Ubisoft actually patched the game to remove UPlay. I had been hoping that would happen and bought it shortly after. Only a few months later, I had been happily enjoying my new game when I launched one day to find UPlay had been patched back in.
Ubisoft, I know you're not listening, but stop punishing your customers for buying your products. You did the right thing once before and removed the DRM from this game. Now that the DRM is back on, I would not be surprised to find the number of seeders for this game on torrent sites has spiked. No one wants a content management system inside another content management system, especially if they only have one or two games in the "nested" one.

This is the RE game that you play on a rainy afternoon in lieu of a marathon on the Sci-fi channel.
The episodic nature of this game really makes me feel that I am playing a well crafted action horror television series that will hopefully get another season. The story was well told through the eyes of different characters and at different times, but it all comes together really well. For me personally, the characters make the story work. Yes we all love Chris and Jill, but to me the stars were the secondary protagonists that you got to play as-Parker Luciani, Keith Lumley and Quint Ketcham. I know I'll probably never see these characters again, but they were nice to get to know in this story. On a personal note, this game made me cry. When I thought a certain character had died, I bawled. Then I felt bad that I had. This is Resident Evil! It's B action horror cheese! Yet, this game quickly invests you in these characters and you bond with them.
The game plays very well. The combat is very smooth, and the atmosphere reminds me a lot of the claustrophobic spaces of the first RE games. The inventory is very simplified but there are also places to store weapons and workbenches to upgrade weapons. The map screen has been done away with and a mini map in the corner of the screen shows the next waypoint. On the whole, I feel that the controls and the interface have been simplified.
This was a nice game to go between RE4 and RE5. If had a lot of action but had a lot of the elements that reminded me of classic RESI: timed escapes, claustrophobic spaces, over the top bosses, and rocket launchers. This was a fun time, and what is comes to Resident Evil, what more could you want?

Review as of 12/30/17
7.4 hours
Summary:
This game is not your regular farming simulator. You start off with your grandfather's old run down farm, repair tools, some scafolding, some sheet metal a weed trimmer, a couple run down tractor attachments and some advice from your friendly neighbor. Your job is to restore your family farm get some farm equipment and start making a living on farming. You will want to talk to everyone you meet because you will need their help and you can also start you're own family.
My Review:
I have played several of the old farming simulator games and figured this wouldn't be too far off and that I won't love it. But for some reason I instantly got caught into it. I like the Idea of starting with practicly nothing and inhereting a farm thats building should probably have been condemend and torn down. Once I finished the tutorial (which I don't want to spoil it for you) I found a weed trimmer (the devs plan on adding a proper lawn mower soon) in one of the building and started to cut the grass, that took a while but it looked much better and you don't want a yard that looks like crap. So then I got to repairing some buildings which suprisingly is my favorite part of the game. Eventually when you have money you can replace the building materials and restore the farm, but in the meantime you don't want a massive collapsed roof over your head when you sleep. Also there are quests that you will get social points, money or maybe equipment which gives the game a RPG aspect and you can also marry and have a wife and kids if you're into that. For a brand new early access game it has a good amount of content and playability. And the best part for me is that the devs are very active, they worked through the holidays when many game studios take off and they released a update. And they are also very active on the steam forums taking note of any suggested features that you give them on their wish list thread and also promptly fixing any bugs that you may find and post on their bug report thread. The only problem which is understandable being a brand new early access game is that some features and mechanics still need to fleshed out and I have spotted a exploit where you can get free materials and once you have it you have an unlimited amount but that will be fixed next week. But that exploit is something that other people like right now and is useful for testing the game and spoting bugs.
In short I think this game is really going somewhere, possibly the next big game. I'm glad that I jumped on when I did. Good game, Great devs and unlimited potential. I would say the only reason not to buy this game if you like the farming type games is if you want a already completed fleshed out game. Then wait a while and come back.
Edit: Oh and deformable terrain is nice.
Also I don't get why people with integrated graphics (not supported) are ignoring the minimum specs and buying it then giving it a bad review for not working on their system that does NOT meet the minimum specs.

This is a really good game, especially for EA. I have never played a Farming Simulator game, so I cannot compare it to that. This is not just a farm simulator game, this has much more to it. You can build relationships with towns people, farm, upgrade and repair buildings. People that I have watched say this feels more real than a simulator because of the other aspects that are a part of the game.
This game starts out like StarDew Valley (a game I enjoyed). You inherit a farm from your passing grandfather. It is run down and needs to be fixed up. You have no equipment or animals, so basically you start with just the farm and 2 fields. You get quests from the neighbors, which help to get you started. The starting quests give you equipment that you can use on your farm. The more quests you do, the more you can do in farming. The quests also give Social Points which allows you to buy stuff at discounted prices.
Game currently has:
Farming (plowing, cultivating, seeding, spreading manure, spreading fertilizer, harvesting, baling hay)
Quests
Buying  of equipment, seeds, animals, fields.
Selling harvest and food from animals.
Fishing (but haven't tried that yet)
Updating and repairing of buildings (you can also customize the look with the building supplies, you cannot build full buildings, only fix or update what is already there)
Building relationships with towns people
Marriage
Devs are actively working on the game and adding new things and trying to balance it as well. They also have a roadmap of items they want to add like AI helpers, traffic, rpg type skill trees and many other things.
There are a few issues, but it is expected in an EA game. The good thing is that the Devs are actively working on it and you can give concerns or comments in the Discussions. They also do receive email (heard from content creators that they have emailed and received responses) about issues as well. I really hope this continues do the road path, because this has been a fun game to play and there are many good features that are supposed to be added.
Do I recommend this game, yes.
While the terraforming looks and works great, the game itself is shallow and it seems more of tech demo than a game.

I have a problem where I get really into a game, and then I just do nothing but play that game until I get to a final stopping point. When I bought this game, I was thinking, "I'll just do the first ending, then wait for a patch to officially fix the graphics." That's not how it works. It became a full time commitment. I just couldn't stop. When I reached ending C, I decided to complete all the sidequests and get all the endings, which means: upgrading all weapons, finding 95% of the enemies, doing all 21 of the joke endings + the main 5. Main problem with this was the enemies, because you have to sometimes rely of luck based appearances, making you reload the game countless times till it shows up. For some people, it could take hours to do this. Eventually you level up enough and you can take out enemies really quickly, so worrying about getting all endings wasn't a problem. Also you have to farm for materials to upgrade your weapons. You will need a guide to get everything, and don't even think about 100%, too much luck based stuff.
When you're playing the game, you may be confused on some plot points, or you're just trying to find something, it can be tempting to look up the answer.
for you can easily run into spoilers, and for this game, it's best to avoid as much story points as possible.
Once you get ending C/D you should buy the DLC, it will unlock cool challenges, which is nice since the game starts to get easy at this point. After that, 100% the quests and do whatever you like then finish the ending again to get ending E. You get the option to delete your save at this point for a cool bonus. Maybe don't do it so you can unlock a little bit more of what you want. If you want to delete, you shoud screencap your progress, cool to look back on.
Really, I wouldn't buy it till they finally patch it, but I had so much fun, and spent so much time with it. It was easily worth $45+$12DLC.

I wanted to like this game, I really did.  While I appreciate what the developers were striving for, I just can't recommend this game to others.  On the surface this appears to be a Zelda clone.  While that sounds promising, on delving deeper into this title nothing could be further from the truth.  While Zelda relies on great combat and clever puzzles, Anodyne relies on unfair combat and ridiculously hard platforming.  Enemies don’t stop in their tracks or bounce back when you hit them, so enemies that require numerous hits invariably result in damage to you as they just plow forward through your attacks.  In addition, the number of times you die from attempting next to impossible jumps becomes too much to bear.  Add in that native controller support simply does not work (in the forums the developers even go so far as to suggest getting a third party program such as xpadder or joy2key to make it work) even though partial controller support is listed on the store page, and I feel you have a product that could have used a lot more polishing before releasing on Steam.  For every moment of fun I experienced with this game, I experienced several more of frustration.  On a side note, towards the end of the game suddenly the F word appeared several times in dialog, whereas the rest of the game had been devoid of swearing.  While I have no problem with swearing in video games, I was playing through this game with my young niece and this sudden unexpected change in tone was not appreciated nor did it seem to fit the game.  Overall I would rank this game a 5/10.

Do you like The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening? OK. Then play that.
Honestly, it's not terrible, but it borrows too heavily from a game that's much better than it is, and it suffers from the comparison. The biggest problem with it is that the overworld is too sparse and empty, whereas in Link's Awakening, every single screen was memorable. Finding things in Anodyne's overworld feels like combing a beach instead of being fun thing to explore in and of itself.

Recommended if you like open-ended exploration/adventure games.
If it weren't for the graphics, most of Anodyne could have been done as a ROM hack of the old GameBoy game Link's Awakening. The basic game mechanics are very close in look and feel to a Zelda game, particularly Link's Awakening. Like that game, the levels are laid out as a series of static screens which scroll when you reach the edge. The main character can move in 8 directions and attack in 4 directions, as well as jump over 1-tile sized pits and patches of spikes. The game controls are simple and responsive and best played with a gamepad or joystick.
Like most of these types of games, Anodyne can get boring at times especially if you get lost or stuck at a point where you don't know what to do next. There's no leveling up or even an economy in this game so if you don't know what to do next or where to go, then you are pretty much going to be stuck wandering around aimlessly with nothing to show for your time until you get back on track. Fortunately the game has a central "hub" world with lots of warp points which makes it relatively painless to navigate from place to place. Additionally there is a good auto-map feature to reduce backtracking, and each of the warp points has a red gem above it which lights up when you have gathered all of the quest items within a given area, so you won't spend time needlessly re-exploing a region if there's nothing else to find.
The core experience consists of exploring puzzle-filled dungeons in search of treasure chests containing "cards" which are used to open up numbered gates which block off different areas of the overworld. Each gate requires you to have a certain number of cards in your collection before it will open. You explore dungeons to get cards, and you use cards to access new parts of the overworld so you can access more dungeons and hence more cards, etc. A few of the dungeons have boss fights as well.
Combat is not as frequent or as intense as in a zelda game - the enemies are mostly slow moving, fairly passive, and come in small numbers. Later in the game there are a few challenging sections, but for the most part enemies are essentially "obstacles you can kill". They do however factor into many of the dungeon puzzles in interesting ways.
Within the dungeons, progress from room to room usually requires some combination of defeating all the enemies in a room to lower a gate, using a key to open a door, or solving a puzzle to remove some obstacle.
Unlike a Zelda game, Anodyne has very few treasures or special items to expand your abilities. Instead, puzzles are solved with the standard ability set and whatever is in the envirionment. Most puzzles involve devising ingenious ways to trigger multiple pressure plates at the same time, while other puzzles require precision jumping and are essentially top-down platforming. I have to give the designer a lot of credit here as the level layouts and puzzles are really very well done and better than most of what you see in the zelda series. One puzzle involves chasing giant silverfish creatures, which retreat from you when you cross their line of sight, onto pressure plates. The silverfish change their facing by 90 degrees at regular intervals, and you have to make sure to chase them in the right direction lest they be driven into spikes or full down a pit. I was reminded of sneaking past groups of guards in the Metal Gear games, except in this case instead of trying to sneak through an area undetected, you are sneaking around to ensure that you will be detected at the exact right place and time. Another creature-based puzzle reminded me of the Dreamcast game Chu Chu Rocket, and involves toggling a switch to raise and lower obstacles within a maze-like area so that a giant rat will pass over a pressure plate. Upon bumping into an obstacle, the rat will turn 90 degrees and keep moving forward. The trick is to time the raising and lowering of obstacles so that the rat turns in the direction you want it to go and doesn't run off to its own destruction. Other types of puzzles involve leaping from moving platforms, riding rafts made out of dust, or luring armored creatures into the path of turret fire so that you can use them as shields. Conspicuously (thankfully) absent are puzzles where you have to push blocks around, pull a series of levers in a specific order, or toggle a timed switch and then run through an obstacle course before the timer runs out.
Visually, the game is 8-bit style pixel art but with a considerably expanded color palette. The scenery is varied from area to area and very well done. Music is minimal and perfect in that it adds to the atmosphere but does not intrude. Sound effects are very zelda-ish, with plenty of audio cues when you discover something or solve a puzzle or anything along those lines.
The overall theme and story was incomprehensible to me. None of the characters or settings fit together in a way that I could understand, and the overall feeling of the game is less like the exploration of another world and more like wandering through a dream. Whether the creator was attempting at some kind of post-modern symbolism with all of the elements in the game or was going for literal surrealism, I don't know. It all went over my head but I will say that the mood created by the various locations and characters was interesting in its own right even if it didn't end up amounting to much of anything (at least to me).
Upon completion of the main quest you are given a special ability which makes it possible to explore previously inaccessible areas of the map and collect additional cards. I didn't bother with this but for completionists it's nice that there's some additional content there.
Overall a positive experience and a good contemplative sort of game to play when you don't have the energy for a faster paced game, nor the attention span for an RPG. It's the rare sort of comfort-food game that you can settle into and play in a relaxed state of mind.

Rising Storm 2 is an interesting game. It is a MilSim, yet it feels almost like Battlefield. Shooting in this game is much easier than in games like Squad and Arma, and the gun mechanics feel a bit like Insurgency.
The graphics are by no means the best, and actually can feel pretty poor at times, which makes me wonder why I only get 120 fps in this game. The official maps in this game are about the size of the maps in Battlefield, and the rest of the game, besides the shooting mechanics, stays true to what Rising Storm and Red Orchestra fans have come to expect.
It already has tons of custom maps, to the point where I have only played several of the official ones, and there are plenty of populated servers at all times of the day. Just like Insurgency, I feel like this is a good introduction for anyone interested in getting into MilSims, although there is not near as much teamwork and coordination as there is in a game like Squad.
Also good luck getting any class other than Grunt...

RS2: Vietnam is quite possibly the most difficult yet enjoyable game that I've bought on Steam. At first, I nearly refunded the game due to the difficulty and performance issues, but with a little tweaking to the in-game settings as well as Nvidia Control Panel, I can play the game on Ultra at 60fps most of the time. This performance improvement allowed me to get a better feel of the fast-paced combat and the movement of my character, therefore, improving the overall experience.
Firstly, if you think that RS2 has simular gameplay to Call of Duty or Battlefield, you're hilariously wrong. This game is up there with the likes of Arma, except with a Vietnam twist. If you plan on buying this game with that wrong expectation, God help you because this will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. With that being said, if you like games similar to Arma, you'll love this. At first, you'll die dozens upon dozens of times before making a good chunk of kills. At the time of writing this review, I've spent 2.7 hours in-game and have already acclimated to it's unique and challenging feel. Don't let the difficulty scare you, just keep playing.
Secondly, I want to dive into the game's performance. On a scale of 0-100, I'd give this game a 75. The engine is on it's last breath of life, yet manages to somehow do the job. If you plan on just tweaking the in-game settings, I'd place a bet that you'll run into some major issues. I am currently running a GTX 660, and this game does surprisingly well with that 2GB VRAM hunk of CUDA cores. I eliminated all performance issues by disabling a few of the fancier options (Bloom, light rays, etc.), as well as disabling V-Sync in-game and instead forcing it through Nvidia Control Panel. Strangely enough, GTA V presented a simular issue in the past, and that same V-Sync trick fixed it.
Finally, the content of the game is on the lesser side as of now, but it's very polished. Weapons look great, maps are amazingly detailed, and the music is *kisses the air* awesome. If you're a fan of those Vietnam movies from back in the day, this will make you feel like you're making one. The weapons are very balanced, and the game does amazingly with delivering a terrifying yet amazing Vietnam War experience.

Its a top down racer that finishes as soon as you run out of petrol. The Main objective simply seems to be to reach level 10 in order to unlock the hardest car to get. Once you have unlocked all 10 cars by reaching level 10 there seems to be little to no replay ability.

* Add 10 more levels with different obstacles.

I really like this game it is similar to the Farming Simulator series but adds interesting elements like social points which allow you to get discounts on new farm equipment and you can get married and raise a family. Which adds many elements from harvest moon in a realistic setting. Also you must eat and sleep regularly and to add more social points you can talk to people on the huge map and build up individual relationships. You can do jobs for various people and they will trade old rusted farm equipment for food or just earn cash.
You use this to build up your income in the beginning stages. Later you can buy new equipment and theres a nice variety of vehicles which all have different driving experiences.
Your rusty old tractor is fully articulated and it putts along as you plough fields slowly churning up the landscape, But of course the new equipment is what you want as it will yield more from your crops faster. As in farming simulator..
You start by doing up your starter farm. You can errect scafolding and repair the roof and most elements of the barn and main house. It has a simplified mechanic so theres no crafting but it works and you do feel your acomplishing something while building and repairing.
Later on when you earn some money you can buy building materials to enhance your farm. You have various tools to work with nailgun and grinder. Which you use on various parts of the house.
For an early access game this feels very complete and polished and you will be amazed at the content on offer here compared to other early access titles. I would say they are just ironing out bugs before the final release but maybe they will add little touches here and there but it's a very fleshed out game mechanic at it's current state..
I did noticed when it rained the game chugged so theres probably a minor bug in the weather system which they will probably fix pretty quickly.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

I never had the chance to play 'Gun' when it was first released, and so these past few days I've been catching up on what I missed out on. At the time of writing this review I've logged almost 8 hours, and I completed the game this afternoon. Given that I also spent an hour or two completing various side quests and activities, it's safe to say that 'Gun' is a rather short game, and can be easily completed in two or three casual sessions. The developers packed a lot of content into the brief play-time, though, and the last two to three hours of the story are incredibly fun.
The world of 'Gun' isn't as richly layered as that of the 'Red Dead ' games, and the action isn't quite as thrilling as that of 'Call of Juarez'. I wouldn't call it an inferior title, though; the balance between gunfighting and adventure is maintained rather well in this game. The storyline is rather standard for a Western, but even the most clichéd moments are fun to experience.
Unless it's a childhood memory of yours and you're buying it on Steam for nostalgia, I doubt you'll walk away from 'Gun' calling it an all-time favourite. But I don't think you'll dislike it, either. For me, 'Gun' stands as a solidly above-average shooter with many more positives than negatives.

Game of Thrones The Role Playing Game
REVIEW FROM LIGHT RPG PLAYER
Story
The story is of 2 main characters that are both playable. Mors Westford a sworn brother of the night's watch who has been a member for 15 years and at the beginning is hunting down deserters of the night's watch. Alester Sarwyck a red priest who dissapeared 15 years ago and has returned to his home town of Riverspring to find it in its worst state poverty, riots and his ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brother Valaar is set to marry his sister and become lord of Riverspring. About half way through the game these 2 characters meet up and together thwart the plot that threatens the kingdom and exact vengeance apon those who have made them suffer.
Gameplay
The combat is a tactical RPG (like dragon age) that has energy involved when you run out of energy you have to wait for it to recharge or use a potion so you can use your special attacks again. It is a very simple combat system to learn but hours to master it is fun and a different take on combat like The Witcher series for example. However towards the end of the game the combat becomes both frustrating and difficult to pull through a fight I played this on the easiest difficulty and I found it difficult till the very end.
Graphics
You normally won't see a graphics section on my reviews but I have to mention it for this game the graphics are awful if you have bought a really good computer to run a really graphically enhanced game like Battlefield 4 don't get this game the graphics really are awful and there should be no excuse for a 7 year project which is what this game was. An example of how bad they are is that most characters will fold their arms this completely ruins the immersion as one arm is inside of the other it looks terrible so again if graphics are your thing don't get this game.
Open World
Now technically this game has an open world however it is in sections like in Assassins Creed however if you are a huge fan of the show like myself then you will love the locations in this game they look almost exactly like they do on the show. An example of this is The Throne Room when you enter you can see all the pillars that are in the show and of course The Iron Throne it really is the best we can get in a video game until we play the telltale version of this world.
Voice Acting
In this game the voice acting is not AAA it is ok the majority of characters you meet have average voice acting but with it being a Game of Thrones game the voice talents of Lena Headey, James Cosmo and Conleth Hill are used with the charcters Cersei Lannister, Joer Mormont and Lord Varys these actors and Lena Headey had an interest in the game and they provided their voice work which is really good it's great to see how devoted they are to the show and the fan base. But now onto Mors and Alester's voices at the beginning Mors sound like a british Batman which is quite hilarious however as you play more you get used to it. Alester is at best above average voice acting which is fine for a main character.
Final Verdict
I will be honest if this RPG was not called Game of Thrones I never would have played it however this game has one of the best stories in gaming and should be played for that, the combat is good, the graphics are awful, the locations are great and the voice acting is ok.

Does Adventure Capitalist need a review? Sure why not; I review everything else on Steam, lets get into it. As with most games like this, there are plenty of unfunny joke reviews that will fill up the front store page for this game so I'm hoping to beat the trend and give some points about the game.
First of all, Adventure Capitalist is a game, about, well capitalism. You are an investor setting out to make your fortune. This game is very similar to the likes of Cookie Clicker, which first came to fame in 2010, is still a mega popular game today. You start off buying lemonade stands, each click on the lemonade stand generates money, with that money buy another stand, so on and so on. Eventually you have enough money to hire a manager for your lemonade stand. The manager acts as the clicker, so you can leave the game running (or close it down) and you will still generate money. You then work up to other investments following the same pattern, and no sooner have you started, you will soon be a millionaire. With your millions you can also purchase upgrades to your investments, such as increasing profit by 3% or something similar.
This is where AC is different to other clicker games, you no longer actually need to spam click in order to make progress, since you have your managers working over time for you. What I really like about AC is that you can close the game down, and you will still be generating money, meaning you can let your funds mount up for a couple of days, log back in, spend it all, and watch your money roll in for a bit, then log out.
The UI is so brilliantly displayed, you can work your way around all the menus with ease, and you can find all of the information you could ever need either on the main screen or within 2 clicks. Be warned, this game not only has highly addictive gameplay, the soundtrack is almost just as addictive. Once that song gets in your head, it just will not leave.
AC is not hard at all, it just seems to be a time-sink, and one that keeps you logging back in on a daily basis. You can see just by the amount of hours I have in this game already just how easy it is to loose yourself in a really simple game. I would say I am not in the game for longer than 15 minutes on a daily basis, but it does keep bringing you back just so you can see what made up number of money you have made over night.
The developers are always adding new content to this game as well; recently there was an update which allows you to continue making your fortunes on the moon! This runs along side your regular empire back on earth, meaning twice as many investments to manage and oggle at crazy sums of money.
Given that AC is a free to play game, you have no harm in trying it out. I would say that even if you just load it up every couple of days to check it out, you will still get a lot of enjoyment out of it. There is also an iOS version of the game, but unfortunately it does not link up with your game on Steam; that would of been just too good if it did. Maybe it's a potential possibility in the future.
I really strongly recommend AdVenture Capitalist; its a simple, yet horribly addictive game, that allows you to pop in and hour of the game with ease for ten minutes at a time. Play in small doses to get the full effect!

To preface this, I have 300 hour in Borderlands 2, all of the expansion DLCs and have beaten the game 7 times.  I love the game, but am not necessarily an uber-fan.
The Presequel feels like a terrible fan game.  I was actually surprised by how much went wrong in the first hour.
- The voice acting is mediocre at best.
- Which makes the main character(s) having a speaking role all the more jarring.
- The enemies and environment feel uninspired and simplistic.
- The humor is all wonky.  I don't know how to describe it but it sounds a bit like a 7 year old wrote all the jokes.
- All of the enemies in the starter area have obnoxious HP and damage and are carbon copies of each other.  I didn't see a new enemy type until the first boss, and his second stage was just to become a particularly tough normal enemy.
- The characters from BL 1 and 2 are talking over the game as narrators, which makes the game feel very disjointed.
All in all, the game feels like what happens when you forget what made BL2 great (haven't played the first), so all you're left with is bad puns and "lul so randum" characters.

Really good game.
A lot of the negative reviews it gets are about the PC port being buggy - I hate to be that "works on my machine" guy but I didn't encounter any game-breaking bugs, there were a few glitches but honestly I found them pretty funny (like people floating outside their cars), and they didn't impede my progress at all. Admittedly it did crash once (and kept doing so at that point), but for some reason putting it in windowed mode fixed it (and I switched back after).
That aside, the actual game is great. Great music, setting, story and characters. Gameplay is a bit wonky but you get used to it. There's also a lot of side missions to let you know more about the side characters and the town, and lots of cool (and useful) things you can find/buy. The only gripes I have are that some sections could drag on for a bit too long, and were quite tedious, like following someone who's driving painstakingly slowly for ages. Also the driving controls are terrible, let's not dance around that. Early cars barely turn at all, and later cars go way too fast and turn too sharply, making them flip over and spin wildly out of control. Lastly, there are extended QTE sequences that are also pretty tedious, and you usually die immediately if you mess up, having to go back and start the entire sequence again.
However, even with all that, this game is one of the few these days that made me actually want to come back and keep playing, and see the story through to the end. The characters felt realistic and had depth instead of being generic flat characters like in most other games.
I don't even know what genre this game would be. It isn't really a horror game, and it's not really a murder mystery either, it sort of combines elements from lots of different genres, and has a wacky humorous theme mixed in with darker elements. It's sort of like a weirder Japanese version of Twin Peaks.
tl;dr I had a lot of fun playing this. It was a great game from start to finish, even with some iffy patches along the way. Contrary to what most of the negative reviews say, it's not "unplayable". It runs pretty well on my mid-tier PC, and has setting adjustment options.
Just try it out if it looks like something you'd enjoy, and don't worry about all the horror stories about the PC port. They're mainly gross exaggeration.

I remember picking up that game for 30€ on Xbox360, close to its release, not really knowing what it was all about, discovering the aliasing, the horrible textures, the stiff animations and the myriad of incomprehensible game-design choices. Like, why the hell does the map rotate in the map-menu? It's confusing as hell, you can't find anything because of that. Oh and why do I have to look at it so closely? Why is the game using the music so strangely? It sometimes feels like there are four tracks and it's using some of them in the weirdest moments. Why are does survival/shooting session so boring and tedious, and why aren't they integrated better in the rest of the game? Why is the car so slow and why is the steering angle so narrow?Why...?
You would think that "what the f*ck?" would be a better question to go along the strange nature of the game. But at first, you'll be far too busy questionning every decision made during the development process, to really, thoroughly pay attention to how much the game is up there in its head. You are probably going to hate it for a while. But you are going to stick with it, wanting to come back.
At first, the main character makes you stay. He talks to himself, to you maybe. And you'll want to hear what he has to say when you'll first him talk to you about "Jaws". Then you are going to stay for the plot, ripping off Twin Peaks so amazingly well and with its very own quirks, with a whole new level of bizarre, that you won't even be able to say that it is plagiarism, when it obviously is plagiarism. Then you are going to understand the crappy controls, deal with it, and actually explore the map, talk to every character and learn about there great and diverse personalities, even with the poor navigation help that the game gives you (it's hard to find anything with the game this ugly). And hopefully, you are going to be touched, creeped out and amused (a lot) by the story, amazed by the twists and turns, the gameplay even, not in it's execution, but in its structure and ideas that wan and will works (sometimes not, let's be honest). And hopefully, you are going to LOVE IT.
That's what happened to me. That's what happened to all my friends who enjoyed it. Give it six hours. Give it the time to lead you to the big reunion in the community center. At that point, you'll be far too concern about the plot to let the amazingly low production value steer you away from the game. Hell, you'll probably even enjoy the game despite AND because of that poor production value that, somehow, adds to the game's personality.

Rising Storm 2 is an interesting game. It is a MilSim, yet it feels almost like Battlefield. Shooting in this game is much easier than in games like Squad and Arma, and the gun mechanics feel a bit like Insurgency.
The graphics are by no means the best, and actually can feel pretty poor at times, which makes me wonder why I only get 120 fps in this game. It already has tons of custom maps, to the point where I have only played several of the official ones, and there are plenty of populated servers at all times of the day. Just like Insurgency, I feel like this is a good introduction for anyone interested in getting into MilSims, although there is not near as much teamwork and coordination as there is in a game like Squad.
Also good luck getting any class other than Grunt...

RS2: Vietnam is quite possibly the most difficult yet enjoyable game that I've bought on Steam. At first, I nearly refunded the game due to the difficulty and performance issues, but with a little tweaking to the in-game settings as well as Nvidia Control Panel, I can play the game on Ultra at 60fps most of the time. This performance improvement allowed me to get a better feel of the fast-paced combat and the movement of my character, therefore, improving the overall experience.
Firstly, if you think that RS2 has simular gameplay to Call of Duty or Battlefield, you're hilariously wrong. This game is up there with the likes of Arma, except with a Vietnam twist. If you plan on buying this game with that wrong expectation, God help you because this will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. With that being said, if you like games similar to Arma, you'll love this. At first, you'll die dozens upon dozens of times before making a good chunk of kills. At the time of writing this review, I've spent 2.7 hours in-game and have already acclimated to it's unique and challenging feel. Don't let the difficulty scare you, just keep playing.
Secondly, I want to dive into the game's performance. On a scale of 0-100, I'd give this game a 75. The engine is on it's last breath of life, yet manages to somehow do the job. If you plan on just tweaking the in-game settings, I'd place a bet that you'll run into some major issues. I am currently running a GTX 660, and this game does surprisingly well with that 2GB VRAM hunk of CUDA cores. I eliminated all performance issues by disabling a few of the fancier options (Bloom, light rays, etc.), as well as disabling V-Sync in-game and instead forcing it through Nvidia Control Panel. Strangely enough, GTA V presented a simular issue in the past, and that same V-Sync trick fixed it.
Finally, the content of the game is on the lesser side as of now, but it's very polished. Weapons look great, maps are amazingly detailed, and the music is *kisses the air* awesome. If you're a fan of those Vietnam movies from back in the day, this will make you feel like you're making one. The weapons are very balanced, and the game does amazingly with delivering a terrifying yet amazing Vietnam War experience.
I rate this game 100/100 rice fields.

Alright, I got this game as a gift, I am just going to say that this game is a must-have if you're into grand strategy, space, or both of those categories. First, I like the game for its randomly generated galaxies (even though some are complete flops, for example encountering a gas-giant civilization or something 3 times in a row), which constantly give you something new to discover or see. I have played this game for a long time, and I'm still finding cool new things that I've never seen before, all while getting benefits for my empire.
Second, You can create and command your own empire that suits your playstyle. This has inspired me to create entire STORYLINES and LORE, Even though you can't design what your species will look like exactly. You can create whatever kind of empire you want, be that A race that wants to destroy the entire galaxy, or turn themselves into androids (which is only possible with the Utopia DLC), or one that wants everyone in the galaxy to worship the religion that your species worships. And that names a few possibilites.
Third, You can research a vast tree of technology, which will benefit your empire in many ways. These technologies range from Fusion power, Cloning, Faster travel, and Colored lasers all the way to Zero-point power, Androids, Instant FTL Travel, and Harnessing the power of supercharged particles!
The possibilities are (nearly) endless in Stellaris, and I am incredibly happy that this game exists.

I have a problem where I get really into a game, and then I just do nothing but play that game until I get to a final stopping point. When I bought this game, I was thinking, "I'll just do the first ending, then wait for a patch to officially fix the graphics." That's not how it works. It became a full time commitment. I just couldn't stop. When I reached ending C, I decided to complete all the sidequests and get all the endings, which means: upgrading all weapons, finding 95% of the enemies, doing all 21 of the joke endings + the main 5. Main problem with this was the enemies, because you have to sometimes rely of luck based appearances, making you reload the game countless times till it shows up. For some people, it could take hours to do this. Eventually you level up enough and you can take out enemies really quickly, so worrying about getting all endings wasn't a problem. Also you have to farm for materials to upgrade your weapons. You will need a guide to get everything, and don't even think about 100%, too much luck based stuff.
When you're playing the game, you may be confused on some plot points, or you're just trying to find something, it can be tempting to look up the answer.
for you can easily run into spoilers, and for this game, it's best to avoid as much story points as possible.
Once you get ending C/D you should buy the DLC, it will unlock cool challenges, which is nice since the game starts to get easy at this point. After that, 100% the quests and do whatever you like then finish the ending again to get ending E. You get the option to delete your save at this point for a cool bonus. Maybe don't do it so you can unlock a little bit more of what you want. If you want to delete, you shoud screencap your progress, cool to look back on.
Really, I wouldn't buy it till they finally patch it, but I had so much fun, and spent so much time with it. It was easily worth $45+$12DLC.

It's easy to describe NieR: Automata in parts, but hard to convey what it's like in an overall sense. All in all, if you enjoy character-driven stories, I'd definitely recommend it; however, if you don't have a high-end PC, you may want to either look into the FAR mod or get the game on PS4.
The graphics are a perfect example of doing more with less. Instead of chasing after the newest, most bleeding-edge graphical techniques like a dog after a speeding car, Platinum focused on the design of the world. Their spaces are gorgeous and serene, relying on color, atmosphere, shape, silhouette, and the openness and closedness of spaces -- all of which are more effective for setting a mood than the highest-resolution textures would ever be. (That said, the game is more graphically intensive than it ought to be given the texture quality. Other users are reporting major performance problems stemming from bad PC optimization, and I'm sure those would be significant on a middle- or low-end machine.)
The gameplay frequently changes between 3D hack-and-slash, side-scrolling combat, and a top-down shoot-em-up. You can become stronger by leveling your character up through combat, upgrading weapons (through fixed ranks) with found materials, and equipping "plug-in chips" -- essentially a lore-based skill point system with re-spec'ing. Combat feels fun and satisfying to master, but difficulty is a bit of a mixed bag. On the one hand, there are some sidequests where enemies have unexpectedly high levels without any advance warning, forcing you to either give up or endure a long slog against a damage sponge. On the other hand, by mid-to-late-game, you'll have the plug-in chips you'll need to be able to tank damage pretty effortlessly, though not necessarily to the point where you can win without paying attention. Something to watch out for: the game world isn't leveled (a la Skyrim), so if you overlevel, you'll be able to one-shot bosses, at least on Normal difficulty.
The game world has a lot more variety than you might expect based on the rusty, industrial first level; the environments range from serene to outright fanciful while still feeling plausible. Zones unlock as you progress through the story; some people describe this game as "open world," but in that regard, the world is less like Skyrim and more like Borderlands and Ocarina of Time. As far as narrative goes, while most games use sidequests to pad out their length with filler material, NieR: Automata uses sidequests to build and expand on its world, revealing more and more about the minds, perspectives, and relationships of its characters and peoples. Even minor, one-note storylines serve to teach you more about the world and immerse you deeper into it, and they seldom feel like lectures or infodumps. That said, quest designs rarely diverge from the usual trio you see in games: "
," "talk to this thing," or "kill this thing."
The character writing is excellent. The key characters -- main and supporting -- each have a texture to them, and often a startling degree of depth. It's easy to describe characters as one-note archetypes based on first impressions, but as the story runs on, you really get to know these people, and they feel real. Few games manage to have even a single character that feels so convincing, and this game has half a dozen of them. It's very easy to get invested in them.
And I think that's about all I can say without spoiling anything.
