Please take into account that a 5 to me means average, anything higher is above average.  5-6 is serviceable but nothing special or groundbreaking, 6-7 is serviceable with some good aspects, 7-8 consists of good to great aspects, but a there are still noticeable problems and annoyances, sometimes to a degree that will turn a player off, and deter it from being a 9-10, or a game of masterful craftsmanship, where a game has very minorest, are either unnoticeable entirely or small enough that the rest of the quality in the game masks it.
The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past.  Secret of Mana.  Hyper Light Drifter.
CrossCode is the result of taking the very best mechanics and design philosophies of these three excellent games, and it never feels like an unispired clone of any, never resting on these laurels, for it never completely replicates these games.
Story: 7.5 ( While they play with tropes, there are still too many )
The first noticeable difference when you start playing is the setting / narrative as a whole.  The plot of CrossCode shares almost no similarities to the plot devices of the other games.  That isn't to say it's completely original, which it isn't.  As it draws from the best gameplay mechanics of the three games already mentioned, so to does it draw from, or replicate the best concepts and themes of existing franchises, creating something better in the process, while managing to feel unique regardless of similarities.
Some might compare it to the .Hack series, but in truth it is more similar to that of the high fantasy series Otherland, novels where people are becoming trapped within it's virtual cyberspace, comatose in the real world. And just like in the Otherland books, CrossCode has a diverse amount of areas, all with important and well-thought out narratives, quests, and characters, each one totally different from the next and never staying on one genre setting, stretching across the fantasy and science fiction genres.  It isn't just a science fiction story and world, and it isn't just fantasy.  It does a great job of balancing the two.  Unfortunately, it still uses tropes that have been repeated ad nauseum in this industry, and that's the anmesiac protaganist.  On the other side of the coin is the developers played with this trope a bit, making your character mute because the code of the MMO she is in isn't working properly with her avatar, causing you to slowly learn phrases over the course of the game.  You get flashes of dreams and visions as you progress throgh the story, but none do a decent job of really hinting at Lea's origins, almost as if the developer cares more the world's story than the character's, but this is only from the perspective of where the story goes to now, as there will be much more to come.
Because it's Early Access it's hard to judge how compelling the narrative is, or might become.  As it stands now, the areas you do get to explore that are essential to the playable story sequences feel like a patchwork at times, with a lot of dense activity in one area but not much further away it feels completely empty of gameplay of any sort.  Fortunately, in these areas you can easily see where something might be added.  Finally, in regards to the story is the Guild that you join, as well as other factions' quests. To put it simply, the Guild is my favorite part of the story so far, has the most promising of the main narratives, and the amount of quests you can find throughout the world that aren't even connected to the guild but to other factions, and even many that are completely unique, is very impressive, especially considering much more will be added.
Gameplay: 8 ( Great Combat Action / Horrible, Micromanagement Economy
The second thing that helps CrossCode stand apart from the other games, where gameplay is concerned, is the by having a combat system that has more depth than what you would except from a game of its kind.  Within the game-world, Leah is considered a Spheromancer class, which is the jack-of-all-trades.  There are five elements, one being neutral, each with their own skill trees and combat arts that you unlock throughout the game, and then switch back and forth between them.  While every element you use has the same type of combat arts ( Melee, Guard, Ranged, etc ), the skills for each of them changing depending on the mode, so you have a nice degree of flexibility in playstyles.  The four elements you get to use are capable of overheating after a fashion, so it forces you switch between attack styles and keeps you on your toes.  Finally, when you unlock a new element and skill-tree you will discover that you have the same amount of skill points to allocate as you did for the others, so every style will always feel equal and not underpowered.
While I applaud the combat and action in general, there are other areas that hinder the game from being truly exceptional.  The first of these issues is the economy and how acquiring gear, items, and materials work.  To be frank, it's obtuse, unintuitive, and downright awful.  It simply becomes a chore of trying to keep track of every material you need to trade for more of another material for more of another, to get a piece of equipment or a certain amount of item.  On top of which you still you need to spend your hard earned money as well.  It makes no sense to have a bartering system where the NPCs charge you for buying items that also require the several different types of materials.  They always require several types of materials, usually multiple of both, and many of these can only be found by trading other materials to vendors at a completely different part of the game-world.  Because materials are the only form of loot, meaning all equipment and items needs to be found via the economy and chests, their is a severe progression problem.
The gear that you do get after the hassle is actually a highlight, as besides the normal attribute changes, they almost always come with unique passive traits.  A gear might give you a bigger time window for making a perfect guard and counter attack, or make it quicker to aim, move faster, more critical hits, etc.  There are a lot of traits to be discovered, which can make a noticeable impact.  It is just unfortunate the amount of unneccesary backtracking and micromanagement needed to acquire items and equipment.  Even for consumables work in this fashion, where you need two to three types of materials, and typically several of each.  When you discover that some of the consumables, be it defensive gains or strength-based ones, come in three degrees of strength and a few degrees of length, the longest being sixty seconds, you will most likely not go through the hassle of acquiring them or will hardly use them because you will want to hoard them, despite them not being all that important.
You will acquire AI-controlled teammates which is a great addition to the game, and also a very perplexing one.  This is where, besides the graphics, the game resembles Secret of Mana the most.  You set tactics for your companions and that's all the control you have over them.  Their addition drastically impacts the gameplay for the better, each companion being a specific class and having their own unique abilites.  Which is where it gets perplexing, and in all honesty, disrespectful to the player / consumer.  The game goes to great length to explain six other classes that exist in this MMO game-world only to force the player to be the jack-of-all-trades.  You cannot switch classes at any point and there are not sub-classes.  The closest thing to a subclass is using particular companions, but so far in the game you basically only have two unique class-based companions available to you.  The reason is balancing issues, which is inexcusable when they basically tease you that they are there and you can't play them.  To be fair, it's more disrespectful than ruinous gameplay.

Great game with tight controls and beautiful retro graphics. Imagine one (three total), big, random Super Meat Boy level. This level will have you go down instead of up. There's also a timer that will force you to keep going. You can extend the timer by killing enemies and collecting their power-ups, or by unlocking certain achievements. The levels become harder the further down you get, and there are some cool boss fights that will remind anyone of the earlier Mega Man games. There are also in-game achievements that will unlock new weapons, abilities and outfits, making the game supposedly easier later on.
The screenshots had me worried this would be 'one of those' games (you know, simple graphics and gameplay, zero heart and fun), but I'm so glad I gave this a try. Super House Of Dead Ninjas is really the opposite. It's a brilliant little hardcore platformer.
And now that the game has proper controller support it's even more fun to play it.
Highly recommended !

Borderlands: The Pre Sequel tells the story of what happened between the two previous Borderlands installments (thus both "pre" and "sequel" i guess :)), but this isn't a game you really play for the story. Don't get me wrong, it's filled to the brim with hilarious moments, but after every quick laugh you'll be focusing on two things: shooting and looting. And this does a pretty good at both of them - Shooting is simplistic but fun and there are about a gazillion different guns, shields etc in this game thanks to random generation and mutliple different stats. Mind you it all get's a bit grindy though.
The game is set in space this time and this means you'll spend about half your time in low gravity environments. This is a double edged sword, as it adds the immensely fun "gravity slam" mechanic (which i will really miss in the next Borderlands game if they don't include it), but also makes the game feel a bit more sad and lonely than Borderlands 2.
Fans of the previous two games should definitely pick this up to see how jack and the other vault hunters come to be who they are and - of course - for the mindless fun that is the Borderlands shoot & loot formula :). New players should also join in in said mindless fun, but i'd suggest playing through Borderlands 2 first - you'll enjoy The Pre Sequel a bit more this way.

While SR2 is quite similar to a GTA game, there are some core differences. The most obvious one is that, while GTA likes to downplay the inherent anarchy that flourishes within the game, Saint's Row embraces it, and lets you go nuts. For example, the notoriety mechanic. If, at any point, you find yourself surrounded by members of a rival gang, you can choose to begin firing randomly at civilians, by which point cops will come running and take the thugs off your hands. Another example is the cars. Saint's Row 2 completely ignores physics for these bits, and just lets you go wild, smashing through groups of pedestrians with not even a scratch on you.

Saints Row 2 is still to this very day an incredibly fun game to play once you get into it. It may not have the depth and content of a GTA game, but it's got a lot of charm and just pure fun.
The city of Stillwater is a sprawling metropolis that feels alive and filled with detail. It may be relatively small compared to the worlds of newer sandbox titles, but each area is unique and memorable.
The gameplay, as I said previously, is incredibly fun. Reckless driving and well-made combat is the essence of the game and key to what makes it what it is. It feels tight (although the handling could be a little better, but I understand in the context of the game it makes sense to be poor) and the systems are easy to get used to.
However, this basic gameplay is somewhat ruined by the Respect system, which I feel brings the game down. The Respect system basically entails that you must fill up your Respect bar to play missions. This is done by doing Activites around the city. My grudge with this is that the game forces you to play what would be considered "side missions" or trivial activities in other games in order to enjoy the main meat of the game. There's about 10 or so of these different activities and 5 levels of them can be completed each, with a higher difficulty each time. They're relatively enjoyable at first, but as I got further in I got frustrated at the fact I was forced into doing these Activities, all of which I had done before but at a lower difficulty, just to play the main game missions and stronghold missions.
The game advertises itself as having a raft of customisation options - while there is customisation options, these are nowhere near as detailed the advertising would have you suggest. There is some nice choices, although I never really saw them as a big part of the game.
The graphics are nothing special, but you do have to remember this was released in 2008 - although it isn't really an issue to me anyway. The controls are pretty much fine too.
The story is actually quite good for a game in this genre. Sure, it has your typical violence-fuelled gang warfare, but it also has an underlying humour about it that makes you love it. On the surface, it doesn't seem that interesting, but as you move forward, you begin to really take in the cutscenes and engage in the story.
My second main criticism of this game (other than the Respect system) is that there's simply not enough interesting stuff to really do in Stillwater. After you get a few hours into the game the Activities feel like a chore rather than a fun side mission, and when you get bored of exploring Stillwater while running people over and attracting police attention there isn't actually that much else to do. This makes the game feel surprisingly linear for a sandbox game, which is obviously the opposite of what the developers were intending to achieve. The world of Stillwater is there, and it's alive, but I felt a severe lack of participation in it.
It's also worth noting this PC port has very, very bad FPS drops and it can be annoying even at the best of times.
To conclude, Sants Row 2 is a very fun game at its core. It has great gameplay mixed with an enjoyable story, and a world that feels well-designed and lively. However, the game is brought down by the Respect system and also the lack of actual content you want to do outside the missions. The FPS drops in this port can also be a general annoyance. However, Saints Row 2 is still a very good game that you'd do well to pick up for cheap sometime in order to have hours of good old-fashioned carnage and fun.

To start off, I enjoy both this and Overwatch, having about equal time in each.
Paladins is one of those games that upon first viewing, looks like an inferior clone of another game, in this case, Overwatch. But if you were to take a *little* more time to inspect why people play both, you may find something to enjoy. Paladins is first person shooter with team objectives, as you can probably see, but it also introduces a few MOBA elements, such as not being able to switch characters and buying items for more power. Many will see both of these as features that only "filthy casuals" enjoy having, but I feel it adds a little bit more tension to each match, where the selected character isn't as effective against the enemy team, or buying certain items can turn a game around if done right.
Personally, I feel as though the Champions to be more creative than Overwatch's heroes. Most of the heroes in Overwatch operate in a fairly simple manner, but naturally have some unique skills - fly, become a turret, create walls, freeze enemies and run on walls, to name a few. The minor issue of repeatability is true of both games, but more variation adds to an experience. The most unique traits of Paladins' champions that I can list off the top of my head are: becoming invisible, throwing weapons, giving teammates shields, and poisoning enemies.
There is also a healthy community. By healthy, I mean there are people playing, much like other games, some players are still.. interesting.
I can't really work this in, but it's free and doesn't run horribly on most machines, old or new.
Those are my thoughts on the game, please excuse me for my messy, unorganized review.

Ok that was a little longer then I was expecting, anyway onto the more detailed part.First this game is set in a setting where you can play as an avatar in an other world. Key word "an other world" meaning people are able to play on Earth as an avatar that will physically be walking and talking on a distant planet in space some where. Every person starts on a place called the bridge where you go through a tutorial so you know how the game is played. At least everyone is supposed to start there... Any way you first play through a prolog? maybe? kinda thing as a girl named Shizuka. She's trying to get to her brother and has to fight aganist some mysterious guy and his robots. When she finally does get to her brother, she gets there in time to see him.. well I'll let you play that part your self. Any way you wake up as a amnesic girl named Lea, who is at the bottom of this big ship (where first time avatars or avatars in general aren't supposed to be). While you are there a guy named sergey begans to talk to you via some kind of personal link connection that he has set up with Lea. We find out that Lea has speech issues with her avatar and sergey will have to help her with a work around for her speech. After the troubles he'll help you get through a tutorial and later on you meet some of the crew. You are finally let off the ship and put back where all little good avatars should be, a place what they call the playground where all the avatarsa are. You find out that since Lea has lost her memory that maybe if she played the game once again that maybe she'll regain her memory. And thats basically what you have to do the more you play the game the more mute Lea remembers. It gets more intense as she remembers more, and frustrating as Lea trys to get her memories out with the speech problems she has. I'll leave it at that so you can play the game yourself. This game is a masterpiece, and nothing short of it.
Pros :
+Enjoyable, and even captivating, story.
+Great artwork
+Beautiful environments. (ties in with artwork)
+Good music.
+Phenominal gameplay. (combat, movement, etc.)
+Humorous where it attempts to be. Dramatic where it needs it. A nice balance between fun and seriousness.
+Full controller support (for those of you who despise mouse/keyboard)
+Easy to learn/manage menus.
+Easy to pick up, harder to master.
Cons : There is only really one or two Cons so I'll be a bit more lengthy with it.
-Could use significant difficulty adjustments. It's very easy to level (and therefor over-level) as you progress in the story. This makes many fights that should be significantly difficult, well, significantly easier. This includes bosses, side-bosses, and just general mooks to be cleaned up. There is no difficulty setting either so you can't make the game harder on yourself to counter act this. For some people, this isn't necessarily a bad thing, but for others it's a bit of an issue.
-Locked class. As we know, there are 6 total classes in the world of CrossCode. We only get to experience playing with one of them however. I have no issues playing with that one class but having the knowledge that there are other classes in the game - it kind of makes me wish you could play with those as well.
Seriously though, buy this game. You absolutely will not regret it.

This game is awful without a controller. Nearly unplayable. With a controller it becomes tolerable, but still has many annoyances.
PROS:
- Could be a decent game.
- Has some good moments in the story.
CONS:
- Almost every aspect of the game is a time waster, meant to hide the lack of content.
- Time savers and increased loot drops are vastly increased as you progress. I can't find a great reason to explore on your first playthrough.
- Combat only rarely is "interesting". Interesting being more encouragement of combos, weapon styles, and enemy attacks and NOT simply upping damage so no mistakes can be made.
- Awful hacking minigame, even by hacking minigame standards.
- Controls are meh, especially in larger horde combat.
First the game's design purposefully adds time to every activity. Do you start running at full speed? No. You build up to it. Do you start out with "fast travel"? No, you wait until you get 1/3-1/2 of the way through the story. Do you start out with timesavers, like auto loot items? No, you get that one near the end of the first playthrough. Fortunately you keep some of these on subsuquent runs. Do you ever get good save functionality? NO. HELL NO. Fortunately you learn to save often, even to the point of taking detours so that if you die you don't lose a half hour of progress and items when you respawn. Most quests are fetch this, then return and maybe repeat 2-3 times. Since you run through the game 3+ times to get the main endings, there's really no point in doing exploration until you have all these timesavers. Oh, and enemies start to drop a TON more chips and items (especially if you equip an +drop % chip), so once again there's no point to doing anything besides the bare minimum on the first run, when you can't even open up half the chests or scan.
Other poor design decisions abound. After a certain point on Normal enemies are a cakewalk, except in a few instances when you run into one that can stun lock you and hits for half your HP. Any other time you can open up your inventory and heal instantly, using very cheap healing items. Weapon damage scales poorly too, and most enemies are simply bullet sponges.
On that note, another AWFUL design decision was losing your chips on death. The most powerful chips take up less room and allow you to equip more of them. So if you're bad and die often... you'll lose your best chips...which makes you weaker... Of course you can get your chips back by recovering your corpse, but you better not die again or the first set is gone for good. Meanwhile players that don't die will generally be overpowered and can pack 2+ times the chips as a poor player. This also discourages playing on higher difficulities, which might actually make the combat more interesting.

After years of getting disappointed by games from big publishers; I've become extremely reluctant to buy any games over 30 euros. As a result, it took me months (until the summer sale) to finally convince myself to get Nier: Automata.
The day I finally got it, I played it for 10 hours straight; the second day for another 8 hours and by the end of the week, I had 100% cleared everything. It has been years since a singleplayer game had me so hooked that I forgot to eat or sleep until suddenly the sun came up. I usually don't play singleplayer games anymore, because without an online aspect, I find it impossible to stay interested for long enough to see where the story goes. In this game however, I replayed the game several times without getting bored for a second, and even though I 100% cleared the game now; I'm planning on playing through the endings A to E on hard mode now, because the game is simply that good.
I don't want to get into the story too much out of fear of spoiling an amazing story that should be experienced going in completely blind. Just know that it's a really gripping story that deals with existentialism in machines and references many great thinkers from the past and their points of view as shown in the character design of certain machines and the quests they give you.
The customization options for your chipsets (basically your passive skills) are so expansive that you can really build the character that fits your playstyle. Want a super flimsy high damage glass cannon-type build? no problem; want your character to regenerate hp on every hit, be super tanky in general and shoot out shockwaves at your enemies with every swing of your blade? no problem. Do you want to go for the realistic approach? no problem, just chuck out any chip that makes up your UI, and fill that space with more damage... because why not? Maybe you're even too lazy to fight at all, and just want to enjoy the amazing story, in which case you can just turn on easy mode and equip chips that do the fighting for you.
Sadly no game is perfect. I was fortunate enough to only get one problem, which I was able to circumvent (at a certain point in the game, I was unable to pass by a certain monster in the game without my game crashing over and over, but for some reason, staring at the floor and walking in a big circle around that area prevented it from crashing... (maybe something that was corrupted that crashed the game when it got rendered?))
I've heard many reports from people even being unable to start the game at all, or getting crashes constantly, which is probably why the community reviews score this game relatively low... I am fairly certain that the bad reviews are not because they think the game is bad, but because of the technical difficulties you can have with it.
Luckily, we have steam refunds for that though, so if you are one of the unlucky ones with issues, you can just refund the game if you haven't played it for over 2 hours and the game hasn't been in your library for over two weeks!
I guess many people might consider the fanservice as a positive thing; but to me it just gets cringy if the game even forces you to indulge in it to get all achievements. (can't be more specific because of spoilers)
Finally, the game is obviously made for a controller; the hacking minigames (little shoot-em-up sections) feel very clunky with mouse and keyboard, and since hacking is such a strong tool in your arsenal later on, I definitely regretted not having a controller.
Of course, these negatives are not bad enough to take away the enjoyment of this amazing game, so aslong as you simply look past that, this game is definitely worth trying, even at full price.

+ Amazing Story
+ Great Customization options
+ Responsive Combat
- Possible Technical Difficulties (if so -> get refund)
- Fanservice can be Cringy at times
- Controller is strongly advised

For what it's worth, I'm running a GTX 1070 and an R7 1700 and had no major technical issues with the game. I also finished the game and found the true ending, while also doing the majority of side quests.
Now, frankly this game feels like one that has loads of potential, but falls flat in nearly every aspect of the game. For the first 1/3 of the game I was seriously pleased and loved the game, but eventually the game revealed it had nothing else to give and was monotonous for the last 2/3 of the game. To keep things brief, I'll have a conclusion as a Tl;dr, and divide specific things into a few subsections.
Conclusion (Tl;dr):
The game had loads of potential with its setup, characters, sound design and combat, but every facet of the game had 1-2 huge issues that spoiled the game as a whole. It was fun for ~10 hours, but after that it got dull and monotonous.
Story:
The story was trying to go for some 'Ahha!' moment towards the end about existentialism and consciousness, but it was such an underwhelming sentiment given that the entire game was supposed to be build up to something more significant. They also did drop a lot of philosophy in the midst of the game but didn't try and tie it together, making the whole story frankly pointless. I won't say much more because I would like to avoid spoilers, but as a summary let me borrow this quote from Zero Punctuation's review: "Despite its lofty philosophical ambitions the plot wasn't making any actual kind of point. It just dumped a load of existential thematic elements on the garage floor and buggered off to let us sweep them up"
Characters:
2B and A2 were interesting characters, and I would have liked to see their characters developed more; however, contrary to what you may have heard the REAL main character of the game is 9S, and he is such a shallow and uninteresting character that I feel like there is a lot of missed potential. Furthermore he tends to come across as pretty arrogant, and is not at all a sympathetic character.
Combat:
Probably the most underwhelming yet highest potential area of the game. The combat has the ability to be amazing - the combination of destructable and indestructable projectiles and high mobility means for some pretty cool gameplay; however, the problem is there feels like there is no build diversity or exploration in the game period. You can get away with the first 1-2 upgrades of a weapon and never change them out again, and your skill system called 'plug-in chips' has the same problem. This by itself isn't game breaking, but the combination of the next two problems is - there is no satisfying difficulty level: Normal difficulty is incredibly easy once you have a few healing chips, and you get 1-shotted in higher difficulties to the point it makes the game un-fun. I urge you that if you want to play this game for the combat, go look elsewhere.
Technical Considerations:
Just a side note on a few design decisions with gameplay: first, the fact that auto-pickup of loot isn't included until the last ~5 hours of the game is insulting, and is such a quality of life impairment that I can't believe they didn't just make it baseline. Furthermore, there are some incredibly obnoxious moments where the game takes control of your camera, sometimes mid-fight - to keep it short, frustrating.
Sound:
A REAL testiment to how good the game could have been - I kid you not in that the game's soundtrack is absolutely superb, and the people who did the sound design for the game did an incredible job. The problem was the game used the soundtrack surprisingly poorly and repetitively to the point that even the exceptional tracks were feeling overused.

The original asking price is absolutely insane (because Activision, obviously) and please do not read the description, because it's a load of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's not necessarily inaccurate, but it's exaggerated, especially for a game as old as this. Still on a sale the game's totally worth your trouble, especially if you haven't played it before.
It's a PS2-era third-person semi-open-world western-themed action game that came out around 2005 and it shows, both in the good and the bad. The visuals are extremely dated and the oveworld is small and dead, but where GUN actually works it's in its style and atmosphere. It's more Call of Juarez than RDR in that regard, but the writing is solid for a spaghetti western and the port isn't as terrible as one would expect it, despite it being very clearly designed for consoles.  The controls are responsive, despite some weird key assignments. There is no widescreen and no AA. There is no one-button-quick save either and the menus are clearly console-designed (mouse is, of course, supported), but the game has the good sense to provide an in-menu quick-save function and is really good about very frequent checkpoints during missions, which means absolutely no frustration.
The story is simple; you're a dude, whose father dies and goes on a revenge spree, only to find out that things aren't as simple as he thought. The story starts off better than it ends and it sort of fast-forwards past the half-way-point mark, as if the developers were running out of time. The twists are obvious from the start, but we're not here for layered story-telling, we're here to get our spaghetti-western on.
Gunplay feels good, despite its handicaps and the constant (often necessary) lock-on aiming. The world is technically open, but small and mostly empty, but riding on a horse through the dusty roads alongside the railroad is still pretty fun, in a theme-appropriate way.
On the not-so-bright side of things,, the content itself can get fairly repetitive, particularly the side missions. You can play poker, you do bounties, you help around the town sheriffs and all that, but most of it is some variation of "ride there, kill bad guys, rinse and repeat". Main story missions aren't terribly varried either, but they put in the minimum effort.
The last level, in particular, is just a  mess. Sudden difficulty spike that relies on crippling the player's options and learned abilities; pretty standard for game design of that era, but still every bit as annoying as it was back then.
Still, GUN is an overall enjoyable experience. It's short; I've logged over 7 hours in it and though I've left several side missions, but save is still sitting on 82% completion, with the main story completed as well. The original asking price is insane, but during a sale, if you feel like you need something old to satisfy your western cravings, you can do worse than GUN.

Never in my entire life would I ever imagine giving Deadly Premonition a negative review. This is a FANTASTIC game, but the PC version is butchered beyond belief. It REALLY is as bad as people say. Heed everybody's warning.
I bought it cheap for about 2 dollars before really realizing what I was getting in to. Simply seeing "this is a bad port," wasn't enough to deter me. I've seen these comments elsewhere for games I really enjoyed playing the PC port of and thought, "It can't be THAT bad." But when your game immediately crashes on start up, you know you're going to have a bad time.
This port is so butchered that somebody (independant from the company) made a patch to try and fix most of the issues that the game has. With the patch installed, I was able to get past the start-up screen. But, it still crashed.
After much trial and error, I got this♥♥♥♥♥♥load of ♥♥♥♥ to run in Windowed Mode in Windows 98 compatibiity (fullscreen makes the game crash even harder). Even then, the MAX amount of gameplay I would get at a time without it crashing was about 45 minutes. With that being said, I'm one of the lucky ones who actually got to play it with crashes that I could overcome. And I don't even know if I'd call that luck.
The crashing isn't even consistant. Sometimes it's during a load screen, other times, it's when you're going to use an item out of the inventory. Sometimes, it's simply right in the middle of walking.. or when you're mid combat. The crashing also seems to intensify during rainy weather. It really ruins the game experience for me when I have to just hope and pray that the game doesn't crash on the next load screen. When I have to constantly say to myself, "Dear god, I hope there's a phone coming up soon."
Your only hope is to save constantly. But the problem is that you can only save at phones, and if you are doing a Chapter Replay, you cannot save AT ALL. This is a huge problem if you're a completionist, or you want to just go back and do sidequests that are more useful (like the one for the radio). I lost so many man hours because the game would crash during a Chapter Replay, and all of my progress that I just made was gone.
The game looks okay (graphically), but the frame rate is crappy. Sometimes York will have that "stutter" run because the game just can't keep up. In combat, I wasn't able to use the Grecotch (OP weapon that carries you through most of the game) because I just couldn't land a hit. Even while standing RIGHT in front of an enemy, hitting it from different angles, etc. Hits just weren't connecting, or it was delayed... I really don't know what the problem is. But in any case, every aspect of this game is ruined simply because it functions like garbage. I would have asked for my Steam refund, but it was already past the date in which I could return it, and I had poured so many "play" time in to it just trying to get the thing to work.. disappointing.

This is by far the best indie adventure RPG I've ever played. It is heavily derivative of top-down Zelda games like A Link to the Past, so fans of Zelda and Zelda-like games will enjoy Anodyne.
Anodyne's controls are very well-designed. The fact that the game is controlled by a grand total of seven buttons (arrows, select/attack, back/jump, and menu) is an excellent design choice: far too often have I played games with separate buttons for every tool or weapon or action, or so many items that additional controls are needed to cycle through them. The menu very rarely has to be used to play the game, only needed to equip the occasional broom upgrade.
The card system is cute and unique, with each card having a funny little quote about the featured character. NPC and enemy design is well done; the sprites are simple and fit the aesthetic of the game, and the AI, while sometimes frustrating, works very well.
Level design, while not exceptionally innovative, is well-thought-out and well-executed, although a compass item for dungeons would be helpful for keeping track of what went where in previous rooms. The overworld is expansive and elaborate, with intricate, winding pathways in some areas and wide, open expanses in others. Again, the menu map could use some improvements, such as region labels, but it may just be a design choice.
Anodyne's 16-bit style is the perfect fit for what it is, and the idea of a Zelda-like game with modern and surrealist twists is certainly charming. The sprites and tileset are all well-drawn and aesthetically fitting, and the selective use of lighting and effects in some areas of the game is a small yet powerful touch.
One of the best parts of Anodyne is its music. The music is calm and distant, yet drives the gameplay in incredible ways. The player cannot help but nod along to the groovy, eccentric beats and melodies of the Hotel, the somber, melodic sways of the Temple, or the hesitant, ominous notes of the Cavern as they roam the halls and corridors and solve the grand puzzles contained within each unique dungeon.
While overall a fantastic game, it could use a bit more in the side quest department, as the game, while nonlinear in layout, is fairly linear in terms of objective.
The bosses, while generally a bit tricky on the first or second try, are overall fairly easy and simple, without much variety in fight style (dodge its attacks, strike strike strike, wait for its anger phase to pass, rinse and repeat until dead).
There is not much incentive to stay alive in the game. Death means being sent back to the last checkpoint, which in a dungeon can be fairly common. Checkpoints are easy to find and easy to use, and saving at a different checkpoint from the previous one fully heals the player, which seems a bit cheap. There is no currency to be lost, and dying does not reset progress, just position: any items collected will stay collected after death, and saving is only really needed when quitting, as there is no volatile progress in need of saving.
If you are a fan of Zelda-like games and have 10 bucks to spare, give the game a go. As with any Steam game, however, waiting for a discount is probably the best course of action, as the $5 I bought the game for was the perfect price for the game in my opinion (but then again, I don't like paying for things, so there's that).

I've heard many bad tales about this game... horror stories how bad it is. How you had to avoid it.
I didn't care; and played it anyway... and I am so glad that I did. This is a GREAT RPG. Great!
The story is intense, adult and interesting. There are some weavements in to the show (and books?) that you probably understand better than me if you watched/read them. Even if you didn't you can still easily follow this game's plotline and enjoy it. It truly is one of the best story-lines I have experienced in a game.
So good infact that yes, it allows one to overlook the weaker points of this game. It starts rather slow, but name me one RPG that doesn't. It's very conversation-heavy, which would scare off some, but is like the perfect thing for me and many RPG-fans. There can be very large stints without combat or "action"
Which is good, since the combat isn't exactly amazing. While complex enough, with various armor and damage types, many skills and abilities it's just... jarring. It's usually not much fun, which makes it fortunate it usually doesn't last that long. Mostly it consists of finding good combo's (x knocks out, y does bonus damage on knocked down foes) and hope for the best. I've lost fights heavily, and then won them using the exact same tactics without loosing any health at all on reload, so the combat results can be highly random.
Back on the good side; this game features *many* great additions many RPG's could profit from having. The 2 storylines that start appart and closely come together and merge and then allows you to make the end-choice is great. It really helps avoiding story-fatigue if you don't get all of it in a large mesh-up. Downside is that you have to pay attention, it can be confusing if you don't. This is not a game just to relax and not think. You need to pay attention. Another great action is the dog, allowing you to sniff out clues, hidden rewards and take down lone guards (very advised since aforementioned combat). The counter-part fire view is sorely lacking in comparrison.
Other great additions you will notice throughout, and might be spoilerish so I wont go into details expect that you really should loose the boss-fight once. That's just pure genious that other games lack, you'll know what I talk about when you see it.
Another downside is the extremely unoptimalised graphics. You'll often notice stuttering, and FPS might drop to it's knees looking at a wall, while a giant city-overview runs fine. This stuttering behavior can make it hard to navigate about and is overall extremely annoying, and probably the single most giant downside of this game sadly enough. It looks good enough, but it's performance is terrible. Some areas of the city I tried avoiding just because I knew they would drop my framerate to it's knees.
However, I really suggest to get yourself through the horrors of the optimalisation and (infrequent) combat to experience  what this game's plotline and conversations have to offer you. You'll not regret it playing to the end and experience it all. Definitely one of the biggest surprises to me these last few years. No RPG fan should miss this one out...

This is a pretty impressive farming simulator, but after seeing the character animations in the videos I nearly passed it by. That would have been a mistake.
I have hundreds of hours in the last three Farming Simulators and enjoy the relaxation of running a virtual farm. This game adds a social aspect that,  while certainly not perfect, adds a build-up to what you can do. And what you can do is really, really good.
From the plowing, cultivating, planting, baleing hay, putting it in the wagon and loading it in the cow barn for moo food to the buying and caring of animals, building repairs and even an excellent weed-eater simulator to clean up your farm. Framed by an excellent, (and excellent looking), day/night cycle that demands your rest and keeping up your strength with food, this simulation always seems to have multiple options for what you can do next. Not scripted either. There are opportunities that open up for you as you progress, mostly helping out the neighbors with a wide-ranging set of construction skills, or with doing some field jobs for cash.
This is a SLOW moving game. If you are looking for any kind of speed build of your farm, or quick riches, a fast-speed button, or AI farm helpers, this is not your game. You do EVERYTHING yourself.
If you are looking for a simulation that builds at a reasonable speed and always keeps you looking ahead for that next piece of equipment you can earn, or afford, and always keeps you busy, then I highly advise trying this one out. If you have any enjoyment of farming simulators, business simulators, or are even looking for a first-person Stardew Valley experience, then give this a shot.
It is early access. There are periodic crashes so save often as there is no auto-save at this time. I zenned out for about 90 minutes when my only crash hit, and it was a bummer. The animations of the people are pretty weak, even humorous, and the voice acting is a little stilted, but these can be improved and do not take away from the gameplay IMO.
Bottom line - Get it!

I really enjoy the basic FPS elements of this game. I don't think any other multiplayer FPS games capture the pure satisfaction of wielding a clunky, heavy semi-automatic rifle, spotting a foe clambering across the street, leading them with your ironsights and aiming high to account for bullet-drop, and downing them from 100-200 meters. It feels fantastic. Similarly, the amount of anxiety this game can instill when you're pinned down in a helpless situation is quite special. No other game series can get me cowering in a hole for minutes like this one.
That said, the higher-level elements of this game are awkward and unapproachable. I have searched online for guides to figure out how to understand what is happening throughout a battle and how to have more control over the outcome, but it seems like the only real source of information is whatever scraps you are lucky enough to hear from a proficient hardcore player who has been following this series for years.
I don't know how to be a good squad leader, how to perform any of the non-grunt roles, and I have no idea how I'd approach orchestrating a battle if I were commander. There is surprisingly little information to be found about any of these things. Once in a blue moon you'll have a good, communicative commander who you can learn from, but I've only had that happen once in ten hours. The tutorial videos provided with the game are poorly paced and throw a ton of info at you at once, rattling off the awkward controls without any time for me to digest them. And they're far from comprehensive.
So basically I just always end up playing the grunt and learning very little, never feeling comfortable enough to try out the other classes and roles.
I've had some strange audio bugs as well. Specifically with some of the helicopters/airships. Sometimes I plain can't hear them, even when they're killing me. Sometimes bombshells are falling and I'll try to time my sprints to avoid being hit by them, but I find that the sounds they make aren't a reliable indicator. Like the sound loop is no sync'd up. I also get some strange audio artifacts -- phantom sounds like the tail end of an explosion with seemingly no source. Sound is incredibly important in these stressful scenarios so it can be annoying.
The maps are pretty well designed and are very different from one another. They're huge, too. The only problem I have with them is that I often find myself in the same situations, holding the same pinch points, and it makes them feel a whole lot smaller because I spend 75% of my time in the same handful of locations on the map.
I'd love to be able to recommend this game to my friends or new-comers, but it seems like it was made almost exclusively for people who are already intimately familiar with this series of games. It does very little to accommodate beginners. There is a lot to love about the FPS experience here, but the game is just HUGE and there are so many details to learn and seemingly nowhere to learn them from. So for a new player, the experience will be dying, dying, dying, for ten hours until you kind of understand how to be a grunt. Not sure how you're supposed to proceed once you've reached that point.

To start off, I enjoy both this and Overwatch, having about equal time in each.
Paladins is one of those games that upon first viewing, looks like an inferior clone of another game, in this case, Overwatch. But if you were to take a *little* more time to inspect why people play both, you may find something to enjoy. Paladins is first person shooter with team objectives, as you can probably see, but it also introduces a few MOBA elements, such as not being able to switch characters and buying items for more power. Many will see both of these as features that only "filthy casuals" enjoy having, but I feel it adds a little bit more tension to each match, where the selected character isn't as effective against the enemy team, or buying certain items can turn a game around if done right.
Personally, I feel as though the Champions to be more creative than Overwatch's heroes. Most of the heroes in Overwatch operate in a fairly simple manner, but naturally have some unique skills - fly, become a turret, create walls, freeze enemies and run on walls, to name a few. The minor issue of repeatability is true of both games, but more variation adds to an experience. The most unique traits of Paladins' champions that I can list off the top of my head are: becoming invisible, throwing weapons, giving teammates shields, and poisoning enemies.
There is also a healthy community. By healthy, I mean there are people playing, much like other games, some players are still.. interesting.
I can't really work this in, but it's free and doesn't run horribly on most machines, old or new.
Those are my thoughts on the game, please excuse me for my messy, unorganized review.

- On top of the little reaction time, the car turns very slowly. This makes it difficult and sometimes even impossible to grab items or get out of the way of other vehicles. An option to change turning speed and an option to turn with the mouse would be great.
- Menu options are unclear with just symbols instead of words or abbreviations
- Menu options counterintuitive. e.g. pressing escape pauses the game but pressing escape again doesn't unpause the game, it brings you back to the main menu and erases any progress you have made, without any warning. Wtf.
- Needs options to change volume of music and sfx
- Could just be me but I feel like in the later levers (5 and up) you lose gas too quickly. I also think you should lose gas slower when not using the accelerator.
- The buffs (speed boost, invulnerability, slow down) don't last very long
Extras ideas:
- Would love to be able to reverse (to grab a buff or gas that I missed). Technically you 'can' but you can only go reeeeeeeeeally slow. Also, you're quickly and constantly losing gas so pretty much you WILL lose all of your gas (and the game) before you ever reach the item.
- The only difference between the unlockable cars is how they look (which isn't "bad"), but maybe you can have the different cars have different strengths and weaknesses. i.e. one car drives super fast, another car turns fast, another is slow but can recover more easily when hitting another car, etc. So many possibilities.
- Could use more variety of buffs. Extra lives, extra score points, temporary infinite gas, etc
Overall, it's a pretty decent casual/arcade game. I recommend it if you're into 80s music and visuals.
And to the devs, thank you for putting the soundtrack up for download. I was actually going to request it before it was up. :)

I don't think I've been so thoroughly affected by a game in a very long time, if ever. I would absolutely recommend this game for anyone that loves moral ambiguity or existential themes. The combat is fantastic and the gameplay is incredible, but it's the plot and the deep themes of this game that make it one of the best games I've ever played.
The PC version isn't perfect (I had some issues right from the start when I tried running it at 4k resolution and was getting roughly 5 frames per second), and I definitely recommend playing with a controller, but with those technical imperfections aside this game is nierly perfect (haha, get it, nierly?)
If you take the time to fully enjoy this game and immerse yourself in the world, then you're in for an emotional (and existential) rollercoaster. The plot is complex, and you'll have to dig deep to grasp the full meaning of the game, but if you do then I can almost guarantee you'll keep wanting more. I stared at the screen for a good 15 minutes at the end, questioning the type of person I am and what it even means to be human. You'll be forced to reflect on each and every one of your actions as you play, and whether or not those actions are justified is a question that exists at the core of the experience.
If plot matters to you, play this game. If you like to think, play this game. If you're prepared to question everything about yourself, then absolutely play this game.

For quite some time now, serial killers across the United States of America have been putting red tree seeds into the mouths of young women & displaying their dead bodies in the shape of the Algiz rune (ᛉ), sometimes referred to as the “life rune”. The most recent case in the (fictional) town of Greenvale, Washington is no different. Anna Graham, an 18-year-old teenager dreaming of making it big in the city, was brutally murdered, her tongue bitten out, her carcass disemboweled, & then hung up on a tree. This calls FBI Special Agent Francis York Morgan to the scene. Though an expert in homicide cases, this eccentric investigator, who only confides in his imaginary partner Zach, proceeds to turn the entire town upside down with his outspoken nature & unconventional methods.
Deadly Premonition is a game with an outright cult following, but also, sadly, a rather problematic PC port. Its initial development started in 2004, but had to be halted in 2007. Eventually, production continued & it was released in 2010. By that time, several of its assets looked outdated, which surprisingly works in the title’s favor. The uncanny visuals, stellar framing, awkward animations, & at times strange voiceover all contribute to a slightly eerie atmosphere, whereas the funny dialogs & outright hilarious sound effects alleviate the mood just enough to not take the game too seriously.
The whole production was also so strongly influenced by David Lynch’s & Mark Frost’s Twin Peaks that it can feel like playing a video game adaptation. The series, like Deadly Premonition, takes place in a small, seemingly idyllic U.S. town where an FBI agent investigates a homicide case of a young girl &, in doing so, unravels a deep & dark secret surrounding the inhabitants while also engaging with ominous entities. In so far, Deadly Premonition, directed by Hidetaka Suehiro, feels like an homage to Lynch’s series, albeit with some prominent Japanese characteristics & tropes.
Sadly, the PC port of this cut suffers greatly under several issues, which buyers should know about beforehand. First of all, getting the game to work can be quite a chore & it won’t run on many a machine. I played this on a 32-bit, Windows Vista Home Premium, Intel Core 2 CPU, Nvidia GeForce 9500 GT, 3070 MB RAM, DX 11 & I know that it runs on a Lenovo G50-80E5 laptop with Windows 10. Despite that, Deadly Premonition: The Director’s Cut only has a 1280×720 p resolution with washed out colors. During sunny days in Greenvale, everything looks almost sepia. Apart from that, it occasionally struggles to keep a steady 30 fps. The situation became worrisome when, after fishing out some documents in Ep 3, Ch 17 & heading out to Harry’s mansion, Deadly Premonition started to suffer greatly with the frame rate dropping down & staying around 9 fps with my peer’s Lenovo laptop heating up from a temperature of 41°C (105,8°F) to 105°C (221°F). Verifying the integrity of the game cache, rebooting the game, or turning the machine off & on did not help, & the situation stayed this way up until entering the Galaxy of Terror pub in Ep 3, Ch 20. The only way the story could be continued at that time was to hurry to some objective, save, shut down the game, wait, start playing again, save, & so on.
Other bugs included one where the game had to be restarted, because a key item disappeared from the inventory, one where weapons could not be selected, York walking through a door heading towards Polly’s room in the Great Deer Yard Hotel & falling through the floor, the character of Quint driving be- instead of inside his car & glitching in & out of Richard’s trailer, the game crashing whenever trying to leave the A&G Diner in Ep 1, Ch 9, Nick Cormack’s car not moving during Ep 2, Ch 12, & frequent crashes throughout. One method to reduce the likability of the last one is, of course, to play the game in compatibility mode, but that increases loading times to almost a minute & it does not help against the memory leak, which will inadvertently cause a crash. The game also comes with previous DLC included, but they will often not be activated in-game. Lastly, the PC port is also supposed to have controller support, but has issues recognizing these.
Overall, apart from the driving, the crashes, the bugs, & the overheating, I enjoyed most of Deadly Premonition: The Director’s Cut. I believe that, provided readers have a platform where the game immediately works as intended, they will have a good time with this game. The characters are fun, the story overall intriguing (apart from the ending), & the premonitions truly work in the game’s favor. Nevertheless, I cannot, in good conscience, recommend a PC port that is this problematic & that might fry one’s computer. Even though I like it per se, I adviseto stay away from the PC port.

Summary:
From Dust is an excellent gaming experiment of sorts that cycles back on itself with its brief yet enjoyable campagin.  You play the rold of a god-esque figure that controls the elements and minimally commands your tribe to do tasks (just some simple "go here and go there".  The gameplay is fairly simple at the core though in later levels there is more thinking and fast adjusting/reacting required to ensure the tribes survival.  The learning curve is fairly steady as it adds elements or powers into the mix but I will say near the last level is a bit of a jump in dificulty compared to previous levels.
Graphics:
This game came out 4 years ago from writing this (Aug 17, 2011) and the charm and style still holds up strong.  The dynamic effects are convincing and the character design is interesting.  I do wish they had more animals that appeared to diversify the map but since this is a fairly minimalist game it works as is.  Ocasionally the tsunami effect would catch my attention because of a steap drop off or rise in the water that looked bizarre like a wall of water instead a wave but it is what it is.
Gameplay:
Simple and intuitive (played with a xbox 360 controller-needed to be enabled in settings each time)  mainly you are just picking up and putting down materials (sand, water or lava, ocasionally plants or totems as well)  The game is a lightly guided sandbox of sorts where you sculpt the land by changing the flow of rivers and lava flows in order to help a tribe of people reach the exit to the level, this must be unlocked by building all of the villiages on the map which are placed on totem locations.  The level design is spot on with these totems being placed in locations that require you to use different elements and tasks to navigate your tribe but the downside is the AI for these tribe members sometimes cripples gameplay.  I encountered them all to offten crying for help because they weren't satisfied with a path to take or a height difference near them requiring some extra sand raising or lowering until satisfaction.   These poor tribesmen (and women) would also freeze up in terror next to flowing water or lava instead of trying to avoid it which often lead to their demise.
Story:
There isn't a strong narrative here, essentially the tribe is wondering through different areas/realms with the story cycling back on itself toward the ened.  I will give them kudos for making it work though since the focus here really is just the sandbox gameplay and the minimal aproach they took works fine.
Note:
Many slam this game for Uplay issues, I don't think this is fair because Uplay isn't the game.  I am not a fan of running through steam to run through Uplay but it just is what it is, the artists and creatives that shelled out heart and soul into this game created something worth experiencing so don't let the game industry politics soil it for you.

An all around good game.
If in doubt, PLAY THE DEMO! - The devs not only put up a demo in steam, but there is an actual IN BROWSER build of it working on their website. Give it a shot.
Excellent combat - Mechanically shallow with sparkling visuals typical of the "beat-em-up" style. It shines in how fluid it is, the developer's description of "butter smooth" does it justice.
Enthralling story - My perception is probably colored with my personal experiences, but the story is really gripping. It has the typical cliches but caters to them well. The front line NPC's feel human, while the unimportant ones (but important enough to be unique) fall into personality archetypes, none of them feel grievously corny. The story is made of several sub plots that exchange time in the spotlight without ever fighting for attention giving it an organic flow tightly linked with progression.
Good music, standard sound effects - The music design is rather good, I won’t be buying a sound track any time soon but it matches environments perfectly and is a joy to listen to. I never felt myself annoyed by its presence and I never found myself forgetting it's even there. The sound effects are fairly bland. Like vanilla icecream, sweet and enjoyable, but sorta meh. It fits very neatly into the world and is everything that should be expected, but it feels as if it fits too well. The sound perfectly matches the 16-Bit love story the devs have crafted, but seems flat in comparison to the more robust effects found in other games. Not good, not bad, just, vanilla.
Graphical Wonderland - The game looks amazing. The sprites and tilesets (assuming their engine uses tilesets, no clue) are bright and flowing. As you play through the game the graphics meld with the game play as the very physics heavy platforming turn minute details into intractable ledges and platforms. Everything about the look of this game is bright and fluffy, it compliments every other aspect from combat to platforming to story. Everything is crisp, intense secret hunting isn’t hindered by muddled obfuscated pathways hidden from view, everything is right there waiting to be seen, the spectacle of it all makes the little things hard to find.
(The jungle could feel more jungly, it feels like a shady forest atm. I never found myself in an “in the weeds” moment you would expect from a jungle area.)
HARDCORE PARKOUR! (sweet guitar riff!) - Nothing is greater than seeing a chest up on a distant ledge only to realize that it is the reward for a zone wide multistage parkour puzzle. Overboard? Yes. A little aggravating at times? Maybe. Rewarding as all get out? Hellz YEAH! Jumping puzzles fill the overworld as you look and hunt in every nook and cranny for my loot boxes, rare plants to harvest, or hidden caves. The trials are tough, the physics are fair, I am rather bad. I found myself failing time and again trying to get those elusive boxes due to terrible user error not mechanical failure on the game’s part. My only complaint, I also see as a good thing, was the eureka moment when i realized that I could climb up the little edges of these ruined buildings i needed to traverse. Harkening back to the 16-bit era, a half wall used to act like a full wall tile, this game does not function like that. It also does not tell you that and you never run into an occurrence when it’s an issue until you're about halfway through and you run into these ruins. Realizing my massive convoluted round about way of getting to a platform to run along the tops of the ruin walls and get the box I was going for was cut down by about 90% because of a little half wall I could jump up and then run up the destroyed bit of wall next to it was at first rage inducing (I had been working on the problem for about 15 min) but then a big ol AH HA as i started realizing where I could apply this elsewhere.
In it’s unfinished state I would give this game a 6.5/10
-This is made with the assumption that the story would fall flat in the end
-If the story pulls off the finale that it promises and feels like it is building to I would gladly give it a 8.5/10 there is just so much left to do, I hope it pays off.

Borderlands; a great game series heralded by many. I can confidently say that The Pre-Sequal follows tradition and creates a game that lives up to the Borderlands title. The Pre-Sequel doesn't stray from the well-known antics of Gearbox Software, with their crude humor and great storytelling. Though the story this time around was a bit oddly paced, with odd difficulty spikes here and their for certain characters, that might just be my inability to focus on any side-quest whatsoever. Many well known guns make a return from Borderlands 2 (or were they originally in this game first?) and the addition of Moonstone infused weapons adds a unique take to more powerful weapons. Although there are no OP levels in this game, which I feel is a loss, the one and only DLC is fantastic and I feel is very worth the price. Another loss is on the removal of Slag, although it does make sense story-wise. Slag really made gameplay at high levels very strategic in Borderlands 2, but the use of Cryo could also be seen as good(?).
The gameplay is very quick paced and focuses on swapping weapon and element types during the right situations. I feel that the game is pretty well balanced, and the weapons are fun to use. The added mechanics of the ground pound (butt stomp) and low-g environments really creates a very unique FPS experience. The characters are each very unique in their own ways, and have powers that back up their back-story. (Wilhelm is a bit under-powered though) The addition  of 4 co-op is also great, and makes boss fights and areas all the more hectic and fun. The humor is great and has left me breathless many-a times. All in all, I can say the gameplay is very exciting and will drive any FPS lover.
Gameplay: 7.5/10
Story:7/10
Difficulty: 3.5/5
Enjoyment Value: 8/10
Co-op: 8/10
+10 for humor
In conclusion, I give this game a 7.5/10 overall, and it adds a wonderful FPS RPG to any co-op lovers games.

Let's start by saying- yes, we all know Borderlands 2 was better. HOWEVER, that doesn't mean the Pre-Sequel wasn't a great game in it's own right.
Now, as a hardcore Mordecai main in the first game, the events of 2 left me rightfully furious with Handsome Jack. And then Pre-Sequel came along and made him a character that was actually witty and charming, and seeing his fall from grace was actually downright painful. The dialogue could get a little corny at times (but what's a Borderlands game without a little cheese), and ultimately the gameplay didn't deviate from 2 that much- which could actually could be considered both a pro and a con. They didn't actually add any significant gameplay, but you could argue that 2 had everything you needed, so why tamper with perfection.
The characters were diverse, likeable, and pretty damn awesome- loved how old characters came back as playabe- and the little bits of interactions that you got depending on which one you played as was pretty neat. Obviously some characters were significantly useful against certain bosses than others, while some were borderline useless (Aurelia vs the Sentinal? Not fun), but generally they were all really fun to use, and their abilities continued to make them fun and unique to play. The references to Tales of the Borderlands were a major plus in my opinion.
Ultimately, the Pre-Sequel was a pretty strong addition to the franchise, and I recommend to all Borderlands stans out there as we patiently wait for the release of 3. (Gearbox pls.)

When it comes to tower defenses, Gemcraft offers a simple, no-nonsense approach. While other TD games will drown you in options that have two to three upgrades before you're better off tearing it down and replacing it with something new, no gem immediately makes the others obsolete.
The game can be painfully slow at times, largely when waiting for the last giant-class monster to get in range, but the speed options help with that quite a bit. Some levels, even without the battle modifiers, can be punishingly difficult, but once you've figured out a tactic that works for you, you'll be just fine.
This game was so good that I decided to make another tower defense game myself.

It's definitely a nice, well-detailed game exploring the subconscious thoughts of Young, the main character. If it were just that, I would definitely recommend this without a second thought.
However, when the game gives up on providing even the basest amount of a narrative, tells you to 'just fetch these 36 cards, then we'll let you finish the game', and starts throwing out some of the most irritating jumping puzzles I've seen in a while, I kind of start thinking about how much better this would be as a novel. Mainly because it's undesirable and almost impossible to implement a jumping puzzle in a novel.

16 hours is good enough time to properly judge this game, I have to say it's been an enjoyable time spent so far.
Rising Storm 2: Vietnam comes from the same developers who've made the kiling floor series and previous RS games, Tripwire Interactive. I've played red orchestra briefly and killing floor 2 for 30 hours, those games are also considered great in my book. So I didn't expect this game to be bad at all, and it isn't. It's tactical, engaging, fun, and realistic. You will FEEL like you are in vietnam. You will RUSH to the trenches to dodge napalm or artillery. You will be able to bring WRAITH to the VCs by BURNING THEM ALIVE WITH SWEET NAPALM AND FLAME THROWER! You will also CONSTANTLY die, it's not for the light hearted.
Tripwire did an excellent job with the gameplay. To quickly summarize it, there are two main sides: Vietnam and US Military, each come with different roles, weapons and equipment. Vietnamese soldiers are masters guerilla combat, making use of deadly traps such as tripwires, mines and punji traps. They may not have the fire power or weaponry, but they certainly know how to keep an area well mined and ready for ambush. They do not have any vehicle access and generally carry more outdated but still effective weaponry. As for the US military, you will get access to modern weaponry, grenades and equipment for the time. You will employ various tactics using whatever weapon or equipment the classes come with such as the engineer who can weild a flamethrower or plant c4 to clear out enemy buildings. You can throw smoke to temporarily create cover. You can even become the pilot of a cobra attack helicopter or a huey, transporting soldiers across the battlefield. This side also comes with the ability to napalm the VCs. Both sides have access to Artillery support.
This area is bit lacking for the game, the game really feels a bit buggy and inconvienent. The best example I have is for how clunky crouching and proning can feel at times. Hitmarkers can also be a bit messy at times and lead to accidental deaths. Regardless, the game isn't TOO buggy and feels like it's made professionally almost all the time. A lot of people say optimization is TRASH in this game, I disagree and agree. For me, I run everything on ultra and can still pull 55-60 most of the time, lowering to 40 in the worst cases. So, bug fixing and optimization is definently needed in this game.
This part of the game is done decently, the post processing doing all of the marvelous visual work. The graphics are a bit lacking for this game compared to AAA titles like Witcher or Fallout but they aren't garbage and work well with the environment and gameplay. The post processing effects are nothing too special either but they add on to the feeling. I hope graphics and post processing gets a bit more work in coming updates of the game.
So the big question, is this game worth the price?
Definently, even more so. For 25 dollars( 22 since the sale) this game is amazing! The gameplay is the heart and strongsuit of the game and makes up for the flaws it has. To rate it on a scale of 1-10, I'd give a solid 7.

Unpopular thing to say, but the game is heavily overrated. By a lot. It is certainly not Jesus second coming, like everyone said it is.
The game has a lot of cool aspects and is overall worth playing and recommending for sure. But it still has all the annoying quirks of a jRPG game, the grind, the incredibly unsatisfying side quests, simplified storytelling, a lot of pointless running and a big chore for the completionists out there that will be bored out of their mind.
But the CORE of the game is fighting, and there can be no bad word said about it. If you don't have to absolutely do a 100% run of everything you play and can just enjoy the story chunks beeing thrown at you when you go over the main story you will have nothing but fun I think.
Anything else is just the artificial padding to extend the game and meta gaming (like grinding chips for dozens of hours to create hyper powerfull setup).
For difficulty, it is well balanced, though I did fish for few hours to have an easier start (hardly fun after the first 15 min).
I had a major issue with the port when it came to playing in 2560x1440, had to use Borderless Gaming (here on steam, additional cost, can be gotten for free with more hassle, a mod can be applied as well, but it's creator is kind of a d**k, so I skipped it). Without it, game had broken aspect ratio and resolution, which looked really bad.
Yes, this is since day one. It was not fixed till the day of the review as far as I know (05.07.17) so a chance is they just don't care at this point and it will never be touched.
No issues besides that, but I have a fairly powerfull PC, otherwise you might have little choice but to get the 3rd party mod.
The price is a bit high. 59.99€ ? Not worth it at all, get it on a cheaper reseller or sale.
Overall a decent game. But no, no 9/10 no 10/10, more like 7+ or 8 if you actually don't mind the jRPG quirks it didn't resolve. That doesn't account for the technical problems.
It's my opinion though and I can certainly recommend getting this on the cheap to form your own opinion.
Just wanted to make it clear that I think it is overrated.

Guns of Icarus.
First you need a mic. It's not mandatory but it'll help tremendously.
Second you need some friends to buy it. That's harder to accomplish. And also, it's better if they speak the same language.
Third you get into the game and play the tutorial.
Fourth you decide if you are the pilot, the gunner or an engineer.
The pilot is, obviously, the helm. Sometimes, depending on the ship, you'll have to repair or man a gun nearby but most of the times, you'll just be piloting.
The gunner is in charge of shooting stuff. That's not as easy as it may sound because you need to carefully select the types of ammunition you bring with you, depending on the gun layout of the ship. Discuss it with the captain. Remember that the best defense is to attack. You might be tempted to go repair stuff when things are going south but try to continue firing and disabling the enemy guns instead, it'll be more helpful if you can do it.
Finally the engineer. You're always running everywhere to repair, buff, put out fires or man a turret when things are going nicely. It's quite a hard job because you need to keep in mind the cooldowns of your tools and prioritize the right things to repair first. And when you're on the guns, you need to time your shoots with the gunner to have a full clip ready to finish the enemy in one go as soon as its armor goes down.
The atmosphere is steampunky and the ships are all very differet with their own strengths and weaknesses. Contrary to what the game tells you, the goldfish isn't actually the easiest to play because its gun coverage is actually quite bad. The Pyramidion is the one I recommed for beginners for his great frontal resilience and his double frontal light guns. Put a gatling and a mortar (it's quite a nice gun if you can aim it) and you're good to make your first steps.
Cooperation is the key. Though sometimes the AI does a better job...
