For quite some time now, serial killers across the United States of America have been putting red tree seeds into the mouths of young women & displaying their dead bodies in the shape of the Algiz rune (ᛉ), sometimes referred to as the “life rune”. The most recent case in the (fictional) town of Greenvale, Washington is no different. Anna Graham, an 18-year-old teenager dreaming of making it big in the city, was brutally murdered, her tongue bitten out, her carcass disemboweled, & then hung up on a tree. This calls FBI Special Agent Francis York Morgan to the scene. Though an expert in homicide cases, this eccentric investigator, who only confides in his imaginary partner Zach, proceeds to turn the entire town upside down with his outspoken nature & unconventional methods.
Deadly Premonition is a game with an outright cult following, but also, sadly, a rather problematic PC port. Its initial development started in 2004, but had to be halted in 2007. Eventually, production continued & it was released in 2010. By that time, several of its assets looked outdated, which surprisingly works in the title’s favor. The uncanny visuals, stellar framing, awkward animations, & at times strange voiceover all contribute to a slightly eerie atmosphere, whereas the funny dialogs & outright hilarious sound effects alleviate the mood just enough to not take the game too seriously.
The whole production was also so strongly influenced by David Lynch’s & Mark Frost’s Twin Peaks that it can feel like playing a video game adaptation. The series, like Deadly Premonition, takes place in a small, seemingly idyllic U.S. town where an FBI agent investigates a homicide case of a young girl &, in doing so, unravels a deep & dark secret surrounding the inhabitants while also engaging with ominous entities. In so far, Deadly Premonition, directed by Hidetaka Suehiro, feels like an homage to Lynch’s series, albeit with some prominent Japanese characteristics & tropes.
Sadly, the PC port of this cut suffers greatly under several issues, which buyers should know about beforehand. First of all, getting the game to work can be quite a chore & it won’t run on many a machine. I played this on a 32-bit, Windows Vista Home Premium, Intel Core 2 CPU, Nvidia GeForce 9500 GT, 3070 MB RAM, DX 11 & I know that it runs on a Lenovo G50-80E5 laptop with Windows 10. Despite that, Deadly Premonition: The Director’s Cut only has a 1280×720 p resolution with washed out colors. During sunny days in Greenvale, everything looks almost sepia. Apart from that, it occasionally struggles to keep a steady 30 fps. The situation became worrisome when, after fishing out some documents in Ep 3, Ch 17 & heading out to Harry’s mansion, Deadly Premonition started to suffer greatly with the frame rate dropping down & staying around 9 fps with my peer’s Lenovo laptop heating up from a temperature of 41°C (105,8°F) to 105°C (221°F). Verifying the integrity of the game cache, rebooting the game, or turning the machine off & on did not help, & the situation stayed this way up until entering the Galaxy of Terror pub in Ep 3, Ch 20. The only way the story could be continued at that time was to hurry to some objective, save, shut down the game, wait, start playing again, save, & so on.
Other bugs included one where the game had to be restarted, because a key item disappeared from the inventory, one where weapons could not be selected, York walking through a door heading towards Polly’s room in the Great Deer Yard Hotel & falling through the floor, the character of Quint driving be- instead of inside his car & glitching in & out of Richard’s trailer, the game crashing whenever trying to leave the A&G Diner in Ep 1, Ch 9, Nick Cormack’s car not moving during Ep 2, Ch 12, & frequent crashes throughout. One method to reduce the likability of the last one is, of course, to play the game in compatibility mode, but that increases loading times to almost a minute & it does not help against the memory leak, which will inadvertently cause a crash. The game also comes with previous DLC included, but they will often not be activated in-game. Lastly, the PC port is also supposed to have controller support, but has issues recognizing these.
Overall, apart from the driving, the crashes, the bugs, & the overheating, I enjoyed most of Deadly Premonition: The Director’s Cut. I believe that, provided readers have a platform where the game immediately works as intended, they will have a good time with this game. The characters are fun, the story overall intriguing (apart from the ending), & the premonitions truly work in the game’s favor. Nevertheless, I cannot, in good conscience, recommend a PC port that is this problematic & that might fry one’s computer. Even though I like it per se, I adviseto stay away from the PC port.

Being the type that doesn't actually write reviews, i couldn't help but make an exception in this case.
First serious-ish review.
An impressively good game! The pixelated graphics looks very good, and this comes from someone who is not a particular fan of the genre. The RPG feeling is well crafted, having an large range of features including the standard menus equipment, quest, items, and others. What i found interesting is that you can call, when possible, NPCs in your party in order to help with grinding or quests. The maps? So much exploring... as well as returning to previous maps in order to uncover the secrets and other things. The jumping off platforms makes an oddly satisfying, and puzzles are well crafted, making you love and/or hate them.
The combat system is unique and surprisingly intense, featuring a combination of melee and ranged fighting topped off with dashing and blocking. Imagine combining all of them against enemies which don't actually wait for anything when you are engaged. The results are very satisfying once the battle ends. Additionally, you can change between 4 elements during the battle, and adapt the skills to your playstyle.
Soundtrack is great, and definitely helps with the immersion. it has been updated and the new battle theme is bae, as well as other songs being added.
The storyline is great, and it is best experienced, so I will refrain from talking about it. But damn son, this game managed to keep me hooked non-stop! It draws some parallels with other Anime MMOs however the characters and the overall premise gets more interesting as the game progresses. It is worth noting that the story is incomplete, yet there is plenty of progress to be made as of now. At the time of buying the game, the story ended relatively short from me. After a story update, and long time in exile from this game because i did all that could be done before, it managed to catch me back immediately.
Speaking of which, the game is indeed in early access and therefore incomplete. After you reach the end of the plot in its current state, you can explore the areas you wish and continue playing like you did before. This means that there are some areas that are available beyond the plot limitations, and if you complete a dungeon before the progress reaches that dungeon, the dungeon would stay complete. At least that's what happened to me.
i am not sure how these fancy steam reviews are supposed to work, but these are my two cents about it. For an incomplete RPG of this type, it managed to pull off (at the time of this review) a good 44.7 hours. Taking time and unnecessarily over-grinding tallyho!
This is a very very good and polished game, even in its current incomplete state. Buy it. It's offers a great and enjoyable experience at all times, and the updates only improve it as the game goes on. There is a demo ready and waiting if the reviews are not enough, but this game has managed to offer an amazing experience well worth the money.

I really enjoyed the early content in CrossCode with a few minor frustrations with the cliff levels and the quest system being pretty barebones, however I found myself enjoying it less and less as the game progressed. The combat was quite enjoyable with a combination of melee and ranged and being able to switch between the options on the fly. However, I found as the game progressed I grew more and more frustrated with the enemies, with a lot of enemies required you to wait for them to use a specific attack in order to actually inflict damage. I found myself straight up avoiding combat in a game where a good chunk is intended to be about combat.
A less significant frustration I had with the game was with the dungeon puzzle design. It's pretty good sometimes, but I found myself figuring out how to do a specific puzzle pretty quickly, but missing the actual action to complete it a couple of times and having to spend more time just going through the motions again. This was mainly in the timed puzzles with things like missing jumps due to icy ground or missing a shot and having to wait a few seconds to retry. A minor sidenote to this was how many puzzles you have to spend a few seconds to line up a shot up, although I can tell that the devs have tried to make this less annoying with the rebound puzzles in particular.
I ended up just giving up on the game partly into Farjo Temple (10-15 hours into the game if you like to complete most of the quests in an area before moving on) just because I found myself playing just because I'd already put in so many hours with several frustrations with the combat and puzzles just piling up into enough of an issue for me to not see the story through to the end and just play something else, which is a real shame because I was really interested in seeing how things panned out and the different town areas (which were really well done and very interesting to walk around in).
On a positive note, Crosscode has beautiful art and music throughout the portions of the game I played, and the character dialog is well written (I really liked the protagonist interactions in particular). I really enjoyed the towns, and that there were almost always things waiting for you to find if you just spend a little time exploring them. There are also a lot of little details (like party chatter and NPC conversations) scattered around the place that really nail the MMO world setting the game takes place in.
Overall, I have to say give this one a miss unless you think the art, music, and story is good enough that you can look past the issues with the combat later in the game and the other frustrating things scattered throughout the game.

I have mixed feelings on this game. Story-wise, it remains loyal to the series and introduces new characters as well as characters from the show (with some of the actual cast providing voices!)
Basically, the game is set in a similar style to the books. You play as two characters, Mors, a ranger of the Night's Watch, and Alester, a red priest who has returned from Braavos to reclaim his father's seat as Lord. You switch between both characters  every chapter. The RPG elements are great, allowing you to choose your style of play. Mors and Alester have different fighting styles, and you can pick which path you want them to go down. You can upgrade your skill tree, add points to weapons etc... all the typical RPG things. What ultimately kills it however is the combat system.  When you engage in battle you select an enemy and you can line up attacks. Using such an old combat model for this type of game is its downfall. I could look past some of the other aspects except this.
Performance-wise, the game is stable and runs smoothly. The graphics are dated, but they're not bad so to say. Just don't expect super beautiful graphics. The enviroments are also a bit shallow. Riverspring, during the riots felt a bit bland to my taste. There was none of that true hateful spirit! You need to play the game to see for yourself. Apart from that the game hasn't aged well. It feels like it was made back in 2000.
But what about the story? The thing that made me a big fan of GoT is the story, which in this case this game has remained loyal to. The game takes place before the events of the first book, in a simpler time when Robert Baratheon was still whoring away, Eddard Stark's head was still on his shoulders and the realm was finally in peace after the downfall of the Targaryens. Some of the cast members from the show lent their voices! I was absolutely surprised when I heard Varys' spidery voice narrating the intro and good ol' Jeor Mormont giving orders to the Night's Watch. It's those little things that make this game so special.
It has it's flaws but if you are willing to overlook the outdated game mechanics, I recommend this. It's a must-get for any true GoT fan (It's better for readers of the book, but show-watchers are welcome to try it!) If you want a proper quality GoT experience, play Telltale's Game of Thrones game. There is far more polish and TV-esque story than this.
EDIT: Oh and I forgot to mention the voice acting. Apart from the cast who lent their voices (which sound just like in the show!) some of the voices can sound uninspired, like when they're saying, "OH MY GOD WE'RE GONNA DIE!" They sound sort of bored. Not all the voices are like that, but some definetly are.

Overall this is a solid game. The combat is a little dull and the voice acting might be nothing to write home about. The story and the writing is the game strongest point. If you enjoy the show or the books you will have a fun time. If you played games like Dragon Age Origins and wanted to play in the Game of Thrones universe instead then you will enjoy this game.

Here's a basic breakdown of Pro's and cons for GOT the Game...
Pro's:
Good Story. GOT from an origional perspective: and written by George RR Martin!
Good graphics. Yeah, some people have said they look a bit "dated" but when has that been terrible? I still think AC Brotherhood has good graphics and that's four years old. GOOD GRAPHICS dammit.
Lots of weapons.
Good Voice Acting
Brilliant Music.
No Impact:
Skills sytem is different but has no real impact on gameplay aside from being an average skills system.
Cons:
TERRIBLE COMBAT!!! : Despite the hype, this has the combat of the average Generic MMO. The only cool part is the ability to "slow down time" in the middle of a conversation, so the speaker's voice gets distorted (heheh).
You spend lots of time "finding" things. IE. "Here's the way into a room you need to investigate to continue the story, which is a really cool story you want more of! Oops, now where was the way out again? Sorry. Guess you'll have to check EVERY GODDAMN DOOR IN WESTEROS!!!!!"
No character customization. Yes, I know you play as a GOT character BUT...
Levels that trap you. "Find the rocks." OK... WHERE exactly? See above. I can't progress in that story I raved about untill I FIND THOSE DAMN ROCKS!!!
Linear. This is not normally a "critiscm" of a game, since there's alot of good "linear" games. Sure, I prefer open world and sandbox because there's much more to do, but levelled games can be fun as well, the same things happen bassically, and they can still get your blood pumping. Some of the earlier COD games and Halo are a good example, as well as various racers, and classics like Mario...
But not Game of Thrones. Oh God no. Because this game has ABSOLUTLEY NO REPLAY VALUE!!! You only play it for the story, and you must do eveything EXACTLY how they want you to (you can't even draw your weapon without permission from the magic devs) to progress, so what's the point of replay?
Some skills are useless: Wild Fire is incredibly rare, and for the first five levels of "fire" skill (there are only six levels per skillset by the way) you need Wildfire equipped.
LONG conversations. Sure, I know this is GOT, more plotting than slaying, but really? A fifteen minute conversation with an NPC (admittedly and IMPORTANT NPC but..) that you can't get away from? How about "choosing options in conversations?" How about three times in fifteen minutes?
"Consequences for your actions" havn't appeared in the 15 hours I've played the game...
BUGS. This game crashes far to frequently for my taste...
Overall: I'd reccomend buying this game for about $5 at max. Its bassically another Game of Thrones novel, yet it bassically tells the same story you've already heard from a different perspective. All the pro's are bassically things they brought over from the epic TV series (like voice actors, music, setting, etc.). However, I can understand a desire to buy this game simply to be able to wander around Westeros (and there's precious few time and far too small locations to do that).
Play at your own risk.

From Dust brings the term sandbox game into a whole new meaning.  You are literally dropped into a giant side box.  A sandbox that you can control and manipulate in order to help your tribesmen find the promised land.  Developed by Ubisoft, and release in August of 2011.  From Dust gives you god like powers over the elements.
The premise here is simple.  With your various powers over the sand, wind, water and fire, guide your tribe from totem to totem in order to unlock a portal to the next zone.  Each level gradually introduces you to new powers and concepts.  The first few levels are pretty straight forward and act as tutorials to help you develop an understanding for the game's basic mechanics and controls.  You can literally take your godly hand and scoop up areas of terrain, or water, or even lava to mold and manipulate the land.
As you proceed farther into the game, these powers are used not only to lead your tribe forward, but also to protect them from the earth itself.  Whether it's fire, floods, giant waves or massive eruptions, you must continually alter the earth in order to keep your tribe safe.  This is where the interaction of the various powers comes to fruition.  Though sand can be piled up and prevent waves of water from flooding the area, the force of the water can eventually erode the sand away.  Combining lava and sand can create rock to solve this problem, but accidentally redirecting lava in the wrong direction can be even deadlier.
This balance of powers, and the addition of various power ups as well map unique quantities like hidden underground springs and other surprises keep you adapting often.  The maps often adapt as well.  Several levels in From Dust change part way through and throw new obstacles your way.  In a first play through these events create greater challenges as now your well planned out modifications to the world need to quickly be changed before your tribe is flooded, or burned alive.
The look and feel of the earth and it's elements is also just a lot of fun to play with.  Terraforming the earth with your various powers is intuitive and the elements react in fairly realistic way.  Water and lava combine into clouds of steam, cooling into ever growing mounds of rock.  Rivers slowly cut their way through sand at the lowest points creating rivers and peninsulas.  It's truly a wonder to just play in the sandbox that is From Dust just to see what will happen.
Throughout all this, a charming story of the cycle of life unfolds.  From Dust is definitely a game you want to give a full play through of to gain the full experience.  The beautiful graphics and physics hold up today against more modern games.  The story, though a relatively simple one of life and death is told mostly visually as you proceed from level to level.  This is a great game, and a gem to try if you have a chance.

GemCraft is a Tower Defense game, with a twist...
You combine different gem types to customize your towers and traps, which you place yourself.
Skills increase the power of your gems and spells. Each map contributes to your XP, best score from each.
In traditional RPG style, more XP=higher character level, giving more skill points to spend.
You can reset your skills if you want to, so you don't have to restart the game to try a different strategy.
There are too many maps (tracks) for me to count and you unlock 3 difficulty levels.
Each level can be played in "Endurance mode", which will max at 999 waves. (I think)
I've only made it to wave 260 or so.
This means that it will take a LONG time to fully complete this game. I have >480 hours in game and I can not see the light at the end of the tunnel. The replay value this game possesses is enormous. But it doesn't feel that way because of all the different maps.
This is why I have nominated this game for the write in category of "Best Replay Value."

Anodyne is a rather charming, laid back game, but it didn't leave any particularly lasting impression on me. It was a nice throwback to a style of game which I once enjoyed, is a little self-aware but not annoyingly so, but the story seemed secondary to everything else and was more there to string together a series of set-pieces. The music was quite good.
It's alright. If you enjoyed Link to the Past or Link's Awakening back in the day, it's worth a look, although moreso on sale when you can.

Anodyne has a great atmosphere and decent gameplay, but its slow pace will be off-putting to many players.
What was awesome:
As I said above, the atmosphere was wonderful. The music really sets the tone the developer wanted and the pixel art was beautifully done. I also enjoyed the diversity between the worlds you explore.
What was okay:
The mechanics the game supplies you feel fresh, but leave you feeling over-prepared in the often empty environment. The ambiguous storyline may be a deal-break for some, so know what to expect before you purchase the game.
What was bad:
Your initial visit to each world is exciting, but the backtracking gets old. The problem is that Anodyne never enthralls the player enough to want to stick around. Just when you start to get immersed in a boss battle or a puzzle, the game decides to slow down.
If you like games that focus on exploration and have the patience it takes to explore the entire game, give Anodyne a chance.

Rising Storm 2: Vietnam comes from the same developers who've made the kiling floor series and previous RS games, Tripwire Interactive. I've played red orchestra briefly and killing floor 2 for 30 hours, those games are also considered great in my book. So I didn't expect this game to be bad at all, and it isn't. It's tactical, engaging, fun, and realistic. You will FEEL like you are in vietnam. You will RUSH to the trenches to dodge napalm or artillery. You will be able to bring WRAITH to the VCs by BURNING THEM ALIVE WITH SWEET NAPALM AND FLAME THROWER! You will also CONSTANTLY die, it's not for the light hearted.
Tripwire did an excellent job with the gameplay. To quickly summarize it, there are two main sides: Vietnam and US Military, each come with different roles, weapons and equipment. Vietnamese soldiers are masters guerilla combat, making use of deadly traps such as tripwires, mines and punji traps. They may not have the fire power or weaponry, but they certainly know how to keep an area well mined and ready for ambush. They do not have any vehicle access and generally carry more outdated but still effective weaponry. As for the US military, you will get access to modern weaponry, grenades and equipment for the time. You will employ various tactics using whatever weapon or equipment the classes come with such as the engineer who can weild a flamethrower or plant c4 to clear out enemy buildings. You can throw smoke to temporarily create cover. You can even become the pilot of a cobra attack helicopter or a huey, transporting soldiers across the battlefield. This side also comes with the ability to napalm the VCs. Both sides have access to Artillery support.
This area is bit lacking for the game, the game really feels a bit buggy and inconvienent. The best example I have is for how clunky crouching and proning can feel at times. Hitmarkers can also be a bit messy at times and lead to accidental deaths. Regardless, the game isn't TOO buggy and feels like it's made professionally almost all the time. A lot of people say optimization is TRASH in this game, I disagree and agree. For me, I run everything on ultra and can still pull 55-60 most of the time, lowering to 40 in the worst cases. So, bug fixing and optimization is definently needed in this game.
This part of the game is done decently, the post processing doing all of the marvelous visual work. The graphics are a bit lacking for this game compared to AAA titles like Witcher or Fallout but they aren't garbage and work well with the environment and gameplay. The post processing effects are nothing too special either but they add on to the feeling. I hope graphics and post processing gets a bit more work in coming updates of the game.
So the big question, is this game worth the price?
Definently, even more so. For 25 dollars( 22 since the sale) this game is amazing! The gameplay is the heart and strongsuit of the game and makes up for the flaws it has. To rate it on a scale of 1-10, I'd give a solid 7.

Deadly Premonition is weird. that is true. it's also eerily close in themes and plot to Twin Peaks, a show which the creator of Deadly Premonition claims to have never heard of. The graphics are uncanny valley, the writing seems purposefully enigmatic and strange, and the plot seems right out of an episode of the X-Files while still trying to play itself straight. But these are all reasons why Deadly Premonition is one of the greatest mystery games of all time. Engross yourself in the culture of a small american town as seen through the eyes of a japanese videogame developer. Take control of Agent Francis York Morgan as he reads the future in the clouds of his coffee, and shoots plant zombies while wearing a bright orange suit. Get paid by the goverment for shaving. And most of all, embrace the weird, and you might find yourself seeing the game for the piece of art that it is.

This game runs poorly, even if you install DPFix. It doesn't look very good. It controls poorly. The combat, hiding, and evasion scenes are even poorly designed, before you get to controlling them. I've had it crash several times. I've only played a short bit on PC to see how it would run, after completiting it on Xbox 360, and I've had force-quits multiple times. I've even heard of bugs that can prevent you from completing the game, which is the entire reason to play the game.
But this game is enchanting. The story and characters, as much as you can say they are stolen from Twin Peaks, are fascinating and engaging. You will likely have numerous fits of laughter as you experience the quirky animations and dialogue. And the plot goes into perhaps even stranger and disturbing depths than Twin Peaks did. It's worth your time to stick with the game, even if the game is not to your liking, because the story is not to be missed.
That said, if a game that has numerous technical issues is going to bother you, then you shouldn't play it. You can experience the story elsewhere, and get most of the enjoyment from watching it as you would playing it, without having to struggle through what most people would consider a negative experience of completing the game's often tedious "dungeon" segments.
I would say to absolutely wait for sales, even if you really want the game, and know you will enjoy it. This game goes on sale for as much as 90% off fairly regularly, such that I've purchased extra copies for others on several different occasions in the last few years, so you won't have to wait long to get a deal. I first purchased it for $15, as the original release on the Xbox 360, and didn't regret it one bit, but not everyone will get that same enjoyment, or have the same feelings. I can't recommend it at normal price, but cannot recommend it enough for $2.50-$5.

There are two things you should know about me: 1) I'm a big fan of story driven RPGs 2) I am not a particular fan of Game of Thrones books/series. I have to say that this game is definitely one of the best RPGs I have played, and I have them a lot played under my belt (including Witcher and Dragon Age series). I will try to review this game by separately discussing 3 major values of any game. Note that I've finished this game on a higher difficulty (Lord)
TL:DR : Highly recommend this game due to it's with complex characters, intriguing story with lots of twists and plots, dialogue filled with tough moral choices that have actual impact, and an overall enjoyable combat system, that admittedly has some frustrating moments.
1) Story: The story is most likely the strongest point in this game. With numerous plot twists and a moderate-to-strong influence on the story through decisions I have found repeatable joy starting each new chapter not knowing how will the story unfold next. The fact that it's is told through the perspective of two characters which you mostly control alternately through chapters makes the storytelling even a greater experence. Speaking of characters, rarely you will see so much effort placed into complex character creation such as this one - each individual, especially the main characters, is well though of, has clearly outlined psychological traits, way of thinking, unique history and temperament. After a while, it is not difficult to bond and side with some characters more than others.
2) Video/Audio: Combat animation can seem a bit quirky as the you deal damage after you finish your attack, not on the actual point of impact. Similarly, skills that interrupt do that as soon as you start casting them, and, yet again, not on the point of impact. The graphics in the games are quite decent though, unlike the voice acting which is superb. I thoroughly enjoyed listening each line in a HUGE dialogue tree, most likely because the voice of the character well matches their unique character traits and current emotions.
3) Gameplay:
To be honest I wasn't quite sure how I feel about it at times. On one hand the battles were fun and so were the skills even though there are not unique. On the other, I found losing a few battles for it's hard to reposition yourself (from arrow fire) if you have a companion. While you move your character to safety your companion, in the meantime bravely rushes to his own premature end, but if you try to reposition your companion, same thing happens to your main character. Also, if you don't stack yourself with potions, you might find yourself not being able to survive a fight, which would mean going back to a not so recent save in a different chapter only to restock. This, however, may be due to the higher difficulty I played on.
This game has done a great job on this. Decisions you make can have a major impact on what happens next. Sometimes the decisions you make show you instant results, but more times than not you will feel their consequences much later in the game. Dialogue is filled with difficult moral choices that could make you think hard for a few minutes before committing - expect a lot of gray area.

This game is absolutely amazing.  I find the gameplay to be fast pased and the controls (gamepad for me) to be tight which makes for a good skill based game, meaning that you can overcome being underleveled or under equipped by the user playing the game better.  The game maintains throughout a good rate of increasing difficulty in congruence with equipment availability and unlocking more skills that make a real difference in gameplay.  In addition to this, you can use the combination of skills and equipment to really change how you approach battles, so you can play in a way that feels most natural to you.  Dungeon battles, not just bosses, are often challenging and require you to be well versed with your style of play.  Enemies also have a "break" state that often require a specific timing or procedure to "break" them for a short time, but allow you to do a significanly higher amout of damage making battles much easier versus brute forcing your way though them.  This creates diverse and engaging combat, especially when there are multiple types of enemies you're fighing at the same time.
Dungeon puzzles start off easy, but late in the game become quite difficult at times, but not impossible, and rewarding when you're able to figure them out.  Where puzzles in many games fail to nail the right level of challenge, this game succeeds.  Many of the late game puzzles are beyond brilliant when you consider how many levels there are to the puzzle yet managing to cram all of those levels into a concise space where many environmental features double or triple in their usage.  I would honestly like to shake then hands of the people who created them.  There are always subtle environmental elements that lead you in the right direction or give you just enough of a hint to figure out what you're supposed to be doing.  I cannot praise this enough as most games focus on creating an environment purely for the sake of immersion and fail to make the best use of the space available to them to enhance the manner in which the player interacts with the game.
Platforming is smooth and jumping is automatic thereby removing jumping fustrations common in many platorming games.  The one exception to this is the rare occasion when you can't tell exactly the height of a platform even after throwing a ball at it making it difficult to judge if you can make the jump to it.  Finding treasure boxes in the world by figuring out the often complex jumping path to get there makes for a great change of pace, though the rewards for doing so are often lackluster.
If you choose to do all the sidequests available to you, you don't need much grinding, if any at all, to keep up in level to where the game has been designed for you to be.  If however you are the type to focus on the storyline and skip a lot of sidequests, grinding will likely be needed on a continual basis depending on how skilled you are at overcoming the power gap.  Also, for those who are less patient when getting into a new game, the "tutorial-ish" section (tutorial + practice dungeon) is just a bit long (about 3 hours) before the game begins to open up.
I feel the graphics, sound effects, and music are all well above average for what it's trying to be; you can easily check them out for yourself above.  But if you don't like them, you don't like them, I'm not going to argue that you should.
At the time of writing this, the story has not been finished, but so far, to me, the story is kind of meh as it uses a slightly overused plot, especially so if you've watched mmo based animes.  However, each of the main characters provides a unique and interesting personality which is engaging in its own right and contributes to a game that succeeds in creating an immersive experience.
The amount of content in the game is good for probably 25 hours up to 50 depending on how good you are and how you decide to play it and the game isn't even finished yet.  It has a fair number of completionist elements, but has little replayability.  I really wish the game would offer online co-op as it is tailor made for it, but it doesn't sound like that will ever be an available feature.
For me (someone who has played video games most of my life), the level of challenge in battle and puzzles are perfect, but may be too difficult for others.  This is what I wish most of the 2D Zelda games were (apart from storyline/lore).

I used to play a predecessor on some flash site a decade ago and had only vague fond memories. Boy am I glad, this game hasn't disappointed my memories of GemCraft - it's freaking awesome!
The main game consists of 168 pre-made maps. Monster spawns and paths are pre-set, while you generally build towers and sometimes mazes. The towers only serve as sockets for gems, which is where the game is starting to open up. There are 9 colours with different base stats and special effects and it is completely up to you how you combine and level up gems. Do you want slow-down, poison and armour tearing in a single gem? You can do that!
Meanwhile each beaten level causes you to get stronger and stronger both via the XP and skill system and via picked-up talisman fragments. You discover new gem colours and 6 different spells (e.g. freezing), adding a dynamic component to what otherwise might be relatively passive levels.
The progression is where this game really shines. If a monster with 1.000 HP seems unbeatable at first, after a few dozen hours monsters with trillions of HP will be trivial to kill. And the most astonishing thing is, the game always keeps up with your power level. After unlocking them, you have available 3 difficulties and 9 different "traits" to enhance each level and after the base level you can always enter Endurance Mode up to wave 999. With the wrong settings you can go back to level 1 and find yourself utterly out-classed. With the right settings and tactics you can go back to level 1 and upgrade your score from 100 XP to 100 billion XP, feeding back into growing stronger.
Personally I really enjoyed the ridiculous exponential levelling, culminating in beating my first Endurance Mode against a final "e45" wave, meaning its monsters' HP were numbers with 46 digits (aka a quattuordecillion). But at this point you are running into severe technical problems. With around 10.000 monsters on screen, my game grinds to a near-halt with less than 1 FPS. So even after 140 hours there is still much content left, but it's super grindy and little fun to stare at a slide-show for hours.
If all that power grind is not for you - don't worry! Grinding makes the game much much easier, but it is not required at all. And if you never crank up the difficulty, the game is actually pretty casual and relaxing. There are 23 "Vision Fields", that fully turn the genre around into a puzzle game. Here your progression doesn't matter as you have to beat challenges with pre-defined tools. This is taken to the extreme in Iron Wizard Mode, where you can run through the 168 levels of the base-game with a capped progression and no possibility to grind. After 80 hours in the main game, Iron Wizard Mode was still a really interesting challenge and made me think about the game in a different way, because overpowering brute force wasn't an option anymore.
There is just so much to do! Discovering 191 different maps, trying out new skill combinations and strategies, revisiting old levels with new challenges, etc! Many levels even feature interesting achievements, requiring you to think and play outside of your comfort zone (e.g. using only poison or building no towers). There is a very flimsy story arc with nice artwork, but don't expect a proper narrative. The graphics are decent, as is the sound. But let's be honest, the focus is clearly on gameplay first and foremost and this is where the game excels.
This is easily the best Tower Defense game out there and worth every penny! I have never seen such a variety and depth in a Tower Defense game with such a rock solid core gameplay. If you are still on the fence, try out the free browser-based flash version before buying.

Stellaris is another one of Paradox' masterpieces. Anyone can judge the Paradox-Policy of Creating DLC content themselves. I for myself am okay with that, since it more often than not means support and updates for games that have been out for years (see Crusader Kings 2 which still gets DLC to this day). So this review is for the GAME Stellaris and not for the company policies of Paradox.
Stellaris is a 4X type space-colonization strategy game in pausable "real time" (daily ticks). The main game is no clear-cut story driven campaign, as in many strategy games and the game does not feature a "story mode" like for example campaigns in Total War games.
Instead you write your own story and history, unbound by preset provinces etc. - similar to Sid Meier's Civilization just not turn based.
You start off by creating your very own "Empire" (or by randomizing it if you want the surprise-factor or are just lazy). You have the ability to choose an appearance for your Species from many partially animated portrait sets, that will represent your population and leaders throughout the game. You customize the appearance of your space ships, cities, the type of climate your species desires on their colony worlds (from arctic over ocean to desert climate - 9 in total) and set what your civilisations original way of FTL-travel is. Some of these choices are cosmetic, others actually have a deep impact on the game. Not to forget: You set your species traits based on a trait-point system and customize your initial government type through the selection of an "authority level" (like e.g. democracy or dictatorship etc.) and ideology traits (like e.g. xenophile or militaristic etc.) as well as fitting civic policies.
You start the game in a Galaxy - which's size and properties you can chose beforehand - and begin your exploration by controlling your ships, building new ones, researching technology and colonizing planets. Or your expansion. Or your domination of the Galaxy. You will run into anomalies, alien species and realms - both sentient and non-sentient, space-fairing and primitive, empires and enclaves - always forced to make decisions. Some decisions you can only take when your empire has a certain ideology (purge indigenous species on colonized planets), other events happen because of the technologies you have researched (an AI rebellion for example). This way you advance through the years, build up your empire, form an intergalactic federation or just conquer it all. The victory conditions are just that: Dominate or Unify.
You can either play the game casually just enjoying the ride, or min-max every aspect of the game, something the game actually allows you, since you can see every little number, percentage and even customize your warships to the single plasma cannon.
The game is technically up to the standards, shows no bugs at this point that I am aware of (the occasionally confused AI is only a very minor issue and certainly not game-breaking) and it is constantly updated, and the DLC will keep pouring in for the next months, probably years to come If Paradox keeps its course.
I can recommend this game to every strategy gamer, and since this is not turn based even to RTS fans, since the Multiplayer actually demands a certain skill level and knowledge of the games features to respond to threats in time, that can even tickle the fancy of deep-core RTS players. The game allows for a peaceful approach with few wars and conquests as well as for a militaristic domination and so even the more relaxed players can enjoy this game just laying back and managing their growing Commonwealth without need for military action, solving a crisis or the other and befriending everyone. The game has an incredible depth, but allows you to go easy on some of these elements until you actually want to learn about them, but gives you constant nudges to try them out in the form of events and problems which could be solved more efficiently by diving in deeper into the game than before.

OK, the review:
From Dust is a beautiful game, and another pleasure-button hitter for those of us that love this type of "God" game.  You control "The Breath", which is basically your cursor, and it can suck up different types of matter and drop it where you like.  Using this ability, you get your Lemming-like tribe to be able to find certain areas that unlock certain things.
The story is...different, but doesn't get in the way, mostly it's about the puzzles.  You'll have challenges you have to accomplish before you're able to complete the map, and also there's extra stuff you can sometimes find that give you perks of some variety.  Some hazards you'll have to overcome are static, like a river you must divert; others are dynamic events that can impact the whole map.
All in all, if you have a decent system, don't mind UPlay, and love the genre, From Dust is worth it, best on sale.

GUN is a very interesting game back from the old days. Well, to be honest, it's not that old of a game, but if you compare games made in this day and age to the tech of the old days, I'd say it's safe to call it old, but not ancient. If you've played Red Dead Redemption before, you'll see quite a few striking similarities between GUN and this game. I wouldn't be suprised if Rockstar got many of their ideas for Red Dead from this game, but there's absolutely nothing wrong with that, since inspiration is part of art anyway.
I personally enjoyed the game and appreciated the open world it had to offer, although I did not enjoy the story. There are quite a few fans of the game that argue GUN is a much better game than Red Dead, but if you ask me, none of that is true in the slightest. Lemme elaborate my thoughts on this. You'll be able to understand this review a bit more if you've played Red Dead Redemption before, but if you're new to this genre, there's still a lot of information for you that's worth knowing.
The Gameplay:
Considering that the tech they had in 2005 was nowhere near as good as it was in 2010 when RDR was released, you can safely say that the open world in GUN is smaller and there is much less content. That doesn't mean the game is bad, and if you ask me, this game was pretty damn good for its time. As far as gameplay is concerned, you can ride a horse, explore the world, take part in side missions, or break the law, just like RDR. Also, remember the Dead Eye mechanic from Red Dead? You know, the one that allows you to slow down time and shoot enemies in slow motion? GUN had this very same mechanic five years before RDR took off where the game left and added improvements for it.
As far as combat is concerned, you'll be put up against hordes of enemies attacking buildings and settlements, and you will take part in battles against your foes with allies. Shooting doesn't work nearly as well as it does in RDR, since aiming is dumbed down. Basically on GUN, if your crosshair turns red on an enemey, even if the crosshair's center isn't even on the target, you still still manage to shoot them regardless. With all that being said, the combat is repetitive but fun, filled with senseless violence and shooting you would expect from a game set in the Wild West. You can throw molotovs and dynamite, use pistols, use rifles, shotguns, you name it. A game like this was undoubtedly awesome for its time, but arguing that this game is better than RDR is completely laughable.
The Story (don't worry, I won't reveal any major spoilers for GUN except the main character's name and personality, but there are major spoilers for Red Dead. I believe it's important to compare these two stories to get an idea of what GUN is all about):
I remember hearing from somebody that GUN's story is better than Red Dead's. Before I played the game, I kept an open mind, and when I finally decided to buy it, I can definitely tell you that the story isn't executed well, even if you don't compare it to RDR.
Am I saying the story is bad? First of all, the story's concept isn't bad, but the way it was executed was terrible later on in the game.
Basically, the plot starts out this way: Something terrible happens to the main character. The main character sets of on a quest after a dramatic event, looking for answers about himself, and also trying to discover the sinister plans of his enemies. Is it different from RDR? Yes. For one thing, RDR's plot was rather simple, but there are complex meanings behind it. John Marstin (if that's how you spell the full name) was a criminal trying to fix his ways when the law holds his family hostage. He is essentially trying to pay the debt. Later on, John pays his debt to the law, which in turn stabs him in the back and kills him. His son grows up seeking personal revenge, and he finds the man who ordered his father to be killed, and kills him in return. What was Red Dead's story about? It was about the struggles of keeping morals when you live in a world where people only care for themselves. It was about dealing with the consequences of your actions, and how the desire to seek revenge for wrongdoings done unto you can turn you into the very people you despise.
So yeah, RDR did have an amazing plot for sure, and the characters? Very well thought out. They fit the atmosphere of the game very well, which I will tell you more about after I talk about GUN's main character.
So what makes Colton, the main character, different from John and his son? Well for one thing, even though this story is set in the Wild West, which means Colton is a gritty, tough hero like all heroes in a Western, one who is also motivated by personal revenge, you can easily argue that he still somehow manages to stick to the more noble path far better than John Marstin and his son.
While many of GUN's characters, including Colt's allies, are believable, there is one villain I highly dislike. This one is a corrupt religious zealot working for the main villain. While I understand that he was a clergyman, the character design is awful. He looks more like somebody from the Middle Ages, and his personality doesn't fit well either. Other characters in the game, including the minions you shoot at, look more like a bunch of giants on steroids rather than humans.
Now, for those of you wondering why I felt GUN's plot was poorly executed later on in the game, let me tell you why. It's rushed way too fast. On some missions, you will find yourself attacking an enemy base, and once you're done, you might expect a cutscene that will further explain the story and elaborate exactly what happened, but instead, you are immediately progress to the next stage. Is there anything wrong with more focus on gameplay? No. But there is something wrong with failing to elaborate on what you have done, and what awaits next BEFORE you progress.
Conclusion:
Yes, GUN is a good game, but considering that its open world has far less to offer, its gameplay has less features, and its story just feels rushed way too fast at the middle and the end, can you really safely argue that this game is better than RDR? There's no way you can. The point is that it is a gem worth playing, and it was definitely an amazing game for its time.

A top down racing game where you have to avoid crashing into the walls (and if going more than medium pace, cars which spin you into walls if you hit them) and run over the petrol pumps to extend your timer - while it seems like it should be a fuel gauge, it goes down at the same speed whether you are going top speed or crawling along at a snails pace, so functionally it is a timer. This gives the odd situation that if you are running low on "fuel" you have to nail the accelerator in the hope you make it to the next fuel station in time.
The early levels (1-4) play quite well, you can go flat out in light traffic, and the challenge of hitting at least every third or so fuel pump while also avoiding cars makes for quite a good balance. This all starts to fall apart from the 5th level with the combination of regular narrow 2 lane sections that make it impossible not to slow down to a much more sedate pace, plus a new type of car in the traffic that bounces from wall to wall, which are bad enough to deal with in the full width sections, but basically make going any faster than about 150 suicidal from that point on.
If you can make it pootling along to level 10-11 it then gets worse, as you end up stuck on an almost continuously 2 narrow lane setup, which briefly widens regularly but no usually long enough to overtake anything. Meanwhile a mass of purple cars that all go the same speed and move to block you appear and quickly there are dozens of them making it impossible to do anything but chug along behind them at a tepid pace.
Overall I can't really recommend this, if the difficulty of the traffic ramped up slowly following the patterns at the beginning of the game it could have been fairly decent, but everything after that is poor and gets worse. This is for all of the people who are calling this game a Zelda rip-off:
Look, I understand where you're coming from.  At many times I would see something in the game and go "OH, really showing your roots there Anodyne, might as well just call your last boss Ganon and slap on a green hat..."  but then, I did something that really helped me appreciate the game, and games in general, for that matter.  I stopped evaluating it with respect to other games.  I considered it by itself.
The art style is beautiful, and it's not fair to say that just because other games have succeeded using a pixel art aesthetic that Anodyne is just riding their coattails.  Is it true?  Maybe.  Is is a fair criticism?  No.  It's really not.  Look at the game again and tell me it isn't beautiful.  I spent so much time in the world of Anodyne not because I miss my old Link's Awaknening game, but because it was a world in which I truly enjoyed to be.
So, the moral of the story is this:  you can tell me that the game lacked meaning, or didn't appeal to you, or that you didn't like the art style or humor or direction or pacing or any other legitimate complaint.  Just at least give it the credit to evaluate it by its OWN merits.
The platforming is fun and challenging, the myriad of ways in which the designers have you exploring the broom mechanic is brilliant, the characters are quirky and fun, the world is gorgeous, and I truly enjoyed every part of this game.  I would recommend this game a thousand times over.

I will start this review with the short of it for those who don't feel like reading: the game itself is wonderful in my oppinion, especially the sundtrack, story and gameplay variety, but the PC port itself has some serious issues that can make it straight unplayable for people who don't want to do a little extra work to fix it.
In more detail, here's what I love about it sorted by how much impact it made on me:
1. The soundtrack is outstanding. It is still playing in my head regularly, and I can recall the different tracks almost flawlessly.
2. Gameplay is very good, combat feels engaging, and there is more than one type of gameplay as most people probably know, keeping one away from boredom.
3. The story is smart and interesting enough to distinguish itself from the avarage storyline in the genre. It touches on philosophy occasionally, but don't expect it to be too much of an intellectual wonder. What it shines with is offering the player new perspectives of what they have been experiencing, causing them to rethink past events on regular basis.
4. The environment and the characters look really good. Graphics are not precisely state of the art, but the style and design are spot on.
5. The game does its best to immerse you into the world by making everything down to the game mechanics seem like a legitimate part of it, apart from a few quirky tropes we have come to expect from certain Japanese titles (such as the fact that the vanguard of humanity and androidity is comprised of android models shaped like young boys and attractive women). For example, the in-game menu is actually the android's self-management interface.
Now, these aside, there are a few things that are a big "NONO"'s in my book. Part of them did not bother me cause I don't mind messing with game tweaks and mods, but a fully released game having such issues is unacceptable in my opinion:
1. Game crashes. I have seen a lot of people complain about this, and while I cannot account for all flavours of crashing, I can tell you what was happening to me: due to the game apparently not being very good at working with multiple CPU cores (a lot of people assumed it cannot work with hyperthreading, but people who have the same number of physical and logical threads also suffered from this so I don't think this was the case), it always crashed before I could even reach the first possible save point. This was completely solved by running it via a script that only allows it to use half of the logical CPU threads.
2. Screen resolution issues. The game's own fullscreen mode caused it to switch to 4:3 ratio even though I was using my native resolution on a widescreen, resulting in everything getting elongated on-screen. The lack of borderless windowed mode forced me to use a 3rd party borderless window software in order to be able to properly play the game on my entire screen.
3. In certain gameplay segments, mouse controls are downright bugged. From my previous experince with the bad DS1 PC port, I assume this is due to the difference in how analogue sticks and mouses work not being properly accounted for. This can be partially overcome by relying on keyboard alone for the short duration of said segments.
4. FPS drops affecting the game in inconsistent ways. With a system that covers everything save for the GFX card from the recommended hardware, and a GFX card that is above the minimum requirements, on the lowest possible graphic settings, the FPS rate made at least one task in the game impossible to complete - due to FPS slightly slowing down gameplay, but NOT slowing down the timer for the task, causing it to run out even if you are progressing with near-perfect player performance.

A hands-down recommendation from me.
On the pro side, the game is extremely polished. Everything from the combat system to the visuals and music are well put together, impressively so.
The biggest con is the sheer fact that the game is incomplete, hardly something you can fault the developers for. I greatly look forward to the completed product.
The developers have delivered an extremely polished experience, even if half the story is still missing (I'm guessing, we don't know where the story is going :D)
The combat system is challenging but visually clear. Openings and attacks are telegraphed but timings and damage numbers can have you sitting at the edge of your seat.
Personally, I found the game very challenging, but this is also something I'm personally drawn to. Your own experiences may vary.
There seems to be quite a bit of depth to how you approach your character's skill development and usage in combat encounters. Most encounters, however annoying, will have a weak spot you can exploit to push the fight in your favour.
Visually and aesthetically, I felt the game reminded me a lot of the Mega Man Battle Network series. The setting of an MMORPG gives a sense of life to the game, as other characters will always be running around you, doing their own quests and having their own adventures. It's simple, but gives the world a sense of being much larger than yourself.
A lesser gripe might be the fact that changes in equipment aren't visually represented in the game (so much so that an NPC comments on this fact during the storyline). Conversely, it doubles down on establishing a dverse set of main characters, colour scheme, contour, and all.
The worst element within the game strikes me as the equipment system. Despite the developer's efforts to make this part of the game more approachable, I still can't get my head around matching a character's level to appropriate equipment. In the end, I ended up slapping on the pieces that gave the biggest boost to the stats I wanted to work with. It's a shame,
In essence, despite a few gaps in the system, CrossCode delivers a beautiful and polished experienced, even at this point of development. If you're a fan of twitch-heavy combat, high difficulty and an anime-inspired art style and storyline,
.
It's one thing to draw on the past, and another to actually make history.

You know, i got all the in-game achievements with just one steam achievement missing. Considering i spent 140 hours (-10 hours afk) and my achievement count still shows up as 100% (418/419) i will call this game done for now.
-
Gemcraft is an awesome and iconic 2D Tower Defense Game with an abundant choice of upgrades and difficulty options that you can change easily between 150+ levels. It got a unique and mystical story that i really got into while playing the game but that's not necessary to pay attention to, if you just want to progress in the game. The art and setting are really fitting as well.
If you're looking for a 2D Tower Defense Game, there are a few things you can expect right away, like different difficulties for different maps, an arsenal of different towers ranging from standard to unique towers all having a place and use case in the game, replayability and upgrades!
In my opinions Gemcraft exceeds in all of the listed points. You get more maps than you asked for but just enough to feed your endless craving for more, you get an extensive unlockable difficulty system to revisit beaten maps, you get levels out the oven to feed an immense scaling system with skill points and there are easter eggs and details left and right. You really feel how much thought was put into this game.
The tower system uses 9 different gems which incorporate skill effects corresponding to their color and you can mix and match them to your strategical needs. You drop the gems in the tower and upgrade them as you go. You can switch them out too, put them in traps, amplifiers or shrines. There is really a whole lot going on.
If you look for a tower defense game or if you're interested after reading this review you won't be disappointed by spending a few bucks.
Notes / Personal Milestones:
- Beat the storyline after 50 hours
- Reached level 1000 after 70 hours
- After 100 hours i reached level 1800, unlocked 98% of the achievements and finished 85% of the maps on a 70x difficulty multiplier
- 115 hours / lvl 2000 / 99% achievements (6 to go) / 90% maps
- After that i just finished the missing maps on hard mode without additional difficulty, started a new run for the last achievement but ultimately the grind grinded my gears and now i'm happy to let this game go, i got a little burnt out chasing achievements :')
I think there are many stages in the game and you have to decide for yourself how much time you want to invest into it. There are probably more casual players who wouldn't have the nerves to finish the storyline but get 20+ hours entertainment out of the game before they feel the repitition kicking in, then there are people who grind another 50 hours for high difficulty in every map, or maybe you want to grind all the 419 achievements.

Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is a fun and immersive realistic multiplayer FPS, with an emphasis on team work, patience, and hitting the deck as soon as you hear artillery near your position.
The good:
- Visually very appealing, from the bamboo houses of a vietnamese village along a riverside, to the dense and claustrophobic streets and alleyways of hue city, the lush jungles and foliage of the vietnam countryside to the desolate wasteland of hill 937, each map is highly detailed and varied enough to keep the player aesthetically pleased.
- Realism. If you enjoy realism in an FPS then you will be pleased. You WILL die to one or two bullets, getting headshot is an instakill, artillery makes you♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself, bullets ricocheting off the nearby surroundings will throw your concentration off and make you vulnerable. Running in guns blazing trying to be a hero will not work, you need to use your brain, and more importantly, cover.
- Combat itself is quite satisfying. Due to the nature of the game and the short time to kill on all weapons, an emphasis on flanking maneuvers, supressing fire and ambushes, most firefights are short and sweet. This means that you won't be in the action all the time, but when you are it is intense. Each weapon also serves a purpose too, the M60 is great for surpressing enemies, but high recoil means it is difficult to use while advancing, the M16 and AK excell at medium range combat, but lose some effectiveness in close quarters combat, which is where the M3 grease gun, PPSH and shotguns excell.
- Teamwork is key. The only way you will reliably stand a chance at winning a game is with good teamwork and co-ordination with your squad leaders and commander. You need to work with your squad to survive and take objectives, cover each others advance over open terrain and watch your flanks, storming a building on your own won't get results, but with a squad, half of which are flanking will. In addition you need to keep an ear out for when your commander is calling in artillery support, recon or napalm and so on; you don't want to be caught in friendly artillery or napalm.
- No progression system that affects gameplay. The only progression is for cosmetics such a different helmets, uniforms and camo for your character. This means a level 25 or 30 player has no unfair advantage over a lower level player (other than experience and map knowledge). This also means there isnt a "pay-to-win" system in the game, meaning all players are on a level playing field.
- Class sytem. Each class serves a certain battlefield role, and are limited to a set amount per side (meaning you can't have a load of snipers on a team not pushing an objective). This adds a bit more variety to combat.
The bad:
- Continuing on from the class system, the limits to each class can be quite low imo. For a 32 vs 32 player game, 2 snipers and machinegunners per team is low, meaning unless you're the first to load into a server chances are you won't be playing them. I understand this is most likely for balance reasons, but it can be a bit repetitive playing a rifleman for an entire match.
- Number of Maps. Although each map (at least the Supremacy and Territories maps, i've not as of yet played the skirmish maps) is visually appealing and quite fun to play, there are a limited number of maps as of right now; numbering a total of 8 maps. The devs have said there will be more maps in the future, and there are always maps made by the community, however the devs have not said when these maps will be coming and i feel the game hasnt been out long enough for any decent fan made maps.
- The movement can be a tad buggy at times, lying down in certain areas will cause you to twitch about until you get up or move to an area which is flat. And i've had a few problems with moving while prone with an M60, but that could be a rare occurance.
- Joining a match can be difficult sometimes. There is only a server browser, and the vast majority of servers are either dead empty or full. This isnt too much of a problem playing solo, as there is usually at least one or two servers with a few spots, but if you want to play with a group of say 5 friends, it may be difficult getting into a game.
- Performance. Can't say much here but i've heard from some that the game isn't optimised that well. I can't comment as i've not really had any performance issues on my computer, but i thought it was worth mentioning incase you don't have the most powerful PC.
- The viet cong voice acting. Personally i find it hilarious, but it is in all honestly really REALLY bad. But this is just a really minor point tbh.
Overall, if you want a realistic multiplayer FPS set in vietnam using authentic weapons and and emphasis on teamwork, short but sweet firefights and PTSD then this is the game for you.

The weirdest adventure Zelda-esque game I have played in a long time. It is one of these games that, after you finish it, you end up: 1. Completely lost, knowing nothing of the hell happened; 2. Searching forums and webs, looking for interpretations, analysis, reviews, wanting to fully understand all the extremely strange stuff you just played. You can love it or being indifferent to it; for me was a worth experience.

This is what you get when you mix the gameplay of the 2D Zeldas with the surrealness of something like EarthBound. I wasn't expecting much going in, but it ended up being enjoyable by the end of it. (Now if only we could open that 50-card door...)
Anodyne has some strong points and good moments that I won't spoil here. It's worth the asking price if you're a fan of the 2D Zeldas, but it needs some polish to be truly *great*.
For starters, as a first impression, when first running the game it asked me to adjust the window's size with the arrow keys (what game does this?), which couldn't even be held down to change the size and then proved to be completely useless when I could just change the settings to presets in the menu later. I understand this was originally made in Flash but the PC port should be more standardized with the resolution and other options.
There's quite a few dead-ends that *look* meaningful, but are really nothing of use and that makes the world feel more empty than it should be. Also the overworld could have been much more interesting but instead is just a bunch of mostly arbitrarily-placed portals to the different levels, of which have no labels to identify them aside from the small screenshot of the area (heck, even the signs in the levels are worn away and as such don't tell you where you're going).
My other critique would be that the pacing/story should be stronger. Finding the protagonist's signature broom is simply a plain chest in a plain room. The item itself is hilarious because there's nothing special about it and yet it's the weapon for the whole game, but the moment of getting it shouldn't have been so plain.
Overall, Anodyne is fairly imprssive considering it was made in 10 months by 2 developers, but it could have used more polish to really stand out as something greater than a Zelda-inspired dungeon-crawler.

An amazing product already with dozens of hours of gameplay for a low price point, and the game isn't even finished yet!
CrossCode is an action RPG following the main character Lea who plays the silent protagonist.  Knowing nothing about her past she is thrust into an adventure of discovering what events have lead to her current situation.  Although a common cliche of RPG's the silent protagonist is pulled off in a unique and amusing way and later dialogue choices are unlocked.  The characters you meet are decently written and the dialogue does a good job entertaining and telling the story.  I just finished the first major dungeon and I can't believe I have almost 15 hours logged (and this just unlocked the first of 4 skill trees!).
The pacing is moderate.  A more experienced action RPG enthusiast looking for a steep challenge can rush through the areas with what equipment is available or you can digest the areas and take time to appreciate the out of the way treasures tucked all over.  The game keeps track of your treasure completion rates and even after sinking 4 hours into the "mine" dungeon I'm still missing 2 chests... how is this possible... what trickery is this!???...
Needless to say for a completionist this game will keep you busy and it does a good job teasing your brain with many solutions requiring planning out from several maps away or looking at puzzles in a different light.
The quests are decent.  Some of the dialogue is charming, for example one quest sends you on an information gathering mission... which proves difficult with your mute characteristic.  Several spirtes for your portrait are in the game and you can watch your characters frustration grow with your own.  Overall the quests add some meat and lighten the mood while providing useful items to advance the main story.
The sound in the game is decent.  It doesn't elicit any strong emotions, but it's enjoyable enough that I can listen to it while trying to hunt down all of those chests without getting annoyed by it.
Controls are suprisingly natural.  I played with a mouse and keyboard setup which seemed to work well.  Aiming with the mouse for projectiles was particularly satisfying since I knew exactly where my shots would land right away.
Combat is fairly challenging.  Even with an average gear level and a good level many fights proved extra challenging and make sure that I'm not dozing away while hacking aimlessly.  Many enemies have weakenesses that can be exploited such as returned projectiles.  The character has a progression tree that allows them to focus on defense, dodging, ranged, or close quarters combat.  These trees expand when the elements are obtained.  This feature isn't fully complete at this time but already adds a good level of customization that lets you feel the effects during combat, sometimes by modifying an attack or adding a perk (regeneration!)
Exploration: There is a platforming element with many objectives that require timed and precise jumps and there are time attack courses.  The puzzles also take some thinking through and feeling your way through them unlocks items so that you feel rewarded for your time investment.
I feel like that is a ton more I could say but this has already dragged on long enough.  For a small development team this project is polished and enjoyable.  The game plays well and is challenging.  Reccomend it to everyone except for those that have a hard time with moderately difficult games as even with gear stacking there are some areas that will take skill to beat without being crushed by frustration.  Two big thumbs up!
TL/DR: BUY THIS GAME.  You owe it to yourself.

This is a labor of love for the developers, clearly. Fast and tight controls, perfect controller support, interesting and well made level design, interesting story, stable, really well made. And it's getting updates all the time, so it's not the usual abandoned early-access game.
But before going into it, be very aware what type of game this is. It's singleplayer, but emulating an MMO. So while there are other NPCs running around acting like players, and continual party chat from your friends, it is an offline MMO. It's also not a typical RPG, but rather an action/platforming game. So there are two MAJOR points to understand:
1. The game is a grind. Leveling up is not fast. Gathering materials for crafting is not fast. Completing collection quests is not fast. You have to be prepared to grind like an MMO to make progress, particularly since most equipment of value needs to be crafted from those rare drop materials.
2. This is a parkour game. Chests need to be jumped to. Crossing many maps means jumps. Even the second city is one big maze of multi-level jumps. Quests have you jumping to hard-to-reach platforms. Many paths take you several screens away to find the route up to where you need to be and 1 missed jump means starting over.
But if you can handle the parkour and the grind, the game is very well made.
