If you know games like Dragon Age you will be quite familiar with this. you can pause (here: slow down) the game and activate skills to kill or interrupt enemies while adding states like stun, bleed, poison etc. on them. There is a cast bar for any skill or action you take, so anticipating moves is often required. A random aggro system is there that depends on damage dealt and there are skills to provoke enemies, but apart from that they often seem to attack randomly. There is also an armor system with different types of weapons having a greater effect on certain type of armor, combined with the ability to switch weapons this makes for a very good combat system - on paper. Effectively this is pretty pointless, as the damage bonus is always the same (15%) and there is no penalty. In addition you would of course need another weapon and the skill to fill the second weapon slot, apart from that you have 3 weapon types but only 2 weapon slots (unless dual-wielding). Add the fact that light armor grants low health and heavy armor high health in general what makes it obviously more beneficial to invest into things that increase damage against heavy armor, the rest dies anyway. There are also criticals, deflection and dodge effects, but I will come to them in the next section. Basically everything your character can do, the enemy can do as well, except for instant interrupts (only the interrupting part is instant, those skills still activate like any other).
There are multiple things that have to be considered: attributes, abilities, skills and traits.
Attributes directly influence your characters stats, like damage or health. An important point is that upon creating your character you can already maximize 2 attributes and set one at 8 (of 10) considered you keep 2 stats at minimum. As you gain attributes very slowly (5 over the course of the game) this takes a lot of momentum from your progression, because you amost cap effectiveness (of attributes) upon creation. There is also some kind of discrepepancy between the (pretty much exclusive) resistance mechanics, deflection and dodge vs health and damage resistance. As abilities always hit once they activate deflection and dodge will not help anything against them, to counter those you would need abilities to interrupt (some ability trees have little to offer there) and enough energy to cast them, so you will probably need to invest a lot into intelligence. After deflecting you still take damage and you can only dodge after a deflection (there is one ability that changes that slightly) so you will still die unless you have someone to take all aggro from you.
Abilities are aquired by investing points in a chosen tree. There are at most 2 trees that can be acquired, the second can be either another weapon stlye tree or a specialization of the first. Some are more useful than others but the majority is balanced. There are some serious issues with trees failing horribly in certain situations, like Mors' Magnar tree only having one costly interrupt that can be dodged unless the enemy has low health, while the defense tree offers way more for way less. It should also be noted that ablities seem use weapon damage, NOT dps, thus slow high damage weapons seems to be the better choice here.
Skills are the ability to use a certain weapon or armor. Skilling anything where you don't get a bonus is pretty useless as you waste too many points. You will have enough to max a weapon of choice and your armor of choice, depending on intelligence even two weapons/armors may be possible.
Traits can be choosen and acquired through the game giving small bonuses to the character. most of them are pretty balanced, but there are some issues here and there where it would seem unfair (if you knew the other bonus at least).
Your progression will be pretty slow at the start and only picks up when your are about lvl 7-8 because you get another tree and level up more quickly after that. you are able to  (iirc) pick all specialized abilities and all but 2 standard abilities upon reaching max level, so you should choose which skills you do not need.
The easier difficulties will be underwhelming. You don't need to think much there, often enabling buffs and just letting them kill everything works. Lord is challenging but I see certain builds that don't stand a chance here. There is also a "cookie cutter" strategy where you just focus the enemy with the lowest health, kill him and move on, as most enemies do the same amount of damage (unless they use an ability that has to be interrupted ofc). This gets a bit tedious later on, as you essentially always do the same. another option is having both charcters pick up AoE skills and nuke the group until only the big ones are left standing. Buying weapons early will make this even easier.
As stated above some builds won't stand a chance in certain situations, this only holds for Lord diffculty however and you can just tone it down for a short time, but that itself is not a good design choice. Some dialogue choices are also unfair, offering certain quests or similar things where you really can't expect it. There are no major issues here but some small things that may annoy you if you ever find out about it. Another bad thing is that at three points where you can decide to undertake a more difficult approach, be it attacking without killing sentries first, not taking an escort or clearing the more dangerous part of the castle. Seriously, if they don't want you to do this, then they shouldn't add that option, as these things are very frustrating on the highest diffculty.
Not much to say here, loot is pretty balanced, you get a ton of gold though and can buy anything without problems once the more valuable stuff drops. Every drop is scripted so no surprises there. One issue is the high drop rate of two handed weapons, that seems wasted, as there is only one tree that can use them at all.
Very interesting quests, at times a bit linear but the conversations are what this game is about. The side quest are really great. Good characters and you almost always have some kind of choice that changes the outcome (mostly kill someone or not or whom to side with but sometimes there are other benefits).
The atmosphere and design of the locations are very well made. There was one door in King's Landing that couldn't be opened at all so you always had to run around (often running into a deadend) so that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off severely.
Apart from that, they did a good job.
Inventory, character screen etc. are pretty basic. It is very easy to get used to it, and everything is easily accessible. But the minimap designer should have been sent to the wall. It can't be called "map", because you do not see any layout only relative distance to points of interest and it's not even locked. Very bad choice here. Another thing is the sheath/unsheath animations at the start/end of battle, staying in battle mode (adding a key to enable/disable it) would haven been way better.
Overall decent game, but way too many minor flaws to be anything more. They should have taken more time.

I am speaking solely on the single player experience because I haven't tried multiplayer, yet.
I like this game. I have fun with it. A lot of races to choose from, or you can even design your own. It's not a turn based 4x, everything is happening in real time. Customization includes traits for your race (long life, fast/slow breeding, etc) and even the type of government you want. (Imperial, democracy, olligarchy, etc) If you think the game is going too slow, there are even speed controls. Graphics look good, You can customize the ship loadouts and have missile boats, or railguns, lasers, plasma weapons, etc. Same goes with armor, engines, and non - offensive systems like sensors and engines.
I won't count the things I don't like as cons since they're more of a personal preference thing than design flaws, but here are the negatives (In my opinion)
First of all, there may be an option that I haven't noticed, but you can't really design your own ships. It's one thing I think is superior with the Galactic Civilization games. Sure, you can swap the loadouts and have them firing different weapons and whatnot, but you can't actually change the look of them. All Mammalian race ships are going to look the same, as well as insectoid, fungoid, and all of the other races included. I thought it would be cool to make ships that look like your favorite sci-fi ships and whatnot.
I feel like the computer builds too fast. Sure, that could be a player skill thing, but for example, I try to keep my research goals somewhat balanced so I'm not really weak in anything, but by the time I get a good chunk of a spiral arm of the galaxy controlled, I might invade a neighbor that is blocking my progression with a 5k point value fleet and they will respond with a few 20k fleets and crush me when they don't even have half of the territory I do. Sure, you could focus on all military related research, but then your empire won't be able to maintain all of those ships so your resources will go into the negative.
The diplomacy menu could be less exhausting. Maybe like a search bar that you can type in the empire's name you're looking for instead of scrolling through dozens and dozens of empires until you find what you're looking for.
I wish the planet menus would classify the planets by solar system instead of listing them in order of colonization. You might start off with Earth, colonize a bunch of system and years later you might finally be able to terraform Mars, and it ill be on the bottom of the list of planets instead of right next to Earth. Developers, if you read this, please categorize the territory by systems instead of individual planets. Same goes with different types of ships. I can understand a whole fleet having it's own tab, but maybe also have different tabs for construction ships and science ships also.
No single player campaign to speak of. Sure, depending on what type of government you choose there will be certain objectives, but a lot of the time for example, if you have to find some artifacts from a long dead civilization, some of them will be in the territory of another civilization that has closed it's borders with you so you won't be able to collect them unless you go to war (and be crushed as mentioned above).
The final thing is, once again, more of a personal preference than a design flaw, but the combat itself. you fly your fleet into another enemy fleet and they fight each other. If this could be more like a Total War game where you can control the fleets and do formations and whatnot, I would say it could be a near perfect space empire game, but the combat is solely who has the better/larger fleet.
Overall, It's a good game, a LITTLE steep in price, but if it were on sale or had a base price of 20-30 dollars it would be pretty good, but I say this because the DLC prices. A couple of them are 10 dollars each, and there's even a 20 and 30 dollar one. If you got it before the Galaxy edition, the game could cost you around 100 dollars for everything.

The graphics on this game are fantastic, no doubt. Furthermore, the customization mechanics are also great, and with an immersive galaxy there are always things to explore no matter how many hours you have already played.
However, i will not recommend this game. This is because i feel that paradox could have done so much more with it.
One problem with this game is how the AI always stay ahead of you in technology. Whilst this isnt necessarily a problem for experienced players, beginners will struggle to keep up and unlike previous paradox games, if you start off behind, it is unlikely you will ever catch up as the AI will continue to build up their technology at the same rate (or faster) than you.
Another problem with this game is the lack of variety in ways to play it. Trade is especially disappointing in stellaris, being simplified to the extent of trade in total war games. This is most noticeable when you compare the trade mechanics in stellaris to those in EU4, in which trade and how it influences the economy is explored in depth. Furthermore, if your galactic empire is to be successful, you will have to maintain a large navy; the largest navy in fact. There is a constant arms race going on in stellaris, and the only real way to win the game is to have a bigger fleet than everyone else. Also, the AI will have all their ships in 1 big fleet, meaning that you will have to as well. This leads to wars essentially consisting of one big space battle taking place between the two belligerants; whoever wins that battle will almost certainly win the war as the loser will be unable to defend their worlds. This means that there is very little if any strategy involved in war, since it will take you a VERY long time to rebuild your fleet by which time the victor will conquer all the losers worlds. This, as well as battles being un-manageable (like previous paradox games) makes warfare (the only way to succeed in the game) very boring, especially in the late game.
Despite its amazing potential, stellaris fails to hit the mark as a truly revolutionary game, and i cannot recommend it until it does it's predecessors justice by developing upon previous mechanics.

The Binding of Isaac is a 2011 independent roguelike video game designed by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl, initially released for Microsoft Windows; the game was later ported for OS X, and Linux operating systems. The game's title and plot were inspired by the Biblical story of the Binding of Isaac. After his mother receives a message from God demanding the life of her son as proof of her faith, Isaac flees into the monster-filled basement of their home, where he must fight to survive. Players control Isaac or one of six other unlockable characters through a procedurally generated dungeon in a roguelike manner, fashioned after those of The Legend of Zelda, defeating monsters in real-time combat while collecting items and power-ups to defeat bosses and eventually Isaac's mom.
The game was the result of a week-long game jam between McMillen and Himsl to develop a Zelda-inspired roguelike that allowed McMillen to showcase his personal feelings about both positive and negative aspects of religion that he had come to discover from his Catholic and Christian family members while growing up. McMillen had considered the title a risk but one he could take after the financial success of Super Meat Boy, and released it without much fanfare to Steam in September 2011, not expecting many sales. The game soon gained popularity partially as a result of various Let's Play videos showcasing the title. McMillen and Himsl released an expansion "Wrath of the Lamb" in May 2012, but were limited from further expansion due to limitations with the Flash platform. They had started working with Nintendo in 2012 to release a 3DS version, but Nintendo later backed out of the deal, stating controversy over the game's religious themes.
Developer Nicalis worked with McMillen in 2014 to complete a remake of the game The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth bringing additional features that McMillen had planned that exceeded Flash's limitation, as well as to improve the game's graphics and enable ports for other systems. Rebirth was released in November 2014 for Windows, OS X, Linux, and the PlayStation 4 and Vita platforms, and later in July 2015 for Xbox One, Wii U, and Nintendo 3DS. Rebirth has since seen one expansion with a second planning expansion in development.

>Pros: Overall it's not that bad of an FPS game, for someone new to the franchise. >Cons: Most of the cons I have for it so far, for the past 26 hours of playing it, are mostly trivial things, like: I can't tell if the bullets are hitscan type or if they have ballistic properties such as bullet drop, muzzle velocity and what-not. Some props, that are supposedly penetrable, such as hay bales and window pane glass appear to be bullet-proof. I have to do hold-unders instead of hold-overs in order to hit long range targets with the high power magnification on DMRs/Sniper Rifles such as the XM-21 and the M40, given that there's no scope-zeroing system afaik. The bipod system is a little iffy compared to bipod systems on games such as BF3, BF4 and BF1, heck... even the bipod system on DoD:S is a lot better. The helicopter controls are a bit glitchy, I'm more used to the helo controls in Battlefield 3 and 4, so I'm a little biased on that regard. The restricted areas should be at least visible on the map in every capture point, I hate the fact that I can't shoot at the enemy after flanking an objective that has been recently captured by the enemy team. This really discourages strategic flanking to cap or retake objectives imho.

Finally, this is just what I was looking for!! Requires a bit of sense to play, instead of just people wading in looking at their minimaps to hunt out easy kills. Beautiful to look at, intense to play, and so so rewarding when you drop into a game with a decent commander who barks out orders! 10/10!!

All in all, this is a 9/10 game by TD standards.

This is a top down action adventure game ala the original Zelda or more specifically the game feels like Zelda: Link's Awakening with the simple color pallet, and music. The screen doesn't scroll. When you get to the edge, you go into a new screen, just like Zelda. Its very simple, with an attack button, movement buttons and a menu button.
It has simple combat with a good variety of enemies, but there are also good puzzles that feel unique to this game. Things like using a broom to collect dust to place that dust to block things. Again, its very simple and easy. There is no hand holding with this game and you are free to figure things out yourself, BUT when new things are introduced they will bluntly tell you yes you can do this. Such as when you attack dust, it tells you, you've collected dust, attack again to place the dust. It will spoon feed you new things as most good games do, but it doesn't force you to do several tutorials. Once to test a new skill and that's it. The game lets you loose. It doesn't feel like you'll get lost, areas are pretty confined and you have a Zelda 1 like map, there are portals that let you quick travel.
Like all Zelda games, there are keys that you'll need. Not just normal keys that open most locked doors, but specific keys to enter new areas. If that wasn't enough, you'll be collecting enemy cards. Enough of these cards will unlock specific gates with numbers on them. Along the way, you'll also find fairies or red insects that will not only fill your health, but also increase your health overall.
The atmosphere of the game is very surreal or creepy, which is awesome, its a different flavor to Zelda that makes it feel unique. You're a janitor in a dark, surreal world. In fact, I think the game is trying to subtly hypnotize you with its music and sound effects like clicking, tick tocking and chimes. Nothing is really explained, it just is and I'm okay with that. I don't need a story, even if there are NPCs every so often to talk with.
One drawback to the game on PC is that the screen is tall and narrow like an old school arcade cabinet. This tall resolution is because Anodyne is also an Android OS game. A fun Android game, but it doesn't help it on PC.
In all, this game feels good and enjoyable. If you're into simple puzzles, action adventure and a SIMPLE old school Zelda that lets you explore a lot; this is for you. If you're into a complex, deep Zelda experience with a rich story, this game isn't for you.
Playing a clone of a nearly 30 year-old game makes you want to do two things: stop playing this, and start playing Zelda.

This game ROCKS!  It is still in its new stages, but it has some really great potential to be the successor to TF2.  You can customize your gun styles in 4 chassis (machine gun, rocket launcher, pulse cannon or zapper), and from that, go into customization from barrels, scopes, stocks, triggers, and different ammo options.  For regular guns such as the MG or zapper your options are slug (normal damage) tesla (shock damage that lowers overall dmg, but deals AoE to other enemies) healing (heals team mates & yourself, including overheals) the "Juice" (boost damage & speed) or lastly, fire (deal increased damage, turn 75% of damage into DoT.)  With the pulse cannon you can get slightly different ammo mods, such as spinning rounds (which since the base slug round is a giant spikey ball, can be comical to see a wave of these flying, spinning orbs of death coming at someone).  The most customizable weapon in the game though is the launcher, which can be setup to fire up to six rockets at once, have triggers to fire x3 rockets at a time, load them up, Unreal Tournament style, to unleash all six at once cluster version, or change the damage spread from normal, to flak, to cluster bombs, up to an x6 spread.  You can imagine the chaos if you have a six shot launcher, and are dumping out shells quickly that themselves explode further into much small, more explosions!  Add tesla in there to damage everything!  Or fire to burn entire teams!  Or health to buff up your entire team as you try to capture a point!
You purchase all of these with in-game currency, "Blutes."  You earn blutes for competing in matches, and every day can receive a "Daily Gift", of between 100 - 350 blutets (most gun modifications cost between 500 - 4000 blutes, you earn them quite quickly.)  Or even you may be giften with a rare item from the Outfitter shop!  (I've only been playing maybe a couple weeks, and in addition to the 2 free items I was gifted for playing post-launch, I have gained a new half-shirt for my black dude, Moses, as well as a pair of jeans & a white bandana for Magnum, my Sylvester Stallone inspired gunner.)  The other items in the Outfitter however require "Spacebux" (IE, gold.)  This is how these guys make their money.  The outfitter parts unfortunately are way, way, WAY too expensive, although the amount you get for dropping say, $20 on the game is rather awesome.  (If you go ahead and buy the Steam pack, you get 3 items, as well as 20,000 Spacebux, to further customize your hero.)
So far, the game is free to play, and also free of any "pay to win" scheme.  The closest you can come, is by purchasing XP & blute boosts, which is essentially trading your money = free time you have to play the game.  If you have the bucks, blow it on the best deal, the $40 Absolute Badass pack, and get a TON of items for not just one, but 2 chars, as well as a huge pile of Spacebux, enough to make yet another of even the most expensive full outfits I can imagine!

Best of all though, the game devs seem to recognize possible imbalances, but don't go about nerfing/buffing far too greatly items in game, knee-jerk style, unlike some OTHER game companies (Riot!  *COUGH COUGH*)  Try out Loadout, it's a good way to waste free time!
Highly recommended!!! If you missed the feeling of UT and Quake, this is the game for you!!! 'Nuff said.

The Borderlands' series main appeal for me has been about frantically fighting through a group of enemies as acid, flames or a Tediore rocket launcher reload obscures your vision. It's about being over the top and fast paced and your friends melting a bandits face with electricity.
For the first few hours of gameplay, I didn't think the Pre-Sequel was much to talk about; it seemed to be essentially DLC for one of its predecessors, but priced as if it was a standalone. I still think there is some truth to this statement, but I'll discuss that a bit later. What changed my mind majorly about this game was how a minor tweak really added to the frenetic pace of combat and made this an enjoyable instalment in the series: namely, the low-grav environments.
It may not seem like much at first, but giving another axis of movement in which to fight and dodge enemies, as well as putting in an incentive for players to get really close to the action through the butt slam mechanic, in my opinion, really improves upon the fast-paced combat that has drawn me to this series. Of course there have been melee characters in Brick etc, but these mechanics have either always felt clunky or Lilith's close combat being insanely overpowered. Low-grav and butt slam, although to me they seemed prima facie rather pitiful attempts to say "look, new stuff means it isn't DLC, please buy our game," really exceeded my expectations and improved gameplay so much. Instead of sitting back with a sniper, I was running into the middle of the action, pistols blazing with my Lawbringer, heavily relying on a second wind half the time. And just on that point too, Claptrap's action skill fits well within this craziness to the point where I'm wondering how he wasn't included in an earlier instalment in the series.
The story was interesting and there were cool moments if you're a Borderlands afficionado and wanted to see how it all came together, but ultimately it felt like the plot was a bit too non-sequitur for me, and unfortunately I don't think that was intentional. It's not that I couldn't follow the story, it's just that it didn't seem to add up. I don't want to say too much for fear of spoiling it, though, so I will leave that as it is.
The humour is same old Borderlands, which in some instances you will laugh along with and at other times will just fall flat on its face. I don't know if the older Borderlands tripe is wearing thin or not at this point, but I found myself laughing less playing through the Pre-Sequel. The Claptastic Voyage, however, I thought, pulled its weight with the humour.
Overall, the game relies a lot on its predecessor, which given its pedigree may not be such a bad thing. However, it can't escape from the feeling I keep getting that it's just a really long DLC with a few cool new features to differentiate it from BL2. I think I would recommend it, but only if it's on sale.
TL; DR: new mechanics greatly add to the frantic combat style of Borderlands, but game can't really justify itself as a standalone title as it does not add enough new features. Recommend you buy on sale.

Aside from the technical issues (which you can mostly get around with a bit of tinkering and the fanmade FAR patch) this game is an absolute masterpiece. The stylish and flashy signature Platinum combat is great by itself. but what truly makes it exceptional for me is the amazing chip system. There's so many different ways to customize your layout and you can even remove HUD elements for more upgrade space! It truly is a fun system to play with and makes the combat even better as you keep upgrading your setup with stronger and stronger chips. Aside from that, there's also plenty of weapons that you can find/buy and upgrade along the way, which introduce different fighting styles depending on whether you use a sword, spear, gauntlets, etc. And every weapon is viable too, which makes it really fun to switch them around a ton and experiment with different fighting styles.
And the thing is, the gameplay isn't even the best thing about this game. The story is the meat here, and it is simply brilliant. This game touches some really deep philosophical topics that will make you think long after you've beaten it. It puts forth some very challenging questions and really leaves the player to come up with the answers themselves. There is also an air of mystery and strangeness all throughout that keeps you hooked. It makes you wonder "what exactly is going on here?" and always keep a sort of uneasiness about everything in your mind. The characters are also excellent and very well written. You'll see quite a wide range of emotion, so expect the feels. If nothing else, this game is worth playing purely to experience the story. Not to mention the absolutely fantastic OST. Seriously, not a bad song on there. Probably one of my favorite soundtracks for any media ever. It masterfully conveys the tone and feelings of the game, to put it simply.
So yeah, buy this masterpiece and play it (endings A-E, don't be fooled by the credits).

NieR:Automata is a post-apocalyptic, open-world, hack-and-slash game. It's very enjoyable and very atmospheric with some grinding mechanics. There are some minor technical problems but that will not change the fact that NieR is a beautiful game.
Pros:
- Mesmerizing music and OST
- Simple yet challenging combat mechanics
- Beautiful landscape and world
- Deep, well written story and plot
- Multiple endings
- T H I C C
Cons:
- 30 fps pre-rendered cutscenes (don't blend in with 60 fps gameplay)
- Occasional frame drops and crashes (for some people. In my case, the game only crashed once after I finished the first boss)
- Resolution and graphic bugs still unpatched officially
- Angle-switching mechanics (switches between third person/sidescrolling/bird's-eye view mid-combat)
- Endings require repeating the whole game, making it repetitive.
- Invisible walls in open-world reduces immersion of world
Overall, NieR is a unique game that is both fun and beautiful. I'm not a very diligent person when it comes to games; I usually forget about it within a few days or give up playing. But NieR Automata is one of the few games that made me play for 6 hours straight in one sitting, and always hoping for more. The soundtrack alone is enough for me to start playing. Get this game fast while it's on a sale.

I'm not the kind of person who generally likes to buy games for more than 10 dollars, but I tried out the demo of CrossCode and decided to take a chance on it. I have to say that I am more than satisfied with my purchase even though the game won't be finished until next year.
The story is very engaging - you are playing as a person who is, themselves, playing an MMO in the distant future. You've also lost your memory, which while a bit cliche is handled quite well, and your server connection is glitched so that you can't speak beyond a couple of hard-coded words which to me is the best implementation of a silent protagonist I've seen in ages. Despite being an entirely singleplayer game, CrossCode manages to create an experience immersive enough to feel like an actual MMO - "other players" can be seen running around on basically every map and have exactly the kind of dialogue you'd expect an MMO player to have. Your party members are accessed via a contacts list and can be called and dismissed more or less at will, but only if they're online and you aren't in an instanced area.
The combat system is pretty great. The best way I can describe it is that it's something of a mixture of Torchlight and Dark Souls. You have access to blocking and dodging from the start of the game and will need to use them constantly to have any degree of success in the game, but the game's forgiving enough that you can take a few hits and still be okay. You have both melee and ranged attacks, and there are enemies that will force you to use both kinds of attacks as early as the first overworld map. Projectile bouncing in particular is a fundamental mechanic of the game and is used in almost every puzzle. Enemies all behave differently and have their own attack patterns and weaknesses, which you will need to learn in order to beat them effectively. If you can stay in combat long enough you boost the drop rate which is very helpful (sometimes necessary) for gathering items, but this comes at the cost of not having access to out-of-combat regeneration. As you progress you unlock elemental modes, which change your damage type and available attacks, as well as your abilities. More on that below.
The gear system is mostly based on trading items with NPCs - these can be found as drops from enemies or destroyable objects, from chests, as quest rewards, or as part of a chain of deals. Each traded item has its own stats and its own special effects, usually up to 2 of them per item, and there are a
of special effects in this game. You could, for example, have improved invulnerability frames on dashing, reduced aiming time, improved damage when hitting an enemy during its attack, added health regeneration during combat (which starts at 0%, so it's actually very useful even at low values), and another 8 or so effects, and this is just from equipment. Gear provides most of your stats, so it's important to keep it upgraded or you'll probably get wrecked when you try to go to a new area, but you should be able to get most of the items for at least a couple pieces of gear just from doing side quests.
The level-up system is a node-based skill tree rather like a simplified version of Final Fantasy X's Sphere Grid or Path of Exile's passive tree. You start with a non-elemental skill tree - its passive abilities are always active but lose 50% of their potency when you're in an elemental mode. As you progress through the game you will gain access to elemental skill trees, which are only active while their respective element is active.
Some parts of the skill trees involving your active skills have two tracks - only one track can be active at a time but you can swap branches whenever you're out of combat and both branches merge back together after 3 nodes. Very few of the active skills feel useless, though some are more situational than others and every player will probably develop their own set of favorites as they play. (One of mine is the non-elemental single-target dash move, which is exceedingly effective at damaging most bosses and conveys a period of invulnerability when its charged version connects that has saved my life on more than one occasion.)
The dungeons in the game are Zelda-style dungeons, and are instanced so you can't take party members with you. The story dungeons are surprisingly long, almost too much so - they're probaly around 1.5-2x as long as what you'd expect from an actual Zelda dungeon. Each dungeon has quite a lot of puzzles, which is most of why they are so long, but they are extremely well designed and build on each other masterfully. In the first dungeon, you go from throwing bombs at rocks/blocks/enemies, to throwing explosives spawned by enemies, to shooting explosives to make them rocket off farther than you can throw them, to throwing and then shooting explosives to get them around corners, to throwing and shooting explosives around corners to launch a block in various directions while you're standing on it. There are also various smaller side dungeons scattered around, most of which are involved in a quest and are usually more challenging than the required dungeons.
There are some jumping puzzles as well, which can be a bit hit or miss as it can be hard to tell whether something can be jumped to or not. The most reliable way to tell is usually to fire a projectile and see how close its shadow is when it passes over your destination, or if it bounces off. When they work, though, they work very well - some of the jumping puzzles are just ingenious.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who likes action-based RPGs. The story is great, the combat is great, the gear and leveling system is great, the dungeons/puzzles are great, and there are even some obnoxiously hard but not entirely unfair parts for the people who like that sort of thing.
At the moment (version 0.9.5-3), the story content ends about 25 hours in but is supposedly 30-40% of the way through the game, so you can expect to be playing for 80 hours or more on a first playthrough. For a 20 dollar game I'd call that a pretty good return on money spent. There's a demo available if you're on the fence - the demo ends just after the tutorial boss so you can get a feel for the story and mechanics of the game and decide for yourself if it's the kind of thing you'd be interested in.

I'm a bit torn on this one. I like the spacefaring, the empire building, the planet control. The visuals are great, the different races and governments and all that are interesting, and there are fun side-quests throughout your development that help flesh out the background of your specific star-voyaging species.
But it falls into a rut of feeling very much the same more often than not. You're tied to ensuring your civilization produces enough energy and minerals, which limits planetary options. The diplomacy feels quite shallow, as well. There are a number of options with each civ you encounter, but half or more of them are locked at any one time based on a number of different factors. You can try diplomacy and trading to address economical needs, but as the game goes on it seems like every empire has an abundance of energy and only wants minerals (and the rare special resource).
Actual warfare is pretty shallow. You can state your goals when going to war, which is a neat concept, but the way the AI builds fleets basically means you need to have a larger blob than them or don't bother. If you were building a galaxy-spanning military, you wouldn't hoard every ship in your central capital, you'd have smaller fleets spread across your zone of control. But since the AI is going to group all of their ships into one deathball and roll in on you, you have to do the same. Military bases seem like speed bumps, until you're able to pour your research development into larger stations and fortresses.
If this were a sequel to the Civilization franchise, it'd be a real cool change of pace. If you're coming from Civ, this is going to be a bit of a deeper game for you to chew into, free of the 4x/hex limitations but with a lot of the same trappings.
But it's a Paradox game, and it feels like they took the "CK/EU are way too complex" a bit too seriously. Your empire management feels a lot easier than the Euro-centric strategy games they've put out, but the lack of depth in diplomacy hurts more than the rest helps.
Overall, still recommended, but depending on whether you're coming from other Paradox games, or the Civilization franchise, manage your expectations.

I started off as a bird species on the far edge of the galaxy. Their average lifespan was around 60 years, but they made every year count. They were obsessed with technology, already building their first robots before they had even left their world. Unfortunately, they were immediately boxed in by empires that had emerged into FTL travel far before they had.
Their dreams of expanding into distant worlds was immediately and brutally crushed, after their first colony was bombarded into oblivion during in an ill-fated first-contact. Instead of expanding into planets, my people instead built habitats around dead worlds, watching with envious eyes as their hyper-religious neighbours claimed lush, verdant planets.
They waiting, watching their old sicken and die, wracked by disease and genetic weakness, while the incredibly long-lived religious neighbours often made it to ages such as 110. Their neigbours scoffed, those Emperors of the Divine. They knew those foolishly materialistic birds could not possibly understand their true purpose in the unvierse. God was on the side of those who hated materialists, after all.
Humiliation after humilitation followed, where my people were used in foreign wars, had their new colonies taken away from them, brave colonists literally eaten as delicacies in certain worlds. The bird's hearts gradually hardened, and they began to view aliens with the contempt they so richly deserved.
The hatred grew, and the people grew stronger from it. One day, a neighbouring empire, a race of disgusting fungoids, had their fleet annihilated in a short-lived war with an impossibly-powerful ancient empire. Quickly taking advantage of their weakened status, my people quickly turned them into tributaries. The bounty of materials allowed a new phase of expansion for my people, and we colonized 3 new planets.
Suddenly, they had become a Great Power in their local area. The religious kings nearby, now the undisputed superpower of the galaxy, continued to ignore them. After all, they were but a gnat in comparison to the territorial holdings of the great Empire. They were soon proven wrong, as in a few short years a massive construction of habitats was implemented across my people's nation. Billions of souls now rested in space, enough to even match the population and might of the Divine Empire.
My people continued to advance, their knowledge of cybernetics second to none. Soon, they had a breakthrough: implants could increase their efficiency to the point where they would become the superpower. After a brief teething period, it was done. Every man, woman and child was equipped with the implants. The Divine Empire was horrified, quickly declaring an unprovoked war. But this was not the same bird people as before.
Now, their vengeance was at hand. They crushed the forces of the False Emperor, casting him down, and taking his holdings for themselves. The long-lived creatures were quickly enslaved, forced to watch their once great empire collpasing into feuding chiefdoms. Soon, the bird race began to challenge even the ancient empires, building Ringworlds, Dyson Spheres, and even an sensory array that let them see the entire galaxy. Furthermore, they discovered a way to store their minds into an immortal body of steel.
This would not stand, the ancient empires decided, immediately declaring war on the innocent birds. Once again, they were quickly crushed, thousand-year old empires grinded into the dust of history. Now, there were only the birds, mechanical gods of the galaxy, encased in empty, undying shells. Every other race was dead, killed in revenge for their cruelty, and their arrogance. A foreign invader came, a biological hivemind from another galaxy. They too, were quickly crushed, and their worlds burned into ashes.
The gods built a ringworld at the centre of the galaxy, to remind those fledgling races, just coming into space travel, of the folly of those who came before, then retreated back the edge of the galaxy, content to explore the mysteries of the universe within their massive ringworlds. Time would only tell if the newer races will make the same mistake.
tl;dr: Get this game, the stories you create will make you addicted. Please send help.

Stellaris is a RTS that falls into the 4x catrgory. In this game you will explore the galaxy, expand your empire, exploit your enemies (or allies) weakness, and even exterminate an entire species. For the unfamiliar, this falls closer to something like  Europa Universalis, just in space, so this may not be for someone looking for a more traditional RTS games like Command & Conquer.
Since this a Paradox game, It will take you a little while to get used to the U.I. So I strongly reccomend you watch some videos on Youtube that will help you get started in the game and use the Full Tutorial. However, after a few hours of playing, I managed to remember where all of the various menus were and their functions.  Or, you could do what I did on my first try, and say "Screw the tutorial. I can figure this out on my own." and proceed to get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you by the A.I within the hour.
The game comes with some pre-made empires  with set races to start you off if you don't want to take the time to build your own race and Empire. If you don't like the empires offered to you from the start, you can go in and change them. Among the types of species that can be chosen are mammals, avians, fungoids, or any one of a number of other weird, alien lifeforms. After that, It can be decided what your race will be. Will they be great scientist and engineers? Fast breeders that help your population grow faster? Or a strong species whos armies can conquer and defend planets easier than others? Overall the Species and Empire builder is pretty simple and self explanatory.
While I do enjoy playing the game by myself. I feel like Stellaris thrives in multiplayer. Especially with voice chat with your friends. With them you can take on the galaxy while knowing that you have an ally that has your back in case things go south. You WILL need them for the End Game Crisis.
The graphics are excellent. The soundrack is amazing. Without it, you would be driven insane. Space battles look a little silly. Especially when all of your ships in a fleet are so closely packed together. I was also a bit dissapointed by the amount of ship types there were. The biggest of the FOUR ship types is the battleship. There are no carrier or dreadnought types in the game. However, there are mods out there that add bigger ship types and space out the ships in your fleet.
Overall, Stellaris is a fun game and will offers a wide variety of ways to conquer the galaxy depending on if you want to do it through diplomacy or military domination, alone or in an alliance. The base game is great by itself but the DLC gives more opportunities, options, and situations to help you conquer the galaxy. To some, the DLC might seem overpriced. I believe they are worth it. This is a game I would definitely reccomend to someone who like a space RTS.

As someone who has been a fan of GemCraft since the beginning, this is arguably the best in the series and one of the best tower defense games out there. If memory serves me correctly, the first flash release of this game had some weird microtransactions in place, which sort of put me off from playing it (I can't remember if you bought shadow cores or what; this was a few years ago). Thankfully none of that is found in the Steam version of the game. Right now I'm 41 hours into the game and it feels like I am only scratching the surface.
In many ways, Chasing Shadows is similar to the previous GemCraft games. However, there are some unique mechanics like opening tombs and wizard towers, more diverse enemies attributes, and unique level designs that encourage you to play differently. Chasing Shadows doesn't necessarily have the charm or character found in other tower defense games like Kingdom Rush and the sheer volume may be off putting to some people. For me, I absolutely love this game. It is overall the most and best GemCraft.

One of the few truly great TD games on Steam that's also *pure* TD instead of some sort of genre hybrid.
Instead of placing towers as you would in other TD games, Gemcraft's towers don't do anything on their own. They have an empty  slot that holds a gem, and the gem dictates what the tower does. The gems themselves don't have much pizzazz, only 9 in total and when placed in a tower they all look and behave very similarly except for color. Similar range, damage, etc. with some modifiers. (Slow, chaining, steals currency,...) The gimmick is that you can combine gems to mix their effects. They don't generate new effects (see the super cool Android game Myth Defense to see what that's like) but that makes them easier to understand, which can be good because the game has a lot going on at any given moment.
Resource management, tower placement, path shaping, are all there, but there's many small systems on top that make the game as a whole remarkably complex. The uses for gems are the biggest contributor - aside from using gems for towers and floor-based "traps" (alternate tower essentially) you can also use gems as bombs, permanently destroying them instead of slotting them into a tower. You can also bomb the UI icon for an upcoming wave of enemies to "enrage" the wave and make it more difficult, increasing the number of enemies and their health and armor. Additionally, each tower has a handful of AI settings as well to fine-tune your monster-killing apparatus.
Outside of the moment-to-moment action, the game is most comparable to Dungeon Warfare due to (1) the ability to use modifiers to make the game intentionally harder so that you can get more XP from a stage, (2) having XP level the player up, and (3) having levels translate to skill points that you allot on various abilities before entering battle. The skills are more varied than DW though, and the penalties you can apply to yourself are in many cases more impactful. On top of this are a couple of interwoven systems of acquiring and leveling up collectible items that augment your game, something rarely seen in TD games and a welcome layer of complexity here. These systems make it so the strategy outside the game, before you even enter a stage, are a game unto themselves.
All in all easily worth $20 so a total steal at the usual $10 and a no-brainer when it's on sale.
Compared to other pure TD games I've played on Steam, it sits alongside Defense Grid, Dungeon Warfare, Defender's Quest, Creeper World 3, and Super Sanctum TD as games that are more than worth their money.

What do you get when you mix one part Zelda, one part Cthulhu, and one part…well, I’m inclined to say Earthbound, but somebody already has and while it’s certainly odd and funny at times, it comes off as more bizarre than anything. Anyway, you get Anodyne, a game about…well, I’m not really sure. I do know that it has a similar look and feel to older Zelda games, but it’s way darker.  The game pokes fun at various videogame tropes, but also throws a few of its own out there, such as collecting cards in order to proceed because doors are apparently…shy…and won’t open if you don’t have them.
No, not keycards either; collector cards for different monsters. Yeah, the game is definitely bizarre.  It’s also very fun and intriguing. There are a number of things that happen in the game you certainly don’t expect, but that’s not saying much from a game like this. Really, I’m halfway between not wanting to spoil anything and also not really understanding what I’m looking at all at the same time. It’s cheap, it’s fun, and it’s definitely worth it.

This game isn't for everyone, but hardcores and nostalgics will both be mystified by Anodyne. This game is not at all what it looks like and it really is greater than the sum of its parts. At times playing this game struck such a chord in me that I couldn't really sleep at night. It gets you thinking, and it's not a comfortable experience.
In order to get the full experience of this game, you'll need to play it obsessively. Then again, if you're not a completionist, this game's message wasn't really written for you.
TL;DR: This is a must play for hardcores, but don't expect it to be fun all the time and don't expect it to make you feel good. Ever.

Original Review:
It's more of a rage game than casual. Imagine going at the speed of sound and seeing enough of the screen ahead of you to make a 0.3 second reaction. The fuel is a timer, not measured off speed which isn't a bad thing, just something to be weary of considering the gas stations aren't frequent and they can sometimes spawn in areas  the player can't reach. Combined with the short reaction time, the gas stations are frequent panic attacks than sighs of relief.
It does fit the bill as a simple racing game and mimics arcade classics, so it isn't terrible. It isn't good and due to not needing much skill to do well in it, lowers the replay value by quite a bit.

Having already played Skyrim, I knew what I was getting into. The story is the same as the original but it is worth mentioning that there are quite a bit of improvements in this version. For one, the game is now running on a 64 bit platform, which is great if one intends to modify their game. While the original 32 bit version of the game has a limit of on the number of mods that can be run (due to the 4 GB of Ram limitation of the 32 bit system), the new 64 bit special edition now allows for a theoretical limit of 16 Exabytes which NO one is going to hit. Therefore, the limits of modifying this version is near limitless! Great game for the story and even more so for the customisation. Highly recommended for people who want an immersive game with no restrictions!

I bought this game a while back (I think at full price of $9.99) but never fired it up- it seemed like a cool idea that was really interesting to me, but I was afraid of the learning curve and accessiablity of a crew-based aerial multiplayer game such as this..
Finially I gave it a shot last week, and it is a ton of fun. The game is way more accessiable than I thought it would be, and the tutorials are quick and helpful. Typical gameplay is deathmatch involving 2 teams of 2 airships each- each airship has a crew of 4 players. A captain steers the ship around while the other 3 players run the deck frantically trying to man the various gun positions, repair damage and put out fires. Team work and strategy are key, otherwise you totally get your ship wrecked hard. It is frustrating to lose, but incredibly satsifying to take down an opposing airship. The community is great, and everyone I've interacted with is very friendly and helpful.
Even just spectating a game is super fun- the action is something to behold.
The only complaint I can think to mention right now is related to the wait time between games. It typcially takes several minutes in the pre-game lobby while the crews assemble and chose loadouts, etc. If one of the teams is missing a captain it will take longer. I'm impatient so I'd prefer shorter intermissions, like 30 seconds between games, but the wait here is typically a bit longer than that.  But once in game, I always find that the action was worth the wait.
Guns Of Icarus is an excellent value even at full price. I'd recommend it to anyone interested in a fun and accessible air (or even sea) combat, or anyone intrigued by the videos on the store page. The gameplay delivers.
And if the game happens to be on sale, I'd recommend it to ANYONE, even just for the fun of spectating other people's matches. You get the thrill of seeing airships destroyed in combat without the frustration of having to be on them as they explode.

I really Game of Thrones TV series, but after all those bad and mediocre reviews, I bought it at sale expecting a disaster from the GoT RPG. I was wrong, very wrong... Gameplay seems clunky and unintuitive at first, but with every new level and skill it becomes more tactical. The combat system resembles MMO games, player is not controling the battles personally, but he's putting abillities and attacks into queue and the character executes them in the given order.  You have to think about, what abillity you use and when, how to combine them to give the highest damage possible. Enemies use abilities too, but with the right skills there is a posibility to interupt them or avoid taking damage. You can deal serious damage by combinig the right skills of yours and of your companions, on the other hand, if you distribute your skill points badly and just click on the abillity icons, you won't get far... The most exiting part of the game however is the story. The story is mature, dark and full of twists. Choices matters, and some of them may bite your a** later in the storyline. It's not about saving the world, characters have beliavable motivations and their lines are well written. I really love, how Cyanide made the plot lines of both main characters merge into one and how they fit them into the world of GoT, with events from series happening on the background. Bioware should takes some notes from this, about how to write a story.
Even though it does not have the neatest graphics, voice overs of secondary characters are quite bad and there are few clipping and pathfinding bugs, I enjoyed it from start to the end, sometimes the story left me with my jaw wide open, which I didn't experienced in a videogame for a very long time.

This is a game that I have had my eye on for many months. It looked really interesting but I wasn't really willing to shell out $20 for it since most early access games have disappointed me in the past. Now that the steam summer sale is here and the price dropped I finally decided to give it a chance. I am only about 4 hours in at the time of writing this but let me tell you, this game is amazing!
The soundtrack for this game is absolutely perfect and, in my opinion, is possibly the strongest point of the game. I have also found myself liking most of the characters that have been introduced in so far and the combat is very fast paced and rewarding. When I first looked at the game I thought the combat would be similar to a hack and slash. Easy, button mashing nonsense. I am very pleased to see that this is definitely not the case. While I definitely wouldn't call it a complicated system it does take some practice to get the hang of it. The game rewards skill and punishes mindless button mashing (at least in the parts I've seen so far). The hardest part, for me at least, is learning the fighting patterns of the new creatures you encounter, especially if you end up fighting a mix of several different monsters at once. The monsters themselves also do a fair amount of damage if you do get hit so it definitely pays to learn how to dodge early. Of course, I do have to mention that the graphics are very nice. Colorful, sharp and just generally pleasing to the eye.
My only complaint is that the start of the game is very slow paced and holds your hand for a bit too long for my liking. On the bright side, once it's over you're free so there's that. I also understand what many other people have said about the quest system. It can definitely be a bit of a nuisance trying to find out where exactly you are supposed to go but it would be a real stretch to say it takes away from the game's quality. Since I like to take my time and explore these kinds of games I usually end up finding my way sooner or later.
Overall I would give this game a 9/10. Excellent music. Engaging combat system. Great graphics. Likeable characters. Challenging gameplay. Thank you for doing an early access game justice devs, keep up the great work!

Was pretty psyched for the game when I checked out the gameplay trailers a couple months back, and I feel like I got most of what I was promised.
Environment is really nice. The respective color schemes for different areas match really well. Music is fun, whether it's the combat theme or the area theme. Overall, the visual aesthetics are really clean. I just wish 80% of the npc sprites weren't generically grey.
The characters in the game are limited, but are expressed fairly well. There's a couple of characters from the introductory chapter (who probably never make another appearance) that I actually liked a lot.
Combat in this game feels really good. It's actually insanely good relative to other games. It's fast, responsive, and impactful. The game does a good job of stretching your combat capabilities to their limits without being too frustrating; I tried to play a lot of the early parts of the game without ever using my shield. Bad idea.
I have OCD, so I spent a ton of time doing parkour trying to collect all the items in the various areas. It♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. Is it good parkour? Probably, but I spent too much time frustrated to appreciate it.
Puzzles in the temple areas were fun. Parkour puzzles, less so :[
Missions were actually pretty fun. There's a nice variety in mission types, so plenty of different things for you to do. Rewards are pretty hefty too.
The game at this point is still in early access, so don't expect a complete product. The most significant portion of the game that seems to be lagging behind is the story. The most interesting story setup and development somehow all happened in the introductory chapter. Pretty disappointing.
I'm going to give it a 7/10 at this time, but I'm ready to change that as the game continues to develop. It's probably worth your money in its current state, so pick it up if you liked the demo a lot.

I'm a bit torn on this one. I like the spacefaring, the empire building, the planet control. The visuals are great, the different races and governments and all that are interesting, and there are fun side-quests throughout your development that help flesh out the background of your specific star-voyaging species.
But it falls into a rut of feeling very much the same more often than not. You're tied to ensuring your civilization produces enough energy and minerals, which limits planetary options. The diplomacy feels quite shallow, as well. There are a number of options with each civ you encounter, but half or more of them are locked at any one time based on a number of different factors. You can try diplomacy and trading to address economical needs, but as the game goes on it seems like every empire has an abundance of energy and only wants minerals (and the rare special resource).
Actual warfare is pretty shallow. You can state your goals when going to war, which is a neat concept, but the way the AI builds fleets basically means you need to have a larger blob than them or don't bother. If you were building a galaxy-spanning military, you wouldn't hoard every ship in your central capital, you'd have smaller fleets spread across your zone of control. But since the AI is going to group all of their ships into one deathball and roll in on you, you have to do the same. Military bases seem like speed bumps, until you're able to pour your research development into larger stations and fortresses.
If this were a sequel to the Civilization franchise, it'd be a real cool change of pace. If you're coming from Civ, this is going to be a bit of a deeper game for you to chew into, free of the 4x/hex limitations but with a lot of the same trappings.
But it's a Paradox game, and it feels like they took the "CK/EU are way too complex" a bit too seriously. Your empire management feels a lot easier than the Euro-centric strategy games they've put out, but the lack of depth in diplomacy hurts more than the rest helps.
Overall, still recommended, but depending on whether you're coming from other Paradox games, or the Civilization franchise, manage your expectations.

Fun to grow an empire, until it gets too big.  The game could do better informing you that upgrades are available, or that your planet efficiency could improve if you rebuild a tile, etc.  The the AI is pretty dumb, so it isn't really that challenging to play solo.  Even the smallest maps take forever to complete so I have no idea how much time you would need to set aside to play a PVP match. Modding support makes the game more interesting.  Definitely needs more ship types and better models.  Clipping is an issue with fleets, where ships pass through each other on a flat plane.  Come on folks, this is outer space here.  There is such a thing as a Z axis.  Different transportation tech is also frustrating, as some species can flit around the galaxy at will, with hardly an delay, whereas other species have to sit and prepare to jump for ever, making the interception of enemy fleets nearly impossible, especially in late game where large fleets mean ridiculously long jump prep times.
Nitpick - I mean come on, really?  The two human races are immediately hostiile to one another once they reconnect after being seperated all those years?  They don't know where Sol is, or anything about that system until it is explored?  If there is a second human faction that starts on the other side of the galaxy, why would the Sol based humans still not have explored their own solar system, establishing colonies and various stations throughout?  You're telling me that the human race went straight from basic space exploration to having a full fledged colony (population in the millions for industrial scale necessary for space flight) located halfway across the galaxy, and we haven't even built out our neighboring planets?  One would think that we would have colonized Mars, or Luna, before we attempted to colonize another solar system.

This is my first ever Steam review and unfortunately it’s going to be more of a fix suggestion than a review (my review was very long initially but Steam wouldn’t allow me to submit it so I had to chop it considerably). I was able to fix this game (so that it ran) fairly quickly. Here's how I did it:
1. Go to where the game is installed on your PC. For me it's at C > Program Files (x86) > Steam > steamapps > common > Deadly Premonition The Director's Cut
2. Open the redist file and double-click the application called PhysX_SystemSoftware (.msi)
3. Select the Repair option and let it run through completely.
4. When that's finished, launch the game again.
NOTE: I should point out that I AM running the game in compatibility mode (Windows XP SP3). For me, this fix worked immediately. I DID NOT download the 4GB patch that's been suggested! I hope this helps some of the people who were having trouble.
Do I recommend this game? Yes! I can't recommend it enough. In fact, it's one of my favorite games of all-time (I played the 360 version previously).  However, if you are expecting not to have to caress this game softly in order to make it purr – it is probably not for you!
If you are willing to put in a little effort though - I think you will be pleasantly surprised at everything you get out of this game.

GemCraft is a tower defense - strategy game. Your aim is to defend your main base with gems from waves of enemies. There are nine types of gems like critical hit gem, poison gem, etc and you can combine your gems. To use these gems, first of all you need to make a tower. All of these costs mana and you gain mana from slaying beasts.
Gameplay is also fun, if you don’t want to wait that much at a level, you can press the 3x speed button. Also, if you count on your defense, you can spawn other waves of enemies at once.
Level designs are good, so you never get bored and feel like you’re playing the same thing over and over again. Moreover, there is a skill system where you can spend your points gained from leveling up.
All in all, i think it’s a must-buy if you love Tower Defense games. Even if you’re not, take a look at it.
I also reviewed it on my Curator Page, i'd be grateful if you could take a look at it and follow.

The most mechanically interesting Tower Defense game I've ever played. Lots of freedom in how you approach levels, maybe even too much -- you can find a strategy that works for you and apply it in every level, with a few exceptions. Usually Tower Defense games have levels that encourage certain strategies or enemy types that make only one approach viable. This is very rarely the case in GemCraft.
The graphics and story are pretty mediocre, though that's par for the course for the genre.
I particularly liked the Traits system, which acts as a dozen or so different difficulty adjustment options that increase item drop/rarity. It made the game feel like I was always pushing my limits, and rewarded me accordingly. Even just thinking about that as I'm writing this review makes me want to play more.
If I could only play one Tower Defense game for the rest of my life, I'd choose GemCraft without a second thought. It's got everything you could want and a whole lot more. Tons of content, more towers than you could ever use, a great sense of freedom and progression. Just a phenomenal game in almost every way.
4.5/5, highly recommended.

Captain's Log Day One: After many years as an officer in the Royal Air navy, mostly commanding the guns, I have finally been promoted to the rank of Post-Captain and I have been given my first command. My first command is to be "The Maelstrom" a beautiful, new, Goldfish. The guns are in good order, the engines are working like a dream, and it comes with an excellent crew of loyal, hardy, and well disciplined Sailors and Officers. I look forward to making a name for myself with this ship.
Captain's Log Day Two: We were given commerce raiding duties in the Fjords along with a small Flotilla of two Pyramidions, one Spire, and one Junker. We managed to take several merchant ships without a fight but then came upon several enemy vessels. The Pyramidions rushed forward and acted as the vanguard while myself and the Junker stayed farther back. The Pyramidions received heavy damage as the enemies had, unknown to us until now, a Galleon. Using my ship's heavy weapons, we disabled its engines and guns, and it was finally taken down by our Junker. With their flagship lost, the rest of the enemy attempted to flee. We were able to capture one Junker and one Squid. We sailed back to port with out prizes in tow, and gave our report to the Admiralty. We were given many commendations, and I myself was gifted with an engraved sword. We will remain at port for a week.
Captain's Log Day Nine: My Men drank, sang, and ♥♥♥♥♥d the week away, spending most of their pay. I, meanwhile, spent most of the week in my Cabin, quietly reading and going over charts and ledgers. The prize money, when split amongst the three Captains was still a substantial sum. When I awoke this morning I was given my orders. We are to intercept a raiding fleet in the Fjords.
Captain's Log Day Ten: What had happened? When my men were to supposed to report today, there were only three! My two gunners, and my engineer. My entire crew has disappeared except for the four of us! Who could fly a ship with only four men?
Captain's Log Day Eleven: The Admiralty has ignored my pleas and told me that the rest of the fleet has already left port and that I should join them. Well, I guess three men is better than none.
Captain's Log Day Eighteen: After several long days of flying, we have finally found our target. We started chasing them at eight bells this morning, and, knowing they were outnumbered, they fled. We were able to seperate three ships though, a Squid, a Pyramidion, and a Spire. Using our main gun, our heavy Hwatcha, we destroyed the Spire in a matter of minutes. The Pyramidion and Squid quickly followed suit. We attempted to find the rest of the fleet, but it seems as though these ships that now lie at the bottom of the fjord were sent to delay us while the rest of the fleet gave us the slip.
Captain's Log Day Twenty Two: I have begun to suspect that my crew has gone mad. Today we encountered an enemy Goldfish, and rather than follow my orders and do their duty, my Engineer kept trying to use the flamethrower, a weapon that he is not trained to use, when he was not manning the flamethrower, he kept trying to buff the guns while our engines were on fire. He did not, even once, repair anything. My gunner kept using the Gatling gun rather than our ship's main gun, and my other gunner just stood in one place, not moving or speaking. In fact, he didn't do anything. I firmly believe that the sun has gotten to him. We only won because of my expert piloting skills, destroying their balloon with our ship's spike.
Captain's Log Day Twenty Five: I am at my wit's end. My engineer has started talking nonsense, constantly ranting about some fellow named, "Trump" and how he's going to ruin some strange land called "Merica" and screaming at the top of his lungs at any other who disagrees with him. My secondary Gunner has remained in the same area. He occasionally complains about "lag" whatever this "lag" he speaks of is, I do not know. My first gunner always fires the Heavy Hwatcha too early, and never follows my orders, constantly calling me a "♥♥♥♥♥♥y♥♥♥♥♥noob." I swear that none of these men are the original crewmen that this ship originally had.
Captain's Log Day Forty Three: I have lost all hope. It is not worth even working any more. My engineer never fixes anything anymore, my Secondary gunner has disappeared. My first gunner constantly runs around trying to fix things, while completely ignoring the guns. It is so much that I have taken to the drink in order to drown my sorrows. To make matters worse, the fleet that we missed last month has moved into our capital city and I have been called to defend the city against  the onslaught. The best I can hope for now is an honorable death and to rid the world of the most incompetent sailors the sky has ever seen.
Captain's Log Day Fifty: We arrived in the city and found that an entire fleet had besieged the city. I moved into the center, hoping for an honourable death and, to my surprise, my crew performed exceptionally. They followed ever order, kept the ship running, and destroyed all of the enemy ships. My ship, the Maelstrom, has singlehandedly saved the city.
Captain's Log Day Fifty One: We have all been made heroes. Every admiral wishes to meet us, we have been given every medal for valor, we have all been given a fortune in prize money, and the Queen herself has personally knighted all of us in thanks. There have been many parades and balls in our honour. My men have all been made officers, and I have been promoted to the Rank of Rear Admiral. I know not by what power, but somehow, my crew, consisting of three people, did horribly, but finally did well when they were most needed.

Overall positive but I'll look at both sides.
What does GoI Online do right?
Great team mechanics - if you're looking for a LAN party game, something to play with a small group of friends online or if you just want to enjoy a team game where you have to work and communicate with other players, it's a perfect game for you. You seriously cannot win in this game without co-ordination between crew members, so it's perfect for that sort of dynamic.
Relatively good graphics - the textures are nothing special in GoI, but a lot of the video effects used can give a great atmosphere. Not only that, but the entire design of the game is fantastic. Every ship and map has its own unique look and feel.
Awesome sound design - There isn't a lot of music in the game, but where it does feature, it's great. Sound effects are also awesome. When battles get intense, you feel it, especially when you have good headphones.
Great concept - the actual idea of GoI is awesome and unique, and something I'm surprised more companies and developers haven't tried to capitalise on. More games like it are springing up, but GoI is still a very unique and exclusive experience. There isn't a game quite like this anywhere else
Now, the downsides.
Low population - probably GoI's most prominent flaw is its low player count. There simply aren't a lot of people playing this game compared to when it was first released, and that's especially bad when you've got a multiplayer game where players are far more valuable than AI. I've experienced instances where one lobby has left and disbanded, only for all of the same players to form up in a different lobby since nobody else is online. You'll see this happen a lot and it can be monotonous.
Long grind - you do get levels, achievements and collectibles in this game, and gaining all of them can be brutal and long. Your levels are divided between three different classes, so you have to level all three to stay competitive, meaning you can't just focus one class and hope for the best. You will spend a lot of time in this game putting effort in and still getting little as a result other than the actual gameplay experience.
Lack of depth - GoI has a solid framework, but behind that, there isn't that much. Little to no lore, no expansion on regions or ships, and also a very basic meta. Some guns counter some stuff, others counter other stuff. It's as simple as that 90% of the time. No combinations or workarounds like in other games like this. Get ready to pick a style and keep it, chances are everyone else is playing the same way. This is also an issue when you consider the price of this game. I was fortunate enough to receive this game as a gift, but I have friends who refuse to buy the game simply because some things (lore, story, gameplay depth) aren't there, and don't justify the price tag for them.
Overall, GoI is a fantastic game, but it is lacking in features which I wish the developers would work on. And honestly, considering the lack of a large playerbase and the lack of effort being put towards the game by the devs, I wouldn't be surprised if this game goes F2P in the near future. Personally, I think it should, this game needs an influx of new players badly. Still, a fun game, and it definitely has features you may be looking for.
7/10

NieR:Automata is a post-apocalyptic, open-world, hack-and-slash game. It's very enjoyable and very atmospheric with some grinding mechanics. There are some minor technical problems but that will not change the fact that NieR is a beautiful game.
Pros:
- Mesmerizing music and OST
- Simple yet challenging combat mechanics
- Beautiful landscape and world
- Deep, well written story and plot
- Multiple endings
- T H I C C
Cons:
- 30 fps pre-rendered cutscenes (don't blend in with 60 fps gameplay)
- Occasional frame drops and crashes (for some people. In my case, the game only crashed once after I finished the first boss)
- Resolution and graphic bugs still unpatched officially
- Angle-switching mechanics (switches between third person/sidescrolling/bird's-eye view mid-combat)
- Endings require repeating the whole game, making it repetitive.
- Invisible walls in open-world reduces immersion of world
Overall, NieR is a unique game that is both fun and beautiful. I'm not a very diligent person when it comes to games; I usually forget about it within a few days or give up playing. But NieR Automata is one of the few games that made me play for 6 hours straight in one sitting, and always hoping for more. The soundtrack alone is enough for me to start playing. Get this game fast while it's on a sale.
I haven't tried the DLC and I don't plan to buy it because I found it unnecessary and overpriced, but it depends on your preference.
Rating: 9/10
