I started off as a bird species on the far edge of the galaxy. Their average lifespan was around 60 years, but they made every year count. They were obsessed with technology, already building their first robots before they had even left their world. Unfortunately, they were immediately boxed in by empires that had emerged into FTL travel far before they had.
Their dreams of expanding into distant worlds was immediately and brutally crushed, after their first colony was bombarded into oblivion during in an ill-fated first-contact. Instead of expanding into planets, my people instead built habitats around dead worlds, watching with envious eyes as their hyper-religious neighbours claimed lush, verdant planets.
They waiting, watching their old sicken and die, wracked by disease and genetic weakness, while the incredibly long-lived religious neighbours often made it to ages such as 110. Their neigbours scoffed, those Emperors of the Divine. They knew those foolishly materialistic birds could not possibly understand their true purpose in the unvierse. God was on the side of those who hated materialists, after all.
Humiliation after humilitation followed, where my people were used in foreign wars, had their new colonies taken away from them, brave colonists literally eaten as delicacies in certain worlds. The bird's hearts gradually hardened, and they began to view aliens with the contempt they so richly deserved.
The hatred grew, and the people grew stronger from it. One day, a neighbouring empire, a race of disgusting fungoids, had their fleet annihilated in a short-lived war with an impossibly-powerful ancient empire. Quickly taking advantage of their weakened status, my people quickly turned them into tributaries. The bounty of materials allowed a new phase of expansion for my people, and we colonized 3 new planets.
Suddenly, they had become a Great Power in their local area. The religious kings nearby, now the undisputed superpower of the galaxy, continued to ignore them. After all, they were but a gnat in comparison to the territorial holdings of the great Empire. They were soon proven wrong, as in a few short years a massive construction of habitats was implemented across my people's nation. Billions of souls now rested in space, enough to even match the population and might of the Divine Empire.
My people continued to advance, their knowledge of cybernetics second to none. Soon, they had a breakthrough: implants could increase their efficiency to the point where they would become the superpower. After a brief teething period, it was done. Every man, woman and child was equipped with the implants. The Divine Empire was horrified, quickly declaring an unprovoked war. But this was not the same bird people as before.
Now, their vengeance was at hand. They crushed the forces of the False Emperor, casting him down, and taking his holdings for themselves. The long-lived creatures were quickly enslaved, forced to watch their once great empire collpasing into feuding chiefdoms. Soon, the bird race began to challenge even the ancient empires, building Ringworlds, Dyson Spheres, and even an sensory array that let them see the entire galaxy. Furthermore, they discovered a way to store their minds into an immortal body of steel.
This would not stand, the ancient empires decided, immediately declaring war on the innocent birds. Once again, they were quickly crushed, thousand-year old empires grinded into the dust of history. Now, there were only the birds, mechanical gods of the galaxy, encased in empty, undying shells. Every other race was dead, killed in revenge for their cruelty, and their arrogance. A foreign invader came, a biological hivemind from another galaxy. They too, were quickly crushed, and their worlds burned into ashes.
The gods built a ringworld at the centre of the galaxy, to remind those fledgling races, just coming into space travel, of the folly of those who came before, then retreated back the edge of the galaxy, content to explore the mysteries of the universe within their massive ringworlds. Time would only tell if the newer races will make the same mistake.
tl;dr: Get this game, the stories you create will make you addicted. Please send help.

Stellaris is a RTS that falls into the 4x catrgory. In this game you will explore the galaxy, expand your empire, exploit your enemies (or allies) weakness, and even exterminate an entire species. For the unfamiliar, this falls closer to something like  Europa Universalis, just in space, so this may not be for someone looking for a more traditional RTS games like Command & Conquer.
Since this a Paradox game, It will take you a little while to get used to the U.I. So I strongly reccomend you watch some videos on Youtube that will help you get started in the game and use the Full Tutorial. However, after a few hours of playing, I managed to remember where all of the various menus were and their functions.  Or, you could do what I did on my first try, and say "Screw the tutorial. I can figure this out on my own." and proceed to get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you by the A.I within the hour.
The game comes with some pre-made empires  with set races to start you off if you don't want to take the time to build your own race and Empire. If you don't like the empires offered to you from the start, you can go in and change them. Among the types of species that can be chosen are mammals, avians, fungoids, or any one of a number of other weird, alien lifeforms. After that, It can be decided what your race will be. Will they be great scientist and engineers? Fast breeders that help your population grow faster? Or a strong species whos armies can conquer and defend planets easier than others? Overall the Species and Empire builder is pretty simple and self explanatory.
While I do enjoy playing the game by myself. I feel like Stellaris thrives in multiplayer. Especially with voice chat with your friends. With them you can take on the galaxy while knowing that you have an ally that has your back in case things go south. You WILL need them for the End Game Crisis.
The graphics are excellent. The soundrack is amazing. Without it, you would be driven insane. Space battles look a little silly. Especially when all of your ships in a fleet are so closely packed together. I was also a bit dissapointed by the amount of ship types there were. The biggest of the FOUR ship types is the battleship. There are no carrier or dreadnought types in the game. However, there are mods out there that add bigger ship types and space out the ships in your fleet.
Overall, Stellaris is a fun game and will offers a wide variety of ways to conquer the galaxy depending on if you want to do it through diplomacy or military domination, alone or in an alliance. The base game is great by itself but the DLC gives more opportunities, options, and situations to help you conquer the galaxy. To some, the DLC might seem overpriced. I believe they are worth it. This is a game I would definitely reccomend to someone who like a space RTS.

This is an amazing game but it may not be suited for everyone.
I'll try to keep this short and simple. Stellaris is a strategy game that falls into the 4x (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate) type. For the uninitiated, this falls closer to a Civilization in space or Europa Universalis so this may not appeal for those seeking a more classical RTS like Warcraft, Starcraft or Command & Conquer.
Pros:
- Multiplayer available in VS or COOP (if you forge an alliance)
- Many races you can pick (ranging from Humanoid mammals, bird type, fungus, etc), each with their own abilities and perks.
- If the offered choices aren't much your thing, you can create your own custom race and pick their traits, abilities, type of politics and more.
- Like most 4x games you get a wide variety of options for your custom maps.
- Customizable ships and stations to fit your desired design ranging from fast hiting dps or expensive hulking tanks.
- Terraformable planets to satisfy your desire and thirst for inter-galactic conquest
Cons:
- There are no skill tree for your techonology research. For the new players it will offer a nice surprise to what you are able to do but may be frustrating if you end up starting in a dry part of the galaxy with little to no ressources to get or planets to colonize.
- You can start in a very dry part of the galaxy with barely ressources or no planets to colonize and expand (not necessarily a con if you like a real challenge)
- Technology research "tree" is random (at least it seems like it, if I find out later that I'm wrong, I'll gladly remove this from the list).
Overall, Stellaris is a fun game and will offer you a wide variety of ways to conquer the galaxy depending on if you want diplomacy and economic influence or total military domination, alone or in an alliance. The real time elements makes it faster than Civ but may be painfully slow for those who crave a more RTS type. The base game is amazing by itself but the DLC (I do not own any yet but was able to try it from a friend) offers your more opportunities, scenarios and options for your domination of the galaxy. I am not usually a 4x gamer and would recommend it to those who like, have an interrest or would like to be introduced to the genre.

Anodyne is an action-adventure game by
and
, released in February 2013. The game seems to be inspired by the old Zelda games in terms of gameplay and features a nostalgic pixel art. The game is all about exploring the dream world of the protagonist, who goes by the name of Young. The player uses a broom for combat and very few other items to proceed through the story. The goal of Anodyne is to collect a certain amount of cards, which are spread all over the world and often require solving puzzles and fighting enemies to progress to the end area of the game.
My first playthrough through this game went fairly fast, there were only a few stages that required some grinding. Considering that, I was happily surprised by the final boss fight, which in my opinion had an adequate level of difficulty. Also there were a few cards that required to solve rather challenging puzzles, but you don't need to collect all cards to finish the game, so that only comes into consideration if you intend to complete the game 100%. If so, the secret "???" items are also very difficult to find and obtain, even if you use a guide.
I really liked the story of Anodyne, even though the dialogues sometimes screwed that up for me, but that's just a small downside to the otherwise so mystic atmosphere and the dream-like feeling which this game provides. All that is underlined by the enchanting pixel art and incredibly suitable and admirable music. This game possibly has one of my favourite gaming music pieces of all time.
All of this matches up to the foggy surreality that makes this game so fascinating for me and which is why I would recommend this game to you. I don't want to spoil anyone's appetite too much, so all I can say is: If you like exciting stories, you should get this game.

If you have never played The Binding of Isaac I would recommend getting the updated version, The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth rather than this game. Rebirth has most of the features and items that this game does with a whole lot more added to it. I could only recommend this to someone if they’ve already played out all the content in Rebirth and want more, there are still a few differences between the two games.
The game is a roguelike top down 4-way shooter. What makes the game so engaging is the dozens of different items that modify your shots speed, damage, size, rate of fire and many other effects. Almost all of the items stack with one another, making for lots of crazy different combinations that alter the gameplay quite a bit.
There is always an item in a treasure room on each floor as well as one for defeating the floor boss. What I found so addicting about the game is after every run I always wanted to start a new one to see what that first treasure room item would be.
I originally purchased the game just because I was curious about the procedural level generation it used. I’ve ended up putting more hours into The Binding of Isaac and The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth than any other game I’ve played in the last 5 years.
-Playtime-
The game requires a lot of skill development and mechanic learning before you will advance very far in the game. Your initial runs will probably be less than 5 minutes before you die. Once you get better at the game an average run might be around 20 minutes with a good run being around 45. The game has to be beaten multiple times to unlock the final levels. You can expect to spend 30-50 hours before completing the final levels for the first time and even then there are still a whole lot left to unlock.
-Achievements-
Most of the achievements in the game also unlock a new item that can potentially drop in subsequent runs. There are also some very difficult skill based achievements, such as completing areas without ever taking any damage. The achievements are challenging and fun to obtain but be prepared to spend dozens, if not hundreds of hours to get to 100%.
Not recommend. (Get The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth instead).

Before I begin this review, understand that I was not a fan of Game of Thrones/ A Song of Ice and Fire and knew nothing about the series other than it had a bunch of main characters die all the time.  Playing it for the first time, I enjoyed how the two main characters were not really good characters but more so severely flawed characters put in desperate situations.  If you are wanting to play a game that had  similar characters to The Witcher, you may also enjoy the characters in this game.  Like most western rpgs,  the branching dialoge choices is a nice touch that adds  replay value and helps you get immersed in the setting of the game.  The gameplay is a cross between Dragon's Age Origin's queuing system as far as stacking different types of attacks/selecting party members and Witcher 2's slow down when you are trying to select attacks.  It works for the most part however I did have trouble in certain segments of the game.
The game has a very decent art style with really nice moon effects in the forest.  However character detail is very lacking and ugly.  The soundtrack was pretty decent, nothing that stood out and made it memorable but it was not bad either, just a bit repetitive.  The voice acting is definitly low budget however, some of the characters really put forth some awful lines of dialogue and made some scenes hiliarious when they were not supposed to be.   In addition, like most western rpgs, there are plenty of bugs and glitches that at one time forced me to load a previous save, 30 minutes back, so be warned to save often and have different save files just in case.
For the current asking price, it is in my opinion too much, wait till it gets on sale for under $10 and you should fine plenty of enjoyment with the game.  I would avoid the dlc however, the dog skin is just a skin pack and adds nothing to the gameplay or story.  The weapons pack is also not very well designed as you still have to pay  a merchant to get the weapons that are extremely expensive, you will eventually in the course of the game, get weapons that rival those dlc weapons. The one story dlc "Beyond the Wall" is okay but very brief,  do not get the dlc at the current asking price.
While the game has many flaws, it is very enjoyable.  I personally am still not necessarily a fan of Game of Thrones but I can say the game did increase my interest a bit into why people enjoy the series so much.  If you are a fan of the series, you will probably enjoy the game a lot and if you are not a fan like myself, you may enjoy it as an okay western rpg set in  a gritty medieval environment.

I've come to learn that Resident Evil: Revelations is not a suitable introduction into the series. As someone unfamiliar with the franchise - apart from the films - there's the matter of being thrown between various timelines and characters with little exposition. Because of this I have almost no familiarity with each character's history or purpose throughout the game, so how can I be expected to care about their situation or understand the chemistry between each other when I don't understand their significance to the story? All I know is that Conan O'Brien's long lost brother, Raymond, makes several appearances.
I did enjoy the game as whole but there were many issues I couldn't look past. For one, the disjointed story, as if inspired by the film Memento. The controls are quite sluggish; turning can be slow, as is aiming, even though the mouse sensitivity is comfortable for all other situations. Dodging may as well be avoided at all times, it's more of a gamble of whether it will or won't work. There's also the matter of an extremely tight and claustrophobic Field of View, please use a program called Widescreen Fixer to solve this as it works really well.
The main missions consist of backtracking, being a semi-Metroidvania layout where further areas of the overworld will become unlocked over time, providing new additions and upgrades to the player's arsenal. The pacing is kept fresh as various secondary and tertiary characters will become playable in their own unique settings, serving to expand on the story, although each mission does not last long.
It soon became clear that many enemy encounters are only difficult due to how claustrophobic the area can be, with its small rooms and corridors, rather than how menacing the enemies behave, and the difficulty is only increased further by the poor controls. An impending sense of doom that I'd once experienced with a game like this is soon lost after making the unexpected discovery where enemies would not continue chasing me through multiple areas. The boss battles can be difficult when ammunition becomes scarce, the way I adapted to this was to try avoiding all conflict with the basic enemies in order to conserve resources in preparation for the real battle ahead. As I mentioned earlier, enemies will not chase the player through closed doors.
The most frustrating part of the game, story wise, is the amount of red herrings the writers threw my way. There are more twists here than found across M. Night Shyamalan's entire career, unfortunately none of them are as subtle.
RE: Revelations really feels like some wasted potential, especially without local campaign co-op. The writing is poor and the enemies are more a nuisance than they are threatening. As this is my first impression of the series I must say I'm left unimpressed, it's pretty much on the borderline of a negative recommendation.

Apparently revelations was meant to be a return to "Classic Resident Evil" style gameplay. A return to item, ammo and health management. It's "attempt" at doing this was to make every enemy and boss be a bullet sponge. Of course I'll be low on ammo if it takes what feels like 100 bullets to take down bosses. Encounters outside the typical standard enemy are not fun and you'll come to hate fighting anything in this game while you struggle with a garbage dodge ability and camera. Outside of the extremely disappointing gunplay the game continues to be a dull and average experience with bland grey corridors and a boring story and characters. It's hard to recommend this game to fans of either classic RE or action RE as it spectacularly fails at both action and survival elements.

Aside from the technical issues (which you can mostly get around with a bit of tinkering and the fanmade FAR patch) this game is an absolute masterpiece. The stylish and flashy signature Platinum combat is great by itself. but what truly makes it exceptional for me is the amazing chip system. There's so many different ways to customize your layout and you can even remove HUD elements for more upgrade space! It truly is a fun system to play with and makes the combat even better as you keep upgrading your setup with stronger and stronger chips. Aside from that, there's also plenty of weapons that you can find/buy and upgrade along the way, which introduce different fighting styles depending on whether you use a sword, spear, gauntlets, etc. And every weapon is viable too, which makes it really fun to switch them around a ton and experiment with different fighting styles.
And the thing is, the gameplay isn't even the best thing about this game. The story is the meat here, and it is simply brilliant. This game touches some really deep philosophical topics that will make you think long after you've beaten it. It puts forth some very challenging questions and really leaves the player to come up with the answers themselves. There is also an air of mystery and strangeness all throughout that keeps you hooked. It makes you wonder "what exactly is going on here?" and always keep a sort of uneasiness about everything in your mind. The characters are also excellent and very well written. You'll see quite a wide range of emotion, so expect the feels. If nothing else, this game is worth playing purely to experience the story. Not to mention the absolutely fantastic OST. Seriously, not a bad song on there. Probably one of my favorite soundtracks for any media ever. It masterfully conveys the tone and feelings of the game, to put it simply.
So yeah, buy this masterpiece and play it (endings A-E, don't be fooled by the credits).

NieR:Automata is a post-apocalyptic, open-world, hack-and-slash game. It's very enjoyable and very atmospheric with some grinding mechanics. There are some minor technical problems but that will not change the fact that NieR is a beautiful game.
Pros:
- Mesmerizing music and OST
- Simple yet challenging combat mechanics
- Beautiful landscape and world
- Deep, well written story and plot
- Multiple endings
- T H I C C
Cons:
- 30 fps pre-rendered cutscenes (don't blend in with 60 fps gameplay)
- Occasional frame drops and crashes (for some people. In my case, the game only crashed once after I finished the first boss)
- Resolution and graphic bugs still unpatched officially
- Angle-switching mechanics (switches between third person/sidescrolling/bird's-eye view mid-combat)
- Endings require repeating the whole game, making it repetitive.
- Invisible walls in open-world reduces immersion of world
Overall, NieR is a unique game that is both fun and beautiful. I'm not a very diligent person when it comes to games; I usually forget about it within a few days or give up playing. But NieR Automata is one of the few games that made me play for 6 hours straight in one sitting, and always hoping for more. The soundtrack alone is enough for me to start playing. Get this game fast while it's on a sale.

Overall positive but I'll look at both sides.
What does GoI Online do right?
Great team mechanics - if you're looking for a LAN party game, something to play with a small group of friends online or if you just want to enjoy a team game where you have to work and communicate with other players, it's a perfect game for you. You seriously cannot win in this game without co-ordination between crew members, so it's perfect for that sort of dynamic.
Relatively good graphics - the textures are nothing special in GoI, but a lot of the video effects used can give a great atmosphere. Not only that, but the entire design of the game is fantastic. Every ship and map has its own unique look and feel.
Awesome sound design - There isn't a lot of music in the game, but where it does feature, it's great. Sound effects are also awesome. When battles get intense, you feel it, especially when you have good headphones.
Great concept - the actual idea of GoI is awesome and unique, and something I'm surprised more companies and developers haven't tried to capitalise on. More games like it are springing up, but GoI is still a very unique and exclusive experience. There isn't a game quite like this anywhere else
Now, the downsides.
Low population - probably GoI's most prominent flaw is its low player count. There simply aren't a lot of people playing this game compared to when it was first released, and that's especially bad when you've got a multiplayer game where players are far more valuable than AI. I've experienced instances where one lobby has left and disbanded, only for all of the same players to form up in a different lobby since nobody else is online. You'll see this happen a lot and it can be monotonous.
Long grind - you do get levels, achievements and collectibles in this game, and gaining all of them can be brutal and long. Your levels are divided between three different classes, so you have to level all three to stay competitive, meaning you can't just focus one class and hope for the best. You will spend a lot of time in this game putting effort in and still getting little as a result other than the actual gameplay experience.
Lack of depth - GoI has a solid framework, but behind that, there isn't that much. Little to no lore, no expansion on regions or ships, and also a very basic meta. Some guns counter some stuff, others counter other stuff. It's as simple as that 90% of the time. No combinations or workarounds like in other games like this. Get ready to pick a style and keep it, chances are everyone else is playing the same way. This is also an issue when you consider the price of this game. I was fortunate enough to receive this game as a gift, but I have friends who refuse to buy the game simply because some things (lore, story, gameplay depth) aren't there, and don't justify the price tag for them.
Overall, GoI is a fantastic game, but it is lacking in features which I wish the developers would work on. And honestly, considering the lack of a large playerbase and the lack of effort being put towards the game by the devs, I wouldn't be surprised if this game goes F2P in the near future. Personally, I think it should, this game needs an influx of new players badly. Still, a fun game, and it definitely has features you may be looking for.
7/10

Anodyne has plenty going for it in concept -- it's inspired by the great Link's Awakening, it has nice graphics and a good soundtrack, and the dungeon design is excellent (the one exception being the circus-themed dungeon). Unfortunately, the best I can say about the sum of its parts is that it's merely an "average" game -- perhaps worth a playthrough if you're desperate for a Zelda-like gameplay experience, but better off left on the proverbial shelf otherwise.
At its best, the gameplay is enjoyable and reasonably challenging. While not nearly as polished as its inspiration, it's not too difficult to look past things such as the lack of hitbox refinement, flighty controls, and strange overworld design. Other flaws are a little harder to dismiss.
Perhaps Anodyne's most glaring flaw is its story and character dialogue, which are all but incoherent. Yes, the dreamlike setting and premise of the game explain this design decision, but there are two kinds of dreams in life: First, there are the strange or eventful dreams that we relate to family or friends for a good laugh or an interesting tale. Second, the kind that are so bizarre that we wouldn't bother retelling them, because all we'd get in return are blank stares. Anodyne is more the latter than the former. The game would have been more enjoyable with no story at all.
Lastly, I'll note that the game is not particularly family friendly as the themes get darker (and the profanity stronger) further into the game. Obviously that's more applicable to some audiences than others.
In closing, while I can say I enjoyed the game enough to go for all the achievements, it's not something I'd want to play again in the future. Buy it on a sale if you must buy it.

Stylistically, this reminded me a bit of Space Funeral, in a good way. It uses tried-and-true mechanics (with a bit of a spin) as part of its storytelling, but in a very subtle way.
The story itself is difficult to follow. The main theme certainly seems to be about some self-centered individual who is in a constant cycle of breaking and mending a friendship with someone else. The story begins with us in the middle of one of the "breaks" in the friendship. Young, the player character, expects it to be easy to fix the friendship, but the friend, Briar, is savvy to the cycle and won't be so quick to forgive. Young's journey is a humbling one, as he has to come to terms with his imperfections in order to show Briar he has changed. However, we can assume the cycle will continue. At least... that's what I got out of the story.
It's always tough with these sorts of surreal games to tell if it's just being weird for weird's sake or if everything has a specific meaning. However, this game at least stays consistent in its presentation, and for that much it's commendable.
The writing is excellent, the visuals are gorgeous for pixel art, the soundtrack is great (and surprisingly deep), and though the game only has one real mechanic for puzzles, it continually finds ways to keep it fresh. Unfortunately, the game is VERY formulaic. It doesn't take long to figure out exactly how each area will play out: enter a region, explore every cell on the map, enter a dungeon, explore every cell on the map, collect cards, fight a boss, repeat.
The dungeons themselves are designed impeccably and the overall pace is good enough that the predictability isn't too problematic. But occasionally I did roll my eyes upon entering a new area, thinking "Well here we go again."
Still, if you like Legend of Zelda and games with a deeper thematic experience than average, I can't recommend this highly enough.

Anodyne is an action-adventure game in the style of Legend of Zelda. You play Young, and your goal is to kill a bunch of bosses so eventually you could save Briar. That kind of sums the whole plot of the game.
The strength of the game comes from it's gameplay and the simplistic puzzles you are to solve, given a limited, but solid arsenal of powers. From the start you get a broom with which you can hit monsters and collect dust. It might sound funny, but dust actually has several uses like floating on water and blocking monster projectiles. Another power is the ability to jump, which will allow you to cross gaps and jump over monsters.
But, for me the strongest part of the game was the endgame. Yes, you actually have new content after finishing the game. You will be able to visit zones you been through already and new zones which are unreachable otherwise.
In conclusion Anodyne brings enjoyable gameplay with some jokes of the genre. I had a lot of fun with it, and it's a good value for the price.

I bought this game many years ago for PS2 and sunk hundreds of hours into and 100% completed it more than once. After what seems to be close to 7 years since i last played it i decided to buy it on steam today and relive it. I have a few grips about this PC port so far. Nothing terribly condemning but it is a significant annoyance. First off i want to say that its annoying this game dosent at the very least support 1920 x 1080p resolution. It max resolution supported is 1280 x 1024. Most games of this time made by big companies usually had native 1080p support on the PC. Why this game dosent i am not sure. Its not a big deal because 1280 x 1024 dosent look horrible. This PC port is graphically superior by a large margin compared to the PS2 version. The bigger issues i have noticed in this port is that it has a plethora of audio bugs. So far since i started playing it on PC 3 hours ago i have encountered 3 different audio issues. The first time was right near the begginning after the steam boat sequence loads. The winchester rifle was bugged with the same firing sound as Ned's single shot rifle. The issue went away after i died a couple times but it is still something to note. The second issue i experienced with the audio was a synchronization issue with one of the cut scenes. The Audio was about 3/4 to 1 second delayed with what was going on in the cut scene. The third issue was after the stage coach mission from Dodge to empire. Well near the river bank on the route that you take on this mission after you leave the canyon there appeared to be one of the ambient sounds from the mission still playing when you got within a certain vicinity of the area. That was the only bugs i have noticed so far. Gameplay wise i havent noticed anything yet. Still feels like the same good old game i played back on the PS2. Overall this game isent bad but it isent the greatest. The graphics where pretty shoddy even back in 2006 so it hasent aged well like games such as GTA 3. Regardless if its your first time playing it ever the gameplay may seem dull, and the world unintresting which for the most part it is. The world dosent have much in the way of detail and things to do but i wont hold it against it to much. The shining part of this game is its short but compelling storyline, playing through it is loads of fun and the gun play is quite entertaining. People that have played this before years ago the hit of Nostalgia is great but Nostolgic or not dont buy this game unless it goes on sale. It was on sale today for 50% at $9.99 and i bought it but i would still call that pretty steep. Ideally if it goes on sale for $5 then i say its a good buy. Its steam MSRP is $19.99 and it is by no means worth that much so if its priced at $20 dont buy it. That money could be spent on a better game.

Don't be fooled by my hours on the game: about 130 was the game being tabbed out.
Borderlands: the Pre-Sequel is by far the worst Borderlands game made so far, failing to even remotely surpass the standard that BL2 set for the franchise. I would even go as far as to dub it a disgrace to Borderlands and its genre.
What I like:
+A more diverse cast of weapons that suit the new setting of the game with new properties such as a cryo element
+ACTUALLY DIFFERENT CLASSES FROM ITS PREDECESSORS
+Gives openess to explore the largely ignored space station of Helios
+Gives more backround to Handsome Jack
+Gunplay is just as satisfying as the previous games, but not much more different
What I hate:
-Clearly pandering to a younger crowd, with a distinct lack of more adult themes or humor, and even CENSORS SWEAR WORDS! Even though this game is rated M!
-It sh!ts on characters from the previous entries by making them act and make decisions completely out of character for what was built around them, clearly by writers who were either trying to mold said characters to their own images, or simply had no idea who these characters actually are. Notable examples are Moxxi, Torgue, and especially Handsome Jack. Character "deveopment" is also abruptly and undynamically shoved into this poor excuse of a story.
-Gameplay, despite solid gun usage, is completely boring. It is way too easy with ridiculously overpowered weapons and you level up so quickly side quests become pointless. You could easily shred through the game without so much as breaking a sweat, exept for like one boss fight near the beginning.
-Oxygen mechanic is to this game what durability is to survival games: A simplistic annoyance disguised as a "unique feature"
-Too lazy to come up with many new characters, all playables are characters seen before in the series and some are clearly more powerful than others.
-An extremely bland world that is larger and more open, but feels as deep as a water droplet.
Verdict:
An absolute bore and a flop in countless categories, The Pre Sequel is undeserving of the Borderlands name in any and every sense.
Recommendation Status:
4/10
Not worth any of your hard earned money under almost every circumstance.

Its a great roleplaying game, plain and simple.  If you are a fan of the Game of Thrones series like I am, and like roleplaying games, its just plain neat.
I really am enjoying being in the nights watch and seeing the ominous, thrilling wall that goes on forever.
The combat is tactical not action.  The game does say that in the description, but I thought it would be somewhat twitch based, it is not.  You choose the actions of the character and they carry them out in real time, but you can pause any time and change and/or que up orders.
Its a role playing game, which means you do get to build up your character, choose attributes and skills, buy, find, and equip different weapons and armor.  I love it.  Exploration pays off in finding new items, etc.
The graphics are fantastic at the highest settings and at 1600 by 900 resolution.  I know that people criticized the graphics for the Xbox, but the computer version to me at least, captures the world perfectly.
The dialogue and story is game of thrones, that simple.  Horrible actions, rough words, and intigue everywhere.  Do not let your children play this game.  The first quest is caused by some horrible, R rated actions.
A few things could be better.
You have to almost be on top of an item before you see it.  For example, you may see a bunch of crates across the room, but you have to walk over there and almost be touching them before you get an icon that there is something to grab.
The game appears to be fairly linear.  I'm very early in the game, but its not a wide open world to explore, its more of a tight knit story to follow.  There are sidequests, and several neat choices in the dialogue, but this is a more linear game.
Needs more actors from the series.  The only voices that I believe are in it from the series are Varas and the commander of the Night's watch, thats it.  Since this takes place parallel to season 1, there are so many others we could have met.  I don't know what other characters may be around, but even if we get to meet them, they won't be the same voices.
Anyways, I don't what was up with the Xbox version, but the pc special edition version is a great game if you would like to enjoy Westeros for a little bit while waiting for season 5.  Right now its on sale for 5 bucks.  Its a steal!

A solid game.   SR2 is more serious, gansta game.  you have your diversions, you can do some funny sh*t, but overall, the game comes across as a serious game with a sense of humor.
The city has a satisfyingly large feel, you can get lost in it.
The cars have a good feel to them -- driving a sports car is completely different from driving a big truck or some little eco box.  you have differences in the weight of them you can feel the heavy ones not wanting to turn, some of them accelerate lots faster, etc.
The music is good, there's a a selection of hip hop, reggae, funk, rock, metal, and some lighter stuff.  should be something there for almost everyone's taste.
The graphics aren't so bad for an 8-year old game, you can turn them up to modern resolutions like 1600 x 900.
Now, the down side.  It's a PC port of a console game.   The controls are ok, mostly, but the mouse is used to aim your gun, not to drive.  This is important in-game, cause you need to shoot from the car sometimes.  But it means you don't have the fine control that mouse gives you.  instead you have WASD controls.   still, for cars, trucks, bikes, boats, and helicopters, it's ok.
But then there's the airplane controls.  they are horrid.  stupidly bad.  I'm not talking "bad enough to annoy you", I'm talking "bad enough to make you want to smack your OWN face up against a brick wall, and then swear off video games for life".  Basically, if you want to fly a plane in this game, you MUST have a controller, don't bother with the keyboard.
According to the game, I'm 18% in, and I've down 11 missions.  So far, I've never needed to fly a plane in order to advance the storyline.  I hope I never do.  (I'll update this review after I finish the game -- to let you know if you ever need to fly a plane)
PS -- I finished the game.  you never need to fly a plane.  so only if you care about achievements are the bad plane controls a problem --
Overall, it's a solid game, get it on sale, and you'll be happy.  I'm having a lot of fun.   Just don't bother try to fly a plain with the keyboard.

Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is an excellent next entry in the Red Orchestra/Rising Storm series and does an amazing job at translating the series’ signature authentic and gritty feel of combat, to the jungles and cities of South Vietnam. Much more than new guns and maps, Rising Storm 2: Vietnam excellently portrays the asymmetrical warfare between the military might of the United States and the less advanced communist forces. Any fans of the series, era or genre would not go amiss picking up this title.
Unlike previous titles in the series, rewards are no longer tied to classes, unlocking weapons and attachments. Instead levelling up unlocks a series of aesthetic changes that can be applied to your character model for all the different factions (US Army, USMC, US Helicopter Pilot, NLF, and PVAN). This levels the playing field more off the bat but still provides interesting items to strive for if you are into character customisation. These items range from clothes, tattoos, sunglasses, hats, helmets and more and really allow you to give your character a unique feel. This also feeds back into gameplay as the changes you make can be seen by everyone else and aid or hinder in target identification, as they would in real life.
The asymmetrical gameplay present in Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is both functional and clearly well thought through with relevance to the real conflict. This can be seem in both the equipment each side uses but also the mechanics by which each team operates. The U.S. forces have access to helicopters (on some maps), more fire support missions available to the commander and a slight edge in small arms compared to the PVAN and especially the NLF. This allows U.S. forces to be more mobile and bring more firepower to bare on a target but to achieve this requires communication and people who know what they are doing. In contrast, the communist forces are equipped with DShK heavy machineguns in objectives close to their spawn, all classes carry mines or traps and squad leaders can deploy tunnels to act as fixed spawn points, offering a well-hidden point from which to strike an unassuming opponent. These assets allow the communist forces to act more independently and use ambushes, and hidden traps to wear down their foes. All of this and more culminates in interesting and creative opportunities to gain the upper hand again the enemy team.
Bar a few miner bugs which Tripwire seem to be doing a good job of clearing up, the only major criticism is that the number of maps at this stage are fairly limited. While there are already community created maps in the workshop for this title, they do not quite live up to the polish of those the game launched with. Game modes too are somewhat lacking with only three at the time of writing but all are diverse and well-constructed. A new addition in Rising Storm 2: Vietnam compared to previous titles is Skirmish. This game mode is a smaller scale mode which pits up to two team of eight players against each other, to control objective areas with few respawns, making for some tense and nail-biting one on one combat. The only issue I have is that once dead, a player can use a free floating camera to ghost which can often ruin the one on one duels at the conclusion of many of these matches.
In summary, Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is a brilliant game which takes Tripwire’s tried and tested gritty first person gameplay and adapts it excellently to fit the asymmetrical infantry combat of the Vietnam War.

This game drove me to complete endings A,B,C, D and E.  The story was compelling and interesting.  The combat and gamelay elements are really enjoyable and well designed.  You get melee action combat with a variation of 3 different weapon types and combinations of them.  You also get to do bullet hell shoot em ups.  The game is primarily in 3rd person over the shoulder perspective but sometimes switches to above or from the side 2d scroller.
None of these mechanics are extremely deep but they are all interesting, enjoyable and well designed.  And the variance makes it so even after 3+ play throughs you won't get bored of them.
You should understand that you will want to play through this game at least the 3 times to get the chapter select mode and so you can see all the endings.  The first 2 are very similar but the 3rd play through may as well be an all new game.
Highly recommend this title.

A friend of mine gave me a physical copy of GUN because he wasn't a PC gamer probably five years ago, and I remember slogging through what's probably one of the most generic,cliche-riddled action games I've ever encountered. I eventually sold the game (back before Steam when selling used games was still a thing; thanks Valve for taking away that revenue stream) but had an attack of nostalgia a few weeks ago and finally decided to pick it up on a Humble Sale for about $5.
I never beat my physical copy of the game, though I was able to slog through to the end and its absurdly difficult boss fight. I never made it that far this time around, mainly because I decided my life was just worth more to me than playing through this truly awful game.
Now, I'll get this out of the way first: certain parts of
are really good. For a game with such awful visuals the voice acting itself is actually quite good, with special mention going to Ron Perlman and Kris Kristofferson, and the soundtrack is also quite nice. That's really the most I can say about the game, though, as the rest is quite garbage.
The story itself is just...I really don't know what to say about it, other than it feels like an absurd, over-the-top genre parody of actual Westerns rather than a serious attempt at making a good Western itself. Keep in mind, this was originally a Gamecube game so it's not really fair to compare it to later titles (most notably
) but the fact remains Westers as a genre had been around for a lot longer than video games, and there was so much other material the developers could've drawn in. Instead, we get a very strange arcade-shooter/RPG hybrid that never actually manages to make use of its own logical core mechanics. For example:
There's an arbitrary stat buff given at the end of ever sidequest. There is not, however, an actual leveling system, so it's hard to really keep track of what these values actually represent.
There are kill chain mechanics for killing large groups of enemies in a row with a specific combat style (i.e., chaining several kills with melee weapons), as well as for getting headshots or shooting weapons out of their owners' hands. Since there's no score or level up system, this mechanic feels completely pointless.
There are several instances where the player is given a mounted weapon with infinite ammo and wave after wave of Valve-level stupid AI to slaughter. While this sort of works when that weapon is a Gatling Gun, it becomes ridiculous when it's a canon (and it's a canon most times).
This, of course, isn't helped by the fact which the game is named after (the guns) are themselves pretty bland. Most of the weapons depicted are lever action, except none of them fire this way: the rifles fire on semi-auto, and the 1887 (the most iconic leveraction weapon in history) is a single shot shotgun. While it's nice to see a wide range of authentic Western shooting irons in the game, the fact the developers went to exactly no effort to make sure they were depicted realistically is disappointing.
There are other mechanics which are handled much the same. Your character, Colton, and most of the people you run into are never especially interesting and it's difficult to take any of them seriously. This is compounded by some of the absurd things you and NPCs will both yell in combat (Colt, for instance, seems to think he's in Vietnam and will shout "Get some!" quite often for no real reason). The models themselves aren't animated well, and there's one constantly reused conversation animation that looks like it'd be right at home in the original
.

I'm generally a fan of old-school RPGs, I'm all in for supporting indie game developers, but c'mon! This entire trend of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games sold as "Indie", "Retro" or "Old-School" is really starting to get on my nerves! I don't mind the lack of voice acting, I don't need long and gorgeous cut-scenes, I can live with the shallow storylines, I can also deal with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics in general. But what really drive me nuts are the small things, such as, for example, me being able to hit an enemy from 100 miles away.... with a melee weapon! Nevermind the fact that all I really hit was air, the monster on the other corner of the screen just dies and disappears.
For me, this is a game breaker. It's like the game devs are telling me, "Hey, it's a fantasy game, right? You only imagine you're an adventurer, you only imagine you're fighting monsters, so what's wrong with imagining you really hit the bat right before it died?"  Well, at this point I put on my Grumpy Cat mask and shout, "NO! I won't friggin' imagine that! It's your job as game devs to illustrate at least the most basic stuff!".
Needless to say, that if in the past I generously shelled out money for indie games without digging too deep, thinking to myself that even if I won't be enjoying the game, at least I'd be supporting the games industry, that is not the case anymore. I'm tired of lazy game devs selling me crap as "Indie". I'm willing to pay for good games, but I work hard to earn that money, and so should everyone else, including game developers.
As far as I'm concerned, Anodyne is a bad game. I can't remember how much I paid for it, I just hope it wasn't much. Oh well, at least I'm wiser and more careful now, when it comes to choosing what games to buy, regardless of how cheap or expensive they are.

I had a good few days invested into this game because, you know, I like to take my time with new concepts, especially if they are pretty.  This game has a lot to offer in terms of beauty and inspiring animations where it comes to the forced generated into the environments.
The problem is that this game feels like it was supposed to be more, couldn't reach its high-end goals, and so settled for being a simple puzzle game.  I wanted to care about the little tribes people, but, because I could really do nothing more meaningful with them than build them paths and tell them to go somewhere, they never really became all that endeared to me.  I mean if they had even been better programmed to be more interactive just with one another and their environments, it would have been sufficient for me to feel like an actual all-powerful god watching over my people.  Fact is, they just threw up cookie-cutter village spheres and then sat around waiting for me to do something.  I would have greatly enjoyed watching them fish and farm and hunt or just about anything which made them feel alive to the gamer.  I really think that, with the bare bones nature of your godly influence in the world of From Dust, this game needed more content and variety within its little living world.
Anyway, going from scripted event to scripted event works well enough for a FPS or arcade modes in other genres, but it does very little for a game like this, in my mind and while many of the natural disasters you are trying to aid your little pointless people in surviving are rather glorious, they actually leave you, a god, feeling rather small and futile when faced with their might and splendor.
I wouldn't really recommend this game for more than a cursory playthrough and a few moments of drooling over the fluid physics.  It's pretty, but its pretty blank as well.

I wrote a negative review for this game about five months ago and see it fit to give it a positive review now as so much has changed in that time. Many issues I had originally have been addressed, such as the screen space-eating HUD, the lacklustre graphics/effects, the lack of content, and the lack of decent maps. The game feels well rounded now with better balance and a more refined refined gameplay experience.
While I'm generally happy with the game and the direction it's headed in, I still harbour some reservations that I hope become addressed long-term, such as:
- UE3 in 2017, no amount of polish is going to stop people from noticing
- The sound effects themselves aren't lacklustre but the overall audio pales in comparison to modern games that use spatial audio
- Each entry in the RO series has been more 'accommodating' (read: casual) than the last and RS:2 is another step in this direction with its audio hit indicators and absurd amounts of realtime tactical information (you can literally get kills from shooting at floating HUD markers on occasion)
...And my biggest gripe:
- Territory and Supremacy modes (ie: musical chairs) don't fit the setting; you'd think an asymmetrical Patrol/Search & Destroy mode would be a staple in a Vietnam game.
- RO games seriously need a hardcore mode if they're going to continue to be so 'accommodating'. There's a reason a lot of RO1 vets won't touch it.
Overall it's a 6.5/10.
I really hope Tripwire stops crowdsourcing/focus grouping its design decisions in the future.

While the game itself overall is not horrible, calling it "the game of the decade" would require a lot of brain damage to the point of not knowing how to breathe.
Combat and the game mechanics in general is an extremely cheap Witcher 1/MMO ripoff based sorely on chance hits. It feels like a chore going from point A to B and back while every other step, there's a combat sequence. Every other step, there's some scripted bad guys you have to meet that initiates a combat sequence where you're quite literally thrown into the foray of big armored baddies which gets annoying after a while, especially when you have no health potions or companions. Alternate mechanics include a lot of talking yourself out of trouble and walking down very linear paths to encounter more baddies or an overly long conversation.
The graphics quality of the game is a tad dated, in which I have no high standards over, however it will upset some, considereing it's a game that had been released in 2012. But the worst part is the loading time to get the god damn textures in. I swear that they load textures and NPCs only within a 20 meter radius of the player character.
I have a Windows 7 64-bit Operating System AMD Athlon(tm) II X2 250 with a 3.00 GHz Processor.
My personal system you see, is no spring flower in full bloom, but ♥♥♥♥ me if I can get this game to not lag horrendously when there's more than 8 NPCs about. I have a far easier time loading high-res textures in Skyrim than I do even trying to load a save file. Hell, it takes a good 5-7 minutes just to get the damn game to launch, just enough time for me to make a filling platter of sandwhiches, chips, and a drinks and come back to find the game still trying to launch. It's quite annoying considering once again, a dated design and simplistic mechanics.
The very redeeming quality of the game which barely lifts it up from being♥♥♥♥♥♥ is the plot. I'm unfamiliar with the Game of Thrones franchise and I hear the story itself is really interesting, and fortunately, I wasn't dissapointed, in fact quite intrigued. Considering the game's namesake, it is of course, feudal politics, feuding, and intrigue, which all makes a great plot. This was pretty much the only reason why you see that I've played the game for so long, sometimes late into the night. But of course, it's dragged around a lot in between all the running from point A to B and all the combat sessons. It's very, very, VERY long, which in a way considering all the other boring♥♥♥♥♥♥you have to put up with in-game. I guess the real flaw in the story is that it constantly pulls you back and forth between two characters, one character who's timeline is happening in "the present day" and the other whose timeline of events occured a couple of months earlier. Obviously, you'll see that the events that these two men go through eventually collide at some point, but that hasn't occured quite yet at my point of the story (which is about 17 hours in), just more evidence on how incruciatingly long the game is. In some way or another, directly or indirectly, choices made by the player influence the future chain of events either immediately or in the long run, which is a very great story mechanic. So in all fairness, the story is the saving grace of this game, but the very annoying combat mechanics, linearity of the story, and an escorting mission finally pushed me over the edge from being annoyed to plain rage inducing fury.
Regular retail price is 20 dollars, and I pity any soul who's actually willing to pay that much. Hell, I spent 5 dollars on this game during the 2014 summer sale and I'm still very much questioning if I actually got my money's worth out of it. It makes me a tad depressed how some games that were actually good, both new and old, were on sale for the same price, much less being the same retail price or lower.

NieR:Automata is a post-apocalyptic, open-world, hack-and-slash game. It's very enjoyable and very atmospheric with some grinding mechanics. There are some minor technical problems but that will not change the fact that NieR is a beautiful game.
Pros:
- Mesmerizing music and OST
- Simple yet challenging combat mechanics
- Beautiful landscape and world
- Deep, well written story and plot
- Multiple endings
- T H I C C
Cons:
- 30 fps pre-rendered cutscenes (don't blend in with 60 fps gameplay)
- Occasional frame drops and crashes (for some people. In my case, the game only crashed once after I finished the first boss)
- Resolution and graphic bugs still unpatched officially
- Angle-switching mechanics (switches between third person/sidescrolling/bird's-eye view mid-combat)
- Endings require repeating the whole game, making it repetitive.
- Invisible walls in open-world reduces immersion of world
Overall, NieR is a unique game that is both fun and beautiful. I'm not a very diligent person when it comes to games; I usually forget about it within a few days or give up playing. But NieR Automata is one of the few games that made me play for 6 hours straight in one sitting, and always hoping for more. The soundtrack alone is enough for me to start playing. Get this game fast while it's on a sale.

Short review: It's the Donnie Darko of video games.
(Note: Nominated for the "Whoooaaaaaaa, dude!” Award and not just because it's the first time I've ever seen a squirrel in a video game scream like a monkey, thought that scene definitely helped)
Long review: A very divisive game -- it's quirky, hopping between tragedy and comedy at the drop of a hat, rife with amusing (and in hindsight meaningful) esoteric movie and music references, awkward jokes and some of the most amazing plot twists I've ever seen in a video game. It references Twin Peaks and Silent Hills quite a bit, but the surreal nature, web of intrigue and bizarre metaphysical  discussions that regularly crop up in the game are more like a cross between Donnie Darko, Hot Fuzz and Youth in Revolt.
- Combat: it was added late in development, and wasn't originally planned. It boils down to third-person over-the-shoulder shooting and melee in creepy "nightmare" levels along with non-combat QTE-smashing chase sequences. Some shooter-enthusiasts might not be impressed, but I actually liked the action levels.
You aren't pressed for resources, since you start out with a pistol with infinite ammo and are bound to find unbreakable or infinite ammo weapons along the way. You can't save whenever, but only in certain places (in combat levels, these are safe houses that are pretty few and far between).
- Open World: a large portion of the game is spent in a sim-like open world, like Dead Rising but without the Zombies. You can go fishing, undertake sidequests, look for collectibles, replay combat levels, or just explore (read: fool around and dig up quirks about the NPCs). There is an in-game clock that you have to pay attention to -- the good news is that you can replay chapters in order to do the things you missed the first time around.
(The sidequests give good rewards and reveal a lot of fascinating backstory, so they're a definite win in my books.)
- Music and Voice work: The VAs are spot-on. There is a lot of dialogue in this game, and more than a few awkward moments, and the performers do a fantastic job in tackling both, in my opinion. The music is pretty iconic. The soundtrack is limited, but the few melodies and songs that it has are memorable and cathartic.
- Genre: This game is definitely /not/ a survival horror. It is a paranormal mystery and a tragicomedy combined with an open world and shooter mechanics. There are some pretty gruesome moments, perhaps even a few eerie moments, but very little that can be considered proper horror (except perhaps the chase sequences, which will catch you by surprise the first time around).
- Story: There's very little I can say about the story without spoiling it or making it sound like I'm recapping Twin Peaks. Believe me, it is a popular misconception that this game is a copy of Twin Peaks -- it definitely is more than that.
The basic premise is that you play an FBI detective who has a split-personality and specializes in serial killings. He comes to a sleepy, seemingly harmless American townlet where a prom queen's been murd- okay, I've started describing Twin Peaks. You get the picture. Although the game leaves off on a premise that is basically Twin Peaks, it deviates very early on into a multi-layered network of conspiracy that involves the military, demons, and more than one serial killer.
- Technical issues: I haven't encountered many glitches, but due to an unfortunate chain of events that had nearly sent the game to development hell -- events that were beyond the studio's control -- the PC port has a serious issue with memory leaks. My GPU was overheating like crazy, followed by crashes and freezing. I got the situation under control with some fixes and patches, and luckily the memory problem didn't get dire until the last few levels. I recommend playing in windowed mode, and leaving open an app that monitors your GPU temp -- if you have the know-how, I also recommend setting up a more rigorous GPU fan profile.

There are three phases to this game:
1) Starting out, developing an understanding of game mechanics, and pushing through levels.
2) Coming to an understanding of what you're supposed to be doing, running around unlocking stuff, checking out guides and videos to figure out your broad objectives and how to most effectively reach them.
3) Mana farming for hours on end. (Seriously, you could potentially mana farm for like 10 hours straight of real time).
Each phase does have a lot of fun to it, but it's really too bad that manafarming is the end game, cause it is time consuming and serves only to mana farm better.
On sale, this game is a fun diversion that's worth the money.

Saying GemCraft Chasing Shadows is a tower defense is like saying Garry's mod is a first-person shooter. Like, yeah, technically it is, but...
If anything, it's in many regards way more similar to old RPGs like Diablo where you'd set up skill points, gear, sockets, loot, and all of that stuff in order to kick♥♥♥♥♥and do a bunch of crazy stuff like chain hits that freeze enemies and leech mana while doing crit damage and whatever the hell.
Everything is put together very cleverly and in a way that lets the player experiment to their heart's content instead of limiting them with garbage caps and artificial difficulty. (Many skills have unlimited level caps, they just increase the point cost per level to balance it out)
I used to play the browser version but now I can finally play the Steam version to let everyone know I'm busy jerking off.
Biggest pro: Lets you get away with hilarious game-breaking combos if you're smart enough and try a lot of things. I've gotten to a point where enemies have broken numbers of hit points IE: 2.7781+e15 and I still one-shot them. (That eventually comes to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥in endurance mode anyway so I guess it isn't that game-breaking)
Biggest con: Very VERY grindy. You technically have to do every field 3 times (there's hundreds of them) if you want to get your hands on every skillpoint you can get from them. Shadowcores used to be the game's freemium currency, but now they just drop normally in this version. (Albeit not enough in my opinion)

One of the best tower defense games I've ever played. The system offers so much depth by having gems that give special abilities like a slow gem and chain hitting gem. You can combine gems together so if you put a slow gem with a chain gem, you'll now chain hit monsters with a slow effect. This gives you countless combinations for different strategies. You can even combine several gems together. There are tons of options for how to approach maps.
I played the flash version for a long time but liked it enough that I purchased it again on steam, as it really is one of the better tower defense games around.

TL;DR - Otherwise seemingly great game, but with the 2 computers I played it on, it had bugs, crashes, and framerate issues up the wazoo. The mouse & keyboard controls were also fairly lackluster as well, though with controller it was fine. While the game is good, be aware that you *may* experience game breaking port issues with your PC set up, with community fixes only *possibly* being able to fix this. -
Nier Automata seems like an absolutely awesome game, but for me & the two rigs I played this on, it was not. Both of these PC's are admittedly behind the times, but this doesn't excuse the inconsistent quality of the port along with poor M&K control choices. On foot M&K controls were ok, though not as smooth as with a controller. The worst instance of M&K controls were the forced bullet hell sections of the prologue, where you seemingly needed 3 hands to properly utilize all of the options given to you.
Rig 1 ran the game as smooth as butter. That is until cut-scenes arrived, and the game stuttered until the cutscenes ended. Oh yeah, and then the game froze during combat. Combined with no auto saving (Along with no saving at all during the prologue), this meant having to replay the prologue multiple times until I gave up.
Rig 2 was having issues from the start. The framerate was tanking for no reason, until funnily enough a cut-scene appeared. During cut-scenes everything was as smooth as a movie. But when gameplay initiated, it was sluggish, delayed, & awful. I luckily didn't experience any crashes (As far as I played...), but the FPS in gameplay as opposed to cutscenes leads me to believe something was bugged, so I gave up.
Now, you might think it's harsh to give up, especially when I had 2 PC's to try it on, but I gave up for a reason. I should have heeded other negative reviewers advice, & just tried to buy the game on PS4 in the first place. If I'm going to buy a video game, I don't want to have to research how to make the game playable, when it should be playable in the first place. As far as I can see, it's a *much* safer bet to buy this game on PS4 if you can, as your chances of having issues on PC may be fairly large. I know not everyone has a PS4, so if you don't have that option then I am sorry. So if you choose PC, try to keep in mind the Steam refunds, in case the game ends up being incompatible with your set up.
I know not everyone ran into problems with this port, & that's great for you, but I'd much rather get a refund & try to play this on PS4 instead. If the game ever gets a major patch fix, then this review will probably be obsolete. But as it is now, Nier Automata was unplayable on the 2 PC's I played them on, making this a negative recommendation from me. I wanted to enjoy the game, but it being broken out of the box is a deal breaker. Even if it is fixable with community mods, the ever looming threat of crashes discourages me, and I'm just going to take the easy route with PS4.

First let me start by saying how I cannot believe this game has gotten all these bad reviews. It's not a bad game at all. Does it have it's flaws? Yes. Does it deserve all of the horrid reviews it's received? No. It's a very story and lore focused game, and if you allow yourself to immerse into the story, I believe you will enjoy it.
The game itself takes place during the first book, A Game of Thrones. You will hear events from the book play out as you progress through the game. I don't think it ever goes as far as A Clash of Kings, but don't quote me on that. During the game you will switch between the two protagonists, Mor and Alester. They are very flawed characters each with a past that still haunts them 15 years later. Typically with games that have multiple protagonists, I usually like one character more than the other. But with the way they were written, I really enjoyed playing as both characters and seeing each of their stories play out. Throughout the game you will come across various characters, some are more "meh" than others. The antagonist of the story was well done imo. You will love to hate him.
That being said... This game will at times will feel like it fits into more of a 'interactive film' sub-genre RPG game. I say that because the cutscenes can be very long winded at times, and they will happen quite often. In my opinion the game's story is extremely well done. The voice acting was actually pretty decent for the most part, even though there are a few NPC's that have laughable voice acting and animations. The leveling system tries to be complex but it is rudimentary and the gameplay will have a feeling of "been there, done that" if you played Dragon Age: Origin's before. The combat and dialogue systems are very similar but it's execution is mediocre at best compared to Bioware's. It feels like a generic copy. The sound track is pretty good, as it complements the setting. But some of the background music can get repetitive at times. Very repetitive.
Some of the complaints I've read / heard talked about the horrid controls and graphics. I've been using the Xbox 360 controller for Windows and didn't have any control issues, and the graphics are a tad bit dated. As you play you will be able to tell where the game was quite possibly rushed in some areas. Character models and animations being one area. But as time went on I didn't mind the weak points of the game as much. Now believe it or not, this is a game where your choices do matter. The decisions you make will have an effect on the rest of the game as the story unravels.
Still, I am surprised and dismayed the game does not get rated higher for it's ability to draw you into such a great story and setting. The morality of this game seems to match up with the books - there is no clear hero. Some good deeds will be scolded rather than rewarded. The villains of the world sometimes win, and innocent's can and will suffer. I would definitely recommend it for fans of George R. R. Martin's work.

Resident Evil: Revelations is a continuation of the action / survival horror hybrid that started in Resident Evil 4 and, in this case, was originally developed for the 3DS. As such, though the visuals have been brought up roughly to a Gamecube-era RE game, the environments are more limited and closed than its predecessor. While you can still leap off of high points, hurdle over some rare obstructions, and aim in first person, a lot of the environmental interactivity is relatively limited. In general it's "Resident Evil 4 Lite: Boat Edition".
Similarly, weapon upgrades are just discovered in the course of the game. In general, the weapon layout isn't going to have many surprises for RE veterans, though there are some nice new improvements in the latter half of the game. The emphasis is largely on action this time - though there's keys to find and some pointedly simple puzzles, for the most part the focus is on aiming and shooting baddies. Shooting enemies remains satisfying, though sometimes feedback on the enemies part is lacking - it wasn't until late in the game I realized you could tell if an enemy was dead or not by whether or not the crosshair is lit. I probably wasted a decent chunk of ammo firing at slowly-slumping, melting enemies where it just wasn't clear I'd already finished them off.
Though it has some tension, the horror is generally absent this time around. While not as enjoyably schlocky as RE4, it does have some fairly ridiculous moments that stand out. The new fish-hybrid enemies aren't particularly frightening, and mostly it just feels you're fighting pale piles of goo without much personality. The bosses are solid, but fall more than a bit into frustration due to their ability to soak damage even on normal.
The big change is Genesis, a first-person scanner akin to Batman's detective vision (in Arkham Asylum) or Eagle Vision in the Assassin's Creed series. This lets you find hidden items (and a set of collectibles), and scanning enemies regards you with extra health kits. It's a bit of a misfire, because though the extra health kits come in handy and it can increase tension early on when you're scanning just to get that extra kit, it doesn't do anything interesting like reveal new weak points or at least give you a library of scanned monsters.
The boat environment is kind of a mix of neat ocean liner nods and boring grey hallways, and the forward motion of the game keeps it from ever developing too much personality. Though there's backtracking, it's relatively mild. Having Jill return (along with her prominently featured third-person butt) as the main character is welcome,  given the treatment she had in Resident Evil 5. You'll regularly swap out to a few other characters for different chapters, including series mainstay meathead Chris. The plot is pretty much just interesting enough to keep you going but its twists and turns are generally predictable for a series veteran like myself.
In general, it's a decent little side game for the series, nowhere near the best but also nowhere near the worst. It does just well enough to hold together on its own and to earn a recommendation, but not a ringing one. If you've already experienced Resident Evil 4 and would like a little more in that vein, this is probably worth your time more than Resident Evil 5 or 6.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

A bit quirky but oddly familiar is one way I would describe Anodyne. It felt sort of like an inside joke that that, while not entirely in on, I could still relate too and appreciate on some level. The same goes for the plot specifically, there is little to no back story or context given but I suspect this was a conscious decision as it leads each player to get a different meaning from various parts based on the context of their own life. Unfortunately it is a little subtle and you're never hit with that moment of introspective clarity that other games manage to deliver.
Mechanics wise the puzzles are nicely balanced between single room puzzles and exploration/ labyrinth puzzles. A few of the platforming puzzles were a little rough, mainly because of bad spawn points, but overall it's straight forward and satisfying. The worlds and dungeons are nicely varied, very nicely actually, and interesting, as are the enemies.
In the end this is probably not for everyone but if you're looking for a throwback to the heyday of adventure gaming or are looking for something a little different with a lot of heart just to burn a few hours then this is as good a choice as any.

I -really- like CrossCode, and there's already plenty of people extolling their love for the gameplay, story, graphics, music and all that jazz. So I figured that instead, I'd focus on some minor foibles you may have with it.
The combat system's definitely a strong point for me, but it's certainly a bit unusual. Positioning your cursor is critical, and it determines in which direction you attack, guard or dash, all at once. Switching between these actions is very fluid once you get the hang of it; nonetheless, it may throw you off initially. Going purely by keyboard is not recommended.
You don't have to grind an ounce if you don't want to, but there's plenty of optional quests that have you do so. If you're like me in that you find sidequests of higher priority than the main storyline, you'll have to figure out some techniques to farm plants and enemies. CrossCode handles this in quite an interesting manner with its combat rank system, but grinding it is, so be prepared for it if you're a completionist.
Any game with sidequests has to balance their rewards to not render the player too powerful for the main quest. CrossCode makes a decent attempt by diminishing quest experience as you overlevel them, but does not resolve the problem entirely.
I enjoy rather difficult games, so overleveling is quite a concern for me. Characters will even comment on your excessive level if you come across a dungeon a bit too well prepared. It's therefore a pity that there's no way to freeze your experience. You can inhibit yourself by purposely equipping bad gear, but the fear remains that I'm not experiencing everything as the developers intended me to.
On the other side of the spectrum, if you're along purely for the story and ignore everything else on your path, you may find yourself in some tougher fights than you're bargaining for.
This is honestly more of a minor gripe with the genre as a whole than with this particular game, but it does suffer from it slightly.
Nonetheless, this is likely the best thing I've seen in Early Access thus far. Plenty of others have sung the praises I have, but suffice to say: strongly recommended.
