Guns of Icarus Online is a splendid cooperative game which provides an experience you cannot get elsewhere. It rewards thought and coordination in a ship to ship steampunk package, challenging you to rule the skies!
At the most basic level, you have two teams comprised of two to four ships, facing off against one another in a variety of modes. There are several unique ships to select, and each ship can be customized with different weapons based on their mounts/slots. Each crew consists of four people, who individually can select one of three classes, and then select class gear which they will use on the ship. This provides for a surprising amount of variability before you factor in player action in the game itself. You have to communicate and plan ahead, then adapt to the circumstances which emerge.
As an individual, you are both essential to and dependent upon your crew. If you Pilot, you need someone else at Gunner to take your shots, and an Engineer to keep you flying. They in turn depend on you to approach, evade, and keep their weapons in arc or range. Even as a Captain of one ship, you need to coordinate with the other ship(s) to achieve your aims. You do not need a microphone - there are voice clips and text chat - but you need to speak and to listen, you all fly together, or you will be dashed apart.
There is a very high skill ceiling which rewards both experimentation and analysis. Players start out with basic notions about roles, then uncover the details of a task (learning about main vs. secondary engineering, and the merits of different fire control tools), then find some tactical awareness (tacking to the side against this ship using this tool will allow us to hit their blind spot), and finally emerge into the strategic plane. Players keep learning and each learning leads to more exciting gambits and outcomes, which is why people can play this for thousands of hours.
The community is close-knit and peculiar, with a strong core of pleasantly eccentric and capable veterans. If you have friends, you can take a ship with them, and if you don't, you'll probably make some in Guns of Icarus over the first weeks of play. You can also find rivalries, form or join clans, and generally have a splendid social time.
In summary, if you are seeking risk and adventure in a high flying cooperative game which rewards both communication and cogitation, come aboard Guns of Icarus Online. We're always looking for fresh recruits, whether you know the difference betweent the bow and the stern, or aught that stems from either.

I wasn't sure what to expect from this game. I vaguely remember hearing good things about it when it came out ten years ago. It definitely looks like an earlyish GameCube era game, and has a few awkward hiccups here and there, but overall it runs well, and I'm thoroughly enjoying it.
My complaints so far are...
-Key bindings could be more customizable. It won't recognize any buttons other than the L/R click on my mouse. I've accidentally button mashed myself to death on a few missions. The key to throw barrels of TNT is the same as the button to throw your selected grenade/explosive type weapon. One minute you're setting up an ambush in the intersection, the next thing you know, you took yourself out, and failed the mission for the tenth time.
-Does occasionally crash. It's a well done port, but it's still a port, and isn't quite as stable as it could be.
-THERE IS NO AUTOSAVE. If you fail a mission, it'll restart you where you picked it up, but if you quit the game, or it crashes on you, you'll pick back up exactly where you last manually saved. You have been warned.
-Missions can be a little clunky. You have to blow up a boulder, but your tnt was dropped a few pixels too far away, and despawned, so you fail, and have to restart. You have to chase down a bandit that changes sprites in the gang every time you play it, and you'll fail even if you still have a direct visual on them, but they've moved just a few steps too far. You'll fail if you're doing an escort/follow mission, and stray too far ahead.
-Crosshairs are more just boxes, and precision shots are tricky until you have a few hours in, and get a feel for how the hitboxes work. The Sharpshooter rifles are precise though, and since unlocking them, headshots are a breeze, even from horseback.
Otherwise, it's a great game. The gameplay's enjoyable, the story's good, the map design is great, especially for as old as it is. I've lived in Colorado since '97, and the scenery really does capture some of the nostalgia I've gotten from travelling across the plains, and visiting old ghost towns and stuff.

The primary mechanic of manipulating the land is wonderfully executed. Every level is creative and interesting and I never felt like I was just repeating the level before it. This game gets top marks for game design.
Furthermore, the presentation is top notch. The water and lava flow beautifully and everything is tied together nicely with a distinct visual style.
The problem with this game mainly comes from the fact that it was designed for consoles and poorly adapted for PCs. The mouse vertical/horizontal axes control a little pointer that tracks the terrain rather than the screen, making it needlessly difficult to click things on uneven ground.
The game is also filled with unskippable cutscenes. Between levels you repeatedly watch the same cutscene. The scene is only about 60 second longs, but it's still annoying. Also, periodically in a level the game takes control of your camera to slowly pan around the new objective, even if you've played that level before and already seen the cutscene. It breaks the flow of the game and, worse yet, the world doesn't pause for the cutscene. I've lost villages while my camera was seized from me. It's not the end of the world, but it's a ridiculous thing for a game studio to overlook.
This combined with the mouse issue leaves me sorely disappointed in Ubisoft's user interface design. Do they have a QA department?
There's also no real story to speak of. You just follow a tribe around different levels. The lack of story doesn't seriously detract from the game, but a quality story or just some kind of world building would have certainly added to it.
That said, the game is still engaging and unique. It's short*, but that's just because it's all quality content that they didn't pointlessly recycle (unlike 90% of all other games out there). If you really want more after the "story", there are challenge maps.
You've probably never played a game like this before. It's worth it on that basis alone. Better still, it's actually quite engaging. This is the best game I've played from Ubisoft that I can remember.
* I consider short a pro, since I don't have 100 hours to blow grinding. But I understand that other people feel differently. If you like long games, don't let this game being short dissuade you.

Beautiful little game that's got some fantastic mechanics here. The only problems are Uplay and the length. I believe the problems with Uplay that meant that this game couldn't be launched have now been fixed (at least, I've never had any issues since I bought it), so that's something.
The gameplay is essentially a puzzle-based god game, where you control the elements earth, lava and water and are able to give basic directions to a handful of villagers in order to help your tribe survive. Levels generally focus on one or two problems building up - an incoming flood, or an impending volcanic eruption - and require you to take action to protect your village from the same.
The game is, though, far too short. It feels more like a tutorial campaign. What little is there is very nice, with great music and atmosphere. If in future the mechanic is expanded upon, that's something I'd definitely pick up. For now, this is a great game that's on sale often enough, and is definitely worth a shot when it's at about half the asking price.

I'm not going to talk about the performance issues some people have been having here, just purely gameplay/story review.
IMPORTANT: If there is one thing that every person getting this game should know, it's KEEP PLAYING AFTER ENDING A!!! If you don't you are missing out on half the game. The story continues after endings A and B. If you've spent most of your first playthrough doing side quests then you will get through the additional endings at a good pace, so don't worry about it taking too long. But it is absolutely essential to getting the full experience from this game.
Gameplay: This game is an interesting mix when it comes to gameplay. The bulk of the game is hack and slash style gameplay, but there are segments that are twin stick shooter and scrolling shooter.
This might not be for everyone, but I found it a really refreshing change and it helped this game feel really unique.
The hack and slash combat is extremely satisfying and there is a decent range of weapons available, all though I found a small set that I used for the majority.
Story: The story is told in a simple but effective manner. The main arc revolves around an Android force which are trying to reclaim earth from an army of machines so that humans can return.
I won't go into any details or spoilers, but I found the main plot good, with a couple of nice twists.
However the strength of this games story is in how it represents the good and bad sides of humanity through the machines developing thought.
Some of the machines on earth have started to think for themselves and imitate humans in some way (as they learn a lot from human data on earth). This allows for some incredibly touching moments of tenderness and joy, as well as moments of true horror and sadness.
You might think that the fact the machines look like toy robots would take away from this, but I found the complete opposite.
Their innocence and naivite/lack of understanding makes it even more powerful. Truly incredible experience.
Visuals/Graphics: Graphically the game looks good. I like the art style and look. I can understand critisisms from some people that the world is a little bare, but I think it fits the theme, and its not something I noticed too much.
One of the strongest elements of the game is the character design and the ANIMATIONS.
I love the look of the characters, but they are truly, truly brought to life by the incredible animation work done by Platinum here. From combat, to movement, to idle animations: they are so smooth and just gorgous. A lot of games could learn from Platinum when it comes to that.
One of the best games I've played in a long time. There's just something special here that really hit met as I played on.
Highly recommended and please don't stop after ending A!

Let's just get something out of the way here: this port is one of the worst ports I have ever had the displeasure of experiencing. Even after following a lengthy list of instructions and applying the DPFIx, DP: Directors' Cut features a butchered, shoddy port that is prone to frequent crashing, weird speed ups and slow downs, bizarre physics mishaps, corrupted saves, and a really, really weird issue where playing for more than two hours in one sitting can result in some... interesting... consequences for the engine.
And even if the game wasn't completely broken, it still suffers from a myriad of problems. The combat is abysmal. Not only does it feel tacked on, it literally is tacked on, as confirmed by Swery65, who explained that his publisher forced the decision in an effort to garner more sales. The combat is tedious, featuring only two distinct enemies: ones that die quickly with no effort and ones that take up five minutes of your time in pure tedium ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If the combat is supposed to provoke a challenge, it is easily negated by how easily you can cheese the gameplay by acquiring infinite ammo and durability weapons early in the game, but not even instakill weapons can save you from a never ending supply of quicktime events.
Disregarding the gameplay, the graphics are incredibly poor. I'm not one to turn my nose at dated graphics, as some of my favorite games are before Steam was even a thing, yet Deadly Premonition released in 2010, the same year as Red Dead Redemption, Halo Reach, and Mass Effect 2. Going up against these games graphically is a bit ridiculous when the game looks like it came out in... 2006, but whatever.
At this point, you may be wondering why there's a postive thumbs up next to my review, since I've done nothing but trash Deadly Premonition. Well, the truth is that this game is the best worst game I've ever played. Like I've pointed out, there's just so much wrong with DP: DC, and yet, it's an incredible experience. All of the characters are well written and lovable, and all form a cohesive, believable community and setting. Dialogue is as bizarre as it is hilarious, and trust me, there is plenty of writing to enjoy. Weird quirks dominate the scene, such as having every single character follow a routine and schedule based on a variety of factors, and allowing sidequests only when the time is right, and pulling those sidequests away from you if you're too slow to grab them. Additionally, Deadly Premonition has care in weird areas that I've not seen in other games before, like letting you use your turn signal in a vehicle, or having your character be able to grow a beard and shave it regularly, or most unique of all, having your character sleep under the ♥♥♥♥ing blankets.
Name me one game that lets you sleep under the covers besides Deadly Premonition.
... *Ahem*
All in all, Deadly Premonition is a bizarre, flawed, hilarious, witty, diamond in the rough. It has a ton of bad, but if you're willing to put up with the bad and push through, you'll discover a truly unique experience that no other game will ever deliver quite the same.

Resident Evil Revelations is a solid port of a 3DS game. The graphics look acceptable; there are some muddy textures on doors, but that is not a bad thing given that it is a port. Controls are a bit awkward, but that is due to game play mechanics.
Game play wise, this game plays like Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5. The notable difference is that in this game, the player can move and shoot which is a welcomed change. The best aspect of this game is the game play. Fans of Resident Evil will like this game. The enemies are disgusting looking and the game aims for a classic Resident Evil type of feel.
Unlike RE4 and RE5 alternative game mode, Mercenaries, Revelations has a new mode called Raid Mode. Raid Mode is fun, but to can become a grind fest. Raid Mode puts the player in certain maps from the main game with an objective. The objective can be get from A to B or eliminate enemies. Enemies health bars are visible and when the player shoots the enemy, numbers pop out. There are different weapons and upgrades to get in this mode that are necessary to progress and prepare player for the difficult bonus stage. To remedy the monotonous grinding, Raid Mode can be played online with another player.
Overall, Resident Evil Revelations a solid port and game that fans of the series most likely will like.

In typical Paradox fashion, after a year of patches, Stellaris has become an excellent game.

I think the fact that this is the most-played game in my Steam library tips my hand a bit here, but: yeah, I really like this game.  It's a thoroughly enjoyable space empire simulator with immense replayability value thanks to how customizable your empire is from the word go.  I have absolutely lost track of how many different empires I've invented over the 15 months this game's been out; it's very high-concept-friendly.  The gameplay experience is also very customizable--if you don't like the endgame crises you can turn them off, you can make the galaxy tiny or huge, you can give the AI empires head starts if you want a challenge, etc. etc.  And while there's a definite learning curve figuring out all of the game's complexities, it is a learning *curve* as opposed to a learning *cliff*.  (Looking at you, CKII.)
For me, however, this game's greatest strength is the robust attention and support it gets from Paradox.  And I'm not talking about DLC; even the free patches will tweak or even overhaul the gameplay to make the game flow better.  Diplomacy used to be nearly impossible because distant empires would refuse to work with you; then they changed it so you get a scaling distance penalty instead.  Food management used to be a giant headache because you had to manage each planet's food supply separately; then they changed it so that it's a universal resource like energy and minerals instead.  And so on and so forth.  Don't get me wrong, I love the Utopia expansion and I'm eagerly awaiting Synthetic Dawn's release, but the DLC is really just the icing on the cake compared to the love and attention the base game continues to get from the devs.
So yeah, whether you're looking for space friends or out to conquer the galaxy, I'd give this game a whirl.  It's one of the most fun time sinks I've ever played.

Great game: terrible PC port.
I was waiting to get this game on steam a long time ago, and then a Volition sale happened coincidentally. So I bought it, started it up, and was excited to play quite possibly the best SR game on PC. After having to click through the main menu using only my arrow keys (no mouse support on the title screen), I was finally able to start the game. The graphics seemed a bit bad when compared to the console versions, but I wasn't going to let graphics stop me from playing. So I created my custom character, and after watching the following cutscene, all of my hope of this being a good PC port officially sank.
As soon as I was allowed to move around (after the cutscene you have to break out of jail), I noticed that
was moving faster than it should have been: character movements, their animations, you name it (though the sound effects were still normal). This makes the game nearly impossible to play-since it's so hard to aim weapons and driving is incredibly awkward (on a side note, they didn't even bother to change the weapon change pop-up from the Xbox version,
). Why exactly is the game like this? Well that's because when Volition ported SR2 from Xbox to PC, they didn't bother optimizing the CPU speed for it (SR2's is about 3.2 Ghz) so that it could work well with the CPU speed for most computers (
, see IdolNinja's 4th post). To put it in English, while it'll run perfectly fine on the Xbox, it'll run like crap on most PCs (this "speed-up" glitch happens on both Windows 7
8). If you think I'm the only one with this problem, check the community hub for this game and you'll see that tons of people have the same problem.
Now I've heard that there is a way this can be fixed by using an external mod known as
, but that's beside the point. The fact that I'm forced to restort to an external mod to fix a game that should have already been fixed is just ridiculous. If you want to play Saints Row 2, pick up an Xbox or PS3 version. Do not waste your time on this lackluster PC port.

There is so much I could talk about in this game, so I'm going to try to simplify it in two ways: as a game, and as a piece of art.
This game is obviously inspired by the Legend of Zelda, and it takes this inspiration well. It's an overhead adventure, in which you explore the world and dungeons as well as you can. To progress throughout the game, you generally must find cards that will help you unlock gates throughout the game that require different amounts of cards. In order to get to the end of the normal, story-section part of the game, you have to investigate places well to find every last card, giving plenty of playability and exploration that doesn't grow too stale or ambigious as new challenges arise to getting each card. You may have to pay attention and give patience, but if you're trying, nothing during the normal gameplay is impossible to find out. In what is technically post-game, you gain no real rewards for what you do except unlocking a few interesting levels. A lot of the post-game items almost guarentee that you use a guide, as they are very hidden and cryptic. However, you don't have to do any of this post-game, and most of these items are pointless anyway unless you're a completionist freak. All of the post-game cards (not hidden items in general) must be found to unlock a special last area, which again doesn't serve too much of a point, but it's a sweet area and gives a sense of accomplishment. There are only two things that I would shame the game in terms of gameplay for, and that is that: 1. when you gain the jumping ability, you cannot jump over enemies or projectiles as you would logistically think, and 2. you can only have one save file, meaning that if you want to replay the game  for a speed-running achievement, you must give up your long and hard progression of card collecting. However, those serve as minor details, and the game is still extremely enjoyable.
If you ever wanted to do the famous "are videogames art?" argument, this game would be an excellent example for proving so. Everything about this game is beautiful, to the point where I'm still thinking about it almost daily, even when I have completed it several months ago. This game is intended to be the exploration into the mind of Young, which means that everything is somewhat of a pre-set dream. And Hell, it truly is like a dream. The soundtrack is absolutely beautiful, and fits each individual event or area all too well. The graphics are purposely 16-bit-esque, which gives the atmosphere a surreal sense and further helps move the game's intentions of the whole story. The whole plot is an ambigious exploration throughout Young's mind, which brings up so much symbolism. You could hire the most advanced English professors of the world to try to dissect this game, and even then there would be so many possibilities as to how you could interpret almost anything. Even the very existence of characters in this dream world are controversial as to what they mean. Some themes of the game are given to you on a plate, and whether or not some purposes of the game are clear or ambigious to you, they all share ideas that the most troubled in life may have, and they may easily reflect into individuals on a personal level. This is not a "princess is captured, go save her" kind of plot for the thick-headed, and that is definitely an up-side.
This game is a masterpiece. If you a few good hours to sit down and play videogames each day, or if you ever wonder about your dreams or life in general, you have to play this. The ten dollars are so worth it.

Can I give a thumbs-sideways?
The word "anodyne" in a literary sense can mean "soothing" or "blandly agreeable," and I can certainly give the game the bland part.
For the better part of three hours playing the game I did not know if I could stomach finishing it. I'm getting ahead of myself.
It's a Legend of Zelda-like with a ton of strange thematic choices, poor writing, too much dialogue and tonal shifts that will give a player whiplash. What few inventive game mechanics it employs are spread throughout an atrociously long and dull climb to nowhere. You might pass through seven screens just to get to the next place: no enemies, no obstacles to speak of, just a march. As if the designers (credited indie devs Sean Hogan Jonathan Kittaka) couldn't be bothered, having come up with the overall map of an area, to fill it in with things. This becomes very apparent when retracing your steps. You will find a checkpoint at the beginning of an area, putting you on guard for the trials ahead. Then those trials never manifest and seven screens later there's another checkpoint.
To what end? Was my adversary through that place boredom? Will checkpoints at the beginning and end of a stretch really help me combat that adversary?
The few basic enemies you encounter are all laughably simplistic. Many pose no threat at all. Some cannot even harm you. This led me to think perhaps they were more of a rhetorical device than a game object, really. The only rhetorical question that sprang to mind was "why am I still playing this?" Then later I encountered fire-breathing lions and they shot my dandy theory to hell.
But I do know the answer to that rhetorical question, as the game is a little more than a poorly-written, bland, easy Zelda clone.
First, even though the various mechanics are spread out way too far, the few that the game offers are very neat. Even with all the crummy verbosity, the game does not tutorialize, rather giving you the tools and letting you figure things out. A good bit of design. The nugget of a good game. I would never have thought that piles of dust could have so many uses, but there you go.
Second, there is at least one boss in the game that requires a neat bit of fooling and approaches a reasonable challenge. Shame that I can only honestly say that about one of perhaps eight or so bosses, but that one is very good and fun.
Third, there are a few counter-intuitive design choices that I won't spoil that I do admire as choices. It is this last point that keeps my thumb pointing up with all I've said about the game to this point. What I will say is that it's a shame you only get the full, mechanically complete game after playing through the whole thing.
Heck I guess that's a second way it reminds me of Fez. The first was the music and sound effects. Which I didn't mention. Okay.
The music is fine if you're into chiptunes and oscilloscopes. Tones, mostly sine waves. Some triangle. There are several good tones.
Which is more than I can say about the jokes. Those are all tonedeaf. And just grating given everything else that happens. I want to say that, as a rule, you don't get to make crappy puns about bicycles with names in the same game where you murder a man and jump into his corpse-portal to go commit an abortion on a tentacle monster. Which is part of what I mean when I say the game is tonally all over the place. Anything vaguely interesting as a narrative point just gets dropped somewhere; crushed away by screen after screen of nothing happening.
Things I didn't like:
bad jokes
boring, longwinded dialogue
blandness
useless screens
lack of difficulty
Things I did like:
inventive mechanics
post-game elements
certain specific challenges
cute enemy names
no navi

I originally purchased this game largely because of the insane amount of overwhelmingly positive reviews. Just reading some of these reviews you'd assume the game desended from the heavens on a golden chariot to lead all the chosen people to the promised land. After about 5 hours of gameplay I was ready to rule this out as people being overzealous; the game was good for sure, but I didn't see any golden chariots around. I'm glad I didn't review the game at that point... Since then my appreciation of this game has done nothing but soar higher and higher. The game is so much deeper than I thought.
Pros: (There are so many)
-> Core gameplay is dynamic and interesting. There is a huge variety of skills to master and you can form different gameplay patterns based on how you want to play the game.
-> Enemies are incredibly well balanced. At no point have I ever felt something was too easy or insurmountable. Strong enemies will almost always take several tries while you discover their weakness and learn to exploit it.
-> Death isn't punishing. Feel free to sack a life to understand more about your opponent. It won't set you back and you'll get back to the action quickly
-> Boss design is incredible. They look and feel intimidating and make your victories feel hard-earned and satisfying.
-> The dungeon puzzles are very well done. Nothing seems obvious. It's very much in the spirit of old zelda games, but because you have different abilities than Link the puzzles are new and interesting.
-> Everything about the game is incredibly well polished: menus, facial expressions, fast forwarding cutscenes, help tips. It all exudes a feeling of "some guy really spent a lot of time on this, good job".
-> The game is VERY deep. There's so much to it to explore and optimize. At the same time, how well the game is balanced let's you work around this complexity if you don't want to be bothered or pick and choose what aspects are fun to you. For example: I couldn't give a toss about the crafting system and don't feel like purusing the traders for slightly more optimal equipment/temporary stat boosts... So I didn't. I completed side quests to improve my stats adaquately through leveling up and played more of a Dark Souls style of 'git gud' gameplay.
Cons:
-> The story at this point is very weak... I know the devs are still working on this, but it has to be mentioned.  Almost 20 hours in and the main protagonist does not seem to have a strong driving motivation. She knows she's lost her memories and that playing the game might help her remember and thus far she hasn't remembered anything of consequence. Beyond that I guess her motivation is "the game is fun so I guess I'll keep going"... which in fairness has also been my motivation for playing despite the weak plot.
Anyways, that's my take. I picked up the game at 30% off. It's been worth every penny and there's still so much more of the game to go.

Right I just want to say I LOVE this game (trust me I'll need to say that before I get into the parts I don't like). I think the story is amazing. It's a very well-written game with interesting and well developed characters. Yorke is wonderfully entertaining especially when you're just driving around and he's talking to his alter ego Zach about 80s movies. A lot of the mini stories are fun and the action is very tense and can be really scary at times. I'm serious this game can be pretty horrifying. I enjoyed every part that didn't involve...well uh... ok...
The controls.
I've read some other reviews and apparently the console versions controls were a lot smoother but the PC controls leave much to be desired. Yorke kinda controls like a tank (which would be fine in a point and click game) but this is a horror shooter so it's a little clunky and awkward.
The real time events are uh... a little difficult. Now I'm slightly biased as real time events are the bane of my existence but Deadly Premonitions are something very special indeed. In most games the real time event keeps the same pattern so that you can kinda power through it after several tries. This game changes the pattern EVERY SINGLE TIME. So it's a little difficult. Though I feel someone with good reflexes could get through it no sweat, I'm just slow af.
When you drive you feel like you're driving on black ice though I will admit it's very fun when you drive really, really fast and crash into stuff.
Also if you're playing on PC be aware this game might crash, several times. It did for me a lot. You can have several days without crashing and it could play smoothly until one day it's like NOPE and crashes on you during a scary part, and oh boy you forgot to save so time to go back into the scary tunnel again with those wall crawlers that take a dozen hits with a shotgun again!
And yet... after all this... I still love it. It's like Taco Bell, even though it hurts and might even be morally wrong you just keep coming back for more. I really do think it's the characters, story, atmosphere, Twin Peaks-vibe, challenging puzzles and fun shooting segments that keep me coming back.
I'd recommend it to people who have a lot of patience and want a game primarily for story. Still amazing though.

The dialogue was unengaging, the story tried to really hook me but has failed to keep my attention by the repetitive and soul-less voice acting. Calling this a budget RPG, or an RPG, is using the term very loosely. The leveling system looks like it would be interesting, but the skills do little unless you put a lot of points in to them (a LOT). I chose one of the character's classes (a Water Dancer), just to have it so down the main storyline I have to wear medium armor. Sure, I can wear light armor still by just re-equipping it, but if I use light armor, everything kills me very quickly. I thought, "Well, maybe I can just get some better lighter armor". I have yet to find a merchant that even sells for cheap enough for me to afford. I can't go out and grind for XP and money, I'm stuck on these rails. Finally I ended up getting stuck in Chapter 4 because everything kills me very quickly (mostly, archers). I even tried turning down the difficulty, and I still get killed just as fast...
This game took no risks, and it feels like a mix between The Witcher and Dragon Age: Origins, with all the good story, choices, and fun combat taken out. They put you on rails, failing to deliver a compelling storyline of any sort, failing to let you truly explore the world to your leisure. Every time I try to get in to the story, I just become disgusted with another thing this game does wrong. Don't buy the DLC, don't buy the game, unless you have a real obsession with the Game of Thrones universe. I'm glad I got this crap in a humble bundle, it's not even worth a fraction of the $2 I spent.
EDIT: Some things I forgot to add: There is no character creation. The most customization you will get is your choice of equipment and most of the other weapons don't even show in the cutscenes. The choices you do get to make during dialogue honestly don't matter that much. Let me put it this way, if you played Dragon Age Origins, loved the choices, then played Dragon Age 2 and went "Euuugh, smh", that's about what I felt with this game's dialogue and choices.

I think the fact that this is the most-played game in my Steam library tips my hand a bit here, but: yeah, I really like this game.  It's a thoroughly enjoyable space empire simulator with immense replayability value thanks to how customizable your empire is from the word go.  I have absolutely lost track of how many different empires I've invented over the 15 months this game's been out; it's very high-concept-friendly.  The gameplay experience is also very customizable--if you don't like the endgame crises you can turn them off, you can make the galaxy tiny or huge, you can give the AI empires head starts if you want a challenge, etc. etc.  And while there's a definite learning curve figuring out all of the game's complexities, it is a learning *curve* as opposed to a learning *cliff*.  (Looking at you, CKII.)
For me, however, this game's greatest strength is the robust attention and support it gets from Paradox.  And I'm not talking about DLC; even the free patches will tweak or even overhaul the gameplay to make the game flow better.  Diplomacy used to be nearly impossible because distant empires would refuse to work with you; then they changed it so you get a scaling distance penalty instead.  Food management used to be a giant headache because you had to manage each planet's food supply separately; then they changed it so that it's a universal resource like energy and minerals instead.  And so on and so forth.  Don't get me wrong, I love the Utopia expansion and I'm eagerly awaiting Synthetic Dawn's release, but the DLC is really just the icing on the cake compared to the love and attention the base game continues to get from the devs.
So yeah, whether you're looking for space friends or out to conquer the galaxy, I'd give this game a whirl.  It's one of the most fun time sinks I've ever played.

It's basically using WASD to move around and then mouse clicks to attack and defend in whatever direction.  If you are close range you'll melee and at long range you'll shoot.    Holding down mouse buttons will do overcharge attacks.  There is a skill tree to choose branching skills, etc
The thing that makes this all come together is that most of the enemies have unique patterns of attack that you have to figure out how to approach them, especially in the boss battles and other mini quests.   It makes for some boss fights where you may die multiple times before you win making it more satisfying.   It also helps that the loading time after you die is so fast that it doesn't derail from the game much at all.  I really appreciate that about it.
Now obviously with it being in Early Access the story is not complete.   As of this review it seems like it may not even be halfway there. I could see myself playing for another 10 hours easy though on what is available as far as quests and such though which would give me almost 40 hours(maybe more) in a game that is at best halfway complete.  Not too bad IMO and well worth its pricetag  especially if can get it on sale at all.

I know the game isn't complete yet, but so far, I've played through all of its available content in several different versions, spanning over a year now.
•TL;DR version•
It respects your time by allowing you to save anywhere, it's overall easy to learn, the combat is fast paced, fluid, and not overwhelming, The characters are adorable. The pixel art is really good and the soundtrack really blends in with the ambient.
•Actual opinion version•
Everything in general pretty refined. The difficulty has a nice pace, It doesn't overwhelm you. The 1000 exp for level up system works pretty well, making lower level enemies give you less experience as you level up, somewhat forcing you to move on forward. The destructible plants also help sell the character's abilities, because everything is linked to the combat.
I'd say that the puzzles, world exploration and combat are masterfully woven together, and I definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes to beat up some baddies and scratch your brains to solve some nice puzzles. It has very well adapted controls for a modern audience (as opposed to older games with stiffer controls and 8 way directional movement), and the pixel art is just to cry for.
The story is simple and accessible, all the characters are likeable (so far).
Emilie really helps breaking some of the monotony by talking to you every once in a while when you're sometimes just walking around to previous areas, getting some S ranks, trying to get all the materials you haven't got yet, or just whacking some plants.
-The amount of initial quests that are given to you can feel a bit overwhelming. Specially for someone who is new for this kind of game (which is not the case for me), but I can see a few people getting a bit confused with switching between which quests are going to be showing up in your HUD initially.
-When I got into new areas a couple of times I couldn't tell the height of some of the platforms to jump onto, but that's a limitation of the camera angle itself (and probably some lack of shading of taller platforms ). This was very very rare but it definitely happened. I got kinda frustrated because it broke my "flow" of jumping around as i got Lea's face smacked against a wall and fell into the water.

Going in, I was a bit intimidated by "From Dust." I was worried that I'd get overwhelmed by a complex, totally freeform sort of experience where deep mastery is required to have any fun at all.
I'm pleased to say that this title avoids that problem. You're generally allowed to ease into the mechanics quite gently, and you also tend to get a lot of warning about things potentially getting away from you. Thoughts like "Oh...what I'm doing with this volcano won't be very helpful in a minute" are much more common than "What the heck just happened?" Your goals are easy to identify, and mistakes are usually correctable. Even when you completely fail, you can usually see where things went wrong.
I also felt that the general mysteriousness of the game world was highly compelling when combined with what you do find out. It all left me wishing that I could have discovered more regarding the goings-on.
It's true that the behaviors of the people you're trying to help can be a bit less than helpful, especially given their tendency to be finicky about where they can and can't go. (There's also the whole problem of them managing to drown in something like one foot of water.) Even so, the quirks aren't so bad as to ruin the game.
"From Dust" is a slightly quirky but ultimately interesting ride. I think it's worth trying.

Now when was 4-5 years old I remember seeing commercials for Gun and always begged my dad to get it for me. Of course he never let and always gave me the speel of "Oh its violent" like any other kid my age at the time. Now 11 years later I now own the game and let me tell ya after those long awaited years my expectations have been none the more met.
The Positives:
For an old game running on a modern opperating system Gun runs flawlessly and despite how dated the game may appear it does pay a lot of attention to detail mainly in character models and atmoshpere. The controls are a little weird at first in my opinion and they could have been better but again this game is 11 years old so I will cut it some slack in that regard. You are also given plenty of variety in side activities that reward you with cash and stat points which give the game some light RPG elements and its almost recommended to do these side jobs when you can in order to progress at a smoother pace with enemies that pose a real threat.
The Neutral:
Despite the given variety in missions is does get a little repetative but not to much to where it will jade any sort of enjoyment for the player.
The Negatives:
Now if your all into graphics this game will dissapoint you since it is dated and it dosent support modern resolutions like 1920 by 1080 and the graphic options are also quite bleek with detail.
Overall its a fun game with some smart writing and characters but overall just being enjoyable

This is a really tough game to review.
Imagine a really bad restaurant. It has terrible service, terrible decor, smells bad, looks bad and is just generally unpleasant. It shows no promise at all. And yet....
...They serve about the best main course money can buy.
Deadly Premonition's main dish is it's completely captivating story, which is brought to life by some excellent voice acting. The main characters are a really well written bunch and I found them quirky, utterly charming, charismatic and lovable. I wanted to know everything about them.
If you have seen Twin Peaks, you will not fail to notice this game has derived A LOT of inspiration from that show. Luckily it does so in a really cool and often suprising way and so it never feels like a bland ripoff. Beyond the Twin Peaks influence, it's pretty obvious the game designer, Swery, likes David Lynch's wider canon of work too, to the point that the game could be mistaken as a collaboration. Being a Lynch fan, that's not a bad thing in my book; I think other Lynch fans will love this too.
So what's not so good? I'm afraid there are quite a lot of niggles that takes the shine off the Deadly Premonition experience.
Here we go:
- My experience was massively hurt by technical problems. The game crashed constantly unless put into ME/98 compatibility+admin mode. Alas, this had the side of effect of gradually bringing frame rates down from 60fps to 10fps within 15 minutes of continued play. Repeated reboots were required to maintain a playable frame rate.
- in compatibility mode, a slew of minor bugs arose, such as gun-aiming glitches, which made the game annoying.
- A unofficial hack (called DPfix) to unlock the 60fps is required.
- Pretty poor graphics with a washed out palette, rough textures, and some very ropey 3D models at times.
- Driving is really tedious. It takes too long to get anywhere.
- The core 3rd person survival horror game is not very enjoyable.
- The RPG mechanics (health, hunger, tiredness, inventory management) are completely superflous
- Time lapse mechanic is frustrating. You have to wait around for certain events to happen. Time can be sped up, but the mechanic means that you can end up passing TOO much time and missing your appointment.
- The game is littered with tedious mandatory mini-games, such as waggling the thumbstick to run away from danger, or hiding from an enemy to escape danger.
- boss battles are a chore
- not scary in the slightest. (even the bits I think were meant to be scary)
- Dull fetch side quests.
- The game is not challenging in the slightest.
- Production values  are not great. Very rough around the edges. Wonky transitions between scenes and parts of the musical score.
- Story got so ridiculous it was immersion-breaking. (A mad story isn't necessarily a problem, but there needs to be some sort of underlying internal logic to make the suprises and twists truly matter)
- no steamcloud
In short, the core game is just not very good. I played this to enjoy the story  and get to know the town and townsfolk of Greensvale, not for the sake of the game.
That's enough criticism. I don't want to put anyone off from giving this a go, because DAMN, the story and characters and atmosphere are SO SO good....Good enough that I can forgive that massive list of faults.
But would I recommend it to you?
Now, that is a tough question. I have to give a somewhat nuanced answer here. I'd have to ask:
- How tolerant are you of bad ports? This is one of the worst I have experienced.
- Do you like brilliant stories so much you can put up with a subpar game which is very rough around the edges?
- Do you appreciate great voice acting, atmosphere, superb characters, and perhaps David Lynch's work too?
If you are pretty tolerant, likes stories, love Lynch and can put up with a game that is a quite poorly designed, go for it. You won't regret it.
If you veer the other way....stay WELL clear.
I few things to add: the game is supported by a deliciously quirky soundtrack, and features one of the most charismatic protaganists I have yet encountered in a video game: Francis York Morgan (who is up their with Garrus from Mass Effect for me)
I LOVE this game, despite its numerous faults, and I can't think of a game so in need of a modern remaster that polishes the rough edges, gives it a nice, glossy coat of paint, and improves the core game so it can be experienced by a wider audience.
It's not a whole hearted recommedation, but if you can stomach it's faults you are in for an unforgettable experience.

If you have ever played any of the Borderlands titles save for the Tales series, then you know what to expect out of the Presequel. With that said, this game did get a lot of flak for not being as good as it's predecessors. I agree in some areas, but in most of the main gripes that players had, I had to disagree.
I will admit that I jumped onto the Presequel hate train early on when I started playing, but the more I delved into the game and completed it, the more I found myself enjoying it. First off the pros: The opening was explosive, and it certainly got me excited to continue with the story. I found that I enjoyed the playable characters (save for Claptrap who was fun for a time due to his random nature). Many of the npcs were fun to converse with as well, and you get to see a lot of old faces from previous games. The new weapon types were also a nice change of pace. Lasers were slightly underwhelming without the right gun or character build, but a couple still stand out and are fun to use. And the cryo/freeze weapons were a welcome replacement to slag as you could slow or even outright freeze an enemy rather than just slagging them to deal more damage. The music at times was pretty awesome and helped compliment the environments and battles that I had. The low gravity is still quite fun to me especially when coupled with good ole' butt slams. Along that note, the O2 mechanic was not as obtrusive as I originally thought it would be and many OZ kits (as they are called) are extremely useful even if they do replace the relic slots of the previous games.
However, there were definitely some cons. The environments, while beautiful and fitting for a moon landscape do get old fairly quickly as they have a rather muted colour palette. Some of the new characters fell into 3 categories for me. Those 3 categories were: loved, hated, or utterly forgettable. There were characters that were introduced for mainly one mission or perhaps a couple missions that are just never heard from again. Basically, they are just an unseen quest giver that you don't really interact with or they may just up and die in front of you as the mission is if it's scripted. Those are the forgettable ones. Others (one in particular: I'm looking at you Pickle!) are just downright annoying and I found myself agonizing over whether it was worth doing another mission for them or not. The last area of complaint that I had was the mission structure.
Most of the time I found that missions went a little something like this: Acquire mission that says to go to objective A. Arrive at objective A. Objective A is locked, blocked, or otherwise inaccessible. Whoops! Go to objective B to get the key for Objective A. Get to Objective B. Do some annoying battle or mind numbing task to get key. Trek back to Objective A now that you have the key from B. Open door to Objective A and hope that there is no Objective C though Z just to finish A. Rinse and repeat (sometimes multiple times per mission).
It got old fairly quickly needless to say, but most of the time the Objective B sends you to a new area possibly, but sometimes it just felt like padding.
Overall, despite its flaws, I did truly find myself enjoying the game. When I finished it, I immediately could not wait to do True Vault Hunter Mode and beyond, but that's just me. It does feel like somewhat of a long DLC for BL2, but it was still fun. My advice is to get it on sale and bring some friends along to share in the low grav and butt slams.
DLC: There are a couple DLCs for the game as well. 2 of them provide new characters which are fun to play as (Jack especially), but perhaps should have been included in the vanilla game. Another, the Holodome adds more levels to be gained and a rather mediocre arena that can be fun, but it easily forgettable (also should have been included). Another is a slaughterdome which is not worth it. The last one is the Claptrap DLC which is definitely a nice addition to the game. Different environments, new weapons, and new characters are a nice change of pace if you are bored of the main game.

Overall Paladins is a well made, cool looking first person shooter/fantasy arena game with some unique characters and some with familiar designs and mechanics. Once you get the hang of it and learn how the mechanics and secrets work, it can be very rewarding, especially making it to the last level with the D6 and getting to reroll crappy items into a really good synergy. Unlocking items and characters through the challenges and gameplay was a good motivation to keep playing, as were the large number of achievements. Since each run is randomly generated, no two runs are ever quite exactly the same and makes for interesting runs each time, though after 140 hours I find that my most successful runs tend to have the same core items anyway.
Some of the hard mode mobs/bosses are really unfair, which can be infuriating, but the final bosses
are challenging in a way that I found fun.
A good game for completionists who like a challenge - there are plenty of items to encounter and try out.

Does game have puzzles? Wait, what puzzles? Oh, you mean this "minigame" with moving wires that you gonna do like 6 times? Hard to call that even a puzzle cos it gonna take you 30 seconds everytime to solve it.
-----------------------------------------
There arent't many guns and even those are lacking anything special unlike other Resident Evil games where you could find grenade launchers or laser cannons.
We have pistols, magnums, shotguns, smgs, sniping rifles and one shoot use, rocket launcher.
There is few weapons per each type but those arent much different from each other, beside number of upgrade slots and very minor stats.
Inventory is really dumped down when comparing to Resident Evil 4.
You can have only 3 weapons at once and you can change them only at "weapon box".
There is also very limited max ammo (you can increase it by finding special items), only healing item in whole game are green herbs (max 5 at once), 3 different grenades and no herb mixing. Also 3D map is really, really bad. You dont have full rotation control and it doesn't even tell you precisely your location in the corridor/room. You gonna end up keep looking at it just to make sure you are going in the right direction a lot of times.
-----------------------------------------
The main feature of this game are two things:
>Unique scanning mechanic
You can scan enemies (both dead and alive) to get free herbs or scan environment around you to solve a puzzle (not really a puzzle to be fair) or get free items. Unfortunately its more like a bad distraction from gameplay, slowing it down even more most of time.
>Weapon part system.
Well this one is a bit more interesting. Almost every gun have more than one weapon upgrade slot, where you can insert different upgrades that you collected around the game (you can do that while using "weapon box"). You can add and remove them for no cost so its encourage you to try out different things everytime. Upgrades arent really that special tho: most of them are very generic, like increase of clip, increase of damage, burst of more bullets per shot or bigger chance for stunning enemy.
Too bad that 25% of the game you can't even use neither of those things.
-----------------------------------------
Another problem that I have with this game is how slow characters are moving making it really hard to strafe or avoid incoming attacks. Well, probably thats why there is dodge system. I see that many people are complaining about it - that its confusing, hard to use or just unresponsive.
Let me tell you ..... thats a lie. The dodge system works very well and its easy to do - just stand still and move forward or do quickturn right before enemy supposed to hit you. Its very easy to use and to abuse, making the game very trivial. Dodge is very generous too - you dont have to even do it with perfect timing and many times you gonna dodge by mistake, cos you just wanted to actually move away and the game registered it as dodge.
-----------------------------------------
Enemy variety is really small. Lets see: common enemy that can only grab you, same enemy but with claws, same enemy but now he can shoot, suicide bomber, big one with instant kill hit, half-shark thing that hides in the water, typical RE dog, mutated fish, enemy using shield and good, old re-used for the n-th time Hunter (that is hands down, the most annoying enemy in whole game. Why? Cos he spend 90% of time jumping left and right so you can waste even more ammo everytime you try to shoot him. Like really, he sometimes do five jumps in row before you can actually even hit him - and they dont even have that much health, they are just annoying cos of those jumps).
Heck, even bosses are weak.
One is just upgraded common enemy that you can avoid (you can kill him for extra weapon part - you gonna meet him few times - whole concept of it is very similiar to Nemesis),
second is also upgraded common enemy that you just outrun and shoot until it die,
third is a generic "I will charge into wall and you shoot me in my weak spot" type enemy,
fourth is half horde mode, half turret section
and fifth is just typical Resident Evil boss (
). I admit, its a cool looking fight that will test your dodge skills but nothing special about it really.
-----------------------------------------
Beside singleplayer mode there is Raid Mode. Nothing much to say about, its just cut out parts of the single player mode where you can play solo or with your friend. Its actually more fun than singleplayer mode but its not very long.
-----------------------------------------
Gameplay is really short (it would be even shorter if not all backtracking and cutscenes).
The story is really meh with lame plot twist (
) , not even much of whole "revelations" going on in it if you ask me. Actually story gives you more plot holes and questions than answers.
Its just generic, typical Resident Evil plot where you go to X place, do Y thing, kill Z enemy so I dont understand why Capcom is trying so hard to make it some sort of emotional movie/serial.
I finished this game as fast I could, didnt enjoyed very much - especially with how cheap enemy placement is (enemies spawning behind you or behind corner giving them free hits) , terrible gunplay (most weapons, including shotguns, feels very weak, enemies wont get stunned that easy and like srsl - where's fun in using just 3 guns?) and boring in-game fillers.
After playing it once, I dont have any reasons to play it again to be fair.
I preffer to just replay for 10th time Resident Evil 4 with good, old "inventory Tetris" instead.
At least I will have more freedom with choice of weapons there (same with upgrades)
and the game wont stop me every few minutes to pull a lever and watch unskippable cutscene.
I expected something better than Resident "Less gameplay, more cutscenes and QTE's" Evil 6.
I got even more dull game with less, both enemy and gun varity, and probably the weakest monster design in entire franchise.
I recommend it only to hardcore fans that just want more RE and people who love third person shooters. Anyone other - better skip it.

Maybe if you're a Game of Thrones super-fan and really want to see what life is like on The Wall, this would appeal to you. Otherwise it's just a weird, clunky RPG-brawler with bad keyboard support.

If, like me, you're a fan of Game of Thrones and you enjoy RPGs mainly for the story, this game is great.  The story is one of the best I've seen in a video game.  However, the combat, controls, and visuals are all pretty much just adequate.  There are a good number of small bugs mainly dealing with the camera and walking controls.  The voice acting is also pretty hit and miss with people mispronouncing names and speaking as if they don't understand the context of what they're saying.

Overall, pretty fun game. If you are a fan of RE4 style of Resident Evil, then this is for you. Mostly action, with some strategy. The story is so-so, and seems to trail on, but has corny lines reminiscent of classic RE, which made it enjoyable for me. Nothing special, but I certainly enjoyed my time with it.
Definitely recommending it. Gameplay was smooth, story's okay, and had no other issues with it.

So, I heard you like GTA....
This might be a common introductory statement when it comes to Saint's Row, as it is just that...a GTA clone. An island based city infested by various gangs (Brotherhood, Sons of Samedi, The Ronin and your own The Saints) as well as the corporation Ultor. Your ultimate goal is to drive every other faction out of Steelwater. This is primarily done through faction missions and stronghold takeovers.
Being a GTA style game there is a number of things you might find to be similar. Various housing, shops, weapons, vehicles, clothes and tattoos can be purchased to increase your "Style" ranking as well as make you funds on a day-to-day basis. Side missions are in abundence and range from escort, racing, delivery, assassination, chop shop, helicopter assault, mayhem ($ value damage time attack) and many more. Completion gives weapon unlocks, vehicle unlocks as well as discounts on clothing, damage type reduction and unlimited ammo.
Personally, I came from playing Saint's Row The Third & Saint's Row IV which both have a much more silly aspect to them opposed to the more serious nature of SR2. More story is filled out as the Saints grow into a proper gang along with much more character development when it comes to Pierce, Shaundi and Gat.
If you are a fan of Saint's Row The Third / IV then pick this up to get some backstory on how the Saints came to be and shine some light on a number of references that get made. Definitely worth it!

Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ where do I even begin with this game?
First off, the bad. The port is very difficult to get working. I'd recommend downloading the 'Gentlemen of the Row' mod to get everything working ok. It sorts out a lot of the major issues with the controls, adds plenty of new custom decals, and generally makes the game much better. The modding community really pulled through with this one.
Now, onto the good. Nay, the great. I'm actually writing a review for it, so that says something.
The story, dialogue, and world building is incredible. For a franchise that grows wackier with each installment, SR2 has a way of making a scene poignant despite your character wearing nothing but nipple tassles and hooker boots. Then there's the little things, the comments that the nameless NPCs throw out when you walk past them, commenting on your characters appearance, deeds, and homies. It's something you really shouldn't notice, I mean, NPCs in a game such as this are basically cannon fodder, things to run over. But it's things like that which make you feel as though you're actually doing something that has a real impact on the world as you progress through the story.
I've briefly touched on customisation, but I really can't do it justice. You can make anyone. Literally anyone. My character is currently Emperess of the Pimps, fur coat, tiara, g-string and all. The customisation of cars and cribs isn't nearly as extensive, but it's enough to at least put your own stamp on things.
Money can be a tad easy to come accross, especially by the time your half way through the game. The only thing I've really had to save up for was a UFO
Oh, didn't I mention that? You can go around in a bloody UFO.
Basically, this game is pretty much wonderful. I prefer it to GTA IV and V without a doubt, it just has so much character!

This game hits all the right places in a tower defense game. I enjoy the variety of towers, the complexity of play, and the storyline followed. It is made very easy to learn by the tutorials and in game tips. Started playing from the first gemcraft and have certainly enjoyed this one the most so far! highly recommended!

As far as tower defense games goes, this is probably one of the best I've played. The original Defense Grid was pretty and the gameplay was entertaining but this one beats that for strategy and gameplay. Let's be clear, the graphics take a back seat to gameplay and challenge here. It's not that the game is "ugly" but the game is far from "pretty" too. Top down 2D with basic sprites for mobs and towers. Just want to get that out of the way.
In every other way possible, this game is superior to other TD games. While the end-game is pretty cookie-cutter in how you design your defenses, early on you can get creative and just enjoy different ways to win each level. Admitedly, the game is a bit easy for the first 100-150 player levels but in order to unlock all the levels and get all the gems / challenges, it's quite the grind but in a good way. There are a wide vareity of level designs from the typical maze that is made for you and those you have to make yourself. Being able to power-up your gems and skills also adds a fun dynamic (although again for end-game it's very cookie cutter but that's not for everyone).
I've put more than 100 hours into the game and I'm still not done. At player level 500, I have all but 2 or 3 maps completed (except the challenge maps) and all but 1 skill unlocked (red gem...I hate that level) but for those into TD games, this is a must have in your collection.

But it takes some time to get there and it can be fun for some people. This is one of the best tower defense games I have played.
Came back to this one after playing newer tower defense games, the game-play still holds up.
I've played tower defense games much beter than this one.

The ultimate tower defense game.
What we have here is the tower defense genre distilled down to its purest form and then enlarged to a truely massive scale.  It isnt flashy and there isn't a lot of style in Gemcraft, but for fans of pure tower defense strategy, this is the game for you.
Even if you are new to the genre, Gemcraft is a great buy as the difficulty ranges from newbie to impossible and the depth ranges from shallow to punishingly intracet.
GemCraft essential offers an endless ammount of tower defense fun; the game is ridiculously massive, and that is only added to by the large number of customization options coupled with your way of playing.
It is simple and challenging.  Massive and complex.  I highly recommend GemCraft for fans of strategy and tower defense, and at the price even more casual players can pick it up and get thier money's worth.
Worth the price. This is an immersive and time consuming tower defense game. Love it.

You are on a ship with 3 other people and all of you must work together to keep the ship running and in firing at enemies.  You also have 1-3 allied ships (each with their own crews) on your team.
What this means is that you want to be playing this game with friends.  Ideally get a 4-pack and give 3 copies to your friends and then play with all four of you as the crew of a ship.  If you don’t have any friends to play with, then make some in game.  Joining a clan will help you develop a group of people that you can play with and that you know you can rely on.
I’m not going to go into too many details about the gameplay, but the rough overview is that you have one pilot who moves the ship and communicates with allied pilots.  You also have three other crewmembers that fire guns and repair components on the ship.  There are different ships, gun loadouts, ammo types, tool loadouts, etc. to choose from.
Cosmetics can be purchased, but provide no gameplay advantages.
The playerbase is usually small (a couple hundred people online at most), although in the aftermath of sales it can be much greater.  You have a generally friendly community and active devs, who you will often find in matches as well.
Yeah, that about sums it up.  Also, prepare to spend lots of time in lobbies.

Nier: Automata is one of the best experiences gaming has to offer. To thank Yoko Taro and company for this game, I'll explain exactly why I recommend you purchase and experience this title.
As a game, there's a unique combination of Hack and Slash action, RPG stat progression, and Bullet Hell gameplay that accels in putting the player in tense situations, using combinations of dodges and slashes to decimate foes into pieces. The action has that smooth feel that you get in a lot of other platnium games like Metal Gear Rising and Bayonetta, made all the more interesting with the bullet-hell components the game has to offer.
The game's visuals are pretty to look at too, with stunning landscape visuals (the water effects look particularly good if I don't say so myself), and the designs of characters create a lot of visual interest (even taking into consideration the anime-styled visuals of the game). I understand not everyone is crazy over the stylistic choices that the anime visuals in their games, but it is an aesthetic that is fitting of the type of action you will experience during this game.
This game has a quirky sense of humor about itself. There are 21 joke endings in this game, most of which are hinted at as possibilities throughout little hints in the world surrounding the player. Also, considering the fairly dire situation that the game thrusts you into, it's nice that it'll let you spend hours upon end to become the greatest fishing android the world has ever seen (Good Luck catching a swordfish or Beetle Fish, BTW).
The music in this game is excellent. This soundtrack places emphasis on using a lot of vocals to create textures along with more traditional elements of "epic" gaming music to create a score that conveys the melancholy of the situation at hand. I would go as far as saying this will be remembered as one of gaming's greatest soundtracks.
However, if you are getting this game, you should get this game for the narrative it crafts from roughly 30-50+ hours of gameplay (I beat my first playthrough in a little under 40 hours of in-game time). Most games give you a single prespective as a Main Character to experience the narrative and action of a game. Nier: Automata isn't like most games in this regard. In order to truly experience this game, you need to playthrough all the main endings. This isn't something cheap like changing the color of explosions, either. Each ending comes from a unique perspective that challenges you as a player to really think about how you play games.
Obviously, no game is perfect, and Nier: Automata does have flaws. However, this story is something that you need to experience, especially if you are a believer in videogames as an artistic medium. Frankly, this is probably one of the best games I have ever played, and I cannot state how much I recommend you give this game a chance and play it to completion.

I LOVE Borderlands, the problem with games in popular franchises is that the developers tend to get lazy. Thankfully, this is not one of those games. As ever, the art style is impeccable and even though the environment is completely different, it still looks and plays just like Borderlands. The attention to detail in this series is just so beautiful. (to illustrate what I mean, check out how the lenses on the guns reflect the environment)
Real love clearly goes into making the Borderlands games, and terrible British accents aside, this is a game I could have paid double for and still feel like I got my moneys worth within the first ten minutes. I recommend playing with a friend, but I imagine it is just as fun by yourself and while it may be a bit samey in terms of 'go here and kill stuff' the characters and scripting are more than enough to keep me interested in continued play. Possibly the only series of games I've wanted to continue playing after I have completed.
The low gravity jumping system at first seems like it's going to be a real pain, but before you know it, you become so accustomed to it that it feels not only necessary but an incredibly enjoyable feature. The new oxygen feature is also something I must applaud, it is VERY easy when adding a resource like that to a game to over do it and turn it into tedious gameplay, again the love put into the game shows through and it has been done so well that it becomes part of the challenge rather than 'one more thing to screw you over'. Overall I didn't expect to like this game as much as it's predecessor but I actually ended up liking it more. Bravo. I tip my hat to you Sir's and Madam's respectively.

ARMA 2 is a military simulation video game for Microsoft Windows, developed by Bohemia Interactive. It is the sequel to ARMA: Armed Assault (ARMA: Combat Operations in North America), and preceding ARMA 3. ARMA 2 saw a limited release in May 2009, and a wide release from June 2009 through July 2009. An expansion pack titled ARMA 2: Operation Arrowhead was released in 2010. In June 2011, a free version of the game was released, featuring multiplayer and limited single player modes. It is also considered the official successor of Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis (which has since been renamed to ARMA: Cold War Assault by Bohemia Interactive). The game had sold 2.3 million copies as of February 2015. And that is no wonder this is the most realistic Shooter you will ever play, I Highly recommened it!

Arma 2: British Armed Forces (BAF) is a first person shooter simulation game developed and published by Bohemia Interactive and released in August 2010. BAF follows the events of Operation Arrowhead when you successfully overthrow the Takistani regime. In this DLC, the British forces commence Operation Crimson Lance to control the rising insurgent activity in post-OA Takistan. You play as Brian Frost, who coordinates with various British squads to accomplish objectives.
In Operation Crimson Lance, you play as Brian Frost. Frost comes across as a completely likeable individual because BAF's dialogue represents him as a driven individual for his nation and also an individual that cares for the mental and physical safety of his teammates. Furthermore, the game successfully attempts to incorporate some personality into Frost's teammates through their heavy British accents. For instance, Frost surprisingly meets an old friend 'Tanny' at the start of a mission. His surprise feels rewarding because it shows that in a short campaign, Bohemia managed to meaningfully and briefly explore the backgrounds and expose the personalities of the main characters such as Frost.
Regarding length, BAF features a storyline-driven four mission campaign. I completed BAF in 5.5 hours, which is a reasonable length. I think there should have been more length to the campaign, however what Bohemia presents is quality. The game excels in realism through its focus on communication and teamwork. For instance, your squad cooperates with other British teams to plan and execute missions. Random events also occur that help or hurt you further into the game.  For example, if you decide to help out an individual who had his goods stolen by an insurgent, then he will gather local troops and help you in further missions. If you do not help him, following missions become more difficult. In other words, you are presented with choice and it can affect the game. The game also incorporates a strong soundtrack that features a compilation of rock and Arab instrumentals into various songs.
BAF feels more tighter and polished compared to Army of the Czech Republic DLC. I did not experience any random bugs and glitches that harm the progression of the game or the enjoyment of the game, so I feel that this was more accomplished in that regard. Regarding AI, the AI feels more reactive towards your commands. However, while better than Czechia DLC, AI driving  still is horrible.
Arma 2: British Armed Forces is a very good DLC. It features a strong four mission campaign that shines in presenting Brian Frost and his personality and background. Missions also vary with optional side missions and missions depend on cooperation and communication. There is also a good soundtrack that complements the environment and operation. My only issue was the AI driving behaviour. I recommend this DLC because it expands on the overall Arma 2 story in Takistan while adding some fresh content to the game. At $8.99, you can't go wrong with this.

This game had promise....
HAD.
I'll start from the begining. I, being a fan of RO2 and Rising Storm, was very excited to hear of a new Rising Storm title, especially in Veitnam. So I subscribed to TW's mailing list for beta news and waited. I got finally get a email and jump in. I ended up participating in two beta tests for this game, and while it had issues, a lot of them, it was a beta and I understood that. I trusted they could fix it up and could launch the game.
So launch day rolls around, and I pick up the game...big mistake. They had fixed almost nothing from the time the last two beta tests had ended, and the release. The game's optimization is a joke. It's 2017, yet this game puts most, if not all of its load on ONE core of your CPU. That means a high end system, like mine(i7 6700k@ 4.5GHz, 32GB ram, GTX 1080TI), can't run it at 144hz because of horrible framedrops every time CPU core 3 hits 100%, which is often. My lowest has been 35fps. On this system(a system that runs BF1 maxed, at 1440p, and 120fps min). Now, I realise this might be acceptable performance for some, especially those of you who 'don't see the need for more than 60fps', but if you have a weaker CPU, like a AMD FX chip, you will have issues even getting 60fps on low, because of the same 'issue'...p*ss poor optimization. That's just one issue.
Other issues include, but are not limited to; a bug that causes all guns to do zero damage, at random. Hit reg issues. Bad audio all around, audio glitches, overall poor netcode resulting in confusing deaths and rather unenjoyable experiences. Bugs in the server browser. Horribly implemented vote kick that can ruin games. Poor game rules making it easy to take over a server for boosting, not that most of you would want to as everything you can unlock is a cosmetic, of which their are few, most just slightly different than the last, and as a bonus, they take forever to unlock because of high requirements. This is just what comes to mind off the top of my head.
Now, this is bad, but it wouldn't be as bad if Tripwire had promptly fixed these issues, but we are 2 or 3 patches in as of me writing this, and the performance issues where supposed to have been fixed in patch 1, then they where pulled last minute, with no comment, and no statement or new date for them was given. I had to check the games subreddit for a link to the devs timeline for patches to find out that they had pushed the performance patch back to August. Meanwhile, the last two patches have done little to improve the game in other areas as well. One of the highlights of one of the patches was how the devs listened to someone on Reddit and removed a single tree. One. Single. Tree.
They where praised for this...meanwhile the game is broken in many ways and has less than 3k people online every time I play it, with my all time low being 2.2k on June 29th.
I eventually gave up on the game being fixed anytime soon, and since I had barely played a hour of the final release(wasn't even level 4, even with the double XP around launch), I decided to apply for a refund...and got a surprise. The final release of the game used the same AppID as the beta builds I had played on steam(that's my theory anyway), and the 15 hours of beta time I had over two betas was added to my final release time...I had 16 hours in game as far as Steam Support knew. I tried to explain that this was almost entirely from beta...but it's Steam Support. Enough said.
So now, I am stuck with a poor performing, UNFINISHED Veitnam reskin of Rising Storm. And not even a very good one at that...
If that doesn't sound like a good time to you, maybe don't make the mistake I did when I bought this game.
