The game has a manual in your inventory that you can read to understand some basics. You also get right into enemy action which is great so that you can do some practice to understand how the game works. I think the game does a great job for first timers. It warns them about the highest difficulty, it offers a game manual and you get in-game tips when you need them the most. Even for bosses!
Now this game is special. Never have I ever seen anything in Resident Evil like Revelations. Revelations has a unique mechanic in the form of a scanner which you can use to scan a area for ammo, herbs, custom parts or just secrets in general. You can even scan the enemies you face, either dead or alive. The scanner is a very useful and cool item that adds a nice touch to the atmosphere and you feel alot more like you're inside the game when you carefully scan each area with caution to find all the hidden stuff. It's a great touch! It makes back tracking way more fun and finding those super cool secrets just makes it extra thrilling. Not to mention that you get a herb (Healing item) everytime your scanner reaches 100%. It's an useful mechanic and I love the fact that they went from traditional items in plain sight to completely hidden items that required you to use an optional yet highly useful item to find the items. It adds to the 'sea' atmosphere. Where divers have to scan for treasures, if you feel me. The Resident Evil series does have sea creatures, plenty of sea creatures to say the least. BUT, I've never seen a Resident Evil with this much focus on sea creatures ever before! The game has a great style in creatures. The creatures really gives a deep sea feeling. They look wet from water and they look very 'sea crispy' - Very strong looks that resembels already existing creatures of the sea. From my own Resident Evil experience have I never seen a 'partner-swap' before. In a story-related moment in the game, the characters swap partners with each other which will obviously add a more interesting twist in story where you get to see new character interactions! Revelations is different, well I'll tell you that the game has no store in the campaign. There are weapon boxes scattered around but that was only to upgrade your weapons or swap weapons but that was upgrades and weapons that YOU HAVE FOUND YOURSELF. Revelations was a straight up exploration game above all and I think it's an excellent move to turn a game with such mystery and atmosphere into a exploration game. That was a thing I highly liked. Obviously the game can be fun with buying your way through but I think it added a bit more of a nicer touch that you HAD to explore in order to get anywhere. Top-notch, full glass for Capcom here!
Similar to Resident Evil 6 you can quickly melee your enemies with a quick click on the left mouse button though it's alot more risky in Revelations since you move slower, you are vulnerable and you don't really stun your enemy when you use your melee attack. I barely used melee at all, only on THE MOST SAFE MOMENTS POSSIBLE. You can also hit F when the enemies are stunned to perform a takedown (Won't always kill) which can save you about 3 bullets or so. The guns were very well played-out. You could use each firearm without ever feeling like picking a side. Handguns were just fine with decent damage and lots of ammo, machine guns were really great if you went into trouble of a crowded hallway if you have fire rate upgrades, Shotguns was used when I felt bullied by the enemies to knock them back to save me some time and ammo so I could get past them. Sniper rifles were used when I got to those sneaky moments where the enemy hasn't detected me yet so I could sneak a headshot on them. Magnums were used for those big fellas that I just wanted to murder away, such as bosses. But I love the fact that each weapon felt useful and that there wasn't a single weapon that just screamed MEH. Ammo wasn't ever an issue. You used your scanner "Genesis" to find ammo until you were filled. And during bosses you could use your surroundings in order to save your ammo. Combat was really fine and fun!
The game is not just on a ship. You get backstories set before the ship and you get to play different sides throughout the story. Keith, Parker, Chris and Jill is all there for you to play as!
I'd highly recommend this for Resident Evil fans! Combat is really well done, game runs super smooth and ost is 100% <3

Don't let the simple graphics fool you- This is a hugely in-depth Tower Defence game, with a vast variety of levels, potential towers & traps (activated by creating & merging the titular gems which define a Tower/Trap's properties), space for maze-building, and a whole lot more.
You level up as a character in an approximately RPG style, allocating points to different skills, while finding different talismans and slotting them into a growing network that can give you powerful abilities. The plot is sparse, but it's there, and the map is vast, slowly revealing itself hex by hex as you spread out in different directions exploring it.
Possibly the best aspect is the sheer customizability- not just in terms of merging gems, but with the game difficulty as well. You earn level Traits which can be used to varying degrees each to change level difficulties in different ways, to gain more experience. Likewise, you can enrage oncoming waves over and over, rush them in early, or leave things as they are- You never feel penalised for playing 'too gently', and it gives you room to expand and push yourself on more axis than just "Easy" "Normal" "Hard" would (though there are difficulty levels on top of all this..!).
So, yes- If you're a Tower Defence fan, this is an insta-buy. If you're not, this may well be the game that makes you one.

Gemcraft - Chasing Shadows represents tower defense game excellence.
It has wonderfully flexible gameplay through its gem combination systems and multiple leveling mechanics, allowing anyone to customize the experience to their own prefered style.  It quickly does an excellent job teaching you its basics, and then has fantastic replayability for revisiting the same early levels later as your experience grows.  That first level you barely cleared? You can play it again later when you return with enhanced gem abilities, and then you can choose yourself to make it still more difficult for further rewards.  It supports changing your abilities during the same game without restarting, and an engaging backstory that drives the missions forward without ever seeming like just another level.  How does the story end?  In a way, I hope it never does and the sequels continue!

This is a *must* if you are both a fan of RPGs and Game of Thrones alike.
You play as two completely independant characters - Alester and Mors. Alester is royalty, while Mors has "taken the black", living a life alongside an army defending all mankind from any and all threats that may lie beyond an enormous ice structure known as "the wall". The motives of these two characters differ on many important points, and this game is a journey to discover how their paths affect one another. Knowledge of the TV series or books is not a prerequisite to enjoying this game, but it certainly is a perk.
Now, I seriously discourage anyone from buying this that has a habit of skipping cutscenes and dialog. Cutscenes and role-playing dialog are more than 50% of this game’s true content. It’s essentially an interactive 25+ hour movie, written by George RR Martin himself. The story is deep, the acting ranges from passable to superb, and it all absolutely ties in to the lore of the TV show.  You make dialog decisions that can and will affect the outcome of the game, and in many cases, affect the outcome of your present mission.  Almost every fight can be talked out of, if you care to figure out how to calm the person you’re speaking to.  Adversely, you could tell the angry person to shut their mouth and prepare for a beating, if you wish.
Combat is cool-down style, and fights can be slowed down to bullet-time to make tactical decisions, which you will be doing A LOT.  Auto-attacking will get you killed, period.  You must use buffs and special attacks which are unlocked with XP, which is gained by completing missions, discovering new areas, and defeating enemies.
Standard RPG fanfare such as inventory, loot, bartering, side-quests, open-world exploration, hidden items, character leveling, upgrades, stats, potions, and armor & weapon slots are all present as well.  Enjoy!

This review is for the game ''Saints Row 2'' a single player(co op enabled),open world action-adventure,video game.
Developer:Volition,Inc,CD Project(for Microsoft Windows)
Publisher:THQ
Series:Saints Row
Platforms:Playstation 3,Xbox 360,Microsoft Windows
Release dates:October 14,2008(for Playstation 3 and Xbox 360) and January 5,2009(for Microsoft Windows in North America).
Plot
You take control of an unnamed player character(The Protagonist) after having woken up from a coma.Apparently you are
a gang member of the now dying out Saints Row gang.Immediately you acumulate command of the gang and the gang members in order to save the gang and bring it from the east side of the Stilwater into actually conquering Stilwater.To do so
you will have to defeat the three existing gangs who all compete over power over Stilwater.You will have to progress through
each gang's story missions,destroy it's strongholds and lastly wipe them out of existence.After doing so you will engage the real threat which is Ultor,a Law Enforcement corporation and the main Saint's Row antagonist.If you manage to survive the story missions and the stronghold assaults you will then own the whole Stilwater.
Gameplay
The game is set in an open world environment meaning that you can do whatever is that your heart desire.You can maneuver through the environment,engage in melee or unarmed warfare,drive around and swim around using various means of transportation etc.In order to play story missions you have to play side missions-called activities- first(minigames such as crowd control,drug trafficking,escort,fuzz,hitman,septic avenger etc.).Those missions award respect points and you can spend those in order to progress through the main game.Additionaly there are other type of activities called diversions such as collection,jobs,stunts and minigames(with the exception of Tagging and CD Collection no other diversion is recuired in order to achieve a 100% completion).
Recap
I loved this game's plot which in my opinion was very consistent with every mission in gang's story missions and Ultor's mission path.The gameplay is satisfactory utilizing many weapons,vehicles,aircrafts and a wide variety of customization over the vehicles,the weapons ,the clothes and jewels,fighting style and even yourself through a plastic surgeon.And many other mods to explore.
Pros
+Wide variety of customization
+Plot
+Warfare
+Co op
Cons
-Over the top gameplay
-No dlc avalaible for the Windows edition
Summary
I definitely recommend this game.Buy it and if you want to make the most of it don't use cheat codes.Cheats will result in making this game dull and pointless.
Thank you Volition,Inc and CD Project developers.Enjoy this game!

tl;dr: A frustrating mess that I wanted to love, but honestly it's just not fun. Go buy something else.
Don't get me wrong, there are actually a lot of great things about this game. But it is very far from perfect, which one might think based on the very high approval and reviews it gets here on steam.
Many, many, battles are long, repetative, boring, and frustratingly difficult. I see many people say they are 'hard', but these battles are just poorly optimized. You know what else is hard ? Lifting heavy rocks, but that doesn't make it fun.
In battle, you have to continue to make near perfect moves and one slip up can often cost you 70-100% of your health...resulting in you having to replay the battle from the beginning (of the first phase of a sequence of battles, as will often happen) and you having wasted ANOTHER 5-10 minutes of your life (depending on end boss, or whatever you're fighting).
The challenges are equally frustrating and I've found myself having to replay each one so many times that by the time I complete it, I can speed run through it. That's the type of profeciency they require to simply move on. It's absurd.
Healing also takes an absurd amount of time. Like 2 seconds of having to stand still during the heat of a fast paced battle. It's ridiculous. Honestly, when using a health in battle I often am hurt 80-150% of how much a full heal accomplishes. Meaning, a heal will usually result in a very small amount of health gain, or more often than not you actually lose more than you gain from having to stand still and getting injured.
I have other gripes too, and may edit them in later.
There's a lot of potential, and I do understand that it's early access (rightly so), but it has a lot of optimization problems to deal with, especially in main battles (which consists of 90% of the game since they take so stupid long to finally win).
In a lot of ways though, it has potential to be a really fun game, but I honestly don't understand why it has such a high rating on steam. It's good, but no way is it that good. So I wanted to give a honest, contrasting opinion to all these 'best game ever created' reviews.
So, while overall I do enjoy aspects of the game, and think that it has the potential to be a great game. It falls flat. It is simply too much of a grind and not an enjoyable experience.

I bought this game for about 3-4 euros when it was on sale and i recommend you do the same. Personally i think it's worth it's full price, but I know most people disagree. Anyway, let's talk about the game itself.
Story: The story follows Colton White during the 19th century. Colton lives with his father and they're both hunters. One day when they're on a ship it gets attacked because some people are looking for an item that Coltons father is hiding.
The boat gets destroyed, Coltons father gives Colton some kind of token, tells him to go to some place in some town and ask for Jenny, then he tells Colton he's not his father, pushes him off the ship and a second later it explodes. Colton goes to the town he was told to go to and finds Jenny.  Then he starts his adventure, trying to find the one behind the attack on the ship and have his revenge. It might sound ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but it's actually really good.
Gameplay: It's an open world third person shooter with side missions and stores where you can buy weapon upgrades, etc. Honestly, it really felt like an RPG sometimes. Singleplayer only.
Graphics: First time you see them you might think they suck, but you'll get used to it.
Soundtrack: One word: Masterpiece.
Score:
9/10

Ahh... sweet sweet nostalgic memories. This is a game me and my father would play when I was just a child. It's an open world western game with a great story, great gameplay, great gunplay, and great immersion. It has character progression; every time you do a side mission or hunt a bounty, or choose to kill or subdue a wanted criminal, etc. you get money (which goes towards buying upgrades from shopkeeps like increased ammo, more horse stamina, or more damage.) and increased stats. Certain types of side missions increase certain stats. Story missions don't progress your character any, but that's what makes the game fun. If you cannot beat a certain part, you can do side missions to increase your stats so you can do so. You get more guns throughout the campaign, meaning the combat doesn't get stale because you always have new "tools" to try out. I recommend playing this game on the hardest difficulty, or second to hardest, because only then do you really get the full experience of needing to increase your stats to progress. If you play it on the lowest difficulty you can breeze through the whole game with eaze. The immersion is so good and so thick (if you can get past the graphics, which to me, weren't a bad thing, especially for the Playstation 2 era.) and they really go above and beyond to make you feel like you are in the wild west. It's brutal, realistic, your character changes clothes over time, and you can play poker. (!!!) This game is a win-win and honestly worth every penny. Also, something to note: headshots are HEAVEN in this game, when you shoot someone in the head  with a sniper rifle, their head just pops. (and at one point, you man a cannon and you can headshot people with that as well, which is pure joy.) I cannot recommend this game more. I constantly had a blast. -EDIT: The story mode on normal difficulty took me 8 hours to complete. I didn't rush through it or try to 100% or anything. A casual playthrough on normal took me 8 hours.

I adore this game and everything about it. The ships control realistically and majestically, similar to how I'd imagine they'd handle in real life. The aiming system for gunning is intuitive and forces you to track your targets to get any hits off, rather than blindly firing rounds into the air. The repair system is simple while still allowing for some complexity, and with the damage you'll be taking on during matches, it's enough to keep you frantically busy.
Teamwork is an absolute must, and captains must have some sensability and experience when it comes to directing their crew. A team that works together as a well-oiled machine will wipe the floor with an uncoordinated opposition, and while it may be frustrating when you're stuck with one such team that can't get their act together, the community tends to be rather forgiving to newbies from what I've seen. That being said, it is rather frustrating when the game starts without a full player crew complement, as the remaining slots will be filled with AI. Suffice to say, while they do the best they can, the AI can't even come close to holding a candle to a real player that knows what they're doing. Furthermore, if a player drops during the match, they are replaced with a bot, which is leagues better than simply leaving the slot unfilled.
Rarely do I have issues finding matches, and the community is often endearing and fun to chat with while waiting for players to join. Sometimes you may have to wait a while before getting a lobby, but once you're in, your crew carries over between matches, so it's easier to continue playing. Voice chat is fully supported, as well as team and crew specific chat options. You can type both in the lobby and in-game, and you are also given a repertoire of barks to give orders and communicate with your team. Thanks to some fantastic fan submitted voice acting, there are also several voice options from which to choose. Though there are the occasional bad eggs that trash talk when your ship is blown out of the sky for the 3rd time in a row, there's never been a match I've played after which the chat hasn't been filled with "gg" from both sides.
The devs clearly put a lot of love into this game. I downloaded it way back around the time when it was first released, and it's come a long way since then. There are a variety of game modes, maps, and an enormous array of ships and weapons to pick from, though some of the game modes may not be particularly well received by some players, mostly the Rocket League-esque capture the flag matches, though I don't mind these too much.
Captains may rearrange and swap out weapons on their ships in the loadout menu before a game starts, and different setups will drastically change a vessels role. Each gun suits a different purpose, and none of them feel useless. Furthermore, players have the option of picking gear to take with them - gunners get more ammo types, engineers get ship buffs and repair tools, and the pilot gets utilities to increase ship speed, maneuverability, etc. - and each class is allowed one item from each of the other two classes. Understanding what each piece of equipment does will definitely give you an edge in combat, and some ammo types work better on different guns.
Finally, the game has Steam Workshop support, and while full on mods obviously aren't enabled, this allows players to design their own ship banners and character customizations, including clothing and hairstyles. Supporting them with a vote grants you access to these in-game if/when they're implemented, but otherwise you'll have to buy them or earn other options with in-game achievements. With that said, the achievement system has an absolutely staggering amount of room for completionists to keep themselves busy, and various milestones will grant you further items with which to customize your character, including dyes, hats, and outfits.
All in all, I give Guns of Icarus a solid 8/10; I highly recommend this game to anybody that has so much as a passing interest in steampunk airship battles with a heavy emphasis on teamwork and tactics. It's incredibly fun, and well worth the purchase, especially considering the low price, and the fact that it goes on sale semi-frequently. Don't miss out; we would certainly welcome more crew members!

TL;DR - Otherwise seemingly great game, but with the 2 computers I played it on, it had bugs, crashes, and framerate issues up the wazoo. The mouse & keyboard controls were also fairly lackluster as well, though with controller it was fine. While the game is good, be aware that you *may* experience game breaking port issues with your PC set up, with community fixes only *possibly* being able to fix this. -
Nier Automata seems like an absolutely awesome game, but for me & the two rigs I played this on, it was not. Both of these PC's are admittedly behind the times, but this doesn't excuse the inconsistent quality of the port along with poor M&K control choices. On foot M&K controls were ok, though not as smooth as with a controller. The worst instance of M&K controls were the forced bullet hell sections of the prologue, where you seemingly needed 3 hands to properly utilize all of the options given to you.
Rig 1 ran the game as smooth as butter. That is until cut-scenes arrived, and the game stuttered until the cutscenes ended. Oh yeah, and then the game froze during combat. Combined with no auto saving (Along with no saving at all during the prologue), this meant having to replay the prologue multiple times until I gave up.
Rig 2 was having issues from the start. The framerate was tanking for no reason, until funnily enough a cut-scene appeared. During cut-scenes everything was as smooth as a movie. But when gameplay initiated, it was sluggish, delayed, & awful. I luckily didn't experience any crashes (As far as I played...), but the FPS in gameplay as opposed to cutscenes leads me to believe something was bugged, so I gave up.
Now, you might think it's harsh to give up, especially when I had 2 PC's to try it on, but I gave up for a reason. I should have heeded other negative reviewers advice, & just tried to buy the game on PS4 in the first place. If I'm going to buy a video game, I don't want to have to research how to make the game playable, when it should be playable in the first place. As far as I can see, it's a *much* safer bet to buy this game on PS4 if you can, as your chances of having issues on PC may be fairly large. I know not everyone has a PS4, so if you don't have that option then I am sorry. So if you choose PC, try to keep in mind the Steam refunds, in case the game ends up being incompatible with your set up.
I know not everyone ran into problems with this port, & that's great for you, but I'd much rather get a refund & try to play this on PS4 instead. If the game ever gets a major patch fix, then this review will probably be obsolete. But as it is now, Nier Automata was unplayable on the 2 PC's I played them on, making this a negative recommendation from me. I wanted to enjoy the game, but it being broken out of the box is a deal breaker. Even if it is fixable with community mods, the ever looming threat of crashes discourages me, and I'm just going to take the easy route with PS4.

This has become one of my favorite games, and I believe every tower defense fan has a good chance of really enjoying this game. Gemcraft - CS is based on the original Flash game (haven't played it at time of writing, but I should get around to it sooner or late). I've played a lot of Flash tower defense games, but Gemcraft is very unique, for many reasons:
Is similar to other top-down TD games, in which your sole objective is to defend your base (in this case, your Orb) from hordes of enemies. You do this by placing gems into towers and traps. It's a simple premise, but the game incorporates so many elements that complicate matters. Every gem type has a different special effect, and many factors, such as the shape of the field, the gems you have available (you don't unlock all the gems for use on every map until later in the game), and the skills/abilities you have, just to name a few. You can also speed up time, which is very useful as things WILL get slow at times, or pause time entirely while you make decisions. This sounds broken, but I assure you, it isn't. You can even play in Iron Wizard mode, which disables most of the extra bonuses and makes the game more like a typical TD experience, with the difficulty being thrown at you head-on. Much of the game is the player investing more in their talisman bonuses and skill points to challenge more difficult maps and make more progress in endurance runs.
Nothing too fancy, the music is ambient and fits the mood of the game, while the sounds do what they need to. Nothing I'd mind if they were muted, but not bad.
Same as the Sound department. Not bad at all, and the gems are pretty to look at, but nothing incredibly fancy. It looks exactly like a Flash game.
The game runs very well overall, but there can be significant lag due to all the enemies and effects on the screen if you progress far enough in waves. A lot of people complain about this, but this is a very common, and often unavoidable problem in games. I have seen a couple of apparent fixes for this, but have yet to try them. However, it shouldn't be too hard to run this game decently.
When the store page tells you that this game has an emphasis on strategy and replayability, it is
lying to you. There are dozens of maps to play and as you level up and discover new strategies, you can replay stages you've beaten to gain more XP and go for rarer talisman fragments to further power up, and you decide how much harder to make your endurance runs. All this adds to many hours of replaying, which makes the game grindy, but to me it rarely feels like just a monotonous grind because I enjoy seeing how much stronger I've become since the last time I played a particular map, and regardless if it is a new map or not, it's fun to me. In addition, there are hundreds of achivements, and while some are freebies, the majority require at least a bit of skill to obtain. Your level can soar into the thousands and there is a lot of complicated math with the game's inner workings, for those who like solving that stuff (too intimidating for me). There is a lot to do in this game for dedicated TD fans, but more casual players may prefer a simpler experience.
I love this game, and out of all the TD games I've played, this is one of the most unique I've played. If you're a longtime fan of the genre, you should give it a chance. You likely won't be disappointed.
- Simple gameplay at its core
- Many ways to customize your abilities and challenge level
- Many, many maps and achievements, offering immense replayability for a TD game; the desire to keep earning things can become addicting
- The many facets of micro-managing various gameplay elements may turn off those looking for a simpler experience
- This game is inherently grindy, especially with the randomization of talisman fragment drops and certain enemies that may or may not appear in a given run, so people who are bothered by grinding in games should probably stay away
- Some people like an immediate challenge, but this game is only as hard as you make it, which some may not prefer

Stellaris is entertaining for a few hours, but quickly becomes dull and tedious. When you first start a game, you're amazed and interested at how indepth the game feels with all the different mechanics. Plus, if you're a fan of the sci-fi genre, it's a blast to just get yourself immersed in growing a space empire. However, once you crack the surface, once you start learning about these mechanics, it quickly reveals itself to be shallow.
Combat is boring and unbalanced. It always boils down to having the bigger fleet, with few exceptions. Ground combat is even more boring and simplified, with no strategy involved at all. Simply move your army to a planet, land, and win. Managing your empire is boring and tedious.
To manage your empire, you have a few planets that you directly control and micromanage, and then have to delegate any other planets to "sectors." These sectors give the AI control over the planets, having them build and develop improvements. A good portion of the game is taken out of your hands and put into the AI's, and the AI is beyond inept. I've had sectors, with plenty of resources, still have empty planets with no improvements while they build nothing else. To try to get the most out of your planets, you have to constantly jockey with the sector system, do the dull and tedious colony development yourself, and then jockey with the sector system again. It's very boring, and adds more micromanagement to a system that was designed to reduce it.
Of course, the sector system is absolutely necessary, because the other space empires are just as inept as the sector AI. The only way to stop a player from completely steamrolling the galaxy is to cripple the player through using the sectors. If you try to play around the sectors, you get the micromangement hell I described above. If you use the sectors "as designed" then the game is still unbalanced, but still better than the optimal way to play.
I tried to like Stellaris, and at first I really did. It just becomes so boring and tedious. It's hard to explain how much time is wasted in this game just waiting. Waiting for resources, waiting for fleets to build, waiting for the invasion to end, waiting for the warscore to tick up so you can end a war, waiting, waiting, waiting. The only things that could have made the downtime between conflicts interesting was the empire management, which is taken out of control of the player through sectors, and then handled ineptly by the AI.
In addition to the problems with the actual game, Paradox Interactive has become a terrible company to support. Gone are the days where Paradox made fantastic, if buggy, games for relatively cheap, with great expansions to enhance the vanilla game. Now, Paradox releases broken games, then releases a constant stream of overpriced DLCs that add one or two features, that are inevitably broken or unbalanced on release. The sad part is, most of the DLCs are great ideas, with terrible implementation, or are great ideas, at the expense of ignoring vital areas of the base game.

So I originally wrote a review that was ranty because I don't like sidequests... much. They 'can' be a nice distraction but they're mostly platitudes and abusive of some of the most ancient cliches. That said, changes have been made where there are fewer of them, and even some of the ones that reamain, are quite interesting. Most noteably is the sub-arc about the girl whose kindness is exploited by a guild to bring in 'Seekers' to help with grunt work for some diabolical plot of this guild..... that hasn't been revealed yet.
Before the change the game was already a 10/10 in my eyes, now it's more like 11/10. I cannot get enough, and I cannot say enough good things about it. It's not just RPG in the level grinds, you can surpass obstacles a variety of ways, including a skill tree that actually makes the character feel powerful, and equipment that can be customized for several different playstyles.
The story starts out with this kind of 'anime' style opening, hooking you with a mystery, a sequence of action-packed events that just leave you wondering what's going on. But there's a catch: Lea is introduced as an amnesiac, surrounded by people who seem to know more about her than she does. This includes the main villain. I won't say any more than that, so as not to spoil, just give an idea of what to expect.
Every character is colorful and loveable. Emilie is a faithful sidekick, perhaps a bit ditzy but not in an annoying way. She is actually my favorite supporting character, an endless source of adorable. Apollo is definitely an over-the-top rival, the kind of obnoxiously righteous punk but fun to be around in doses, which is exactly how you're treated to him.
But by far the most important thing in any video game is the gameplay itself. And CrossCode delivers immensely. Switch between melee and ranged combat seemlessly; dodge attacks gracefully or put up a directional shield; use circuits to buff your abilities and add a variety of new ones; use elemental attributes to exploit enemy weaknesses. Almost everything flows in this beautiful dance and you can always learn a new technique or adjust your patterns. And if you use a gamepad, you will be delighted by how buttery smooth Lea can move.
Seriously cannot wait for full release. If you value 'fun' and respectable challenge curve more than pretty graphics, buy this game.

text: A throwback to the old topdown legend of zelda games. Because of a relatively short story length, the repetative nature of the combat and puzzles does not become frustrating. I personally wad not a fan of some of the bossfights and the discrepancy of difficulty between most of the early bosses being a cakewalk but a couple, including the final boss, being annoyingly difficult for no adequite reason. there are only 6 achievements and three of those come from the main story, while the other three are from the additional achieveable content and gameplay. Overall i would give this game an 8/10, it was well written and ended as soon as it needed to to not overstay its welcome.

On the whole, if you want a fun and unique Zelda-like action-adventure game with puzzles you couldn't go wrong with Anodyne. The music is good, the look is interesting, the gameplay is generally solid. It's not without flaws. When it comes to jumping, you will probably be swearing a lot because the game feels "slippery" when it comes to edges. There's also a fair bit of tedious exploring at the end of the game to get the necessary items to progress to the final area. But overall, it's a pretty solid and fun game that will take you between 3-6 hours to beat on your first try.

I was a big fan of the old 2D Legend of Zelda games like Link's Awakening, and Anodyne effectively recaptures their spirit with some...very strange new twists.
Um...minor spoilers, I guess.
So it's like...a broom instead of a sword? What? Like, one minute you're floating down a river on a pile of dust, the next you're falling down a whirlpool into a weird land with walking trees, and then you climb a windmill and get to outer space, which is ruled by cubes wih faces, but it's actually a hotel filled with evil ghostly cleaning ladies, and there's a town where everything's in black and white and shadows are chasing you and...well, don't get me started on the ending. It's ridiculously surreal.
Therein lies Anodyne's brilliance--unlike Link's Awakening, which had some weirdness but was always internally consistent, Anodyne perfectly recreates the fuzziness and weirdness of an ACTUAL dream. And it does it well! A work of art, really.
The gameplay is great too, of course, standing on the shoulders of giants and whatnot. If you've played the top-down Zeldas, you should feel right at home. Frankly, it's a better Zelda game than some of the actual Zelda games we've seen recently.
Anyway, thumbs up.

First had this game back in 2005 on my ps2 but decided on a whim to re-buy it for my pc after seeing it on sale. The game itself is one of the best for the limited choice of cowboy games on PC and in my opinon across all platforms. Although some of the negative reviews have said that the game hasn't aged well i'd have to say that i do agree with some points but as a whole disagree.
I've finished the campaign in just over 5 hours but in all honesty the map size for what we would call open world in comparison to a game like Red Dead Redemption is of its time and frankly that is understandable when trying to create a campaign that wasn't overly boring within a relatively small open world. The one bad thing i would say about the short length of the campaign is that you can feel like the story lacks depth in some senses but i feel that as a whole it stands strong as it tries to not make boring repetitive core missions in a limited space.
As far as side missions there are plenty and of a wide variety be it your classic bounty hunter posters (which in mission do include an option to subdue your bounty which i found surprising for a game in 2005 for which i expected to be find bad guy shoot bad guy policy upon first playing it so long ago) you have the option to help out on a ranch herding cattle, delivering mail or even hunting wild animals (the hunting missions dont include way points on your map which really ups the open world exploration of the game). You can even just go out and hunt buffalo if you feel like it a true variety on display throughout.
The game has a basic weapons collection system which allows for a bit of variety when it comes to combat both in ranged and melee. Although you can't go to the store to buy your weapons as they can only be unlocked through campaign progress, their is a general store which sells upgrades for those weapons to improve things like damage and accuracy as well as other miscellaneous items including the nice little feature of a pick axe to go and mine gold allowing you to become the true claim jumping 49'er you've always wanted to be.
The graphics are again understandably low quality and are of course of their time. Cut scenes can be a good laugh watching the characters mouth move in random contortions which apparently are producing words as their gun jaggedly no-clips through a horses head. I feel that it gives the game a bit of atmosphere i mean it wouldn't be expected now, but hey as i keep saying its a classic from 2005 and the game holds up so much more than just graphical quality.
The game does have both mouse+keyboard and controller support though the controller will have to be manually mapped out for those who wish to truly experience the old-old-gen console experience.
But hey real nostalgic trip a true classic and a worthy title to a returning fan or a new one. i'd have to give it a solid 9.5/10

You know that game, that comes out pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ on release date,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of people that were following the hype, expecting a similar level of quality as the previous entry of the franchise and not receiving it?
Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel wasn't a game like that, contrary to popular belief. It was a great game on release, improving almost every single aspect of the franchise... for casual players. I loved every single second of it and it's one of my favorite non-PvP shooters to this day, but it severely lacked in one aspect veterans of the franchise loved: End-game grind. In fact, it was so bad that it didn't have anything like an original raid-boss (it being a rehash of the final boss) and normal bosses didn't even respawn. The Borderlands community was in an outrage, reviews at the time severely bashing on the game, a great game, that didn't live up to expectations it didn't give in the first place.
Then, the patches came, fixing a lot of stuff that veterans were mad about (except the holodome DLC, that was just dumb gearbox, kinda impossible to defend you there), but unfortunately the damage was done.
If you're looking at this review now, looking to see if you should buy this game, then yes, absolutely... if you're a casual. "but Arara, didn't you just say they fixed the grind for hardcore people?" Yes they did... but that can't bring the playerbase back. If you don't have a dedicated team, you'll probably have better luck in Borderlands 2, even if this is an improvement in so many ways.

I think its a little unfair to judge this game simply by the shortcomings of Ubisoft and their terrible DRM. This game is wonderful.
Thankfully someone here in the review section has gracefully provided a very useful guide on how to get the ungodliness that is UPlay to work.
So, I'm not even going to talk about that. It is what it is. I never had any problems with it.
From Dust on the other hand, is actually an insanely addictive game. My only wish is that it was longer. I absolutely love the combination of simulation god-game and the challenges you are given to overcome. Every time I put this game down, I consistently had the nagging urge to play it more.
You can play the game however you like, whether you want to speed through the challenges or take your time unlocking everything (the extra challenge mode levels are unlocked by various things like finding totems on the landscapes or getting 100% vegetation on the current land). The game is a challenge, but there is no time limit for completing the levels and you can take your time if needed. Its actually fairly relaxing. The extra challenge levels you unlock are fun also.
The nature simulations are very fun to play with and it controls very well. The controls themselves are very easy to use. I recommend playing this game with a gamepad. (I use the xbox 360 gamepad for windows.)
And yes, this game is absolutely gorgeous to look at. The music, the sounds; everything is wonderful. The simulations in this game - the water and volcanoes expecially - are really amazing and fun to manipulate.
Its not very long, I completed the main story in about 9 hours, but its a very nice, satisfying experience all in all. I think I may play it over again, and see if I can complete the challenges using different methods. It doesnt seem like any two playthroughs of this game will be the same. I still have many extra challenge levels complete too (there are lots of them).
Dont disregard this game simply because the DRM is bad. If you can put up with the bit of extra effort it takes to get UPlay running, I promise this game is worth it.

Starts out a bit slow, and with really simple, linear levels. After a while you start receiving upgradable gemstones for your talisman that give you passive bonuses. They might be x% damage to a specific enemy type, faster tower reload rate, more mana, slower killchain decrease rate etc. That alone lets you build a "character" for a specific playstyle.
But wait, there's more!
We have skills that also give passive bonuses, different tower types of course and combination of those tower types. You can either build a "pure" tower with one element, or a combination of 2 or more different types. So far i've been in levels that offered me 6 different types at the same time, and i could make a combination of all of them in the same tower. It costs a lot though! In addition to towers we have traps that are built on the ground for bad guys to walk over. Like towers, they can be equipped with one element, or a combination. We also have spells that give special attacks to your towers or traps.
There are a lot of levels. Some of them are pure classic tower defense, some feature additional objectives like destroying a certain targets before the last wave, either by simply shooting them with your towers or using some specific spell/level gem to bomb them with. The design seemed first very linear, but after a while they started opening up, and we can build proper mazes on many levels! That's the most fun part of TD game in my eyes, and not many TD games offer us that, for some strange reason. After the waves you can start Endurance mode for more exp, enemies and talisman stones! If you want more challenge on the levels, you unlock battle traits when progressing in the game. They increase the exp in addition to the difficulty.
I haven't experienced a single bug, everything runs smooth.

GemCraft: CS is easily one of the best tower defense games I've played. Highly addictive, challenging, an immense grid of levels to beat, and very clever gameplay mechanics (gem combo formulas) make this a must-have for tower defense fans.
I am a huge fan of tower defense type games and this is one of the best ones that I have played.

I've played a number of tower defense games over the years, but never seriously. I thought it was just a genre full of fairly generic, brief diversions. None of them seemed to be serious games. None had any real depth. After an hour, you'd seen everything the game had to offer.
With GemCraft - Chasing Shadows, that hour will give you just the briefest glimpse of what the game has to offer.
This game has so many fantastic and innovative concepts brilliantly intertwined that it's hard to even know where to begin to describe it. Just covering the individual features like the amazing trait system, which allows you to tune the difficulty for increased XP gains, or the deep skill system, which give you the ability to tweak the power level of every tool at your disposal each game, or the wide array of gems, each with unique characteristics and the ability to combine with others, will not come remotely close to doing the game justice.
GemCraft - Chasing Shadows combines all of these elements and many more in a seamless whole. Every single part of the game is smoothly intertwined with others. Leveling gives you skill points, which tweak your gems and spells, which define your towers and play style. All of this is impacted by fragments, allowing you to further tweak your build and play style. Even getting achievements is tied into the game by giving you skill points!
Even with everything I've said, so much was left uncovered. This game is crazy with content, all of which is fantastic. It even has an interesting story! This is not your usual tower defense game. It's the pinnacle of the genre. If you don't play this game, you are doing yourself a tremendous disservice.
Buy this game.

In quality and overall fun, it far outstrips its status as a mere "gaiden" game!  Lightly textured but nicely modeled and animated, it exhibits an attractive "Hyper Dreamcast" style that doesn't overload the optic nerves with absurdly realistic textile weave.  Limited ammo and herbs make things a lot more survival horror-esque than 4, 5 and 6, but when you run out of something, you can scan your surroundings with a little viewfinder that identifies hidden items.  It's a great crutch to have if you find yourself in a sloppy gameplay session!  Viewfinder usage is never too onerous, and it's downright AWESOME if you've got an obsessive-compulsive inner beast that craves a massage.  The contextual dodge mechanic (you joggle the stick in a certain direction right before the blow falls) is a little weird at first, but it actually works beautifully in one-on-one encounters.  You're better off running from mobs, but let's face it; what game lets you duck an entire
of misshapen gropers?
has a perfect RE story, one that's even worthy of a mainline game.  You know what that means, RE fans:  it's a convoluted, monster-packed mess dripping with so much cheese sauce that it will give you gout, and it is positively glorious!  Let me explain something to the uninitiated; RE stories are good not just because they're cheesy fun, or just because they've got oodles of hideous monsters, but because they are leavened with real creativity and intelligence.  It's wonderfully dumb spectacle plus deep mythos.  Unkillable action heroes with one-liners striving against organizations with (sometimes insanely) complex motivations.  Ridiculously twisty plotting with expert pacing.  Not many AAA actioners (game or film) can suck you in like an RE can into its coincidence-laden universe of pustulant monsters!
Tbh, if you're a resident evil fan, try the game out. It's pretty cool to get something a little different. Plus taking on an abandoned ship, pretty cool setting.

Wow, time to write my first review, huh? This game is definitely worth it. I found this game on accident. Since then, it has become one of my favorite RPG's ever. From the exploration of the beautiful areas, to the intruiging story, to the whole feel of the game in general, it is the only game that I have ever wanted so badly to finish. The movement system in itself sets it apart from any other game ive ever played. That, combined with the ingenious combat styles and the layout of the game world itself is god-like.  If I could give two thumbs up, I would.

EDIT:  I now have hours on Steam because I had to play through it again.  This game is just so fun.
I have no hours on record on Steam because I pirated it first to see if it was any good.  I'm reluctant with 8/16-bit games as I've been burned too much in the past.
That said, I got to the "current end" of the game as it is in that copy I got.  I was floored.  This game is amazing.  The combat feels so good and so rewarding.  The story is adorable and it pulls you in rather quickly, I am actually upset it isn't finished.  It takes place in a fictional world called CrossWorlds.  You are an MMO character named Lea and you meet friends along on the way.  There is something different about your character, but none of your "MMO friends" pick up on it.  I almost felt like your fictional friends were real people.  The world feels alive with random NPCs dashing around.
It feels like Diablo and Chrono Trigger had a child and this was the game.  I normally hate A-RPGs, but something about this game just feels so rewarding when you play it.
The only cons I can think of is the quest interface and questing, and the vendors.  To trade pretty much any item, you don't just trade Gold/Credits and receive the item.  You also have to trade components from around the world.  I am not a fan of that.  If I grind the money, I'd like to just buy the item without any additional items needed.  That was frustrating.  And the quest interface leaves a lot to be desired.  A mini-map with directions would be nice, you get pretty overwhelmed with the amount of quests in the early game and trying to clear them all out is a hassle because of the interface it gives you.
Other than those two gripes, if you are on the fence, pick it up so you can also be disappointed when you get to the "end" of the current iteration of the game and just want more more more.  I'll be keeping my eye out for the official release so I binge play it for days on end.

GUN can be basically thought of as Call of Juarez, albeit more shooting and less running around dodging stuff. As Colton, you grew up under a harsh father learning to hunt and live off the land and horses and the rest. Until one day, your father told you he's not your real father, then to save you he threw you off the boat you've been defending as the boiler exploded. Your only clue is a token to the Alhambra Hotel, and Jenny, and a preacher Josiah Reed, who is working for someone... And it may involve Indian gold gathered up by Spaniards...
The game involves shooting... LOTS of shooting. Pistol, rifle, shotgun, even a few whiskey bombs (i.e. molotov cocktails before Comrade Molotov changed it to gasoline) and later, precision rifle plus a bow. As you go through the plot missions, you'll unlock new weapons. And as you go through the game world, you can travel anywhere (between towns if you like) and indeed, some of the "gold deposits" you can mine requires buying a pick in town.
A story mission would be escort the wagon through Apache territory (resulting in a couple checkpoints, including on horseback, static defense, go forward to find dynamite to clear a passage, then railshooter.  Another mission would be clearing the bridge of Apache presence, as they rush the bridge, check for explosives (you have to grab them and chuck them into the river) then escort the Chinese coolies to finish the job as Apaches attack, then finally defeat the Apache warrior leader with quickdraw and shoot fire arrows out of the air then kill the minions and finally leader himself.
Betweens story missions you are encouraged to do the "side missions", which would give you bonus in various areas, such as pistol, rifle, shotgun, horse (speed), quickdraw, and so on if you complete them. The side missions are quite varied, including wanted posters (best if you wound the perp, then grab and knock out), but usually it's dead or alive (alive worth slightly more). Each town has a sheriff who will ask you to do things, basically run around town dealing with various troubles, usually involving shooting, but sometimes melee. There's also pony express where you need to make deliveries on a timer. There may be additional missions in town. Finally, there's usually a shopkeep where you can buy various upgrades, from fastloader for pistols to better knife to pistol upgrade (bore enlargement kit).
There is a lot of terrain between towns, and lot of places to explore, and as mentioned before, there are gold in those hills (and you'll need a pickaxe from a shopkeep to get them). Finding them is part of the fun.
As this game did come out more than 10 years ago, graphics are low-fi but good enough. Music is quite good, very orchetrally western. Voice acting is above average, though somewhat cliched. Gun sounds are adequate.
The main problem is you basically spend your entire game depopulating the West, of one unsavory character after another. The game doesn't reallly have you do anything else (other then grabbing TNT barrels and chucking them, either into the river or put them at places where you do need to blow them up). The only time you really need to think was the wanted, where you TRY to sneak up on the guy but it probably doesn't work.
While the controls can be mapped to gamepad, the game is best play with mouse and keyboard, where the added precision makes gun fights easier for you to pull off headshots or weapon shots (i.e. shoot weapon out of enemy hands). And in this game, you CAN blow enemy's head off. Rare, but it does happen, esp. with shotgun.
Still, the game holds up even after 10 years, and IMHO, at some places, better than even Call of Juarez (the original) which has a very similar premise of sorts (in CoJ, people are also after the gold hidden and the protagonist is chased after by a nasty preacher with gun). If you can get it at bargain bin prices, it's worth a couple hours for sure. Just beware of certain nasty segments, like the quickdraw segments that require a lot of retries. And remember to save. A LOT.

The Good: The game has a decent plot--although there are some pretty major holes. Cole is a likeable protagonist, bordering on an anti-hero. The game also allows you to continue playing after you beat the main questline, in case there were any side missions that you missed before taking down Magruder. While I wouldn't play this game again right away after beating it, it does have some replay value, and the soundtrack is reminiscent of both Firefly and Tombstone.
The Bad: The side missions can get repetitive after a while, and the A.I. isn't great on your allies. They're more likely to walk into a bullet than avoid it, and there are plenty of missions that you'll fail if they die. The game also has an odd habit (particularly during the Magruder fight) of not giving you instructions on a mission until your health is nearly depleted and you can't do much other than die and start over. The Pony Express missions are also kind of pointless--at most, your horse gets more health and you get $5 for essentially running a horse race back and forth across the map. Pretty dumb.
The Ugly: Some of the writing in this game is downright laughable, and most of the side characters are cardboard cutouts. Apart from Cole, there really is no character development. Magruder and his posse are evil because the game needed antagonists--no other reason. Likewise, you as Cole don't particularly gain anything by completing the main quest apart from having the satisfaction of killing all of the bad guys and feeling like the Man With No Name out of an Eastwood western.
All in all, the game is pretty good and definitely worth playing at least once, but the creators could have done a lot more with this to make it even better than it is.

EDIT, I've got it working. I'm keeping it "Not Recommended" for the faint of heart.
What worked:
Set compatibiltiy mode to "Windows XP SP2", run as administrator
Delete LAV Extensions
Reinstall Physx
Launch from the DP application and not the launcher
Using these setting will launch in windowed mode, if you want to run fullscreen create a shortcut of the DP.exe and then in properties type in "-fullscreen" within the target field.

Deadly Premonition is a homage to Twin Peaks, a show that inspired video games like Max Payne, Alan Wake, and Silent Hill. A show that ended too soon, yet the concept found new life in video games. It's how game writer and director Hidetaka Suehiro molded the Lynchian framework into something more akin to his style, while still respecting the inspiration, that made the game shine. This is art, plain and simple. And no word has ever been more fitting for the most polarizing video game of all time.
And there you have it.

So, from a technical perspective, it's a solid game.  Good graphics, tight controls, a lot of varability and customization, fun (if slightly repetitive) combat.  Music is mostly good to great, but has some headache-inducing tracks too.  It's fun and challenging to play through to the end, for the most part.
But the story is completely flat.  Its the story of androids fighting robots for reasons that aren't ever truly defined.  The characters are bland and wooden (or slightly annoying), and it was impossible for me to really understand what they were doing and why they were doing it, at least at the end when the story sort-of reveals itself.
And maybe that was their point?  Something something existentialism?
I don't know, I feel like they were trying to do something profund and meaningful, but in the end wound up being vague and boring.
Or maybe I'm just as dumb as a bag of hammers.
At any rate, it's a fun enough game from a technical perspective, but if you were interested in the promise of a deep, meaningful story, you'd best look elsewhere.  Or else, be prepared to spend a lot of time researching WHY it is a deep and meaningful story.  Which I frankly don't care to.  If they can't be bothered to explain the story and character's motives in-game, I can't be bothered to do research onto the topic.
It's honestly a little hard for me to hit the thumbs up/down, as I'm a bit torn, but as I apparently must choose one, I've got to say no. And the gameplay alone isn't quite good or unique enough to recommend on its own, but it's close.

Loadout is a game that I would recommend in a heartbeat to any and every casual gamer who enjoys a good "Shoot Em' Up" style game as well as anyone who just like good violent fun with their PC experience while gaming in general.
The first thing that attracted me to this game was the customization. Usually that's a big deal in a game for me, because I like to create things or insert myself into a game and take it from there. Though this time was different. I bought two starter packs after a week of playing this game and I only used one to customize my appearance, whereas the other went to me buying weapon slots. The combinations for guns and weapons that you the player can both make and see in matched as a whole on this game is ♥♥♥♥ing crazy. Not to mention the different abilities you can come across as you level up and work your way through the tech tree like disguise for one instance. I encountered that ability in the middle of a match not even knowing it was in the game and I freaked out for a second because of all the explosions.
I'm usually a story-driven gamer, but this game and it's entertainment value crush any need for it to have a story campaign or anything of the like at the front door. The matches are simple and while only a tad bit hard to understand your first time playing through one like Extraction matches, it doesn't take more than he first or second try to get the hang of it. If for some reason they make an episode-like capmaign you can co-op or multiplayer with your friends or just anybody in the lobby with all of the comedic-sociopathy and hilarity of blowing things up...I might have to batten down my hatches and stay in my house for a few months.
Though honestly I can say that there are a few issues that only make the game more challenging. The only thing that comes to mind to mention at the front door is that If you're a gamer who likes the option or relies on going to cover during your shooter...this isn't the game for you. You'll get blown up, burned, zapped, and pumped full of lead. This will happen a lot if you try and use something for cover, sometimes several at once for. Though that's the real fun in it. You can watch your character running one minute and they will KEEP RUNNING after they've had their top half or leg blown off. Literally every death in the game is played comedically and despite some people in the lobby or community catch COD syndrome and raging over the lobby chat about how their team sucks or someone is a hacker when they die I've found that most of the players are casual about it...then again I only do casual play.
All and all, Loadout is a great game for when you just wanna blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and have fun while doing it. The game is only a few months old and already they've got a lot to offer. If and once the year margin comes around I'm a bit anxious to think about all of the expansions they'll make to the world they've already created for us to just go insane in.

The GemCraft series changed my entire perspective on how a true Tower Defense game should be. Playing these games made Kingdom Rush and similar look so boring and dumb that I never even bothered with them.
GemCraft plays differently than other TDs. It starts out painfully easy, but as the game goes on you unlock various ways to make the game harder for yourself, increasing both difficulty and rewards. Endurance mode is the epitome of all this; most "infinite" modes are just that, infinite. GemCraft's ends at 999, and it's no cakewalk.
Here's generally how the game goes, from what I can tell:
- Early-game: Playing maps on easy, playing with difficulty as you unlock it, gaining skills/power
- Mid-game: Finishing up the remaining maps, going back to earlier maps and overloading them with difficulty modifiers to get lots of XP, completing challenge cheevos
- Late-game: Endurance runs
- Post-game: Trying to beat your high score on that max difficulty endurance run
Since GemCraft ends up being quite a different experience, I recommend playing this and its earlier titles online first (but not the first one, it's not as good). You can find them on Armor Games or Kongregate.
Also, Mac or Linux users: just because this game is Windows-only doesn't mean you can't play it! Just run Steam inside of Wine, install the game, and you should be good to go! (Disclaimer: Not all games work that well with Wine. This one just happens to be one of the good ones. Look up your game first to see if others have tested it!)
The best tower defense game you're going to find on Steam.

Gemcraft is by far the best tower defense game/series I've ever played, even better than Bloons, and Chasing Shadows continues that streak. There are a lot of levels to try to beat your previous score (sometimes by several million points), and in the addiction of leveling up your skills you can easily clock over 100 hours into the game - and you don't even have to be paying attentions! You can just run the game in the background or a small window while you do something else and check back every so often. That's how I reached 175 hours, and I could keep going.
The one bad thing about the game is that during endurance runs, which can go for quite a long time, the game starts slowing down to unbearable levels. I think I've read that this is because the game if Flash-based, and Flash can't handle large loads of objects. Hopefully, the developers will port the next game in the series to Steam in something other than Flash, or whatever causes the obnoxious slow down. This would easily cut the length of endurance runs by half.

The Legend of Zelda is without any shred of doubt one of the most important and influential games ever made. Nintendo’s landmark release has inspired hundreds of games and mechanics within them, and you can't take two steps without hearing a developer site it as one of their biggest inspirations when developing their own games. Indie game Anodyne is one such example of a very close replication of LoZ's core gameplay, which isn't necessarily a bad thing in and of itself, but unfortunately fails to bring anything new to a very crowded table that results in but another poor attempt to recapture the magic of a classic.
You take control of Young, a man who wakes up in an unknown realm called the Nexus. You are told that you must protect Briar from the darkness, but first must prove your worth by scouring the land for cards. And, that’s pretty much all you need to know. The story unravels in a nonlinear way, leaving much for you to deduce for yourself and numerous questions without straight answers. Unfortunately this initial air of mystery falls apart after you've progressed further into the game and come to realize the developers have no intention of ever answering or even elaborating on the many threads making up its haphazard plot.
You run into a lot of characters during your travels, but none of them have anything relevant or useful to say. One of my biggest issues I had is that the dialog aspires to far more lofty and philosophical heights than it has any hope of reaching, ending up feeling pointless and pretentious, while at the same time completely throwing off the tone of the game. A lot of heavy subjects are brought up, from antisocial paranoia, to self worth and parental neglect, but they are never expanded upon or even discussed beyond a cursory overview (which comes across as forced and in poor taste).
It’s clear this was a very personal experience for the writer behind the dialog, but putting all of your problems and insecurities into your game is a sure fire way to lose your audience. Adding to the disjointed tone is a bundle of worthless profanity that was unneeded and serves absolutely no purpose. I'm not sure why the developer felt the need to include random four letter words, as it doesn’t jell at all with the rest of the game, and even as someone not typically bothered by profanity felt a tad disgusted when presented with it in this context. The ending is the final nail in the coffin, coming completely out of left field and not giving even a remote sense of resolution. I will be the first person to advocate artistic expression, but the story fails on so many levels it had me wishing it hadn’t been included at all.
From a gameplay perspective Anodyne fairs a bit better, but on the whole still fails to do enough with what it attempts. You spend your time split between exploring an overworld, collecting cards and filling out your map, and then dipping into dungeons which comprise some basic puzzles and the occasional boss fight.
It's a formula that works, but in this case quickly becomes repetitive as you neither gain any new abilities, nor encounter consistently interesting puzzles to solve. So much of the game is comprised of nothing but wandering, that many areas feel like nothing but filler, featuring no purpose but to elongate your adventure and keep you away from the handful of smartly designed dungeons that could have made for a much tighter experience on their own.
The extensive backtracking also contributes to much of your time feeling like a grind, occasionally even breaking the game as paths close and you become forced to retread even more ground taking the long way to wherever you were headed. Simply put, it's poor design that frustrates and belittles the player, dragging the experience on longer than it needed to be and making the enjoyable sections a lot farther apart. It's a shame because at times I really felt Anodyne was onto something, but each time my hopes were shot down as I cursed the many aggravating design decisions the developers made.

Truth be told, there were moments when I actually did enjoy my time with the game. The true problem is, to reiterate, the fact that Anodyne does absolutely nothing we haven’t already seen and not well enough to compensate for its lack of innovation. It has it’s moments, but by and large feels all too familiar, and ultimately had me wondering why I was playing it instead of so many other games. I never felt compelled to continue, and I doubt it will be finished by most.
If Anodyne does anything right, it’s the game’s music and art. The graphics wholly envelope the 16-bit era, with a wonderful pixel style that is both beautiful and varied. Each dungeon has it’s own look, from a noir inspired town, to a neon maze it is constantly evolving and giving you something new to look at. It may not all flow together, but it was the one thing that made me want to search out new dungeons.
The other half of the presentation is the music, which does a great job of selling the somber, lonely tone of the story, even when the dialog can’t. From gentle piano melodies, to a pounding jungle beat, it is just a great set of songs, and some I could actually see myself listening to outside the game. They are that good, and easily the best part of the game.
In the end though Anodyne left me wanting. Wanting for better levels, a better story, a better ending, but mostly, a better game. When I first began, I had little idea what to expect and was actually enjoying myself more than I would have expected. But as time went on, the gameplay never evolved, and the story only strayed farther and farther off course making me want to jump ship before it had completely sunk (which by the end it had definitely done.
By the time the credits had rolled, I was all too happy to be able to wash myself of the experience. I don't say that lightly, and hate to have to be so critical, but I simply cannot advise anyone to play what was one of the most disappointing games I've experienced in a long time.

The base game was incredible when it first came out in 2011 and when the special edition arrived, it arrived upgraded with new graphical features, new immersive features and a new, more stable engine.
The base game was incredible for new players to the series. I for one pre-ordered and played for two weeks straight back in that cold november of 2011. It introduced the lore filled world to young impressionable people like myself. Filled with little side stories, books and history. Little stories that I still encounter to this day that I missed over and over again with every playthrough. But sadly the small aspects are overshadowed by the basic main storylines.
The Civil War questline is basic at best and can be completed fairly quickly. The same goes for the Dragonborn questline. The guild questlines leave you feeling like you earned nothing but a new outfit or a weapon. Becoming the leader of a guild should leave you with more todo, not less.
Combat is clunky and basic. It's Hack 'n' Slash at best.
Now what stands out about this game is the player base behind it. The modders more specifically. All the problems listed above can be fixed with one of the 70,000 mods that are available to download (for free) and install straight away.
With each little mod you can customise your game to work in the way you want it.
• Want to expand on everything within the game like 155 more spells or more shouts?
• Think the skill system is too basic?
• Hate how the animals react to you or want them to actually drink water and breed?
Bethesda may be ruining the original model they provided us with the Creation Club, but they provided players and content creators with fantasy sandbox to make their own and that's worth something.

Deadly Premonition is a game you need to play,
For Director's Cut on PC, though, you should not pay.
So says Mr. Stewart.
Deadly Premonition is one of my absolute favorite games. The Director's Cut, however, and especially the PC version are something to avoid.
Deadly Premonition was a flawed, but amazing game full of charming personality with every of it's lots of characters. What it needed is some additional polish, some rebalancing, some QTE removal. Ideally an engine port to make the world feel even more complete by removing the loading screens or at least making them less frequent. It needed something that will make the original strange beauty preserved for generations to come.
Instead it got The Director's Cut. A version that is worse in pretty much every regard. With slightly better visuals in some parts, worse in all others. With all the game breaking and lighter glitches, typos, mistranslations and other issues intact. With next to no changes to actual issues. With one non-issue made better (the controls). With pointless DLCs. With horribly voiced and animated new cutscenes that break the flow of the story, spoil things and add nothing of value. And, especially on PC, with countless crashes. Crashes that you cannot avoid no matter what you do, just make them slightly less frequent.
If you can, find the original for 360, play that instead. If you absolutely must play Director's Cut, do it on consoles. But this version? This version is the one to avoid at all cost. It will ruin the game for you. And the game is very much worth it.
