Loving the game thus far. If you’re on the fence for this game but have a strong fondness for Action games and/or JRPS with great, unique stories, I’d say the game is worth it during the current sale. However, just know that this is a (still) an unoptimized PC port before you buy it. If you’re like me and have AMD, here are my recommendations:
1) If you encounter the white screen of the death, click here. This fixed the issue for me. Essentially, I was running on the most recent AMD driver, but the game files (as the time of this writing) was not able to recognize the latest version of my driver. Basically, I had to download an older AMD driver for the game to recognize my graphics card.
2) To optimize performance and stabilize fps, download the FAR mod (which is a google search away). Hopefully this will help improve performance, as this mod did for me.
For reference, here are my specs:
Intel Core i5 6500
AMD R9 380 4GB
8 GB of RAM
If you have specs similar or greater than mine, I think you’re in good shape to have 1080p 60 fps for the most part (but I’m still a PC newbie, so sorry I mess anything up :/ ).
For the review bit:
It takes some patience to get the port running decently, but once you do, the game really takes you on a ride, at least based on the 8-9 hours I played so far. Highlights include:
-	Fluid combat system, but takes a while to get used to
-       God-tier soundtrack, and might be the best of 2017 so far
-	Fantastic art direction and character design
-	LOADS of side quests and content to discover
-	Fishing (?)
-	Great story and unique premise
-	Interesting mix of Platinum Games combat and some Dark Souls aspects sprinkled in here and there (makes more sense once you play it)
-	2Booty
Obviously, as with all other games, Nier: Automata may not be for everyone. But like I said, if you fancy Action games and/or JRPS with great, unique stories, you can’t go wrong for this game.
Note to Square-Enix: try not to rush your PC ports next time. I noticed that Nier wasn’t your only game to encounter some major PC drawbacks, especially in the cases of Just Cause 3 and Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. It’s clear that your company publishes good games, but major performance issues and the following negative word of mouth has alienated some eager consumers from purchasing more of your products, me included. Just a pro-tip

Borderlands: the Pre-Sequel – many people compare it to Borderlands 2. Here's how I see it:
In terms of the base game, Borderlands 2 was terrific and hilarious all the way, and introduced us to our favorite "villain", Handsome Jack, as well as a slew of other lovable lunatics. The Pre-Sequel builds upon this established world and its inhabitants, and gives you even more toys to play with, including lasers, ground-pounds, and a new elemental – freeze. As such, I recommend playing Borderlands 2 first, and follow it up with the Pre-Sequel if you like it, which hopefully you'll enjoy even more.
Now, if we also count the DLCs, BL:PS is much, MUCH shorter, but I wouldn't say it's lacking. The length of the campaign feels just right, and it's as hilarious and action-packed as Jim Carrey playing a unicorn with explosive rainbow diarrhea. In addition, the few DLCs that it has are all terrific (everything except the Holodome of♥♥♥♥♥♥. The 2 characters – Handsome Jack's Body Double and Hammerlock's Ex (I think?) – both bring fun and fresh dynamics to the game, and Claptrap's Totally-Not-Inception not only introduces dozens of new creatures to fight, but also a brand-new game mechanic: glitched guns, which is oh-so-exciting when you get some of the most OP combinations. DO buy the Season Pass if you want to play The Pre-Sequel. It's still totally worth it, even if the Holodome isn't.
Bottom line: if you're the type of gamer that likes grinding and meticulously training your character to become as good as it can possibly be, you'll love Borderlands 2 more. On the other hand, if you just want a fun time hanging out with stupidly funny characters wielding ridiculous powers, you might, like me, enjoy the Pre-Sequel more. Neither game is superior, and to each their own.
With all that said, just buy both games. They're both super ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.

This game has almost everything going for it.. great graphics, good story, good voice acting, and even though it's meant for controller, the gameplay is still palatable via the keyboard/mouse control scheme.  Despite this you need to be aware that it is an unforgiving "START OVER IF YOU DIE" based game.  What makes this worse, is you have to find out how to save, sometime later, after a major boss battle.  No auto-checkpoints here.
If you are one of the mega-god gamers that never die in a game, great, this review isn't for you--move along.  To those others who do not find the no save/no checkpoint type of game easy... Is it worth it to persevere, get better and get to the end?  Yes.  However, the beginning experience of the game may also make you want to get a refund (many in the community forums have indicated they've done so).
Next, getting out of the game (or rather back to the main menu) can't be done during combat segments in the early part of the game where you don't have a menu.  So if you're still stuck in the repeat ad nauseum hell of a beginning, don't try letting yourself die--you'll have too much auto-heal power, that will take you to the end of the opening segment, so best just ALT-F4.
While someone may have thought that "saving" could be part of the story, that person was a moron.  If you consider the "auto-healing" mechanic they've added, and that we're dealing with bots, I'd expect the standard checkpoint system in most of these console conversion games to be more on par with the story than a manual save.  This design is an obvious time-gating mechanism to allow them to increase the average playthrough time against a short story.  Mr. Developer, I see through the thinly veiled attempt, and am not amused.
Finally, there are some wierd glitches, and strange camera behavior during boss battles.  It's very easy to become trapped, and not really know all the details of your situation ("where am I?" -- "your grave"), and sometimes that situation means you're simply in a position where you can't move, and die after you run out of auto-heals.
In any case, be forewarned, that if your skill level isn't high-enough, you hate practicing, or you don't like (or aren't good at) non-checkpoint/"save when they let you" games, this might not be the game for you.  Despite this, the game IS fun, looks good, and plays very well, which is why I will still mark it recommeded--but get it on sale, it's not worth full retail.

Your quest in Anodyne is to save the Land from the darkness that has come over it in the form of The Briar.
Throughout the game you face many bosses who seem to know deep truths about who you really are. They hint at the fact that you play video games to escape from reality, and that one day you will have to learn how to deal with people.
The collecting aspect of the game is very engaging. You must collect cards and keys in order to unlock new areas.
Anodyne offers a beautifully realized SNES-like game world. It has a intriguing story and there are some really great songs that capture the mood of the game quite well.
Anodyne is a good designed old school adventure game and a perfect choice for those who liked the old Zelda games.

I know George RR Martin can tend to be a bit flowery in his dialogue, but this game has you going "Who the hell has ever talked like that ever" too many times.
After enduring the first few cutscenes I was already on the verge of quitting (seriously it felt like the writers were trying really really hard to remind us this was a Game of Thrones game, shoving completely awkward, unnecessary references to lore). But when I actually tried the combat and gameplay I knew this game was unsalvagable trash. I felt like I've seen that same skills tree in a dozen other games, the camera itself is probably an enemy character given how much it hindered you, and "combat" conists of queing up three actions repeatedly.
To be fair, here are some good points I can think of: The graphics are decent, and the two main characters are very different and play that way as well. The story is worth playing if you can bear bad lines and acting (I couldn't). Music is good, it's basically the show's.
Overall: Poor gameplay and camera, some very bad voice acting and dialogue obscuring a great story. Definitely not worth more than 5$, this is a game where its better to just watch someone else play

Finished Game of Thrones last Thursday. Even though the game has a decent story it bursts and get shattered on the shortcomings of the graphics engine.
You play two characters: Mors, "the butcher", Westford, a loyal warrior of the Night's Watch and Alester Sedwick struggling to regain his heritage as Lord of Riverspring after been away for 15 years.
The story is really great and contains all the ingredients the famous Game of Thrones series features: honor, love, fights, betrayal, debauchery, violence, mystic and magic, deception, heroism, and cruelty. It's all in there. This is a true Game of Thrones story.
Also if you watched the TV series you'll recognize some characters: Cersei Lannister plays the plotting ♥♥♥♥♥ and you simply can't get behind Lord Varys motives and schemes. As a goodie: you have a Cameo-appereance of Mr. "Game-of-Thrones" himself: George R. R. Martin is the Maester of Bergholz. Running a little Q&A with him is quite hilarious.
Ok, there are some irrational items in there: e.g. it takes you 3 months game time to travel from Castle Black at the Wall down to the Riverlands, but after chapter 8 you are free to simply click anywhere on the map and are there within a blink of an eye.
Or: at some point Alester murmurs to himself: "pillagers will be executed" during a riot ... which does not keep you away to grab and loot anything which is not nailed down. =)
But then there is the story. And what a story it is! I can remember the events in chapter 11 leaving me with my jaws wide open: WTF! The game overdoes this theme and attitude of the core Game of Thrones nature in the end like in the final events in chapter 14, but all-in-all it is a great story to experience. Westeros is here.
This is the very strong part of this game.
Then the combat techniques is quite interesting and has some charm: like in a Dragon Age 2 manner you slow down time - it actually never stops - and issue some actions. This interface is not that easy to get your hold on but after some encounters you'll learn this new experience. And it
fun. As time does not stop you feel pressure to get to your decisions rather fast. I finished the game on normal level and every now and then I lost some combats and this is a real good experience. Be demanding so that success is sweeter.
This is the interesting part of the game.
... and then there is the game engine. They say it does not take a good graphics for a great game to tell thrilling and fascinating story. True. But the engine should at least bare some minimums. This game is an example to stress this principle.
As the audio and speakers are ranging from ok (average peasant) to excellent (Lord Varys) the Graphics are weak. All in all the textures are squishy, some motions clumsy. You find a lot of people sharing the very same faces and if I don't know it better I would say I've been witness to the impossibility of the
Seriously, you have to be very capable of suffering and be very high pain tolerant accepting this. Walking around the great hall in Castle Black is ... well ... demanding. Even though some places are nicely rendered like the Gift at the Wall.
If the developers had more time to improve the graphics engine this game would have been rated much higher in the critic's world.
This is the very poor, ugly part of the game.
For the record, I needed about 36 hours at normal difficulty level and finished the story with Mors taking care of the baby outside of Westeros.
I award this game 3 out of 5 stars, thanks to the pretty cool Game of Thrones story line ... nearly ruined by the half-baked graphics textures and graphics engine. It could have been better. Much better.

I thoroughly enjoyed GUN when it was released and I replayed it endlessly; it was so successful where Red Dead Revolver fell short - playing both of them back-to-back was very fulfilling.
Despite this, for the so-so quality of the port (which I'm beginning to think is inevitable when porting old games,  Shame), $20 is STILL too high.
If I was given the opportunity to buy a console version for $20, that would be a steal! Seeing as how, on PC, if you ride too fast through the relatively small world all hints of scenery, except for static objects, are prone to disappear, leaving you riding in the sky (but not for too long) – $10 would be more than fair, if you had an inkling of replaying this game. The more I've played it, though, the less often I've found such glitches.
Remember, circa 2005, much less was expected from games. There is a respectable amount of diversions; I'm 6 hours deep and about 60% through - just sayin', don't expect an older ReDead Redemption. This is not that. If anything, it's ReDead Revolver with PERHAPS less refined combat but much more freedom and Native Americans instead of Mexicans, Animals instead of Carnies.
Aye, when I recently replayed both Red Dead's, I kept finding myself thinking "When is [major incident from the story] going to happen?!" Every time I was anticipating such an event, it was always one that took place in GUN. So it seems, at least to me, GUN beat out ReDead in being epic... indeed, sometimes, while riding aimlessly around, the music can become TOO epic.
As evident from the publishers, I really do stand by my saying that GUN is Tony Hawk with guns, regarding the sense of the controls/feel of it. Mind, I am playing with a controller - IT DOES HAVE CONTROLLER SUPPORT, YOU JUST HAVE TO MAP THE BUTTONS YOURSELF - when I first started the game, if you take a few steps and then stop abruptly, Cole continues sliding ever so slightly. LOL it's as if a remnant of the engine that defined the skateboarding. The longer you play, the less you'll notice it. Also: Never ride your horse with gun drawn unless you are in combat; having your weapon holstered, your horse can maneuver just as well as anything with wheels. I exaggerate only slightly when I say you can drift around corners on horseback.
The gunplay is acceptable but nothing fantastic and you can't take too many bullets, even on Normal. For every few bullets, you'll have to take a shot - of Whiskey, oh yeah. Often, especially when horses are involved, it can be aggravating to try and line up your shots. Sometimes, it comes down to: drive your horse in circles, drive your horse in parallel lines, get off your horse. There is hardly ever that appropriate speed at which horse-to-horse combat can be fluidly achieved. The speed of things was something to be reckoned with in all games back then; remember how ANY time you had an escort mission or had to follow a story-dictating character while they walked and talked – if you moved at full speed, you’d leave them behind; if you walked, they’d leave you behind. So it comes down to Start.Stop.Start.Stop.Arggggh.
…anyway, I don't know if I'm just lucky in doing this/lacking in skill for having to do this, but a tried and true method for me, that I've employed in several games when I can’t figure with the camera(/)speed: swing the camera haphazardly to aim, shoot, pray... watch it be a headshot... er, watch your enemy's head explode. Yes, there's chunky gore to be seen in GUN.
Pistols, Shotguns, Rifles, Bows, Dynamite, Whiskey Bombs, Knives, Hatchets... 30(?) weapons in all. There are Stats that get upgraded when you complete missions, to help you in the progression of the story; it's a tale of revenge steeped in a revolutionary atmosphere - your actions throughout the Story make you more and more enemies, you'll be ambushed constantly by parties of 2 or 3 Bandits; sometimes the towns will be (")off-limits(") as the residents will seek your life.
A typical half hour in-game could be something like:
Shoot bandits off their horses (again, because of the iffy/sluggish camera controls (ON CONTROLLER), I usually will get off my horse and run around whenever enemies ride in on the beasts, it's much easier – just don’t get trampled) and then scope the scene for gold veins to mine, go back to your incapacitated enemies and scalp them, go to town and play Texas Hold 'Em, pick up a Pony Express mission that takes you to the Ranch in-between the two towns (Empire, New Mexico and Dodge City, Kansas), go check the store in the other town (while avoiding/destroying the Bandits/Indians/Haters-in-general), pick up a Deputy mission, dispatch with criminals, then go to the wilderness and find the Native American shopkeep and Hunter, all the while using your Quickdraw (GUN's Dead Eye) to kill birds and other wildlife.
You cannot aim down sights with your pistols; not really sure why but that’s that. You can aim in the first-person with two-handed weapons, poppin’ dudes with your rifle, rippin’ ‘em in half with your shotty, or huntin’ the murderous Great Animals with your bow (really cool, really annoying). It has been stated elsewhere that, at least for controller, ADS is a toggle – if you continue holding the aim button and try to shoot, it’s a no-go.
The Cast Includes:
Whistler from Blade as your father, Ned.
Hellboy as the criminal Mayor Brown.
The Punisher as Cole, the hero.
Keeping in mind that this is an old game, ergo perhaps lacking in content by today’s expectations:
$5 = WIN. $10 = DEAL. $20 = LOL.
Addendum: Playing on Normal, I've quickly found any sort of challenge to be nonexistent. I still stand by my recommendation, seeing as how, no doubt, only fans of Western Shooters or those of the game when it was originally released would seek this game out.
For those who have not played it, it's (EITHER "is" or "was," sorry I can't commit to one or the other) a good game. I just have to stress once again that, despite being a technically open world, there's nothing but hand-holding; there's little in the way of difficulty; there's fun to be found, should you acquiesce to its age.

When I first purchased Stellaris I was amazed. It was like everything I wanted in a 4x space game, but after you play for a while, the critical flaws quickly become apparent. This game is wonderful on the outside and a rotten, hollow corpse on the inside. Consider this, 1 YEAR after release and there is still yet no way to mass-build fleets. Oh, you have a 800 fleet cap? Guess what you get to individually click to build every single one. Why in the world isn't there an option to have fleet templates? It's god-awful and makes the game tedious for me. There is a great many other reasons for my dislike of this game and i'll list a few of them below.
Positives:
+A lot of different types of government
+Terraforming
+Different weapons for your ships
+Hive mind species
+genetic alteration
+slaves
Negatives:
-No quality of life updates a year after release
-combat hollow
-diplomacy hollow
-warfare with other empires is a chore
-feels very unfinished
And many more. I honestly doubt any of these problems will be fixed. Stuff like the templates might be, but a few other reviewers share my thoughts that some of the major problems in this game might be rooted too deep in the core of this game to be fixed at all. Plus, this being a paradox game you'll more than likely be paying for any fixes to this game anyway. Don't buy this game at this point. It is not worth $40 USD at all.

As much as I love Stellaris for the ability to be whatever kind of space empire I like, and do recommend the game overall, it truly does need some deeper expansions to flesh out the game.

I've been supporting CrossCode since around 0.1.5, and it's one of the few games I can completely recommend to anyone.
I could fairly easily make a long, extended review on why CrossCode is amazing, but the best way to show why Crosscode is such a gem, why it is so beloved by many is to think about this question:
What if Link to the Past had full JRPG mechanics?
Lttp is a game about exploation. It has mechanics that refuse to allow the player to get any extremely powerful skills to blaze through enemies and has expert design so every screen you walk to has a different feel to it.
CrossCode creates a world just as alive an expert and turns it on is head. It focuses heavily on ranged combat and timing your dashes to maximize damage output against every enemy, and gives it traditional RPG mechanics around that exciting core to make it feel like a fresh experience. \
It feels like what Zelda would be if it was a traditional RPG; that is, not traditional at all, and absolutely amazing.
very fun to play alone and even more fun to play co-op. I highly recommend to people who enjoy b film noir type actions.

One of the best story directions in a video game! Story and character development is amazing here.
To get the full experience you need to finish the main endings A,B,C and D. Transition from A->B can become
a bit boring at first but the outcome is an amazing story and world that you get to appreciate even more.
Then on C and D the game becomes a masterpiece!
The game structure and deeper meanings seem to be based on philosophical concepts like Nietzsche's perspectivism and this is a very rare find in a video game. I was blown away!
The combat system is fast and fluid. Fixed camera placement in certain parts of the game just transform it to a different game. 3D space melee combat transforms (free camera movement) to a 2d platformer and then from bird's eye view to a roller coaster shooter and then back again. Crazy amounts of actions and a very intuitive upgrade system for your characters/androids with the use of chips and memory banks.
It is a game that questions reality itself even its own existence. I have not seen a game that prompts the player to delete its own saves at the end! If you are a person that wants to dig deep into a game's story and the concepts of the messages it broadcasts this is a game for you! I want to read Nietzsche now!

I would love to recommend this game, because for what it is its a wonderful experience - however I have to address the single reason its not currently a good investment:
The game is dying.
As it stands right now (before Alliance is officially released) PvP is the only gamemode. And there are hardly any players left outside of peak gametimes. Even at peak gametimes, its not really that great - mainly 4 semifull lobbies.
Its bad. And Muse does little to help address fundemental matchmaking problems. Guns of Icarus is a PvP game (right now), but in matchmaking lobbies all players can see the weapon layout of enemy ships. Which makes literally no sense, because it turns lobbies into drawn out countering matches and forces a handful of meta-ships to counter specific meta-ships. Lobbies are "balanced", but ship crews are often composed of full-clan ships with crews that have hundreds of games under their belts. The other ships are often newer players trying to dip their toes in the game.
And wouldn't you guess who gets gunned out of the sky?
Look I understand its how the game works. Its not really anyones fault, thats just how it is. But the simple facts are as follows:
1. Many new players stick it out for a few games and then quit and play other things.
2. The pool of existing players is shrinking, as vets leave for other games.
3. The game is requires a substantial playerbase to continue to be enjoyable.
I'll let you figure it out from there. I sincerely hope to see some of you in the skies.... but I'm not misleading anyone into wasting their money. I enjoyed the game, but when 90% of my so called gametime is me alt-tabbed out and waiting for matches to start I can't recommend this in good conscience.
--- Edited below for those who are still interested ( As of November 11th, 2016 )  ---
Its now only a short time before Alliance is released, and I've been asked by several people if I would be willing to give the game a follow up try.
I did. And I would recommend the game even less now.
The userbase that plays this game has decayed to a somewhat horrifying point - people play, but there are serious issues with the game that have become painfully highlighted due to lack of players.
For one, all the same issues persist in PvP, which is still the games primary gamemode. All players can still currently see the layouts of enemy ships, which forces a horrible counter meta into the game and saps the ability for captains to comfortably diversify loadouts.
Clan ships still dominate the lobbies, although this has been lessened by the fact that so many people have simply quit the game - logically leading to less clan players. Still, the norm is to see one or more highly veteran ship crews sitting in a lobby and chewing through all comers. Etc.
The real issue is with the upcoming DLC, and the worry that once the DLC comes out, Co-op vs. AI matches will sap even more players from the already struggling PvP modes. Theres also the underlying issue that aside from the addition of a few maps and decals, not much has been added to the game in quite some time - and PvP is planned to remain the same.
Don't get me wrong, flying an airship is fun... but not everyone gets to fly, do they? Those of us who typically crew the ship (gunners and engineers) are usually stationed on meta ships (because of the bloody see-all lobbies), in relatively familiar combat scenarios, for the majority of our games. Tedium (tedious) is the word I feel best describes PvP as it stands now.
Guns of Icarus is more than worth the asking price for the game. No question, its a great value buy. Personally I've gotten more than enough hours out of the game to merit the money I put down for it.
I just wouldn't recommend it. There are other games that I feel would have been better uses of my time.

Man, I wish that I could simultaneously 'Thumbs up'
'Thumbs down' this game. As it is I can't recommend this game but I can't recommend it
either.
The game is
developed on the PC. It basically won't run without using
and even then, with the latest version of that, it has issues like HDR style bloom occasionally flickering and blowing out the screen, an aimbox that doesn't let you aim outside of a
fraction of the screen, a screeching sound loop when you're in a car and crashes ever 25 minutes on the dot. Still, it's a really,
great story with really solid gameplay. On the one hand, if you have a 360 or PS3 then just pick it up used for one of those systems but, as of the time of this writing, it's on sale on Steam for $2.99 with the soundtrack and the OST
is worth that money (listening to it right now). The game's not unplayably broken (with dpfix and compatibility mode for XP SP3/98 set) but it does have enough issues to make it a conditional recommendation even on sale.
Gameplay wise it's an open-world game set in a small town that feels realish. There are two major "centers" to the town (downtown and a smaller business/residential area) and a bunch of places off in various parts of the countryside all connected with roads that feel planned rather than designed for sandboxing/gameplay. In many ways Greenvale feels more like a town than any other open-world location that I've played because of that.
A day-night cycle is present, as you'd expect, but unlike most open-world games it's not just a perfunctory addition that has no gameplay impact. Rather, NPCs have a routine and are available at certain places at certain times and not at all at others. This impacts when you can start sidequests and when missions can be taken. On top of that NPCs actually drive around Greenvale to get to their various locations. The first time I saw this in action I was standing outside a particular main character's house waiting to be able to start a side mission and I saw her drive up, get out of her car, walk into the house via the garage door (and then the mission still wasn't available so I "peeked" inside the window and she was in there puttering around).
The story is one of the best told murder mysteries that I've played through. It's got elements of cosmic horror as well as "good" old-fashioned depravity. As you progress through the missions you're going to be picking up clues that allow you to "Profile" what occurred (basically a cutscene that starts out unclear but clears up as you gather clues) that will eventually lead you to the killer and uncover what the craziness that goes on in the dark, dark hours of the night is all about.
The shooty gameplay isn't particularly good but, thankfully, it's also not particularly necessary. A standard wrench (that you can get with infinite durability from an early sidequest) will do you well for most of the enemies through most of the game. Shooty wise it harkens back to the Resident Evil style aim and stand mechanics but you'll only hit an enemy if your sight actually crosses them and turns into a reticle. It's not great but it gets the job done and, aside from the three bosses in the late game, it's not really required. Just make sure you do the quests to get a .34 with unlimited ammo before you get to them.
All in all the game is flawed, critically so on the PC, but it's still such a satisfying game with an
story and a soundtrack that is silly, cheerful, haunting, beautiful and sad all at the same time. Definitely give it a shot in some fashion. Whether that be on one of the last-gen consoles, a PC with dealing with the issues that crop up or even

A great game in a bad port.
The bad port comes in the form of horrible graphics settings and crashes. Fortunately I was able to find workarounds for these issues making the game less of a “bad” port, and more of a “decent” port. The first thing you will want to do is download the DPfix mod which will clean up some of the graphics for you. This does not solve the issue with crashing however. My experience with crashing was that the game would always crash at specific parts of the game, usually at the start of a cut scene. By this, I mean that the crashes were not random. The game would crash, I would reload the game, and it would crash at the exact same spot again. I found a workaround, which involved running the game in compatibility mode until you pass the part that crashes then disable compatibility mode after you save past the crash. By doing this I was able to enjoy the game and complete it with only a few technical issues.
Now for the game itself. The game in my opinion has a great story and cast. The characters have developed back stories, and the game keeps you guessing as to who is guilty of murder. The main character is particularly interesting in his mannerism. All in all, this is a case of a great game that didn’t have enough money for that extra polish.
I would recommend this game to anyone who’s looking for a good 3D adventure game with an interesting cast and story.

This game is one of the worst I've ever played, and I love every single second of it.  From the begining, it is clear that a lot of love went into it, if only that love and care were equaled by skill and budget.   The port is perhaps one of the worst ever made, lacking any graphical options whatsoever and being unplayable without a controller, to get any kind of control at all you need to install a fanmade patch or two.  This isn't even getting into  the myriad of glitches, poor audio mixing, and graphics that would make a dreamcast look down in shame, but there is way more too this game than all the technical problems.
You see, here is where the love comes in.   From the begining, every character in the game is memorable, each has there own personality, traits, and even a unique schedule.  The plot is fantastic and engaging, and at times even heartfelt and moving.  It has a fantastic sense of offbeat humour that will remind enlightened players of Twin Peaks.  Actually, the entire game will remind people of Twin Peaks, because from the setting to the characters to the music this game is a love letter to all things David Lynch.  It should be no surprise that its flaws are just part of the charm, and together they make the game seem more complete for it.
Seriously, buy this game if you haven't already, you won't regret it.

This is THE tower defense game that all other tower defense games want to be when they grow up.
You could spend 30 minutes here and there and have a great time, or you could devote hours upon hours to trying to perfect your strategies for each map. So many different combinations of abilities, powerups, and effects make each scenario have multiple paths to completion. Plenty of different maps with tons of options for scaling the difficulty up or down in different ways make for high levels of replayability.

GemCraft - Chasing Shadows is one of the many web-based TD game "GemCraft." But before you turn this down as 'another web game that is a waste of money to get on steam,' the game has, in my opinion, the best mechanics any TD game could ever have. The 'Gems' are more customizable than any other game I've ever played. The game itself can get repetitive but there are special levels that will change your game plan every now and again. Recommended.

I've been playing the freeware games in this series for years so I'm glad to pay for a game that stays true to its predecessors.  The same GemCraft tower defense combat gameplay is present with many welcome refinements.
Beyond the tower defense game, the player is given quite a number of ways to upgrade their power with a lot of options to choose from, though options need to be earned.
The game will always present a challenge for you to overcome with the ability to give yourself larger challenges along the way.  Each scenario also allows for an endless mode after the objective level is reached, though it seems as though the game wants you to power up significantly before you get serious about trying them.
If you like 'tough but fair' tower defense this is a pretty good buy.

I am tempted to call this the ultimate TD game. It's a TD game that everyone looking for a new TD game should pick up and try. It has numerous levels. It has interesting upgrades. It has a good amount of grind that is made interesting by a variety of valid strategies. It has interesting and unique concepts.
But there is one thing that really sets it apart from other TD games: there is a highly mathematical late game that has spawned a community of math heads searching for the perfect gem. At a certain point the game isn't any longer about beating the levels. Instead it is about coming as far as possible in an endurance run, using the most cost efficient gems and deploying your strategy in a way that minimizes lag while stile allowing you to farm the enemies with mana gems (=gaining currency). Suddenly everything happens in orders of magnitude.
The lag is the only downside really. It is a flash game originally, and at some point you start sending continuous waves of enemies with increased speed. This kills the fps. So playing an late-game endurance run is kind of a nerd thing. It can easily take 5-10 hours and it requires maintenance.
But it's a great TD even without these endurance runs.

Anodyne borrows heavily from early Legend of Zelda, but manages to stand on its own just fine.
A lot of familiar mechanics are present here: pressing buttons, running through mazes, solving light puzzles, and jumping across holes. However instead of a large repertoire of gadgets and items, Anodyne sticks with one main weapon and a very small amount of items. The mechanics, from boss fighting to exploring, are largely focused around platforming. Jumping at the right time and angle will be essential at certain points of the game. Given the game's rather brief life, it is understanble that gadgets and mechanics are kept fairly contained.
Layered on top of the game is a bizarre narrative. There is certainly some failed humor every now and then, but you will also receive eerie messages, cryptic details, and what seems like nonsense. Also included among the dialog and regular text are the cards hidden throughout the game that act as indirective narrative. It is certainly an intriguing aspect, but don't expect to be rewarded with sure answers.
Anodyne is not without its flaws though. The mix of humor, nonsensical dialogue and strange text will definitely turn away some players. The art style might scream Legend of Zelda, but this adventure has been pared down quite a bit and this is most noticeable through the lack progression and gadgets. For those of you that like secrets there are some pretty extensive ones here, but if you are wanting everything up front, a large portion of the game is kept hidden away.
With a charming aesthetic and surreal narrative, Anodyne is a neat hidden gem. Those that like some mystery and an adventure that's smaller in scope compared to Link's adevntures will get the most out of this one.

Anodyne is a delightful, surreal, pixel-art masterpiece. Total gameplay time for the main storyline is a bit short (6 hours at  the most) but there are a lot of end-game secrets. Challenge level is minimal, but the environments are spectacular. Unfortunately the various levels do not tie together especially well, so it will probably take a bit of digging on your part to make sense of the world of Anodyne and how its levels relate to one another thematically. Still, it's a solid game for fans of Zelda:LTTP, surrealism, or gamers who love the 'indie' vibe.

Pro:

Cons:
From the technical aspect the game is far from up to date. Also the intput and GUI is "consolish" and needs some time. Over all I would NOT recommend the game for somebody who looks for a RPG without interest or knowlege about "The game of thrones " series/books.

Game of Thrones
Concept:
An RPG taking place in George R.R. Martin’s rich fantasy world. The story takes place just before
the events that happen in the First Book and HBO’s T.V. Show Season 1.
Graphics: ★★★☆☆
The graphics are pretty good as are the recreations of the scenes from the T.V. show. The games camera or FOV are too close and feel very cramped and claustrophobic however with a few simple tweaks the game improves immensely.(See Below for instructions on how to tweak your game)
Sound: ★★★★☆
The epic musical soundtrack from the T.V. show is great throughout the entire game. The voice acting is also done nicely.
Playability: ★★☆☆☆
The gameplay combat is clunky, you set up actions in a three-slot queue, then watch your commands get carried out in sequence. Apart from your basic attack, no abilities are mapped to any face buttons, so you frequently need to pause (though the action doesn’t stop entirely) and pull up an ability wheel to issue new orders..
Entertainment: ★★★★☆
George R.R. Martin collaborated with Cyanide to create the story and I got say it is as good as the books and will keep you coming back to see what is going to happen next?.
Replay Value: ★★★☆☆
I feel the game has a good replay value with all the choices you make throughout the entire game which effect how people react to you and of course the end game. Also replaying with different classes adds to a new experience. There are five different endings based on what you do in the last chapter, but the bigger changes occur throughout the adventure as characters are either present or absent based on how you treated them earlier.
Overall Rating: ★★★☆☆
MY PERSONAL REVIEW
Game of Thrones is split into chapters, and control alternates between two protagonists. Alester is a red priest returned from a 15-year exile in the east, and Mors is a skinchanger in the Night’s Watch. Though the two plotlines are initially unconnected, each story arc is full of interesting developments and surprising twists, making their eventual convergence quite satisfying.
Mor’s is a skinchanger so he can inhabit the body of his lovable dog and scare attackers with his mighty bark, or lunge at their throats with its chopping teeth. You can control your dog outside of combat as well, to track the scent of a fleeing coward or squeeze through a hole in the wall, and this adds some diversity to the exploration. The dog also has a skill tree to level up with Mors. Certain animations for  the kill scenes are quite entertaining. In many RPGs, good loot can make some long fought battles worth the wait but that doesn’t happen in Game of Thrones. Nearly all of the good items from shops are unattainably expensive until the game is practically over, leaving you to scavenge for gear suited to your particular armor and weapon specialties. Overall  I feel Game of Thrones is purely story fleshed out through  its two characters as you delve deeper into all its lore. If you enjoy great story telling with a lack of good game mechanics than you cant go wrong with Game of Thrones.
2 Tweaks I found that greatly improved the game for me are:
**Turn on Vsync**
Edit configuration file
Go to %USERPROFILE%\My Documents\Game of Thrones\UnrealEngine3\AGOTGame\Config
Open AGOTEngine.ini with a text editor.
Find a line: UseVsync=False.
And change it to: UseVsync=True to enable Vsync.
**Adjust the Field of View**
Edit input configuration file
Go to %USERPROFILE%\My Documents\Game of Thrones\UnrealEngine3\AGOTGame\Config
Open AGOTInput.ini with a text editor.
Find the section [Engine.PlayerInput]
At the end of it, add the following lines:
Bindings=(Name="F1",Command="FOV 75",Control=False,Shift=False,Alt=False)
Bindings=(Name="F2",Command="FOV 90",Control=False,Shift=False,Alt=False)
Bindings=(Name="F3",Command="FOV 120",Control=False,Shift=False,Alt=False)
Modifiy FOV values to your preference if needed and save.
Launch a game.
While in game, press F1, F2 or F3 to change FOV.
Hope this helps as I found both work and make the game alot better.

Paladins is a game that doesn't try to reinvent the wheel in many respects, but in general takes the parts of hero shooter FPS games, and combines it with some rpg/moba elements to give you very fun experience. I typically don't really enjoy any FPS type games, but i've actually been really enjoying this one.
So the MOST obvious game that it's going to get compared to is Overwatch, which is fair since its VERY similar, but it has enough differences for me to enjoy it much more. Customizing my character (in a playstyle way, not just visual ala skins) has always been super fun for me, testing out different bulids and seeing what works for you and what doesn't ect. This alone makes me enjoy the game a fair amount more, but I also hugely appreciate that characters in this game seem to be a bit more beefy and you get 1 shot a lot less, allowing you to stay in the action for way longer. I've enjoyed a lot of the characters too, even if half of them may be VERY similar to champions from other hero shooters, its ok cuz they still have enough of a unique feel to them and they're done well.
The only few bad things about the game i can think of, is if you don't wanna spend money to unlock champions, you'll easily reach high enough rank to participate in ranked play before you actually have enough champions to do so. But $20 for the all characters pack feels very worth it, as a lot of the characters are a blast to learn to play. Also characters have voice packs which you may need to purchase for in game voice commands, but you literally need to buy them (with in game currency or real money) or else you just get the standard voice over lol. People are also cheating from time to time, I haven't encountered it very often but in the 2-3 games where it was very obvious, it was very annoying. I feel like most of the complaints i have are very minimal, but worth noting for new players.
It's free, give it a shot, play a few different champions, playing with friends helps, good times.

From the time I've spent in CrossCode so far, it's absolutely fantastic, and it only promises to get better as it approches the big 1.0, which it's getting quite close to at the time of this review.
Whether it's worth getting during Early Access or better off waiting for the full release is up to you; it's a great game either way, and if you like action RPGs you will certainly not be disappointed.

So, what is this game?
Is it Chrono Trigger?  No, there is no time travel or parallel universes (that we know of, this game's story is only at the start of the beta, the rest is just gameplay) but the visuals and the music make it feel very much like it.
Is it Legend of Zelda? No, but the puzzles and dungeons require players to pay attention to the controls and push the game's physics and their own understanding of the game's limits to advance.
Is it Guardian Legend?  No, there's no flight, but Lea is very much inspired by the NES heroine, and her 'spheromancer' abilities make her very adapatable to your own play style (Like melee? Increase your melee and defense stats.  Like range? Increase your attack and HP.)  Like Guardian Legend, the game looks fun as a spectator, but is deceptively harder than it lets on.
Is it Final Fantasy X?  No, but the circuit system is very reminiscent of the Sphere Grid.
It's a well thought out 2D Platformer mixing together what works in a lot of games into one cohesive RPG.  And it's enough to forgive the 'grindy' nature of the quests and missions.  Yes, there's a lot of defeats on mobs needed to collect 7-20% chance drops of items you need, but with a diversity of quests to choose from, a lot of the missions overlap, so progress on one mission helps another without you realizing it.
And yes, the jump puzzles can be frustrating.  But that's because they're EVERYWHERE.  Crosscode loves hiding things in plain sight.  If you walk past a location on a map to head from Point A to Point B, you'll ignore the shrubs and bushes hiding items.  You'll miss where the screen scrolls past a drop-off to a hidden cave.  You'll miss treasure.  And Lea's jump ability can't really be enhanced.  You're just as capable to find these places at the start as you are at the end.
And like Metroid, Crosscode is meticulous in it's 'fencing'.  Without earning 'shades', you can't get past fences to high-level encounters, so there's little chance of stomping into a place where a Robo-Goat will kick your teeth in.  Certain areas, you'll need elemental powers to bypass barricades.  If someone can figure out a way to 'cheat' these barricades, you kind of have to respect them for doing so, as again nothing in this game is easy.
I fell in love with this game on GOG and I bought it a total of three times to support it... (once on GOG to play it, twice on Steam: as a gift to someone else, and again to write this review for you) that's as good of an endorsement as I can give to Crosscode.  I'm excited for the progress, and can't wait to see what they do next.

Gun is the underrated masterpiece that too few had heard of. Gun is the game that Neversoft quietly made while most people were eagerly awaiting their next Tony Hawk game. Gun is the open world western of 2005, 5 years before Red Dead Redemption would hit stores as a critically and commercially successful western. People praised Rockstar for doing an open world western, but forgot about Gun.
Gun is a gem, and everyone should play it. The story is strong. The voice acting from the leads, Thomas Jane, Ron Perlman, Kris Kristofferson, Dave Wittenberg, Lance Henriksen and Brad Dourif, nuanced and unequivocal. The soundtrack is perfect. The animation is outstanding. The gameplay is pretty good, but not perfect. There are so many reasons for owning this game and literally just one fallacy; the graphics.
The only issue in Gun is the poor time release; late 2005, before the first next gen console would roll into stores, therefore, only taking advantage of what power the PS2 had left in it; and that's what PC gamers are getting, the PS2 port. It's not bad, hell, you can use a controller and configure it to your liking, all buttons mappable in the menu.
Concering the plot, you are Colton White, voiced brilliantly by Thomas Jane. You start the game with your father, Ned White, hunting along the Missouri River. You fight some bears and this acts as the tutorial, learning how to shoot and whatnot. I REALLY don't wanna spoil anything, because the plot is so damn good. For the time being, consider this the closest thing you can get to RDR on PC. It's a fun game, but unlike Redemption I feel like a lot is missing. The map is small and the campaign seems kinda short. The world doesn't feel as alive and vibrant as it could be, and graphical bugs seem frequent (Weird walk cycles, people moving without a walking animation from a distance, etc.).
But my complaints of GUN end there because the game is an excellent western title. You play as Colton White, a young man who has to carry out missions to find a crook reverend named Reed after he ambushes a steamboat you were on, taking your father and a ♥♥♥♥♥ he knew to the river deep. You play between Dodge City and Empire City in Kansas (Both well known as the pinnacle western cities in popular culture, along with Wichita and other towns) fighting off gang members, raiders, Apache Indians and so on.
If you've played Red Dead Redemption before this game then you should feel right at home. It has a pretty straightforward third-person mechanic where you can get weapons like a Schofield revolver, a lever-action rifle, Winchester Shotgun, tomahawk, whiskey bombs (Essentially a Molotov cocktail) and much more. Gunplay is very simple and intuitive, normal for a TPS, and you can use your revolver to slow down time with a Dead Eye-esque mode called Quickdraw. Plus, you can ride a horse. Why would you pass that up?
While not as developed and gritty as RDR's excellent western epic of a story, the story is still well-thought-out, although from what I've heard it's relatively short. You can also do side missions such as being a ranch hand, helping the local sheriff or marshals, and, a wild west staple, hunt bounties, among other things. The score fits so well with the game and story, that I could see it very well in a spaghetti western if the graphics weren't so...you know...2005.
Overall, it's a great game and I'd recommend it if you're a fan of the wild west, Red Dead Redemption (Much like myself), or just games like these in general. It's a smaller-scale RDR and despite its dated and sometimes buggy graphics and small map, I suggest you give it a look.

From a non Resi fan: Revelations is great!
OK so I don't like the series on the whole. Kinda liked the Alone In The Dark adventure game roots of the first game, and the more natural controls that came with 4 (and the creepy atmosphere in the slower, early parts of both games)... and that's about it. I heard the two revelations games felt like a return to Resi roots so I decided to give this a try.
I loved it! What you've got here is some very light puzzling that recalls the earliest Resi, and straightforward but challenging combat with controls that improve on the changes 4 brought to the series, while ditching some of its annoyances. To my delight, there is no inventory tetris and weapon upgrades can be removed and reused on later weapons. The scanner is a pretty nice touch, and combined with the setting reminds me of an old Dreamcast Resi clone called Carrier (this is much better ;P ).
The story is the usual Resi nonsense (had no expectations here; wasn't disappointed). I'm a huge horror fan, but this ain't it, it's just monster schlock with a few jump scares. Having said that, some of the combat and action sequences really do ramp up the tension in a satisfying way. Chris and Jill are totally bland, but it was a nice surprise to find some of the supporting characters quite likable and entertaining. And, considering its 3DS origin, the game looks really good too (and works in 3D - more on this below*). The episodic structure really works; the pacing is good, the occasional, brief changes to different characters and locations keep things lively, and it helps with the mundane task of fitting a bit of gaming into the inconvenience of Real Life. My only (minor) gripes with the gameplay are that the puzzling elements and scanner could have been developed into something a lot more interesting, and the final boss was poor (but even the best games fail that test).
Another nice surprise: the UI, options and keyboard & mouse controls are great. The menus aren't exactly what I was used to but are smartly designed and work really well during play. There's a 30, 60 or uncapped frame rate option**, which is fantastic. The mouselook felt a bit odd at first (bit of inertia) but I got used to it in no time. Overall a much better PC version than I'm used to when it comes to big-name, primarily console titles.
All in all, my favourite Resident Evil so far. I'd say it's worth the full price (campaign is 9+hrs) and a bargain on sale. On to Revelations 2!
* I played in Nvidia 3D Vision with Helixmod fix applied, on default settings. I thought it looked great with negligible issues (eg markers on your map at wrong depth; nothing during gameplay). Note, crosshair is switched off by default, enable it each time you run the game (I used F11. Read the instructions!)
** I played at fixed 60fps, but it forgot this setting and I had to reset it each time I ran the game. Check your options before you start. All other settings saved fine.

Some tips:
-Those who don't understand reverse slopes for placing artillery units will have a hard time in this game. Place AT guns on the reverse side peering just over the edge. Doing so will provide much needed cover.
-Units zero in on enemies with each missed shot, move a tank or retreat a gun down a slope thats under fire to throw off enemy aim and force them to zero in again.
-Caveat: Moving your own units, messes up their aim as well, trade-off accordingly. More experienced crews can fire while moving and maintain zero-in aim. (this is the era before gyrostabilizers)
-Use tanks in hull down positions on slopes
-Inexperienced gunners/drivers cannot fire while moving, they must come to a complete stop
-Units with direct attack commands will zealously carry out their orders and chase enemies if they don't have clear line of sight. Be sure to cancel any attack orders with the stop command if you want them to acquire different targets.
-Anti tank rifle infantry is great at finishing off wounded/disabled tanks. Remember that tanks poor vision near them and infantry can crawl around undetected.
-Keep experienced soldiers alive during your campaign. An AT-rifleman/marksman or a tank gunner with good aim can make mincemeat of inexperiencd tanks--especially at a distance.
-Units may panic if they have low leadership or no one nearby is around with a high leadership value.
-Penetration values are ideal circumstances. That H35 with 35mm penetration probably won't kill a Panzer 4 with 30mm frontal armor unless some plating has already been blown off.

After 17 hours I feel like I've got some strongly formed opinions on at least the world, graphics, story, writing, voice acting, controls, and animations.  I understand this game "requires" multiple play-throughs and I freely admit I've not yet completed my first.  Having said that, I am not sure I'm interested in finishing the first run, hence the review at this point.
I'll just admit right off the bat two things:  I despise anime and I just finished the main story of Witcher 3.  I freely admit that these two things probably set me up to be more critical than I might have otherwise been.  But, reviews aren't meant to be written by only loyalists to a genre or fanboys.  I could care less if you think "I don't get it" when it comes to this game or anime.  I bought the game just like you, I get to review it just like you.  And if I hate anime, then why did I get this?  Because I love open world games and will give them a chance even if they aren't in my favorite genre.
WORLD/MAP
So...when it comes to the world, all I can say is...holy cow it's bad.  I have read review after review of people saying the world is beautiful.  WTF?  What games do these people play?  Beauty must really really be in the eye of the beholder because this world is drab at best.  If extremely minimalistic is your thing, then I guess this world is great.  To everyone else, no.  There are some decent vistas and the lighting can be decent at times.  Just having played 100 hrs of Witcher 3 might have spoiled my opinion on this world.  But, come on...there are basically 3 main assets that are placed everywhere.  1) Ruined bulidings with NOTHING worth exploring, 2) big trees, 3) and mobs that are basically just minor variations of each other.  Yes, there are some cool bosses and some unique mobs, but for the most part, you are basically looking at the Google Android symbol with nearly every mob you face.  The variation is appaulingly bad in this world.  It feels like I'm playing a game on the PS2 or PS3 back when worlds were largely devoid of details that made them truly feel real.  And while nostalgia can be good, a world that is this empy in an age where we have games like Horizon Zero Dawn, Witcher 3, or Tomb Raider is just unacceptable at the $60 price point.  I wouldn't complain this much on the world if the game were $30.  Lastly, there are invisible walls and gaps in textures everywhere.  For some reason, they felt the need to design buildings with lots of visible rooms and hallways but you can't go into even the most accessibile entry points at ground level, you just smack into invisible walls.  At the edges of the map or in some outdoor cooridors, you can sometimes see large gaps in the assets where they didn't bother to patch up the hole that allows you to see through the world.  Again, this is a $60 game.  Some have defended the drab pallet and buildings saying "But it's post apocolyptic!!" So is Fallout and a ton of other games.  Each of them are more interesting to run around in than this world.  Apparently in this world, the only thing that can survive the end times are concrete buildings and giant trees.  There is nothing else to look at.  You will be running back and forth constantly through the same drab landscapes.  Textures are also poor.  I am playing on max settings.  There are areas in the desert for example where one texture on a rock is overlayed on another texture that is completely different.  They don't match at all.  These aren't out of the way or obscure either.  They were just looked at by devs and shrugged off apparently.  This is rookie level stuff that you'd expect to see in an early access game.  Apart from that example, textures in general and shapes show little effort.  Just stop in the amusement park area and really, really look at the textures and blocking of the shapes.  It's literally the same quality you'd find in an old PS3 game.
STORY/WRITING/VOICE ACTING
Oh man, if you hated my opinion before, you're gonna really hate me now.  The writing is just...elementary at best.  There is so much cringe here.  Your fighting companion literally says the stupidest stuff.  There is a moment where the head android chick explains that the aliens were coming from a certain location, which explained why the landscape had changed, and this idiot boy then comments "I wonder why that giant crater is there?"  I don't know who wrote these lines but they are filled with ultra stupid anime commentary.  I don't know if this game was written for children, but it seems like it was written by one.  No matter who you are, you can't possibly defend this writing, it's appaulaingly bad.  The voice acting was tolerable for an anime style game I guess.  That isn't saying much though.  The story isn't anything unique.  Again, it's basically a child's take on the question of "what it means to be sentient/human, etc." or "what does it mean to be alive."
ANIMATIONS/COMBAT
This is the only thing that kept me going for this many hours.  The combat is fun, challenging, at times frantic.  2b moves very fluidly and she's fun to control.  Definitely use a controller as keyboard and mouse with this game is a nightmare.
Evading seems a little overpowered since you can evade repeatedly to avoid damage.  The animations are pretty decent but when sprinting, the map seems to have lots of "trip you up" spots for some reason, where 2b will just trip up for no apparent reason, such as the transition area from desert to city.  I don't know where to comment on this part, so I will stick it here:  the transitions from side scrolling back to 360 isn't enjoyable.  I like the style it brings to the game, but that damned boy android that follows you everywhere gets in the way constantly.
MUSIC/SOUND
Pretty good all around.  It seemed like they didn't shower me in anime-hype-battle music all the time which was nice.
QUESTS
Not that great.  After the initial quests that take you to new areas, future quests just keep sennding you back to the same drab landscapes.  None of the quests were even remotely interesting or engaging to me.  The only side-quest that was fun was the monk ninja robot.  If you're gonna make me run around constantly in this tiny world, your quests better be some of the best quests ever written.  They aren't even close to that.
FISHING
Why?  Just why?  Why put fishing in this game?  Lol
DLC
They want 14 bucks for some skins instead of put some costumes in the game.  You apparently need to make it through 3 playthroughs to get 2 skins.  Seriously.
CONCLUSION
I can't figure out why this game is getting so much love.  I can only guess it's the anime folks that love it, which is fine.  Perhaps it makes people feel nostolgic but that can be acommplished without making the world and textures look like it was made in the era you're trying to honor.  I just can't recommend this game at the full price point.  Get it on sale and enjoy the combat for as long as you can.  But unless you love anime, you will get tired of this empty, boring, and bland world pretty quickly.  I cannot fathom how anyone could play it through 3x just to get the entire story.  Even if the story was great or fresh, requiring multiple playthroughs is just ridiculous and reeks of a lack of effort in building the entire game.  It's a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥effort at giving you more hours of gameplay without the extra work by the devs.  I would say if you can get it for $40 bucks or less and you've got the spare change, go ahead and give it a whirl.  If you're on the fence, pass until it's super cheap.

Let's get this out of the way. The port is bad. No graphics options, 720p only. This can be fixed by using the DPfix by Durante, and downloading HD fonts, HUD and icons.
The game likes to crash for many reasons and in many different ways. Most of them can be prevented by smoking cigarettes (in the game, but I can assure you it also helps IRL), editing the exe file with CFF Explorer, running the game with compatibility mode set to Win98, running the game in window mode and/or changing default controls to a gamepad.
There's apparently a bug that corrupts your save file, but I luckily haven't encountered that one.
During my 29 hours of gameplay at least 5 of them I had to replay because of the crashes. Googling, setting and fixing stuff to be able to even play the game took me around another 3 hours.
It was worth it.
Deadly Premonition is an open-world survival horror detective action adventure game. You can explore (by foot and by car) the town of Greenvale at your leisure, doing side activities, like quests, fishing or collecting stuff. However, you need to eat and sleep (or drink coffee).
During the main questline you mainly travel around, talk to people, solve simple puzzles and shoot some undead zombie-like things. There are also boss fights.
The combat generally resembles that of traditional survival horror games like Resident Evil or Silent Hill. Walk away from the enemies, turn around, prepare your weapon and shoot.
The attention to detail is especially worth the praise. You need to wash your suits and shave if you don't want to look like a hobo. When you pass another car at night, its front lights reflected in your own rear-view mirror will blind you for a brief moment. And car mirrors don't even work besides that. Other mirrors you encounter do work fine though.
Let's not forget about the ridiculous, idiotic and totally uncalled-for QTE sequences. They're so bad, it makes them almost good.
FBI agent Francis York Morgan arrives in the town of Greenvale to investigate a case of murder. Then appear the aforementioned zombie things making the whole plot a hillarious mess. The story is great, even though it doesn't make much sense. At least there are some nice plot twists and everything gets explained by the end of the game.
The cutscenes and dialogues are simply a piece of art. Thanks to the music completely unfitting the situation in most cases, they are genuinely funny.
This has to be the selling point of DP. There's a lot of different characters and the great most of them have personalities of their own. York himself is quite an individual. He talks to his second personality, Zach, all the time, even with people around, without a trace of embarrasment. He's also a walking bag of strange habits and mannerisms.
The whole Greenvale looks like an uncanny valley. Getting to know those people is totally worth the effort.
Don't be discouraged by all those technical problems I mentioned
- Deadly Premonition is a great game and the quality of the PC port doesn't change that fact in the slightest.
Objectively 9.5/10.

Space Civ 5 with a bit of Sci-Fi roleplay.
If you like space games and you like civ 5 you will probably like this game.
Every game starts with the hard choice, what race do you want to play (create). This choice will determin the strategy, moral choices and tactics.
Pros;
* super fun early gameplay where you rush to colonies as much space as you can and build up your empire.
* great looking univers and maps.
* very cool mods that extend the content and gameplay
* fair and entertaining random events that spice up your early/mid gameplay
* very deep and interesting diplomacy options that really shape your gameplay. Its very important to have the right friends and enough friend with shared interests or common enemies.
Cons;
* lacking end game content
* terrible battle system ( you have one try, one big battle, the one that brings most ships normally wins. The winner of that battle will dominate the opponent for the rest of that war)
* Conquering planets is a boring mechanic (place starfleet at planet-->weakends their defenses until 0 defence left-->send in ground troop which are more than the defending troops, wait again and conquered)
* expensive DLC with average added value
I did enjoy playing the game and learning tactics and strategies. If you take your time and micro manage as well as zooming into the action, you can experience the full space feeling. I did find myself macro managing and just looking at the starmaps and fast forwarding to the events after a few play throughs though. The mid-/End gameplay can be boring until something happens where you either lose loads or gain to win alot. These choice and events is what makes the game entertaining, cause you stand to lose a lot of be rewarded greatly.

Mid to end game needs a lot of balance. Lost quite a few games where I had more research than the AI, and therefore I should have better tech and more core planets available but somehow the AI had 3 times as many planets as I did with about 30% less research. Resources also feel unbalanced, you'll never have to worry about food while managing some stupid influence that you can hardly do anything to improve. Energy will be your bottleneck while you sit at max minerals after about 3 mins of playing. The game is fun overall, but the balance issues kills it after a few hours of play.

A bit hard to learn the basics, even with the tutorial, but easy to master after that. The gameplay is RTT (Real Time Tactics, you can still pause). You can't build bases but you might get reinforcements and call out for support aircraft and artillery, although I can't compare it with Sudden Strike or Blitzkrieg because it's much more realistic, the weapons and equipment (including the might Tiger and IS-2 tanks) are modeled after real life, with accurate range, armor, reload, speed, sounds, etc. so it's definitely not like in BF1942, for example, where hand grenades can take out a tank, you have to know how and with what to attack certain targets. The only thing I regret is that there aren't more games like this and that it's sorta limited in equipment and scenarios although it has what most of us probably want: the Battle of Kursk. 8/10

I would really like to recommend this game: it is quite cheap now, it still looks good and it covers most of the European theatre of WWII. There are a lot of different units and it tries to be realistic.
However there are so many issues that it turns into a definitely no:
Aiming is unrealistic. If your tank crew is not exceptionally trained, they can't hit the enemy even from 20 meters. Fortunately it goes to the enemy as well. Same for penetration rules. Even when there is a hit from 20 meters and from the back, it just bounces off. I know that the gun of the R35 is not the ultimate tank killer, but it should be able to kill a Panzer IV with less then 8 shots from point blank range...
The AI is terrible, but the enemy has the numerical advantage. In campaign most missions boil down to this: the useless infantry charges ahead, but they can be ignored, because in most cases they can't hurt the tanks. The player should have wait with its tanks and its highly trained crew until the enemy tanks get in shooting range, then the player should concentrate fire and destroy the enemy tanks one by one. Once it is done, the enemy infantry can be executed. It is important to protect the tank, bushes, terrain and especially buildings can help with that.
Most campaign missions are setup in a way that it is disadvantageous to the player. The first step in almost every campaign mission is to concentrate the troops at one place or at a different place where the game suggests. If there is a small town on the map, it is the best just to collect the troops there, and wait till the enemy tanks come and can be shot down one by one.
And let's not forget about loading times which are simply too long.

Definitely not an example for ease of access and intuitive controls, as it feels unwieldy and clunky, but it is a real beast of complexity and a heaven for diehard tactical RTS fans of realistic gameplay. Realistic in this instance means physically correct and therefore - speaking in layman's terms - mindbogglingly unfair and frustrating mechanics.
Not for everyone, but almost could have been used by real WWII generals for actual warfare planning and simulation in regards to the love for realistic detail.

I had heard mixed things about the game and was afraid it was just a cash grab but was pleasantly surprised that it shared much with RPG favorites of mine like Dragon Age and The Witcher.
The biggest strength of Game of Thrones is the story. I thought it was actually really good. The characters were well written with interesting backstories. Like the source material, there were no “good guys” – the protagonists had as many flaws and as much blood on their hands as their antagonists. The story overlaps with the first book, A Game of Thrones. Fortunately, even though you run into characters from the book (modeled after the actors from the HBO series) and events from the book, there are plenty of original characters and locations too. You decisions do impact the story and the gameplay. Certain decisions give your character permanent perks that are bonuses in gameplay (+x to attach, or +% to item drops). There are dialogue trees as well when talking to NPC’s. However, for the most part, your choices never feel as consequential as the Bioware games until the very end of the campaign.
Visually, the game is modest. It has decent backgrounds and character models but it looks dated for a 2012 release. I heard it runs the Unreal Engine 3 and there are definitely better looking games on this engine out there. The art design is faithful to the HBO series and looks as expected.
Gameplay-wise it plays like many other modern RPG’s. It is very similar to Dragon Age as you can control one party member (and you can switch between party members) and queue up various actions in combat. Unfortunately, Cyanide doesn’t allow you to completely pause during combat to issue orders instead it slows combat down. Some people might not find that a problem but I thought it was inconvenient when trying to manage multiple characters in combat. Sometimes the camera would get in the way during combat as well with insufficient zoom and angle to see what you were attacking.
I played with an Xbox controller which was fully supported and very enjoyable. As this game was also released on consoles, the controller seems the ideal method to play it. I never had any performance issues and the game never crashed on me.

Oh my, an excellent game. A true strategic 4x game. This game sets itself apart in my opinion by use of an extremely friendly user interface in combination with excellent game play mechanics. There are also a number of nice touches like the ancient civilisations with conciderable firepower and no interest in diplomacy that dot the map. Furthermore, the gathering of resources is straight forward, once occupying a territory, one can build mineral, energy, science or special resources collectors on applicable astriods or planets. simple. There are also extensive micromanagement options for resourses, territories, diplomacies and ship construction if one chooses to utilise them or they can just be left in their generic state.
All in all it is an excellent game that fully embodies the ideals of Extermination, Exploration, Exploitation and Expansion

Stellaris, oh how I feel about you,
The things I hate:
1: To make this game playable, at least for me, you need mods, lots of mods, this isn't that out of the ordinary for me, because almost as soon as I get a game I mod it like crazy, though this game is almost unplayable without them, because certain things are just pointless, such as defence stations, for some reason the developers thought making them have no reason for existing would make for good gameplay.
2: Scale, while you can build a massive fleet of amazing looking ships, the fact that everything is cartoonishly large and all the ships seem close in size to everything, including the spaceport they were built in, in many cases it looks more like you would dock the spaceport to the ship than the ship to the spaceport, don't get me started on the fact that ships look LARGER in some cases than the planets, even if this was how things look smaller at a distance, you'd need to be at an incredible distance from the planets, a way to fix this is with mods, like Downscaled ships and Realspace, two mods that make the game playable for me.
3: Battle and war, War just feels empty, unfinished, battles are purely blobs of numbers going after blobs of numbers, sure having the correct mix of point defense and other things can be useful, but at the end of the day it's just blobs going after blobs, and after a while war is a chore, no fun.
The things I don't like:
1: Diplomacy, it feels unfinished, I know you can only do so much with AI, but there are so few options and it almost feels like federations are intended to punish you, because you lose something like 20% of your naval capacity, and the other members of your federation don't seem to build up or even upgrade the ships in the 'Federation fleet'
2: I'm not sure if this should go into the Things I hate pile or just dislike, but ship upgrading is absolutely terrible, when you research a new tech you can upgrade an existing ship, while a cool idea the, fact that you have to click so many times to simply upgrade something like an FTL drive seems insane! The power system is intended to keep you from rushing all the best weapons or whatever and not upgrade your ship powerplants, but the fact that you have to click so many times to upgrade something is terrible for gameplay, and the autoupgrade button, is totally worthless, it will sometimes work, and others do nothing, and then sometimes it'll upgrade your power plants even when there is no need! All that does it drive up the purchase and upkeep prices!
3: Fleet upkeep, I understand a fleet upkeep cost, but if you have a large fleet it seems what little strategy in this game goes out the window because you burn more power and minerals when your fleet is out, because the fleet upkeep is so high if you have a big fleet you can't execute a slow strategy, it's mostly a rush to their fleet so you can start landing troops on the enemy planets.
4:Planetary invasions, I understand this isn't the game you're looking for if you want ground invasions, but they are way too simplified, usually it's just you make a fleet of 100 assault troops and land them on enemy planets with at most 25 troops plus a few millitia, and then after the planet is taken the population will actually fight FOR you if the enemy lands troops to take the planet back.
The things I like:
1:The encounters are pretty good at first at least, I can imagine they get old quick because there are so few.
2: Early game, it's fast and it's full of mystery, the mystery of who you'll meet next, because you may find your greatest ally, or enemy, and at this point the arms races are real.
Things I love:
1: The game is very pretty, other than the fact things are scaled like toys, the systems are pretty, and the ships look pretty good as well.
2: Species creation, you get to name your species and pick ethics and government types, outside of roleplay this is pretty useless though, as there are only a few differences in how empires play.
3: naming and building ships, instead of building a pre-made ship you get to design your own, of course with limits, but sadly as you research things it gets tiresome to upgrade them, and it really gets tiresome to upgrade them when you are focusing on a research empire, and upgrades come in quick.
Things I cannot stand, AKA game killers for me.
1 after a couple hundred years the game starts freezing at the start of each month, it's almost certainly due to the economy being calculated at the 1st of the month. (NOTE: this probably takes longer to occur without the massive amount of mods I use, so it may take longer in vanilla but it's probably going to happen) I suspect it's because the game is maxing out a single CPU core, and it's freezing up while calculating.
In short, it's pretty, and the early game is fun, but I wouldn't recommend it unless you get it for a 50% or so deal like I did.
