Stellaris was never a very good or well-polished game – it was a bug-ridden, rushed release, and instead of fixing it, Paradox went straight towards releasing overpriced DLC without fixing the core issues of the game, such as sectors, bad AI, and the unbelievably terrible warfare design which takes more inspiration from EU4 (whose combat is decidedly lacklustre) than HoI4 (whose combat is the point of the game). While it is indeed an empire builder, it's an empire builder whose warfare is more chore than game.
That they keep pushing DLC, then, while leaving the game fundamentally broken, is an insult to the consumer. Putting more band-aids on a pustulent, rotting mountain of gaseous lard isn't going to make it any more appealing, and it certainly hasn't for me. The worst insult of all is that, after complaints that the game had no built-in auto-explore feature, one was released – locked behind a mid-game research option, which forces you to tediously queue your exploration manually for hours before finally getting to focus on the rest of the game.
While it's fun watching the numbers go up, the rest of the game is grossly underdeveloped, and will remain as such permanently, since Paradox builds its games' width rather than fixing their crippling shallowness, should it be present on release. You'll see more features, but they won't meaningfully interact with one another (see EU4), and the fundamental issues present will never be fixed. You might have fun for a few hours to begin with, but you'll be left with ashes in your mouth as more and more intentionally overlooked design problems keep nagging at the back of your mind. The only thing a responsible consumer can do with a product like this is to simply not buy it.

"After beating the dungeon I now know the truth. The developers feed on the rage of the players. Without our agony the developers cannot succeed."
I almost cried reading that, and I understood why.
I have been looking for an actual RPG game for a while now and CrossCode filled that void. A great story, great combat, and a very pleasent developer team. Being a fan of the whole variety of games, CrossCode was a bit of a shock when I realized the game wasn't just another cut out of the RPG cloth.
It carries elements from several genres:
RPG (Obviously): Giving into the classical feeling of a Megaman or Zelda-esk stlye CrossCode has an "almost" cliche story involving Amnesia and a broken voice module. Avoiding the classic silent protagonist and going with an almost silent one (Who by the way has a very wide range of reactions even without most of her speaking abilities) allows for solid communication and in most cases relatability.
RTS: The entire combat system is Real time, and YOU have the decision to keep going on your fighting streak. (Although the terminology BLOOD LUST comes to mind) The games fighting aspect is not easy either, most enemies require a specific strategy to deal damage, and in some cases, won't even take damage unless you perform a set of actions before hand. (I'm looking at you Phoenix, I have a special set of words for your ice dungeon BS)
Story-Driven: Or if you'd prefer a visual novel. Every character you interact with has a personality, random people hanging out nearby, random people in the combat areas, every single NPC. There isn't a single NPC who doesn't feel unique from the other, and the developers have done an amazing job at upholding this level of seriousness. Your party members feel like real people, they have lives outside of CrossCode and it works as a solid excuse to pause the game and add to the building story of Lea. Oh yes, Lea, you amnesia ridden woman you. Besides having amnesia, Lea has a speech problem, apparantly, in which is made up by her sense of humor expressed through her responses.
Grinding: I LOVE BL2 and grinding was a huge part of it, so to face a small amount really didn't phase me much. This game does have a grinding aspect (It has a mission literally built on grinding, but more on that later.) but it isn't as bad as some RPG games would make it. The chances of things dropping are relatively high, and if you are willing to search, you will find what you need.
Puzzles: NYEH....Thats dead now.
To put it simply, this game has a major play on the puzzles aspect, and is the thing that the dungeons are built on. If you play this game, don't go in not expecting your brain to be challenged, because I can promise you, you will not get away without feeling slightly aggervated at one puzzle or the next. Don't worry, you'll figure it out, it might take you a few days, but I totally believe in you. (Please make guide on how to puzzle, these developers abuse my puzzle privledges.)
In all, CrossCode, is it the next big thing?
Possibly.
Is it a definite success?
Pretty sure it already is.
Is it worth my money?
Yep, if you want it in early access that is.
Normally, this would be the point I go on some rant about early access but I cant help but praise the developers on this.
In two years they succesfully stayed on track for updates and releases, and I have yet to see them fail.
So, congrats on being an actual succesful early dev team, you just outdid 90% of the other teams.
Good luck on release day, I see this game exploding on that day, its got a wonderful community and a great team to keep it together, and I look forward to seeing whats next in your work.

CrossCode...Boy oh boy, where do I start.
I'mma start at the fundaments of this game, while trying to not spoil any little thing.
The design of the game and it's mechanics.
If you've played lots of Zelda games in the past, like me, you'll soon realize that CrossCode feels very reminiscent of The Legend of Zelda's Dungeons, even though they are far from being alike.
And I can tell you why that is.
PLAY stands in the center of this game.
While these days, most titles like the Uncharted series or Outlast have the common theme of having a set story in mind, where a game is designed around, which is not bad don't get me wrong-
CrossCode is wholely designed around it's base mechanics, which are a well balanced, quick paced with a smooth feeling action combat system, simple but hard to master movement, an easily learned level-up and skill system, latter one being called "Circuits" in this game and the means to balance all that out.
What this game does is work out a basic mechanic for whatever place you're in and build the entire world around it, placing tricky but great puzzles throughout your way, making those progressively harder to ease you into using your abilities, while also offering a fantastic pacing.
Did I mention how great the puzzles are in design and theme?
I dare say they even outmatch the ones in classic Zelda dungeons.
Now, with that out of the way, let's address the Characters, World and Story.
This one will contain very, very mild spoilers about the basic idea of the setting.
CrossCode places you inside the world of the online game "CrossWorlds", which is basically an enhanced version of a VR game, where you control a virtual character in a physical enviroment.
It's not actually a multiplayer game for you, though.
That's just the story.
That concept itself isn't THAT new, I guess, but it's put out in a very charming and appealing way.
The characters are a bit stereotypical, but also that- in a very charming way.
They all have their very own, intriguing personality and I must admit that they kinda grew onto me while I played through the several parts of the yet unfinished story.
That story by the way, I'm VERY eager to see how it ends up.
With what's in the game so far, I'm super excited to experience more of it.
And before you worry about the game never being fully finished, you should check the release-schedule for the game.
You can find that in the forums here on steam, or on gamejolt.
That being said, the game devs are ever working on this beautiful masterpiece and it's steadily growing bigger and better.
All in all, I could not NOT recommend this game to everyone.
YES, it is unfinished, but it's SO GOOD!
From both, a personal, and an objective and substantial point of view.
Do not miss out on this game, you would regret it.

I'm not going to totally recommend this game, but here is what I can say.
The game is an open world game set in a city in campain. You are an FBI agent sent there to solve a murder mistery who happened in that city.
The game has a vey nice story, a murder mistery with some fantastic element, since you will mostly fight zombies like enemies born from the mind of the main character.
I can assure you that you will surely play this just for the sake of knowing who the culprit is, but here is some flaw in the gameplay
The game is too easy.
Enemies are always the same slow walking "zombies" who takes one or two hits to the head to kill. There is really no challenge at all and the only way to really game over is by either failing some quick-time event or by getting killed by getting hit on purpose. Same thing for the bosses, whose almost every attack can be avoided by quicktime events. Moreover, your weapons are all over powered, from the basic pistol whith infinite ammos to the magnum whose hits can really one shot enemies. why does this game even has melee weapons, don't ask me.
All of this makes the game really boring and doing the secondary missions, which are a lot, becomes something one does just for the achievements.

On the positive side we have the story, I really enjoyed following it all always wanting to know more about it and every murder so particular. But what wins the oscar for me is the main character, who suffers from double personality, with a know-it-all behaviour, we really see him change during the game, and the voice act really fits him.
In conclusion I recommend this game only if you like good plots like I do. If you hope for something more FPS like, forget this. If this was a visual novel or a Telltale like game it would have probably been a better purchase. Definetly not to buy at full price and If I should give an objective rate, I would give a 6.5 / 10, although I still enjoyed playing this

The characters looks decent in comparison of some meshses from Greenvale. But the amount of work done on each road of this city deserves a bit of understanding. The goal was to achieve the detective experience of solving this murder in a non-linear way. Each part of the city has some collectibles and some clunky or funny designs that tells the player "go there!...is funny isn't it!?" for instance when you go through a forbidden road or a field filled with animals. I just beat the game a minute ago, and I'll base this reccomendation on the time i spent on it.
First off, I reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys western films. You're a cowboy seeking revenge on whoever killed your father, who was involved with a madman looking for a fabled city of gold. I'll rate the game on a few criteria.
Story/immersion: 9/10
-The story  is great. Each character brings something new to the table. Each of them have their own unique personalities and are important to the plot in one way or another. The voice acting is also pretty good. Sure, it may be out of sync at times, but that never got in the way of me enjoying it. Also, it feels like I'm playing in a westerner, and although some of the scenes portray a few negative Native American stereotypes that seem to be a bit outdated, it feels genuine. I loved it, but honestly, the story should've been a bit longer. I beat it in 6 hours which, although average for the time, seems short for the kind of game it is.
Controls: 6/10
-This is one of the few places in which the game suffers. Moving is standard, as well as aiming, jumping, and crouching. What really could've had some work was the weapon system. You have plenty of weapons, don't get me wrong, but it's such a hassle to switch between them that I wound up using the rifle for most of the game. This could've easily been fixed if you could just cycle through with the mouse button. Instead, you have to use either the numbers or hold alt+the corresponding weapon key. Really bad in the heat of battle.
Graphics: 8/10
-By today's standards, an 8 seems a bit generous, but considering the fact that this game is from 2005, they really stand out. Even today, they don't look horendous. One thing I must say is that character models, such as NPCs and enemys don't render at full motion unless you are closer to them. If they are further away, they look like something out of Doom 3D. Anyway, the camera controls nicely, which is great considering the time this game came out.
Extra: 7/10
-Throughout the game, there are plenty of side missions you can do to improve stats, gain money, and take a break from the main story. They're fun, and adds to the feel of the wild west. My only complaint is that it feels like grinding. If you don't do side missions, then the main story gets very difficult towards the end. This makes it not feel like something extra, but rather, something you have to do and part of the main game.
Overall: 8/10
-Highly reccomend. Don't buy it at full price. It's a short game worth a smaller price.

God Games have always been one which you've have the overall power the wield the world at your fingertips, with each God Game type having their own different style to give, showing the emphasis of what type of god you are in that specific universe. Sometimes the wielding of nature (which is most common in god games) is used to a much greater advantage, one of which provides the player to have much more strategy that simply clicking on the environment. From Dust perfectly does this.
From Dust developed by Ubisoft is a game where you play as a deity which has the power to shift the lands underneath the native people's feet for their own means of survival. From Dust's story synopsis is about a group of native in which their land is torn by the natural causes, until they summon their god (the player) to help them strive to a new land in which they may find a peaceful location to settle on with any nature causes harming their colony.
The Story is told through a more native style tale which help give a more tribal and authentic feel to the games' art style, with such a story it can be consider to have contain a hidden message or parable. (Though I'll overlook that)
The gameplay is pretty much like other god games. You have to move around the natural element of the world to help suit the needs of the native people, to get from point A to B, which 'B' is a tunnel to the next level. The native people set up camp near a tribal totem pole in which it gives you various additional power to prevent natural disasters or pave way to an exit. This is the games' strongest point: the powers that the player has. The game makes it clear that you can grab and bend the natural element to your will. Ubisoft was clever with this technique as each level gives a limited amount of supply of a certain element. This is to make you strategise the current situation and makes you focus on rationing certain elements. Sometimes they give too much of an element and its up to the player to prevent that specific element destroy the tribes people. Sometimes this can done through kites which give special powers prevent certain elements from destroying the tribe.
The art style of the game is somewhat unique, in that it uses more tribal colours and texture which exist in more tropical environments, like Hawaii and Togo. The graphics are technically well designed with very little glitches or flaws that exist within the game.
The flaws that exist within the game are the sometimes unfairness of a certain level, elements attacking the tribe too quickly and giving a game over. Another is the AI which has a lack of pathfinding when going to a location which is perfect valid with no obstacles in the way. Last but not least is the somewhat lack of a sandbox mode or more time to use your creative skill in building nature constructs. Personally I had a great time using some elements to create damns and bridges, changing the flows of certain elements is what is highly enriching besides the strategy element of the game.
Overall From Dust is a great game which I highly recommend to anyone who loves God Games and want a bit more strategy as well.

An amazing little godmode game, where you can handle the elements earth, water and lava. I think it's too small, only 15 levels, more like an advertising game. But the concept is quite good and challenging. On the one hand you have to protect your people from deadly floods, on the other hand their villages get burned down by fire caused by the lava. Sometimes you have to fight all the elements together at once. Then you should have the right strategy to survive...

It's a little hard to tell from the trailers, but "From Dust" is a full-on puzzle game. You play as a tribal spirit or god, but your power is far from absolute. The world is made of a few fundamental puzzle pieces: rock, earth, water, lava, and several landscape-altering varieties of tree. It's your job to assemble those pieces in a way that achieves the objectives of each level.
The graphic design of the game is amazing. The tilt-shift blurring and low camera angle give the levels a sense of hugeness. The textures are lovely, and they always blend nicely across the constantly changing terrain. The foliage looks thick and lush, and the flowing water and lava look excellent, although they don't quite come as close to photorealism as other parts of the game.
Perhaps most important, the little villagers are amazingly well-designed. In some ways they look similar enough to real-world tribes that they seem familiar. But little details like their oversized masks and strange huts give them a bit of an alien feel as well. They're tough little guys trying to survive in a world that is completely indifferent to them. It makes you want to help them.
Overall, the setting is beautiful and strange and brimming with hinted possibilities. It left me wanting something like an RPG set in this world - something where you could be surrounded by it, rather than looking down on it from a distance.
The gameplay itself is fun, sometimes challenging, and occasionally irritating.
Shaping the world is intuitive, and the excellent physics simulation makes it a joy to dig a hole or build a hill, and just see what happens as a result. Unfortunately, the results are often unpredictable, and a single wrong move can wreck a great deal of work before you realize what's happened. Additionally, many of the levels have problems that need to be addressed in a limited time frame, and the added rush makes screw-ups even more likely, but last-second victories are that much more euphoric.
If you like puzzle games, and especially if you prefer a bit of frantic action over contemplation, "From Dust" is worth getting.

Why you should get NieR: Automata
It is easily one of the best games I've ever played in my many years of gaming. It connects to you on a personal level and enraptures you with the beautiful music and art. You get to experience the game through a few characters instead of a lone hero, allowing you to view battles and choices from different perspectives. It perfectly plays out like a story book, with twists and tragic turns, it is never boring.
You might think that it is just another game overly hyped to be full of feels and somewhat lacklustre action. Yes it is very touching because they executed the atmosphere perfectly. The appropriate music is played whenever an action is taken. If something took a turn for the worse, an immensely dark music will play and make you wonder why did they do it. Gameplay wise, it is very challenging if you played in on hard mode. Just a tip: don't choose hard mode until you reach the first save. it requires you to be on your toes at all times just like dark souls; loss of items on death. The evasion mechanics is very fun to play around with and it takes some skill to handle some of the bullet hell moments.
Sure, there are technical difficulties surrounding the game. It is unfortunate that Square Enix has not produced a fix as of now. However, the fan made mod, FAR, has done a decent job. Great job eliminating pirates and the technical faults. I have not encountered any problems at all after using the mod. Currently on GTX 1060 and i5-6600. Just save regularly to avoid disappointments. Don't let the reviews on technical difficulties bother you. The installation of the FAR mod has made the game immensely playable.
A little sad that Square Enix jacked up the price in SEA. But seriously, buy this fantastic game!

One of the best games I have played in recent memory. With The legend of Zelda: a Link to the Past being on of my favorite games of all time I just had to give this a download and was not dissapointed.
The gameplay is very reminiscent of old school ALTTP/Links awakening Zelda with an emphesis on puzzle solving and revisiting previous locations. During the game you will come across gates that require cards to get through. The game gives you enough cards to let you experience tha base game but becomes much more difficult and unique with its puzzles if you want to enter the deepest areas of the games.
The game world is very large and extremely varied with many different locales that can be traversed in a very non-linier fashion. Very late into the game you may notice that you are missing a large number of collectables and will gain an ability unlike any other game in order to fully explore the nooks and crannies of the maps. While doing this you will also be able to discover some very well hidden easter eggs from other indie titles.
The story is vary sparse and leaves a lot of the reaction up to the player to figure out in an attempt to understand the world you are currently in.
The soundtrack incredibly well done and can range from slightly eerie and mysterious to down right scary in some sections.
Overall I cannot recommend this game enough for anyone who enjoys Zelda-like, puzzle or artistic games, or something that requires massive amounts of world exploration.

Imma start off by saying:
Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is a realism based shooter set in the open rice fields, dense jungles, napalm torn hills, and condensed towns of Vietnam during the (YOU GUESSED IT!) Vietnam War. Play as the NVA or Viet Cong, and the U.S. Army or USMC in 64-man battles.
If you're like me, you'll feel a sense of insecurity walking through the Jungle and not knowing if there a VC awaiting you around the corner or a Punji Trap lurking on the ground. You take no more than 2-3 bullets in a life so it really adds on to the cautious atmosphere of the game. As you progress you'll get more used to pushing up, but you'll always stay cautious.
-Damage Ratio in weapons feels right

Note: Ignore the comparisons to Team Fortress 2.
Loadout is a really good game. It is multiplayer only (PvP or Player v. Bots) and free-to-play.
Focusing on the actual game: it is very chaotic. Allowing players to make literally billions of combinations (2 guns which can be one of four chasses and each with different stocks, barrels, projectiles, etc.), Loadout keeps people on their toes. You see a lot of the same ideas, though, in slightly different manners. The worst part about the customization is that guns that are "in the middle" are not very good. I do very well with a Heavy-Pyro-Rocket Launcher and a Light-Barrel Assault Rifle, but making a semi-auto marksman rifle wouldn't do very well. Many combinations are pointlesss (Sniper and extralarge magazine, shotgun with burst fire) but they are occassionally used anyway. Some combinations are a little too strong and some are too weak, but the developers have been working hard on updates and seem to care a lot about issues players have.
Looking at its free-to-play status: It's balanced. Paying money can give blutes (in-game money) and experience bonuses and Spacebux (real money). Blutes are for buying new weapon parts and paying for a weapon level-up gotten by experience. Spacebux are for in-game cosmetic items. Cosmetic items do nothing for you and can be found in the daily chance rewards. I see no advantage for paying for the game, because alll gun unlocks can be gotten eventually and pretty easily, and I can't ever see myself buying an experience booster. I've put $5 into the game so far (Feb 2014), but I plan on putting more in during the holidays.
Looking at its players: They are mean. Not in-game (well, many are, but it's kinda the average player in all multiplayer games) but in their reviews, on their twitch.tv account (Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday Loadout streams their progress in the game) is nothing but begging for free items and complaining that cosmetics cost real money. Cosmetics give no advantage and can be found randomly in the daily chance (I have found 4 items already). This game costs money to develop, you ought to give at least $10 to the developers if you care about them.
However: the packs are really expensive. I wish their were cheaper ones. The price of spacebux is kinda high, but understandable. I would never buy a $34 Mardi Gras pack for a new game.

Game of Thrones
Ratings
--------
Engine:         6/10
Gameplay:    6/10
Narrative:      5/10
Emersion:     5/10
Overall:     5.5/10
TL;DR Review
Half-Pretty Linear Box world, with interesting RPG elements, and fresh combat system.
Original characters, good parallel story to first season/book, although the story drags with false endings.
Review
Game of Thrones is a Third Person Perspective Role Playing Game that attempts to immerse the player in the world of HBO's adaptation of George R R Martin's, "A Game of Thrones." The story follows two original characters, Mors Westford and Alester Sarwyck. Both characters are sanctioned, and yet lack a lot of the flare of the characters from the book series. That said, those who like watching the show will find they are fine.
The unreal engine isn't utilised to its maximum capacity, however, it is more than adequate for those looking for an interesting story to parallel the characters they enjoy from the main series. The graphics are fine, but nothing to write home about. There are a few graphical issues here and there, with objects/bodies clipping through walls, sconces, etc. The world design is a little linear, and fairly "closed off," however, there are some neat features like hidden doors and alternative paths that will be discussed later. That said the weapons, armour and body/face art is not too bad, not the best, but still, the graphics utilisation for the characters allows for a deeper emersion.
As with all RPGs the RPG elements are going to be important. There are plenty of good items, that seem impossible to buy, and some even stay that way, so this makes the game's item dependency fairly well balanced. The character building is pretty good, and probably one of the better features in the game. Both Mors and Alester have 5 sections to do with the character building side of things: Characteristics, Stance Skills, Ability Skills, Stats and Traits.
Both characters having to choose one of three stances, and getting to specialize in a second or "doubling down" on their original stance at level 7. At the beginning of the game you have to place your Characteristic points much like most RPGs, these should be stacked with your stance, especially if playing on a harder difficulty. The Stance skills give your characters their combat abilities based around their weapons, whereas the Ability Skills give them abilities based on their unique abilities, that is, Mors is a Warg and has a dog (aptly named "The Dog" GG for creativity...) and Alester is a Red Priest of R'hllor. The character's stats affect the armour and weapon proficiencies, however, the stance they choose doubles the points placed one weapon type from each of the three weapon sections, and one armour type, obviously allowing for a more rapid spec, and increasing the gameplays dependence on items. The traits are interesting, as the name suggests, they are traits which have little bonuses. However, the starting traits require a balance between positive and negative effects. That said, as the game progresses, many other positive traits can be unlocked.
Gameplay revolves around three central sections: Combat, Narrative and Exploration.
Firstly, combat is not what most might expect from a 3PP RPG, there is no hacking and slashing, no button mashing... Both Mors and Alester (and the odd companion you meet throughout the story) have three orders you can place from amongst various abilities you have, these are placed in a somewhat bullet-time initiated by pressing the space bar. This is pretty cool as it allows the player to assess the situation and look at armour types, etc. Ahhhh, something I haven't mentioned yet, Armour types. There are 4 Armour Classes in Game of Thrones, unarmoured, leather, mail and plate. These correspond to three weapon types, cutting, perforating and bashing. There is a bonus 15% damage increase when using the matching weapon type, so it is important to try and match them. This is also a bit of a flaw, as you are only allowed two weapon sets at a time to switch between and changing items in the inventory is not allowed in combat, this isn’t really an issue, and most combat is fairly straight forward and victory is nearly always achievable without the need for this, but it would have been nice to have the third slot, just to even things out (as clearly it is the intention from the start to have a proficiency in one weapon type from each section, cutting perforating and bashing, yet you will assuredly find yourself sticking with, most likely, only cutting and perforating throughout the entire game). I digress... The abilities you cast/order/whatever, use a mana like resource called energy, this regens at certain rates and can be near fully regened using a restore ability once every 20 seconds.  Combat difficulty scaling is a bit unbalanced, Squire is winnable without any effort auto-attacking will win most fights. Knight will take a minor amount of effort, auto attacking will be your majority of damage which does help with energy maintenance. Lord, however, will melt your face and have you retrying most fights half a dozen times.
Secondly, the Narrative sections are pretty cool, giving some depth to the story and allowing for some player choice responses, much like mass effect or knights of the old republic. These can change the course of the game and unlock traits. This is the main story telling vehicle and allows for some time to sit back and be immersed... unfortunately, towards the end of the game, I found myself fighting to stay my patience at the false endings. My housemate, Paddy, was having a good old time listening to me become enraged at how the game was being dragged out. As for the story itself, it isn't bad. I think that those who are more interested in the TV series would find this more appealing. Initially I thought the other way around, that the book fans might be more interested, however, I realise that the character depth which looked to be developing, fell off the face of a cliff and died as the two character's paths crossed over... making the title more appealing to the TV show fans, as the characters are far less complex. That said, the title IS based off the TV Canon and not the book canon.
Thirdly the exploration section has some unique features, but does leave a lot to be desired. Frankly, the world map is tiny... especially for Westeros... Kings landing is smaller than my inner-city apartment, and other areas are equally small... I was expecting far more in this area. There is one saving grace though, MAGIC!! Both Alester and Mors have unique abilities, as a Red Priest of R'hllor and a Warg respectively, that they can use to interact with the environment. Mors can skinchange and use the dog to scout around, find hidden items, track scents and rip enemies’ throats out, which is neat. Alester can use his powers of R'hllor to find hidden items and door switches (usually hidden as sconces on the wall), which is less neat, but you know, we can’t all have overpowered dogs. There are some interesting sections where you have to solve puzzles and find your way around mazes, sometimes being allowed to think outside the box and avoid combat, or at least take on fewer opponents, which gives you the false illusion of free will, in an otherwise very linear, boxed off world.
This game, whilst not horrible, has some woeful issues. These include world design and extreme item dependency, however, if you play on the easier difficulties, you should be able to carve through the game with little worry. Taking care to remember that this is a semi-cannon game, you won't be playing as Jon Snow, or some other ♥♥♥♥♥♥y character you heart from GRRM's♥♥♥♥♥♥fest, but you will be given a somewhat interesting storyline that parallels nicely with the first season and first book of the series (thanks to GRRM having input in the script so he didn’t have to retcon the ♥♥♥♥ out of it later).
GG.

CrossCode, while unfinished as of writing, hits every note perfectly.
The game uses a pixelated retro style, with a high amount of variation in scenery, bosses, enemies, effects and different attacks. If you like this kind of art you'll be very pleased.
The gameplay is extremely fluent with a physic based projectile system. The game teaches you how to play in a very intuitive manner, you barely noticed you played a tutorial. There are no difficulty settings, which is for the better since the game wants you to be good in nearly all aspects to continue, which story-wise fits the character being a "balance-type".
The story has multiple layers, a more mysterious opening about your origin (which is not heavily followed on as of now), and the players quest to retrieve her memory.
There aren't any dialogue options, but the game has plenty of humour.

Don't let the beautiful pictures on the Steam shop page blind you; this is -in 9 of 10 cases- not what you'll actually see while playing the game. I'm not saying that the graphics of From Dust were ugly, they are not. But you watch the world from high in the air, and the tiny people of this world are just that: tiny, tiny people. But that's not the problem of the game. I admit, I was hoping for a modern version of "Populous". A proper God-simulation. But your powers as a God in this game are highly limited. Everything in this game is highly limited. Your tiny people have to discover or populate around certain obelisks before you can work wonders. Those "wonders" allow you to manipulate the world to a degree. I'd say 80% of the play time, you pick up sand and drop it somewhere else. This way you create land for your tiny people, or you dig ravines for controlling the flow of waters. It's actually quite fun for a while, but pretty soon it gets old. You are doing pretty much the same all the time. From Dust clearly is not the new Populous. The old hit from 1989 beats From Dust in the categories fun, length and complexity. The world of From Dust provides only roughly one dozen maps, and those are not really huge. Between the maps you watch the same boring sequences again and again, you do the same things again and again, move tons of sand from A to B so that after some settling you can get your tiny people to make it to the exit of the world. Maybe that's why we only got a dozen or so maps (of which the first few are pretty much meant as tutorial maps...), because the developers realized that the game concept is simply not complex and entertaining enough to motivate for more than 10 or so hours. French games are often pearls of innovation and creativity, but this one sadly, is not.

A poor man's "Graviteam Tactics Operation Star," this game will give you a nice introduction to realistic WW2 tactical wargaming for a modest price. The game comes with several campaigns and includes events/nations rarely covered in the war (you can play the Invasion of Poland and France from both sides). The graphics really aren't terribly bad by today's standards, and the combat is slow and realistic. All of your units carry on from mission to mission in the campaigns, and they gain experience accordingly (they are all named and have semi-independent portraits so you can follow individual soldiers or squads if you are so inclined). The game also comes with a nice editor and plenty of user made missions on sites like Moddb.
Overall, for $5 its a steal. It is the only game in the series that actually works on my PC without huge frame rate issues, and it is the most diverse in terms of units, dates, scenarios, environments, etc. You more than likely won't regret the dropping the modest price on it.

An excellent game in the now very competitive 4X/Grand Strategy space game renaissance we seem to be enjoying right now.  Personally, I like to play the game on slow and let everything unfold before me.  During slow or down times, this gives me an opportunity to read a bit or just relax.  Others prefer to crank up the speed to get to the good stuff and that's fine too--I like flexibility in these things. The ship designer gets the job done for me and there are plenty of mods with excellent designs--as with most Paradox games, Stellaris is mod friendly.  There are several storylines in the game.  That, along with the ethics, civics, and government system provides an almost infinite amount of playability.  Added to that, more stories are being added on a regular basis through DLC.  Getting to DLC, I've noticed that seems to be a bit of a sore spot among some players.  Speaking for myself and myself only, I have no problem paying for DLCs--the designers and developers put in time and effort to create them, I think they should be compensated for their labor.  I don't find the prices that expensive--sales are frequent here and elsewhere, so if you're patient, you can generally get good deals on DLC, but if you want it immediately, the price isn't that high--I'll definitely be picking up the new expansion when it comes out.  Your milage might vary of course and that's fine.  If I come across as a Paradox fanboy, well, the simple truth is that I do enjoy their products--sometimes they hit a fly ball or ground to short, but usually when I see Paradox I can expect a good game and that's what's important to me--a good and fun game, good customer service, moving quickly to fix problems, and continued love and care for their products is what I expect from a game company and, for me, Paradox has never failed to deliver and it most definitely delivers here with Stellaris.

I strongly disagree with many of the negative reviews. For that I'll probably get thumbs downs on my review, but I stand by my thoughts on this game.
For Borstal:
You get a quick introduction with a short story, and then you're thrown into the randomly generated map.  You can only see one tile in any direction, but each time you move more appear. There are houses, hills, rocks, and other events that come up as you move. You can find useful or rotten items in various places in each map, but there aren't any random events that will kill you or damage you. You have to eat food, rest, etc. to stay alive while you try to find the Borstal. You must also be cautious of the weather, staying out or sleeping out in the rain will give you sickness. There are a fair amount of items you can get for the length of the game, such as food, matches, lanterns, wood, aspirin, apples, jam, and a knife. Once you get to the Borstal, depending on the supplies you have and the choices you make, you'll get one of a few different endings. It's a simple concept but very interesting for me.
For Mountain:
This mode seems much more difficult to stay alive in, due to altitude sickness. In this mode, the randomly generated map is completely filled out for you to see from the beginning, and you can generally see the "peak" flag that you have to get to, then get back to base camp, in order to win. Items in Mountain include food, tents, an altitude tracker, altitude sickness tracker, and rope. There are different and more difficult mechanics in this novella than in Borstal, in my opinion. It was much harder but certainly still enjoyable.
There are some "bug-like" things that I and a friend found. You can stay in a house and spam 1 and Z (Rest, confirm, rest confirm, rest, confirm...) and you'll stay alive infinitely, with no need for food, although it has a flashing red "you need to eat" indicator. There are also some ways to seemingly "cheat" the game, so I don't know if they're overpowered strategies or design flaws or something else.
Overall, it took me 1.1 hours to beat the game and get all achievements, but $3 is a low asking price, especially if there's more content to come. I plan to play more to test different strategies and find more endings, but that being said, I'd be happy with paying $3 for what I got (although I did get it in a bundle, it was one of the main reasons I got it).
Final Rating: 8/10

When I first purchased Borstal, it was still in an early stage of development and had many glitches.  The mountain scenario, especially, felt very random, and certain events made absolutely no sense.  For instance, I recall when if I simply moved, I would die suddenly and without any prior warning; essentially for no reason at all.
While there are still some random events in each scenario, you are not always destined to doom or success based on how the map generates during a round of play.  I think that aspect of the game could be fine tuned even further, but then, this is a game about survival.  Sometimes, despite our best efforts, things happen.  The real question is that of how you will adapt to your environment and which resources you will choose in order to face the expected and the unexpected challenges ahead of you.
Both scenarios are short and can be completed in less than 10 minutes, but you will not discover everything about each scenario in one round, or even two rounds.  Until this week, I encountered storylines that I had not previously seen, having already played each scenario dozens of times.  So replay value is high.
This game will not appeal to everyone, but if you are a casual gamer or you need a short game to play everyday before work/school/bed, Borstal may be just what you are looking for.

Unfortunately it didn't, and eventually gave up after about 3.5 hours of gameplay. So what makes this game so unbearable bad? Well lets start off with the gameplay itself, if you can even call it that.
So when you first start playing the game you get the option to gather some supplies from a crate that you are next to. You are able to go back to these crates to continue to grab supplies as and when you need them. You are then given a couple of slots in your inventory to pick up a few items of your choice. So after you have chosen these items you are then able to move around. Now even for a cheap game I would expect to see animations when you move your character. Well guess what? There is no animation, which really makes the game fall flat. That on top of the game being like a grid when you move around really isn't very impressive for todays average indie games.
The map that you are presented with isn't very good, with the crates that you spawn on top of you are constantly going back and fourth to the crate to make sure that you don't starve to death or die in general. Now throughout the map you can find a few places such as houses and caves that you may think that you can enter and it might have some actual content to the game. But it turns out that you get some text and options when you enter a house and that's about it. The game REALLY needs to have more content, because for a game that costs £1.99 I would expect to be more content than what is in this game. I think that it's also fair to say that his game has WAY too much RNG throughout. For example the houses might say that is abandoned, but if you exit it and then enter it, it might say that the house was a fisher mans. This just shows that the game has too much RNG for it to make sense.
The graphics of this game is just pixel graphics. It seems that pixel graphics are rather other used in todays gaming age and only some games really nail it and work well with it. Borstal isn't one of those game, the graphics just don't work with the sort of game that the developer was trying to make.

Disclaimer: This is an early-access review of CrossCode. I have not completed the game, and some parts of this review will be out of pure speculation. I will update this review at some point to reflect the final version.
CrossCode is a top-down hack-slash RPG that takes place inside an MMORPG. And it is awesome and immersive. No seriously, at times, I actually felt like I was playing CrossWorlds, the MMORPG that CrossCode is set in. Players (as in "you") play the role of Lea, a mute amnesiac who was a former player of the game but, due to the amnesia, had to start over (with the help of the game's programmers), which unfortunately caused problems with her voice module (making her mute). Her eventual goal is to get to Rhombus Square, which was the place she last was before she lost her memory, in the hopes that that'll fix things. Along the way, she partners up with a player named Emilie and another player named C'Thon.
Oh right, you want to know about the gameplay. Alright then.
CrossCode is, as I've said, a top-down hack-slash RPG. Lea has three main attacks; a melee swipe, a quick projectile throw, and a slower, charged projectile throw. As you defeat enemies (which respawn periodically around the map, and usually don't attack you if you just leave them alone), your rank goes up (rank functions like a combat meter), and a higher rank gives you better item drops and more XP/currency. Accruing enough XP allows you to level up, which allows you to unlock skills, abilities, and upgrades via the in-game skill tree. Currency is used for buying and trading items, which will further serve to strengthen Lea's stats.
(It should be noted that while you only need 1000 XP per level to level up, the XP gains of everything decrease per level. It helps to think of the XP gains as permillages of the required XP to level up.)
At the start, enemies in the game are fairly easy to beat and require no skill or thought at all; just mindless attack-attack-attack. However, this soon gets thrown out the window with the first boss, which requires you to be able to dodge attacks well. A fair amount of the game's combat is based around dodging, at least if you're not strong enough to completely pulverize everything in your path and/or tank the damage; often in the game, you can end up in a situation where you fall prey to a short series of high-powered attacks from different enemies and have half your lifebar depleted.
Besides the dodging, almost all enemies seem to have a different strategy for tackling them. This is most pronounced with the bosses, which are often armoured, and usually require you to attack them from behind, or hit a weak-spot enough times to stun it before going in for the kill. However, many non-bosses also follow a similar pattern; attack them at just the right time (usually when they're charging for an attack), and you can completely stun them for a bit.
The aforementioned skill tree allows you to unlock skills for use in combat. One skill allows you to do a giant whirling slash with your blade; another allows you to fire a quick volley of projectiles in a narrow beam, and so on. These "combat arts", as they are called, require 1 SP each to use (out of a total SP of 4). The first SP recharges over time, but the other 3 SP need to be gained by attacking enemies with normal attacks.
The game has four different "elements" you can use when in combat, plus a fifth no-element. Each element can damage some enemies more than others, and each has their own specific combat skills. That giant whirling slash? That's now a whirling slash, ON FIRE. However, it should be noted that using an element in combat for too long results in "elemental overload", which forces you into no-element combat for a cooldown.
Emilie and C'Thon, the two other members of your party, will naturally fight alongside you. You can command their combat behaviours (e.g. which enemy they attack) via an in-game menu (which also allows you to use healing items, as well as point out key items/NPCs/enemies on the screen). If either one dies, they come back into battle after a minute or so; if you die, however, it's game over and you start from the very beginning of the room, having lost all your loot and XP from said combat session.
In short, the combat is very smooth and, in a way, therapeutic. It is, however, not easy; especially in some areas of the map, where your party members aren't with you. It can be easy to get complacent with letting them do the work, until you stumble upon such a region and everything becomes three times harder.
In addition to the hack-slash gameplay, the world also has some number of puzzle dungeons with switches in them (I think four, but I'm not too sure as I haven't get played that far). Said puzzle-dungeons are Legend-of-Zelda-like, in that they first introduce some new mechanics that work with the tools you already have. Then you're given a new tool (which also grants you an element to use in combat), and presented with some puzzles involving that. Overall, the puzzles can be very difficult at times, but all are fair.
Interspersed within each puzzle dungeon are a number of combat sections (without Emilie and C'Thon), which must be passed in order to progress. I'm not a huge fan of these as I'm not quite so great at hack-slashers, but I'm sure many people do need breaks from puzzling (unlike me), so while I personally might not enjoy these sections, I'm sure others won't mind it.
There are multiple "secret" crates scattered around all the levels, too. These are usually tucked away in locations that aren't easy to reach; oftentimes you'll need to jump up a few ledges, then parkour your way across the map to get to said crates. Later on, you'll need to hit switches to open up paths so you can keep parkouring. Said crates contain useful loot, like health/quest items or weapons.
CrossCode, being an RPG, obviously has sidequests. These can be of the form "acquire these set of items", "find these things on the map", or "defeat these enemies". Each sidequest comes with a recommended level, so you know when a quest is out of your depth. Still, there's nothing stopping you from just going around and accepting every single quest you come across, while biding your time before you're of a strong enough level to do said quests.
The humour in the game is quite nice. Owing to Lea's muteness (except for the word "Hi" which was manually programmed in), a good few conversations of the game make some reference or another to this (e.g. "If there's anything that's troubling you, just say! I feel better talking to you already!"). Some other conversations make reference to the NPCs not being actual people and hence having limited interactions (combined with Lea's muteness, this results in the NPCs just saying their pre-scripted dialogue). There are puns (the main part of the CrossWorlds world is called The Crossant due to its shape, and one important item you can get is called the "Hi-Sandwich").
As it is now, remember that the game is still in Early Access, so the game is indeed incomplete; at one point, a dialogue box popped up saying that "This marks the temporary end of the story for this version" (but it still allowed me to play on); at another point, I collected a key to a building only to find that the interior of said building was inaccessible. However, in this case, I think it's justified; the scope of this game is so large that it's not at all unreasonable to ask for feedback/bugtesting from a community.
In short, a well-crafted game. It's the only game so far that I've actually had to stop playing because my eyes hurt. I've clocked over 20 hours so far, and I'm still not halfway-through. If you're at all interested in hack-slash puzzle RPGs, CrossCode is DEFINITELY a game I can recommend, even while it's still in development. If you have any doubts, check out the ~45-minute demo, which is in fact playable in-browser at
.

This is honestly one of my Favorite Games Ever, and the game that got me into the Resident Evil series (i played RE2 back in the day, but never liked it as much as i like this). The story Isn't Terrible, which places it above a lot of games, and i really enjoy the sort of deliberately unrealistic and colorful characters that the series is known for-- it's preposterous, but on purpose, so i like it. Jessica thought the Mediterranean was a lake, your boss is Columbo, the obvious traitor is obvious, the Dante-quoting terrorist is the guy from Breaking Bad, Rachael is ON THE SCENE, everything is Italian for no apparent reason, the women are all going commando (in every sense), and Chris has the personality of a block of wood but gosh darn it i like him anyway. It's Big Fun and i love it. And i haven't even mentioned the Raid Mode yet, which exists alongside the story mode, almost as an entirely separate game...
...And it is by god the most capital-f Fun i've had with a game in years. If you like DOOM or Serious Sam-style shooters that are defined by matching the correct weapon against a varied set of visually distinct enemies, always prioritizing the most dangerous thing in the room, then this is precisely for you. Raid Mode in this game is a huge, sprawling thing filled with probably way too much gameplay, and frankly i'm still not really sick of it after more than a year. The challenge is just Exactly Right, and while there's admittedly a bit of grinding involved, beating the ultra-tough Ghost Ship is the rare achievement in video games that's actually worth doing. At first it seems literally impossible, but eventually you own it, Dark Souls-style, and the comparison is a fair one.
Atmospheric, endlessly replayable, good Achievements, sexy people, addictive Raid Mode, and just flat-out FUN-- it's the best, i tell you. A millon out of ten.
PS: the camera is zoomed in way too much, so download Widescreen Fixer and set the FOV to about 75 and you're good to go-- it's a super easy fix and makes it way more playable.

Being an HD remake of the original 3DS game Revelations is not going to win awards neither on ps3 or pc for its visuals. Character models are decent, while most of the environmental objects are rather simplified and textures are also quite low resolution. While I traversed through the "world" I got used to it however. In the end the muddy visuals even add to the atmosphere.
Controls while being the best in the series, still far worse than most of the shooters I have played. And believe me I tried a few really bad one. I used keyboard and mouse, which is far better than anything on console, even modified the fov to 85 degrees, so I had the most pleasant way. Still, as the previous titles, RE's controls are still rather clunky and they simply cannot be compared to a refined control system.
Revelations mostly takes place on a luxury cruiser abandoned in the open ocean. This means that there are rather dark and tight corridors in the crew area and a few more open and better lighted spaces like a hall, a solarium, a casino and a cafeteria. The overall feeling while exploring is quite similar to the first game's. You have to collect a bunch of different keys to open up initially closed parts of the ship. Bactracking is quite usual. Resource management is also taken into account, however it feels somewhat simplified. In addition the player has a scanner which can be used to search for hidden items in the vicinity. I think that exploration is the strongest part of the franhchise and Revelations definitely has some of it. My biggest problem was the other half of the game which was featured sequences. In these parts of the campaign the player controls different characters in various places and dates. This pretty much adds to the story element while basically negating any advancement the player gained through item upgrades as these segments are using separate and partially fixed weapons and ammo. I feel that there is a need for these snippets to glue the story together, but there are too many of them, some of them even being annoying and almost pointless.
Music is a mixed bag. More intense scenes have annoying background tracks, while the slower exploration parts have less prominent, but decent enough soundtrack to aid the the atmosphere. Overall sound quality is decent. Guns and monsters sound generic, but they are immersive enough. Voice acting is acceptable.
Raid mode lets players replay segments from the campaign with unique enemy spawns and scattered loot. It is pretty simple and cheap at times. There is a score system based on accuracy, finish time and taken damage similarly to the campaign. Finishing longer levels with the no damage medal is frustrating due to mechanics and monster spawn. Better gear can be gained and upgraded with parts which also gathered through levels. Additional upgrades can be bought from the raid store which expands inventory size for various items for example. A few of them carries over to the campaign, I heard. I did not see any of it, but who knows.
In addition for those who are finished the campaign there is a NG+ mode with all the weapons and upgrades maintained. An option to change outfits will also appear in the campaign menu. This is definitely adds some variety on the second run.
Overall, I am not a big fan of the Resident Evil series, mostly due to the infamous tank controls scheme. This is the first game that I could play through. I like the exploration, but I need proper mechanics to enjoy it which is while far not perfect, but still decent enough in Revelations' case.

I've never played a Resident Evil game before, and for my first one, Revelations did a great job keeping me on my toes. It was constantly dancing the line between survival horror and traditional third-person shooter, and I never felt like I had enough ammo to feel fully comfortable. The Genesis device was used to its full potential due to the myriad of hidden objects, invisible/difficult-to-spot enemies, and the storyline was full of cliffhangars and drove me insane because my work only gave me enough time to finish a single chapter every night.
I have two major criticisms: the dodge mechanic is unreliable at best, I never used it because it didn't seem to do anything. On occasion my character would dodge an attack but it felt completely divorced from whatever buttons I was pressing at the time. This meant that I mostly shot my way out of situations, which necessitated heavy usage of the Genesis device and my AI partner to keep my limited ammo stocked up. But complaint number two is that your AI partner is almost useless. The doors in this game only allow one charcter through at a time, meaning your partner shows up late to every fight, never seems to bother shooting anything and can't seem to hit anything with the few shots they take.
But all in all, the game is well worth playing. The swimming mechanics are some of the smoothest I've seen in this sort of game and the arsenal of weapons and enemies is diverse and keeps things interesting. Wish more PC ports were like this one.

Why you should get NieR: Automata
It is easily one of the best games I've ever played in my many years of gaming. It connects to you on a personal level and enraptures you with the beautiful music and art. You get to experience the game through a few characters instead of a lone hero, allowing you to view battles and choices from different perspectives. It perfectly plays out like a story book, with twists and tragic turns, it is never boring.
You might think that it is just another game overly hyped to be full of feels and somewhat lacklustre action. Yes it is very touching because they executed the atmosphere perfectly. The appropriate music is played whenever an action is taken. If something took a turn for the worse, an immensely dark music will play and make you wonder why did they do it. Gameplay wise, it is very challenging if you played in on hard mode. Just a tip: don't choose hard mode until you reach the first save. it requires you to be on your toes at all times just like dark souls; loss of items on death. The evasion mechanics is very fun to play around with and it takes some skill to handle some of the bullet hell moments.
Sure, there are technical difficulties surrounding the game. It is unfortunate that Square Enix has not produced a fix as of now. However, the fan made mod, FAR, has done a decent job. Great job eliminating pirates and the technical faults. I have not encountered any problems at all after using the mod. Currently on GTX 1060 and i5-6600. Just save regularly to avoid disappointments. Don't let the reviews on technical difficulties bother you. The installation of the FAR mod has made the game immensely playable.
A little sad that Square Enix jacked up the price in SEA. But seriously, buy this fantastic game!

An excellent game in the now very competitive 4X/Grand Strategy space game renaissance we seem to be enjoying right now.  Personally, I like to play the game on slow and let everything unfold before me.  During slow or down times, this gives me an opportunity to read a bit or just relax.  Others prefer to crank up the speed to get to the good stuff and that's fine too--I like flexibility in these things. The ship designer gets the job done for me and there are plenty of mods with excellent designs--as with most Paradox games, Stellaris is mod friendly.  There are several storylines in the game.  That, along with the ethics, civics, and government system provides an almost infinite amount of playability.  Added to that, more stories are being added on a regular basis through DLC.  Getting to DLC, I've noticed that seems to be a bit of a sore spot among some players.  Speaking for myself and myself only, I have no problem paying for DLCs--the designers and developers put in time and effort to create them, I think they should be compensated for their labor.  I don't find the prices that expensive--sales are frequent here and elsewhere, so if you're patient, you can generally get good deals on DLC, but if you want it immediately, the price isn't that high--I'll definitely be picking up the new expansion when it comes out.  Your milage might vary of course and that's fine.  If I come across as a Paradox fanboy, well, the simple truth is that I do enjoy their products--sometimes they hit a fly ball or ground to short, but usually when I see Paradox I can expect a good game and that's what's important to me--a good and fun game, good customer service, moving quickly to fix problems, and continued love and care for their products is what I expect from a game company and, for me, Paradox has never failed to deliver and it most definitely delivers here with Stellaris.

This game is hands down my favorite 4X strategy game right now, and it has been for a very long while. It's interesting in that it plays mostly in real time, rather than being turn-based. Combat can be fairly in-depth, or you can just let the game auto-design ships for you and usually turn out fine, but either way it mostly does amount to watching your fleet shoot at the enemy fleet. (What did you expect? It's a 4X game, not Starcraft.) The tech tree isn't so much a tree as a cloud; you get a semi-random selection of possible technologies to research each time you complete one, and some technologies can improve your options for the future. The AI works surprisingly well, becoming a fair challenge with the right settings. And, most importantly for me, you get to customize your species from their appearance to their preferred type of planet, from major traits to minor abilities... and, with the right research and the right amount of planning, you can change these traits some more while the game is already in progress.
I'm the ruler of a galactic empire of jungle cats, and I love it.
Now, bear in mind: I haven't bought any of the DLC, I haven't installed any mods, and I haven't played multiplayer. This review is based entirely on the vanilla single-player experience. So if you're looking for a review of Stellaris's multiplayer and/or extra content, you'll have to ask someone else. But if you're after a great way to spend a week or so (which could very well be a century in-game) conquering the galaxy by yourself – which is exactly what I'm after – then Stellaris is the way to do it.

This game's gotten some good and bad reviews, and I'm not 100% sure why the bad reviews except for maybe a bad port to PC. There is a solution for that: it's called a controller. It took me all of about two seconds to realize I needed to pull mine out of the drawer and connect it in order to have a better experience with this game. Do that and remember you're playing an RPG (because fighting is a pause-and-plan affair), and it's a good and immersive game in the style of the books or the show. You'll start as one character, a member of the Night's Watch, play a chapter, then switch to a noble--with a twist (the screenshot should clue you in to what the twist is)--and by about the fourth or fifth chapter, you start to see how they're tying it together. Story-wise, it's done in Game of Thrones style, combat-wise, it's a standard RPG, pause-and-plan with a means of controlling various members of your party and a means of regenerating energy for attacks without requiring potions (though they are available if you want them).
I highly, HIGHLY recommend a controller if you have one because without one, it's a bit of a hassle to deal with clunky controls. With a controller, though, it's a decent game with a decent story...though a bit too 'on rails' with a lot of invisible walls preventing players from really getting to explore some areas. As small as some maps are, the invisible walls aren't really necessary. It is worth noting, however, that some of the main characters, such as Mormont and Varys are voiced by the actors who portray those characters on the show, though Cersei is not voiced in the game by Lena Headey--which is a bit of a disappointment after hearing James Cosmo as Mormont and Conleth Hill as Varys.  Clunky PC controls requiring a controller and invisible walls make me only rate it about a 7 overall.

Also the AI is pretty dumb in most situations, but the combat, once you get used to it, feels solid and challenging enough to not get boring, and the AI being predicatble can be considered a good thing, as it allows youto build up your own strategy of how to deal with different groups of enemies.
Plays well with KB/Mouse, no problems at all. And the graphics options and toggles that you would expect a PC game to have are all there.
Final thoughts:
Great game, with a great story, that looks a bit dated, but doesn't have any major glaring bugs and accomplishes what it sets out to do, which is tell you a story while giving you enough gameplay in between to make you feel apart of the story and that what you do matters.

Borstal is an interesting duo of miniature survival games in which you play as the most fragile human beings on planet earth. Pitched in the description as more interactive novellas, the two scenarios provided play out like only the most classic turn based survival, harkening more to the style of NEO Scavenger than Rust in that the most engaging aspect is the text based story and randomized encounters rather than the graphics and crafting and whatnot.
Even though both scenarios are similar in structure, I feel that they provided such different experiences that I'll be addressing them seperately. You'll understand why in a moment, as I feel this may make or break a purchase, or at the very least provide some input to the developer.
Borstal, the titular title and "main campaign" is one where you play as a young boy who's trying to find his dad that worked at a--you guessed it--borstal, which in american terms is a Juvenial Delinquency center. In the game's world, the borstal is on an otherwise deserted island. Don't ask how this works, because I have no clue, but don't let it ruin the fun either.  Every time you start a new game, the map is completely randomized, and there are obstacles and threats around every turn. You can find clues as to what happened to your dad, and encounter rogue bands of kiddies who, depending on what you've found and how good your RNG is can give you good stuff to help you survive or beat your head in. It's constantly raining, and you need a decent stream of sleep and food to survive until you find your dad. The sooner you do, the better the ending, but when you find the borstal and what you've experienced up to that point can influence the turn of events greatly.
I think I experienced 4 different endings in my time, and there were still options I hadn't made which makes me remember this one a bit more fondly. The over all story is a bit too vague, and I feel as if I missed some huge context clues, but the change of pace and setting to what I've been playing recently and the dumbed down but reasonable survival mechanics made it a joy. Plus, there are some exploits that I discovered that made my later journies much more bareable, though I won't spoil them here as the difficulty is part of the charm. The titular game will take multiple tries, but the rounds are bitesized and I genuinely learned from every mistake I made.
Now we get to the stinker of the bunch, called Mountain. Now, I can see the appeal to making a deathly realistic simulation of scaling a massive mountain, and for the most part, I feel that Borstal succeeds in emulating the experience. But--and this is a big enough but for a Sir Mix-a-Lot song--Mountain suffers from some game ending glitches that shocked and baffled me each time they happened. Now the conceit is more or less the same if a bit more straight forward; reach the summit then make it back to the basecamp. Along the way, there are abandoned tents and what not that have randomized events and visible obstacles that need to be navigated with rope. Your needs are about the same, but the demand for rest and food is increased the higher up you go, and requires you to strategize your ascent so you don't get to the top and not have a way back.
In theory.
The problem is--and there are plenty of problems with Mountain--is that for every other death I had, there was absolutely no warning or justification for any of it. Now keep in mind, this is a text heavy game; I'm not criticising it for that. However, for every death where I was offered a bleak end to a risk that backfired or mistake I made, there would be points where I wouldn't have a single indicator on my screen that I was low on sleep or health or close to death, and I would take a step forward on completely clear terrain and just get a YOU DIED screen. Then, in an insanely insulting and borderline rage quit moment, I reached the summit, got a standard "you have a headache" type message that you get throughout the climb and made it all the way back, only to realize that that message OVERRIDED the "Good job, now go back." I died almost immediately after. This situation in which the progess message was overrided happened multiple times. Often times I would get to the summit in perfect health, get a "your head hurts" message and then immediately die. Other times I would be in fine health, with no warning signs, get a warning sign that I'm near death, rest in a tent and then die the moment I hit the button. This happened a handful of times. That was also pretty awful. Are you starting to see why this is the bad egg?
After 77(!) tries, I discovered an exploit, did a sidequest, and made it to the top and back without a hitch. I made it back fine because the base camp was only a few tiles away. It was a combination of what was basically cheating and a whole lot of luck. Hopefully the developer sees this and polishes out the bugs, because that ain't good at all.
But Razorbitz, is it worth the 3 dollar price tag? Absolutely. It's definitely old school and the cards are often stacked against you, but for both scenarios you're provided the tools to survive.  It isn't a masterpiece, but it's cheap asking price and experimental style makes for a flawed but genuinely engaging adventure. Assuming the kinks are worked out of Mountain, this is a nice surprise from the indie front and I'm glad I picked it up day 1. I never do that. Here's hoping that the developer makes some more stories to throw in over time as well!

There are plenty of extra features in the multiplayer Raid Mode, which is mainly re-runs of campaign missions with twists on them.  Namely, you'll be able to play as other characters, get other costumes for those characters etc.  It may sound like it's cheap to just re-do the levels, but I assure you that they are much more difficult in the Raid Mode and will provide a good challenge for someone who has already experienced what the campaign has to offer.

Anodyne is one of these short sweet indie games that offer a great experience while it last. The story stars with a character named young waking up to find himself in a dreamrelm. He then comes across a sage who says he is the chosen one and must   defeat the creatures in order to escape. What makes the story special is how the bosses and NPC's seem to have different ideas about what is going on and sharing them with you. The gameplay is very similar to the old Legend of Zelda games. Both have an overhead view and use a weapon for stabbing your enemies. The main differences come with the limited items and main weapon. You use a broom throughout the game to dispatch enemies and activate switches and the only usable item you obtain is some jumping shoes that allow you to jump which is used allot in later areas. The game looks fantastic with a retro art style. It fits the world and setting nicely and the game isn’t afraid of some dark tones when it wants to. The settings are also quite unique where you find yourself in a hotel or a strange universe instead of your usual dungeons and temples. Music is nice most of the time and has some nice tracks that I wouldn’t mind downloading. Anodyne mages to bring back the dying overhead action adventure genre and does it in such a well way. The game may only be 5-6 hours long but it is well worth the money and it was only made by two guys in less than a year. Pick it up some time and experience it for yourself.

tl;dr : Super fun TD with a simplistic approach but a lot of depth.
Extremely fun and addictive TD game with a simplistic (but super efficient) approach. You can always be challenged more. And you can always progress.
Just 3 monster types but many modifiers. And enraging. And occasional special monsters (flying ones). And beacons to take care of. And things to destroy. And special objectives to unlock skills and traits.
Just 9 gem types but all the combinations are possible. And they do different things in towers, traps and amplifiers. And you can also use them as bombs. Or to enrage waves for more challenge.
The game is simplistic but never boring thanks to a lot of variation in what happens, what you need to do (apart from building towers), and what you can do.
Dozens of levels, very cool "spell crafting" mechanic, very customizable and rewarding difficulty system, hundreds of achievements (which give a bonus so you're motivated to get them). All the systems (looting, crafting, talisman, skills, environments, achievements, traits, gem bombs, enraging, towers/traps/amplifiers, flying ones, beacons...) everything is well designed and smart. And the game is still interesting even after you played hundreds of times because it's never the same thing twice, and by increasing the difficulty you are always challenged.
I'm almost 400 hours into the game and I'm not done. I haven't even finished every map on every difficulty setting. And I even have a few achievements left to unlock.
What other game can keep you entertained for hundreds of hours for that price ?

With hundreds of hundreds tower defence games it's easy to get lost in tons of clones and mediocre titles. Looking at GemCraft's screenshots or even trailer, I've put it in "No, thanks" category. It looks like another generic, Adobe Flash based tower defence, and it's true. This painfully simple looking game has it's roots in flash, as it was released in web some time ago. What caught my attention were positive reviews of GemCraft. I bit the bullet and boy was I surprised!
Quickly, you are enveloped in minimalistic but eerie and mystical atmosphere. Curious, slowly unfolding story and dark music made it complete. With that, you slowly get to know GemCrafts mechanics. As you progress, you'll be gradually realising how big of a game GemCraft is. Though gameplay rules aren't revolutionary, the amount of features is overwhelming.
As the title says, you'll be crafting gems to defend yourself from incoming waves of monsters. That's simple, right? You'll receive a massive amount of gems that have different roles and characteristics. You'll have basic attack towers, enhancement towers and traps which you can upgrade. That's still simple and familiar. Now, here's the thing - you're free to combine and mix gems you want. You want to have highly damaging tower that also freezes enemies? Or maybe you want it to also poison and lower armour grade? Sure you can. Everything combination you can think of is possible. It's the core of the game - not only you have to decide where to place the towers, what gems to choose, how much to upgrade them but also mix them just right from your own recipe.
And it gets better. Looking at the map in between missions you'll see how gigantic it is. Even more so, you can shape missions just like a mix your gems. As you level up, gradually unlocked game modifiers can drastically transform the mission so much that your previous, perfect tactics become completely uselss. Many skills and mods offer a high reward at a price of high risk. That breaths a new life in levels that you would normally tick off as completed. As a cherry on top of the cake there are secrets that are cryptical enough to keep your curious.
That being said, GemCraft is a top notch tower defense game that despite poor initial impression will keep you playing for long. If you plan to highscore endurance levels, it will perhaps last a lifetime.
Final score : 8/10

This game is way too simple, way too RNG, and just feels rushed, lazy, and randomly put together.  It's not the overly simple graphics that make this game fail, because I am one of the few gamers these days that can have a hell of a lot of fun with simplistic graphics.
You start the game off with two choices, Borstal or Mountain.  Either choice puts you into a spot on a map where you can move one block at a time and then get completely random feedback.  Every move feels like life or death because of how fast hunger, tiredness, and ailments move on you or just "pop" up.  Theres no skill or strategy here, it's just 100% RNG, combined with utterly simple graphics.
