I’m glad I decided to play this game! The only reason I started playing it was because I finished Saints Row 4 and loved it, which made me want more. As it turns out Saints Row 2 feels like it hardly belongs in the same franchise as the fourth game. Volition have truly reinvented the franchise as they’ve gone from title to title, only keeping the characters and setting as they go. This explains why the people who loved the second game and wanted more of that tend to complain loudly about the third and fourth games. They’re just not the same. Personally I think reinventing and iterating are both equally valid approaches for a series to take. I like the variety, and you certainly can’t accuse them of retreading the same ground like I’ve seen some do with Rockstar and the GTA series.
Saints Row 2 came out in 2008, and it feels like a game of its time. It might not seem like 2008 is that far back, but when you play games of that time they all feel old now, as does Saints Row 2. At that time I remember games journalists were talking about emergent gameplay instead of story, and it shows in Saints Row 2’s design. Compared to any major game released in 2013 this feels like complete chaos. Instead of the world acting like a virtual movie set with carefully staged combat, the game instead relies on world simulation systems and AI to act on its own. This approach makes it nearly impossible for a developer to tell a story during missions, because the minute to minute gameplay is completely unpredictable. Instead the designer only choreographs the action with commands like: Go there, kill that, chase that car, etc.
Even during missions the world simulation present in the free exploration mode is in full effect. So when you take over areas of the map you’ll have friendly thugs spawn there. If a mission happens to take place there, or a car chase goes through neighborhoods controlled by your gang, groups of friendly thugs will spawn and rain bullets on your pursuers. If during a mission an enemy shoots a civilian standing near you, police will arrive on the scene and start fighting the enemy gangsters with you. The last time I saw this kind of three way combat break out spontaneously was in the Stalker games. I wish we had more games like this, especially on the next-gen consoles where the extra memory and power could allow much more elaborate world simulation. That would in some way fulfill “the point” of next-gen hardware. Making something you couldn’t do on 360/ps3, just like this game is something that couldn’t exist on PS2.
Anyway, I had a great time blowing through this game. It’s messy, ugly, glitch, but it all comes together to create something special. One thing I was pleasantly surprised by was the quality of the cutscenes. In Saints Row 4 they were generally very high quality, but in a couple scenes I found the sound to be a bit crap. In Saints Row 2 the sound during cutscenes is phenomenal. It’s raw, violent and has about as much impact as you could hope to have. It fits perfectly with the story itself which in the “Brotherhood” missions turns into an ugly conflict where neither side appear noble or heroic in any way. It’s dark, gruesome and I was even shocked at one scene where the game made it abundantly clear that the player isn’t a hero anyone should aspire to be. So I finally get where the hype about Saints Row 2 has come from. If you know you’re a fan of slightly janky games with outstanding qualities you’ll probably like this. Those wanting a slick, modern, controlled experience should avoid it like the plague.

This game is a huge letdown.  I bought it after seeing videos of Rebirth and Afterbirth on YouTube, thinking it would be similar, but with a worse engine/platform and fewer items.  Actually playing through the game, though, is a much worse experience than I expected.
Between 90 and 95% of my runs are bad because I can't find any good items, and most of the remainder are often screwed over by unfair rooms.  For example, one of the rooms consists of a bunch of 1-character-wide "bridges", and it often features a bunch of suicide bombers and other enemies that charge at you.  They're impossible to kill before they get too close unless you have an incredibly overpowered build or flying.
Another grievance I have is that hitboxes are based on the shadows of projectiles, enemies, and your character.  This makes it extremely difficult to dodge bullet hell areas, since avoiding the projectiles themselves often doesn't work.
These and many other things about the game make it not worth the money unless it's on a great sale.  All in all, it's not a very fun game.  It punishes you for what amounts to not winning the RNG lottery, and I don't think anyone would count that as good gameplay.

- Raid mode (coop mode) is quite fun to play with your friends, you can unlock funny/odd characters and weapons and it has 20 stages with 3 levels of difficulty each (Chasm/trench/Abyss) plus one extra stage called "the ghost ship".

Amazing tower defense game with astounding - at some times, intimidating - depth and customization.
Every facet of the player's build can be customized, with skill points obtained as the character levels up and glyphs that fit in the talisman providing passive bonuses in battle. Wizard scrolls add set difficulty penalties to levels, but allow for much greater experience gain. In battle, tower and trap locations, gem strength, abilities, & range, and even the number and strength of enemy waves can be controlled and micromanaged as much or as little as desired.
Many levels have optional challenges or strategies that can be employed, and the later levels open up greatly, allowing the player to contruct intricate mazes for the monsters to traverse.
There are definitely optimal set-ups, and the game loses a bit of charm once these optimal set-ups are discovered and utilized, but it is still very compelling and fun.

- Depth
- Skill System
- Map Diversity
- 20+ Hour Campaign
- Replay Value
- Community Guides
- Gem Combining
- Repetitive
The depth of GemCraft lies within its strong crafting system.  By the end of the game you are given nine seperate gem colors that all affect the battlefield in a diffferent way.  Along with this you are given traps, towers and amplifiers which all use the gems differently on the battlefield.  Combining the nine gem colors in different ways alters the way that the tower, trap or amplifier fight for you on the battlefield.
The skill system is a great way to boost your performance on a level to level base.  The great twist is that you have to complete levels throughout the game to unlock these skills and then decide how you want to spend your points.  They can affect anything.  From directly boosting all gem damage to allowing your amplifiers to increase attack, you get to decide what the best lay out is for your play style.
After the first few tilesets, the maps really branch out in interesting and unique ways.
The campaign for this game lasts for quite some time.  You are offered several paths to go as you progress through the game, each allowing you to unlock more game features.  Even after you beat the game, there are three difficulties tied to each map.  On top of that you have the option of setting traits before each map starts to make the battle harder for you, but as a reward offering you more experience.  Additionaly once you beat the game, you can unlock iron wizard mode which is a fun challenge.
One of the best features of this game is the community.  There are several great guides out, and after you have progressed through the game on your own I encourage you to look at the great work in the community tab to help you further your progress within the game.
There are unfortunately a few negative things within GemCraft.  One of the biggest problems is not being able to save or macro gem combinations.  There are a couple external programs, that the truely devout use, but it would have been great for them to include a save mechanic in game for commonly crafted gems so you didn't always have to combine them by hand or use and external service.  DO NOT GET ME WRONG, this is in no way game breaking and does not affect someone who is just playing through the game the first time.  This is a grievance for end game play.
Lastly, one of the biggest let downs with GemCraft becomes the repetitveness of the actual game.  Once you understand the key fundamentals at all difficulties it is more or less a rinse and repeat.
Overall, GemCraft is in my opinion the pinnacle of what a tower defense game should be.  This game should be an instant buy when on sale.  And at full price is a great game for people who enjoy the tower defense genre.

For those of you who are reluctant to buy because of controls: The controls for shooting on an XBox 360 controller will definitely feel a bit awkward at first but over time you will become acustomed to them and it will feel more natural. I started out using an XBox controller (first 5 or so hours) but I had ordered a steam controller which, in my opinion, is the absolute best control option due to how customizable it is. Using the tracpad to aim and rebinding the right stick click to shoot while also having attack on right bumper for melee makes it very easy to quickly switch between melee and ranged combat. for those of you who don't know, the combat is a little unorthodox but I think the system works well. If the right stick is in the neutral position, pressing right bumper will do a melee attack. if you move the right stick, an aiming reticle will show up in the direction you point the stick and pressing right bumper will throw projectiles. since both attacks are bound to one button, you may occasionally do a ranged attack instead of a melee attack or vice versa. this isn't really a huge issue since both are very powerful if used effectively. I haven't beaten the game yet as of me writing this review, but the 22 hours I have spent were an absolute blast. The combat is this game's strongest point by far, only matched by the diversity of the countless quests you will come across. Some quests have you helping someone track down a thief, while others have you fight a horde of regular enemies followed by a really strong version of an enemy you've fought before which forces you to apply everything you learned fighting the regular enemies. between dashing, blocking, ranged attacks and melee attacks, and specials for each of the categories, the combat is incredibly fun and deep. This is one of my favorite games on steam right now due to how jam-packed it is with things to do. One of my other favorite games at the moment is Secrets of Grindea. If you like this game but can't get over the controls, Secrets of Grindea plays very similarly but uses a much more controller friendly experience.

If you enjoy retro, especially if you enjoy Metroid or Zelda and games in that vein, don't miss Crosscode.

Guns of Icarus Online is a multiplayer FPS/Strategy game of sorts. Teams of 4 work together and manage an airship, one that is fitted with various weapons, perks, and/or stats that vary from airship to airship. The objective is simple: down enough enemy airships to reach the goal. However simple the objective may be, the game itself is a myriad of strategms. Teamwork is essential in this game; without it, a crew will not be able to perform at maximum capacity. However, with teamwork, skill, and a bit of luck on your side, your crew can turn a harmless looking airship into a powerful, dominating dirigible in the skies.
The mounted weapons on each ship, coupled with the tools that each class is allotted, are quite balanced and fair. No slot should be left empty, everything must be carefully selected and used. The game itself is not difficult, nor is it frustrating. Rather, it is user friendly and has quite the low learning curve.
The community in this game is quite friendly and very mature. No problems with it.

If Legend of Zelda were set in the bizarre fantasy world of a dreaming child, you'd have Anodyne. It's a top-down dungeon crawler that features a large and diverse open-world that makes exploration and discovery quite enjoyable. The game doesn't hold your hand and only offers some subtle hints of direction, although it's never really all that challenging in regards to its combat or puzzle-solving. The 16-bit pixel art style is really well done, thanks largely in part to the terrific use of color that makes for some beautiful locations. The soundtrack is memorable and helps set that dream-like atmosphere that the devs were going for. On the downside, the gamepad controls can be overly sensitive and jumping puzzles tend to become frustrating as a result. Also, while I like that the story is abtract and open to interpretation, it feels unfocused and seems to serve mostly as an excuse to explore some eccentric locales.
In all, Anodyne is a solid Zelda-clone that's able to thrive on its colorful artwork, well-designed dungeons, and a soundtrack that is worth the price of admission by itself.

I don't mind games that offer challenges. I actually like games that offer challenges.
But when I need a freaking PhD in game mechanics just to get past a boss, I have to say F*** this game.

Revelations goes back to Resident Evil's roots, playing as series veteran Jill Valentine investigating an abandoned cruise ship in the middle of the ocean, while trying to survive the horrors lurking all over the ship. Revelations also adds a new mode called Raid mode, and it's very addicting. Raid mode lets you run through multiple sections for the main story facing leveled enemies in an arcade like mode. As you keep playing Raid mode, you will level up and unlock more weapons. The weapons also have a Borderlands like flair to them, with some of them having special effects and some being rarer than others. In short, Raid mode is a very fun, very addicting new addition to the Resi series.
However, the main downsides of the game is every section that doesn't take place on the ship. The sections outside the ship feel more like Resi 6, where you fight wave of enemies with plenty of ammo to go around. The survival horror aspect is thrown out the window during these segments. The game would've been much better without these segments.
Other than that, I'd give Resident Evil: Revelations a
. Would've been a 7, but again the aforementioned action segments of the game aren't great, and there's a lot of them. If you like horror games but don't mind a bit of action on the side, then you'll enjoy this game.

This is what I expected the Codename Panzer series to be (which was an huge disappointment beyond the graphics) and it is everything I have been looking for in a RTS/RTT type game. The level of realism is well beyond any other game of this type out there. Improper planning and use of tactics are punished over and over again by a good AI. Hundreds of units are modeled and at your fingertips and variants within each vehicle type are meticulously researched and detailed. Elements such as range, armor penetration and the intangibles such as shock and moral are accurately represented. I love the fact that you can actually use infantry for more than cannon fodder and can build an actual combined arms plan of attack for a given objective.   For those who are saying this game it too difficult or the scenarios take too long, fret not there is always the arcade build and unit-spam RTSs out there like Command and Conquer and Age of Empires……this one is for the big boys.

This, is a game for Die Hard Strategy fans, and I mean DIE Hard, the kind that will micromange and face extreme Difficulty and Realism, wait hours for anything to happen, and still be entertained. Well, I come from this point of view.
This Game is not for the faint of heart, so if you've only played basic, or no RTS games, you really should steer clear of this one, and try some more popular titles. As for those who are experienced, this review is for you. Theatre of War is a very advanced strategy game, that is very hard, a challenge i'm sure you and I would gladly take. TOW combines Historical Accuracy and somewhat realistic gameplay to create a real platoon commanding feel. Extreme detail had been given to every object and how it interacts with others on the battlefield. You can play as the obvious All-Stars, USSR, USA, and UK, and some underdogs such as poland and frace are included (underdog if you look at it like I do), and each of these playable countries has a wide variety of units and missions to choose from. Missions are usually fun, however sometimes it can get tedious, defend this, attack that, over and over, but it varies in mission and out from time to time. Unfortunately, some common problems do plague this game, as with most realistic, large scale RTS games, the storys are quickly fed to you in a short amount of writing, and then its off to unscripted action, I know a lot of players enjoy a detailed RTS story, so you won't find one here. Further more, unit responsivness is slow, and will not act in a way a real battlefield scenario would play out, standing around, not reacting to rather obvious things, and would stare at an enemy, only firing a weapon slowly. However on a large scale, details can be put aside and the gameplay works and isnt unbalanced, using the right tactics and playing smart will always fetch you a win. This game really reflects 1C as a whole.
--Pros--
+ Realistic and Accurate
+ Long Campaign Time with Plenty of missions
+ Hundreds of different units all very well detailed
--Cons--
- Freindly and Enemy units are slow in response
- Hardly a detailed story
- Repeditive

So I'd heard various things regarding Pre-Sequel. I managed to pick it up on a sale with all the current DLC available. As I had an Aussie friend that had played it before, I went on his advice of playing the Baroness. He knows I like marksmanship in the series, playing as Mordecai and as Zer0 in the two previous games. I was slightly skeptical... but I found right away this was perhaps the best choice to go with. Reminds me much of Mordecai really.
Starting off, I was chuckling at various story elements, knowing full well the events of both games and Jack's involvement. This game still shows how much of a jackass he can be... but at times just can't help but feel like he's a jackass for a reason I guess. I haven't gotten that far, but parts of the story make you feel for him.
Additionally, playing this with my Aussie buddy, who might I add was -very- enthusiastic that I play it with hiim, I'm laughing so hard at some of the humor in this game. To me, it's not riddled with pop culture references and the like. This is a similar kind of humor, but it's so culturally different at the same time that I can't help but go "huh?" at times. It helps that my friend not only played through the game, and wants to play it again with me, but that he's actually familiar with things that -I- wouldn't be.
I'm unsure the reason people don't like this game that much. I thought before: "Sure, this is like a stand alone expansion to Borderlands 2." "Sure, it's perhaps a cash grab when they could be adding more to Borderlands 2 but instead make a whole different game." "Sure, why is there so much room for additional characters when making a new game, yet they only have two DLC characters for 2, and they have 2 more for Pre-Sequel already? Can't there be crossover or the like?" "Sure, there's no slag, but this cryo element... what gives?" "Butt stomping... the heck? Double jumping too?"
I have to say... it's fun. I'm liking the cryo ability to freeze then shatter enemies, and the butt stomping is already engrained into my techniques of how to approach a fight. My long standing choice still remains just camping at a spot and providing cover to my buddy, but I feel like in this game I can actually stand my own ground up close and personal now, with the confidence of a shotgun or other strong firearm, and butt stomping along with my special class ability.
(And wow... getting my friend to sign a contract to provide us both bonuses? I'm exploring that tree for now but will most likely branch into my own two personal trees for superiority once I get to a high enough level later on. >:3 )
I whole heartedly recommend this game... Even if you have friends not familiar with the Australian culture, but especially so if you have as great an Australian friend familiar with that neck of the woods as I do. It could very well be a grand adventure for the two of you, yourself delving into the unknown, and a friend there to guide you through it.

This is a strangely addictive game. First couple of maps that one plays won't probably leave lasting impressions. The graphics are ok but nothing special, the storyline (there actually is one) isn't memorable and initially the tactics at the player's disposal are limited. You may even be tempted to put the game back in your (virtual) library shelves, but you'd make a BIG mistake.
Give it a few rounds and you'll start unlocking skills and building up an amulet that can enhance specific traits. And your scores start to soar as you unlock more maps, So you start thinking: "I'll give it just another go" and then something new pops up.  Eventually you'll get stuck on a seemingly impossible level. But then you realise that if you go back to older maps and replay them with the newly acquired skills your old score will multiply unlocking even more skills.
And that's when you get really hooked!
You play a wizard committed on stopping a demon called "The Forgotten" that will summon hordes of monsters on each map level hurling them at you. Basically it's a matter of constructing "choke points" manned by towers and traps to obliterate ever-larger waves of fiends preventing them to overwhelm your "Orb of Presence". Towers and traps are powered by gems. Gems can be combined to achieve powerful combos, or used as "pure" (convinient if high on the "Pure Colours" skill), On completing maps players will acquire skill points that can be spent to get more powerful levels of particular skills as well as amulet fragments. Skills need to be unlocked by acquiring the relevant wizard skill tome in some maps, a sub-objective of the main objective of staying alive as long as possible. Invariably you will eventually be overwhelmed on each map, but the challenge is to push that boundary a little further each time, unlock new skills and try new tactics.
Skill points can be reassigned at the beginning of each map so you are not stuck with a bad choice of skills and this encourages the player to experiment. I have changed tactics a few times and the results are not always predictable but that's part of the addictive fun of this game.
Give it a try. Actually give it a few... And then you'll probably write a review similar to mine.

So, what is CrossCode exactly?
Well let me tell you, my dear friend.
CrossCode is an 2D Action RPG which is presented in the
pixelart i've ever laid my eyes on.
Right at the title screen the game greets you with smooth visuals and a calm music that evokes memories of PSO.
Graphically the game is great. Every area of the game is chock full of amazing pixelart and so much charm oozing out of it.
The music in the game is also phenomenal and consists of many styles, from boss tracks that get your fighting spirit pumping, to the calm friendliness of Rookie Harbor's theme.
The artstyle of the game is sort of a hybrid between Secret of Mana and Phantasy Star Online and creates this vibrant and colourful look to the game.
The game looks and sounds good yes, but what about the gameplay?
Luckily the combat is as every bit as fantastic as the Art and Sound design. It's responsive, fast and definitely well balanced with the emphasis based on the players skill. The leveling is luckily very fast with the help of Quests and the game doesn't turn into a grindfest, so you can enjoy the game at your own pace.
To spice things up the game also features
, which are full of all kinds of challenges for the player to tackle. At the end of a dungeon there is usually a bossfight, which usually put up a good fight.
Set in a VRMMO called CrossWorlds, the player assumes the role of Lea. An amnesiac, mute, girl who is playing the game in order to get her memories back. During her adventure she meets other players such as Emilie, a competetive young girl, Apollo, the overdramatic wannabe superhero and many others.
I think CrossCode is a phenomenal experience and well worth your money, but the game is in Early Access and as such is not complete, which is a damn shame, because the story is really well done and suffers heavily from the bit-by-bit form of releasing the main story, and even though the dungeons are fun, some of them are a bit bland and the music may get repetitive to some people.
Overall, the game is bloody fantastic. Well written, great looking, good sounding and greatly playable, This indie ARPG does so many things right it's downright amazing how much Radical Fish Games have put their effort in this.
But if you are considering buying this, be warned that the story is not complete.

Anodyne is a game which I bought for $3 along with a bundle of other assorted indie games. Having finished it, I can wholeheartedly recommend it, even at full price, for it imparts simplicity, solitude, and subtlety that I find rather underappreciated or ignored these days.
The story, ostensibly about a human named Young attempting to protect "The Briar" from "The Darkness" that has spread across "The Land", would be rather uninteresting if it were not for how the game's description directly states that it all takes place within Young's subconscious. Resulting from this is a somewhat lonely journey which focuses more on succinct phrases rather than grandiose spiels and atmosphere over tangibility, overall akin to going through a series of dreams within a larger dream (which is no surprise as Yume Nikki is cited as one of the inspirations for this game). Later on in the game the ideas and caricatures presented occasionally get a bit too obtuse for me to understand, but the main theme of the plot is still clear and I was quite satisfied by the ending. Moreover, Anodyne never interrupts its gameplay for an extended period of time to exposit or pontificate, which is nice as it means players are not forced to care about the game's script if they do not want to. That would be a shame, however, as the multiple lines of dialogue from the game's NPCs and signs tend to be incredibly humorous or chilling, sometimes both at the same time.
Mechanically, the game is not particularly complex; imagine Link's Awakening but with no items outside of the Sword and the Roc's Feather. Although Young gains several equippable upgrades throughout the course of the game, the majority of them just increase the range of his broom, and the enemy and obstacle counts are not particularly high either. As such, the majority of the game consists of exploring the overworld (surprisingly large and spanning multiple environments), slaying enemies (both passive and aggressive), clearing dungeons (about as much as you'd expect in a Zelda game), vanquishing bosses (all of them uniquely designed and fairly tough), and ultimately collecting cards which are required to progress further in the game.
Nonetheless, the rooms of each dungeon tend to be designed well enough that old adversaries often offer new challenges. There are also some tricky puzzles and platforming sections as well, the latter sometimes becoming a bit too tricky due to the top-down perspective. Honestly though, there are only two points of contention I truly have with the gameplay. Firstly, the collection of said cards might put off players who do not enjoy backtracking and exploring EVERYWHERE. I was personally okay with it, though Young's mediocre movement speed made the task plodding at times. Secondly, the post-game is rather lackluster, basically furthering the card seeking with a late-introduced gimmick which can be hard to control along with literally exploiting glitches; it feels like an afterthought. Other than that, the simplicity of the game is a mark in its favor.
Moving on to aesthetics, the game describes its visuals as "GBC/16-bit", which is certainly true and they are sprited very well in that style, but what really stood out to me were the gorgeous overlays that complimented many of the game's areas. I'm particularly a fan of the cliffs (pictured above), which are bathed in a warm sunset's glow, along with some later, gloomier areas which would be a shame to spoil. The sound design is excellent as well, especially the "Obtain Key" noise which is utterly jarring and I love it.

After the action-packed Resident Evil 5, Resident Evil Revelations looks back to the series' roots for an experience that many old-school fans will recognize. Revelations adapts the pre-rendered titles' defining traits to the modern RE, bringing back the series' name to a more grounded state, and actually knows what it wants to be this time: a survival-horror game that focuses on the atmosphere. Revelations reinforces this in the earlier hours of the campaign, where the player is greeted by distant eerie sounds, dark corridors, and the occasional jump scare that's done so effectively due to tension build-up. Some of the scariest parts of the game are the paths leading to the bosses because you can hear their cries echoing the hallways, either laughing from the thrill of the hunt or desperately crying for help. The tension does slow down during the latter half of the game, but the way leading there has been consistent in tone and quality.
Revelations uses an episodic structure to move the plot forward. This was done by the developers because
regarding the the original 3DS release. The 12 episodes featured in the game contain different scenarios from the perspective of three playable characters and their partners, all contributing small pieces of information and some backstory for the grand finale. While the game starts and ends exactly how a Resident Evil fan expects it too, this has got to be the most complicated series entry to date because there are a lot of character motivations to factor in, and the most important plot points are shown so poorly, with little explanation on why things happened the way they happened; Revelations isn't as straightforward as the games before it so some time is needed to fully grasp the story.
Overall, a good game and a great entry to the RE franchise. It retains the B-movie feel that the rest of the series is known for, and the gameplay combines the best of both worlds to deliver a solid experience. Definitely a must-have for the RE fan.
And there you have it.

Honestly, I don’t know where to start. DEADLY PREMONITION is one of the most memorable games I have ever played, but sadly not always for the right reasons. There is so much wrong with this game it’s not possible to list all its flaws in a brief review like this. Suffice it to say, it runs terribly on the PC with the longest load times I have ever encountered and more glitches than I could shake a stick at. The graphics are pretty awful (I used the DP patch which supposedly improves performance and graphics but it still looks like something from the early 90s). The controls are awful and if I hadn’t discovered a tweak that fixes a ridiculous aiming problem I would probably have given up on the game. The combat is hideous too, with the aforementioned dreadful aiming system and poor mechanics. Even the UI is an irritating mess. And yet despite all this I’m glad I stuck it out until the end (incidentally, despite having completed the game I only found a handful of the many side quests, as they are often time-sensitive and way off the main story track). So what’s good about DP? Well it certainly is quirky, and it’s easy to see why it’s gained such a devoted cult following. At its core DP has a very strong story backed up by solid voice acting. It has many weird and interesting characters and some crazy dialogue. Although it is derivative (Twin Peaks and Silent Hill are often-used comparators, and rightly so) it still has a unique personality. There’s no doubt that if DP had been produced to the same standard as a AAA game it would be outstanding. But unfortunately I can only recommend it if you have a slight masochistic streak, as, it appears, do I. There’s a five-star game in here struggling to get out but due to all its faults I can only give it 3.5/5.

So I'd heard various things regarding Pre-Sequel. I managed to pick it up on a sale with all the current DLC available. As I had an Aussie friend that had played it before, I went on his advice of playing the Baroness. He knows I like marksmanship in the series, playing as Mordecai and as Zer0 in the two previous games. I was slightly skeptical... but I found right away this was perhaps the best choice to go with. Reminds me much of Mordecai really.
Starting off, I was chuckling at various story elements, knowing full well the events of both games and Jack's involvement. This game still shows how much of a jackass he can be... but at times just can't help but feel like he's a jackass for a reason I guess. I haven't gotten that far, but parts of the story make you feel for him.
Additionally, playing this with my Aussie buddy, who might I add was -very- enthusiastic that I play it with hiim, I'm laughing so hard at some of the humor in this game. To me, it's not riddled with pop culture references and the like. This is a similar kind of humor, but it's so culturally different at the same time that I can't help but go "huh?" at times. It helps that my friend not only played through the game, and wants to play it again with me, but that he's actually familiar with things that -I- wouldn't be.
I'm unsure the reason people don't like this game that much. I thought before: "Sure, this is like a stand alone expansion to Borderlands 2." "Sure, it's perhaps a cash grab when they could be adding more to Borderlands 2 but instead make a whole different game." "Sure, why is there so much room for additional characters when making a new game, yet they only have two DLC characters for 2, and they have 2 more for Pre-Sequel already? Can't there be crossover or the like?" "Sure, there's no slag, but this cryo element... what gives?" "Butt stomping... the heck? Double jumping too?"
I have to say... it's fun. I'm liking the cryo ability to freeze then shatter enemies, and the butt stomping is already engrained into my techniques of how to approach a fight. My long standing choice still remains just camping at a spot and providing cover to my buddy, but I feel like in this game I can actually stand my own ground up close and personal now, with the confidence of a shotgun or other strong firearm, and butt stomping along with my special class ability.
(And wow... getting my friend to sign a contract to provide us both bonuses? I'm exploring that tree for now but will most likely branch into my own two personal trees for superiority once I get to a high enough level later on. >:3 )
I whole heartedly recommend this game... Even if you have friends not familiar with the Australian culture, but especially so if you have as great an Australian friend familiar with that neck of the woods as I do. It could very well be a grand adventure for the two of you, yourself delving into the unknown, and a friend there to guide you through it.

One of the worst RPG games I've played in a long time. Even though the plot seems interesting, it has a lot of issues that make it, in my opinion, unplayable. The battles become repetitive too early in the game, and it has a graphic glitch in some places where you just can't look at some parts of the scenario because it freezes for a while.

For a game based on a TV show*, it's pretty good. While I normally prefer turn-based combat, the real-time-with-pause works pretty well. You have to balance inflicting status effects (on fire, stunned, knocked down, etc.) with matching extra powered attacks while always saving a bit of power to throw in an interrupt. You're often controlling 2 characters (and sometimes also a dog), so there is a lot of room for strategy. Like most real-time-with-pause systems though, the fights always devolve into a big pile of guys bouncing all over the place.
The story is really about as good as it gets for something like this. It all takes place before the show starts and focuses on new characters who often run into characters from the show. The writing is ok, and the story is interesting. Some of the side quests are fun.
There are a lot of negatives though. Some of the quest are really wonky - you have to basically try every dialogue option. It seemed like a crap-shoot to figure out the best dialogue option. The results were just too random.
The visuals are all over the place. The main two character's faces look great, but some of the cast members are almost unrecognizable. The texture quality is often pretty bad. For example, the doors look like something from a 10-year-old game: just a flat texture on a very thin bit of polygons. Like, the handles are never modeled making them look really out of place. Tree, flowers, etc. often look terrible. Oh, it's also worth mentioning that the game is over-the-shoulder third-person, so it can be a real pain to look around. As far as I could tell there was no first-person "look" option. The FOV was really low, as well.
The difficulty curve is a bit off. Most fights were easy, even many "elite" or "boss" fights, but a few were suddenly extremely difficult.
In the end, Game of Thrones RPG is a fun little game that fans of the show can get some fun out of. It has some flaws, but overall I've had a good time.
* It features the likeness and voices of actors from the TV show, which is based on the books.

Oh where do I begin on a behemoth franchise such as Game of Thrones...
Well first of all, I can probably say that you are not going to like this game, why you may ask, because considering this is a title released in 2012 you will be expecting it to maintain a certain quality about it which it sadly lacks. Allthough my complaints are few and mainly focused around the camera being centered to close to the protagonists back, I do not believe people who dislike this game are wrong.
To break it down, the one point people seem to agree upon is that the story is what drives this game forward, it's a very interesting take on the events taking place during the first novell of the "A Song of Ice and Fire" saga, all be it not entirely canon unless we've been kept in the dark on some major nuggets of information both within the books and the HBO show.
The errors I've heard about it is that the combat is way to repetative, and many people dislike the way it's done. For you who have played 'Of Orcs and Men', the combat is very similar to that, as is the gear system, only Game of Thrones seem to have a bit more indepth inventory. I personally enjoy this combat style, but as my favourite parts of the books are the priesthood of R'hllor, and my favourite part of the HBO show is Connleth Hill, it's hard for me to look down at this game too much. (Yes, Connleth does do a guest appearance as Varys).
Another issue I care to mention that I personally struggled with was the portrayal of women, and whilst I am not a fan of the heated pro or cons of feminism debatte raging online, let me just tell you that even I who generally doesn't mind exploitation or characters not being described to their fullest was shocked with how there seems to be no noteworthy woman in this game at all, but hey, atleast the protagonists are allright. (Warning, one of the voiceactors for the protagonists sound like coarse stone).
So to summarise, as much as I personally enjoyed this game, it probably isn't for you. I can live with the poor graphic, a handful of bugs and an uncomfortable camera angle as I am so interested in Westeros, but I wouldn't expect many others to put up with so much. But at the end of the day, I really enjoyed the game, it was fairly lengthy if you did the side missions and it never felt to easy or to difficult. But if you against all odds find it in you to deal with all of these things I've warned you about above here, I strongly recommend the game simply on the basis that I enjoyed the combat system, and the story is good.

The game is fun, don't get me wrong. The story is great, combat and gameplay are great, animations are great, soundtrack is godlike. English voice acting isn't perfect, but doesn't make me want to impale myself like other dubs do. The game is fantastic.
Why a negative review then? I think most people already know most of the major issues with this port, but I'll explain it anyway. In fullscreen mode, the game only supports up to 900p even if it is set higher than said resolution. The game engine is more demanding than it should be. With a GTX 1060 6GB OC, i5 3570k stock, and 8GB of dual channel RAM at 1600Mhz, I get dips as low as 40 fps at 1080p (with FAR, slightly worse with Borderless Gaming, more on that in last paragraph) with everything maxed except for using 2x AA and AO off. Anti Aliasing and Ambient Occlusion, when both are enabled, screw up the pop in draws, making them vary jarring. (AA is better than AO, so just leave AO off if you get the game). If you are to Alt-Tab out of the game and go back into it, it will register the Tab button as being held down when it is not. Won't affect gameplay until you get to a cutscene and it will skip it. (pressing tab once you get back into the game fixes this problem, but I missed several cutscenes before figuring out the problem and learning how to fix it).
Nier Automata has been out for several months and already has its first DLC out. All we've heard from the devs in terms of a patch is "we are investigating" and since then its been complete silence. Several outlets have called it ridiculous that it still hasn't been patched yet, including Kotaku, Digital Foundry, and Rock Paper Shotgun. PC Gamer just had in article about how Steam Review bombing is affecting games specifically mentioning Nier Automata and GTA 5 (which admittedly is the reason I'm doing this). It is inexcusable that Square Enix/Platinum Games have done nothing to resolve these problems
There is a mod known as FAR (Fix Automata Resolution) that fixes the resolution/fullscreen issues, but that also has some serious problems since its creator, kaldaien, pings the users' steam accounts and gets their information. Excuse is an "anti-piracy" check, but if he doesn't like you for any reason at his disgression, he'll ♥♥♥♥ with your account and your game files without disclosure (aka its malware). Its the reason the mod isn't pinned on the Nier: Automata steam forum anymore. Use borderless gaming instead since windowed mode does support higher resolutions.

That said, the combat is solid.  The variation of the world and the wonderful soundtrack helped maintain my interest.  While the story felt fractured, the dreamlike atmosphere worked well with the overall nostalgia.  Me likey.

This is what I think about the game after 6 hours of playtime.
Pros:
- This game is challenging. It's not like cod or bf1 where anyone could get a 20+ killstreak because 1-2 shots to the body and you're down.
- Realistic gameplay, despite this game not having the best graphics you will always see that player movements are realistic. This includes recoil, leaning left and right, switching weapons, running, reloading, checking how much ammo you still have, proning, crouching, flying helicopters.
- Long rounds. This might be good for players who despise games where rounds take like 10 minutes only. Well this game is different, some gamemodes consist of 3 rounds where every round could take more than an hour.
- Fairly good playerbase, well considering bf1 has 10k this game reaches half this number and it's only weeks old. That is a good start in my opinion.
- Hardcore 1shot 1 kill; literally, one shot can take you down sometimes even with a pistol. A sniper shot hit is definitely a kill, like 100% of the times i hit someone with a sniper it was a kill. for other weapons it all depends to be fair, sometimes you need 3 bullets with the AK to kill someone.
- Game modes, although they are kind of similar but it's good to have a variety of game modes.
- In-game communication, you can mark literally anything using "z" on your keyboard. you can hear ally soldiers saying "enemy spotted". This game features ingame voip and that's good, you could talk to your squad, to your whole team and even a public chat. To be honest haven't seen anyone abusing it so far.
- In-game performance, I get 120+ fps running on ultra although I have a fairly good gaming rig. i5-7600, 8gb ram ( not even in dual channel ), and an ASUS dual 1060 6gb. I stutter sometimes but in rare occasions but I have never seen my fps drop below 55.
Cons:
- Some slight bugs, not really noticeable but one, which is the prone bug. When you're in prone position sometimes you just can't move forwards or backwards and all you have to do is stand up.
- A huge delay in the kill feed, I honestly don't know if this is intentional or not but sometimes you'll see your own kill 5 seconds after you kill your ennemy. Kind of annoying because you can't know if you really killed him or not, there are no messages on the hud confirming the kill or anything.
- Servers, well this is kinda annoying considering the fact that my normal ping to almost all EU servers is around 60-70 sometimes in RS2 it goes beyond 100 but this issue has a simple fix, get better servers I guess ?
- your allies are marked with a tiny blue triangle when aiming at them, some times the triangle doesn't even appear but you'll get used to it, you will definitely know who's on your side after a couple of hours of gameplay. I only killed my teammates like twice in the very first game. And if you just say sorry in the chat they will definitely forgive you. ( By that i mean they can type NP in the chat and you'll have your 20 second penalty removed from your spawn timer)
Overall, I highly recommend buying this game if you are a veteran at these types of war games. We're waiting for you on the battlefield.
Oh and, you could grab a copy of this game for less than 22$ if you know what I mean. ( You didn't read that )

A much-needed change from Borderlands 2, and a welcome one in many places. It might not be better, but it's different, and that's what I wanted.
Core game's Borderlands 2. Same UI, same shoot/loot gameplay, same levelling and such. It does however throw a lot of other stuff into the mix, which I'll quickly go over:
The game no longer starts at the pace of Claptrap climbing stairs. You stand up next to a crashed rocket with two non-pitiful weapons and start shooting dudes. Action skill unlocks at level 2.
The Grinder lets you "trade up" weapons to higher quality. I can get purples without tryharding for fifteen hours. I approve.
The low gravity serves to make exploration a bit easier and allow ground slams, which are incredibly fun. Oz kits replace relics, which I thought were a bit underpowered in BL2, and they have all sorts of perks to take over the role, which I like. I didn't have issues with the oxygen mechanic, it makes things interesting getting from A to B, but I can see how some people might. Tip: Claptrap doesn't need air, if you can bare playing as him.
TPS's 4-6 vault hunters are a bit niche for my tastes, with skills that seem to cater for very specific play styles, and if you choose the wrong one at the start you're out of luck. Their skills are however fresh and interesting, if of limited usefulness.
Laser weapons, which come in varieties mimicking the other weapon types, are a bit uninspired, but whatever, lasers.
Cryo damage freezes people in place and makes them take increased damage. Cryo replaces slag. It's like slag but cooler. That pun was unintentional.
Enemies are about the same. There's a few new ones, like the swarming Torks and duplicate-on-death Kraggons, but most of the others are reskins or very close relatives to Borderlands' Bandits (Scavs), Hyperion Soldiers (Lost Legion), Buzzards (Dahl Fighters), etc. Also, stalkers for a single level! ASSET RECYCLING HO!
This game also marks the triumphant return of the Eridian Guardians as enemies, which are some of my favourite baddies of all time, mostly because they and the places they spawn in look sick as hell.
TPS really shines in the presentation. This game looks freaking
The Elpian landscape, frozen, superheated, abandoned and bustling all at once, is more high-tech and futuristic than Pandora ever was. The Helios space-station's scale is unimaginable, not just from its eclipsing figure from Elpis, but when you get to explore its halls and facilities yourself later on. Fighting through all the areas that gave you grief in BL2, like the supply cannon and Jack's office, is awesome. Much later in the game, you once again delve into Eridian ruins, and holy hell, they look better than ever. The final area genuinely took my breath away. Look forward to it.
It's also brillaint to be playing as the bad guys for once, and seeing the whole Borderlands scene from the other way around. The GUN Loaders are your allies. Helios Station is your base of operations. Wilhelm, Nisha and Athena all have actual personalities and react to things that happen in the world. I can finally appreciate the exquisite human being that is Jack without feeling guilty.
Writing remains solid: Jack is tremendous as previously discussed, the characters catch you off guard with jokes, and the term "Paedophile mustache" is used unironically.
Soundtrack is 99% retro sci-fi synths and it fits perfectly. Features the return of our lord and saviour Jesper Kyd. Praise be to his Nordic excellency.

This is my first Steam review and it's also the first early access I bought. For the time being as of the current version (0.8.5), Steam says I played for 42 hours, in-game time 34. The only things I have yet to do are completing the botanic analysis and finding about 20 chests in the jungle area.
I discovered this game while checking my Steam recommandations and I remember quite well thinking upon seeing the character design "this one seems nice, might as well checking the store page". At first, while looking at the screenshots, I wasn't really impressed, since the game seems to have been made using RPG Maker (it's not, it uses HTML 5 and another engine don't remember the name), although I was quite intrigued by the overwhemingly positive reviews. Then, I noticed there was a demo. I tried it the day after...
Upon playing it, I was amazed : " This game looks like the perfect combination between Zelda, Seiken Densetsu (Mana Series), YS and Alundra gameplay-wise. And the world's background seems like a mix between Phantasy Star and .hack// , That's an awesome idea !". And you know what ? That was only the prologue (the original indiegogo campain demo was much bigger).
Eager for more, I instantly bought the early access, and then, I just could'nt let go of this game (I still can't actually). Let's see why.
The game takes place on another planet, CrossWorlds, which is actually a MMORPG using augmented reality. You'll be controlling Lea, a female avatar belonging to the spheromancer class (That means throwing BALLS everywhere). However, Lea has two important problems : she's an amnesiac (Yeah, that's cliché, but I don't mind it) and has a disability with her talking functions. In short, she's almost mute, only able to say basic words such as "Hi !". Then, Lea travels trough CrossWorlds, looking for answers, helping and being helped by various characters along the way.
Yeah, nothing special about it, still I can't really judge the story in this version : it ends before going in the second temple, and the adventure is still about discovering the world at this point. But I can say for sure the main characters are charming, especially Lea. Do not misunderstand this : Lea is not almost mute to make the player identify to the character, she's really, REALLY expressive. Just by looking at her portraits, you can easily imagine what she's thinking, and you will love her for that. The world's backstory is also pretty interesting, and I want to see more of it, hopefully soon enough ^^
The game looks better in-game that on the screenshots : Detailled background and sprites, smooth animations and some very nice views. Exploring CrossWorlds is a pleasure to the eyes, if you like 16-Bits artsyle (Although, I think a game like this never could have been released on a 16-bits system at this time, it probably had to wait until Saturn and PSX). I'll nitpick only regarding the basic NPC portraits, which contrast a lot with the others, but Radical Fish members are working on it.
Music seems like a combination between Phantasy Star Online and Secret of Mana, most of the themes are very peaceful and help you throughout thinking (and you will do that a lot). Battles themes are more aggressive. Overall, a really good soundtrack, maybe it lacks for the time being more battle themes.
And the gameplay... where do I begin with ? There are not that much different environments and areas (except the jungle, which is huge), but I can assure you : there's a lot of exploring to do if you're just a bit curious. Most of the chests or plants are in plain sight, reaching them though... that's another story. The game will then takes the form of parkour puzzles, and you will search an answer to it just because this chest is looking down at you, mocking you. Each new zone gains in complexity regarding level-design, and you'll soon discover you'll have to navigate through different screens in order to discover alternate paths.
As of now, there are 5 dungeons in the game, the sixth one will come on February 28th if it's going well. Those dungeons are massive, the first time you'll visit them, you will easily spend 3 hours. Almost each room is a puzzle, save for a few dedicated to fighting. They are quite balanced, it's difficult enough to force you to think, but not ridiculous to the point you'll say "Screw this, let's check the answer on Youtube !". However, I do think timing-based puzzles are sometimes a bit too strict. I have no problem with it whatsoever, but people who are not in the good pace might be discouraged, it could be sad...
Combat in CrossCode are really smooth and nervous. Controls are responsive using a X-Box 360 controller (please note that the game's engine only accepts X-Input controller, you might want to avoid unpleasant surprises), I did not try with keyboard/mouse, but I believe aiming should more precise, the analog stick is sometimes too sensitive for predicting the right angles in order to bounce the balls you shot where you want them to land. You can also dash, guarding and use melee attacks. Each of these abilities have access to a superior level, called combat arts, gained by using CP in a skill Tree granted by leveling-up. The tree will appear small at first, but don't forget : there are four more branches, unlocked by acquiring the elemental powers.
Ennemies are quite a challenge : they're fast and deals a lot of damage . There's quite a lot of strategy involved in order to find their weakspots. Don't worry about dying though : you'll respawn in the same area you died, most of the foes doesn't attack you unless you hit them first and you auto-heal outside battle.
There are also a bit of crafting and a lot of side-quests. Most of the latter are fetch quests, but you won't feel that doing them is a chore, since you'll do them along exploring the places. Well.. except the botanic analysis which is a bit tedious, because the only plants who count are those who give a drop. Maybe Radical Fish should take into account all plants destroyed or lowering the amount needed.
Radical Fish says the full game will need 30-40 hours to be completed with a 100% rate. Sure... if you know already where everything is hidden. I think a more accurate time should be around 60-70 hours, which would be really impressive for an A-RPG. I think the twenty bucks they're asking for are almost a gift considering the amount of content and the overall fun of the game.
Now then, the question is : should you buy CrossCode ? If you have a soft spot for 2D A-RPG, absolutely, you cannot miss a game which has so much love and care about it. I keep hearing how early access are a bad thing, but this game is a perfect counter-example, this is EA done right : CrossCode is perfectly playable in its current state, the minor glitches you might come across are not game-breaking (and quite funny, watching Emilie jumping to her death repeatedly killed me XD) unless you don't play fair by abusing the game, and the germans from Radical Fish are very attentive to their community. I love those guys so much that I already bought three copies (The other two were for friends who were interested in it), just to support them as much as I can.
Still, since there are only a few development months remaining if everything is going well, maybe it's a wise move to not play the game until the full release or just adding it to your wishlist.
CrossCode has only a last pre-requite to fulfill before falling in my top of best games of all time : the full story. Otherwise, it would only be a really fun game, which doen't take its players for fools and respects them. That's not so common in our time, right ?

Only a little ways into the game (recorded playtime is pretty inaccurate, in reality I've only got maybe 3-5 hours logged), but I'm loving it so far. The overworld style is very reminiscent of the best of the best RPG's from the 16-bit  era, but the character portraits really make it pop. The gameplay is a fun action-y real-time battle system that I can't quite describe properly, but it's absolutely fun.
I will say this though: it does frontload a LOT of information early on. You start by getting dropped into a strange world where you (and your character) have basically no idea where, who, or even what you are, and a large amount of my playtime so far was spent reading various in-game infodumps regarding the setting, lore, etc. While I don't know how much of that is made redundant later on, in that maybe it gets explained as the game progresses, I think the developer could stand to do with a healthy dose of "show, don't tell".
That caveat aside though, this is one of the most fun games I've played in a long while, and frankly the only reason I noticed it and harped on about it was because of how well-polished everything else about the game is by comparison. I'll come back to this review once I've had a chance to play more and beat the game, but for now it's definitely a solid winner- well worth the price and easily an 8/10 or better.

This is the best co-op experience I have ever had.  In this game, you are on a steampunk airship with three other people and you have to work together to stay alive as well as take down other airships that want to permanently ground you.  This game rewards coordination and cooperation not just with the crew of the ship you are on but also, if you are the captain of the ship, with the other ships on your team.
Outside of the game or while you’re waiting for a lobby to fill up, you will have plenty of things to do while you wait like check your achievement progress, build and customize the ship you will bring if you are in the position of ship captain, and customize your character with a steadily growing list of things that you unlock.
On the ship you can be one of three classes that each have a job on the ship.  You can have at least one piece of equipment from each class and technically you can do any of the other jobs if the situation calls for it but everyone brings three pieces of equipment from their own class that makes them better at that job.
The engineer makes sure your ship stays in one piece an in the air.  You primarily repair damaged or destroyed parts and put out fires using a variety of tools at your disposal.  You also have the ability to sprint for a short time to quickly get to that pesky hull that just went down again.
The gunner brings the pain to enemy ships.  They can bring three types of ammunition that each have their own ups and downs that benefit different types of guns.  You also can quickly reload a weapon you’re on.
The pilot, which is normally the captain, navigates the ship through the map, lines up the gunner’s shots, and moves to try to give your engineers enough time to repair the damage you have inevitably taken.  They can bring special charms and tools to perform special maneuvers such as quick turns or smoke clouds even though most of them tend to damage the ship in some way they can really give your ship the extra edge.
There are a few things you should know about this game though.
First off it has a very steep learning curve.  The tutorial gives you the basic controls but there are so many tools, guns, and ships that figuring everything out is a real challenge for new players so asking for help and directions early on is a good thing to do.
Second you are probably going to want a microphone.  While you can play without it, not having it severely handicaps you and your ability to coordinate with other captains and crew.
Finally, as of this review, the number of people playing this game is really small.  It’s such a problem that I would suggest using this site (
) so you can play it when there are a fair number of people playing. (about 150 finds me a game and it’s easier if you play with friends).
Overall, if you are looking for a real original and great co-op experience to play with friends or with others in a small community then this is definitely something to pick up.

I'll update this review as i play along, but for now, a thumbs up !!
Level 25, first play through:
Pros:
-The hovercraft vehicle is way fun, much like the sand skiff in BL2 CS DLC.
-Cryo is different than slag and very fun.  Cyro doesn't have the overall damage buff of slag, but it freezes the target for a while and has massive buffs to crit and melee damage.  There's a slagga type cryo weapon available.
-Weapons machines actually sell good weapons, purples, red text and legendaries, unlike BL2 where the machines were worthless.
-laser weapons add a lot of depth to elemental weapons.  Rail guns can be used as an alternate sniper rifle with a huge ammo pool.  laser weapons are like smgs.
-Aussie characters are cute and preserve the light tone of BL2.
Cons:
-Low gravity movement is awkward, and feels like slow motion.
-The air mechanic is awkward and sometimes irritating when you're in the middle of a fight.  You may have to break off and find an air source.  It's also stupid game design when people with lasers and teleporters can't compress air long enough to last more than 3 minutes.  Heck, i can go scuba diving and stay down an hour
-Maps tend to be confusing and paths to objectives are often very confusing.  the big arrows of BL2 are missing.  I want to spend my time fighting bad guys, not figuring out which obscure route to take.
-Fire weapons are EVERYWHERE and are USELESS about 80% of the time because you're fighting 80% of combat in vacuum.  Maybe 50% of elemental weapons in the vending machines are fire weapons that are mostly useless.  Also, when fighting in vacuum, your fire weapon won't set anyone on fire, but fire barrels create huge fires and will burn you.  Totally stupid.
Summary:
The basis of the game is all BL2, so if you like BL2, this game is more of the same with a few interesting variations and a few annoying design flaws.

Fetishistic and otaku aspirations are satisfied fully in this action romp developed by Platinum Games. Action sequences feature tight control and wide open space, and a varied means of defeating opponents. These are augmented by the game's RPG inventory and character customization. A very nifty way of expanding upon the solid gameplay and inviting experimentation and replayability. The graphics make the action fluid and full of sparks and speed and bring some interesting and varied environment to the proceedings, although they do tend to be rather drab in spots.
The soundtrack is pretty good, as nice accompaniment to the action and also in quieter moments. The music overall is vibrant and never lets up unless for an effect. Its scope and energy lend a ton of dramatic flair more than what the game's graphics can accomplish. The raspy vocal work do tend to grate the ears, but the soothing tunes in transition wash over any inconsistencies.
A lot has been said accompanying numerous accolades of the game's plot and characters, and I think it deserves a mention as something that can only be possible within this interactive medium. The story takes shape in various forms as the point of view changes between characters, and each iteration or incarnation of the story is realyed in different pieces and revelations. The pieces do relate like a roughly drawn puzzle and give you a sense of the general plot, while not especial in of itself, transcends the normal storytelling in a feat of exuberance and indulgence. Some might think how the story was handled ham-fisted and artificial, wresting control and sense of immersion away from the player as deemed fit by the designer. I kinda enjoyed the rollercoaster ride through the loops and turns.
There are some technical issues and console roots rearing its limitations, such as the game's cinematic pre-rendered videos limited to low resolution while taking up half of the game's 40gb or so installation footprint. And there hasn't been much in the way of technical support from the publisher. However, the game and content presented within persevere to the end and give you a unique experience that has to be played to be believed. That's one of the highest acclaim one can give to a game nowadays.

This game was largely panned and I'm sure if you want to hear about what's wrong with it it won't be hard to find negative reviews, but this is all about why I loved this game.
I heard going into this game that it had terrible gameplay but I actually found the combat system very engaging. For the most part it revolves around using special abilities to interrupt enemy attacks, keep them stun locked or provide power combos with status effects. Fighting one enemy at a time is quite a simple task but the game really shines in crowd control: Facing off against a room full of enemies you must be constantly mindful of all of them. One successful special attack against you can turn the tide of the battle drastically.
There are two main characters and they can be spec'd very differently. Making one a tank and one a glass cannon results in some varied gameplay between chapters early on and once the two heroes join forces later in the game synergy between them can make clearing out rooms of soldiers both efficient and satisfying.
I think the dialogue system is worth mentioning. Instead of simply stating what your character is going to say many dialogue options are presented as part of your characters inner thoughts and, giving you a slice of something familiar from reading the books. Some options are even just two parts of the same thought. "I don't trust him..." "...but I have no choice" are just so much more interesting as choices than "refuse" and "accept" and after a while I found myself reading them in the characters' voices. It's a very elegant implementation of an old fashioned system that shows that actual care and thought went into this game.
Story is were the game really shines though. It's not on the same level as the A Song of Ice and Fire series proper (it suffers from some awkward and sometimes over-expositionary dialogue and poor to atrocious delivery by the actors) but it's a solid addition to the franchise and as video games go it's terrific.
As already mentioned there are two main characters: Mors Westford is a sworn brother of the Night's Watch and a secret skinchanger. Alester Sarwyc is the heir of noble house who left Westeros to become a Red Priest. Their stories start off seemingly entirely separate but as the game progresses their stories begin to converge both as you learn the connections between their current situations and their past history together.
Despite being old friends Alester and Mors are quite different from each other with motivations and world views that are very much at odds. Alester is quite pragmatic and willing to stoop as low as he needs to to reach his goals. Mors is more driven by a sense of justice but also a rage that is always bubbling under the surface. When the tensions between them come to a head it's one of the best moments in the game and the voice actors (particularly Mors's) actually manage to summon up some real emotion to their performances.
The intrigue itself is complex and slowly revealed with many twists. These are twists of the good sort; they take you off guard when they happen, but once out in the air you'll slap yourself for not having seen it coming (though admittedly some are a bit obvious or otherwise cliche).
There is some conflict with the source material (some of which can chalked up to gameplay necessities and some not) and there are a few moments where the story falls flat. But these are rare enough and stand out because they contrast the largely good writing. If this were a tie-in novella rather than a video game I would have been as glad to read it as I was happy to play this game (though I'd expect some the dialogue to be brushed up a bit and the body count drastically reduced).
The game is a diamond in the rough but I would recommend that anyone who is a fan of the franchise and a fan of WRPGs should at least try it out. I'm sure many of you have it sitting in your library unplayed after the game's inclusion in a Humble Bundle.

*Disclaimer, I only played this game for an hour, so take this opinion in that context and weigh it accordingly*
Picked this up for 65p, and I'm glad I only paid that. The reviews of this game were pretty mediocre and I knew that going in, however I thought playing it knowing of it's dodgy quality would somehow make me tolerant of it's shortcomings. I was wrong.
In the main, it was the voice acting and dialogue which killed this game for me, I just couldn't get over how bad it is. Does that sound snobbish? Perhaps... but when every conversation had me wincing internally...  I knew I wouldn't be able to plough through this game.
That said, in my opinion I think the combat  is actually worse. It is a kind of real time, MMORPG style combat reminiscent of World of Warcraft. You queue up actions and attacks with special abilities taking up "energy", while standard attacks can be laid upon your enemies forever. There is no blocking animations or reactions to being hit, they just chop and hack away at one another until one falls down... very much like the early MMORPGs.  The only difference to the formula here is you can hold in space bar to slow the game down to a crawl, like a real time active pause.. should you feel the need to do so.
Special attacks might hit multiple enemies or add a status effect like "stun" or "bleeding" but it is really unsatisfying. Those of you who like that kind of combat...  I'd say you should still steer clear of this. I played WoW for years and believe me when I say whatever itch that game scratches with it's combat... Game of Thrones doesn't.
These two elements alone were enough for me to abandon Game of Thrones only a hour in. Some may argue I hadn't given it a chance... but to be honest first impressions stick with me when it comes to games, mainly because there are just so so so many others in my collection that I could be spending my finite free time on. Perhaps that is shallow...  but I suppose I'm so long in the tooth as a gamer now, you just know when a game isn't going to improve.
So be warned... Winter is coming... but you can spend it indoors playing a lot better games than this.

Gemcraft was always the daddy of tower defense games and kept me entertained for a long time, but this one is simply not as good.  I have persevered with this game for a long time (years in fact), coming back to it several times since I purchased it, but ive come to the conclusion that its just not that enthtalling and I often find myself looking for alternatives.
As good as previous episodes of Gemcraft were, this is WAAAAAAAAYYYYY too micro management intensive and has an almost impenetrably dense damage calculation system that you have to learn if you want to progress in the game.  its a bit like learning to speak a foriegn language just to ask for a sandwich.  Once you have learned it, you realise very quickly that 80% of the game engine is pointless fluff and you just need 3/4 colours of gems to do anything in this game.
Also, I think for any new player, be aware that there are far too many eliteist players on forums not willing to help new players and have turned this game (and i fear the entire series) into a complete waste of time.  Gemcraft: Labyrinth was amazing, but the micromanagement changes to this game leave you cold.
The graphics and sound are amazing and epic and set the mood nicely, and the narrative story is enthralling, but as soon as you get to the point of completing the single player campaign, it soon becomes a repetitive grind/slog through endless and unbeatable endurance runs to increase your level to the point that you have enough skill points to actually stand a chance to get past level 400.
As much as the online guides are good, the fact that someone has made a guide that calculated damage output to such detail fills me with a deflated sense of "why am I playing this?".  What first seems to be endless fun becomes an endless drag.
Quite simply, after the initial enthrallment of this game, the boring endless annoyance sets in and you ask yourself why you are bothering.  If playing 45+hour levels are acceptable to you, may I suggest as an alternative that you turn the computer off and go outside?.  Theres a whole life out there that youre missing out on.  Life is too short for the level of dedication you require to just complete ONE LEVEL OF THIS BLOATED GAME, let along progress to the point where you can clear 999 waves of monsters consistantly.
And thats before we get to the lag..... OMG YOU HAVE NEVER SEEN A GAME LAG LIKE THIS!!!!  this should be the defacto standard of playing games.  If your system can handle an endurance run without lagging, its good.  if not, dont bother!
Ive played this game many times, completed the single player campaign, completed all fields on every difficulty with every trait enabled... completed all the vision fields and I am currently level 2764..., but I am still nowhere near completing a single endurance run on this, and that is why this game fails.  buy it because its cheap... lament at the stupid comments on forums and the unplayable endurance mode

This may be the only game where I put out an actual, serious review.
CrossCode is an SNES-styled action RPG, and one that sets out to be as genuine to the hardware at the time as possible. Not unlike Shovel Knight in its tribute to NES platformers, CrossCode is similar in its tribute to SNES RPGs. The aesthetics, the graphics, and the gameplay, all feel as if I'm playing a long-lost cartridge discovered from a time capsule in 1995.
Comparatively, it is the perfect mix between Secret of Mana and Phantasy Star. A few other elements remind me of .hack, as well as Ragnarok Online, for reasons that you'll see should you play it.
A few minor notes:
- Currently Early Access, so this game is not story/content-complete until its full release in May. (There's still a lot of content in its current release, though.)
- Unlike Secret of Mana, there is no multiplayer co-op. Sadly!
- There's a playable demo on Steam, and an in-browser demo on RadicalFish's website.
- Yes, I know Phantasy Star was for the Genesis, you jerks.
This game has endeared itself to being very near and dear to my heart. I hope that you find it as charming as I do.

This is my new favorite game.
The game is actually set within a VR MMO, so, it's sort of like playing a game, ina  game, while discovering both game's stories. It's a top-down game-game with the ability to melee and use ranged attacks at the same time with your mouse. Special abilities mix fights up a little and there's tonnes of MMO tropes to help you along. (Other 'players' running the course, enemies don't often attack unless provoked. Certain areas are 'Instanced'.) The art Style is great, the combat is fun and intuitive. The puzzles are freaking hard, yet fair, and the story thus far is wonderful.
The only down-side? It's early Access. As of writing this (Xmas beta), the sandy area is the end of the road. That being said, I've only encountered one bug thus far. The allied AI's a little wonky, sure, but she's still a helpful ally.
I would buy this before the price gets jacked up. It's a very, very good game.

Excellent game, even in early access.  I don't think i've ever seen a better menu UI in any other ARPG, and the GUI in general is excellent.  The developers are very responsive in the places you can talk to them at, and if you have a suggestion or question they usually respond.  They also do streams of them working on the game,  and it's interesting to watch how they make it.
The combat and locales are some of the best I've ever seen, and when you level up and get to try something new out in the perks "circuit" screen it's like christmas every time.  Puzzles get very complex, and the first time you solve them feels very rewarding.  While the story isn't up to where the content is, the game lets you play up to the point where the developers are at working on the content.  As of the time of wriiting this, all 4 elemental catagories (including most tier 1 abilities and most of the perks) are in the game, and there's 2 dungeons and 2/3 mini dungeons (forming a third dungeon, so esentially 2/3 of a dungeon) that are complete, and there's plenty of other content like the quests and the botanics list if you get bored while waiting for the next update.
All in all, I can't really recommend this game enough, and I can't wait until it comes out completely.
