Game Of Thrones: The Role-Playing Game (GoT: RPG) feels like a game from yesterday and yesteryear, while also certainly delivering its own spin on the RPG genre. The story is Chapter-based and switches b/t two characters: Mors Westford (of the Night's Watch) and Alester Sarwyck (a Red Priest) - old friends who have not seen each other in numerous years. They are both trying to find a certain girl that some groups and those on or near The Iron Throne are looking for, in this excellent story loaded with a web of secrets, lies, twists, turns, and (of course) conspiracies.
Combat feels somewhere b/t the combat of the original campaign for Neverwinter Nights [NWN] (have control on two party members at once) & Dragon Age: Origins [DA:O] (real-time combat with a pause allowed for strategy). Though, parties you control never get as big as DA:O (even if there are other NPC's who help you and you have no control over) and the pause isn't a full-blown pause - here, the "pause" only slows time here, which makes the game feel more action-like. Once you have more skills behind you, the gameplay certainly gets better and a bit more strategic. The combat here though lacks the flashy & showy nature that made games like Dragon Age 2 just look awesome.
The graphics technically often come off as dated & looks like they should've been released back when DA:O came out. While some character models & and areas look fine, others who aren't as important often come off as bland and/or are just there. The voice-acting is all over the place, ranging from poor to really good - where most of the best acting comes from either the main characters in the story & also those actors and characters who are also on the GoT HBO TV show (like Varys). Interesting enough, there is an option in the game menu to even mute/turn-off the voice-acting completely. Also worth noting - sometimes, the dialogue might come off a bit stilted, unfortunately.
If there is anything that this game nails and other companies should take notes on, it's the actual storytelling, characters, lore & GoT universe. GoT: RPG delivers a fantastic story & plot. B/c the game is done in a Chapter-based format & will often hit you with a cliffhanger just like the TV show does, you'll want more - though since this game is complete here, you'll have the feeling of wanting to just keep on playing to see what happens next; or maybe continue even further than that to see maybe even what happens a bit later; or maybe even be compelled to continue even more! Throw on top of this that there are constant jaw-dropping plot twists & even moral decisions for players to make in the main story and even on side quests, this game will certainly keep the player engaged and immersed into the story and actual game-world itself.
Even despite its dated nature in some regards and a bunch of minor issues, that can't stop GoT: RPG from sitting on its very own throne. It's the game's characters, lore, GoT universe, the actual adventure itself, & its lengthy story (which took me somewhere around 42 hours, BTW) that are excellent and certainly do make GoT:RPG as memorable as it is.
Final Grade: B-

Why a negative review then? I think most people already know most of the major issues with this port, but I'll explain it anyway. In fullscreen mode, the game only supports up to 900p even if it is set higher than said resolution. The game engine is more demanding than it should be. With a GTX 1060 6GB OC, i5 3570k stock, and 8GB of dual channel RAM at 1600Mhz, I get dips as low as 40 fps at 1080p (with FAR, slightly worse with Borderless Gaming, more on that in last paragraph) with everything maxed except for using 2x AA and AO off. Anti Aliasing and Ambient Occlusion, when both are enabled, screw up the pop in draws, making them vary jarring. (AA is better than AO, so just leave AO off if you get the game). If you are to Alt-Tab out of the game and go back into it, it will register the Tab button as being held down when it is not. Won't affect gameplay until you get to a cutscene and it will skip it. (pressing tab once you get back into the game fixes this problem, but I missed several cutscenes before figuring out the problem and learning how to fix it).
Nier Automata has been out for several months and already has its first DLC out. All we've heard from the devs in terms of a patch is "we are investigating" and since then its been complete silence. Several outlets have called it ridiculous that it still hasn't been patched yet, including Kotaku, Digital Foundry, and Rock Paper Shotgun. PC Gamer just had in article about how Steam Review bombing is affecting games specifically mentioning Nier Automata and GTA 5 (which admittedly is the reason I'm doing this). It is inexcusable that Square Enix/Platinum Games have done nothing to resolve these problems
There is a mod known as FAR (Fix Automata Resolution) that fixes the resolution/fullscreen issues, but that also has some serious problems since its creator, kaldaien, pings the users' steam accounts and gets their information. Excuse is an "anti-piracy" check, but if he doesn't like you for any reason at his disgression, he'll ♥♥♥♥ with your account and your game files without disclosure (aka its malware). Its the reason the mod isn't pinned on the Nier: Automata steam forum anymore. Use borderless gaming instead since windowed mode does support higher resolutions.

This is not a bad game, but it certainly is underwhelming for people, who played Caesar or similar games with quite annoying game mechanics. Little to no depth.
The most annoying thing for me was the evolvement of houses. In Caesar you had full control over where evolvement takes place, since you were the one chosing which goods and services are provided to the neighbourhood. For example, I had whole quarters dedicated to making wine, pottery, oil and so on. Those quarters were provided with everything they needed to evolve to some moderate levels and they were happy with it. It would be ridiculous to provide them with all the luxury goods and services needed to evolve to high class patricians with mansions.
And that is where this game is different: You have basically zero control over evolvement of the houses. They just WILL evolve. That would not be a problem, if they were not demanding new stuff and if you don't provide them with that riots will start and they will burn the city down. That is a major flaw for me, since it forces you to basically build a new subcity around EVERY area you want to expand to and there is no way around it.
There is no way to stop this, let alone build dedicated quarters for certain industries. If you expand it is just building the whole city again next to the city with some minor exceptions and it gets old very, very soon.
If you have no experience with these games this might be for you. I rather play Caesar again.

This game has one of the most amazing potentials of almost any game I can think of. The game has alot to work on, but is already hitting the mark on alot of fronts.
some of the pros:
-Early game is strong, as the exploration is exciting, and random events that can trigger are diverse enough and evenly spaced enough that they feel impactful.
-The galaxy has the ability to feel forboding and mysterious and old. The Fallen Empire system already works well, and makes it so that you cant be the big kid on the block until the later parts of the game.
-Amazing mod community, and a decent (albiet not as equally amazing) set of modding tools.
-the game gives you the options to min/max like a fiend or slack off a little in the name of RP.
some of the cons:
-Combat is breathtaking to watch, and your first war will likely have you one edge. But the balance that is placed on warfare is atrocious on two major levels. The first is withing the ship designs themselves. Ships are not well balanced against tech (i.E. upgrading your ships makes them less copst effective). Small ships evade too much and large ships can only effectivley fight other large ships. the second issue is that there is no reason to not stack all of your hsips into a death ball; in many ways, you get punished for not doing so. This makes wars tiresome and uninteresting.
-Diplomacy is shallow. Too few factors and actions are possible for diplomacy to be complex.
- the mid game drags. I dont mind thisso much, because i tend to play the game on very slow setting while I watch stuff online, but I can still see how the middle game is devoid of substance.
overall, I tyhink the game is amazing. I think the issues I outlined will be adressed in time, and boy am I excited to see how this game will evolve.

Megabyte Punch provides an interesting combination of super smash bros and Mega man in the form of a 2D action platformer. The premise of the game is collecting pieces from your defeated enemies and using them to augment your own suit. The powerups provided can be anything from a base damage upgrade, to a new ability like a laser shot. The powerups are assigned to specific areas like core or arms and you can only have so many, like 2 arms. You can only have 4 active powerups at a time, these are assigned to your special via your standard special, side special, up special, or down special. These are very similar to the up, down, side, and standard B's of super smash bros. I really like how they allow the powers to be customized to certain spots, which help you become most comfortable with the controls.
Speaking of the controls, they are very tight, with quality bindings that can be changed and gamepad support. Gamepad support is essential for 2d platformers and I always appreciate when it is there.
This art is interesting, I really haven't seen something like this and I am not sure how to classify this. It seems to be a combination of bright colors, with sharp polygon voxel-ish objects. I really love this and this is a unique style that reminds me of what mighty number 9 wished it was. The bright colors and sharp angles really pop and stand out from a lot of games.
the music is fine, there isn't much to it, but it does its job. The soundtrack consists of basic techno music that is pretty vibrant and uses a variety of sounds to create a feeling of action. I don't have too much to say about this music, other than I like it.
The game also has boss battles that all have unique parts that you can only get from them. These parts can be something like an arm or leg that have unique abilities such as a drilling ability that act as both a combat ability and an environmental modifier. For example, you can use the drill to dig through certain materials, and that is how you get to level two.
This game is all about customization. You customize the color of your armor with color palettes you collect. You customize your aesthetics and stats with body parts. And you customize what abilities you want and what slot you want it to go in. This is the one that really stands out to me as I don't think I have seen something like this before in other games, but I feel like it should be commonplace. I can put the most comfortable setup of moves for myself into the bindings I want and it is super convenient.
Overall, this game hits a lot of strong points and is definetly worth a look (unlike some other action platformers). With customization, fun, and challenges abound; megabyte punch earns a 9/10 with a label of "unique".

- Main and Side quests with interaction between the various NPCs.
- Create and manage a team.

Obviously there are some bugs and imperfections, for example, sometimes animations are trivial and cumbersome, you may encounter problems starting the game (of course there are already solutions to make it all work) and also the lack of a crafting/building system can be a problem ( replaced with different skills like repair and modification of objects ) but in my humble opinion and for the price of the game, it is really worth it if you're looking for a game where kill many zombies without neglecting the survival element.
Recommended.

Coming from only having played the sequel, Saints Row 2 is a fun game that has held up pretty well 5 years later. Bloody hilarious, with heaps of one liners, (at times very) dark humour, and full of odd references to pop culture. Story is good, and completing the missions is quite satisfying. I didn't like the necessity of repuation to complete missions, but that is attained easily enough by completing side missions that were slightly amusing and quickly over with.
Graphics were nice enough, but the view distance is poor, and so cars just "appear" from nowhere, making driving annoying some times. It's also annoying when you look away from a car, then look back and it has also disappeared. Music was great (since I loved their selection), and the radio adverts were amusing (though there wasn't that much variety).
My only real gripe with the game was it's lack of solid controller support. Sure it worked, but the games interface and instructions didn't change to reflect that, leaving me to guess which key did what, and at times using the keyboard even. In addition, some of the chase and shoot missions were impossible, leaving me to resort to using a mouse and keyboard to complete the mission. Probably should have just stuck with that haha.
But yeah, good fun, worth the lowish price it's available for now if you're a fan of SR/GTA games and have some time to kill. I myself got 26 hours of play and 65% completion on normal, so you'll get your moneys worth out of it for sure.

At the end of the day, Saints Row 2 is nothing more than a sub-par GTA clone in terms of quality, both graphical and gameplay.  That being said, Saints Row 2 leaves its mark by boasting the true spirit of the sandbox genre better than any game I've ever witnessed.  Comparisons to GTA IV are unnavoidable - the trailer itself makes multiple references to the acclaimed title - but this title's largest claims to fame against GTA are its innumerable efforts to be wacky, over the top, and at the end of the day, fun, while its competitor has taken the path of harsh, gritty realism.
One of these efforts has drawn me to the conclusion that someone on the dev team was psychotically mad, and that is the sheer extent to which you can customize your, well, everything.  From the type of paint on your cars to the angle at which you wear your bowler hat, Saints Row 2 is also one of the best Second Life simulators you can dream of.
The story and characters aren't very engaging, but at the end of the day, this game isn't about the story, but about the gameplay, which can be described with a very hard to come by word in today's gaming industry - fun.  Sure, it's fun to an extent of near insanity, but it's fun none-the-less.

A spin-off of the main series of the Biohazard/Resident Evil franchise, Biohazard Revelations expands the lore of the core series and offers a good challenge to players. Set between the events of Biohazard 4 and 5, the player controls Jill Valentine, Chris Redfield and a cast of new, interesting characters, trying to gather information to bring down a bioterrorist organization known as Il Veltro. The player should expect plot twists, of course, as we're dealing with a Biohard game over here.
Graphics are A-OK, with good character and environmental modeling and nice special effects. Great voice acting (well, at least the original, Japanese voice acting is excellent), sound effects and good soundtrack comprise the sound department. Controls are pretty much the same as Biohazard 4, with an over-the-shoulder third person view and good input response. Sadly, the horror, which made the franchise so famous in first place, is nowhere to be found. The game has its moments, and the relative lack of ammunition, herbs and other items scattered across the different places that the player gets to explore makes things a little bit harder, requiring strategic use of such itens and good reflexes in order to dodge enemies and run away safely, but, in the end, it still is an action-oriented game, much like Biohazard 5.
Biohazard Revelations may not be a real classic like the three first iterations of the series, but it is a very fun game anyway, and its difficulty and secrets may keep the player busy for quite a while. A must-buy! - 9/10

Summary: A solid exploration platformer without much depth.
This is a simple platforming game in the metroidvania style. The basic controls are responsive and there are plenty of areas to explore, so it's an enjoyable game overall. If you're a fan of shorter, simpler games, this is an easy recommendation.
However, if you have a lot of experience with other metroidvania titles, you'll notice many things this game lacks. There are no boss fights, you have no health bar (and thus there are no health upgrades to collect), and the only combat upgrade you get is a gun with extremely limited ammo. Upgrades feel more like keys, getting you past a few doors without really changing anything like if you got a double jump or a new weapon instead.
The map does show you where important items are (which is better than a lot of mediocre metroidvanias), but it doesn't show one of the main collectibles, so it's only of use for reaching the end of the game and not for completionist item hunting. Completionists may also be annoyed at the score mechanic - your score increases when you collect gems and coins, but when you die it resets to 0 and they all respawn. It feels out of place in a more exploration based game like this.
If all you want is a simple exploration game with light platforming, you'll probably enjoy this game. If you're looking for a deeper metroidvania experience with more completionist item hunting, you may be disappointed. I'd still recommend it on sale, though, as the basic gameplay is solid enough to be fun even though it's lacking more depth.

You play as an Indiana Jones wannabe, complete with whip and gun, exploring underneath a pyramid.  The people have been captured by some bad guy who stole all the relics.   Jump, roll, and use weapon are your abilities.
When you find a relic you have to take it to a pedestal and it opens up new areas, but there's no way to tell which relic is supposed to go on which pedestal so there's lots of backtracking and trial and error.  The gems and coins you collect don't seem to do anything, just add to your score.  You lose them when you die but other than that there's no penalty for dying, you can restart your progress in the same room.  The good things is you don't lose any keys or special items when you die.
The enemies always reappear in the same room even if you've killed them, so watch out.  There are simple puzzles such as switches that need to be hit.  Early on the enemies will die with one hit but later on they take more hits to die.  There are mummies, spiders, bats, and other such creatures.  You can't kill anything underwater so just avoid the jellyfish.
There's no life meter--you die if hit once.  But thankfully there is no fall damage, you can fall at any height.
I've been playing for 2 hours and it says I'm 40% of the way through, so the game is probably pretty short, unless the later areas are tougher.
Graphics are cute, cartoon, pixel style.  Very colorful.
Sound effects are okay, but I didn't hear any background music except for the opening screen.
I like this game so far.  It's fairly easy, and I find it fun to collect the gems and coins.  People who like more difficult metroidvania games will probably be bored.
UPDATE:  I spoke too soon about it being a short game.  I'm another hour or two in and only 49% now.  Mostly I'm wandering around places I've already been trying to figure out how to open up new areas.

Video Review:
At first glance Megabyte Punch might just look like a side-scrolling platformer with three dimensional graphics, and although the game does feature platforming, the real gameplay focus is on the combat. The fighting system is very satisfying specially due to one core mechanics of the game: the ability to switch the body parts of your character. These parts can be obtained through various ways and collecting all the different parts, exploring the different powers, set ups and building any character you want is what makes this game differ. Sadly there is no online multiplayer to be found. The potential for one is immense but only local multiplayer is really available.

In terms of plot Megabyte Punch actually tells a good story. There are two factions warring for control of the village you were made to protect. The intrigue here is that these factions will help you to take down the other faction and even persuade you into thinking that they are friendly when they are in fact just waiting to backstab you. The problem here is that the story itself its not very well delivered to the player and the characters are always so lifeless. This might have been thought out to make the experience of the player feel more "retro" but I fear that most of the players will just skip the dialogues and miss out on the plot.

Megabyte Punch has a good balance between Retro and Modern and the soundtrack is one perfect example of this. It sounds very modern while having a more retro feeling. The "blocky" graphics are somewhat resembling of a pixelated sprite and the gameworld is actually side-scrolling, both working towards that "retro" feeling. The world is layered through different levels each one with an unique look and feel to it. On the end of each world there is a boss fight that will reward you a special part from himself. Theese boss fights are the climax of Megabyte Punch. The overall Artificial Intelligence of the game is well done, proving to be somewhat challenging and all the bosses are unique both in design and skills wich make them real fun to beat and very rememberable.
• Final thoughts
In overall Megabyte Punch is a very entertaining experience and a greatly well done game. It has everything to be an excellent game: wonderful gameplay and mechanics, an awesome soundtrack, an interesting plot and a colorful aesthetic but has little issues that prevent him to become so much greater. The lack of Online Multiplayer really hinders this game. But still this is a must play for any type of gamer and I hope that one that day we see a sequel to Megabyte Punch.

Long version:
Ok, so this is a great psychological thriller revolving around fears of a child growing up in a dysfunctional family, being raised by a mother with paranoid schizophrenia, who is experiencing imperative auditory hallucinations which are rigidly and delusionally interpreted and provoke verbal and behavioral responses including obdience. Delusional interpretation manifests in, among others, grandiosity, feeling of a mission, delusions of guilt and sin (the latter being transferred to her child). These result in inappropriate and irresponsible actions which jeopardize the safety of her son, Isaac.
Isaac, trying to cope with the family situation, is facing his worst childhood subconscious fears. Subconsciousness is traditionally represented as 'basement' (similarly to e.g. Hitchcock's Psycho). His weapon in fighting those fears is crying and thus, relieving negative emotions. As Isaac goes deeper into the subconscious cleansing himself in a psychoanalytical way, he discovers his most concealed desire - to kill his mom.
Short version:
It's the only game that your wife will encourage you to play ('Have you killed your mother already?').

NieR: Automata is a game designed to leave a very strong impression. It's the sort of experience that sits with you long after you put down the controller.
If you somehow haven't already encountered spoilers from another review, do yourself a favor and tread carefully. A large part of why this game is praised is because of what its narrative accomplishes, and it's difficult to explain why it so strong without giving away examples and moments from the story.
I'd almost say this game has a niche appeal, but it seems to have resonated with so many that "niche" might be an inaccurate descriptor.  However, it is a bit strange. This game is part action jrpg, part open world, part top down / side scrolling shooter. I initially picked this up because it looked fun, and I had been looking for a good take on AI + philosophy. I personally went into this game completely blind, I had not played the original NieR, nor the Drakengard series, and I can confidently say that they are not at all required to get full enjoyment from Automata, especially because there are multiple thousands of years canonically separating each installment. Same universe, but only loosely related, at most.
Gameplay: At a baseline, combat is fluid and fun, controls are smooth and responsive. But if you are unfamiliar with action rpgs, it may take a little bit of time or possibly some controller remapping to get used to it. I cannot personally speak to the keyboard and mouse experience, but it's probably best played on a controller. While Automata's gameplay has a strong foundation and has a lot going for it, it is also far from perfect. There are several instances in the game where the viewing angle and controls will sudenly shift from free roam to top-down, or side scroll, and it's not often a smooth transition, sometimes occuring while you are already engaged with enemies. Camera troubles aside, the changes in perspective do at least offer a wide variety of experiences which is a bit refreshing. Combat has several different weapon types, each with their own style of combos. While the game starts you with short sword = fast attack, long sword = power attack, you can actually experiment and do some mixing and matching, such as having the long sword as your fast attack with a fist weapon as your strong attack. Different configurations lead to varying attack styles and animations, which is really cool. Additionally, the game allows you to customize your character strengths through the use of chips, which give various bonuses to enhance your combat efforts. While many chips are a basic sort of 'do more damage', 'take less damage', some actually modify game mechanics, like adding invincibility frames, automatically popping a potion at low health, adding a ranged rippling effect to each swing, or applying slow motion to your enemies for a couple of seconds after you perform a perfect dodge. There's also special attacks your pod assistant can perform, such as a large lazer, or a ranged attack barier. However, for all of the intricateness of the combat system, nuance is generally unecessary as you progress in the game, as the bosses start to reuse attack patterns without introducing enough to really shake things up. The gap between difficulties is rather steep; very hard makes every source of damage including minor hits instantly lethal; hard makes a number of attacks in the game instant death unless you invest heavily into defense; normal is fairly forgiving, and allows you to lock-on; while easy gives you access to chips that can automatically attack and dodge for you. Personally I would have been most comfortable with a difficulty step between normal and hard, but I eventually found myself enjoying hard. Finally, while the tutorial is serviceable (and wonderfully cinematic), it may leave you underprepared or fail to clarify some key concepts (such as the fact that you can interrupt your own attack animations mid-swing with dodge, or that sometimes it's necessary to chain-dodge to survive). On that note, death is brutal, as it will leave your chips in your corpse, and you have to fight your way through enemies to retrieve it and get those mods back, or else. Additionally, if you happen to die before accessing the game's very first save point, you have to start from the begining again, which I unceremoniously found out the hard way. Criticisms and nitpicks aside, again, the core of the game is really fun. Also there's pig riding, I feel like that's worth a mention.
Presentation: The soundtrack is phenominal, character models are fantastic, the setting is interesting, the environments are memorable, but the graphics leave a bit more to be desired. With the OST, there's not much more to say than it's really beautiful, and suits the emotional twists and turns of the narrative quite perfectly. With the character models, I took an initial interest in the way 2B and 9S look with their black attire and blindflods, but perhaps the true winners here are all of the adorable, rusted, highly configurable machines you encounter in your travels, even as they try to murder you while flashing red eyes. The setting is a far distant future where you are playing as androids in the conflict against alien created machines, trying to protect the final remnants of humanity. Immediately you are given a conflict and a purpose, and are dropped in on the action. As you explore the world you'll encounter a variety of scenery, there's something to be said for that initial moment you land in the city overtaken by nature, or your first nervous steps towards the eerie amusement park. But this all brings me to my last point on presentation; while the aesthetics are on point, the graphics feel a bit muddy, kind of lacking the vibrance you would expect out of today's standards.
Theme: Automata fancies itself as a mysterious, deeply emotional and highly philisophical narrative. I would say it accomplishes what it sets out to do with an uncommon maturity, albeit, you might be fooled into thinking otherwise given 2B's risque attire. Again, it's hard to discuss this at length without giving away spoilers, but I will say that it rewards those who read between the lines and have an eye for detail. Also I have to give it to them, the game legitimately tugged at my heartstrings at several points, it made me cry.
Now the final note I'm going to make in this review is about the quality of the port. It's bad. There's no sugarcoating it. In fact, a lot of the negative ratings are due to the bad port. There's issues getting fullscreen & borderless window to work, the game may randomly crash on you, you might encounter performance dips in certain sections. I would normally expect better out of Square Enix. Personally, none of these things prevented my enjoyment of the game, I didn't encounter the problems too frequently, but this could be a dealbreaker for some. Hopefully we'll see a patch sometime.
All in all, it's a lovely game and I recommend it. But if you have a chance to play this on console instead, you may want to do just that.

A lovely little gem of a game. A .hackish setting, gameplay that's like a somewhat faster-paced and more in-depth Secret of Mana, and plenty of charm. The worst thing I can say about it is that the perspective kind of screws with the auto-jumping puzzles on occasion - gauging the height of some platforms isn't always easy - but overall this is shaping up to be a great package. With the version number sitting somewhere around the 0.8 mark, I have little reason to think this won't be done.
EDIT: Having put in more time,I'm going to re-word that sole criticism more strongly, and add an additional one: the perspective absolutely skewers the platforming segments by dint of being completely unsuitable for it. Very poor design decision. Destroys any ability to accurately gauge distance/height in a LOT of cases - almost every jump feels like a gamble.
In addition, evasion isn't nearly as effective as it should be. While it works fine against projectile attacks, the majority of the enemies have melee attacks that either have turn-on-a-dime tracking, tells that are too quick/subtle to reliably spot in the middle of a busy combat encounter, or some combination of these. By and large, an enemy that goes in for a melee attack isn't going to care how many pirouettes you pull trying to slip away, or in what direction you do them in. They're just going to turn around and kick you in the face anyway.
Considering these are two significant flaws that affect two of the games most significant facets of gameplay - combat and platforming - I'm tempted to flip that thumb downwards. I'm still charmed enough - and frankly, at this point, invested enough - to give it a pass and keep trying to work with these problems. I would think carefully about these aspects of gameplay before picking it up, though. They can quite easily cause frustration.

I remembered to review something finally!
So HOG wise, I'd say it's an okay game overall. Definitely not the best, and definitely not remarkable. The only thing that stood out to me was being able to put clues together and make deductions to help your case (and further the storyline). I haven't encountered that in a game yet, so I'd say that was new and interesting.
The storyline was alright, felt pretty cliché to me for the majority of it though. There were also a few jumpscare moments, but not enough to actually make you afraid. And some sounds, like thumping, can be heard throughout the gameplay.
Voice acting was meh. There were moments where I expected the voices to rise, etc. due to rising emotions, but there wasn't, so it just felt odd to listen to, among several other instances.
As for the game play, the hidden object scenes are decent. There were quite a few times I had to sit and stare, then give up and consult the HO guide for that one last item, but overall the scenes were good. I wouldn't say too terribly difficult, but enough of a challenge. Most of the scenes repeat at least 3 times, so they get old quick. Also, there are only two, or three, instances where you have to complete something in order to unlock a hidden object. I'm used to having several every scene, so this was an odd experience for me, and I'd have to say I was disappointed.
As for the puzzles, there were very few of them! I was surprised by how little there was, so that was another area of disappointment. They weren't too difficult though, and I actually found some of them fun. And thankfully this game provided instructions, though they aren't the most clear sometimes.
Also, there is no teleport function, so if you get annoyed easily with backtracking I do not recommend this game, as there is quite a lot of it.
Overall, I recommend the game if you get it in a bundle or a cheap sale, but don't pay $10 for this game. It is a nice distractor for a few hours.

(original review, ~16 hours)
This game will be great for some people, but it started to get really frustrating for me. Like some other Paradox games (Crusader Kings comes to mind), there is a large focus on diplomacy, with warfare occurring comparatively infrequently. This can be fun, but unfortunately fleet sizes and resources are rather unforgiving. Perhaps it was just bad luck with regards to whatever modifiers the empire had, but the first empire I went to war with had a fleet about half again the size of my entire fleet capacity (we had the same number of colonies, and I had more territory, filled with mining stations). I hate strategy games that decide to give the AI more resources to increase the difficulty, which seems the case here.
Additionally, which tech you can research is essentially random, so there isn't that element of strategy common in most other games of the genre, and you can't trade tech, either. Even with multiple unilateral research trade agreements, I still was one of the lower tech empires for some reason, which made it clear the tech trading was about useless. On top of this, I often like creating a network of alliances (especially in games where I don't expand fast enough to avoid becoming an underdog), which is made far more difficult by the desire to form mutual defense pacts being quite low in the AI, and having almost no desire to form more than one.
Other nitpicks I had included that space battles take weeks to play out (real time battles in a real time system). For realism, it seems like it would have been prudent to have separate battle screens so that naval battles could play out in the space of a single day (as they typically do, in both real life and pretty much all scifi), while movement and ground combat could remain on the week-month scale. Further, it would be nice if it weren't so hard to expand. For some reason, it costs you personal influence to expand your empire, even if major factions want you to do just that, and colony ships are massively expensive in terms of almost every resource. Also, why do you only get resources on the first of the month, if each day is effectively its own mini-turn? It's a pain waiting for a full month to pass just so you can get a very small part of that income that you needed to finish a building.
There are a lot of good points to this game, don't get me wrong, it just isn't the best for me. It has nice shiny graphics, apparently good mod support (Though I haven't tried modding it, yet), and the diplomacy heavy nature of it (including the war dynamics) are an interesting change of pace from the average 4X game.
(Additional thoughts, ~93 hours)
After getting frustrated, I went back and modded this game (doing so is incredibly easy) to give myself more resources. Even so, the sheer build times of ships, the chaotic research system, and the limitations of resources (even modded to be about 6x higher!) made for an incredibly slow slog. I found myself waiting for hours, just micromanaging construction ships, waiting to have enough ships to be able to attack the weak empire next to me, so that I could spend about 20 minutes to capture 5 planets, and then go back to micromanaging construction for another 2 days (out of game) until the automatic 10 year truce expired.

What a mixed bag and yet a profoundly enjoyable game, although generally flawed, this Game of Thrones turned out to be in the end. Game's story is unpredictably interesting and doesn't stoop to merely rehashing the familiar tunes from the books, but it carries their tone and atmosphere perfectly into an interactive medium while its two protagonists are some of the most layered characters I have ever played as in any game and as a result it's incredibly satisfying to watch their grim tales unfold over the course of the game, all the while bringing the story's peculiar framing into foreground and delivering one of the more compelling experiences in recent years. Sadly, this is where the other side of the coin comes into play - game's technical and mechanical aspects are questionable at best and a mess at their worst. One glance at these graphics will tell you they weren't where the budget went and the sound department didn't fare much better, VA suffering in particular with not even the main characters managing to avoid the brunt of the damage, for the most part. It's clear the voice talent wasn't given much direction to work with while they were delivering their lines and this vague design philosophy carries over into other things like somewhat archaic combat and arguable direction when it comes to gear design, secret finding and other systems.
I should point out, bold and underline that I still enjoyed Game of Thrones immensely when all the good and bad is tallied at the end because, in my opinion at least, game's strong story and narrative manage to FAR outweigh it's technical shortcomings. If you enjoy a story with an edge that doesn't hold back any punches and without the proverbial knights in shining armor, this just might be the game for you.

If Borderlands2 was "The Little Mermaid (1989)" then the Presequal would be "The Little Mermaid II: Return to the Sea (2000)" Or, like when "Transformers" came out in theatres again, and you could accidentally rent "Transmorphers" at Blockbuster if you you weren't paying attention or weren't hip to the scam.
Graphics:  6/10
When I played the original, I sneared at the cell-shading. I thought it was poorly done, but it grew on me. I BL2, they spruced it up and made it look good . . . or so my brain told me. In this, the pre-sequal, it looks like no effort was made to improve upon the graphics, soapy texture pop-in, or anything like that . . . but it's not worse. So, as the saying goes: If you're not getting ahead, you're falling behind.
Art Direction: 7/10,
see above for my opinion of the cell-shading. The character designs are solid enough. The sets are layed out in ways that are interesting enough, though there is a lot of filler and clutter where everything is stuffed . . . then there are the vast characterless expanses of nothing that reside beyond the playable area. Again, they did a good knock-off of the previous 2 entries but did nothing to improve. But, some the new characters are ok. Some of the set pieces look thought out.
Writing: 4/10.
Right away ,pick Athena if you are playing alone . . . or the story makes NO sense. To start, BL2's writting was friggen great, through and through. In BLPS, so far, the writing vacillates between mediocre and ear bleeding aneurysm inducing garbage. The story pacing is such that it pushes you to urgently complete the story missions, but ya know . . . no rush.♥♥♥♥♥♥ you know the main plot. It's predictable to the max, so what it needs to lean on is not THE suprise reveal, but awesome action, a false sense of urgency, maybe a personal transformation, the strength of relatable characters, plenty of lore easter-eggs, and for you to get into the moment -despite knowing the end. So go do some side-missions at your own pace. Claptrap, is his usual blight on the game. Dear god, kill the whole line off already. Please give me the ability to kill them. I want them and their creator destroyed. I want the voice actor and the person who signed off on claptrap, as a concept, to be slapped in the face for every time anyone ever wished claptrap would just shut - the - hell - up. No, that would lead to death. Nevermind, it's just wrong of me to want someone tortured to death for creating a terrible cancerous bleeding polyp of a character. Little of BL2's charm remains in this entry. Many characters are lifeless zombies that speak gibbirish. Litterally . . . I have no friggen clue what many people are saying. It's in some sort of outrageous moon-speak that sounds like a red-neck and a kangaroo simultaneously farting through a bullhorn. Also, ZERO VOLUME CONTROL DOES NOT MAKE WORDS FUNNY!

Quality Control: 5/10,
Lots of garbage textures next to hi-res textures, characters running through walls, stilted animations, same mobs over and over, killing a giant floppy monster and when it dies it hits the ground like a giant rock-hard turd and tumps over . . . then disolves . . . aparently to be respawned by Hyperion. The big "H" in the sky was painted by someone with a different artstyle than the creator of the rest of the universe. Did I mention that animations were stilted and rigid andcharacters had lifeless faces? Would you like to cover at a corner and shoot at doods? Nope, you hit the wall. You'll have to step a good 5ft away from that corner before your exploding frosty mirv bullets of O2 replinishment actually make it to the enemy. A lot of the problems the other entries in the series had, but in greater quantity with no solutions.
Sound: 7/10
claptrap and meh music and nasally voice actors being outrageous. Moxxi is still alright, good things happened there. The rest is re-used assets or so-so implimentation. Still disapointed that BL2 promised Dub-step (Nero level quality) and did not deliver. You ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. But at least this time they didn't promise me anything they didn't plan to deliver.
Controls: 8/10
There are some weird choices on what buttons to stack up. What if I don't want brakes and grenades to both be the G button? For the most part, controls are good. Vehicles, meh. Double jumps are jfun and easy to control. No beef with the control, but platforming can still be a beast with the occasional poor level design or huge collision box on a small object.
Gameplay: 7/10
Not really open world since it's all difficulty gated with drastic damage spikes. It does give the illusion of open-worldiness by allowing you to play the story and skip the side-stories (which are looooooong and drawn out- never being as simple as they let on- always an understated goal- but you'll still be killing the same ol mobs everywhere you go) and just try to beat the story missions at a higher difficulty. If you wasted your time trying, and a strategy change doesn't work, you can grind on a side-quest for loot and XP and badass points. Basically, the same as the previous 2 . . . except its in low gravity. That's pretty neat. My only complaint is that the gravity should not change depending on the presence of atmosphere. Gravity should be pretty much constant on a moon, lower on the space station- done. Otherwise there's LOADS of things to open, which you can ignore unless you really actually need ammo. You could buy a ______, but meh, a good one will come along. Most of the game is really just standing around sorting through♥♥♥♥♥♥in your inventory and deciding what a name implies that is NOT in the god-damned description and shooting at walls to try and determine which gun is better. If you like loot management games, this one is for you. Or, you can just roll with whatever you have ammo for. That works too. Guns are a dime for 10,000 in this game so screw em. Go places, kill stuff, get things, deliver things, sell rewards. Nothing new here, but fun enough.
Overall: 6/10
Basically it's a rip-off/ standalone expansion of the previous game with poor writing and a low-gravity gimmick. I would not say it's a good use of your money. Just make up your own prequal story and play BL2 again.
***Edit: 22 hours of torture in. My review has not changed. I'm even at a point where I should grind on side missions to level up so I can just finish the damn game . . .  and it was getting fun for a bit there, then pppppppppppppppppppppppppttttttt. Still thumbs down. This review stands.***

Resident Evil Revelations is fun at some points, but yet feels like a chore to play at other points.  I am a big Resident Evil fan, although I must admit I favor the classic style of RE(1-3, CV, Remake, 0) to the newer ones (4,5, 6).   However, despite that I still am capable of liking the new style of RE games because RE 4 is one of my favorite games of all time.
Revelations, I feel tries to mix the two together somewhat.   Certain points of the game where you play as Jill, mostly the earlier chapters in the game, you get  a sense of classic RE elements (minus tank controls in favor of the over the shoulder style) such as finding keys for certain doors, "puzzles", tight corridors and dodging.  Ect.   However its very dumbed down in a way, and the "puzzles" I speak of are all the same puzzle basically.  I appreciate it nontheless, but sadly after midwayish into the game, it mostly loses this type of gameplay it felt like and favored a more linear style.
At other times the game has these boring shooting/"action" sessions that just drag on sometimes.  It seems anytime you're not playing as Jill, the game is just simply lackluster and generic.  Sessions where you shoot what seems like a million hunters can drag on at times. (Despite all episode "parts" being pretty short in all honesty")  They aren't fun at all.
I played on normal difficulty and it wasn't that hard of a game to me in all honesty.  Lots of ammo, health, ect ect.  However they do add harder difficulties which is also appreciated.
A positive thing that comes to mind, is a couple of the "bosses" in this game I found to be pretty creepy and scary.  Which is sort of odd for Resident Evil, as most of the time the bosses come across as "scary, but mostly threatining"  rather than having a super "Creepy" aspect to them.  2 bosses in particular I feel were pretty creepy, and they did a good job to set the tone with them.  Other than those two bosses, the game really isn't that scary and honestly there are a few, but not a whole lot of jump scares surprisingly.
Overall, the game was worth the playthrough for certain chapters, but some were just lackluster.  This game is very average to play on PC.  Now as this game was originally a 3DS game though, not bad for a 3DS game from 2012.   Overall I would 5.5/10.  So I recondmend only if you're into the RE series.

This game is the perfect mix of terrible and worse; it's the expired milk in the fridge you know is bad, but that you know you're gonna smell anyway .  It's polarizing because everything from the voice acting, to the mechanics, to the graphics are mediocre, if not downright terrible, YET, the absolutely addicting story and the kooky, surrealist overtones make this game well worth the money (pro tip: play this game with a controller or not at all; it was never meant to be a PC game).  I don't care how pretentious it sounds, most people just don't understand this game.  It's meant to be a joke on itself in a sense because of how silly and cartoony everything seems to be, but don't let that fool you.  This game has a story of unparalleled depth in terms of video games,
If you like surrealist art, if you enjoy the Monty Python films and the Flying Circus; if you like getting wasted and listening to The Bends while watching every Wallace and Grommit movie ever made with the volume off so the claymation sheep sound like Thom Yorke, I promise you will love this game more than most members of your family.
The reason it was never commercially successful was because it is meant for a certain kind of player who's in a certain kind of mood for 8-12 hours every so often.  This game can be fun multiple times through because the combat, while admittedly pretty clumsy mixes things up enough to keep you on your toes, and the various things you can buy and the mini-games make sure the experience doesn't become too heavy.
To sum things up, don't buy this game if you're looking for a typical shooter or a typical survival horror game, or a typical anything.  This game is truly one of a kind, and if you can learn to appreciate is flaws, you will understand where I'm coming from.  I've never played a game this truly original in my whole 15-odd years as a gamer.  If it weren't for the original KOTOR, this would be my favorite game ever.  10/10.

"I Shall Remain" is a wonderful ARPG that has nifty and fun features which remind me of Dungeon Siege 1 and 2.
TL;DR: I recommend you buy it.
Now, for a slightly in depth review, I'll do the cons first:
CONS:
*The story's more of "tell don't show," character wise, with the protoganist literally saying what he's feeling and thinking about at the moment, but that's a slight complaint.
* Early-game is hard, but that should be manageable once you find a way to get more serum.
PROS:
* The doctrine system and Dungeon Siege like character development. I think more ARPGs should follow this format. Your character progresses by using a weapon. Using a shotgun increases your skill for that, which in turn increases your rifle skill and in turn increases agility.  Once you level up, you gain a "doctrine," which are essentially skill trees which help you customize your character even further, as well as research points for further specialities. You can build your character to be a leader with buffed NPCs, or a solo rifle wielding killing-machine.  The system is fun because it feels natural...why would I ever put my hard-earned points into small arms when you've been killing enemies with your trusty winchester shotgun?
* New spin on post-apocalyptic games: When you think "post apocalyptic," you think of Fallout, right? Past a future time with robots and computers? Well, this game takes place in the 1940s, sometime after WW2, and things have gone terribly, terribly wrong. Its a cool and novel way of looking at an old trope.
* Serum: You're also infected. Which means you have to kill zombies to gain their zombie blood, from which the serum's derived. BUT the main currency in the game is serum. So there's a tight balance between getting skill points (by selling serum) to keeping some in stock for you to use before you become too infected that you can't fight anymore. It's a tight balance that keeps you on edge.
Bottomline: Game is Fun, pay and play as soon as you get the CashMoney for it.

Hi everyball!
I'm going to start off by simply stating that this game is awesome. I'm a huge fan of the pixel art style, so if you are too, this game is a must. I bought this game knowing it was in early access because I just couldn't pass up on the art style and the slew of positive reviews.
- This was actually the selling point for me. I love the art. I love, love, LOVEEEEE the art. Developers, I believe you made a great decision reworking the portraits of the characters within the game, as they made for an excellent presentation.
- Really immerses you into the world of CrossCode.
- And boy is the physics butter-smooth. The physics is great in that when I make a mistake, I know it was of my own accord and not the fault of the game itself.
- The combat in this game is quick. Once you get into the later areas of the game, standing still while you're in combat for even a split second means certain demise, and the game teaches you this right from the get-go.
- The level designs are outstanding and feel like a lot of care was put into them. I enjoyed all of the areas I explored in the game.
- The type that makes you go: "Yeah, I did that! Feels good!" when you beat it! I really love how some of the puzzles revolve around a certain element and start off easy, then progressively get harder as you progress, which makes it twice as rewarding when you beat them.
- I literally clapped when I reached the end of the story implemented. I adore the characters in this game oh so much! I need plushies!
Now that we're past the overview, I'll offer a more personal perspective. The way I'm going to format this is by having two sections; story run, and 100% run. The difference between the two is that a player only doing the story most likely won't encounter the same things a player doing a 100% run will. In doing this, I will be offering two different perspectives on the game.
A 100% run for those of you who don't know, is basically exploring all areas, obtaining every item, and completing every side-quest alongside the story quests and many other things. I kept this explanation brief, but I hope it's clear and get's the point across.
- Soundtrack will be pretty enjoyable since you usually don't stick around some areas for too long.
- Looks pretty neat, fun to traverse in.
- It's going to get really repetitive, really fast. You're going to be hearing the same soundtrack for the area you're in over and over and over, and it get's to the point where you just want to get to another area as quickly as possible, just to get a new soundtrack playing.
- Sometimes I can't tell when a platform is above the character, so a lot of the time you're going to think "Oh I'm on a high platform, I bet I can reach the one across from me." until you try to do so and you smack face first into a stone pillar and drown.
I actually had to devise a strategy in order to tell if I can jump on a platform or not; throw a ball. If it looks like I'm above a platform I try to make sure by throwing a ball at the platform I want to get to. If the ball flies over it, I'm in the green, If it doesn't then no-go.
For now this will be all. I know the 100% run review above may seem unfair, since it's the price you pay for going for a 100%, but I feel it's worth noting regardless since different people play games differently.
Thank you everyball, and thank you especially to the developers for such an endearing and fantastic game! CrossCode holds a special place in my heart.
If you're a fan of Dead Frontier, this game is for you!

I honestly don't know - why this game is rated Very Positive (at the moment of writing my review). I don't know - maybe it would bloom at the late game, but this far game feels highly unfinshed - more like a beta test, where testers have to pay to test the game.
The game is not without positive points - but this far - I've found 2 of them:
- Advancement system, based on 'you are what you use' and unlocking 'perks' that further shape you into desired hero, which is both nice and annoying (because you can't save some points and invest them into firing rifles, for example, all of a sudden - you need to tediously go from missing every second shot to being able to hit zombie into eye from great distance)
- Setting - most of zombie games happen in modern/futuristic settings and there are not many WW2 zombie games.
But negative points are plenty:
- Graphics - that's my first problem.
Sometimes I couldn't see my character in that mess. Quite often I couldn't see enemies. And flashlight doesn't help much. And to add to all that - after they are killed common enemies dissipate into red mist which obscures your vision even more.
Update: Thanks to developer's reply - I found out that there is 'aging' affect in options that makes things more brown. So, turning it off helps somewhat and returns colors to the game. Stil - other graphic problems stay - hard to spot enemies, hard to notice character (there are still moments when even without 'aging' character blends with back ground perfectly), blood mist into which dead enemy turn (imagine backing off from a horde of zombies, while shooting at them - and every shot enemy bursts into cloud of mist to cover its buddies). Also, found another problems - when your character gets covered by a wall - you can see his outline through it. But when enemy gets covered by one - there is no outline, even if the enemy is hitting your character.
- Sound - or mostly lack of it. There are sounds of gunfire and background music mostly stays very quiet, aside from moments when it plays compositions 'cat jumped onto piano and we've decided to include it into soundtrack'. There is NO in-game voice, which brings you to another problem - sometimes character tell their thoughts/feelings/else, sometimes there is even a narative, but it's all (except some dialogues) made as a string at a bottom of the screen, which is hard to notice (most of the time you'd be focused on shooting things or looking at other parts of screen).
- Level design - levels are a mess. In some games - there is a difference between one building and another - but here they are almost same. And maps are a mess as well - sometimes you see a passage on the map only to find out that it's blocked by something. And yes, things that block your passage add insult to the game - game tells you that you are a soldier, so you expect to be trained in things like jumping ot stepping over things... but, no. A couple of tires is an impassable object. Knee-high barier - also.
Sumarizing my opinion - the game HAS potential.
After fidling with graphical setting - game stopped being unpleasant, but it's still clumsy. So, I still won't recommend and name it a risky purchase - but at least now I see why SOME people may like it. I'll try to update this review if there would be any significant changes in game or my opinion.

Even though it is overshadowed by the somewhat superior Rebirth, the original Binding of Isaac is worth checking out. If you can get past its framerate issues and lack of controller support, you'll find an enjoyable and addictive (yet challenging) game that offers endless replayability at a relatively low cost (which is made even lower when on sale).
Pros:
+Terrific Artstyle
+Awesome Music (Superior to that of Rebirth in my opinion)
+Gameplay is very straightforward
+Tons of enemies and items
+Randomly generated levels means each playthrough is different
Cons:
-Keyboard controls and lack of controller support
-Severe framerate issues
-Hit detection can be very wonky
-Item descriptions are very vague, leading to a lot of trial and error
-High difficulty can be frustrating, especially for newcomers
All in all, The Binding of Isaac is worth cheecking out, but if you are looking for a smoother and more coherent game, Rebirth is a safer bet.

First things first - terribly cluttered, same colored, indistinct, logic-free Hidden Object Scenes. They contain no objects that require actions to obtain (stuff like “combine statue and crown to find a Queen, use the axe on the tree to get some Wood”) which are apparently one way to force some logic onto the scene, but do have plenty of miscallenous drawers that neither hide nor reveal anything of use. Never before have I had to resort to hints in
single goddamn HOS.
While double-dipping into HOS’s is extremely common, this is the first game I’ve had using the same HOS three times. Might have been four for some of them - the HOS's are samey enough that I couldn't keep track.
There's no guide (Enigmatis 2 didn't have one either, but it was well constructed enough that I didn't feel it needed one). There's no map - not even talking about fast travel, there's no map period. Want to know where to go next? Just follow the hint button.
Constant backtracking. Row across a lake to look at some moss covered rocks, then row back across to discover an HOS scene which gives you a scraper - back across the lake you go to use it. Go all the way to the site of the final confrontation, enter the correct sequence of demonic runes to open the gate to the underworld – and then backtrack way back to the town for a rope ladder that will allow you to descend.
Puzzles are♥♥♥♥♥♥ No on-screen instructions (hit the instructions button for an explanation). They involve ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like a compiling a picture that was torn apart – with the pieces being only
the shape of the cut parts, so take a wild guess and try to jam them in, even if the silhouette does not match.
The game is not an adventure-lite, like the second, but very much a series of arbitrary obstacles that you backtrack through.
Constant ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jumpscares - half of them come when you're discovering corpses, and half from your freaking
in the investigation. The big bad actually doesn't do anything for the entirety of the game.
The protagonist is a ♥♥♥♥ing moron. She isn't too bright in the sequel either, but this version can give Alex Denton a run for her money in sheer cheerful cluelesness. As you're examining the evidence inside your hotel room, a hand reaches into the closeup from offscreen - someone apparently barged into your hotel room, grabbed some evidence right out of your hands, and jumped out the window without the protagonist ever getting a good look at them. Though as of writing this review I have 76.7 hours, I must have played this for at least another 100 hours in offline mode. I'm usually not the kind of person to play Tower Defense games. The only TD game I have ever played aside from this was Fieldrunners 2 on iOS, and even then I played it very little. That being said, this game is VERY fun and quite addicting too. Got this on sale a while back, but now that it's on sale again for the 2016 Summer Sale, I wanted to take the time to recommend this game to everyone.
This game plays just like any other TD I have seen: enemies walk along a path, you build towers along said path, and defend a certain end point of the path by shooting at enemies with those towers. But what really makes this game stand out is the customization of the towers and the possibilities and potential they have based on the gems that you create. You have gems of different colors, each color having their own effects, which you can put into towers and traps to damage enemies and apply those effects. However, you can combine gems to combine their effects, as well as applying a boost to overall damage at the cost of lowering their overall special power. These combined gems are perfect for towers, but for traps you'll want to stick with single color gems to get the most of their effects (until you get certain gems later that you can still combine with them and get an even more massive boost), as traps will greatly lower damage but will boost specials.
There are many skills to unlock, as well as new difficulties that also increase your experience gain, not to mention hundreds of achievements. Thus, you get a lot of value for just a few dollars.
However, there is one qualm that I do have with this game, and I know this is mainly an issue with it being a Flash game and all, but...when you get far into the game, to the point you have thousands of monsters on your path, the game will lag intensely. Even if you have a good computer, it'll happen. But, you'll only have to worry about that when you get really far into the game and you are farming for large amounts of experience. As of this review, my wizard level is at around 5,000, and I have had sessions where I would play on a single map for 6+ hours
Pros:
* In-depth customization of gems (you'll see just how customizable when you learn about things like 32-spec gems)
* Lots of things to find and unlock, and great replayability
* Very nice skill tree system that helps boost your gems and overall abilities
* Talisman system, where you can insert collectible fragments that boost your stats
* Practically endless, skill points being purchaseable with shadow cores (dropped from enemies) and some skills having no cap
(I read somewhere that theoretically the level limit is around 50,000 but don't know if this is true)
Cons:
* Very laggy when you get a couple thousand monsters on the path. This is to be expected since it's a Flash game but it can be an annoyance, especially when it becomes a necessity when trying to max your experience. All I can suggest is keeping your speed low (1x or 3x, I heard that with 9x enemies can even bypass some of your traps) and just doing other things at the same time to help pass time. Still, this is not much of a big deal and won't happen until you are really far into the game, so it's not something that should turn anyone away from this wonderful game.

This game feels like it throws every possible upgrade mechanic at the wall just to see what sticks. It's not that the core tower defence system is unenjoyable, it's that when I try and play it like a tower defence game in the way I think of games in the genre, I find that all the ancillary mechanics end up stripping away the core motivation I have to play these kinds of games.
It all ends up boiling down to optimising for experiences points and item drops. It has to be said that my strong distaste for this game is not unrelated to my strong distaste for MMOs. The whole justification becomes circular, and in the never ending loop of grinding for more stuff in order to get better at grinding, I just don't feel like I am getting anything out of the experience.
I'm relatively sanguine with TD games that have a few modest upgrades here and there, but this goes so far overboard that I can't actually see the game through all that noise.

Although I had to tweak the video graphics down, this game was surprisingly playable on my computer that has only an AMD A8-5500 APU with 8GB RAM and AMD 7400M video on Windows 7 Pro SP1.  It got pretty choppy if there was a lot of action, like when you've got 4+ stars of notoriety and things are swarming you.
I had no problems getting the game installing and running, but every now and then, it would seemingly minimize unexpectedly.  That may have been due to other programs I had running, though I'm not sure -- when it happened, the other programs were not showing a pop-up window or any other alerts.  By the way, at some point during installation, I had to edit the SR2_PC.EXE file's compatibility settings to disable desktop composition on Windows 7.
The game itself crashed a few times, generally during missions -- so when it happened (which was rarely), it was annoying to restart the mission because in doing so, you may have lost whatever vehicle and followers you had before the crash.
I could never get a USB controller to work, and steering vehicles with keyboard/mouse takes getting used to -- it's very twitchy, depending on the vehicle.  During a heated chase, it was bothersome to accidentally drive off of a bridge and automatically fail the mission, or waste time being stuck on a tree or a cement barrier.
The music is fun, with a variety to choose from -- yet if you play a lot, you'll start to hear the same songs.  I eventually adjusted the configuration to turn-off the car radios by default, whenever entering a vehicle.
Some of the missions had me confused on what to do or where to go, so I had to pause / minimize the game, then look-up tips on various wiki pages and forums.
Finally, the graphics do indeed look dated as of 2013 (after all, Saints Row 4 is out), especially the cut scenes.  Still, it's a fun, silly game to play.  Be wary that there is a lot of violence and cruelty in the game, so it's not for kids.

4. The Stellaris dev team does implement their own political ideology into the game. Decent, but noticeable. That wouldn't be this bad if their political opinion wouldn't be leftist-socialliberal-SJW. If you're at least part-time-marxist, you will like it, but I can definitly not agree with Stellaris' world view.
I don't like to "thumbing down" Stellaris, but I just have to do it, when I see how the dev team/publisher acts.

People prefer TD;DRs to be visible, so here's my summary before the review:
Good game. Unique customization system, battle physics, and nice art style to it. The game should run flawlessly on most computer setups, and look nice while doing so with little to no compromise needed.
I'd give it a solid 8/10.
Now for the bulk and detail.
Gameplay: 8.5/10
------------------------------------------------------
This game delivers a hardly-done combat system that is both unique, and frustrating to get the full hang of at first. The core mechanics are not unlike Super Smash Brothers physics to fighting. You beat up an enemy, and as they have more damage to them, they fly further from your hits. If they hit a wall too hard, or fly out of bounds, they die. There's a default cap of 1000 damage before you simply drop dead, however. This is an entertaining concept, and it's done fairly well. The customization, however, leaves you feeling at times like you need specific parts on to get a certain edge in exploration and combat. An example would be the first major piece you get, a "core" that allows you to do super jumps into the air. Once you have this, you will most likely never be able to not use this ability anymore. Despite these sometimes almost-forced pieces, the game is more than fun enough to keep players' attentions for hours.
Story: Hard to Score
------------------------------
This game's story is hardly a driving force in actually playing. It's more of a guiding template for progression. You won't find yourself performing quests, no NPCs will be particularly important to you besides giving tips, and overall, mean nothing. It's a good system in place as-is to just familiarize you with how the game works, and that's about it.
Sounds: 8/10
------------------------------
Not much to say here in all honesty. The game's sounds and music match well with the atmosphere, and help bring you into the game further. It's not remarkable by any means, but it's a lovely side to the main course that is the gameplay.
Style: 7.5/10
------------------------------
There's nothing groundbreaking here. It all looks nice, has a fairly unique look about it for the characters, and all the customization options, but nothing that is jaw-droppingly good. There's enough TLC that the devs gave under the hood to keep things looking nice, but not enough to warrant acclaim for the art.
Multiplayer Elements: Unrated, will change when I actually try them.
------------------------------
This game is said to have a good multiplayer system, and I plan on trying it out proper at a later date. All I have done so far is the single player.
In short, good game, I'd wholeheartedly recommend trying it out.

Resident Evil: Revelations is the first game in RE's "Revelations" series, it's mainly focused on events that are not directly connected to the main series.
The game starts with Jill and a new character, Parker Luciani, as they are ordered by the BSAA to look for Chris & Jessica (another new character) on a ship called "Queen Zenobia". The game takes place in 2005, about one year before the events of "Lost in Nightmares".
First off, let me start with the setting. The "Queen Zenobia" makes for a great setting, it's atmospheric, mainly consists of tight corridors, and feels great to explore. Some other scenarios include Chris & Jessica or Quint & Keith (Again, new characters) wandering through a snowy mountain region and a kind of "flashback" scenario that shows the Terragrigia Panic. I don't want to talk further about the plot, since it would just spoil things.
I think that the Queen Zenobia is overall the best setting.
Secondly, the graphics. This game is a HD port of a Nintendo 3DS game, meaning that the graphics are not anything to brag about. However, I think they are sufficent enough to underline the mostly dark atmosphere. All the cutscenes are pre-rendered aswell.
The gameplay is fairly slow-paced. It mainly feels like RE4/RE5 with some modernizations like walking while aiming/reloading. RE3's dodge mechanic also makes a return. Each character only has one, unique melee move. Ammo is very important, and enemies will be able to lower your health considerably with just one hit. The healing mechanic is simple: You press a button, your health refills. You can aquire a variety of weapons, but as so often you start off with your trusty old Beretta (Yes, this game uses real life weaponry). You can upgrade your guns with parts that you can find throughout the levels. These parts will, for example, increase the critical hit chance, damage or firing rate. Each weapon only accepts a certain number of parts at once.
Something I somewhat dislike about the game are the silly character designs and some story elements. Most characters look out of place compared to the rest of the RE series, while others look as you would expect a BSAA/FBC field operative to look. The worst happened to Jill, as they decided to remodel her face for some reason. Horrible design choice.
The whole Terragrigia plot seems to be a bit too sci-fi to me (
), and again, dosen't really fit into the rest of the events.
Other than that I thought the plot was pretty good, better than Revelations 2 if you ask me.
This is also the first time we get to play Raid Mode. This gamemode is focused on combat, and is mainly about getting from A to B, destroying foes and looting ammo/weapon cases/parts on your way. I'm a big fan of Raid mode, in both Rev and Rev2. It's a huge grind fest, but if you are into that kind of stuff then you will love Raid Mode. The Trinity reward makes the mode more challenging than in Rev2, since it requires you to take no damage throughout the whole stage (among two other requirements).
Overall, I really like Revelations, I think it's a good mix between survival horror and action. Get it during sale.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
-------------------------
The sole reason I bought into this Early Access project was that I liked the premise of an ARPG with firearms.
One that preferably wouldn't turn into a pure bullet-hell late game, but took a more serious, even tactical approach.
Playtesting it, I was thoroughly surprised as to how well made it already was.
"I Shall Remain" offers a well thought-out experience even in its current state, you can feel from the very first minute that this is Scorpius' most ambitious project up to now and that a lot of work and love have already been invested.
The RPG-mechanics are by FAR surpassing what I had anticipated or would even have asked for, honestly.
ISR makes use of an Engine built in-house by the devs, seemingly built with the top-down perspective as a focus.
Nice to see some craftsmanship instead of Unity for a change, especially when it performs and looks very well.
Of course there are a few rough edges (mainly animations IMHO), but the devs are very open minded and already aware of what needs to be done. The biggest issues that have been brought up are already being adressed, THAT is how Early Access should work.
All in all, I am very much looking forward to the release and hope that ISR and respectively Scorpius Games get the attention they deserve.
My gut tells me they're going to finish this game 100%, no questions - and then probably pack another 15-20% on top of that, just because they're
1) awesome

So, if you came here looking for the game that would've been the outcome of "Diablo" and "Commandos" making a baby while "Hellgate London" was spying creepily through the keyhole, this is as close as you'll ever get to that!

I played through this game on the Xbox 360 years ago, the play time listed for this version doesn't reflect that.  Bought this a second time on sale because it's good and I like the developers.
When Deadly Premonition released years back, it was slammed by mainstream sites such as IGN for its subpar graphics and archaic controls.  Technically these reviewers pointed out the flaws this game has as a reviewer should, but they missed the magic this game seems to have for the players that love it.
For everything this game seems to get passable or "middling", there's something that makes you smile.  Driving is boring, but the conversations York has with himself make the long trips you have to take early in the game worth it.  You also do unlock and find better weapons and even some helpful abilities that make going around town easier later in the game.
Fans of Twin Peaks will get a more out of Deadly Premonition than other players.  I'll even go so far as to say that this is a must play if you like Twin Peaks.  There are plenty of subtle and not so subtle nods to that short lived television series.  The protagonist loves his coffee.  The town this game is based in feels quite similar to Twin Peaks and has quirky, memorable characters.
This was one of my favorite games of 2010.  If it's on sale I strongly recommend giving it a try.

I went from Atari to Commodore 64, then PC gaming. So I don't have nostalgic memories of sitting in front of a Nintendo, although sometimes we'd rent one or I'd play one at a friend's house. I can see the appeal, and people who would pick this game up obviously know what they're getting into.
I got this game as part of a bundle for next to nothing. If not for that, I would have left this one alone. In fact, I had it marked "Not Interested" after it coming up in my discovery queue. Anyhow, it's just like what you'd expect. Dicey chiptune music, quick zooms after battles, a bit of camera shake, and tons of dialogue. This game is one of the highest rated RPGs on Steam right now, but make no mistake, this is more of an action game than an RPG game. After an hour of playing I didn't see a single piece of loot or stat screen. Combat requires twitch reflexes as you block, dodge, and aim your attacks.
I can see the appeal. I totally get why so many people love this game. Personally, I just don't care for the style. I left this stuff behind in the 80s and I was anxious to move on even then. Bring on the polygons, pixel shaders, and texture maps!
