Amazingly fun parts-collecting beat-em-up local co-op/multiplayer game.
These aren't all the Pros and Cons, but ones that stick out, to me:
PROS:
- Great fun running around in Adventure mode collecting parts to upgrade your bots. Multiplayer Adventure especially.
- Versus is enjoyable, when enough parts have been made available via Adventure to lend builds some variety.
- Custom bots means your bot suits your play-style, skills on your designated inputs rather than based on equip slot.
CONS:
- Adventure Mode: When another player kicks the bucket, they are out for that entire adventure. No way to give one of your lives to bring them back into the action, even if you are sitting pretty with a surplus.
- Walljump: Jumping off of walls is simple, just bump your stick over. No need to Direction+A. However, more often than not this screws you in tight situations where you need to be agile while falling down a narrow shaft. Get too close to a wal and bump over, you've just flung yourself towards that red-hot damagepad and hurled yourself into a world of hurt, or worse. A simple choice in the input options to make walljump require Direction+A would fix this issue.
- Controller per Player: Need to go into options and designate who gets what controller number. The game doesn't have a bot select screen on startup to detect what player is using what controller.
OVERALL:
I'd highly recommend it. Having a blast in Adventure right now, and Versus should be better once we have more parts and colors unlocked. Great couch co-op/multiplayer game. If you are playing solo, I'd imagine it would lose some of its attraction (at least, it does for me. Then again, I do mostly multiplayer, so tastes will vary).
If you are looking for a title to play with friends couch-side, one that can be both co-op and competitive, this is a great title for that. I have over thirty five couch games, and this easily rocketed to the top five. Easy to pick up (Smash Bros is a good analogy for Versus and Boss Battles), concept is simple (It's an adventure-platformer/beat-em-up), and the customization to make your very own fighting robot to fight with, or against, your friends is great fun. Both Adventure and Versus (with adequate parts available) are easy to jump into and run with, as well as hop out of (bits and parts are saved even if you wipe in an Adventure Level).
Rating: 9/10
( 10/10 if Adventure Resurrection is added in later. It's just a bummer to blow up and have to sit there watching the rest of the crew play on without you, despite someone having a pile of lives they'll never use. )

After the first hundred hours, I still feel like I'm not even halfway through this game.  Well built Tower Defense game -- arguably the most solid one I've played.  While the graphics leave something to be desired, the replayability and massive amount of customization possible make this game nothing short of addictive.
The best part, for me, has been being able to reset traits and bonuses you've earned entirely, and even between fields.  This feature has significantly decreased the amount of grinding that one sometimes needs to do in order to advance in a TD game.  However, even grinding doesn't feel like the right word -- playing the same field on a higher difficulty, or with newly defined gemstone parameters, makes the field suddenly feel like a new game, with new challenges.  And with better than 100 fields, it never gets old.
Get this game if:  You are a tower defense fan, even a casual one; You enjoy puzzles and strategy; You like a lot of playtime for the dollar input.
Do not get this if:  You need maximum use of your videocard; you dislike grinding to level up, even a little bit; You require roleplay elements in your game at all.

Being a person whose played a lot of hidden object games, the Enigmatis series is pretty great. It's got a plot that's suspenseful with that whole murder mystery stuff going on, some paranormal wackiness, and overall it's pretty fun to play.
Neat Stuff:
* When taking things from Hidden Object puzzles, they STAY taken. Like, I don't know what this detective does with the crap she doesn't need but she doesn't toss it back in the puzzle, and new junk doesn't just randomly appear either. It makes the scenes more challenging as the hidden objects actually look like they belong, and it makes them easier as the game progresses and the more you complete a particular scene.
* The junk in the Hidden Object puzzles is relavant to the scenes. The piles upon piles of nonsense make sense in the storm-stricken areas, where houses have been blown through and wind dumped stuff in a tangle of laundry lines. The 'scary' places don't have stuff like bowling balls just hanging around (though they do have some weird stuff)
Lame Stuff:
* No fast travel through the map. Have to tediously go through each part of the map to get where you're going - no shortcuts.
* Despite claiming to be a detective, the heroine doesn't keep things that are obviously useful after using them. Sometimes they'll stick around for the next puzzle, but she discards them pretty quickly. I know this lady's concussed and all after that car accident, but get it together girl.
* The detective takes forever to piece together evidence and form a deduction. I understand, she's concussed and stuff, it's a wonder she's thinking clearly, but still.
* The detective keeps a deduction wall in the hotel room - even after someone has obviously broken and mucked with stuff. I know, she's concussed, fine.
* Crappy instructions on the puzzles that weren't immediately obvious. They stay the same quality for the entire series.
* There's one puzzle I didn't get at all - it was one of those "guess the hidden password based on nothing." In later games, the herione will staunchly refuse to muck with stuff until she has an idea of what combination or password she needs. I don't know if I missed a hint or what, but that puzzle made no sense to me.
A lot of my problems with the game can be explained away with the detective's concussion, so overall I really enjoyed the game. Good puzzles, good hidden object scenes, and a story that manages to keep interest.

While I can't call it a perfect rendition over the madness, the wacky level design, the witty humor or the re-playability of Borderlands 1 or 2 – Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel gives a rather neat addition to the franchise and, for once, worth a try even if you're not a so-called ״diehard״ fan of the series. Initially the game revolves around Handsome Jack; the ״Super-Evil״ maniac that ruled over Pandora on the last game is being presented here as the hero of this little adventure. For the first time we've got the chance to see Handsome Jack's story unfold, and witness his own persona falls into some deadly dark intrigues that made him who he is in the second game.
But the story doesn't end on the happily ever after note...
I found the story lacking in-depth to the point it felt like it was being told in a very niche aspect narratively, very one sided and not in a two-way fashion that passed through a multitude of different perspectives throughout the campaign of the last games. Some of the replacement characters you'll encounter (such as Nurse Nina for Dr. Zed or Janey Springs for Scooter) really aren't as funny and immersing as some of the most notorious NPCs we've ever met on the last two games (such as Tiny Tina and Tannis, for example). Another problem I've had in the game was the problematic level design; many times through your gameplay you'll find yourself pretty much lost on a dead-end and you'll have to go the other way around to get back to your mission – and that's WITHOUT mentening all the randomly-generated marks that appear abruptly on the map and basically confusing you as to where you should go next.
And because the entire game takes place on a moon orbiting the planet from the 2nd game, the environments are very samey and repetitive. It's essentially all gray moon-wastes and building interiors. The campaign DLC that's out there for the game, Claptastic Voyage, helps a little on this matter with all of the hectic concept designs running amok around the mind of Claptrap, but yet it doesn't solve that issue completely as the DLC is around 3 hours long, which is about a fifth of the entire playtime of the base game.
As a final thought: If you're a fan of the franchise, you'll have to play it. If not for Elphis, Pandora's moon – then for Handsome Jack – It's a pretty solid experience really. But if you're not as much of a fan... then I'll recommend you to skip this one and play the second game instead. Trust me, it's a real blast.

I wanted to give the game a fair shot as it's a VERY slow burn, especially for a 4x. The fleet battles are, frankly, a joke. Technological advancement just makes ships exponentiall more expensive, with a power level that doesn't scale the same (this is a well documented issue). It's purely a death-stack game. There are certainly missed opportunities for tactics using formations, planetary cover, and techs that would make fleet battles more interesting like stealth, subsystem targetting, etc.
For the first few encounters, the little story missions are interesting. That ends fairly quickly as you repeatedly encounter the same ones over and over. The RNG of universe generation seems to be a total crapshoot, with massive distances between ANY systems with planets (not to mention whether they are even habitable). This can make the early game really slow, especially if you have a close neighbor breathing down your neck.
The game lacks real depth. That is not to say that it isn't complex, but I've yet to see how the political and social systems really impact the game in a meaningful way. Everything is, eventually, overcome by tech or traditions, making the evolution of your empire feel artificial. The complexity, therefore, is smoothed over into a bland mid-to-late game experience that relies on 'crises' to give you a reason to continue playing.
EDIT 08/12/17: I wanted to see if there was something about this game that I was missing, so I kept playing because I WANT to like this game. Here's what I learned: the only means of vicotry is war. That's it. There is no political, scientific, or social means to win. There might be the appearance of such means, but they do not really exist. Federations are a joke. If you're in one, expect to be the only person contributing. Because the pace of the game is so terribly slow, expect to devote days to a single game only to have a surprise fallen empire show up, declare war, and wipe you out of existence.

Stellaris is entertaining for a few hours, but quickly becomes dull and tedious. When you first start a game, you're amazed and interested at how indepth the game feels with all the different mechanics. Plus, if you're a fan of the sci-fi genre, it's a blast to just get yourself immersed in growing a space empire. However, once you crack the surface, once you start learning about these mechanics, it quickly reveals itself to be shallow.
Combat is boring and unbalanced. It always boils down to having the bigger fleet, with few exceptions. Ground combat is even more boring and simplified, with no strategy involved at all. Simply move your army to a planet, land, and win. Managing your empire is boring and tedious.
To manage your empire, you have a few planets that you directly control and micromanage, and then have to delegate any other planets to "sectors." These sectors give the AI control over the planets, having them build and develop improvements. A good portion of the game is taken out of your hands and put into the AI's, and the AI is beyond inept. I've had sectors, with plenty of resources, still have empty planets with no improvements while they build nothing else. To try to get the most out of your planets, you have to constantly jockey with the sector system, do the dull and tedious colony development yourself, and then jockey with the sector system again. It's very boring, and adds more micromanagement to a system that was designed to reduce it.
Of course, the sector system is absolutely necessary, because the other space empires are just as inept as the sector AI. The only way to stop a player from completely steamrolling the galaxy is to cripple the player through using the sectors. If you try to play around the sectors, you get the micromangement hell I described above. If you use the sectors "as designed" then the game is still unbalanced, but still better than the optimal way to play.
I tried to like Stellaris, and at first I really did. It just becomes so boring and tedious. It's hard to explain how much time is wasted in this game just waiting. Waiting for resources, waiting for fleets to build, waiting for the invasion to end, waiting for the warscore to tick up so you can end a war, waiting, waiting, waiting. The only things that could have made the downtime between conflicts interesting was the empire management, which is taken out of control of the player through sectors, and then handled ineptly by the AI.
In addition to the problems with the actual game, Paradox Interactive has become a terrible company to support. Gone are the days where Paradox made fantastic, if buggy, games for relatively cheap, with great expansions to enhance the vanilla game. Now, Paradox releases broken games, then releases a constant stream of overpriced DLCs that add one or two features, that are inevitably broken or unbalanced on release. The sad part is, most of the DLCs are great ideas, with terrible implementation, or are great ideas, at the expense of ignoring vital areas of the base game.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. The game is boring and unbalanced, plain and simple. If you think you cand find some enjoyment in this game, perhaps through modding, then I still don't recommend buying this game, if only so that Paradox doesn't get your money.

This is more of a review of the Star Trek New Horizons mod than of Stellaris, although I did play vanilla Stellaris when it first came out. I've played the Star Trek mod with two races.
The first game was with the Romulans. The start was slow, but enjoyable. I like building up my empire, exploring and researching new tech. The original Stellaris was much the same, I recall, but dealing with familiar Star Trek races makes it more fun. Then the annoying pirates decided to appear. Suddenly the game announces that some members of my race turned traitor and became pirates, i.e. the barbarians from Civilization. I find this to be an annoying and gamey mechanic. Sure, it's nice to have some random NPC enemies to fight, but Stellaris already has space monsters to fill that role. Moreover, if there are pirates, I'd like to have other options of dealing with them, such as trade, diplomacy, bribe them to attack other races instead. They're just a classic chore like the rebel whack-a-mole in Crusader Kings 2.
When my Romulan Empire was strong enough to have a decent fleet to start a war, I chose the puny Bolians. I had a bigger fleet, more star systems, I even had a vassal, whereas the Bolians only had one planet. Still the war lasted decades. I don't even know how long. Let's say the first time I attacked my fleet's power was 550, whereas the Bolian fleet was 300. However, they were next to their spacedock, which has a power around 900. So each time I attacked them, half of my fleet got wiped out, the rest escaped, I rebuilt my fleet a bit stronger and attacked again. I did this maybe 5 times, maybe more. Each time the victorious Bolian fleet only stayed in their home system. They did not pursue my fleet, didn't attack my planets, didn't try to make allies. They would just sit on their asses, next to their seemingly invincible spacedock. After a while though, I managed to beat them. This was probably due to me developing better weapons and learning to design my ships better. So I managed to destroy that spacedock, their fleet and invade their planet. Finally I enslaved those blue ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s! This whole was war very silly and gamey, but at least I felt like I accomplished something.
Soon after some race called the Nomads came to my territory and offered to sell me some of their ships for a hefty sun of energy and minerals. I could pay-up so I tought, why not. At that point my fleet power was around 2000, I believe. When I got the Nomad ships, it was over 6000. That pesky United Federation of Planets was next to my Empire, and according to intel, their fleet could not match mine, so I decided to start a war. I chose modest war goals, the Andorian capital and three other Andorian colonies, as they were the ones closest to me. Indeed the Federation's fleet could not match mine, and the process of eliminating the fleet and defences of a planet, and then sending down an invasion army, began. This wasn't very challeging. Just tedious and bureaucratic. If I have to do something like this, I'd like get paid for it. After the logistical victory of the Romulan bureaucracy department, I was in possession of the four planets I set as wargoals. That wasn't enough to win the war though, for some reason. I decided I'll invade earth then. I destroyed their defenses, and my Romulan masters with their Reman slave warriors fought a hard battle against the humans. For a while I wasn't sure if we were going to win or not, but we did, and we got those Andorian planets. But we had give earth back to the Federation as we hadn't allogated it as a war goal initially, which seems silly. At least we should've been able to loot everything of value from earth or purge the planet of all life.
After I recovered from the war, I started thinking which race's territory I should invade next with my overpowered Nomad fleet. The thought horrified me. I didn't want to go through with the logistics again. I quit.
Star Trek-wise the mod seems pretty good. The people have really gone through the effort of adding all kinds of races. They seem to adhere to what the TV shows and movies did. The other Romulan homeworld, Remus, is inhabited by Reman slaves, which is canonical. Or is it? This was from the move Star Trek: Nemesis, which I wouldn't necessarily call canonical. Gamewise though, I don't think it matters much. There are some custom Star Trek events and anomalies as well. They're pretty cool, although some of them have been taken directly from a Star Trek episode, such as Inner Light. A probe paralyzes your captain, and you have to decided what to do. I've seen the episode, and I know what to do you, so it has really nothing to do with going boldly where no-one has gone before. It's not a mystery or a puzzle how to solve the challenge.
In my second game I played with humans, or the Federation or whatever it was called. I guess I got unlucky with the world generation as it was hard to find other planets to move to, I was also suffering from lack of energy resources most of the game. The Vulcans were my good buddies though, and helped me out. Then there were same annoying pirates again, which were quite easy to crush this time. I saw a few of the same events as in the Romulan game. Then the Xindi event chain happened. This was taken straight from Star Trek: Enterprise. Earth is attacked by a probe and you have to send a captain to deal with it. Eventually you're rewarded with an overpowered ship, Enterprise. I'm not sure how I feel about this thing, since, once again, I know what is going to happen. I've seen the show. I think you can turn off the story mode in the beginning to get rid of this, which I probably will do if I try the mod again. Soon after this event chain, I got bored again.
This is Stellaris in a nutshell: it's fun for a few hours, but the game itself if too shallow and tedious so you'll quite. Has anyone ever actually completed the game? The diplomacy, the combat, the exploration are very simplistic and shallow. The exploration is really fun, for a couple of hours, but then it too becomes monotonous and boring. In the Romulan game I had one ship far away from home (sort of like Voyager, but not as far). Sending to to the next system each time to explore became a chore, and I didn't yield much benefits for my empire anyway. Talking about exploration, there's one thing where Star Trek and Stellaris clash. In Stellaris, there are separate ships for exploring and fighting, but in Star Trek, the best explorers are usually also the best fighters, especially if the ship is called Enterprise. The Federation does have dedicated science vessels, but ships like Kirk's and Picard's Enterprises study spatial anomalies, conduct diplomatic missions, and fight wars. This is not how it works in Stellaris, which is kind of dumb. Sometimes when you warp into a new star system, there is an indigenous space monster. In Stellaris, the science vessels has no option but to run away, you have to send the fleet to destroy it afterwards. In Star Trek, the explorer would deal with the monster, then explore the system.
Star Trek New Horizons does seem like a competent mod. It worked perfectly, btw, didn't crash once. And it is still in development, but the question is that can the final product overcome the drawbacks set by the original Stellaris?

You're alone in the park, bloody from the last safehouse you just emptied of infected, searching for a doctor that might help you with your infection... It's getting dark, you're tired and you're down to your last couple of flashlight batteries. You have to go on, you need the blood for the serum and you need the serum to hold off the pain...
30 rounds in the SMG are not enough! You're not used to it, but today you're going to fire your shotgun too. These new guys are bigger and the SMG is too light for them. Ah... the goddamn flashlight is flickering again!
is all about the alternative history "zombie apocalypse" type atmosphere and the ongoing pressure of survival. You have to get guns to kill infected, you have to kill infected to get serum, you have to get serum to keep your infection under control, you have to find safehouses to rest, you have to kill infected to empty the safehouses... Constantly you have to be on your toes, to use all your resources, to even run away if necessary!
is skill based and depends on your weapon choice. Your weapon choice depends on the "luck of the drop" mainly and you also have to adapt to the enemy types, because they have different resistances and you can't afford wasting bullets that only deal half damage. On the other hand, if you use weapons that you are not used to, your chance to hit drops, so you may be firing bullets that deal no damage. The game makes you pay attention to these kind of decisions and sometimes you have to make them on the fly, because encounters tend to be unexpected and in high numbers.
Other than that, you get "doctrines"(which work like passive bonuses) for every level. Some doctrines are skill specific and you can buy them with research points.
is easy; your main concern is to have a mixed collection of weapons and sufficient parts to repair them. Some batteries, juice and medkits are also necessary, but nothing tedious is going to keep you away from the action.
The flow of the game is exactly as detailed in the intro. You always have to keep an eye on your tiredness, infection level, serum, ammunition, flashlight battery, health and stamina. You have to keep going and you have to find time to rest. You get to interact with the world and the story through written dialogue and sometimes you even get to team up with some of the survivors. The AI is decent and the story, even though it needs retouching, here and there, helps the atmosphere.
The graphics are not mindblowing, but they do what they are supposed to. The "infected" models are varied, the weather effects are beautiful and the GUI does its job. The environment really sets the tone, you'll find yourself in damaged homes,  broken down hospitals, streets full of vintage crashed cars and blood smears. The lightning effects are quite nice, a lightning strike during nighttime that reveals a couple of hungry "infected" walking toward you is always a thrill.
Walking on the streets, fighting for your life is complemented by a smooth soundtrack. The weapon sounds are okay, as well as the sounds the enemies make. Especially in the sewers, things can get pretty scary. Some speech would've been nice, but it's only early access, so who knows?
The game has an old school single player experience feel to it, it greets the player with great atmosphere, has a good story, meaningful quests, interesting character development and leveling system and good level design. All in all "I Shall Remain" is a good game, with lots of potential to paint a compelling "alternative history" picture.

Fantastic game! I thought it will be just another fun action Diablo-ish version of a game set in a post apocalyptic setting. Boy was I wrong!  I found beneath all of this a very complex RPG system. In I shall Remain this is wonderfully done by balancing this exploration feeling with the treasures and dangers of the unknown world. It always feels like an adventure to explore some new building or new map never knowing what you may encounter.  Also the great ambiance and atmosphere provided by the music and art style augment this feeling.  I also like the mechanics in the game, the scavenge, night-day, stamina and infested state are greatly enhancing the atmosphere and are very well integrated in the story and the survival feeling that you have when playing.  I’m having a blast with this game so far and I highly recommend it to anyone who is looking for a good thrill but also for those searching for a game with a little more depth!

Having worked on a bit of art of this game as a freelancer, i have spent quite a lot of hours also playtesting the game.  It did take a short while for me to get used to the game control and mechanics, but then it grew on me rather quickly as it has a lot of old-school charm i haven't felt since staying awake nights as a teenager exploring the dungeons of diablo 1.
Now to review the main parts of the game:
-The loot system is well done and ballanced as it gives you enough ammo to shoot at zombies, but never more than it takes to make you feel that ammo is in short supply and not to be wasted (actually the best parts of the game for me was when i was very low on ammo and had to make each shot count).
-The skill system is the best part of the game for me, there are the main weapon categories each with their bonuses (doctrines) as you progress, wich are well thought out and fit each weapon type, giving it a different play-style. On top of that there are books spread through the game that give you extra bonuses to skills that are not accessible through leveling them up via experience, so finding these thoughout the game is really rewarding.
There are also some minor negatives here, like the shotgun and sniper rifle being in one category and sharing some bonuses and  enemy resistances that don't make a lot of sense intuitively, but it's by no means something game-breaking.
-The replayability factor is suprisingly high for a game with a more or less liniar structure in the levels available so far. Having tried out different builds (melee and heavy weapons are by far my favourite) they play and feel different enough to make it rewarding to replay the game over and over trying different things. On top of that the randomized loot also adds a lot to the replayability factor , and a good drop actually means something in a game that doesn't spam you with loot ala diablo 2.
-The visuals are very fitting for the game , adding to the nostalgia feel it has going for it. It is still rather rough around the edges (the animations are pretty lacking at the moment) but there are a lot of things to be still added to that aspect that should make the game really shine. In the couple of months i have worked with the team the game has improved noticably in the visual department and if they keep it up they will have a real polished product by the end of development
To sum it up the game is not without flaws currently, but it has a lot of heart and potential, and is a welcome addition to the RPG genre bringing back some old-school gameplay and mechanics in a good way. Keep at it :)

A friend recommended me Enigmatis 3, so when the trilogy went on sale, I decided to pick them all up. For the oldest of the set (five years old now), this game held up really well, and was a fun and engaging hidden object game that I can recommend wholeheartedly to fans of the genre.
It does have a few rough edges. Artifex's nagivation system has improved a lot since this game, especially the ability to navigate using the map. This game has a *lot* of walking around from location to location. Also, they did a slightly poor job of making sure that when you're asked to find something, there's only one of it in the scene. (A good example is a scene full of skulls that asks you to find a jawbone. There are at least ten on screen, but it's a specific one that it's looking for.) Also, there are some odd translation and/or word usage errors. For example, the game uses "shoe" interchangeably for shoes and boots. That wouldn't be so bad except that sometimes there are both shoes and boots on the screen. In that case, "shoe" always refers to the boot, not the shoe. Despite all of that, though, it's a really fun game.
I wish I could say the same for the bonus adventure. It's short.... that's about what it's got going for it. The translation issues abound -- keep your phone or a web browser handy to look up words that aren't in use anymore and then be prepared to figure out what kindasorta but not exactly matches that word anyway. There's a lot of pointless reuse, some depending on you to see things in locations you've visited several times that are next to impossible to see, and just generally a lot less cohesive of a story. Also, the voice acting is terrible.
That said, if you finish Enigmatis, you'll probably want to play it, and it doesn't take all that long. I just wouldn't pay extra to get access to that bonus adventure part if I were being asked to.

I’m writing my review for
from an interesting perspective; I’ve played it twice. I first played this game a year ago and jumped into it again to do a revised review and prepare for the release of the third title in the series. Since my first playthrough, I’ve played many other hidden object games and I feel I have a different perspective. That all being said,
is still an amazing game. It’s an older title, from 2011, but the fact that it can still hold up as one of my favorite games now in 2016 shows how well it was made. Great story, good gameplay and fitting aesthetics all come together making this title shine.
You’re put in the role of a detective with a slight case of amnesia, she knows who she is but not why she’s in Maple Creek. Part of the story’s charm is learning everything that is going on which technically the main character already knew about beforehand. You’re on the case of a missing young woman in the town and soon find out from your notes that many other ladies have been disappearing for years in Maple Creek. As the protagonist is a detective, she sees everything from a logical perspective while in truth, the events happening in the town are far from logical or the norm. She has stumbled upon a world of ritualistic sacrifices, mind control, demons and death; a world that will follow her to the next game in the series. Along the way she meets other characters, most notably Detective Richard Hamilton who had a loved one go missing in Maple Creek. Hamilton has a vendetta against those that took his beloved away and aids the protagonist with her adventures in this game and the sequels.
This game and others in this series are hidden object games, and are very old school. The game has more hidden object scenes than puzzles so that may turn some players off. Also, you’ll be visiting the same hidden object scenes twice or more as well. I counted five hidden object scenes in the first ten or twenty minutes alone. Another thing to note is that the hidden object scenes are difficult. They’re pure clutter and can require a player to stare for a while trying to find an item, some of which are hidden in tricky spots. I often found myself trying to find that one last item and spending a few frustrating minutes squinting at the screen. The game is light on puzzles, as mentioned before, and none are too difficult. A nice feature the game has is an evidence board, since you’re a detective, you use it to try and piece together facts and remember things and also solve the case. A feature I did not like was the inability to teleport. You do have a map which shows you places you need to visit but you can’t teleport to any of them which can mean a lot of backtracking.
For an older title, the graphics in the game are pretty good. The tone is well set with music and dreary colors making the town of Maple Creek even more ominous. I only have two issues. Firstly, the hidden object scenes, as I said, are very cluttered so if you have bad eyes be warned. Secondly, the animation isn’t too great, when characters speak their mouths don’t move realistically. That, however, is minor. The game also has full voice acting which is very well-done, despite the lack of lyp-sync. Well, the main character and the preacher are good, anyway. Everyone else is satisfactory, but I wasn’t a fan of Hamilton’s voice acting.  Good to great voice acting kept the story compelling.
All I can say is buy
, play it and then grab the sequels. I enjoyed the story, I enjoyed the twist of the main character having memory loss and forgetting she had already solved the case, I enjoyed the gameplay, it’s just a well made game all around. Sure, there are some flaws and some things I personally don’t like. The game is an older one but despite that, it stands up well against some more modern games that don’t offer nearly as much. If I could use the map to teleport, it would be a perfect game. Despite how frustrating I found the backtracking I might play this title a third time at some point. It has Steam trading cards and achievements and it should be in your library if you’re a fan of hidden object games.

Enigmatis: The Ghosts of Maple Creek is one of the best saga (Enigmatis) of Artifex Mundi.
You awoke, as a female detective (FBI or something) after a powerful storm knocked you out. As you revive, you’ve lost most of your last memories as well as most of your notebook pages and evidence. The more you’ll explore the more you’ll recall and be able to stop a very dangerous and evil person in Maple Creek.
As every Artifex Mundi game you can move freely in different area (of Maple Creek) and need to solve some puzzles and find all objects in hidden objects scenes. The game has (2 or more difficulties?) a guest feature: every one of the family can play an independent save and resume the game where they left it. When you first play the game you’ll have a notebook where you have all your objectives as well as all your notes. Adding to that you’ll have a hint button that will help you in many ways but be warned that you may not use it in any puzzle or hidden object scene (HOS)or investigation scene (IS). Hints can be used to know where you need to go, where is the next interaction or to show an object or clue in an HOS or IS or to skip a puzzle. To conclude this part, you’ll also have an inventory to store useful items through your journey.
One of the very good thing of this game is that there is a unique feature you won’t find in any other Artifex Mundi game:
•	You’ll have a separate inventory for your evidence. You then need to match evidence with the right deduction in order to go further in your investigation.
(*) :
In addition to no skip or use any hint while playing every puzzles and Hidden objects scenes, there are more missable achievements. Two of them requires you to complete a puzzle and a hidden objects scene under one minute. And 2 others hidden objects achievements ask you to find 3 objects within 3 seconds or to finish a scene with less than 4 misclicks.
Finally if you missed anything while finishing your first playthrough, you’ll need to play the game again with the same profile I guess. (achievements are linked to the profile: you may be able track your achievement in-game I believe) The good thing is you only need to succeed where you failed to get the achievements left.

More people need to be willing to try this couch monster. Yeah, lack of online multiplayer is a drag, but since the playstyle is familiar you should be able to find people who can pick up on it quickly locally (and the singleplayer is good enough on its own anyway, way better than most fighting game story modes).
Whereas the Smash Bros franchise has more of a floating, bouncy feel to it, Megabyte Punch is tight and snappy. It's a lot more satisfying, and seems to make it easier to work with the trajectory a robot takes when it’s been punched into a stage hazard (or wall, or other robot, or a projectile you previously fired). Keeping an enemy juggled by knocking them around like anime jai alai is the best.
They also did a good job of balancing the customization system. You can be loaded with recovery-focused moves and nothing else, or be a zero-abilities tank, and it all feels fair. There are a few really bad builds you could make, but by and large, no matter how stupid you want your fighter to be/look, it'll be fun to play.

I just wrote a review for Borderlands 2, and I wanted to come here to talk about what they fixed in this game from Borderlands 2.
One, the game doesn't feel slow. It flows well both in missions and combat. It didn't feel like 12 minutes reloading my SMG,  it felt like the 3 seconds the item card says it is. Missions weren't constant backtracking and had interesting naratives to their own. The main story while much shorter, also had much fewer moments where you were waiting for the story to progress.
Two, combat was much more complex. Both action skills and passives felt more game changing. Instead of 2 really overpowered skills and 28 other skills that only provided stat boosts, every single skill felt significant in some way or another. Shooting people increases your fire rate, dealing elemental damage boosts your elemental damage, shooting while sprinting, subroutines. It all just felt so much more active. Enemies also got a boost to AI and new abilities. Completely new enemy types. No longer just skags, rakks, and threshers. More verticality with jump boosts, booster pads, and unique O2 kits to replace relics and offer a new slam attack. Mechanics involving oxygen and atmospheres and fire. Weapons had more quality at the cost of massive loss in quantity.
Three, visuals. Two words. No deserts. And thank god too. I was getting bored of the wasteland of pandora. You get to explore Helios, abandoned Dahl facilities, Eridian fortresses, and the friggin moon. Textures are clean and crisp, models are smoother, and the shading is much better now. Color pallete features purples, blues, greens opposed to brown, brownish green, brown with yellow. Brown but it's pale. Enemy designs are bright, colorful, completely unique compared to other games in the series.
Four, writing. Two words. Unique personalities. Sure everyone is an aussie, but also better written and with much better dialogue. Ten year old boy interested in machinery. Random soldier who likes pizza parties. Mercenary who's addicted to cybernetic implants. Gunslinger whose only pleasure in life is in torturing others. Mayor/Sheriff that's a complete failure but still wants the best for the town. The characters really feel unique. I'll never forget pizza party dude. On top of that, story feels less contrived and to my knowledge has less plot holes. Better story, though admittedly much shorter too.
Five, music. Somehow the music is slightly more memorable. It fits the more sci-fi theme and I can actually remember more to a track than just a few strums on a guitar.
Six, co-op. It's dead. Nobody likes this game with the two biggest concerns I'm hearing being about the lack of farmable items and bosses, and the lack of main and side mission content. Because of this, co-op is dead. It pretty much never existed, and I played the game on release. I think these games are much more fun solo anyways, but that's just me.
So overall this game has one message running across my mind. Quality over quantity. Borderlands 2 had so much to do, to discover, and find for your own, aswell as just general content in the form of locations, missions, and items, but tell me a moment you would prefer any gun over a harold. I've found that all the content in this game is high quality, polished to shine, and with little to zero bugs. With Borderlands 2 I felt like for as much as there was, there was only so little worth experiencing with the rest feeling like padding, but with this game I was legitimately happy with everything there was every moment of the way through. I liked every quest and combat encounter. I liked the music, the one-liners, the speech. I liked the story. All I could wish for is more quality content like this. I was happy the entire time through all three of my playthroughs. Nothing annoying or troublesome came up. It was just fun the entire way through and something I would gladly play through another 10 times.

These Japanese developers cannot hide behind the quality of their games anymore, when offered on consoles. They need to put forth the effort to make them playable on PCs as well, something they seem reluctant to do. It's unfortunate, because I love a lot of the games Japan offers, but I cannot in good conscience stand behind something that is so obviously  flawed in the PC market.
Even the much maligned Konami(boy is that a change given how much they were loved through the 80s and 90s) offers ports that are better performing than much of the Japanese games in the PC games market. It's really unfortunate, since I don't think PCs are beyond Japan's understanding. They seem to be people with a great understanding of electronics, yet play by the rules of consoles, and not the openended way of PCs. I hate to break it to Japan, but choice is a way of life, and rigidity enforced by consoles is simply a way of the past. The PS4 and XBone are proving that. They came out recently, and yet are far behind the PC market. People who want more power, and are willing to put in the work to access that, will always be far ahead of the console market. Many developers recognize that, and make games catering to the PC market. Even guys like Totalbiscuit will recognise that in the beginning of his reviews, highlighting what the options portion of the game allow a player to customize.
The old ways of the console have become antiquated. The personal computer, while being around since the 80s, if not farther back than that, offers more choice and customization, and the offerings of hardware allow multiple different price points of entry. That is the way of the future, rather than a one size fits all console offering.
Most of the world has accepted this. Japan would do well to join the trend. Now I realize I am singling out this developer, who may have felt backed into a corner, with consoles the best chance of success. However, I realize that in today's times, 2015, consoles are NOT your best choice, regardless of the market. You adapt, or fall behind.

Quick Summary: Third person action shooter very similar to Resident Evil 5, but at times noticeably lower graphics and some actual downgrades in gameplay mechanics. This is likely due to the fact that Revelations is a port of a Nintendo hand held game, later upgraded with HD graphics, and was never meant to be the next “great” Resident Evil game. Still, it’s fun and time consuming so you’ll get your money’s worth even if you didn’t buy the various DLCs.
Despite the fact that Revelations was released a few years after Resident Evil 5, the story of Revelations actually takes place earlier, as a kind of prequel (though unrelated plot-wise). You play BSAA agent Jill Valentine for the most part, but in each chapter you’ll regularly control different people such as Chris Redfield or other BSAA agents.  You know Jill is the main character though since she’s the only one who can mod her weapons with upgrade kits, and swap guns at the various loadout crates scattered around the area. Jill and her partner Parker are on a mission exploring an abandoned cruise ship related to terrorist activity from years before. As usual in Resident Evil games, “terrorist” means bio-weapons that create monsters to be unleashed on the world. This time around the weapon in question is the T-Abyss virus, that doesn’t make traditional zombies, but instead makes “oozes” which look kind of like humanoid tubeworms with claws and spiky teeth. Of course, that’s just the weak stuff. There are a bunch of giant bosses and super creepy monsters wandering the cruise ship as well.
If you’ve played Resident Evil 5, the gameplay should be very familiar to you, except that now you can just press the mouse button for a quick jab attack. Just like in RE 5 though, regular melee isn’t much use except for breaking boxes in the campaign (it’s more useful in Raid mode). You still have special contextual power hits that do a lot of damage to stunned enemies, but it’s a lot harder to set up stuns in Revelations. To kill most enemies you’ll have to rely on your guns. Various guns are found throughout the game (you can’t buy them in campaign) and they can only be upgraded with weapon “parts” that you find lying around. For example, your basic pistol may have 3 upgrade slots so you can add up to 3 weapon upgrades like + damage, faster shooting, and larger magazine, and swap for better ones that you find later. There’s no “money” used in the campaign for buying upgrades. Also note that even though you are usually with a partner throughout the campaign, this is not a co-op game. You cannot go through the story with a friend.
Another new feature for Revelations is the Genesis device, which is just a scanner despite its fancy name. You can quickly switch to the scanner at almost any time to scan enemies (alive or dead) and it adds a % to your “data.” For example scanning an ooze could give you 10% and scanning a tougher enemy might give you 20%. Every time you reach 100%, you get a healing herb added to your inventory, and the % resets to 0. It’s a slow but steady way to gain herbs at various points in the game. The Genesis can also be used to locate hidden items (like ammo or herbs) lying invisible on the ground.
Pros:
+A spooky Resident Evil game with enemies more gruesome than zombies, and no “human” enemies so you don’t need to hide from enemy gunfire (though there are some ranged oozes). There is a lot of backtracking in this game, and you’re going to go through most areas of the cruise ship several times. This means you have opportunities to pick up things that you missed the previous times through.
+The story is compelling, but it’s episodic which means every chapter starts with a “previously on Resident Evil Revelations” cutscene to catch you up in case you didn’t buy every episode.
+The Raid mode is the highlight of the game and allows you and a partner to level up by playing through areas from the game’s campaign. You also acquire BP (kind of like money) that you can use to buy weapons and weapon upgrade parts. You’ll need to get new gear when you level up because weapons have fixed levels. For example you start at level 1 with a level 1 gun, but when you’ve advanced, you may want to buy a level 2 gun, etc.
Cons:
-Since this is a mobile game port, the graphics and handling isn’t quite up to snuff compared to Resident Evil 5 or 6. There’s some frame rate stuttering on my computer (which ran RE 5 smoothly), and like Resident Evil 6, every time you start the game there are half a dozen little load screens to wait through.
-The game’s co-op Raid mode doesn’t have that many people playing anymore apparently. This may be because you can’t “drop in” to someone’s game. The host has to set up a game and wait for people to join, sometimes for a long time if nobody is searching for a match that very second. Most people probably don’t have the patience for that. This means if you want to play co-op, you need to set it up with a friend beforehand. Also, like RE 5, there’s no text or voice chat in the co-op.
Overall, the game is a fun continuation of the action shooter style of Resident Evil games, and the creepy deserted cruise ship has a nice atmosphere for horror. Raid mode will occupy a lot of your time after you’ve finished the story. Once you’ve mastered Raid mode’s Abyss tier of levels, the campaign’s Infernal difficulty (hard mode) will seem like a walk in the park.

Alright, let's cut through the BS you read in other reviews and get down to it.
The good,
The writing, yes, the writing, it's succinct , punchy, and entertaining. The character known as Parker really tugs on the heart strings, and is genuinely relatable. Anyone complaining about the plot obviously never played RE1. It's always been hokey and awkwardly paced. This game is no different.
Level design and art direction, everything feels creepy and alive.
Overall flow, fun and easy to get through, with new game plus options.
The Bad
Gone are series stables such as, complex puzzles, green/blue herbs, inventory management, ammo scarcity, and most of all, areas to explore that function as open area puzzles, like the mansion, or police station.
While I was most disappointed in how linear it was, it's still fun to play and has some eerie moments. It is slight, being a handheld port, on unique interactions with the environment, I find it still scratches the RE itch.
The shooting, you basically just dump ammo into to things. Once you get and upgrade your auto-matic weapon of choice, that'll be your main stay anytime you have ammo. The reason being is that combat is just too fast paced over short distances to try and use you're rifle (which will miss) or handgun (goes in the trash asap), or magnum (three enemies later, no more ammo). It's pretty much smg/shotgun all day once you get the ammo capacity upgrades.
The cut-scenes, we are talking MGS levels here. Cut those out and your playtime will he halved.
in conclusion. It's a good game, just not the return to roots people have been saying it is. Just solid all around, while being just two shades away from borderlands.
If Capcom just (they won't) slowed it down, made ammo scarce, and made the protagnist not a super solider, we'd be right back to our roots. P.S. please bring back Carlos and HUNK.

One of Artifex Mundi's earlier games, it lacks some of the great features incorporated into their later work (e.g., fast travel map), but it's easy to see the quality foundation that has led to them to the top of the hidden object puzzle game genre.
As far as detective games go, I LOVE the evidence mechanic that allows the player to be more involved in making deductions that further the story. The haunting music is perfectly themed and remained stuck in my head long after the game was over.
The prequel bonus adventure provides great backstory but is more susceptible to the idiosyncrasies of this type of game, such as a convoluted coffee machine puzzle that would ensure no one would ever buy a beverage at the gas station. It also seemed to have more confusing translation errors in the hidden object scenes than the main adventure did.
Although the game is not without its flaws, if you like fantastic original detective / mystery stories, then I would highly recommend this game and its sequel.

Loadout is a very entertaining game that my friends and I enjoy a lot. Although starting out may be hard, it's worth spending an hour getting used to how the game works.
Some things I enjoy from Loadout:
-Weapon Customization: Plenty of options to chose from. Snipers, Medics, Heavies, Light assault, you have it all.
-Looks: The game has a Team Fortress look to it that I enjoy.
-Tech Tree: Many people have different opinions on the tech tree, some are good and some are bad. I personally enjoy it. It gives me something to work for in the game. I can't have the best pulse gun untill I've played around with it a bit.
Some things I don't enjoy from Loadout:
(I understand this game is still being worked on, these are things that could possibly be fixed on later dates.)
-No voice chat: It would be really cool to talk to my teammates about where I am and how we can work as a team, but currently that is not an option.
-Matchmaking: There is no option to exclude certain maps or gamemodes from your matchmaking queue. Also, sometimes when playing with a party you are split between teams. The only reason I play with a party is to play with them on the same team.
-Limited Loadout and Weapon slots: For the begining part of the game, you start off with one loadout/weapon slot. Thats cool, start with nothing and make your way up, I like that. What I don't like is how it stops giving you more loadout/weapon slots around level 20. After level 20 you must pay for more slots.
Thanks for reading my review and I hope it doesn't discourae you from playing it. At least try out the game for an hour before you give it a bad review. :D

Plus, if you're a fan of the sci-fi genre, it's a blast to just get yourself immersed in growing a space empire. However, once you crack the surface, once you start learning about these mechanics, it quickly reveals itself to be shallow.
Combat is boring and unbalanced. It always boils down to having the bigger fleet, with few exceptions. Ground combat is even more boring and simplified, with no strategy involved at all. Simply move your army to a planet, land, and win. Managing your empire is boring and tedious.
To manage your empire, you have a few planets that you directly control and micromanage, and then have to delegate any other planets to "sectors." These sectors give the AI control over the planets, having them build and develop improvements. A good portion of the game is taken out of your hands and put into the AI's, and the AI is beyond inept. I've had sectors, with plenty of resources, still have empty planets with no improvements while they build nothing else. To try to get the most out of your planets, you have to constantly jockey with the sector system, do the dull and tedious colony development yourself, and then jockey with the sector system again. It's very boring, and adds more micromanagement to a system that was designed to reduce it.
Of course, the sector system is absolutely necessary, because the other space empires are just as inept as the sector AI. The only way to stop a player from completely steamrolling the galaxy is to cripple the player through using the sectors. If you try to play around the sectors, you get the micromangement hell I described above. If you use the sectors "as designed" then the game is still unbalanced, but still better than the optimal way to play.
I tried to like Stellaris, and at first I really did. It just becomes so boring and tedious. It's hard to explain how much time is wasted in this game just waiting. Waiting for resources, waiting for fleets to build, waiting for the invasion to end, waiting for the warscore to tick up so you can end a war, waiting, waiting, waiting. The only things that could have made the downtime between conflicts interesting was the empire management, which is taken out of control of the player through sectors, and then handled ineptly by the AI.
In addition to the problems with the actual game, Paradox Interactive has become a terrible company to support. Gone are the days where Paradox made fantastic, if buggy, games for relatively cheap, with great expansions to enhance the vanilla game. Now, Paradox releases broken games, then releases a constant stream of overpriced DLCs that add one or two features, that are inevitably broken or unbalanced on release. The sad part is, most of the DLCs are great ideas, with terrible implementation, or are great ideas, at the expense of ignoring vital areas of the base game.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. The game is boring and unbalanced, plain and simple. If you think you cand find some enjoyment in this game, perhaps through modding, then I still don't recommend buying this game, if only so that Paradox doesn't get your money.

This is more of a review of the Star Trek New Horizons mod than of Stellaris, although I did play vanilla Stellaris when it first came out. I've played the Star Trek mod with two races.
The first game was with the Romulans. The start was slow, but enjoyable. I like building up my empire, exploring and researching new tech. The original Stellaris was much the same, I recall, but dealing with familiar Star Trek races makes it more fun. Then the annoying pirates decided to appear. Suddenly the game announces that some members of my race turned traitor and became pirates, i.e. the barbarians from Civilization. I find this to be an annoying and gamey mechanic. Sure, it's nice to have some random NPC enemies to fight, but Stellaris already has space monsters to fill that role. Moreover, if there are pirates, I'd like to have other options of dealing with them, such as trade, diplomacy, bribe them to attack other races instead. They're just a classic chore like the rebel whack-a-mole in Crusader Kings 2.
When my Romulan Empire was strong enough to have a decent fleet to start a war, I chose the puny Bolians. I had a bigger fleet, more star systems, I even had a vassal, whereas the Bolians only had one planet. Still the war lasted decades. I don't even know how long. Let's say the first time I attacked my fleet's power was 550, whereas the Bolian fleet was 300. However, they were next to their spacedock, which has a power around 900. So each time I attacked them, half of my fleet got wiped out, the rest escaped, I rebuilt my fleet a bit stronger and attacked again. I did this maybe 5 times, maybe more. Each time the victorious Bolian fleet only stayed in their home system. They did not pursue my fleet, didn't attack my planets, didn't try to make allies. They would just sit on their asses, next to their seemingly invincible spacedock. After a while though, I managed to beat them. This was probably due to me developing better weapons and learning to design my ships better. So I managed to destroy that spacedock, their fleet and invade their planet. Finally I enslaved those blue ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s! This whole was war very silly and gamey, but at least I felt like I accomplished something.
Soon after some race called the Nomads came to my territory and offered to sell me some of their ships for a hefty sun of energy and minerals. I could pay-up so I tought, why not. At that point my fleet power was around 2000, I believe. When I got the Nomad ships, it was over 6000. That pesky United Federation of Planets was next to my Empire, and according to intel, their fleet could not match mine, so I decided to start a war. I chose modest war goals, the Andorian capital and three other Andorian colonies, as they were the ones closest to me. Indeed the Federation's fleet could not match mine, and the process of eliminating the fleet and defences of a planet, and then sending down an invasion army, began. This wasn't very challeging. Just tedious and bureaucratic. If I have to do something like this, I'd like get paid for it. After the logistical victory of the Romulan bureaucracy department, I was in possession of the four planets I set as wargoals. That wasn't enough to win the war though, for some reason. I decided I'll invade earth then. I destroyed their defenses, and my Romulan masters with their Reman slave warriors fought a hard battle against the humans. For a while I wasn't sure if we were going to win or not, but we did, and we got those Andorian planets. But we had give earth back to the Federation as we hadn't allogated it as a war goal initially, which seems silly. At least we should've been able to loot everything of value from earth or purge the planet of all life.
After I recovered from the war, I started thinking which race's territory I should invade next with my overpowered Nomad fleet. The thought horrified me. I didn't want to go through with the logistics again. I quit.
Star Trek-wise the mod seems pretty good. The people have really gone through the effort of adding all kinds of races. They seem to adhere to what the TV shows and movies did. The other Romulan homeworld, Remus, is inhabited by Reman slaves, which is canonical. Or is it? This was from the move Star Trek: Nemesis, which I wouldn't necessarily call canonical. Gamewise though, I don't think it matters much. There are some custom Star Trek events and anomalies as well. They're pretty cool, although some of them have been taken directly from a Star Trek episode, such as Inner Light. A probe paralyzes your captain, and you have to decided what to do. I've seen the episode, and I know what to do you, so it has really nothing to do with going boldly where no-one has gone before. It's not a mystery or a puzzle how to solve the challenge.
In my second game I played with humans, or the Federation or whatever it was called. I guess I got unlucky with the world generation as it was hard to find other planets to move to, I was also suffering from lack of energy resources most of the game. The Vulcans were my good buddies though, and helped me out. Then there were same annoying pirates again, which were quite easy to crush this time. I saw a few of the same events as in the Romulan game. Then the Xindi event chain happened. This was taken straight from Star Trek: Enterprise. Earth is attacked by a probe and you have to send a captain to deal with it. Eventually you're rewarded with an overpowered ship, Enterprise. I'm not sure how I feel about this thing, since, once again, I know what is going to happen. I've seen the show. I think you can turn off the story mode in the beginning to get rid of this, which I probably will do if I try the mod again. Soon after this event chain, I got bored again.
This is Stellaris in a nutshell: it's fun for a few hours, but the game itself if too shallow and tedious so you'll quite. Has anyone ever actually completed the game? The diplomacy, the combat, the exploration are very simplistic and shallow. The exploration is really fun, for a couple of hours, but then it too becomes monotonous and boring. In the Romulan game I had one ship far away from home (sort of like Voyager, but not as far). Sending to to the next system each time to explore became a chore, and I didn't yield much benefits for my empire anyway. Talking about exploration, there's one thing where Star Trek and Stellaris clash. In Stellaris, there are separate ships for exploring and fighting, but in Star Trek, the best explorers are usually also the best fighters, especially if the ship is called Enterprise. The Federation does have dedicated science vessels, but ships like Kirk's and Picard's Enterprises study spatial anomalies, conduct diplomatic missions, and fight wars. This is not how it works in Stellaris, which is kind of dumb. Sometimes when you warp into a new star system, there is an indigenous space monster. In Stellaris, the science vessels has no option but to run away, you have to send the fleet to destroy it afterwards. In Star Trek, the explorer would deal with the monster, then explore the system.
Star Trek New Horizons does seem like a competent mod. It worked perfectly, btw, didn't crash once. And it is still in development, but the question is that can the final product overcome the drawbacks set by the original Stellaris?
P.S.
Something I noticed is that half of the races seem like they're Militaristic, Materialistic and Xenophobic. I'm not sure if this is just a Star Trek thing, that when you compare minor NPC races, they resemble each other, or that the attributes just show the lack of variety in Stellaris.

This game is really easy to spoil, so be careful what you read. However I cannot recommend this game more highly if you have the cash and the time (50 hours for 100% completion for me).
++What it does well++
+ Platinum combat. If there is anyone in the industry who knows how to do combat, it's Platinum. This game is no different with platinum at the wheel.
+ Diverse, replayable story. In fact, "new game+" logic doesn't apply to this game even though it is "NG+". If you completed a quest in the previous playthrough, you don't have to do it again, saving tons of useless grinding. I'd even go so far as to say that the "NG+" is actually saying "I'd like to continue the story" instead.
+ Incredible and creative soundtrack, sometimes even using the enemies to then create soundtracks in a way that is neither annoying or intrusive. Very rarely do I ever feel so emotionally moved by a games soundtrack and this one really pulls at me. I'd say the soundtrack is on par with DOOM (however obviously not the same genre of music!).
+ Character builds can actually be as diverse as you want them to. If you try you could get a very solid crit build, a counter build, dodge build, XP farm build, Item farm build, aoe build, etc.
+ You are not punished for your difficulty choice and if you're new to this type of game you can use the Auto chips to give you a much easier time. Hell if you hate grinding you can use auto chips to do grinding for you while you afk if you build your character correctly!
+ Grinding is not necessary! Even more so if you do the sidequests! Only for the 90%-100% completion players does grinding matter.
+ Very well fleshed out characters with loads of backstory that are even tied in to some of the "weapons stories". I can't go further without spoiling anything.
+ You don't need to play the previous games at all.
+ English VA's are very good at their job!
-- What it does wrong --
- Camera can be a bit disorienting at very specific times in the game because of forced perspective.
- To get the full impact of the game you need to invest more time in doing the sidequests as well. However, it is time very well spent.
- Sidequest aren't particularly >time efficient< until you get fast travel, which is a few hours in. That said, again they can still be worth the time emotionally and in terms of in game rewards. If you aren't worried about the time efficiency then this is a non-issue,
- Combat will definitely feel strange at first. (this is remedied quite quickly)
- Death is more potent than in Dark Souls, so try to avoid getting killed out there.
- The game does not autosave unless you unlock an ending, so you can get "fix" mistakes like death by just loading your last save.
- You MUST save often or you might be SOL.
- If you overlevel content it is trivialized. (So yeah, don't go out of your way to grind levels, let it happen)
Just know that I have sacrificed my save data to help you for when the time comes.

The Bottom Line
With HBO's brilliant television adaptation skyrocketing George Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire saga to the forefront of pop culture we were undoubtably going to see ventures into the realm of interactive media. Martin's world is incredibly ripe for all kinds of game genres but one of the most obvious is certainly the RPG - enter "Game of Thrones: The Role Playing Game".
Unfortunately GoT is lacking in quite a few places. While the storyline is fairly on par with what you'd expect from the novels Cyanide Studios chose to create a game that looks and feels like it should've belonged in 2003. The combat is more or less the same model found in KOTOR, the graphics and visual design are severely lacking polish and modern standards, and the voice acting (aside from the contributors from the HBO series) is laughable at best.
Overall the game has an interesting story to tell if you can stomach through it's many shortcomings. I'd only advise a purchase if you're waist deep in the GoT craze.

Even if this game is $20 for early access, it is well worth it. The game has quite an interesting story that keeps you going with a satisfactory fast pace combat. Just imagine a Zelda game that is more difficult, faster pace, and a "Sphere Grid" System for stats and skills. Throw in some .hack// elements and you have this awesome entity known as Cross Code. There is some "cons" but there not really "cons" but more of a quality of life fix(s) that the developers can adjust before full game release.
Story - The story as far as early access goes is you take the role of an amnesiac Player name Lea in a fictional game call Cross World. Thinking that Cross World can help her regain her memory, she takes on the Plot of Cross World. However, Lea had her speech "module" corrupted so she becomes a silent protagonist. But Wait! unlike most silent protagonist, Lea still "talks" in the game. You start out with basic words but its quite comical to see her interact with other characters and see her limited choice of words. Of course she still nods up and down or left and right to let the other characters know her decision.
Pros:
Combat - The combat of this game is, in my opinion a pretty face pace game for a top down Action RPG. You have a basic combo, a dash/dodge button that is shared with guard. The game punishes you pretty heavily with amount of damage you take so dodging or guarding is key to surviving. The idea of "chaining" battles by constantly initiating a battle by attacking a monster is pretty cool. The higher you rank up your battle by constantly being in battle, the more EXP you will get and a pretty high item drop boost at the end. The developers were able to incorporate skills in a way where it does not "interrupt" combat. For example, you do not have to "pause" the game during combat to initiate a skill but rather the player can just hit the dedicated skill button. It is up to the player to charge the skill or not but charging the skill does slow down everything around you. Pretty Nice if you trying to aim a Range skill. The usable item menu though, will be a "pause" in combat. There is elemental(s) in this game. The elements provide advantages to monsters that are weak against an element or is key to exposing enemies weakspot/breaking armor. What is nice though is the developers has made it easy to switch elements on the fly with the D-pad. So unlike Zelda, the items or abilities you earn through temples are reusable elsewhere. The amount of fluidity of the combat controls in this game makes the combat system pretty fun and satisfactory.
Puzzles - So far from what I have played, the puzzles are really well designed. Though they are not over the top hard but at the same time, they are not really that simple either and will make you "step back" and assess the situation. While some of the puzzles now and days in games requires you to find a button, key, or moving blocks to help you get a cross a platform, most of the puzzles here requires you to set up what you think will work and execute it by using the a bouncing charge shot that Lea can do use. Some puzzle will require you set up and also move fast. For example, You can set up a ball to bounce corner to corner, however one corner is blocked by an ice block, You then have to Shoot a charge bounce ball and run over to melt that ice block with a fire element before the ball is blocked by the said ice block. Yes, the elements you learn from the previous temples will be useful and will reuse for some puzzles which is nice. Some of the mechanics of the puzzles are pretty unique. For example changing the elevation of the charge bounce ball or melting an ice ball with a fire ball to create steam to turn windmills. All these requiring setups, execution, and following up with the execution to ensure the execution goes smoothly.
Visuals and Audio - Not much to be said here but the visuals of this game is that of 16 bit. The game is 16 bit with a top down camera angle. So if you really enjoyed these type of games from the PS1 and NES era, than the visuals here is a plus for you. A lot of my friends said the game looks like the zelda series and Ys series. The Soundtrack so far has been pretty good. Each song seems to fit each setting or background.
Notable Mechanics- There is some sort of jump "quest" in each map to get treasure. The player is freely to attack breakable objects to collect or gather items for side quest. On the topic of side quest, there are quite a bit of side quest that has me doing the first set of side quest for 8 hours even though they are technically within the first 1-2 hours of the story. There is fast travel, so backtracking for some side quest won't be an issue. Inviting people to join your party is similar to the .hack// games. You open up a friends list, and call them up to join your party. Though at this time of early access you have only 1 contact in your friends list. Each element has their own "sphere grid" and does not share skill points with other "sphere grids" which is a blessing. Being a spheremancer you can equip 2 one handed weapons, so maybe we'll get to see a mix and match of weapons in full game release.
Cons (not really cons but QoL changes):
Difficulty - Not really a con to me because I like challenging games but to some, it maybe difficult at first. You are heavily punished for not dodging or guarding successfully so it makes it feel like even though you are 10 levels higher than the monster, that monster that is 10 levels lower than you still have a chance to knock out 1/3 - 1/2 of your health if you are not careful. It can give off a feeling that you are not actually getting "stronger" per level. The player can also be interrupted while using an item and might not get the healing effect of items. At the same time, this difficulty can be a Pro for some, thus not really a con but a potential QoL change.
Drop rate/gathering rate- Though the idea of using a rank system to determine higher drop rate is a good idea in my opinion, the rate(s) can get some players frustrated. For example, if players need to find "Raw Meat" from a cow, players may need to preemptively initiate other battles before engaging the cow to boost the drop rate for the said quest item. Some of the drop rates from breakable gathering objects are pretty low. I took about 2 hours to find 4 Bear Cicada from breakable gathering objects for a "beginners" quest.
Determining Height - Since this game is a top down view, determining if a platform is in the same elevation as the player can be quite confusing, especially with the amount of plants and other objects that are displayed in each map.
Summary:
Overall This game is an amazing game that can be come a masterpiece here on steam. With a very satisfactory combat system and have puzzles that will give players a sense of a achievement, this game is in good hands. The Developers have done so far a very fine job. Just maybe adjust some rates here and there. I will probably add more to this post as I delve deeper in to the Early Access Version.

Despite my relatively short time playing the game, I can definitely say that I recommend it, especially if you have friends willing to play it with you. Even if you don't have friends who want to play it, I'd still recommend it. It's a team based game where communication actually matters, unlike many of your modern "team" based games. (In which a single good player can carry an entire team.)
The objective of a match varies from a mode where you must capture a point and defend it, to a simple deathmatch in which you must take down a set number of enemy airships, to something called a VIP Hunt, in which you must take down a specific enemy airship. To accomplish these goals, you're given a variety of ships (Seven, I think. If I'm wrong, I'll come back and edit this.) that range from the nimble Squid to the devestating but slow Galleon, and a variety of weapons ranging from a missile launcher that can fire twenty shots in a single barrage, to the classic flamethrower, to a ship-mounted sniper rifle, to numerous sorts of artillery.
A crew consists of four people, each with an important role to fill on their ship. Crews are broken down into three classes.
The Pilot is the captain of the ship, and brings various tools to improve different aspects of the ship. These tools, however, are not without a cost to the ship and will often damage whichever part is improved. (Much to the dismay of his engineers.) Using his stamina, he can also give the ship a temporary speed boost. I would only recommend this role to the more advanced or competent players.
The Engineer is exactly what you think he is. They come equipped with the tools needed to repair, rebuild, buff, extinguish, prevent, and otherwise stave off your imminent destruction. By using their stamina, they can sprint across the ship to get where they're needed faster.
The Gunner is also self explanatory. They bring three different types of ammo, each with bonuses and debuffs, that can be loaded into the ship's guns. Their stamina boost allows them to turn the ship's guns farther than any other class, and lets them reload faster.
I'd break down the guns and ships, but that's a job best left to the wiki or guides. So, if you just scrolled down to the bottom of this, the game is one I highly recommend.

I thought this game to be great, primarily for the story mode.
I played the story mode in co op, and didn't dabble much in the general fighting. But I feel the game shines the most in story mode, especially in co-op.
For one, the levels are very non-linear. I'd kind of equate it similarly to old-school Sonic the Hedgehog levels, in which the ending may be in the same spot, but there are a vast array of ways to get to that end.
There are a plethora of paths and secrets, most of the secrets may just be hidden money capsules or part, but the fact that there are so many well hidden things encourages you to explore these well-designed levels even more. There's also colors you can find to change the appearance of your robot more, which is heckin stylish.
The actual fighting is as you probably know, very similar to super smash bros but simpler. Due to the fighting not being very complex this might be a turn-off for you, but I found it to be very satisfying. The moves are meaty (even though you're a robot) and have a lot of impact.
Finally, the customization is pretty nice. Finding a new part to equip to your robot that may give you a sweet new move or maybe you want a loadout that allows for 4 extra jumps! I do wish there was a bit more variety in the amount of moves though, as there's "only" around 15 or so.
Overall, I'd highly reccomend this game. I feel not many people praise the game for its levels whereas that's what me and my friend liked the most about it. A very nice adventure-fighting experience that shines more in co-op.
