Oh yeah, Deadly Premonition. There is so much you can say about this game.
First of all: Yes... yes I know the graphics may not be so gentle to the eye sometimes and yes it might be a little glitchy here and there, but to be honest, I dont really pay much attention to that.
I would describe DP as a rare species. Why you ask?
Graphic:
Eventhough the graphic may not be so 21st century and wont kill any big product such as action movie-game
Resident Evil 6 (which is very bad in its own way), it just wont take that long to get used to it. You only really see that problem during forest scenes when the grass textures are flickering a little. But despite that, come on guys, is graphic really that great? Look at Call of Duty. Great HD graphic, but always the same crap in it. Shoot shoot shoot.
Glitches:
To be honest, the only real glitches I have noticed were spinning cars or my tie running through my body lol.
The tie get unstuck fast thought and it only happened once. That thing with the car, well, it does weird things sometimes, for example spinning around itself for a splitt second and... yeah. Hehe but these gliches are not game breaking or frustrating, in fact they are really funny to watch and add up to the games humor a little, even if unintentionally. Sometimes they can even work for you.
Gameplay:
Having the two issues out of the way, we only have the major reasons to buy the game left. The gameplay is easy to understand and a ot of fun. Like in Resident Evil 4, you play York in a third person (over-the-shoulder) perspective, when aiming with the weapon you have you have to aim yourself or use the auto aim. Killing ghosties in this game is super fun due to the awesome atmosphere, the creepy enemies, the huge variety of weapons and the amzingly high amount of side quests like investigating old abandoned haunted places. Good thing is, I dont even spoil you things becuase there is so much to do and see in this game that I only scratched the surface. So to sum it all up:
-Easy handling (except for the cars)
-Very atmospheric
-Big town to explore freely
-A lot of side quests
-Very fun battle system
-A lot of very funny and extremly awesome weapons
-A lot of stuff to unlock
-Very well made creepy creatures
Sound:
The music in this game is amazing! Yes it maybe repeat itself a little to often, but hey, its always very fitting and it never gets old hearing these tunes. Especially during action sequences it can really bring you onto your toes, and while exploring something creepy or eary it will please you with a very ambient and... more eary track. To be honest here, it doesnt happen that often that music really melts into the game, at least not in my opinion.
Story:
And now we got to the cherry on top of this very strange cake that is Deadly Premonition.
If you are like me and graphic isnt everything, then you came to the right place. Remember when I said this game is a rare species? Well it surely is. I never saw a game that is a mixture of many things.
Resident Evil 4, Silent Hill and even a little bit of GTA is in there. Its funny and cheesy, its creepy and serious.
You have to eat and sleep to survive, you earn money, you can do this and that and wow...
But... NOTHING can be compared to the story. This real, at the beginning seemingly slowly starting story, will turn into a big and complicated, and at the end really mindblowing masterpiece! The combination with the music, the way the story tells itself, the whole atmoshpere the world builds around the character Francise York Morgan, the dark and creepy environments and an ending that stays stuck in your throat even days after. Not in a bad but more in a bittersweet way. Heck even if I would try to explain the ending here I couldnt even do it justice, neither would you understand it.
Long story short, the story is one of a kind and frankly said, I never ever witnessed a story like this before... just amazing!
So yeah, if you love very good stories and gameplay such as the good old Silent Hill or Resident Evil games,
you are not so interested in graphics and you dont mind the slightly cheesy dialogues sometimes, you should really give it a try. If the price is too high for you wait for the next sale but, still, people dont really give the game as much credit as it deserves. Out of all the games out there these days, this one is a hidden gem and should at least be played once.
I promise you wont regret it. I already played it on the XBox 360 two years ago and downloaded it again as directors cut a few days ago, and it still give me the chills when I hear the story. It also extended story wise, which makes it even more awesome!
Sometimes great things come in little packages, keep that in mind.
Deadly Premonition will forever be one of my all time favourites.

This is one of the greatest games that I have ever played. It will definitely stay within my top 5 games for a long, long time. I plan to at least do a second and third playthrough, if not more.
Before buying, there are 2 things that you must know:
1. This is the very definition of a cult classic. If you find yourself only enjoying huge budget AAA games and never really straying into anything else, then perhaps this is not the game for you. This game must be played with an open mind, as it is very unique. Also, it is worth mentioning that the game really doesn't pick up until an hour or so into it.
2. The PC port is not very good. I would only recommend buying it if you have intermediate computer skills, as you are going to have to edit a few files as well as apply a user-made patch, DPfix.
The story: Simply put, it's amazing. You play as Francis York Morgan, an FBI agent sent to the small town of Greenvale to investigate the murder of a local teenager. The story quickly picks up from here and sucks you in. I wish that I could be less vague about the story, but I risk ruining the game's 20+ hour run. This is the kind of story that keeps you wanting to play the game to see what happens next. It takes many sharp turns and streches across several different genres, including, but by far not limited to: horror, mystery, survival, comedy, and even some romance. I consider myself to be good at predicting storylines in games and movies, but even I could not predict hardly any of this game. It truly kept me interested until the very end. Speaking of the end, you may just shed a tear.
Characters: The characters in this game are incredibly varied and all have distinct personalities. I will certainly not ever forget any of them. The voice acting is great and really helps to bring the characters to life.
Gameplay: The driving is pretty awful but far from the worst I've ever played. The pause menu map only shows your immediate surroundings and cannot zoom out, rendering it useless. You'll have to pay close attention and learn the town if you want to get around. While this map issue was mildly annoying, it made the game a little more challenging. The rest of the gameplay is good, but nothing new or super polished. I would recommend using a controller, as the keyboard and mouse control for this game just feels clunky. The game is open world and each character has a routine that they do. This is important to remember, as they may not always be home for you to ask questions. There are some points in the game in which you must wait a certain amount of in-game time before moving on to the next portion of the story. This gives you time to explore all that there is to do in Greenvale, including a ton of side missions and collectible items.
Soundtrack: The soundtrack in this game is great, and very memorable. I love the acoustic guitar song that plays at the main menu and at various points in the game. Each track suits the level that it was designed for, and nothing seems out of place. The only complaint I have is that the music volume levels occasionally overpower dialogue in cutscenes.
Other thoughts: The game crashed to the desktop about a dozen times during my playthrough. The crashes all occured at set points in the game's story, so they are not random. There are some suggestions to remedy this with a quick search online though. I had luck passing these crashes by setting the game's launcher and .exe to Windows 98/ME mode and running as administrator. I am using an AMD gpu with the latest drivers (15.7.1 at time of writing) and Windows 7 64 bit.
Bottom line: If you don't mind the possibility of some technical issues and you are a fan of survival-horror/mystery games, by all means, buy this game.

The curious case of Deadly Premonition.

Furthermore, you need to use fixes to change the in-game resolution. The graphics lie somewhere between badly aged and horrible. And finally, the game mechanics are often stiff, walking on the border between being boring or laughable. Using a gamepad is recommended.
But with that said, what is offered if you fight past these issues is in my opinion nothing short of amazing. A quirky, twin peaks-esque world full of strange characters, weird happenings and charming dialogue, and a story that more often than not is wonderfully over the top.
This is not a game you should play for the gameplay or the visuals - its all about the experience of visiting the small town of Greenvale and its residents.

The setting is a post-apocalyptic world where androids and machines are at war with each other. At the beginning of the game, you control an android named 2B. Throughout your journey in the vast world of

Despite my relatively short time playing the game, I can definitely say that I recommend it, especially if you have friends willing to play it with you. Even if you don't have friends who want to play it, I'd still recommend it. It's a team based game where communication actually matters, unlike many of your modern "team" based games. (In which a single good player can carry an entire team.)
The objective of a match varies from a mode where you must capture a point and defend it, to a simple deathmatch in which you must take down a set number of enemy airships, to something called a VIP Hunt, in which you must take down a specific enemy airship. To accomplish these goals, you're given a variety of ships (Seven, I think. If I'm wrong, I'll come back and edit this.) that range from the nimble Squid to the devestating but slow Galleon, and a variety of weapons ranging from a missile launcher that can fire twenty shots in a single barrage, to the classic flamethrower, to a ship-mounted sniper rifle, to numerous sorts of artillery.
A crew consists of four people, each with an important role to fill on their ship. Crews are broken down into three classes.
The Pilot is the captain of the ship, and brings various tools to improve different aspects of the ship. These tools, however, are not without a cost to the ship and will often damage whichever part is improved. (Much to the dismay of his engineers.) Using his stamina, he can also give the ship a temporary speed boost. I would only recommend this role to the more advanced or competent players.
The Engineer is exactly what you think he is. They come equipped with the tools needed to repair, rebuild, buff, extinguish, prevent, and otherwise stave off your imminent destruction. By using their stamina, they can sprint across the ship to get where they're needed faster.
The Gunner is also self explanatory. They bring three different types of ammo, each with bonuses and debuffs, that can be loaded into the ship's guns. Their stamina boost allows them to turn the ship's guns farther than any other class, and lets them reload faster.
I'd break down the guns and ships, but that's a job best left to the wiki or guides. So, if you just scrolled down to the bottom of this, the game is one I highly recommend.

Some examples are in traversal; players in zero gravity move in a much more floaty fashion, but Oz (O2) kits allow the player greater control over their gliding movements and can boost themselves into the air. For the most part everything works as expected. Occasionally you will drown or burn some of your people but almost always it's because of your own mistake. That being said, occasionally the AI has some pathing issues that lead them into unnecessary danger and get them killed. More common though is having trouble telling where the AI will allow you to go, mostly involving how steep a slope they will walk up. This can cause problems when you think you have a clear path but the AI refuses to move and reverts to complaining about how much they are now on fire. It was never bad enough for me to make me stop playing though.
From Dust is a nice change of scenery and play style that is definitely worth your time.

This review is for the base game, I haven't played the DLCs yet. Scroll to bottom for final verdict.
The game has alot of interesting features, but I just can't recommend the game in it's current state. When picking your empire you can customize the culture and politics, but your physical appearance I found too limited. At first you really feel like an explorer, there's a fair amount of unique mission chains you can pick up just by exploring star systems. That's the best part of the game. Once you've established your empire (unable to expand without declaring war on someone) it's all downhill from there. Here are my main concerns, in no particular order:
-The AI is just stupid. They'll declare war when they have no reason to or are pathetically weaker than you. They're very conservative and won't take risks to cripple your empire. Instead they'll attempt to wait you out. Their only chance is if you make a really dumb move or don't know what you're doing.
-The lists and map modes are ♥♥♥♥ing terrible. This really surprised me for a Paradox game. In CK and EU you can easily find out who's at war with each other, the diplomatic situation between empires, military size and organization, technologies, trade, and many other useful things just by looking at a list or map mode. In Stellaris I have look at each empire individually. Sometimes I can't see what their relationship is with another empire because they have so many relationships the icons overlap each other. If I want a certain resource I have to talk to one empire after another just to see if they have what I want.
-Only certain planets qualify to be terraformed, but there's no list! So I have to manually check every planet in my empire for a special modifier.
-Diplomacy gets incredibly repetitive and boring. Why do I constantly have to renew my treaties+trades? I get that some empires like you more if you change the length of the treaty, but there should be an option to maintain treaty until one party wants to modify or cancel the deal.
Some things I like:
-You can automate groups of planets called sectors. These sectors also have the option to build up their own military bases for defense.
-You can uplift primitive alien races and encorporate them into your empire in a variety of ways.
-There are no machine races, but you can research technology that gives AI's sentience and make them a part of your empire in a variety of ways.
-The graphics are nice. I especially liked the way terraformed Mars looked.
-Fallen empires. These are ancient high level technology empires that are usually dormant. They'll attack you if you get too close to their borders, but may also help you with gifts.
-Federation victory. Basically you form an alliance with other empires, if you can get more than 60% of all habitable planets you win the game.
-You can have a migration treaty with other empires. Aliens from that empire can become citizens of your empire. This is really cool, because each alien race will have their own traits. For example some may be better at physics research, while others can make really good soldiers.
-You use armies to conquer and defend planets. You can research technologies that will give you interesting units like xenocalvary, genetically engineered super soldiers, and many more! Although these battles aren't intersting to watch.
*****Final Verdict*****
You can really customize you empire with unique features, but the core of the game is too repetitive. I'd only recommend this at 50% off. Keep in mind you'll probably want to buy the DLCs to make the game more interesting.

I try to go out of my way sometimes to at least experiment with new games, titles, software, and what have you. Resident Evil Revelations was one of those times. I do have to say, Revelations didn’t fail as much as Resident Evil 4 did in my eyes – you can read my review on RE4 in about 30 seconds.
I knew fully well that the Resident Evil series is one heck of a console port family, but I gave it shot anyways. The Humble Bundle offer was too tempting not to take, heck I could even make sure the developers didn’t get any coin from me. So it ticked all the right boxes from the start.

With all of the negatives, there are fixes luckily. I was able to use a save file from someone else to match their progress, and there are widescreen fixers that work with this game.  Using fixers for the FOV do cause issues with COOP, so be forewarned.

If there is something that I hate, it's to see that I didn't review all of Artifex Mundi's games, whether they're the publishers or the developers. I was convinced to have reviewed Enigmatis: The Ghosts of Maple Creek, that I was making big eyes when I saw that, no, I didn't.
I reinstalled the game and replayed it. I wasn't going to use my memory for this one.
Enigmatis: The Ghosts of Maple Creek is the first Enigmatis and is developped by Artifex themselves. In it, you wake up in a town, without any recent memories. You just know that you were there to solve a disappearance. But the more you're learning about Maple Creek, the more you'll understand that the reverend is behind something monstruous.
The story is well-written as usual and is using a feature used rarely in the genre: amnesia about the case, meaning that you'll investigate everything again, though there are now more obstacles: Maple Creek got some damage due to a storm, the residents are going to the church, with a bell that doesn't end to ring, your own car has an accident and now, Hamilton, a missing detective, is showing himself.
The gameplay is pretty quite the standard one: find items, use them to reveal new paths or puzzles, clear hidden objects scenes, etc.. However, I can tell that the game is an old one: indeed, you have a lot of hidden objects scenes, which you're often visiting (though previous items found aren't put back, which is nice) and with a lot of items in them. Some objects are hard to find, as they can be mistaken for an element in the background. Puzzles, however, are easy to do.
There is a specific feature: you have a case board, where you'll pin clues, which will lead to new questions. It's a nice way to focus on the case, instead of reading a diary and trying to find solutions in the pages of it.
However, there is a large problem for the navigation: indeed, some arrows are close to each other (like the balcony on your hotel room) meaning that some misclickings will happen: I wanted to go back to my room from the balcony but because I was going too fast, I wasn't pointing on the right area and I ended up to the garden. Also, the map isn't interactive at all: you can't use it for fast travel.
The graphics are very correct, like with any Artifex Mundi's game, and are sticking to the story in itself: don't expect any sun, as you're doing everything in one night, in a deserted town, with some exploring in the forest and with some damage due to a storm.
As usual, the soundtrack is very good.
As it's a special edition, you'll end up with a bonus chapter, with Hamilton's first contact with Maple Creek 30 years before the plot of the main story.
Enigmatis: The Ghosts of Maple Creek is as usual a very good title for playing casual adventures, with an important presence of hidden objects scenes as it was released first during a period where the genre was aiming towards its actual version. While you don't need it to understand the sequel, I recommend to begin by Maple Creek, to really have a better connection with people you'll meet in Ravenwood.

The GemCraft series has pioneered my absolute favorite concept in the tower defense genre.
The idea of directly spending resource to generate higher risk/difficulty/reward. Spending resources to make incoming waves more difficult, which in turn, end up dropping even more resources. This ensures that GemCraft will be able to *always* challenge you at any phase of the game, on any map, because you will always have incentive to make each individual wave as difficult as you possibly can.
Now, what I'd say the GemCraft series does very poorly is balancing its gem(tower) types and encouraging variety. Instead, there are very super optimal setups that are very homogenous (ie, not diverse). I will not give these away in the review, since discovery is one of the few fun parts available due to this.
Check the hours played of myself and others - there is clearly a lot of content here to properly hook somebody.

I have played all the versions of gemcraft and they become better and better. Gemcraft Labyrinth was perhaps equal to this one. I played the limited free flash versions. So I picked this up on a bargain and played with access to all the elements of the game, and it is nearly poorer than the limited version. And I am sad to give it a negative review. For these reasons:
It's strong suit is that you can scale the difficulty quite well by cranking up the challenge. However if you get good at it you end up with getting to big of a reward for this and with the added bonus you get from things the pay version it soon becomes to easy. You advance way too fast and nothing becomes more of a challenge than you make it and even that becomes hard after a while. By playing skilled through maybe a third of the stages you can easily just click "send all" on the rest of them and finish them in seconds, if you like.
The above would be fine if you could actually scale the challenge up, but can't because it lags really bad after a certain point. My rig isn't the best of rigs, but it plays worse than the web browser flash version. So at some point you start not play the best you can, but rather at how you can avoid lag. Which only works so far before that also more or less breaks down because even that becomes easy.
Then it is the graphics itself, I kind of expected this to be scaleable so that it would render to any screen resolution. It doesn't, so if you go full screen (which increase lags) it is gets grainy and blurred.
If you have never played it and it is a bargain I can recommend it for the time you spend to learn it, which is enjoyable and less laggy. Also if you have played previous free versions and wanna throw Game in a Bottle a few coins. And maybe the iron wizard mode is enjoyable which cranks up the challenge by removing some of the things that made the series great.

Let me give you a quick and easy way to describe this game in general:
Super Smash Bros. + MedaBots = Megabyte Punch

I received Megabyte Punch for free in some giveaway.  And I finally booted it up about a month later.  It's a novel idea, but it heavily suffers in that it's not a very unique game outside of those ideas in my opinion.
The game is clearly influenced from both megaman and Super Smash brothers.  The player runs through Mega Man style levels and uses Super Smash Brothers combat to fight.   In addition there's a rather involved system for equipping items that will help change stats, give new abilities and get new attacks.
There's even different levels, every level has a theme, and each level looks different.
So on paper so far, that should sound good.  The problem is there's a caveat to almost every thing I've said.
Megaman had amazing levels, I'm sure if you can think of two different levels, you can come up with at least ten differences between them, Megaman's levels are iconic.  Megabyte Punch's levels are not.  For the most part they are pallet swaps with very little life to them, you can look at the images above and notice, that the "ice" world looks the same Dirt world, and the Metal world is only slightly different.  They handle the same, they act the same they are the same.  There's no different controls or different "theme" it's really just a pallet swap.  What made Megaman iconic is the characters and the levels all have a single solid theme that really stand out.
As for the combat.  I have to say that is the highest point, and then I also have to say the lowest point.  The combat feels SO fresh when you beat up the first enemy, and when you beat up the same enemy for what feels like the 50th time (which actually is the 50th time) before the first boss, it's tiring. Megaman has a lot of enemies, but it threw a lot of low health enemies at you.  Instead in this game, each enemy takes 3-4 hits to kill, using Smash Brother rules (higher damage means they fly higher).  Boss battles are FANTASTIC with this system, because they have special attacks and different tactics.  They even have a life system with it.
Regular enemies though are repetitive as hell.  When you have to beat everyone by hitting them 4-5 times, the novelty of the combat wears off and you're just like "I want to get through this level".  It's sadly tedious.
Smash combat works well when you're fighting hard enemies on a single level, but trying to make a full level based game with it, is tiresome, and while it was good enough for Super Smash Brothers Melee, it wasn't required to stand on it's own, but just be a side diversion.  Plus you had the iconic characters Smashing it out.
And finally the item system.  Again novel idea, horrible execution.  The images up top look good, and they are good, the problem that is in game, at least in the first three levels, you never really look "good" you don't look iconic, you look like a jumbled together wreck of a machine
It's a really great concept though, but the fact is nothing really works exactly like it should.  I actually got bored of it by the third level and went to play something else.
I got the game for free, but I had to ask myself "How much would I have paid for this game?"  and well the answer I ended up with is, I wouldn't have paid for it.  I just didn't like it that much, it really was a great concept, but the overall execution bored me, and I feel it missed out, because a game that plays like Megaman but with a smash gameplay could work, but it needs a lot more iconic levels, and less Smash gameplay (or at least less enemies you have to fight).

Please be aware, when I originally wrote this review, I had played the game for around 1.3 hours. I will update my thoughts and impressions as the game continues to be updated and as I continue to experience it.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CrossCode is by far one of the most charming games I have played since Stardew Valley. From the very beginning, it is easy to see that the devlopers poured their hearts into the game.
Here is a short list of things that I like about the game:
-The developers have done an exellent job of easing the player into the games various mechanics. There is some hand holding in the beginning, but it isn't overbearing.
-The combat is very engaging. This is due in no small part to the obvious amount of thought that went into the different combat mechanics.
-The controls are very fluid and responsive.
-The art is beutifully drawn, and does an incredibly job of conveying the characters emotions.
-The level design is thoughtful and engaging.
-There is just the right amount of dialogue. Enough that you can understand what is happening and appreciate the story, but you don't have to spend an eternity reading it.
So far, CrossCode appears to be far more than the sum of its parts. I am incredibly excited to see how the game continues to evolve and change as it is being developed. I haven't been this happy, or pleasantly surprised by a game purchase in a really long time.
I encourage everyone who reads this to try the free demo on Steam. I am sure that you'll be glad you did.

Just so no one gets me wrong, there are a lot of things to love about this game. It's open-world with numerous mini-games, and it has some excellent voice acting from the likes of Brandon Keener, Eliza Dushku, and Neil Patrcik-freakin'-Harris. The half-baked plotline is an object of adoration for me.
However, this game was meant for consoles. The controls, as of the moment you get in a car, are waaaaay too sensitive. That thing will drive like a schizophrenic on eight cups of coffee. Keep this in mind, get a control pad, do something to prepare for it; or the last few missions will be just about impossible.
Edit: It's been a few years since I wrote this, and as far as I can tell, Volition is still hammering out and perfecting that PC port. It still isn't spectacular; but driving is much more manageable on modern graphics cards (and for those of us with Steam controllers, while the keys are still presented as keyboard keys, it works quite well). For the price, it's a win.

It is my understanding that the start is meant to rush you to the prologue where you meet the actual
heros. The characters in Balthus Requiem + Emo Natsu are supposed to be very over powered as they
are the heros of yesterday and etc. So the battles are quick, the towns are sparce and the
dialogue is rushed because they become way more important later on. As the game opens up very
slowly like Game of Thrones, it starts to get better and better. But it sort of takes awhile :/.
If you only play Balthus Requiem to the first part of Chapter 1...you won't like it. But if you
stick around and vanquish Sylph Cave, the game gets more rewarding. The hidden items and secrets
appear like crazy. The jokes keep you entertained and the fights get more challenging and more
fun. You have to really play your cards right to survive, but it does get easier as your characters
not only grow to become strong, but eventually they get stronger then the characters in Balthus Requiem.
Once you finish chapter 1; the plot thickens and the actual story of what the heck they are mean't
to do unfolds. From this point on it starts to grab a hold of you and reel you in. You are rewarded with
sellable items every new town you enter. The save points are at every resting lodge/Inn and every field.
From Chapter 2 and so on you unlock the Weapon Shop, Armor Shop, Accessory Shop, and so on and so
forth. They introduce fresh new items that alternate in stock as you reach new towns. Every time you unlock
a shop or finish unlocking all the items in said shop you get rewarded with items that make your journey easier.
I found the characters cute and endearing. Although, some were sort of boring, I think
together they had a realistic family bond going on for a band of rag-tag individuals.
In chapter 3 there is the fishing and fighting mini games which I found quite enjoyable. There was also this
card game that reminded me of a card game in ff8 that was hidden in a wall in chapter 2. There was also
these alter boys hidden in a priest's basement lol. It also had a mini game in which I was also offered drugs
and played as someone called Big Beef Gai and was trying to feed people the Big Beef Sammich in a hallucination.
As you progress more and more things become available to you, things get harder as enemies level up
with you, and you have to gear up and learn new skills to stay ahead of the game. The main healer
comes around mid chapter 2 and it gets easier from then on out. Balthus does learn cure a little
later in chapter one though. There is secret bosses, secret dungeons, secret final weapons, secret quests.
secret unlockable characters and secret chests. Lots to explore. Past chapter 3 it starts to slow down again,
but by then you'll be so invested you'll hang on. Around chapter 5 you get hit with something fierce and it
wraps it up beautifully with no stones left unturned in chapter 6.
Then there is this end game resort where you can purchase every single playable character from the story and gear them up as you fight monsters in a dragon quest x like arena mode. All and all, a lot of effort went into this game. I honestly think that it deserves a chance. You will NOT like the very start as it's very unprofessional compared to the rest of
the game, but it's obvious to someone who has actually played the rest of the game. There is also a 90 page
short story sequel that finishes the entire series. If you really enjoyed the lore, I'd read it find out what
happens after you beat the game. The game is definately worth beating, but you can't just play up  untill chapter 1
and expect the game to be like that the whole time, as it gets so much better.
Graphically though, it's not all that great and it is pretty default, but honestly it really doesn't matter. It's so clear that a ton of effort and work has went into this game and most people who use rpg maker to make games aren't as crafty as most people in the game industry tend to be. When I take a step back and look at the bigger picture as a whole, I think
I see a struggling developer who has spent an enourmous amount of time trying to get his story out into the world
and deserves all the positive recognition he can get. Just give the game a chance and no...beating the prologue
isn't giving it a chance. Game of Thrones sucked for many seasons, but when it came to season 6 and 7 the build up was
so great that it exploded in such a fantastic way that it was ultimately enjoyable. But if all there was, was only
5 seasons I would have dropped that show so long ago.
The point is you won't like it if you only play until chapter 1. But if you play chapter 2 and onwards then it's safe to say that in total; Solenars Edge Rebirth is a rare gem that shines bright in a sea of crap. I cannot wait to see more from
this developer.

I really tried with this game, because it's oddly compelling in a what not to do in a game, yet let me see what happens next way.  First of all, the mapping is atrocious, with vast expanses of nothing, but lines of rocks or trees making you zigzag through the vast expanses of nothing.  Towns mostly, as far as I played, have houses with no doors or you can't go in--or, as in one town, they are just giant rectangles of nothing.  There is nothing to explore; you just follow a linear path.  It took me over an hour to get out of the prologue, and I still don't really have a clue what's going on.
You can only save when you come across save crystals, which normally wouldn't be a problem, but they are sparse.  I went through tons of dialogue, opened a book, and apparently my character got sucked into some vortex never to be seen again. Game Over.  Granted, the book did ask if I wanted to open it, but being curious. . .  Unfortunately, that meant going back through about 5 minutes or more of dialogue.
Another point where this save lack  became detrimental was after advancing quite a ways past my last save point, I encountered snakes that could poison.  The first and only item store I encountered had no remedy for poison, nor did I have anyone in my party who could cure. I had one resurrection item since they were extremely expensive and a few tents, which supposedly allowed you to heal the party outside of battle.  I had no option but to let the character die. I decided to use a tent, since I had only the one resurrection  item, but nope, the tent only heals the living members--dead member was still dead.  My options were to go back to the last save and get more resucitation items or just quit. I decided to just quit.
There are mini games, but the vast majority aren't really explained (other than the self-explanatory hit the right sequence of keys ones, which rather suck), and I don't have a clue what to do with them.  The speed at which I've been adding and attaining new party members is almost dizzying, most of whom pop up for a battle and then go away.  And as for the battles themselves, it is baffling how characters can one hit an enemy during one battle, then barely make a dent in that enemy if they encounter it again.  There is no rationale as to the amount of damage characters do, and it seems that battles actually get more difficult as you level.  I don't know if the monsters are leveling with my party or it's just poor settings or a combination.
The story itself might not be so bad--especially if I could manage to stick it out, but there defiitely is some cringe-worthy dialogue.  Yet, the game is filled with odd absurdities--baffling and weird things that made me keep going.  For one, some of the characters are named things like the "Evil King of the West." Although, the poor king of whatever town in the beginning doesn't even get a castle, but just a set of vast and grand steps leading up to his little cubicle.  At one point in the very beginning, you can go into a priest's house. You can uncover a set of stairs that lead down to his dungeon, with cells full of people. Nope, not a clue why they were down there at all.

I've enjoyed this game very much.  I've played Clash of the Continents scenario, very good way to learn the game.  I've won that on Grey (Amsterdam) easiest, Orange (China) and Yellow (USA) both slightly more difficult.  I'm currently working on winning as Red (Chile) definitely harder.  I think that both Blue (South Africa) and Green (South Australia) will be another notch harder.  I'm currently working on the Rise of the Reich scenario 1 game with USA the other with USSR.
My Tips to people new to the game:
1. Coal is king, you need it to build anything, improving cities, making Goods, making Arms, building troops, did I say anything.  Set production of any Coal resources you own or acquire to Maximize ASAP.  Make capturing Coal resources a high priority.
2. Improve Cities.  If playing Clash of the Continents you only have 1 city and it is max production, make some mobile units first turn to immediately capture surrounding countries.  When you capture a City if it's production is less than 10 set it to build Light Industry.  If it can build Basic Infantry in say 6 turns or less do that so you can defend you new territories.
3. Research WAIT on it.  You need to capture a good number of territories before you worry about research.  IMO start researching Improved Infantry first, Light Tanks next.
4. Check on other countries Cities regularly.  Then bottom right button that looks like a fold opens information about the world.  Click 2 button from left on Top the the far right tab (Cities) then at the headings click IPO.  That rearranges all the Citties of the World to show the highest production Cities first.  Any of these close to you are a priority to capture.
5. Amphibious Assaults are tough.  You suffer a large penalty for these assaults.  NEVER try this on a Capital, instead do a massive assault on a territory next to or near them, hopefully one that shows level 1 or 0 Fortifications.
6. Tanks are great for assaults.  High Offense ok defense.  I have noticed that the AI is smart enough that if you assualt with only Tanks you suffer a penalty (25 %) against Infantry so take some Infantry with you, remember I said Improved Infantry is first to research,

This is the story of how the mighty Karskrin imperium (a race of blue reptilian humanoids) colonized a planet, how they lost it to a terrible enemy and how they finally won over their foolish enemy.
The Imperium needed to expand, we needed resources, we needed territory. So our all-mighty emperor in his majestic wisdom decided that we would colonize RB-346 and so we did. The colony ship "Voyager's Hope" reach its destination 3 moths after its departure from imperials docks and started to build the first settlement ofthe new colony. The marshall of the colony reported tons of minerals and plenty of land to build. The mission was a success and so we all praise our immortal Emperor... but it would not last.
After a year of prosperity the colony now called "Paradise" began to send reports of minor but ever more constant earthquakes in the area and that they decided to investigate the epicenter of this events. only a week later we recieved a second message... the expedition to the epicenter had found something incredible, being as gigantic and tall as the sky itself, they called them "Behemonths". It turns out that the earthquakes were a result of this creatures waking up from their slumber and now they were starting to roam the land once again. Our scientist ask permission to study them and we sadly... agreed. That was the moment when everything collapsed, no one knows what the scientist did but we all know what happened after... Settlement after settlement ravaged by the enraged Behemonths, the people of Paradise asked for help but before we could answer we lost communication with the colony.
The Imperium send the holy fleet and its armies to retake what was ours, and when we arrived to the colony... when we landed.. all hell broke loose. The Behemonths attacks were terrible and just one of them could take on a battalion with ease... The Paradise war was just starting.
It took us years to finally win and retake the planet. millions of deads both civilians and soldiers alike. I don't know how I survived those hard and horrible years of screaming, deployments, orbital bombarments and suffering, but what I do know is that not even those gigantic creatures could beat the might of the Karskrin people. We fought for our colony and we won for our Emperor.
Long lived Emperor Argron! and eternal be the glory to our Imperium!.

From Dust is a god game, but not in the way that you might think. Instead of leading a civilization into expansion, you're instead trying to guide them through the world, "fighting" against the forces of nature themselves.
Tech-wise, the game looks gorgeous, and more importantly has this fantastic physics system in which fluid and dust settle realistically. This is important, because those are what you'll manipulate most of the time, be it to open a path, to let forest spread, to stop fires, whatever is needed. It's an experience unlike any other game out there.
However, as much as I like it, I have to say that it's best to pick up the console versions. For a very simple reason, the PC one brings the uPlay DRM, a highly incompetent piece of software developed by Ubi that has a 50/50 chance of denying you the game you just bought. Myself, I had to spend just under an hour tinkering and watching "update" bars fill up before the game worked. Even if it was worth the trouble in the end, this sort of abuse with your honest customers is simply ridiculous.
If you do want to pick it up on PC anyways, good luck, and have a pad ready. K&M controls here are a love-or-hate thing, and you might want to try both out to see which suits you better.

From Dust, however, shuts down too frequently to really do much in a playing session.

From Dust is a fun physics game that won't keep you coming back again and again to play it, but luckily the technology itself has aged well. What other game has free-flowing water, sand, and lava that can all be mixed together to create rock, land, volcanoes, mountains, earthquakes, and tsunamis? If you are hoping that the very end of the game unlocks a no-strings-attached sandbox mode, however, you may be slightly disappointed. The sandbox mode that you get at the end is another level where you get to use all the abilities you gain across the rest of the game to beat the level. After you beat it, you return to the main menu. From there you can choose to play it again, but it doesn't feel at all like a truly free sandbox mode. If you can get past that, then I would recommend this game simply so you can playing with water, sand, and lava.

Absolutely amazing Tower Defense game. If you don't like TDs, you'll hate this, but if you do, you'll love it.
As you can see, the graphics aren't great. However, the strategy, customization, and gameplay are what makes this game so worth it.
This game does what TDs should do; allow complete customization of everything. It's not just a matter of finding that ONE way to beat the level, like some other TDs do. You can develop your own play style, and yet still play in a way that is always challenging. The game is built in a way that it can ALWAYS be challenging. You can make the game harder, in order to get more XP, or easier if you're having trouble with something. Really great concept that I haven't seen many games do.
Also, there's a ridiculous amount of achievements, that are a lot of fun to try and unlock (not just "get to this level" achievements, but lots of interesting things that will cause you to play the game differently).

Ok, so for the actually review, i have to say that i really loved the game. Its very unique as a game since it features some gameplay aspects that i never saw together in one game. For example in Deadly Premonition you have a open world factor, you are free to explore the town of Greenwale as you please. You can do this on foot or in your car, kinda like in GTA, but you will have to make a good use of your time since you are an FBI agent who has a case to solve afterall so, while you can go out and explore the town as you please, you will also have to show up for work in a certain place at a certain time, and that brings me to second gameplay factor in this game, time.
This game has active time system and dynamic day and night cycles. You cant go to police station at 3am and demand that everyone is present there so you can start the next part of yout "main quest" just because you are the main character, no, you have to show up at the appropriate time when the station is working and when everyone needed for the quest are present. You can just sleep it off untill the time is right or you can try to locate and complete some of many side quests that this game has.
Yeah, its a horror game withopen world and side quests, pretty crazy, right. Oh and did i mention hunger and tiredness? Yes, you actually have to sleep and eat regularly so you dont suffer a penalty or eventually die. Miss a good night sleep and you will be tired, it will reflect on your stamina, you will get fatigued super fast and you wont be able to aim your weapon properly or, ignore your hunger and eventually your health starts draining.
Speaking of health loss, there is ofcourse the action part of the game where you will have to beat or gun down creepy enemies before they take you down. Now, this part of the game is, in my honest oppinion, not so good since you have a gun with infinite ammo and as far as i remember, it never takes more than 2 headshots for the enemy to drop dead(frustratingly slow). Action parts lack any form of challenge and you will probably finish the game without dying a single time even if you are bad at shooters, It could be just my oppinion but i think that no one will enjoy these shooting sequences the way they shoul be enjoyed.
Now, even with the games action sequences as bad they are, this game is still amazing because, to play this for the sake of action and challenge is to miss the point of theis game entirely. It shines when it comes to storytelling and character developement. It held me nailed in front of my PC, wanting to get to the bottom of the whole thing and solve the case. It was thrilling from the start and it left me wanting for more when it ended. Characters are deep and alive, you can see and feel their personalities in  everything they do, from their motion when walking and talking, their responses to events and their attitude towards each other. Tho none shines brighter than York himself when it comes to this with his frequent dialogues(well, monologues technically since we never hear a reply) with Zach, his imaginary friend and pretty much everything he does, from the way he introduces himself to people, lights his cigarettes, starts a profiling, etc, etc... Excellent personality 10/10
If you havent played it before and have no idea what it is but are still willing to give it a go even with all the bugs and problems exclusive for the PC port, i say go for it, it surprised me and its probably gonna surprise you too. Its definitely one of the better games that i ever played and i have been a gamer for a while now :)

I'll start with the cons:
- Bugs and crashes galore, be prepared to deal with issues, more so if you're going to use Durante's Dp Fix mod (which is essential).  A great place to start is the pinned "Techinical Support Topic" in the forums if you decide to start playing this game (which is worth it, despite how this critique starts).  This is an issue that I wouldn't blame people for being really upset about but if you have the patience it'll work out fine.
- No in-game graphic settings, no AA, no resolution settings (defaults to 1280x720)... zip, nadda, nothing.  Unless you use the afore mentionned Dp fix where Durante the modder added the ability to tune various settings in the mods .ini file.
- Graphics are hit or miss, some areas in the game will leave you scratching your head wondering if the textures were vomited into the game as oppossed to programed.
Sort of in the middle:
- Some Controls/gameplay:  There is controller support (I use an Xbox 360 wired controller without issue, thankfully...), haven't tried the keyboard and mouse controls.  Control is serviceable, I can vouch that the default settings are actually better than the xbox 360 version of the game, you can react a little faster and aim better with this control scheme.
- Driving! Oh my...  Picture driving a giant heavy brick with wheels that are smaller bricks.  It's almost hilarious, it's a universe where turning down the street can only be done in small calculated increments. Miss a turn in one the games side races and then marvel at the excrutiatingly slow reverse function complete with the back up sounds of a forklift and the engine power of a small lawn mower.
Finally the pros!
- The story is fascinating, the characters are eccentric and a joy to interact with. The main character is absolutely fantastic!!  He's funny, smart and a bit smarmy, it's a lot of fun to watch him rattle the towns folk.  The voice acting is pretty good as far as I'm concerned and each character exudes uniqueness, personality or eccentricity.  There are some pretty laugh out loud moments too!  Also helps that I'm a Twin Peaks fan as the game makes no bones about taking direct influence from that material.

- Albeit the graphics are a bit dated, there are areas that have really good art style: like the interiours; the diner looks really cool and each house you can enter has  distinct personality and depth.
- It's an open world, you are given plenty of time between points in the main story line to explore the town.  Nice details peppered all over the place and collectables to grab.  Lots of side quests that aren't too taxing and also some that add some extra context to the main mystery at hand.   Every interactable character seems to have differenct routines, so you won't always find characters in the same place.  For example: you can observe from the windows on the outside of some homes that have characters in them, one time I observed Emily the police officer, it was about 10pm game time, wearing a blue dress (which I've never seen her wear) and casually enjoying her living room or the time I peeked in on the Ingrams around dinner time, the whole family was there.  The twins appeared to be interacting with themselves while watching tv.  Mrs. Ingram was making dinner in the kitchen and then Keith walked in through the front door (I was there because I decided to follow him from the milk barn, not creeping, observing!!!), he went to the fridge grabbed a beer and sat next to the twins (how's the peeping Tommy... how's the peeping). I thought it was kind of neat because there was effort to make the world feel like it was living around you.
- Some really tense moments in the game, especially the moments where it turns into screen on screen, your characters perspective and the killers perspective.  Those parts are amazing!
I originally played and finished the game on the xbox 360 and now  i've been compelled to play it again, this time the  directors cut on the p.c.  It's a budget game but get past some of the foibles and  you have a very unique and memorable game!

I realize an hour is not a great deal of time to spend with a game, but considering I found five, game breaking design choices (?) in the first hour, and the best thing I can say about it only cost me the bandwidth that it took to download it, I do not like Loadout.

Casual Gamer (or whatever my steam name is at the moment)

I'm going to warn people - I'm still getting the hang of this game.
I bought this on the strength of the trailers, I am a sucker for grand concept ideas.  I love space opera, and it seemed right up my street.  It was one of those times I decided to pay full price near the day of release as I was so smitten.
Unfortunately, my idea of what the game would be and what it actually was were two different things.  I spent the first 5 hours starting and re-starting games.  The concepts in it were *ahem* 'alien' to me.  It didn't click with me, unlike Civ V or Endless Space had.
That was at release.  I kept track of it, occasionally trying it after updates.  Still not liking it.  It gathered virtual dust for a while instead.
After Utopia, I started watching some youtube videos, getting an idea for how to tackle this behemoth of a game.  The in game assistant wasn't, in my own opinion, very helpful.  It actually confused me further.  I tried this game again after purchasing the DLC so I had EVERYTHING installed.
I don't know what changed, but it made sense.  Over a year from release, I am now engrossed in this game.  I love it.  I'm not a super-strategy nerd, but I do like the genre.  The flexibility in this game is immense.  It's one of the few games where I feel I could win without going to war with anyone.  Where diplomacy may actually work.  I see myself going from the fine, granular control of everything at the start to a grand wave of the hand to take over a quadrant at the end.
There's a lack of mention of mechanics and bugs in this review, because I a: don't understand it all (yet) and b: have yet to encounter a bug.
So to sum up:
Pros:
It does feel epic.
There is a ton of stuff to do.  I always find myself thinking of the next steps, even when away from it.
Looks great.
Music is top notch.
Cons:
Tutorial/VIR is not that helpful to me.
Initial playthrough is confusing and bewildering
Not cheap, but does feel like you get a lot for the cash.
There is tons of stuff to do.  I am not getting as much sleep now.
Overall, it's pretty solid to me.  My previous strategy experience ranges from RTS (C&C, Dark Reign, Homeworld, etc) to turn-based (Civ V, Civ BE (yuk), Endless Space, WH40K Armageddon).  I'd recommend it for any space opera fan, but it may take some time before you 'get it'.

I usually don't write anti-recommendations but in case of this game I felt compelled. I've played and loved many Resident Evil games since the original release and my favourites are Code Veronica, Resident Evil HD remake, Resident Evil 4 (with Wii controls) and Resident Evil 5 when played as co-op.
While I used to enjoy Resident Evil games I am afraid their design has become archaid and stale. Game is neither survival horror nor action game, but tries to incorporate horror elements into action by having a horrible control scheme. Most of the game play consists of wandering same stale environments looking for a lever or key while getting streams of same type of monsters thrown at you to try and take a shot at them while game's control scheme does everything in it's power to make second to second game play frustrating.
You do manage to kill off the beasts time after time, but it's not fun and hardly feels like an achievement. But worse than the combat is game's lack of focus and uninspired story telling. First of all pacing is off the wall, there's a flash back after a flash back that leads to constant change of scenery and chararacters, you don't get hooked by the story and just when you have forgotten what were you doing, you'll get pulled back to the original scenery where you started at. Then the "episode" ends and there's a video explaining what happened last time in Resident Evil Revelations. Okay uh, I guess this game was originally released in episodic form or something? Still it feels weird to watch a video about what happened when it literally just happened 3 seconds ago.
Characters aren't interesting, especially female characters are just for showing skin,  environments are boring mazes full of key & lever hunting. There's a lot of time sink type of content, I suspect they got away with it due (assumed) episodic structure? Game builds no kind of tension with it's "horror parts". Game's full of Hollywood-envy, it wants to be a movie an action game and horror product. Unfortunately it just feels unfocused and repeating.

In beginning of a boom of Indie games back in 2007 and 2008 it saw a number of casual games featuring graphics much like these. I am going to try to be respectful in this review, but this game is very bad and easily the worst I've played in a while.
First of all, Arcardia fails at the basic requirement of being functional software. I was not able to get a working controls either by keyboard or mouse or my gamepad. There is no help menu or even a key binding screen I can tell what keys I need to press. If you want to rebind the gamepad keys you need to edit the configuration file manually. If you want to rebind the keybaord keys then you may be out of luck as I saw no configuration file for the keyboard.
Gameplay wise, this game really wants to be Geometry Wars. It's to the point where it follows Geometry Wars home and Geometry wars should consider getting a restraining order. If this game was commercially successful the developers of Geometry Wars should consider legal action. You might think I'm exaggerating, but I played them side-by-side and the difference is uncanny. The only difference is that Geometry Wars actually works and is a lot more polished.
Acardia mimics Geometry Wars in the following ways; grid background, distortion effects, weapons and weapon progression, controls (best I can tell anyway, seeing as they didn't really work for me). Even much of the enemy AI is a mirror of Geometry Wars. It's even to the point where the same AI had the same rough shape and color as it's counterpart in Geometry Wars.
Just buy Geometry Wars if you don't already own it. It's much more polished and, most importantly, it actually works.
Score: 0/10

I see all these negative reviews complaining about lack of support and replay value, but I just want to say that despite its problems, this game is really fun for the 2$ I paid for it on sale.
The gameplay gets pretty intense, especially late in a round when tons of enemies are spawning, and it's an enjoyable challenge figuring out how to best kite and kill enemies and when to use bombs and such.
When you buy this game, be aware what you are paying for.  Arcadia is a casual shooter (As clearly mentioned) that is not meant to entertain you for long periods of time like other games.  This game is fun to play on and off when you don't have time for other deeper games, and it fulfills that goal excellently.  Don't buy this game if you are looking for a hardcore game to sink many hours into to beat or to become the best at it.
Whether this game is being actively updated or not isn't really relevant.  The game mechanics are solid and very entertaining in a casual situation, and I'm happy having given a one time payment of 2$ and receiving the end product I got.
One point that I want to given special mention to is the music in this game.  Hearing the music in this game is like half the experience of playing this game.  The dev of this game put together an awesome soundtrack for this game, which ends up making it extremely relaxing and enjoyable to play.  The music in this game is techno and trance from Newgrnds (Steam censors the full site name for some reason), so if you like that kind of music you'll probably enjoy this game
As the description clearly states, "Arcadia is a fun, casual little shooter." And that's exactly what you get when you buy this game.  Hardcore gaming experience for hundreds of hours of evolving gameplay, no. Fun 2d bullet-hell shooter with awesome music that's worth a few bucks, yes.

Arcadia looked like a budget game in the vein of Geometry Wars.  It even spoke of controller support back when I first bought it.  No such support existed at the time.  The developer claimed that he would fix it, but years later it doesn't work proper.  Even claiming partial controller support should count as a lie at this point.
The gameplay itself is rather bland, the visuals limited and the enemies lack any real diversity.  Even if you wish to play withj Mouse and Keyboard, this will likely bore you quickly.  It is, in my opinion, not worth the money (even in a sale), and a shame that the developer doesn't support his own work.

The game has many flaws. Gameplay, replay value and controls are rather bad.
If you are thinking this is like Geometry Wars you will be very disappointed.

Enigmatis 1 is good for the most part, but there are definite points worth complaining about. The other half of the game, the point-and-click portion, isn't bad.  Most of the items and their uses are pretty, only got stumped 1 or 2 times.

Megabyte Punch is a great indie title that combines the gameplay of Super Smash Brother with the customization of many arena robot games as you fight through a variety of environments packed with collectables and secrets as well as randomly constructed enemies. The game offers a story mode, bot-matches and up to 4 player co-op or versus mode.
This game is well worth it, both at normal price and especially when on sale. If you want a further look at my opinions a more detailed review is just below.
The gameplay is very similar to that of games like Smash Brothers and Custom Robo Arena. You begin the game with a basic robot with no abilities other than the basic combat abilities which are always available independent of what robot parts you equip afterwards.
The combat consists of normal attacks which change depending on whether you're in the air or pressing a directional button (In total, 8 different attacks), special attacks which are limited to 4 abilities gained by equiping a variety of robot parts and are again changed depending on the directional key being pressed in combination with the Special Attack. In addition, you are able to block using a shield system that you can toggle at will similar to that of Smash Bros and a thrust attack that stuns enemies when they are shielding.
Although the game offers 150 different robot parts, there are only a few abilities, which consist of both active and passive abilities. But they are in fact, different, sporting many styles and allowing you to create a variety of different robot loadouts to suit your taste. In addition, there are 50 color schemes that can be found scattered across the levels to give that extra little touch of personality to the robots.
In Megabyte Punch, there are two gamemodes with the primary mode being the ADVENTURE (AKA, the Story Mode) which is where most of the content will be unlocked. The Adventure is fairly short but is long enough to teach you the mechanics of the game, the mechanics of the terrain and allows you to unlock a good amount of parts for the second game mode.
The Adventure is divided up in 6 and a half multi-staged levels with different environments, enemies and a boss at the end of each level.
The story isn't much to talk about, you play as a young robot protecting the Heartcore of your village from the larger robot clans and empires. Much of the exposition can be found by talking to the villagers in your home-town as they receive new dialogue whenever you finish a level.
You can play the Adventure alone, which I did, or you can play with up to 3 other local players in a split-screen mode.
For me personally, the selling point of this game is the FIGHT section of the game which is split between the Tournament Mode and the Versus Mode. The Tournament Mode, serves as a test of skill, as the robot AI becomes significantly more difficult than the Adventure Mode enemies and can easily juggle you with combos and knockout moves if you aren't careful.
The Tournament Mode is an 8-round, 1v1 against Robot AIs where you start off with 3 lives while each enemy has 1 life. By winning the Tournament you can unlock special parts that can only be unlocked in Tournament Mode as well as a lot of credits which can be used in the Adventure Mode.
The Tournament Mode offers a replayable mode which allows you to either play an over-powered robot stomping the enemy AI or challenging yourself by trying to defeat the eight rounds without dying once or without equipping any non-standard parts.
Similarly, the Versus Mode serves as the 4-Player couch Smash Bros mode, where everyone can make their own robot and fight each other.
Although the game has a fair share of content and a good amount of replayability, it does come a bit short when it comes to the complexity of the combat. Small things like not being able to turn around while shielding can easily turn a fight from difficult to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
A minor note on the game is what I personally found to be a very mediocre soundtrack, although this is a subjective opinion the soundtrack never really caught my attention. This isn't necessarily a negative thing but it might be taken into consideration.
In addition, the abilities don't seem that balanced as some are particularly stronger or more useful than others. For example, the late-game ability to increase your attack speed seems very very minimal as the 12% increase feels non-existant in practice. On the other hand, the drill move allows you to bypass tons of terrain in addition to being able to near stun-lock many enemies.
But the most annoying of things in this game is the way that the game handles enemy health. The game damage system is near-identical to the SSB damage system where the more damage you have taken, the easier to be knocked out easier. The problem comes from the difference in knockout tolerance you have in comparison to the enemies. The player is generally sent flying once the damage racks up to 150 or above, whilst the non-basic enemies take up to 400 damage before they are sent flying across the map.

I'll start with the cons:
- Bugs and crashes galore, be prepared to deal with issues, more so if you're going to use Durante's Dp Fix mod (which is essential).  A great place to start is the pinned "Techinical Support Topic" in the forums if you decide to start playing this game (which is worth it, despite how this critique starts).  This is an issue that I wouldn't blame people for being really upset about but if you have the patience it'll work out fine.
- No in-game graphic settings, no AA, no resolution settings (defaults to 1280x720)... zip, nadda, nothing.  Unless you use the afore mentionned Dp fix where Durante the modder added the ability to tune various settings in the mods .ini file.
- Graphics are hit or miss, some areas in the game will leave you scratching your head wondering if the textures were vomited into the game as oppossed to programed.
Sort of in the middle:
- Some Controls/gameplay:  There is controller support (I use an Xbox 360 wired controller without issue, thankfully...), haven't tried the keyboard and mouse controls.  Control is serviceable, I can vouch that the default settings are actually better than the xbox 360 version of the game, you can react a little faster and aim better with this control scheme.
- Driving! Oh my...  Picture driving a giant heavy brick with wheels that are smaller bricks.  It's almost hilarious, it's a universe where turning down the street can only be done in small calculated increments. Miss a turn in one the games side races and then marvel at the excrutiatingly slow reverse function complete with the back up sounds of a forklift and the engine power of a small lawn mower.
Finally the pros!
- The story is fascinating, the characters are eccentric and a joy to interact with. The main character is absolutely fantastic!!  He's funny, smart and a bit smarmy, it's a lot of fun to watch him rattle the towns folk.  The voice acting is pretty good as far as I'm concerned and each character exudes uniqueness, personality or eccentricity.  There are some pretty laugh out loud moments too!  Also helps that I'm a Twin Peaks fan as the game makes no bones about taking direct influence from that material.

- Albeit the graphics are a bit dated, there are areas that have really good art style: like the interiours; the diner looks really cool and each house you can enter has  distinct personality and depth.
- It's an open world, you are given plenty of time between points in the main story line to explore the town.  Nice details peppered all over the place and collectables to grab.  Lots of side quests that aren't too taxing and also some that add some extra context to the main mystery at hand.   Every interactable character seems to have differenct routines, so you won't always find characters in the same place.  For example: you can observe from the windows on the outside of some homes that have characters in them, one time I observed Emily the police officer, it was about 10pm game time, wearing a blue dress (which I've never seen her wear) and casually enjoying her living room or the time I peeked in on the Ingrams around dinner time, the whole family was there.  The twins appeared to be interacting with themselves while watching tv.  Mrs. Ingram was making dinner in the kitchen and then Keith walked in through the front door (I was there because I decided to follow him from the milk barn, not creeping, observing!!!), he went to the fridge grabbed a beer and sat next to the twins (how's the peeping Tommy... how's the peeping). I thought it was kind of neat because there was effort to make the world feel like it was living around you.
- Some really tense moments in the game, especially the moments where it turns into screen on screen, your characters perspective and the killers perspective.  Those parts are amazing!
I originally played and finished the game on the xbox 360 and now  i've been compelled to play it again, this time the  directors cut on the p.c.  It's a budget game but get past some of the foibles and  you have a very unique and memorable game!

This game is excellent. It was fairly easy to learn.  I like the look of the units, tanks troops etc.  It has a lot of replayability. Different world powers face different difficulties.  For instance Germany should store up plenty of oil or research how to make it out of coal before alienating the entire world and having no trade partners.  China produces tons of food so they are either a good ally or someone to invade.  A lot of people have commented about no problem going into debt but there is a  penalty that will eventually wear you down if you get to far in debt. The good news is it's not overly difficult so you can enjoy the war.  I mentioned lots of replayability. I found I had to take out a portion of the US first and then make peace so the land I had conquered would produce at full capacity. There is also a way to play as one of ,i think five, imaginary countries where you grab as much unoccupied terrirtory as you can while building up to take out the other powers.  I've had a lot of fun with this game at less than a penny an hour so far.  I haven't played in awhile but will return to it.  It's that good once you get the hang of it and play as different world powers.

Ok, so you have to spend time and money to be formidable in this game.  I'm Free to Play right now while checking it out and I'm already getting my butt handed to me by players who have spent money to upgrade their weapons.  I can't tell you how often I'm fragged by someone halfway across the map simply because their weapon is that powerful.  The only kills I've managed to achieve (which are very few) are close to mid-range (and even mid-range is a longshot).  Weapon customization looks awesome and there seems to be a lot of choices, which is great, but am I willing to pour so much money into getting those upgrades?  Basically, it's a P2W game and calls out to those with the deepest pockets.
Character animations are SAAWEET!  Controls are tight, very responsive and easily executed; and when you jump...you jump, easily accessing areas of the maps with ease; and none of that crouch jumping BS that I can see so far.
All in all, the game feels more like a casual arena shooter to me; one which you would log into just to pass some time and not really get competitive with (unless you're willing to spend a lot of money).  And speaking of log in, probably one thing I really hate the most is logging in to a match.  You have to sit for a set period of time while the timer counts down before it's actually time to play a match.  You can fiddle around with your loadouts and access the menus while you wait, but I'm kind of used to games like TF2 where you can just jump in a game already in progress, no waiting.  I know a lot of games are like that when it comes to matchmaking, but it's just my pet peeve.
Loadout - You'll either like it, love it or simply enjoy it.  You will have fun playing it, but that fun may be short lived unless you go Minecraft all down in those pockets.

Bear in mind I played the older Resident Evil games more than the newer ones, so my experience with the game might be different from someone who started with 5.
This game is kind of strange as far as Resident Evil is concerned. It's got some decent scares not unlike the original games, as well as a really interesting setting for half of the game that FEELS like a genuine horror experience, but it also has the third-person behind-the-back camera of the later games as well as some segments that are heavily action-focused. As far as the action is concerned, it's fine, but the way the game switches from standard horror that seems like a shout-out to previous games and heavy action set pieces is kind of jarring.
I feel like half the team working on the project wanted to make a game closer to the older Resi games, while the other half of the team, or corporate, or someone thought they should focus more on the action-oriented later games since they sold well, and as a result the game is a little messy. Is it fun? Yes. Was I into it? Yes.
Did I care about the story? Well....half of it.
Just don't pay full price for it.
