Quick review: Hearts of Iron - Space Edition
Now for the longer part.
Like all Paradox games, I really want to like this game, but it suffers from the same glitches and quirks that nearly every Paradox game shares. True to form, Paradox lures the unsuspecting gamer in with a polished trailer and the promise of a customizable gaming experience. Sounds great, no? This time, we are in space! One would think that given Paradox's knack for economic/military sims, that this would be the next best thing since MOO2. And one will find, that like most Paradox games, Stellaris comes frustratingly close to greatness but the engine and the AI steal that potential away like pitbull and a pork chop.
The good:
1) Like all Paradox games, the gamer can make as many or as few choices as he/she wishes. I particularly like the ability to group your planets into sectors and have them specialize in terms of resource production. Another interesting aspect is that some of those sectors will grow separatist movements, and if left unchecked, they will break away into a separate empire. (ouch!) So while not a particulary difficult challenge to address, it is indiciative of the little things that Paradox does so well.
2) New concepts. Space 4x games, have lacked imagination for a long long time... okay, there have been a few here and there that brought a hint of an interesting idea, but nothing mindblowing. Stellaris takes many of the things that made Paradox successful with HoI and incorporates and takes a space-4x twist.
How, you ask? Well dear reader, I'll tell you!
One of the most frustrating developments in 4x games in the last 20 years has been this concept of "star lanes". Now maybe the IFL Facebook page has some legitimate explanation for these, but frankly I don't care. Personally, I like pointing my ships in whatever direction that I choose, and going. Well, in Stellaris you can do both. Plus, for kicks, they throw in a third kind of propulsion system that, if you master it, is superb.
Also, the diplomatic options are actully very good! Whoa, a 4x/strat game where the diplomacy a) matters and b) isn't completely hosed? Paradox does such a good job of the diplomacy in this game that you can take a long-time rival/sparring partner, and turn them into a close ally. Want to form your own space-NATO, yep, you can do that, too.
3) Ship design. Who doesn't love good ship design? The user gets LOTS of options with different types of weapons, chasis, propulsion systesm, etc. One can even choose the AI behavior of the ship class. The ship design allows the user to try and find the right balance of power, firepower, and protection... same kind of choices faced by engineers designing military weapons today. The beauty of this system is in its simplicity. Paradox makes it drag and drop. However, the discussion of ship design leads me into the first....
Not So Good:
1) Ship combat... ugh. Okay, so as with HoI, Stellaris does not delve deeply into tactical combat, nor should it. However, as currently configured, the combat system essentially rewards brute strength and ignorance. If that is your playing style, then you'll be happy. If sleek tech combinations (such as phased cloaks and time-warp facilitators in MOO2) are more your style, you will be sorely disappointed. Basically, the game rewards operational and strategic manuever, which is fine, but it really diminishes the importance of your tech tree where weapons, armor, and shielding is concerned. Another review called this "doomstack vs. doomstack". He was right. Tech may be a tie breaker, but if your combat value is much smaller than your opponent's, prepare to build a new fleet.
Another frustrating feature about the fleet system how the game manages "alliance" fleets. Yes, when you form your own federation with a few of your friends, you get to pool your best technologies together and take turns commanding your alliance's fleet... it is a *really* neat idea but... Their are several problems with this feature. First, although your facilities can magically produce tech that you have not researched, you can't even gain research points from that tech to begin developing your own version of it. Second, the AI constantly overwrites your version of allied ship designs. Finally, even though you may give the fleet orders when it is under your command, expect it to do its own thing. What starts of as a unique feature of the game winds up being a nuisance do to the resource drain and the limitations on diplomatic choices.
2) AI. AI is a constant weakness with Paradox games. It is erratic at best. At worst, it simply does nothing. There were moments when I enjoyed the erratic nature of the AI. It sensed some deep strategic weakness in my empire, attacked me and wiped out my fleet. Then it stopped. I had enough time to cobble together my own diminished doomstack and force a confrontation with the enemy fleet. The tough decisions and the ensuing campaign were quite fun in the mid-game. As your empire expands, and you can swallow lesser empires with impunity, it feels like the AI almost gives up.
3) Finally, the grind. Much like this review, the game is a grind to get through. Further, it grinds your computer's processing power to a halt, and several times, the game just quits. As it progresses, the processing times on turns get longer and longer. This is a problem that I've noticed with all Paradox games, and Stellaris is no different.
So, dear reader, if you made it this far, congratulations. Take the time that it took you to read the review, and quadruple it. That is the amount of time required to process a day-turn deep into the game.
There are some great points to this game, and Paradox explores some pretty neat concepts that can help push the genre. However, Stellaris has flaws endemic to all Paradox games that cause it to fall vastly short of the galactic glory that it promises. Ultimately, I have to give it a thumbs-down.

If you have never played a "geopolitical" wargame before then this is the one you should play to introduce yourself to the genre.
It is a simplified version of Hearts of Iron 1 and maybe 2. Especially due to all nations using only a small handful of "generic" units and a very simple tech-tree. But the AI plays a much better game and MH : TCatS is much, much, MUCH less buggy than HoI1.
Big design flaw has to be the resource management. No matter what country you play your demands for all resources (metal, oil, food etc) will far outstrip your production - you will continuosly have to spend millions importing everything from friendly or neutral countries. When I'd finished playing as Italy I was 200 billion in debt! Still - this does NOT stop your game, nor absolutely cripple your country / industries. The designer also forgot to add the ability to trade in UNITS, so Britain could not buy any of the 1000's of American built destroyers like they did in real life, or lend/lease tanks etc.
All construction and research projects are very expensive and very lengthy too!
Other than this, what is there to say? It encompasses all the WW2 period and pre-WW2 conflicts from 1930 - 49. You can play ANY nation - but most are too weak for you to even be able to "move"..... even "mid-power" nations such as Italy I had a struggle with to achieve much. For a strong game in which you really can dominate the world you have to pick the USA, Great Britain, Germany or Russia..... even Japan struggles (the game's AI doesn't handle nations heavily dependant on maritime actions well).
Like most older "geopolitical" games, all GFX and SFX are very minimalist. Action freaks and lovers of GFX to make you gasp need not apply. Also seasoned "geopolitical" players might not find this one complex enough - they may consider a bit of a "kid's" strategy game.
Still, I like it, and it's cheap!

If you are really bored or new to the genre, then go ahead. It's 5 Euro.

Base industries (steel, coal, oil) in England, Germany and so on will produce 80-150 units per turn, while a good industry in any other country will produce 9 units. But again, it's 5 Euro.

Want a grand strategy game that doesnt require you to "study" for endless hours how to play it, AND is not so simplistic that it doesnt feel like a grand strategy game?
Then Making History gold is your ticket!
This game is the perfect balance between simplistic and too complicated.
You get most of the aspects of other GS game, like your economy, industrial production, resources, diplomacy, etc. Just like in other GS games, but at a much simpler, easier to learn and faster to manage level. Yes, at the cost of some flexibility of course.
About the only negative i can find for this game, is the combat system is a bit over-simplified. Here is mostly about your "attack value", all armies/units have an attack value, and battles are mostly decided on who has the highest number. I wish more weight had been put into tactics, like flanking, encirclements, type of units used, etc. But dont let this mislead you, the strategy and large scale tactics are still here, just not as detailed as i would like.
Still, its a very fun game to play. I have (and really like) Hearts of iron 4, wich is the one i go to when i want a deep, long (as in several day to finish a game long) and complex playthru of ww2, but when i want a faster paced (e.g. end ww2 in one night), not so complex but STILL deep enough game, i come back to Making history Gold.
If you are even remotely interested in Grand Strategy WWII games, dont think about it, just go buy it!
I almost forgot...
Dont make the mistake of buying Making history 2 thinking it will be a modern & better version of this one. Trust me, its NOT!.
Get this one instead.

Loadout is an insane shooter, reminiscient of popular multiplayers such as Team Fortress 2 or Borderlands. The game is effectively a multiplayer arena shooter, similar to those we are most familiar with. It offers a third person perspective, which feels disorienting at first, but soon feels perfectly natural. The game modes are nothing strictly unique, although they feel fluent and work as they should.
The main selling point for this game is its weapon customisation, which is effectively it's point of focus. There are a wide range of customisation options, allowing you to switch out barrel, stock, scope, and payload, which gives the weapon an extra kick. You can even adapt weapons to heal allies. The game will offer up four base weapons, and you can adapt them from there forwards.
Although the game to me is fanastic, it does still have it's negatives. Microtransactions lie at the center of these. You need to pay to get decent character cusomisation, extra slots for more weapons and loadouts, and other little extras which feel as though they make a big difference. Whilst I can't really argue about a game I got for free, these little extras seem to drag the game down somewhat.
Overall, it all works together; fantastic customisation, smooth gameplay, a lot of fun, though riddled with microtransactions as you would expect it to be. I still feel like I may end up putting hours into this game, and for that, it at least gets my seal of approval.

This is an awesome little game! It is a hidden little gem i picked up for $0.21. This is a puzzle platformer that is so fun because the puzzles are very satisfying to solve. At the beginning of the game i was a confused but I quickly picked up the game mechanics due to the games perfect learning curve. In other words when the game teaches a new mechanic, it starts off easy until you are familar with the mechanic, then harder till it becomes secondhand knowledge, and THEN thats when the game shows you the next new mechanic. Of course this is not to say that you will never be stumped at some parts, after all it is what makes a puzzle game a puzzle game and takes some creative thinking BUT is never anything ridiculous to solve. The main part about this game that is kept me so hooked were all the puzzles. The harder puzzles are extreamly satisfying to solve (plenty of "OHHH!!" moments) and secrets are very rewarding to find. The puzzles in this game will never become stale, thats because even though the puzzles are essentially the same, the variations and new mechanics keep it very fun, enjoyable, and interesting to play. One more thing is that great soundtrack, props to them!
PROS
-Great learning curve
-Puzzles never get boring
-New Mechanics add depth
-Puzzles are very satisfying to solve
-Puzzles are so clever (I know i've said it a bunch but I really love the puzzles!!!)
-Great price
-Secrets keep the game interesting
-Never too easy or too hard
-Awesome music to play to
CONS
-None (I can't complain as the game has everything advertised plus much more and FAR exceded my expectations)
The game is short and can not really be a con for being so, as it cost me a mere $0.21. (But the game is so awesome that I wanted more)
The reason I have more than 4 hours is because I tried to get all the "Abandoned Cores" and "Ancient Artifacts"
Bottomline : get this game while it's still on sale, but if it's not... still get it cause it's awesome.
P.S The very beginning with the old arcade shooter mini game is an awesome little "backstory" and an interesting way start off the game and if you survive long enough it will explain what the "Abandoned Cores" do and what the boss looks like (you can't defeat him!)

Allow me to tell you a little story.
On Sunday, December 25, 2016, I was browsing the Steam Winter Sale and had CrossCode appear in the recommended section. I thought it looked interesting, so I clicked on it.
That night, in the hotel we were staying at for the holidays, I downloaded the demo for the game, slowly but surely, at a blazing 500 KB/s. Once it was done, I proceeded to stay up until 2:00 AM to finish the entire 60-70 minute demo. I have never finished a game demo in my life, mind you.
That right there should tell you plenty about the game's awesomeness.
The following Tuesday, I talked my dad into buying the game for me (as I had no other way of purchasing the product). I've already invested at least 3 hours into the game, and have loved every second of it.
The game's storyline and premise are very interesting, and I wouldn't mind seeing them expanded upon in a sequel, if the devs get there.
The graphics and audio just scream Gameboy Advance era, only they're much better quality than such a console could have produced.
The characters, even though we don't know a ton about them, seem very developed and realistic for the setting. You'll see what I mean when you play it.
I think my favorite part of the entire game is the combat, though. The game has crossed all of the best RPGs into one game, in a sense, with its own spin.
This is the game I have, almost literally, dreamed of playing all my life. The only real issue now is going to be getting myself to finish Final Fantasy VII before this, as I don't want to run into issues with the game being incomplete.
Obviously, I'll be playing it again, but you know what I'm saying.
Speaking of, I'd even go so far as to say that this game gives even FF7 a run for its money, in a sense. FF7 is known as one of the best RPGs of all time, but somehow I feel that it just doesn't quite have the charm that CrossCode does.
Anyway, what the heck are you waiting for?! Screw food and other necessities...use that $20 on this instead!
I made it to the first "real" dungeon in the game, and boy oh boy, is it impressive. I've seriously been in the dungeon for 3 hours and now I'm going to bed because I don't want to stay up any later (it's almost 12:30 AM).
The dungeons appear to be like Zelda dungeons, with some almost Metroid-vania-like elements in them. It's an interesting design concept, and I'm legitimately impressed with the amount of fun I've had so far.
Nice Sonic reference, btw. And don't think I missed the Back To The Future reference or the vague Final Fantasy VII reference, either.

Straight to the point; Absolutely fantastic. 9.5/10
Great graphics, good dialogue, AWESOME talent tree(s), cool attacks, extemely diverse enemies, puns galore (ie The Goatfather), Saitama in a Santa outfit, nice soundtrack, challenging puzzles, game isn't even completed yet (review being written as of patch 0.8.5-4) and it took me about 40 hours to "complete" (have like 95% of all treasures, Encyclopedia filled out, best gear, highest level without grinding out monsters for 1 XP each), which is more than a lot of AAA games these days can boast. An encyclopedia in game that fills out as you kill monsters/destroy nodes, and will give you drop rates after you loot X amount from each specific monster/node. AN INDEX OF SHOPS SO YOU CAN LOOK AT WHERE YOU SAW A SHOP SELLING A SPECIFIC ITEM.
Trading system in game, where you don't just straight up buy a new set of armor/weapons every time you reach a new town, but you actually collect materials and trade them in for pieces. Equipment also makes you think about what you want. Increased Focus (crits) in exchange for less HP and defence? More HP and HP regen in exchange for damage and Balance (lets you use elemental attacks more, which is required against some enemies)? To go with that are huge talent trees, think Final Fantasy X, where you have Neutral and the four Elements (Fire, Cold, Shock, and Wave), which each get their own talent trees and points every time you level up, each offering different Melee, Ranged, Guard and Dash Arts, plus all the passives you'd expect like Max HP, elemental resists, Attack Power, etc.
Variation in characters is really nice, too. Your best friend is French, and her friend
is German. Your own character is a mute so-to-speak, but the different facial expressions she makes are very well done, so you're able to communicate through that. You also have the aforementioned Saitama dressed as Santa, there's a dandy on a hunt for a stylish tophat, a character who somehow is using armor from every class, the nerdy guy that needs your help with research, etc. No two characters are alike.
The Dungeons are just amazing. After having completed the four Dungeons for all of the Elements, every single one of them posed a challenge to me, and I would have to stop, take my hands off my keyboard, and think about how to solve the puzzles. They really make you think outside the box. In Fajro, there's even a puzzle that you start it by shooting a ball, then as the ball travels around the "track" of the puzzle, you have to interact with the course, moving blocks, freezing/melting water pillars, lowering barriers, to change it's path, and the puzzle is roughly the size of two screens. Absolutely loved it. Each of the four Dungeons has a specific theme to it, to match the element it is for. As an example, in the Shock dungeon, you create big balls of energy and shoot them off, maneuvering them around to get them to power up circuits. The late Dungeons also utilize the previous Dungeons elements, so it's not like you go get the Fire element first, and then never use those mechanics/methods again.
The only things that were sort of downers for me, was that equipment doesnt change the look of your sprite at all (save the santa hat, which I think looks really nice). You always look the same. Even recolors and a slight amount of detail would be kinda nice. Maybe add on some cool effects to attacks for some higher level weaponry, or effects based on what Modifiers are on your weapon/armor. Also some of the areas got very confusing because from my experience, the map does not accurately portray your position in the current map, and there are A LOT of treasures that I can't seem to get to. A lot of them require you to enter an area from the previous/next map from a vantage point. But maybe that's just because I'm stupid. I dunno. Also, some of the puzzles annoyed me, because there are pillars you have to move around, but you can only push them forward/backward, not side-to-side. Not a big deal, but just annoying. There are also some spots that are like landform bridges, but I can't tell, and I just think it's a wall, so I don't even go in that direction.
(Edit in after more gameplay; After actually going through and finding the treasures, it is definitely possible, but they can be very challenging! And in regards to the landform bridges making me think they are walls, the developers DEFINITELY did that on purpose, which I understand a lot more now. They make you consider all possibilities when trying to solve puzzles, maybe try going from this way, well how do I get there, maybe enter in through the previous area, well maybe that "wall" there isn't a wall, etc. I quite like it.)
Small sidenote; even has the cocky rival that you just love to hate, and you get to duel him. But he's kind of cheap, basically if he hits you with a melee attack, he's gonna take like 2/3 of your HP bar. Despite that, it is very possible to beat him as long as you utilize your guard and dodge mechanics, and if/when you do, it really feels good to beat him.
Basically, amazing game. One of the best that I have played in recent years. Very much looking forward to the full release.

Story: The player is a female detective commissioned to find a missing girl who disappeared in the fictitious hamlet of Maple Creek, VT (USA).  The game starts with the detective having temporary short-term memory loss and as she retraces her steps in her investigation she recovers her memories of the previous events.  Her investigation becomes a suspenseful murder mystery that borders on horror with supernatural elements.
Disclaimer:  I really do not like horror of any kind and this for me borders on it.  Seriously, I gasped out loud and quite literally nearly jumped out of my chair at the major jump scare and that alone set me on edge for the rest of the game.  And I was extremely glad I was playing during the day.
Gameplay: Engaging and suspenseful as the detective retraces her already completed investigation (she does not remember yet) and tries to find the missing girl.  Now if one takes into account that in a real investigation there is a lot of back and forth movement, retracing of steps, and re-visiting of locations then one should not get too annoyed the game does the same thing.  As new evidence is revealed, locations are re-visited.  Unfortunately this game lacks a fast travel map. As the investigation unfolds from a missing person case it becomes a mystery, a very dark and sinister one.
One of the most unique elements of the game is the "evidence wall".  As clues/evidence are collected (and recollected) it is put on the "evidence wall" (which can be accessed at any time from the main play screen).  Between the notebook and "evidence wall" the player gets the "feel" of a "real" investigation.  As the investigation continues the player gets involved in a murder mystery.  (Too many spoilers if I say more.)  I highly recommend reading the notebook, too, so much information in such a little space.
Since this is a Hidden Object game all I have to say about the HO finds is: "jerks".  There are three types of "jerk" find objects by my definition.
1) One is an find clue that can be many things.  For example: Bow.  Bow on a gift package, bow in the hair, more obcure bow tie, bow as in bow and arrow, or the bow of a boat.  The Ravenhearst HO games by Big Fish Games (found on steam) are full of those.
2) The second "jerk" object is one so hard to find, so well hidden, it is nearly impossible to find. This game is full of those.  Even though every hidden object scene is played three times each time with different objects (and fortunately the last group is not re-added) there is at least one object that makes me, at least, say, "jerks".  (After over a 100 HO games I had to consult a guide to find some.)  An example is the clue: crumbled paper.  Generally that brings to mind a wadded up ball of paper, in one particular scene, it was a wrinkled up flat sheet of paper fit nicely against the light colored floor with the edges covered up.  "Jerks"
3) The third type of "jerk" find object is also in this game.  Though not as prevalent as the second type.  The third "jerk" object is a deliberate mislead.  For example calling a top hat a cylinder, or a horse saddle a seat.  Yes, a top hat is a cylinder, as a saddle is a seat, but cylinder and seat is not what comes to mind first or even tenth.  "Jerks"
However, once the player realizes "they" are doing that, one adjusts and moves on.  At least I do.
One of the things I was amazed about was the actual length of the game.  It is quite long.  It plays as a quite logical progression of an investigation.  Everything is ordered, and as new evidence is pieced together the player wants to revisit a location to look for more clues or evidence.  I am fairly sure the game also does not reveal future evidence/clues/needed objects until the necessary prerequisites are meet, keeping the game fresh, and the player engaged.
Overall a great game to play, despite "them" being "jerks" in find objects arena.  It is a long, involved, slightly convoluted missing person case turning into a murder mystery.  OH YES cannot forget the "to be continued" tag at the end.
Just a note of trivia:  Yes, Vermont does look like that (I live in Massachusetts) especially in the autumn and hoardes of people drive along designated scenic roads or hike through the mountains just to admire the turning and turned leaves. (It is even possible to drive through sleepy little towns like Maple Creek, some that even claim to be haunted.)  Yes, those are real mountain names too in the Appalachain Mountians.  The information given about the wildlife is even accurate.  I was quite surprised by all that actually since many games call moths butterflies or vice versa.

The game is not for everyone. You will need incredible patience and strategy to even sit still long enough for this game. Now, past the patience and strategy, you need to be able to think quite a few steps ahead. Personally I love grand strategy games like this but unlike this, they tend to have better balance between supply and demand equality across the entirety of the game. However, this is not the case here. Only few, and I mean
, countries can really balance this and keep their economy and trade up. Otherwise, you end up requesting more than offering as well as delve into debt pretty quickly. Thus, you end up being forced to play one of the preset countries instead of the other ones that are available. This forces pretty repetitive gameplay if you play through the entirety of the singleplayer 'campaigns'.
While I enjoyed my short time with the game, I have to be honest with my review. While I truly enjoy grand strategy, I found the supply and demand system on the international market rather ridiculous. Either countries will rise their imports tremendously and cause you to lose instead of producing surplus or suddenly lose all interest in your trade and cause you to lose money. Either way, you end up losing in one part and gaining on the other. While others may see this as realistic, I would rather have it be a bit more balanced. I mean, seriously, only the preset countries for scenarios and maybe two or three other countries can properly hold their supply and demand good enough to sustain their economy and their own surpluses. Past that, this is one of the easiest and simplest grand strategy games out on the market that I've played.
Despite its simplicity, I would only recommend this to those truly interested in grand strategy games. Those that want a game to waste time or to just occasionally play, I would not recommend this. On that note I don't recommend this to those with short amounts of patience, lacking good strategy or forethought, as well as all around time. A game like this requires time to play and really enjoy. However, to those that have played or enjoyed grand strategy or wish to really get into it, I truly recommend this game. It's easy to pick up and even easier to master (if you ignore the supply and demand system as well as the apparently higher tech nations you initially have to go to war with sometimes-even on the easiest difficulty) That said, I wouldn't recommend this to the general public that has no real interest in grand strategy but I wholeheartedly recommend this to the grand strategists out there looking for an easy game to pick up.

Sooo... This game is from Resident Evil series, but it's less of a survival horror, filled with puzzles and secrets and more of a shoot-the-zombies kind of game. I won't tell you about the story, since there will be spoilers and some reviews already covered that part of the game. I will tell you my impressions instead.
-The first thing I noticed is awkward movement of the main character. It does not go smoothly, but I suppose it's because the game is designed to be played on a console on some sort with a joystick.
-Cheap scares. Like, moviement in the ducts, an unexpected corpse falling from nowhere with scary music on the background. Or you are all like "It's a zombie" and nope, those are rats... Stuff like that, to keep you tense on the transition of the story... In theory. This one is an old formula from scary movies and games.
-The game itself is pretty much has been made to connect the dots between the story lines of previos and next game. It's made to fill the gap holes in the main story of the Resident Evil games. So, if you are more interested in action game and you want to know a little bit more about the Series and why the ♥♥♥♥ zombies suddently become parasitic worms, infrecting the host and such... This game is made to supposingly explain it to you.
-The characters are looking a little bit weird. But maybe it's just me.
-Also, you get to scan stuff. Which would be allright as an optional game dinamic, but it's mandatory one and sometimes the game become a sort of "Scan them all" kind of game. Which is exactly as fun as it sounds.
-The inventory is weird, different from the previous games. So, you just go there... Scan some♥♥♥♥♥♥ kill some bad guys, look for ammo, medkits and grenades... Which is okay for shooter game but kind of dissapoining for resident evil series.
-There aren't much puzzles, it's more like the 4th and 5th RE, but here it's more of a "Go and find the item X to activate thing Y". So... Yeah. That sucks too.
-The game itself is pretty short and it feels more like a series of short interactive movies, rather than a RE game.
So, in short. If you are interested for a Resident Evil series main story, you should get this game. But it's pretty much just that. A series of short episodes made to close some story gaps and connect the games between themselves. So... Yeah. It's not entirelly bad, but it's not a big deal.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel felt kind of like some sort of expansion pack for Borderlands 2. The HUD and UI remains the same, and it keeps some weapons (for example, Nukem). Obviously, though, that's not the case, since it has its own full story line and set of characters.
I liked it.
The UI staying the same gives you a sense of familiarity, which is good for Borderlands veterans, and also welcoming for new players.
The Oz kit is a mixed bag for me. As soon as you go through the intro, you're thrown onto Elpis--without an oz kit, and so, without oxygen. This is perfectly okay, since you get an Oz Kit later on. The only problem is the O2 bar itself.
If you play any character other than Claptrap, your O2 rapidly depletes. If you run out of oxygen, you lose the ability to boost, and also slowly lose health. This on its own is perfectly fine, but throwing something like this early on in the game is not really that good an idea, especially if someone is just starting on the Pre-Sequel. That just adds a whole new level of difficulty, which might cause new players to struggle. This is somewhat excusable, considering you can learn stuff pretty fast, but I just feel like the O2 should deplete slower.
The characters are different, since this is on Elpis. Marcus still sells ammo and guns, but Scooter and Dr. Zed are replaced by Janey Springs and Nurse Nina, respectively. People say it's not the same without the original ones, but I've never had a problem with it. I welcome the addition of new characters, so long as it's not an army of them.
The lasers are AMAZING. There are a few different types of lasers. I only know a few,, which are beams, blasters, railguns, and projectile(?) lasers. They all go in the same weapon category (Laser), but can be identified by their names.
Beams contantly shoot a straight laser until you let go of the trigger, blasters are laser AR's, railguns are snipers, and projectiles are projectiles. Lasers have actually become my favorite type of weapon now.
The Pre-Sequel also came up with a new weapon rarity, the Glitch rarity, which I thought was pretty cool. If you don't know what it is, I won't spoil it for you.
Overall, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is a pretty good game and I'd recommend getting it while it's on sale, due to its large price.

I'm not the sort to prejudice games over things like their being hidden object puzzlers; and the Artifex Mundi games are by far the best examples of the genre. Nonetheless A.M. has followed the method of if it isn't broke don't fix it, meaning they reuse their puzzles with cosmetic variations from one game to another. This has the unfortunate result that if you've played one of their games you've played them all.
That's O.K. if you think of the games as more visual novels with bonus puzzle content. Granted the writing isn't amazing; but it isn't bad either. I know I've yet to play an A.M. game I could make myself stop playing before the end. That's, on average, over 3 hours in one sitting. And, most of their games include a bonus chapter that extends gameplay another hour.
They do manage to do this without unnecessarily padding game length that overstays its welcome. I know that doesn't sound like much in an industry with triple AAA titles that boast hundred of hours of gameplay. But, for cheap casual games this is an achievement.
My recommendation, because of the "if you've played one you've played them all" problem, is pare your selections down to their better games. That would be Enigmatis 2 (but not the mediocre Enigmatis: the Ghosts of Maple Creek) as a top pick, Grim Legends 1 & 2 if you liked that, and the Nightmares from the Deep trilogy if you just can't get enough of these games.

The story is far fetched and generic. The “solving the mystery” part is so implausible all you do is discover things and make wildly outrageous assumptions to find the killer. This just kills the game for me, I can't get over the writing. I know I have slightly high standards (from playing visual novels which are about the story) for writing and that's not the point of this game but when the story is so bad and cliché that it actually takes away from the game you have a problem.
The puzzles are fine but nothing terribly hard and far too much running around IMO. Maybe one day II will find a truly hard HOG but I'm not expecting that any time soon.

Not as refined as some Artifex Mundi titles.  It has some bugs for sure, but they are minor.  The main one that CAN throw you is if you use the in-game tutorial.  One of your tools is an evidence screen which is introduced at the beginning of the game.  There is a LARGE magnifying glass at the bottom of the evidence screen (not to be confused with the cursor magnifying glass icon).  The tutorial instructs you to pick it up and use it to examine your evidence more closey.  While you can pick it up, it doesn't do what the tutorial says it should do; therefore, you cannot advance any further in tutorial mode.  So, don't opt for the tutorial instructions when offered at the start.  You CAN examine your collected evidence closer just by simply clicking on the evidence without using the large magnifying glass at the bottom of the evidence screen.  That said, you can complete the game and bonus chapter.  All Steam Achievements worked as of July 26, 2015.  The bonus chapter had a missing description when hovering over an item in one scene (a long number appeared instead).  Some of the object names in the bonus chapter are not what most would think of when describing some of the objects in some hidden object scenes.  The bonus chapter just doesn't have the same quality as the main story.  The whole story (main and bonus) isn't a "page turner"; however, the background music, art, hidden object scenes, and puzzles are typical of other Artifex Mundi titles.  Overall, if you enjoy Artifex Mundi games, you will probably enjoy this one once you get going.

I bought God of Word in the CAPSLOCKDAY bundle. Of the five games available, God of Word looked the most appealing on the surface. When I started playing it, I wasn't disappointed with what the game had to offer.
In God of Word, the player controls a warrior battling through various monsters and beasts based on Greek mythology. In order to slay each creature, the player has to spell out words with the tiles the game provides. The tiles can be traded in for a cost, but for most creatures, trading isn't necessary. Tiles can be selected with the keyboard or the mouse.
Pros:
- Controls are easy.
- Game is easy to look at and read.
- Goals are clearly explained.
- Bosses are challenging but not impossible.
- Many levels to play through.
- Words already spelled are displayed onscreen.
- Unlockable items add to the game and look good.
- Some achievements feel like they have to be earned, but they're not unbearable to get.
Cons:
- Little replayability after the story is over.
- One or two achievements may feel like a chore.
- Can get repetitive.
- Story route is not a straight line. Map has shoot-offs that the character may skip over if left to his own devices.
- Everything has timers.
People looking for a fun word game with good achievements will find a fun challenge here. Others looking for a great word game will likely have a good time with God of Word.

I haven't played any other making history games.  I got this game, because I was looking for a 4x game based in WW2.
Initial Impression:
I would say this is a fairly complex game, offering a variety of mechanics that can be worked in different ways.  There are resources, economy/industry building, trade, military supply management, ,research, and combined arms tactics (infantry, tanks, planes, etc) - maybe I'm missing a couple...
Gameplay:
I've played as the UK, Germay, and France thus far; and I've played about ten games at various easy and hard type settings.  If I had to describe the gameplay in a few short phrases I would say:
-It feels like a race to assemble the best industry and militry possible before world war breaks out
-resouce and supply management is very key, more so late game where your ability to fight can degrade
-managing both the industrial and military side can either be very precise or very forgiving depending on difficulty
All in all, I would say that I have never felt the need to micro manage too much. Instead, I found my self skipping 5-10 or more turns in a row, until I accomplished a goal, and then tweaked my industry before skipping a few more turns.
Military engagements are more complex and can happen very quickly if you are not micro'ing your units.  I ended up having to give a lot of thought on what units I attacked with and what units I used to defend my territory, in order to avoid stranding a unit or pushing my military beyond what my economy could support.  Of course, this varied with difficulty and nation played, since resource/industry matters quite a bit.
I found research in the game to be important, but not the deciding factor.  The country that does the best, will also have managed resources efficiently and conservately pushed it's armies to conquer the enemy.  Consequently, it is very important to find ways to undermine your opponents' strengths, often by attacking their ability to collect resources.
Multiplayer/Singleplayer:
There is a multiplayer mode, which I haven't tried.  And, I will say that against an AI opponent, I was able to abuse certain patterns to win at times.  For example, as Germany, I started out with a very weak navy and did not build one large enough to defeat the Allied navies at sea.  Instead, I was able to use bombers to destroy most of their ships in large packs, since bombers to dont return until all the units in a given tile are dead.  The AI kept replenishing the units, but in the end I was killing them faster.   A real person would most likely find ways to reposition their navies until they were ready to perform an attack.
Other Thoughts:
I've heard some compare this game to Axis&Allies, and I wouldn't say I disagree - mainly because this game feels a lot like a board game.  It's definitley more detailed than Risk.
The graphics are fairly bland, and there aren't action sequences.  I havne't checked into modding, but on it's own the game is pretty fun. In short, a good distraction from more intense games - it definitely is a beer in one hand video game.
I would say that you should be careful running it on low-end machines, because in general it does seem to use up resources.  I played one game to 1000 turns and the game was just chugging away with noticeable lag.  In general, you should find that it runs well on most systems.  I had no issues with erros or crashing, so it seems like a stable game.
TL;DR  If you like the idea of an imperialist style 4x game set in the action pack time of WW2, and are looking for something more like a board game rather than a Total War, then this game is for you.

Recommended for people who really like tower defense games. If you "kind of" like tower defense, you should probably just play the flash version, and you'll get bored before you hit the point where you would need to pay. If the prospect of >100 slightly varying tower defense maps appeals to you, and more so when I tell you you can go past 100 waves of monsters on each, and then more when I tell you about all the difficulty dials you can fine tune, then this is a good tower defense game to spend 100+ hours on.
I particularly recommend GemCraft for the highly customizable difficulty. Over the course of the game, you unlock nine different difficulty dials, like "more and stronger giants" or "send mana every minute instead of as I accummulate it", and three difficulty settings; plus you can increase the difficulty of a wave by calling it sooner or "enraging" it by dropping gems on it, spending your mana to make the waves tougher and increasing the number of monsters; plus achievements for level-specific handicaps like "only use slowing gems"; plus an "Iron Wizard" mode that takes away your ability to out-level the difficulty curve. Just beating the levels is not all that difficult, apart from scattered puzzle levels. GemCraft excels in letting you make the game as hard as you want it to be, and it rewards you for pushing yourself to the bleeding edge of how difficult you can make it. And with those rewards, you can play the level again, with difficulty turned up just a little higher... (Avoid grinding: your xp is your highest score for the level, so there is no gain for repeating a level without turning up the difficulty.)

Megabyte Punch was not even on my radar, but it's right up my alley. I received an email for a free Steam code from
via a
promotion, and I figured, why not? Free is good. But in this case, free is good, and the game that you get with it is even better.
Probably the easiest way to describe Megabyte Punch is to draw parallels to the Super Smash Bros. series of games. You're a robot beating up on other robots, raising their damage levels with each attack and combo landed, and eventually you send them flying into the environment to explode and leave behind either Bytes (the game's currency) or parts (which can be equipped to grant stat boosts and special abilities). The controls and game play are very responsive, and you'll have no trouble traversing the colorful and non-linear levels, pummeling other robots and finding hidden Byte and part caches all around. On top of it all, the game seems to have a pretty bizarre sense of humor, which is always a plus, so I intend to spend quite a bit of time with it and see where it takes me.
With quite a bit to unlock and find (there are 150 unique parts to discover), this is a highly recommended game if you're a platformer fan or a fan of Smash Bros.-esque mechanics.

This game is really fun, like an updated Vectorman with Smash Bros-esque boss fights, stylized with some Custom Robo or Virtual On. Definitely worth checking out.
However, a few personal cons:
-Salvaging multiples of the same part is mildly annoying since you can only break one at a time, and every time you do so (per item), it backs you out of the Break Parts submenu, forcing you to navigate back to the item again to salvage another.
-The Break Parts mechanic should really just be a button press within the Inventory submenu. It gets really tedious going back to the Inventory to see a part's stats and features before you consider breaking it down more bits. If the reason they did this was for difficulty (Inventory menu isn't paused), then I guess I understand, but geeze does it get really tedious with all that back and forth navigation through menus just to break a half dozen common parts.
-AI difficulty is kind of wonky. Basically, the overwhelming majority of the baddies you crush are absolute cakewalks, leaving you ill-prepared for the radically tougher boss fights (second boss absolutely annihilated me). I'd love to see the difficulty get a little more balanced
All in all, I'd give it an 8/10 so far (for what I expected). It's a great call back to the Megaman and Vectorman era, and launching baddies into nearby walls is incredibly satisfying. I don't know if I would pay full price for this without having first played it, as it didn't really wow me until I I actually gave it a go.
If the devs make a sequel, I hope they fix the tedious menu design.

If you are in for a good-old school resident evil experience you are in for a disappointment. While many people talk about RE going back to its roots with the revelation series the honest truth for RE veterans is that Capcom is very far from it. For me RE last root installment was Code Veronica everything afterward is closer to being a shooter than a survival horror.
Let me start with what I look for when talking about "root RE experience":
- Teasing, mysterious, cold, intriguing and uneasy atmosphere and level design
- Limited resources that forces you to strive for any items/ammunition you can find and think once, twice and five times before firing a bullet
- Narrative driven enemies that you are both annoy and scare the S#$t out of you and yet compel you to respect their presence
- Music that defines the installment and propels the atmosphere and level design.
- Puzzles, locked doors, some positive back tracking to find out what's behind that door or corridor that you couldn't explore before
Now back to Revelations. Apart from the "Resident Evil" title and the presence of known characters from the franchise it has non of the elements that defines a root RE experience for me.
- The game is basically a shooter. The main value of the game if running around shooting creatures.
- Narrative is laughable and reminds me of RE arcade shooters. I think resident evil survivor has a storyline way better then this game. You can barely relate to any event or character in here
- Atmosphere and nostalgia is a thing of the past. Here you will be going through various shooting galleries where you walk in shoot a bunch of enemies and scan stuff and move on to the next gallery

So, let's get this straight: this is a TERRIBLE game. But I love it so much. Now to explain why I feel this way.
Deadly Premonition follows the story of a quirky FBI detective, Francis York Morgan (just call him York), as he and his imaginary friend Zach solve the mystery behind the murder of a young women, Anna Graham, in the fictional town of Greenvale, Washington. It's a classic "who dun it", story, which slowly melts more and more into the bizzare, and stange as you get further along into the game. It should be said, that this game clearly takes HEAVY inspiration from the 90s TV series Twin Peaks, which follows a similar story of a detective unravelling the murder of a young women, which also slowly gets more and more surreal as the series gets further along in it's story.
The gameplay, and graphics are by far where most concerns arise regarding the game, with shoddy aiming, terrible driving while you drive around the town doing either the main quest, or the various other sidequests,
bad textures, some character models look like ones you'd see in PS2 games, bad framerate, etc. Some gameplay decisions made in this game can be extremely baffling in how poorly designed they are. These are by far the games weakest aspect, and are honestly sometimes a hassle to play through. But, however I believe the game makes up for what it lacks in its characters, and overall quirkiness.
I cannot tell you how many times I smiled, or gave a chuckle to the characters interacting with each other, I won't spoil any of these moments, as you should most definately experiance for themselves, but I can say that if the game hits any nail on the head, it is most definately in this aspect. Some may find some distaste in the campy/cheesy/sometimes downright TERRIBLE diolouge in this game, but I personally loved it, and I found myself getting excited when I was playing through the game, and a cutscene would appear, because it meant I would get a chuckle or two out of it. Something should also be said about the soundtrack, as it fits the surreal, quirky atmosphere of the game perectly. The game is also quite lengthy, with various sidequests you can do, in addition to the main story.
Now, many people wouldn't find this justification to buy this game, that the gameplay and graphics completely ruin the experiance, but I would seriously disagree. It seems to me that this game had a lot of love, and effort put behind it, but the game developers skills just didn't match up to what they were hoping would turn out. As I said, some may not like this game, some may even hate this game, but to those who want a different experiance, something that is out of norm, and completely changes the way you would normally think about games, I'd say give this game a go. I've bought this game three times already, on the Xbox 360, PS3, and of course PC, and I haven't regretting buying a single copy. This game will give you a unforgetable ride, which must be played to be believed.  In my opinion, this is without a doubt, the best worst game I have ever played. AND I LOVED EVERY MINUTE OF IT.

If you enjoy deep, detailed strategy games, you should go ahead and try this one. Note: This review is based on the game as played with the Utopia DLC.
Good:
There is a lot of breadth and depth to this game.
Players get a lot of choices about a lot of things, and there are a lot of player actions that can lead toward a goal.
The game designers have built a big universe with plenty of room for content expansion.
Existing content is decent. Music and art are good. Quests are satisfying. There is a true sense of mystery when you play this game without spoilers.
Like all Paradox games, Stellaris employs a relatively deep system of asymmetrical diplomacy. Becoming a vassal or overlord empire are definitely on the table here.
There are three separate research point resources for three distinct disciplines of technology.
One of the coolest features of this game is the ability to genetically engineer entire species.
Ironman mode puts the pressure on.
Mixed:
The level of detail and balance is satisfying, but some aspects of the game can feel a little like micro-managing or balancing a budget.
The combat system gives the player some control over when and where to engage an enemy, but other than that, there are no battle tactics. Biggest stack of firepower wins.
The pausable real time system has its merits, but turn-based is my preference. Sometimes there is a bit too much happening--or not happening.
Lots of angry reviewers speak of the DLC profit strategy. But the prices seem fair to me, especially if you get it on sale.
The unity points system (Utopia DLC) feels a little tacked-on, because it is. The traditions and ascendency perks are basically a poor man’s version of how social policies worked in Civ V.
Bad:
This game is a tremendous time-suck. It can make you a bad person.
The pace of the game slows down in the late game. A single game can drag on and on.
The user interface is astonishingly clunky and unhelpful in certain tasks.
Planetside development (placing buildings on a grid) and ground combat (landing troops and waiting for battle to conclude) are boring and uninspired.
The player gets zero control over what skills a leader acquires as they level up. This will probably change in a future DLC.

It's been over a year since the game's launch.
It still does not have the midgame as a concept. It still does not have a meaningful endgame - declarations of war on cooldown over and over until you win is not meaningful. Megastructures are irrelevant - you'll realistically win the game before you could build and reach ROI on a single structure. Fleet composition, weapon technologies, and ship designer are irrelevant: you are punished by the system if you try to have any kind of ship diversity or upgrade the ships. Space warfare is reduced to a single battle of doom stacks that decides the entire war. Land warfare exists only as a concept, not a system. AI is essentially non-existant, both enemy empires and your own sector one; it can't even recognize endgame crises. Diplomacy is non-existant. The dev team does not know what "playtesting" means, pushing major updates without any QA whatsoever. Numerous bugs that persist through patches, with more bugs added with each update. Anti-consumer DLC and pricing policies by the publisher.
What this game does well is the thrill of exploration, all the events and writing are really nice (if you care about lore). The early game is pretty much the only strong side of Stellaris. You could extract some fun by playing multiplayer with a curated group of role-players, but that's it.

Simply love this game. For being in early access I'm impressed by the quality that the developers have brought to this game. The art, the characters, the gameplay are all fantastic. I love checking and seeing what the developers are working on and just knowing that it will be amazing.

As of the current moment, Crosscode is definitely a game to keep an eye on, if not purchase immediately. While Early Access is definitely a giant red flag to most steam users (and for honestly good reason), I believe that this game is fairly trustworthy. The devs are quite transparent, with each of their updates noting issues yet to be fixed, delays in release dates, and what's going on in general. There is also livestreams which I have yet to check out, which likely go into much more detail of upcomng content.
Pros
-Fluid gameplay and combat
While it definitely takes a bit of getting used to in the beginning, within a few hours I was dashing all over the place firing shots and using specials with ease. On keyboard the game is quite easy to use, haven't used any other medians as of the moment though. The management of special attacks and dodging and using weak spots creates a very hectic and high pressure atmosphere, while still being very fun.
-Story and Dialogue
The story is, as of now, unfinished. However, what is here is still a fairly hefty amount and has been good so far. The main character, Lea, is unable to speak except for certain phrases (largely consisting of "Hi!" "Bye!" and "Lea!" for a good bit early on). Upon hearing finding this, I assumed dialogues would mainly be between other characters with her sitting on the side listening, but she does seem to input quit often through the use of "..." "...!" or "...?" and a facial expression. The facial expressions are quite good, often relaying her inputs quite well alone. You do gain a few more words as time goes on, and I assume the story will continue adding more as it progresses.
The dialogue itself between characters or NPCs often poke fun at other MMOs or make somewhat referential humor. I wouldn't necessarily call it subtle, but it definitely isn't blatant enough to seem like it was fishing for laughs. The dialogue seems rather real between the team characters you get and also between the players NPCs.* I often pause to read the dialogue because it is entertaining, although because it is chat bubbles above their head you can continue running by while reading. As a quick example, the boss of the demo can be found in the bestiary under "Behemoth Hostile Crab" I believe.
*To help clarify things a bit, there are sort of multiple levels of NPCs to explain. As you run around, there are NPCs that are NPCs. These are people running shops and giving quests like those in an MMO. Next, there are player NPCs. They are NPCs running around in game as if they were players playing the MMO. They often use more aware terms (patches, updates, raids, etc.) when chilling at 'player' hubs, and can be seen running around in the fields as you are fighting monsters. On a side note, when lost it can be beneficial to follow the player NPCs because they run between areas and can lead you to exits if you get lost. Lastly, there are party member or story character NPCs. These NPCs are much more present and converse much more with you, the rest you can find out. As strange as it is, being aware that certain characters are NPCs along with the other characters actually helps build immersion, since they think a person welcoming you to town with the same line 800 times is as stupid as you do.
-Tutorializing
I think this game does tutorials fairly well. It is somewhat hands on in the beginning when it initially teaches you all your moves, but it gives you a lot more freedom as you enter the full game. Even early on it is more of telling you and letting you experiment compared to making you watch it over and over. After leaving the initial zone, about when the demo ends,s all questions and tutorializing is basically optional from then on.
-Difficulty (Bosses)
I personally think it does a very good job of creating a rewarding difficulty. When I fight the bosses of the game, it is often very hectic and challanging, and contains a few deaths while doing so. However, when I do die, I generally retry with more knowledge of the bosses patterns and what to avoid or take advantage of. Instead of feeling like I'm playing a very biased game of russian roulette, I actually do see myself progressing each time I fight a boss, and not because of stats. Also death puts you directly at the beginning of the room when you die, so failure doesn't stop you from diving right back into the action.
-Difficulty (General Battles)
The game seems to prefer actual fights compared to grinding, so any enemies you fight in the field that are worth their time in EXP will put up a fight. I find this enjoyable, as new areas aren't bogged down with annoyances but instead full of actual danger even without a boss. Plus, when high enough level and traveling through fields they often don't bother you if they wouldn't be worth your time.
-Difficulty (Dungeons)
I'm just going to say I love the dungeons. They are often large maps with multiple rooms filled with puzzles, enemies, or both at once. However, the pacing is often done quite well on them. Instead of telling you what everything in a room does, it will often give it to you in a puzzle room first. You get to spend time playing around, finding out what your abilities do to whatever object is given to you. Next, it often gives you some enemies that are affected by whatever you just learned, so you can try it out on them. Later, it mixes the two by including one of the puzzle objects that can be used to inflict bonus damage on the enemy or open up breaks for massive damage. Later, the boss combos this by making you use the mechanics you learned by using the puzzle objects on the enemies to open up the weak spots on the boss and attack it. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the dungeons I've played.
-Cons
Yes, even though I love this game a lot, it still has some issues.
-Lack of Story (Likely to be fixed)
At the current moment, the story is rather unfinished and cliffhangery, and leaves a good bit to be desired. This is definitely on the list to be added obviously, but this is just a warning as of now. I personally think this is a solid dev team that will add more, but you never know.
-Lack of PvP (Likely to be fixed)
There is one point in the game where you have a battle against another 'Player' in game, and it is 5 out of 9 battle of hectic, chaotic fun. When I played through it I was basically sweating by the end of it through the careful spacing, dodging, and use of specials. But there is the issue. As of my knowledge, this only appears one time early game and it doesn't happen again for the rest of it. Again, I believe this will likely be added in the future, but just in case this game doesn't get updated anymore (which, again, I highly doubt) I'll leave it here for now.
-Bugs/Glitches (Might be fixed?)
This is almost a pro based on how few I ran into, but I did have one issue that recurred a few times. At random points (I run the game full screen) it would basically freeze the frame onto the screen and reformat it to roughly windowed size, and only update that corner, which left about 40% of my screen a frozen frame. Even after it resized it, the mouse acted like it was still in full screen so the center of what I saw wasn't what the center was to me. I posted this issue to the forums and got a response within a day or two (yay) that said it was fairly hard to replicate so may be difficult to patch (boo). This wasn't common, but it didn't recur enough to make the game unplayable. So while it may be a bit to get this issue fixed, possibly even never, it was nice to get a dev response quickly and it isn't enough to deter me from the game.
TL:DR Good combat, good story (albeit unfinished), good dialogue, good controls, good devs, good fun. Try the demo if you are unsure, but it should be noted that while the core gameplay remains the same, you get some additional abilities and the difficulty ramps up over time. (Also I should stop trying to write reviews after midnight)

GemCraft - Chasing Shadows is arguably THE tower defense game to play. Well-balanced with fair challenges.
GemCraft is my favorite Tower Defense series because of how involved the player must get to succeed in progressing through the games. GC-CS is particularly involved, adding more content to test the player's ability to devise level strategy. The story is well-integrated into game mechanics. The skill tree is balanced. The level difficulty scales well.
Some characteristics worth noting:
-GC naturally discourages grinding because only the best performance on each level is counted towards XP. About midway through the game it becomes possible to farm XP, but a lot of strategizing has to be done before that.
-Unlike many other TDs, structures are not limited to set positions on the level, leaving more options for the player.
-The concept of combining gems (defenders) for combinations of abilities gives even more options for strategy.
To developer: Please release the rest of GC on Steam eventually. Gotta have it all together.

On its face it's probably one of the best tower defense games out there. But there's a point in the game where you go from having nothing to having everything (and beyond) and the challenge fades away.
Once you "get" how to really play this game, it becomes very repetitive and unchallenging. Certain gem combinations mean easy access to literally billions of EXP. I played this game from level 1 to 130 without using these especially deadly/plentiful gem combos, but as soon as I found them, I went from level 130 to 2200 in a matter of days playing pretty casually (I left the game open, so my hours plays doesn't really mean anything).
Also, because this game is built on Flash, it runs very poorly on even the best of setups – the problem being thousands and thousands of monsters on-screen at the same time. When every wave has 999 monsters coming and you're sending them in advance at the highest of speeds (which you'll have to do, since you'll be pretty bored watching everything die), the frames hover around 10 fps for me. It doesn't matter that much because I'm not doing anything besides upgrading gems (to 45+) and enraging waves (which includes repeatedly clicking everything... also boring).
It's almost as if people figured out how to exploit this game and then the developers sort of went along with it. If this is actually what happened, good for them for adapting how their players "game" the game, but in reality, it just doesn't work that well.

This game is time-leeching(Mana Farms FTW). From the very start you are underwhelmed with a simple tower-defense game that runs smoothly and entertains you even when you lose. Achievements are abundant and pleasing to, well, achieve, and it will take you hundreds of hours to complete all of them. Later on, you are overwhelmed with gem-recipes and strategies that will take you into the thousands of Wizard Levels and hundreds of endurance levels. The goal? Beat endurance. Sure, there is a heroing story line following the wizard you play as, destroying the evils that curse the land in their seemingly infinite numbers. But that isn't as important as the dedication of upgrading your gems individually and in the right pattern to create the mana leeching gems that farms need. Confused and slightly scared? You should be. Gem-crafting is no laughing matter. Math like you thought you would never have to use again is useful to an infinite degree in this game, as gem-recipes can become so complex that it may make the faint-of-heart whimper with fear.
Have you bought a game and finished it in a day and loved it? Each level can be played for many hours on end, gaining you billions upon billions of exp. Some players go on 20-100 hour games to farm as much exp. in the hopes of beating endurance. Plan on putting a couple hundred hours in this game, because it is fun, it is addicting, and you will love it.

This is by far my favorite WWII strategy game. for its great diversity in game play makes almost every game diffrent. For i tend to play more as Germany, and most of the time i employ a similar stratagy; which is to bulid up industry, as to allow for mass production of primaraly tanks. Also as for playing as the smaller nations it can be a struggle, for i have been recently playing as Canada and aside from the lack of raw materials, the small population makes it impossible to industrialize every one of your citys. Over all i would recomend this game to all stratagy lovers, especially those who have playes Axis ans Allies, for this game has a very similar feel, for although it does not let you command individual regiments in a battle, its attantion to detail when it comes to the global map, and all of the little things such as city development, research, and resource management results in a rich but not overly complicated game play.

Overall the game was alright.  The majority of the game is a simplistic "come up with words from a 7 letter scramble".  So gameplay gets pretty repetitive as you do a lot of the same 3-4 letter words over and over.
But every so often it does have unique and interesting challenges for you to do.  Such as to open a Treasure Chest to receive a bonus where you have a limited amount of time to come up with a single 6 or 7 letter word;  or another challenge where you have to guess a word ala Hangman-style to also earn a bonus; yet another one where you'd have a long series of words you had to type rapidly.
The game also introduces varying tiles which when used offer various bonuses or buffs, or can also cause negative effects.  When a tile is used it can cause more damage, less damage, give you more time, or more health, or even less damage, or become locked where you can't use that letter again for a period of time, etc.
I also really liked the idea of the 'bosses' which had a lot of health and introduced a different aspect to battle them.  Some may be immune to 4-letter words, others had to be finished off with a 7-letter word or it's head would grow back (ala a hydra).
On the downside, the dictionary used could use some help.  Some serious help.  There are some very obscure words used, and some I'm pretty sure are not even words.
One place a better dictionary could have been used is the Marathon typing challenges (the rapid sequence of words).   It just seems a missed opportunity where the rapid sequence of words could have all related to a theme of whatever was occuring at the time, but instead, just random (and sometimes obscure) words plucked out of a dictionary.  Here's a sampling of the words I faced (captured through screenshots while playing):
just random obscure words.
Another place a better dictionary would benefit is the on the Treasure Chest challenges (where you have a very short time to make a 6 or 7 letter word out of the letters).  Here's actual two 7-letter words you were supposed to come up with (on different challenges):
.   The level does allow you to come up with 6 letter words to complete the challenger for a lesser bonus, but those are almost as obscure as those 7 letter words for these 2 words.
+ Neat story idea for a typing game
+ Great variety of bosses, each unique
+ Great sprinkling of various challenge levels+ Graphics and Art Style
+ Nice campaign for a typing game
+ Typing Challenges, where it's a rapid sequence of words
+ Variety of weapons with different special abilities
- Some very obscure words (if even words) in the dictionary used
- No consequence or penalty for simply randomly making up words or guessing
- Missed opportunity when the Typing Challenges are just pools of obscure, random words, and nothing to do with the theme or battle at hand.

God of Word is a typing game that has a pretty good overall feel to it.
God of War has an smooth and fun gameplay to it, especially if you like typing games. The way the game is made is a sleek and follows traditional typing games. The setting of this game is that you are "putting on a show" so the graphics match that accordingly (it is all play like). There are a multitude of levels and for me the game took 8 hours to beat (Oh and beating the game gives you an 100% completion :D). There are powerup blocks and basically you have to meet the score needed before the time runs out. So in God of War, you are against the timer. However, you can buy powerups from the store making the game scale as you level up and move up. The music for the game is good as well, and it fits the style of the game.
On the other side, God of War was a bit repetitive because I ended up using the same words almost over and over again. There are difficulty levels in the game so you can choose to make the game easier or harder, but overall it is kind of repetitive. You end up fighting the same kinds of bad guys and monsters (apart from the bosses) over and over again, although it doesn't really matter because you are focused and concentrated on the typing. I am generally a fast typer, so once I started to realize the pool of words I could spam, the game became not much of a challenge. I think I only failed and died 4 times in my whole run.
Overall, good typing game and a relatively easy 100% achievement game.
Rating: 7.9/10
Recommend Price: $1.99 or below

RE Revelations is sort of a re-do for the Resident Evil franchise. While the excellent 4 and 5 took the series to a more intense, action game path, Revelations tries to bring it back to it's survival-horror roots with mixed results.
Back are the narrow corridors, and bullet scarcity of old, combined with modern day control schemes and the ability to move and shoot for a bit more control.
However, Revelations does many things wrong. The partner at many times is useless. They don't do any damage, often just stand around doing nothing when you need them the most, and really contribute nothing to the game other than banter. The enemies are not as varied as past games. In fact, most of them are the same enemy, but with different arms. The bosses are often BS and just act as big damage sponges, making them uninteresting battles of attrition.
Despite these flaws, the over-reaching conspiracy story of the game is still interesting enough to go through, and the Raid mode is actually very engaging.

CrossCode is wonderful isometric action RPG.  Though it is in early access, the game is incredibly polished in virtually all aspects.  The controls are fluid and the combat and plaforming elements are very satisfying to say the least.  On top of the core gameplay, the world is vibrant and the characters are memorable.
So far I've played around six hours or so without moving very far beyond the first major area, mostly doing the various sidequests and exploring, so I already feel that I'm getting a good value even if the game were to remain in its current state.
That said, the developers are some of the most transparent I've seen, and they do a great job of communicating their progress to the community.  They even hold livestreams on a semi-regular basis during which you're free to ask questions and sometimes get to watch them implement different features/ideas as well.
Overall this game encapsulates everything I love about the genre while still feeling fresh and refined.  I wish the best of luck to the developers as they continue to work on this wonderful project.
If you still have reservations, you can do what I did and try out the free demo.  You can download it on Steam, but it is also available to play in a web-browser (Chrome/Firefox) since the game is coded in Javascript/HTML5 via the ImpactJS engine.

But I cannot recommend buying the game due to Paradox Interactive increasing prices just before the Steam Summer Sale. Many of their games were increased by approximately 20-30%. In the case of Stellaris, the discount was upped from 40% to 50%, but because of the base price increase there was only a $0.40 cent drop rather than a $4.40 drop. On many other games the discount percentage was not increased, meaning the sale price was more expensive than usual. This is absolutely a shady tactic to increase sales due to a perception of getting a better deal than you are actually getting. I would much rather the discount be kept at 40% off the original base price, yes I would be a little disappointed if I was looking to buy, but I wouldn't be angry at being manipulated.
I only ever expect price increases to occur when a game exits Early Access and during Early Access itself. Perhaps even if it was a massive update to a finished game, increasing the price would be reasonable. But this was a clean sweep across most of their catalog, without reason.
If you purchased any Paradox product between May 17 and July 6, please claim your games/DLC here:
While you read that thread keep in mind that Paradox is in full damage control mode right now. If you read between the lines you will notice that this is not an automatic refund, and you only get 1 key regardless of how many games you bought. This means they get to keep whatever extra money they have made from this exploit, and lose out on 1 potential future sale if you assume that the customer was even going to buy the game in the future. Plus, you have to CLAIM the game by August 9, which I can guarantee you a decent percentage of people will not do due to not knowing about this. 1 month is a ridiculously short amount of time to submit a claim for something that was their fault in the first place - at the very least it should be a year or two. They have profited through their price manipulation, and are continuing to profit by not doing automatic refunds (you can say that it's not "practically possible" all you want).
The fact that they are taking steps to rectify the situation does NOT excuse them from their actions. If they were truly acting in good faith, they would not have initiated the price increases in the first place.
