Hello and welcome to my review of Megabyte Punch, since everyone ever knows what Smash is, and MBP is a triumphant attempt at bringing SSB to PC, let's just get into it.
In Megabyte Punch you are a Megac on a mission with an energy shield, a pelvic thrust to break shields and stun, a jump, a regular attack, double tap to dash, and five special attacks. You utilize these abilities to get through the story and your enemies to beat the game, which starts off basic and easy. As you beat enemies, you collect parts, which can boost your abilities or give you unique attacks. There's a large variety, and enough overlap that you can pick and choose based on aesthetic and still get the bonuses/moves you want.
As you encounter more enemy and move types in more challenging levels, the game becomes progressively more fun and engaging. The story is sparse but actually relatively decent for its type. Still, for the most part the aim of the game is to beat things up, and I'm here to report to you that it excels at this, being just as fluid and fast as Smash while adding its own innovations, and keeping a great sense of balance with the cooldowns on the various attacks, be they big and satisfying or short and sweet. There are mid-range, long-range, and close-range options, with a roughly 40/60 split between ranged and melee variants. You can stack parts providing defense, offense, jumps, ranged/melee attacks, or more for specialized or fun builds, so the gameplay promotes a lot of individual technical skill while retaining a lot of fun. Basically, I'm telling you to buy it if you for some reason haven't already!
The graphics in Megabyte Punch are downright gorgeous. They retain a vibrant blocky style that would be at home in a NES Zelda title but they don't rely on pixels or take any shortcuts to look good. There's a very good spread of variety to the levels and environments, and plenty of skin colors to unlock and you can definitely make some great looking megacs to dish out the beatings with.

The music and sounds while perhaps not universally appealing are all very high quality. Well produced, sensible, and satisfying.
While I still wholeheartedly recommend MBP as a solo experience, if you have even just one friend that you can couch party it up with, I can confidently recommend you buy Megabyte Punch at:

The original game, at release, was gutted of a lot of 4X/Strategy staple features. They released a game specifically tailored towards expansions and DLC. After getting feedback, they trickled content into the game with free updates and patches. Great, right?
It was, until they left out features that easily should have been part of those updates and charged $10 for them. Leviathans, specifically. Species packs. It's a fun game, but Paradox cut it up and sold it for future DLC at meat market. Prepare to spend more than the steep entry fee with 3 versions, especially if you aren't from the US.

Resident Evil Revelations is a third-person survival horror game. To many this may come as a surprise because Resident Evil 5 and 6 pretty much abandoned the survival horror aspect of the series. Revelations though takes inspirations from the newer titles while staying a true Resident Evil game at its core.
For the most part of the game you are playing as Jill Valentine who is accompanied by her new partner Parker. However, for a majority of the game the action alternates between three teams: Jill Valentine and Parker Luciani, Chris Redfield and Jessica Sherawat as well as Keith “Grinder” Lumley and Quint Cetcham who are basically Cool Guy and Comic Relief Guy. This might sound as if I would not like the characters but they are actually pretty enjoyable.
The plot takes place between Resident Evil 5 & 6. One year before the futuristic floating city of Terragrigia had been attacked by the terrorist organization Il Veltro. Veltro had released the new T-Abyss Virus as well as several packs of hunters, ultimately leading to the FBC using Terragrigria’s solar energy satellite to completely destroy the city in order to stop the spread of the virus. After the Terragrigia incident Veltro had completely vanished.
Jill and Parker learn that Chris went missing during an investigation and set out to rescue him. Chris’ signal has been lost somewhere over the Mediterranean, not too far from the ruins of Terragrigia. Jill and Parker find the cruise ship Queen Zenobia that had been used by Veltro during the attack on Terragrigia and had not been seen since.
Resident Evil is played in a third-person shoulder perspective like most entries in the series since Resident Evil 4. The camera is zoomed out a bit more though. The controls are slightly different from RE 4 and 5. You are able to strafe and to shoot while walking. Generally the player movement feels a tad faster than in previous Resident Evil games. Some of the enemies are pretty fast too.  Resident Evil Revelations also re-introduces the dodge move from RE 3. You can dodge pretty much anything if you time it right. Depending on the enemy it can be quite hard but it is always removing when you dodge successfully.
The inventory system is streamlined compared to previous games. You have three weapon slots and can carry up to five herbs as well a fixed number of every type of grenades. It is a strange choice to remove every form of inventory management from a Resident Evil game and I have to say that I probably liked the way it was handled in RE 4 best. While the inventory system in Revelations is clearly not my favorite it does not hurt the game much.
Weapons can be swapped and upgraded at boxes that are found on the Queen Zenobia. There are a lot of weapons to find or unlock. Most of them are not flat out better or worse than other. They all have their upsides and downsides. The upgrading system works differently from the previous games. Instead of spending money to apply fixed upgrades to your weapon you can find weapon attachments, most of which can be applied to any weapon. Every weapon has a certain number of upgrade slots. Upgrades can be switched or removed at the same boxes where you can swap your weapons. The system works pretty well but there is one thing I do not like about it. Personally I like to have all my weapons upgraded and ready for use. However since you will not have enough upgrade kits to put in every weapon you would like to use you will – at least in the beginning – be forced to swap upgrades when changing weapons, which is an unfortunate interruption to the gameplay.
A completely new addition to the series is the Genesis. The Genesis is a scanner that is able to find hidden objects and enemies. While you are using the Genesis the game changes to a first person perspective. You can still move slowly but you cannot fight while using the device. Frequent use of the Genesis is highly recommended since you can find loads of ammo, upgrade kits and healing items with it.
The thing I like most about Resident Evil Revelations is that it nails the atmosphere. While there are some changes to the Resident Evil formula Revelation has everything a good RE title needs: claustrophobic environments, hilarious puzzles and scary enemies. The plot is told in the style of a TV show and there are frequent recaps, which works fairly well. It reminded me of Alan Wake to a certain degree. The story has a lot of twists and while I think that the developers overdid it at times some of the twists were executed beautifully. Especially the “Semiramis” twist left my staring at the screen with my mouth open.
The thing I like least about Revelations is how the developers handled the AI partners. The damage they deal is unbelievably low. Here is an example: At a point where I was able to kill basic enemies with two close range shotgun hits I shot an enemy once. After that my partner shot the same enemy four of five times. With a shotgun. At close range. However, the enemy still was not dead. That is how low the AI damage is. You should never trust the AI to handle anything on their own. Their damage is just sad and most of the time they cannot even tank because enemies mostly ignore them. At least the AI partners cannot die, so that is a plus.
Aside from the campaign Resident Evil Revelations also offers Raid Mode which basically is the Resident Evil version of a dungeon grinder. There is a bunch of characters to choose from, all with their respective strengths. You can then choose a stage that is heavily inspired by a part of the single-player campaign. Your mission is always to get to the end and if possible kill all enemies. On your way you level up and get items drops that can either be weapons or upgrade kits. There is a surprisingly high amount of content here. It is also possible to play Raid mode in online-co-op.

While I have some minor complaints about Resident Evil Revelations I think that it is a really good game. It tries out new stuff without abandoning what makes Resident Evil… well…  Resident Evil. I highly recommend it to veterans and newcomers alike.

I recommend Deadly Premonition to everyone who likes kind of weird characters, good storytelling (that takes it's time) with multiple perspectives from different points on the timeline. You should be stress resistant, because the game will probably crash just before your next save, so you will do some things twice. That should not bother you. It is a kick, because the game itself is not much of a challenge. If you can live with the flaws and see it as an Indie game you got for less than 3 bucks, it is an immersing adventure.
Since the beginning I like the habit of the main character "York" to talk to "Zack". It feels like he is talking to you, the player. It is fun to see other people being puzzled by the actions of the protagonist (as talking to Zack, a person no one can see) and not asking a question. That's what you as the player do: make a list in your mind of things you want to find out and hope that you will get your answers to the right time. Or at the end, at least. Because of the way the story is told you may guess some things and resolve some mysteries for yourself, but I assume that you will still be surprised sometimes. You won't find an answer to everything in the game, like with most scary stories, but that's fine. You will get all important answers to what is important in the game's universe.
Some insights of my journey with the game:
I was well aware of bugs because I read other reviews. I installed DPfix.  I can highly recommend that. By doing so, crashes did not occur too often and because I saved a lot I managed to play the game without becoming depressed. ;) I can only complain about spending too much time on loading screens. Moving the game from my HDD to my SSD did not seem to boost the time on loading screens. Too bad.
In chapter 7 I started to explore the vast world. I should have done that sooner (chapter 2) to have advantages in the game early on. In the first chapters you have time limits, but the game is nearly in real time, so you can do side quests. No worries. Do them! I got my radio, which allows me to drive to different locations in no time without really doing it] after chapter 21. I could have saved a lot of time, not driving myself through the world. You find information about the side quests in the game and also through the descriptions of the achievements.
After you finished a chapter, you can replay it. During a replay you cannot save. A replay is nice if you want to do side quests that may be easier in that level or not doable in another. Everything you gain will be available in any other replay and also in your current game progress. A replay only changes at the end (if you save after finishing the chapter) your inventory, trading cards and the quests you finished. So if you keep dying in your current level, do a replay to get food and medipacks in your inventory. Nice cheat. :)
I used the replays after I was stuck in chapter 22. I was too lazy to open the archive and therefore I did not find an important key. The game is in general, amazingly straightforward, because it shows in red where you need to go to or interact with to proceed. That is nice, as you always know what to do. (But you still have to solve the puzzles by yourself, the game only indicates where the important puzzle is.) You are never lost.
I like the chilling atmosphere of the game, the horror story itself and especially how it is told. One last hint: Don't miss to have lunch with your colleagues. Eat with them in every chapter possible. It's fun!
I am happy that the reviews I read convinced me to play this (indie?) gem.

Over the course of the several hours spent playing, I developed a love/hate relationship with this game. I fortunately did not run into any of the game-breaking bugs that others have mentioned. I did have to use the hint button more times than I care to admit. It wasn't due to the game being difficult, however. It was more due to things like the aforementioned word choices for the hidden object portions. Some were downright misleading and I wondered many times if something was lost in translation (was this translated to english? I never did check...but it gave me that impression). Also, I too noticed that the "hit box" for some objects was a bit off or small. Damn you, fur hat! Most of the puzzles were decent, except the sliding tile one. But that's a matter of personal hatred and not due to it being a bad puzzle.
The graphical style was right up my alley. I loved it. It was like wandering around a dismal, eerie painting. The background music/noise was spot on, and especially creepy during the hidden object portions. The feeling of rummaging around someone's shed while someone creeps up behind you was very real.
The story was better than I'd expected. A bit predictable, but still intriuging enough. There were times, though, I cursed the lack of common-sense logic. "I need a fishing pole for that? Really? Are you serious? What was wrong with all the god-d----d sticks laying around everywhere?" I also came to utterly loathe the amount of back-tracking. Be prepared for that. Just take a deep breath and pretend the protagonist has suffered a nasty head injury. Which she probably has.
All in all, the combination of great art, chilling atmosphere, passable story and decent puzzles make it worth playing, despite moments that will make you glare at the screen in utter hatred.

I'll recommend this one, but only hesitantly. The atmosphere tends to be great, the voice acting isn't bad, and the story, if thin and transparent, is at least interesting. The problem is that the actual puzzle/hidden object gameplay, while solid, is just so flawed. The puzzles tend to be of the frustrating "keep starting over until you hit upon the exact sequence" variety - expected of an Artifex Mundi title, but still inviting many Skip-button presses - and the hidden object portions are a mixed bag. Incredibly, if you replay them from the Extras menu, one of the HO areas doesn't even include one of the objects you're supposed to find (the "horns" in the Chapel), making it literally impossible to get one of the achievements unless you go through them all perfectly when you play the initial campaign. Still, this game lands at the upper end of the genre, so if you can get it on sale it's still worth it.

Compared to the other Artifex Mundi's games, this title has some lackings that made me lean toward the thumb down; but let's start from the beginning.
Enigmatis: The Ghost of Maple Creek is a point and click hidden object adventure.
Your goal, as a Detective, is to find a missing girl and to unveil the mystery that lies behind Maple Creek.
For the ones that have already played the next chapter, Enigmatis: The Mists of Ravenwood, there is a little but singular problem: You already know what happens. (I won't go further to avoid spoilers).
The problem of this two titles is that they are strictly linked between them and on Steam they have been released in opposite order (first the second chapter and just recently the first one).
A really bad thing for the fans of this genre and this software house that seen the fun of unveil the mystery took away.
Other than this "little" problem, what made my decision go toward the "no" is:
- Too few puzzles.
- Those ones are too easy making the already short game even shorter.
- A really bad translation (at least in Italian) leads you to the mistake and to use the Hint in the hidden object sessions.
- The story, the setting and the characters are only sketched and made with the obvious purpouse to push the gamer to buy the second chapter, making the game not so addictive.
If you still want to try it I would suggest to wait until it will end in some bundle.

Rispetto ad altri titoli sempre editi dalla Artifex Mundi, questo gioco presenta varie carenze che mi fanno propendere per il pollice verso; ma andiamo con ordine e partiamo dall'inizio.
Enigmatis: The Ghost of Maple Creek è un'avventura grafica punta e clicca hidden object.
Il vostro compito, in veste di Detective, è quello di trovare una ragazza recentemente scomparsa e svelare il mistero che si cela dietro Maple Creek.
Per quelli di voi che hanno già giocato il capitolo seguente, Enigmatis: The Mists of Ravenwood, si presenta un piccolo quanto peculiare problema: sapete già cosa succede. (Non entro nel dettaglio per evitare ulteriori spoiler).
Il problema è che questi due titoli risultano essere legati fra loro, e su Steam sono stati rilasciati in ordine inverso (è stato pubblicato prima il secondo capitolo e solo recentemente il primo).
Brutta storia per gli appassionati come me di questo genere e di questa casa editrice, che si vedono portare via il gusto dell'arrivare fino in fondo per svelare il mistero.
Al di là di questo "piccolo" intoppo, ciò che fa oscillare l'ago della bilancia verso il "no" è:
- La presenza di pochi enigmi
- La facilità dei suddetti, con il risultato di rendere poco longeva una già breve storia
- L'approssimativa traduzione che ti spinge a commettere errori ed eventualmente ad usare l'aiuto nelle scene hidden object (un esempio su tutti la parola Pipe tradotta come tubo e non come pipa)
- L'evidente abozzo di storia, personaggi e ambientazione fatto apposta per spingerti a comprare il secondo capitolo rendono il gioco poco coinvolgente
Se proprio siete convinti di volerlo provare, posso solo suggerirvi di aspettare che finisca in qualche bundle.

Greetings Everyone!  It’s time for round 2!  Specifically the game “On a Rain Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two” which is the sequel to well…the first one and you are here to read a review.  So what do we have here?  Eh, the continuation of an RPG that comes straight from Penny Arcade, which should be enough to buy it immediately, but is the game itself good?
Home Wrecker:   The game starts off more or less the same way it begun previously and in most games that might be annoying but I found it humorous at least.  This is much like the rest of the game, more of the same.  If you liked the original you will enjoy this and probably don’t need to read this review to begin with.
Call Me Kratos:  The game seems to have learned a bit from the original, it keeps the graphics and sound effects but the enemies are a bit more dynamic (though the bosses can be a bit easier) and the abilities you unlock are interesting as well.  You ultimately get part two of the first game polished a bit with additional options and some interesting storyline.  You aren’t going to have jaw dropping inspiring events but you may find a perpetual smirk on your face as you are murdering millionaires or baking pies.
Die Robots:  One annoyance of the game is that there seems to be a lot more ‘back in forth’ by that I mean that you are required to go back and forth between zones to accomplish stuff, I do not know if this was to pad game time (doubtful as the game is short unashamedly) or just a design that wasn’t thought through thoroughly.  You also get more of the same as far as targeting issues and I did notice that the game’s enemies seem to heal a lot more, this never caused severe issues but I did find it annoying from time to time.
This isn’t an epic 99 hour RPG but it is an enjoyable tromp down memory lane and an interesting story told from one of my favorite comic strips.  If you don’t already have this game you really should grab it if you are a fan of parody, RPGs or Penny Arcade.  But, while you decide I’m going to start into the third game, enjoy!

I have pretty mixed feelings about this series. On the one hand, I greatly enjoyed Episode One and Two. The comic book style is quite endearing, and plot is pretty interesting. Humor is on point, as can be expected from Penny Arcade as a whole.
However, the fact that the developer and overall style of Episode Three and Four changed makes me want to caution new players from diving into this world. I could not bring myself to finish Three, as the enjoyment died off entirely. The latter half of the series looks like it was made in RPG maker, which by itself isn't a drawback, but is pretty stock combat/features with no flair. The storytelling/humor seems to have left the series entirely but that point.
One and Two are definitely still worth playing, even if you don't plan to play the rest, but it seems pretty hit or miss as to whether people enjoy the latter two. You've been warned.
I still can't get over the Fruit Fckers in this series. Whether fighting them or watching them destroy property, they angrily hump the air with vigilance.

At the price point of 10-20$ (what i paid for it during a Steam summer sale) I would say its worth picking up, however I would NOT recommend this game at its 40$ price point, it feels like a lazy attempt that was rushed out the door while still chock full of bugs.
What kind of bugs you ask? How about the classic kill this entire wave of enemies to progress the mission and the last enemy either doesnt spawn, or falls through the world making it so you must leave the map area and come back to reload the fight and have the final enemy spawn where you can actually interact with it? Remember that classic? Yup, seen that one 5+ times in the past hour in different missions...
Hey, by the way, do you per chance enjoy playing this game on PC with an Xbox controller? So do I, but there is no option in any menu in the game to turn vibration off completely, so be prepared for random vibration when you do random things, like scoping up with some weapons but not others, or walk away from a vending machine and its talking to you, or any number of other random activities...
Also should you have a beast gaming computer make sure to never set your Physx settings above high, or you will experience random game freezes and crashes with varying frequency (I of course found this out the hard way, and after experiencing 4 or so crashes within an hour I had to search the internet where a forum was filled with people who had experienced the same random crashes and concluded they were caused by the PhysX settings...
If this game were to be patched to fix all of the obnoxious bugs
TLDR Final Verdict: Is the game worth getting? Wait for a sale because its not worth 40$ in its current state. 10-15$ is acceptable, 20 is pushing it. Unless the devs come back and fix some of the obnoxious bugs, and throw in the option to turn controller vibration off completely thats my final verdict as someone whose put several hours into the game. Is there a rich story line full of classic humor good voice acting and witty quips like BL1 and BL2? Yup. Minus the bugs this game is SOLID, but the bugs that have gone unanswered really detract from the games overall score

I'm not a good writer, but
quickly established itself as one of my favourite pieces of media ever, and I'm still constantly thinking about this game months after finishing it, which is why it's important to me to put down my thoughts on it somewhere. Anyway, on with the damn review.
If you don't know Yoko Taro, he's the crazy, brilliant genius behind
. You know,
. In any case, I'm convinced that Taro's (semi-spiritual) sequel to the 2010 cult classic
is a powerful display of what true authorship in video games is capable of, utilizing its inherent potential as an artistic medium to its fullest and beautifully integrating narrative, aesthetics, thematics and mechanics to deliver one of the most thoroughly absorbing and deeply heartfelt journeys I've ever experienced in any medium. It's a flawed game for sure, but as someone who values scope and personality more than formal perfection, most of
's flaws ended up being very negligible to my overall experience. But yeah, this game offers no shortage of personality, and indeed feels very much like the eccentric vision of a true auteur director through and through. One who is keenly aware of player expectations and uses that knowledge to convey his ideas with sincerity and ingenuity, not to mention a unique sense of humour. Clearly frustrated with how formulaic a lot of the modern gaming industry has become, Taro makes a lot of unconventional and bold choices in this game, the most controversial of which being the decision to force the player to replay a good chunk of the game's first half (albeit from the perspective of a different character) to unlock its second half. This may sound a bit arbitrary at first—and some players will undoubtedly consider this too high a barrier of entrance and (understandably) refuse to meet the challenge—but I think this decision does have its proper place in the grander scheme of things. Indeed, if you look closely, you may gradually discover that all these eccentricities do point in a unified direction and eventually tie into the game's greater artistic and thematic ambitions. The final stretch in particular is a stroke of genius and connected with me in a way that will probably prove to be a singular experience in my life as a gamer. In any case, unless you are immune to Taro's specific charm as a director and storyteller, I think you will definitely realise that
is a special kind of game. Maybe it's even best described as a niche game at heart, albeit one that was made appealing to a mass audience by teaming up with the people over at PlatinumGames, whose technical experience with aesthetically and mechanically acclaimed action titles such as
and
finally made it possible for a Yoko Taro project to have a level of gameplay and polish that it deserves (but more on that later).
Let's get the most obvious things out of the way: the narrative style of
is clearly not everyone's cup of tea. For one thing, the plot is full of crazy anime and sci-fi trappings, and let's not get started on the vast ocean of background lore involved in the Drakengard/Nier franchise, which is, uh,
. If you're a fan of anime or just weird sh*t from Japan in general, that's just part of the charm, but if not, you might look at this game's (pretty shoddy) trailers and say to yourself "a weird Japanese video game about leggy androids battling alien machines? no thanks". While certainly understandable, you would be doing yourself a huge disservice by skipping over this game based on those factors, because
's narrative exemplifies the very meaning of "more than meets the eye" as well as "more than the sum of its parts". The plot of this game is one thing, but the
it tells is something else entirely. Like
, this game is not about winning a war against space monsters, and like
, it is not even about the question whether machines can be humans. Those aspects of the story are all well and good, but I consider them to be merely vehicles for greater narrative goals. What this game is really trying to do is best explored for yourself, but to give you a general idea,
's core ambitions include an oftentimes painful but nonetheless deeply sincere and actually thoughtful essay on the nature of humanity, a poignant therapy session on coping with existentialist dread, and a metanarrative examination of why we play video games in the first place. And it does all this without ever coming across as needlessly didactic or anything, so there's plenty of room for you to find your own meaning in all of this. In any case, I recommend checking out the links below for detailed discussion on this game, but I hope I was able to shed
light on why I think that
absolutely deserves to be remembered as one of the most narratively ambitious video games of our times. Or, to quote Jim Sterling,
One common complaint often heard is that this game's combat gets a bit repetitive atfer a while. I can definitely see where these people are coming from, and anyone expecting another
is surely set up for disappointment in that regard. However, I still think some people are selling the gameplay a bit short; at the very worst, one might describe the gameplay as serviceable, but it's certainly not anywhere near bad. Sure, you can ultimately get through the game with mere button-mashing and some dodging if you want, but I nonetheless genuinely enjoyed the fast-paced and unadulterated nature of the combat, and similar to the narrative department, there is a lot more to the mechanics than meets the eye. In fact, most of the subtler details of the combo system are left unexplained and have to be figured out via experimentation. Furthermore, the player characters have incredibly eclectic movesets with outright beautiful animations ("ballet of death" hits the nail on the head), ensuring that every encounter is visually and viscerally stimulating at the very least. However, the real highlight in terms of mechanics reveals itself when combining the combat mechanics with the incredibly enjoyable and fluid movement controls. I absolutely loved traversing the world via a mad combination of dashing, jumping, kicking, sword swinging, pod gliding, sand surfing and even goddamn boar riding, especially since your primary means of motion can be chained together skillfully with the numerous combat mechanics to bridge large distances and gain extra height.

Solid, if unimaginative tower-defense mechanics. Everything you'd expect to see is here: building towers, walling-off enemies' paths into serpentine mazes, upgrading your defenses. GemCraft has an simple and intuitive take on tower design.  Gems provide the stats for each tower. You can swap them in and out of towers, upgrade them, and combine them for increased effects. All of this takes place while managing your mana pool. Mana is gained passively and from destroying monsters, then used to create gems, towers, walls, traps, etc. The economy of this system is rewarding for those who like to micromanage but no so punishing as to discourage experimentation.
Outside of each level, you can unlock new skills to improve various aspects of your experience or hold onto those skill points for more mana at the beginning of levels. This trade-off is a nice change of pace from blindly allocating points as soon as they become available. In addition to skills, enemies may drop glyphs which can be socketed in to a grid and upgraded, providing further customization and buffs. Additionally, traits can also be found that are used to increase and customize the dificulty of  any level. Did I mention the levels? There are so many. A great deal of content is packed into this game.
The only area where GemCraft is lacking is in the graphics and presentation. The entire game has a semi-gothic, old-school vibe similar to Diablo or any other notable RPG to come out the 90s. This style may appeal to some, but overall, the look of the game isn't very memorable.

I strongly recommend this title to all tower defense enthusiasts.
If you havent played any TD games yet, you might want to try out previous GemCrafts online first, since this one somewhat throws you in at the deep end with a few things.

GemCraft is an interesting beast, and if you like tower defense, then this game is for you. That is unless you like having your hand held through the process. This is a game that commands your understanding before you can succeed, and unless you're planning out your skills and utilising your talismans, it can quickly get the best of you.
As far as I have seen, this game offers a wealth of replayability, with the ability to go back to any map you've completed and play it with difficulty-increasing modifiers, and also just harder difficulty levels, not to mention an "Endurance" mode. Ultimately you could spend a tons of hours just work through the levels, and it's a greatly soothing game to play when you just want to chill.

"The Ghosts of Maple Creek" is a beautifully rendered hidden object game

but I found this to be one of the best.
Pros:
- Once you remove an object from a scene, it stays removed for future iterations
of playing that scene.
- The map clearly marks areas where there are actions available to you, so you
never feel lost or wonder where to go next.
- It's immersive.  The music and story can reel you in and make you feel like you're
racing against time to save the missing girl.
- The game includes other types of puzzles which are also well done.
Cons:
- There is no fast travel between areas.
Overall, I recommend this to anyone who likes puzzle games.

An exciting and long hidden object game with not exactly top of the line graphical presentation and a well-balanced difficulty. A solid Artifex Mundi title.
Enigmatis: The Ghosts of Maple Creek isn’t the kind of game that knows how to set a tone, but when it eventually gets the story rolling, it suddenly turns one of the most overused HO clichés (heroine searches for someone in a small town ruled/haunted by a supernatural evil entity) into an electrifying serial murder mystery. With a really decent voice acting to boot.
There are very few conventional puzzles and even the item usage is quite straightforward and limited; the focus is on the hidden object scenes, crammed full of items, giving a surprising level of difficulty. A welcomed change for experienced HO gamers.
The only real problem is that the map: you cannot fast travel with it, even though there is a lot of backtracking– the story requires you to do several laps around the town, easily reaching 4-6 hours of game time.

TLDR: Didn't play single player (not what I bought it for). From a technical perspective co-op is so broken it's not worth trying to play. Just search for ReR co-op issues (lag/desync), they're widespread.
Bought it specifically for the co-op. First off, IT'S NOT campaign co-op. If that's what you want, look elsewhere. Co-op in ReR exists entirely in a new Raid Mode, and if you're thinking it's anything like mercernaries, it's not. It's almost like playing campaign co-op but without any story whatsoever. It simply drops you in an area and you start moving through  killing stuff. It has persistent leveling and tons of guns/gun mods that can be unlocked with the points you get from the levels. It actually seemed really neat (particularly some of the gun mods, huge variety, some really neat stuff) HOWEVER... crippling performance ruins the entire experience.
There seem to be massive network problems with the game, it almost feels like you're constantly having massive lag spikes. Your partner can run halfway through a level, but on your screen they will still be standing at the beginning. Every once in a while the game will update your partner's position and you can get a general idea of where they actually are. Oddly enough it seems to register all actions pretty well, so even though I can't see my partner move, he can still shoot at enemies and I can still see the damage that he's doing to them... It's just that from my point of view my partner is hitting the enemy through walls and whatnot. The whole experience was really bizarre. Searching online for ReR co-op issues shows we're not the only ones having problems either. There seem to be technical issues going back to the game's release that have been completely ignored by Capcom. Saw mostly positive reviews on Steam but very little feedback on the multiplayer, so I thought I'd get this in.

At the price point of 10-20$ (what i paid for it during a Steam summer sale) I would say its worth picking up, however I would NOT recommend this game at its 40$ price point, it feels like a lazy attempt that was rushed out the door while still chock full of bugs.
What kind of bugs you ask? How about the classic kill this entire wave of enemies to progress the mission and the last enemy either doesnt spawn, or falls through the world making it so you must leave the map area and come back to reload the fight and have the final enemy spawn where you can actually interact with it? Remember that classic? Yup, seen that one 5+ times in the past hour in different missions...
Hey, by the way, do you per chance enjoy playing this game on PC with an Xbox controller? So do I, but there is no option in any menu in the game to turn vibration off completely, so be prepared for random vibration when you do random things, like scoping up with some weapons but not others, or walk away from a vending machine and its talking to you, or any number of other random activities...
Also should you have a beast gaming computer make sure to never set your Physx settings above high, or you will experience random game freezes and crashes with varying frequency (I of course found this out the hard way, and after experiencing 4 or so crashes within an hour I had to search the internet where a forum was filled with people who had experienced the same random crashes and concluded they were caused by the PhysX settings...
If this game were to be patched to fix all of the obnoxious bugs
TLDR Final Verdict: Is the game worth getting? Wait for a sale because its not worth 40$ in its current state. 10-15$ is acceptable, 20 is pushing it. Unless the devs come back and fix some of the obnoxious bugs, and throw in the option to turn controller vibration off completely thats my final verdict as someone whose put several hours into the game. Is there a rich story line full of classic humor good voice acting and witty quips like BL1 and BL2? Yup. Minus the bugs this game is SOLID, but the bugs that have gone unanswered really detract from the games overall score

The amount of hours in game is probably more than the time i actually spent playing. As of me writing this review I haven't finished all the playable content that is available, and I haven't played in a while. I have finished the Faj'ro Temple, in which
, if that gives you a better idea of where I am. It is by no means a bad game; it just falls short of the potential I saw in the original demo and has some caveats that make the game unenjoyable at times, which I currently don't see reflected in the reviews.
There are a lot of good ideas behind this game. However, due to the nature of the many features (like leveling, an expansive skill tree, equipment, and consumables) that they tried to shove into the game in combination with the existing combat, the balance has suffered and your character is incredibly overpowered. To compensate, they just made many of the generic enemies harder to hit, which just makes the game more frustrating. You spend a lot of time running around not only to avoid getting hit, but just to get the right timing and aim necessary for a few hits on your evasive enemies.
The player's strengths and weaknesses are not as reflected in these enemies strengths and weaknesses as they should be. The experience gains are also ridiculous. Just the quests alone will overlevel you, not even taking into account grinding with the exp and item drop boosts of the rank system, or the puzzle dungeons.
Overall, the devs seem to have bit off a bit more than they can chew at this time, and the execution has suffered. It's not a bad game, but there are games with similar combat that play better.
Also, for anyone wondering, this game does support the Dualshock 4 controller.

CrossCode has great, fluid combat, it is difficult yet fair, easy to pick up, but hard to master. The rpg style progression is well done (lots of skill tree choices, the ability to swap branches). The loot system is the best I've seen, it actually makes sense what creatures drop, and that you trade those drops in to traders for goods and equipment. The story shines, and although it obviously has influences from popular shows and games, it still keeps itself unique. The characters have great personalities; Emilie is a fun and relatable companion; and Sergey, while mysterious also is likeable. I've not seen enough of the other characters to form an opinion on them. The artwork of the game is a prime example of pixel art done right, it truly is beautiful. Between the gameplay, story, and beatuiful artwork, it is hard to find a flaw in CrossCode, but if I had to find one, it would be that, between quests and traders, the drop rate on some loot items isn't enough to obtain them in a reasonable amount of time. I often found I would be overleveled for the quest rewards once I managed to finally collect the resources.
Although the game isn't close to its finished form, it still is a blast to play, and doesn't lack for content. The story stops at an early point (for plot purposes), but has other content to keep you playing. Unfortunately I prefer to complete the story slowly and explore everything at the same time, so I will not play until more is released. That said, even if you find that an issue like I did, it shouldn't keep you from supporting the developers through early access, they definitely deserve it.

In Deadly premonition you play the role of FBI Special Agent Francis York Morgan, but you can call him York, everybody calls him that, sent to a town to investigate the murder of a young girl. While the premise sounds generic and cliche, Deadly Premonition is anything but that and is by far one of the most unique games I've ever played. Deadly Premonition features dated visuals, mediocre gameplay and more bugs than in your backyard yet it's still an extremely memorable and unique experience that shines most brightly on it's plot and narrative.
While I'm first and for most gameplay over everything when it comes to gaming, Deadly Premonition is one of the only, if not the only game I'd recommend based on it's setting, plot and characters. The game is a mixture  of Thriller, Horror and Dark Comedy blended together in a extremely unique manner.
While you may be put off by the dated, crude presentation and bugs this game possesses, it's still an experience that I couldn't recommend enough if you can overlook it's faults. It's so bad that it's a masterpiece, think of the film Troll 2 which is widely regarded as the 'best worst film' of all time and is an absolutely hilarious masterpiece for all the wrong reasons. The gameplay itself is somewhat reminiscent of Resident Evil 4 but has some awkward controls, thankfully this does little to affect the game as the focus is on it's incredibly strong writing.
The story is absolutely brilliant thanks to the writers eccentric and quirky style, there really is nothing out there like this. Again I do recommend caution when buying this game, you'll need to tweak a few things in order to even get the game to run and there are a few mods which enhance the visuals and allow the game to be played 1080p but that aside this is an experience that should not be overlooked if you're a fan of crime stories and unique writing.

You want Resident Evil Revelations? I will give you revelation -> this game sux. I could not stand playing for more than 3 hours. Just... impossible.
TL-DR : I got this game for free. And I did not even get my money's worth. I do not recommend it at all.This was the first Resident Evil game I played and I believe it will be the last.
Protagonist is a crippled person, uncappable of anything but slow walk. So you charge at your enemies with agility of 95 yo grandpa with clutches. You can not even move a chair if it blocks your path. You shoot zombies that hardly notice it. You scan desks with scanner to find hidden ammo. You look for keys to find doors to get you to doors that you need to find key to open, to get to door that you have no card to open and need to slowly walk to another door that magically opened at your convenience to get it...
Terrible. You can not dodge or block in normal way, nor jump or crouch. Not even run. You just walk with zombies behind you. And if you shoot them, even in the head, they do not even react, they do not flinch. They are not thrown back even if you shoot them with shotgun to the chest at arms length. And you must be almost stationary to shoot. No Run and Gun. Nope. If you try that, you swing knife at enemies... You want to spray them down while backing like hell? Nope, not here.
Ah, there is a door! (the corridors are a few metres long, then there is a door. Always a door... every few steps. And the monsters disappear or appear when you go through that door. And you always close the door behind you. Smart). There is some debris blocking your path, that you coul walk over (not even need to jump) ? Too bad, you need to take a de-tour.
There is NO place for cyber-athletics, no agility.  No using corners, ducking, running back and charging at enemy when you see fit. Nope, not here.You just walk at enemies at the speed of dying turtle, shoot them (shooting makes no difference until enemy suddenly drops dead) and open doors.
Ah, and eat a plant that grows everywhere to magicaly restore your health. And use super-advanced scanner to find ammo you can not see otherwise.
Every zombie runs at you. Every one tries to kill you. Unless the zombie carries a key that you need. Then, for some reason, it runs away from you... and you need to chase it to the start of the level, so the game  seems longer and not so linear. So you end up walking here and there like a confused freshman looking for his class. Go get the key to get through this door. Ah god, why not learn how to pick that locks, they seem to be everywhere...
It has no real effect on the enemy, apart from lowering their health bar. So you are stationary, can not run, and can not use guns to clear some space. You just stand, walk back slowly and shoot. It is extremely boring.
There is actually no atmosphere at all. The game controls feel so unnatural that it just will not let you fall into the story. The battles are so dull you will get no rush of adrenaline. They try to make it scary, and they fail miserably. A zombie attacked me from a washing machine... seriously? A lot of jumps scenes that try to scare you, but they simply do not work at all... The only "scary" moment is when the game crashes and you are afraid of losing your save file.
You want a good horror-shooter game? Go and buy Metro 2033 redux and thank me later. Leave this be. It is not worth your time.

Shows the history from a specific enough perspective that the vastness of the events is easier to understand and provides plenty of additional reading for the curious. The gameplay is largely branching dialogue trees and video/animation with a few minigames that don't feel too trivial, including a clever "stitch together the sentence" approach to some scenarios. There is plenty of reading at times but because the story stays focused it never feels overwhelming. I also REALLY dug the soundtrack, wish it was available to download!

This game came to me via Twitter. A person I know is friends with someone who worked on it and they were lending a hand by promoting it.
Being interested in history as well as how video games can serve as a medium to convey history, especially history from places and about events that aren't touched upon often, I decided to give this a shot.
Mind, I have not played all the way through all the endings of this game nor did I do it in one sitting because I had bought this game in the middle of the semester at university. I had just finished my first playthrough of the game immediately before starting to write this.
However, I at least have gathered enough to put down a review of my thoughts:
I like how the developers mixed animation and live action cut scenes to convey the story. The art was good and the people who acted out the live action cut scenes were also quite good. It reminded me of when I played Her Story a few years ago but the animations and the mini-games in the animations really helped give the player a more interactive role in the story. It was also great that I was not having to type literally all the words of the English language order to dig for video clips.
This is definitely a game where your choices matter both in the mini-games and the interviews. For mini-games, I had a difficult time trying to figure out which choices were best and they weren't always obvious. The game is looking for you to really think about what you would do if you were running from Lety to Prague or where you would hide sensitive documents if the Gestapo were coming to get you. There is no obvious "aha!" answer to some of these games, sometimes even choices you thought would work may not have been the best choices for that game.
Fun Fact: there was a cypher mini-game where I nearly had a heart attack because I thought the game had switched back to Czech for no reason. The fact that coins could be earned for reaching a certain goal in a mini-game kind of helps. The coins then offer an opportunity to go back and fix any errors.
Then there are the interviews, where choices also matter. Depending on what questions are asked determines what you are able to get from the character you are speaking with. Even with no time contraints, these are tough choices to be made. It kind of felt like having an actual conversation with someone--every time I spoke with a character, I chose dialog options that were more diplomatic and congenial or chose not to press a certain button. This game makes it clear that this is not the best route to take if you are looking to get certain bits of information. In all honesty, though, I was afraid some dialog choices would potentially end a conversation or make a character more hostile towards my character. Luckily, after completing a run of the game, you then have the option to go back and talk to certain characters to attain any information you may have missed. It definitely saves the trouble of having to start all over again in order to fill in the blanks.
The historical element was interesting and did as much as it could to relate the history of World War II and what was occurring in Czechoslovakia at that point. Being an American, this is not a part  of history that is widely discussed in standard American schooling. Central and Eastern European countries are rarely if ever talked about. As a uni student studying in the UK, I have now at least taken one class about Central and Eastern Europe in the 20th century where Czechoslovakia was one of my countries of focus. Some of the events and things I studied I could almost immediately recognize while others I honestly did not know but am now glad to have learned through the game.
The Encyclopedia feature is pretty great--I got really excited whenever I talked to a character and a notification popped up saying that I now had gotten new information in my encyclopedia to read. The fact that I can go back and read it is a wonderful thing as well. This game would probably make a fun interactive resource for a class to allow students more active engagement with the source material.
I don't have many complaints about this game other than the fact that sometimes the dialog could sound or look stilted. While I am not a Czech speaker by any stretch of the imagination, certain bits of dialog didn't sound organic, coming across as monotone or over exaggerated. Sometimes, I could even see that in the English subtitles. It could at times interrupt the flow of the game but it was not jarring enough to where the immersion was totally lost.
Also, there may be a bit of a glitch when you talk to a character where the "continue" button will stay there during the cut scene and dialog choices.
Overall, however, this game was a fun, interesting way to engage with an historical event and region that generally does not receive much focus. The developers and the people they worked with should be proud of what they made.
Please show them some love by purchasing and playing this game. Thank you!

GIANTS are a software company i have long linked with my beloved Farming Simulator 15, so when i found this little gem for £6 and being made from them i had hoped to find a game which would prove to be well made and enjoyable, and for the most part this game lives up to the description.
The Vehicles:
the controls are fiddly to get used to but once you do you will find you can get most tasks done quickly, the Wheel Loader is the worst for me, i had a horrible time at the start keeping rubble in the bucket, likewise the truck is a real pain to drive once loaded but other than that the rest were enjoyable, i wont go into to much detail about what vehicles there are. if you want to see them then i would suggest either go raid youtube or buy the game.
The Map (Career Mode)
This is no open world roaming game, it would have been much more entertaining if it was in my opinion, there is a map with different districts on it. each district has a level requirement and a series of missions for you to complete. they get harder as you progress into the higher zones but likewise the vehicles you get to play with can get the job done with ease. for me the map/districts were too small, the game started well but once you get to level 8 the game gets quite short and i personally found it to be over much to quickly. not complaining to much as it was a nice cheap game and you really do get what you pay for. but even though i found it short it was very fun wiping out the various buildings and structures.
Missions
this mode is much like career mode and in most cases its just a repeat of career mode missions but with these missions you dont have the vehicle restrictions you have in career (until level 8 when you can pick your own). again, this mode is more aimed at pointless destruction.
On the whole i would say this game is well worth the price i paid and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys blowing apart things. if there was to be a sequel to this game i would certainly consider it but would very much like to see either many more districts or a game that plays much to the theme of farming simulator where you have a larger single map and take on contracts to demolish buildings and so forth and a company that you can build up from the bottom, employing npc's to do jobs and gradually buy in new vehicles and abilities.

I paid $10 for Demolition Company and it's a fun litte game. On many levels, it's really well-made. The equipment and vehicles are detailed and some of the controls are complex and will take a bit to get used to. The missions are straightforward, don't require anything overly complicated and the tutorials are adequate enough to give you a good understanding of how to use all the machines. I have only one main complaint and that's that the physics need a tweaking when it comes to hauling debris in either your loader or the dump truck. 2/3rds of your hauled materials will bounce, unnaturally, out of your loader's bucket while moving. The same thing applies to your dump truck. Acceleration and deceleration is very herky-jerky and the materials you're hauling will violently shift around and spill out on all sides. I also stumbled upon  another physics bug where, using your jackhammer, you can turn oil drums into projectiles, causing them to instantly break apart solid walls.
Overall, the game's worth the 10 bucks. Who doesn't like breaking or blowing stuff up? It doesn't appear the developers have done anything with it in a couple of years, so it seems unlikely they'll address the physics problems mentioned above. They're aren't game breakers... they just cause some frustration and eye rolling.

The controls are very unpolished, making combat and platforming a chore.  The developers seem to realize that the controls are incredibly difficult to use with any degree of precision because it seems that they have designed the levels and the combat AI to take advatage of this.
Examples:
Damage Plate environmental hazards that send you pinballing around the level if you so much as brush against one, placed where you would have to have precise control to get through them without dying or getting bounced back to the start half-dead.  The controls are the type where if you try to turn around you end up sprinting in the opposite direction.
The combat AI spams quick special attacks and regular attacks like a 6 year old in a fighting game.  Just sitting in the corner spamming ranged attacks so that you can't get to it.  The melee variants aren't any better as the computer doesn't have the controls to contend with and can just jump right behind you and start pummeling you while you're still locked in the delay after an attack.  Not that they need to do that.  Almost any enemy attack seems to cancel out any attack you're in the middle of, even at the point of contact.  You can be in the middle of attempting a combo and start getting annihilated like you were standing still.  I say attemping a combo because every attack in this game has a delay either before or after it's performed, so there really isn't any way to chain a combo.  It's all hit and run tactics, which makes every fight, through every level drag on.

If you have a controller and are looking for a fun platform, you should pick this one up. Great feel to movement and combat, colourful visuals, fun interchangeable part system, and it costs peanuts. Peanuts!

-The AI is stupid, and higher difficulty levels only give them resource boosts instead of actually making them manage their stuff better. It's the reason I stopped trying to build federations, because not only do they all f**king hate eachother after a while (YOU'RE ALLIES NOW, GOD DAMN IT!  YOU F**KERS COMPLIMENT EACHOTHER'S FLAWS, YOU PIECES OF S**T! YOU WERE COOL WITH EACHOTHER BEFORE, WHY ARE YOU LIKE THIS) and they are s**t at managing the Federation Fleets, all of that not being worth the naval cap and influence costs. I haven't had any problems with the sector AI, but that's because I only give them the right to upgrade their buildings.
-Combat is Doomstack vs Doomstack. Just get the thing with the biggest numbers and you'll win. The only strategy that exists is, when you're in a system with various enemy fleets, try to aggro only one at a time and try to steer clear from stations until you've killed the fleets.
-Building bigger ships is just not worth it. Just spam corvettes. Give them missiles on the front and something with shorter range but higher dps in the other slots. Upgrading them is only worth it if you have a low naval cap and you need higher numbers with the same amount of ships (and you have the minerals to spend. Get a corvette building station in your spaceports when you can, as it makes your maxxed out corvettes ALMOST worth the cost). Plus, an all corvette fleet means that, whenever you lose one ship, you lose very little fleet power, while with bigger ships, lose one, and your Doomstack becomes a lot less... uh... Doomy.
-Even though most tech ramps up decently (being mostly percentage based), the ship part tech does not. It should ramp up harder to make the extra costs worth it.
-Unity becomes useless late game. There should be a way for it to be useful after you have all the traditions, like, 1% of produced unity starts going into influence or resource production or something. The first case would make it easier for late game diplomatic players, since all the pacts and alliances and stuff drain a huge amount of influence. The second case would make it easier for late game warmongers (although the influence case would also apply for them, as integrating vassals is expensive).
-I was going to b**ch about Hive Minds having to spend Unity on Traditions that are useless for them and their event descriptions sounding like they're just like every other regular empire, but they're fixing that next patch. Still, Hive Minds being universally disliked makes me sad. What if I just want to be friends with everyone? *sadface*
So, with all these flaws, why did I buy it? Well, because the devs are actively trying to make the game better by working out bugs and balancing stuff, and I both wanted those improvements as soon as they're live and I wanted to support the devs to help them continue to improve the game. Would I buy the Base + Utopia for full price? Not right now, no. But it's definitely worth the cost during the sales.
So, get it on your wishlist, buy it when on sale and have fun.

For some reason I feel a bit of "sword art online/portal" vibe going on. Not only is the storyline great, but the fast paced gameplay and puzzles tie together make this a pretty solid game. In simple terms, I'm not bored and believe me, I do get bored easily. This game will make you think and use that thing upstairs we call a brain. Time to get the hamster wheel spinning.

• If you're looking for high resolution graphics and mainstream 3D technology, you won't find that here, instead you'll find old school graphics that might bring back some memories of the great RPG era of the 90's. Remember Chrono Trigger, Thousand arms and Lunar? It will be a nice dosage of nostaglia. Just let soak in…  :)

• I will be updating this review when I have completed the game in full. As I've mentioned, this game is interesting, fun, challenging, fast paced and includes a great storyline to keep players coming back. I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of RPG, puzzle solving, Sci-Fi, fast paced, action games.   5/5

Deadly Premonition is a flawed masterpiece. If you are not computer savvy and comfortable with troubleshooting, installing mods and tweaking files, this game is not for you. No matter what hardware configuration you have, you will run into technical issues. These can usually be overcome, but it will require extra effort on your part.
Still with me? Well, on top of the technical issues, the game gives off a pretty bad first impression. The controls feel awkward, the graphics are unimpressive and the early part of the game seems like a lackluster knock-off of Resident Evil or Silent Hill. So, is it really worth all of the trouble? Absolutely!
If you can push past the shortcomings, the game opens up and becomes a delight. The characters in Deadly Premonition are fully developed and the deeper you dig, the more you'll find out about them. The town feels alive and has a quirky charm about it. The people and places all have a schedule they follow, so you can uncover interesting situations and events depending on when and where you encounter them.
The story is offbeat and absorbing. This is the kind of memorable game experience that will stick with you long after you've finished playing. I can't recommend it highly enough, but only if you think that you can deal with the technical issues and the rough start.

TL;DR funny idea, boring gameplay
The idea behind the game is fun, but the mechanics are boring. I'd have had just as much fun reading about the mechanics than playing it, which I did. Don't get me wrong, it was fun naming a grayscale picture of a butt "Steve will buy anything", and selling it to an old guy named Steve. But after 45 minutes of selling fourty-four poor mspaint quality drawings (according to my Steam Achievements), I had to Alt+Tab out of the game to see if I was playing right, and if there was actually anything else to do. There was no sense of progression, and no indication of progression to be made.
It turns out there is a branching path based on who you impress with your paintings. You learn your audience (old guys like one style, punks like another), paint the paintings that they like, and the game moves you on to a new gallery with new people to impress. However the game doesn't tell you this at all. The only reward structure was "make money" so that's what I was doing. I was appealing to both of the audiences as a highly successful street artist, and the game didn't know what to do with me.
Once I read about how to move on, I booted the game back up and settled in to create more terrible paintings. But then I realized, I already got the joke, and that's all the game had to offer. "Minimalist AI likes when you paint like x; the expressionist AI wants you to paint like y; appease this algorithm to move on in the game." The game itself wasn't fun, just the idea of it was fun.
The one thing that would have kept me going is to get a gallery of the paintings I pooped out, just so at the end of the game, I got the payoff of watching Passpartout's style change to the whims of the AI. I just want to see a painting of a grayscale butt called "Steve will buy anything" just one more time.
Just don't get this game.

Mehhhhhhhh. This was okayish. Essentially, this game has a couple of preset encounters which your team of soldiers must defeat. You've got tanky soldiers, archers, mages, healers and mobile knights which you control on a battlefield. The main gameplay comes from the tactical decisions you make on the battlefield, such as positioning, target prioritisation, and advancement. The tactics portion of the game is sound as long as you avoid the trap choice classes.
Some of the classes are poorly conceived. The dancer is the big example: she looks useful in concept, but in practice her usefulness is severely limited due to context. She's a melee unit designed to do additional damage when hitting enemies from behind, but is too fragile to be wandering out into the enemy backlines herself. If battles were smaller in scale and you could hold down the enemy frontlines more easily to protect her, she might have been more useful. As it is, she's a poorly designed trap choice which is especially useless in sieges.
But I digress. Other than that, the game's encounter designs are decent and the tactical considerations are fairly good. I completed the game, but I have zero intention of a second playthrough. Many people compare this game to Battle Brothers. But in reality they are not so much alike as you would think. Yes, both games about mercenaries, both uses tactical combat and random number generator (RNG) to determine if you hit your target or not. But otherwise they are two different game. You can watch videos about both, so you can see for yourself. I like both games very much.
But let's see Warbanners.
This is a classical fantasy game, so there are humans, orcs, undeads, monsters, elves, dwarves. In your army you can use humans, elves and dwarfes. There are about 15-16 different units to choose from. Meele, ranged, magic wielder, horse rider. They have special skills and they level up after enough XP.
Apart from them there are heroes too. Additionally you can buy assistants - they help mostly at the beginning of the battle, f.e.: kill one random enemy; curse the enemies, etc.
The maximum of your army is 16. But in certain battles you have allies too so there will be even more soldier on your side (but the player doesn't control the allies). However this maximum size is reached in the game later, at the start you have about 5-6 mercs and you will be able to hire more at certain points of the story. (But you can fire your soldiers and hire new ones anytime).
The missions are mostly linear (sometimes there are multiple choices but these are rare - and there is an arena which is independent from the story). Practically you play through about 42 pre-defined battles (the enemy and the battlegrounds are the pre-defined not your band).
The battlegrounds are well detailed - with trees, hills, objects (f.e.: gunpowder barrel, fallen tree trunk), houses, walls, etc. You can (and have to) use your environment to your advantage. There are different environs too: forest, swamp, riverside, town, castle, caves. Some objects are destructible - a fallen tree can cause serious damage. There are siege missions too (both on the defensive and offensive side).
You can use different tactics to win. I find the cautious, defensive approach easier than outright attack but sometimes you are forced to go forward as fast as you can.
You can use potions during bottles - heal, mana, fire (to be able to see in the night - or burn some enemies), poison, rage (to become berserker), purification (negates all effects) and more. And of course your magic wielder can use spells. They are the classics: fireball, heal, etc. There are some special equipment too.
Maybe at first the game seems hard (even in easy) but later you will realize your tactical options and it will be very enjoyable even with difficult battles. Many are the complaints about the RNG. Yes, it sometimes seems very unfair. But I don't think that the AI is cheating. I have killed strong enemies with 20 percent chance-to-hit in very dangerous moments. And yes, blotched a sure killer hit with 90 percent. But a good tactic is so much important than pure luck, so you will not lose only because a few hit goes aside. Reading the manual (press 'h' ingame) is strongly recommended (same goes for the ingame tips).
After a battle your mercs will heal instantly and there will be no permanent injuries.
Currently I am playing the easy difficulty but I will play normal after that. So I find it replayable - I will use my collected wisdom next time and most definitely will try out other units too.

I'm not gonna lie, Paladins is a game that is very similar to overwatch. With the rapid success of Overwatch, it is clear to see why people would try to mimic this game. Although the games are similar, they aren’t exactly the same. Like Overwatch, Paladins is an action packed first person shooter with various playable characters. The main difference would be that Paladins’ story focuses on a more medieval time era instead of the more futuristic and scientific one that Overwatch follows. It is clear that the developers(Hi-rez) wanted Paladins to be it’s own identity and not a comparison to something else. They focused on improving the aspects of the genre which Overwatch ignored. Doing so, paid off. Paladins offers a greater range of playstyles that the players can enjoy, AND, best of all, it’s completely free.
My first experiences with the game were very enjoyable. The game had easy-to-learn, hard-to-master controls which made me a little more invested in the game. You can either practice your aiming against bots in the game’s training room, or you can try to fight against other players in the ranked or unranked online matchmaking. The matchmaking queue time are pretty quick and each game lasts around 15 minutes. With over 120 hours into the game in the past month, I think it’s safe to say that I’m pretty addicted to the game.
The developers are doing an amazing job at maintaining the game and providing the players with new content frequently. The fact that they’ve made such a great game for free, shows how much effort they’ve put into it. If you’re ever bored at home, and would like a quick game to invest a little bit of your time into daily, show Hi-Rez some love, and download Paladins.

Hey ! Here's a noob's (30 something hours of playtime) review about this game, which happens to be my first ever MOBA/MOBAFPS.
Compared to other players, I have never played Overwatch, so I won't compare.
Let's go.
General Feeling :
I like it. But before going further, remember that the game is still in BETA, so yeah, there are a few problems. You should expect it. Server failures, ups and nerfs, not many game modes (3 that are pretty much the same objective-based gameplay, + one that's more of the same but on unfinished maps)... If you don't pay right of the bat, you'll only have a few champions available at first. Which is both good and bad; Players not willing to play will really train with their favorite champions and get to know their playstyle. But if you don't find what you like in the first six or seven starting champions, you're going to feel trapped until you can buy another one with Gold. And that may take quite a few games. And even then, since you haven't tried your new champion, you're gonna hope it suits your needs.
Community :
I've read some topics on the official forum to try to get to know the community. Some say it's less toxic than in other MOBAs. I don't know. Very few players talk in game, and there's only one who was nice to his team and tried to give them advice and general information. All the others were like "omg noobs sh*t team unranked ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (even though we were in casual matches)" etc. I haven't tried ranked matches, because I'm fairly confident I'm not good enough yet. I've never expected much of MOBAs communities, so there's no surprise for me there.
Gameplay :
Three modes that are basically the same; Payload, Siege, and Onslaught. All three require standing in the objective area to score points while fighting off the other team. Granted, said like that, it may seem boring. But boy, do the fights get intense sometimes. I haven't counted, but there are close to 30 champions, each able to build a deck of cards to boost their abilities, allowing for champion-gameplay tweaking. You want a Sniper that'll rip a new hole to a tank with his pistol ? Well you can have that. A tank that regenerates health when his shields are up ? Be my guest. That means that each time you encounter the same ennemy or allied champion, you'll have to adapt to which abilites the player choosed to boost. All of this combines in fast paced, tense matches. Although, if you're playing against an organized team while you just joined a bunch of randoms, you're almost certain to loose.
Also, you'll sometimes encounter a very frustrating thing : players obsessed with kills. That translates as no support or tank in a team, or tank/supports leaving the objective to chase down kills. And that can turn a hard-won victory in a frustrating loss in the blink of an eye.
Originality :
I have mixed feelings here. Some champions are really original in their desing and abilities; a dinosaur with a rocket launcher, or a fiery king who throws bombs everywhere.. But others, oh god. Generic CoD soldier ? Check. Generic knight who can deploy a huge shield ? Where have I seen that before. I won't talk about game modes. They're all the same. Although I expect it is only because the game is still in BETA.
Do you need to pay :
No. Paying gets you faster access to champions and cosmetics. That's it. Anything else can be obtained by simply playing.
Should you try this game :
I think you should give it a chance. Since, you know, it's free and all that. Personnally, I like it. I don't have friends willing to play it with me, so I join with randoms and still manage to have a lot of fun. I expect it is even better playing with friends.

What NieR:Automata does right is taking a very fluid combat system and implements it into different genres of games.
The story telling is rich and will leave a lot of questions unanswered, but later on will come to a conclussion if you will continue to play the game.
And this is where the beauty of NieR:Automata comes in.
The game does not end when you complete it the first time with the main character 2B.
What NieR:Automata does exceptionally well is trying to project the many social constructs that exists in our real world and try to implement them into a fictional scenario where the world is overrun with robots and try to do the exact same thing.
Things such as religion, monarchs and simple things such as family.
It is beautiful in its own way and without spoiling anything, please for the love of God play the game multiple times, even after the first 3 endings.
Or as Pod 042 would say: "Proposal: Play the game multiple times".
Definitely tugged my heartstrings more than once and the voice acting is so good.
Give it time, it'll be better.
Some of the voice actors really put in the extra effort and is definitely shown at times where the voice  acting is just so good that it is almost haunting.
And you cannot review this game without talking about the music.
The music and sounds in this game is beyond compare.
As MagikarpUsedFly said in his NieR:Automata ACTUAL Game Spotlight: "It is if Undertale came inside your ear and told you not to assume it's gender".
It is just that good.

The gang from Penny Arcade are back in this sequel. And as such, here's a review!
Story- You return as your created character (if you wish) and in trying to rebuild your home after saving the world, Gabe and Tycho return (again destroying your house) and beg for your aid in their latest supernatural case. Again, you now travel around the city looking for a new place to live while saving the world from a tyranical (and fruit-horny robot god). Again, following the same gothic, lovecraftian style of comedy and horror, the story draws you into its world and its characters. But, as in the first game, it will only do so for a couple of hours before the credits roll. A-
Graphics- The game is exactly the same as its predicessor. Nothing truly great but works well with what it's got. D+
Sound- The voice actor for the narrator still does a terrific job and still has that dry wit. Music is recycled from the first game, not a bad thing but nothing really new either. C-
Gameplay- Still needs a controller option and still suffers the same problems. The battles are similar but the mini games that powers up the special attacks are different, which is good. Not an improvement but switches things up a bit. C
Overall- I kinda got lazy with this review but really, it is a continuation of the first game so I really can't say anything new about it. It's fun, and I like the fact that you can transfer your created character from the first game. Also, it does keep you intrested in it and makes you want to see what happens in the next episode. So... buy it and enjoy. C

A lot of the missions can be cheesed in some way. For example, there's one where you have to take the top floor off of a building and make sure as little rubble as possible falls on the sidewalk. You're supposed to carefully destroy it with the long-arm jackhammer machine.
Instead, I used the machine's arm as a ladder, went up there myself, dropped as many explosives as I could, and blew up. Stellaris is an amazing game, full of replayability and enjoyment for hours. The race creation is fun to play around with and making new combinatons to play as is quite interesting. Although it can be daunting at first to new comers to this type of game and somewhat confusing to people who have played some strategy games before (I can say I was confused myself) I found that trial and error is your friend in this game. Always start small if you're confused, play a tiny 4 player galaxy, turn off additional features like end game crisises and fallen empires and when you feel comfortable, kick it up a notch. Play around with government types and traits, find which suit you the best. It took me a long time to find my favorite playstyle and even with 300+ hours I still find new things or ways to make it more efficient. There is also a LOT of potential for roleplayers and from what I've seen and experienced, the community for this game is very nice and accepting of new or unexperienced players.
TLDR:
Stellaris is a fun game, I reccomend the game highly but strongly suggest you to give it time to grow on you.
