Warbanners is a delightful experience for fans for turn based strategy games.  As a bonus this one has an RPG system as well.  You recruit members of your mercenary group from a expanding role of classes varying from knights, archers, mages, rogue type, horsemen, etc.  Each char has a set of skills that you get to choose 1 of 3 to improve with each level and each char can carry 1 artifact (gear).  You play looking overhead at a hex divided map.
The stages can vary from land, to water/swamp, towns, forests and even boasts a night/day into the missions which will change your strategy.  For example, if you are human you get bonuses in day light but at night the skeletons and vampires get bonuses so you can light fires, use potions and cast spells to turn it against them.  Putting a skeleton or vampire in light makes them lose bonuses.
I actually beat this game on my first play through although i admit i had to use the cheat codes for the final battle to level my chars up a bit before i could beat it.  The last mission is a beast but the rest of the game is pretty well balanced and challenging enough to keep you going.  I had to replay a few battles through my play through.
It took me 27.9 hours and some was not actual play time so it can run a bit on the short side considering there are no other modes or campaigns to play.  Its also sometimes not clear if the next mission is a side mission or main story mission as doing the main story mission will progress the map and it seems you can miss a few side missions this way.  Probably my biggest gripe.
I dont see much reason to play through again except to possibly do the  few quests i didnt get to or choosing different dialogues to see the different results.  The story was fun and well written.  I enjoyed reading Roderick's run through this.
Overall a pleasant experience and i hope to see it expanded on in the future.  I do recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of turn based, grid rpg's.

I just finished the campaign on this the other day and this is an easy recommend. Hex, turn-based strategy battler. There's a decent selection of unit types and some unique heroes you have to keep in your party. Units have their own inventory and can sport a single piece of equipment. In battle it plays similarly to Wesnoth (without the in-battle recruitment). Also, between battles, you'll resurrect dead party members, hire more party members and buy potions/assistants. In this regard, I'd argue that the gold you have to spend is rather limited and the options for what you can buy seem a bit limited as well. A lot of reviews I've read mention the difficulty and I agree that the difficulty for this game is quite hard. Part of the difficulty stems from the degree to which hits rely on a straight percentage roll, and the Random Number Generator (RNG) here can cost you some battles, even when your strategy is sound. That can be frustrating, but it's not a deal-breaker.
Pros:
Good campaign
You can name each unit
Units have inventory
Battles are all challenging
Strategy and positioning matter
Cons:
Only one campaign, with very specific rewards and progression, so limited replayability appeal
Some battles lost due to especially poor RNG despite strategy
Somewhat limited strategic options as far as party composition and equipment, more flexibility would be better
This game could be vastly improved with a couple changes: a campaign builder tool and more diversity of things available to purchase (armor, weapons, scrolls, other unique heroes, inventory slots, spells, army slots, etc.).

Fear of piracy is not a valid reason to treat your paying customers poorly. This review regards the port quality, not the quality of the game itself. This game is broken in a technical sense on PC. If you own a PS4 you should probably buy that version instead.
I pre-ordered this game out of a desire to support Yoko Taro and Platinum, despite knowing from past performance that Square Enix would inevitably botch this port, but I'm still amazed. From its month-delayed release on PC, this game has still yet to be patched, which as of November 28, 2017, has been 256 days. Square Enix has abandoned this game. This game still has Denuvo implemented despite the version in use being cracked; strong DRM should not be an excuse to avoid making the necessary fixes a port requires, either before, or especially after it's been cracked, if the company respects the integral content of their own product, and their paying customers.
This game is plagued by a wide range of technical problems. In addition to the poor performance mileage for your hardware, avoid this game if you run an AMD GPU, or specifically a GTX 780 or GTX 780 Ti; the game is prone to going into a state of White Screen of Death for hardware configurations including those GPUs, however other Nvidia GPUs are not immune. They still have not patched basic things, like rendering at 1080p fullscreen without upscaling from 720p, that have a fan-patch (FAR by Kaldaien & co.; if you buy this game you need this); the fan-patch, unfortunately, does not fix everything. They still have not patched more in-depth problems that there is no hope of a fan-patch fixing because it would require source access, like botched implementations of graphics elements that have been around for multiple generations, and as evidenced by the widespread WSOD issue, basic hardware compatibility. If you decide to go ahead with this purchase, I hope it works for you, but for your own sake, keep an eye on the refund clock.
Square Enix is aware of these issues, and by their own claim are 'investigating' them, however I have no confidence that they will make good on it, because that would involve them spending more than nothing. The Nier Automata available from delayed-launch will in all likelihood be the same Nier Automata available after a year, and the same Nier Automata available after a decade, except the online elements will probably be shut off by then. If the game will run on your current hardware, now's probably the best time to play it, because with the amount of compatibility trouble this game has with existing hardware that they theoretically tested on, I've got this worry that it might not work at all with future hardware. When it comes to PC, Square Enix is a brand you can trust, to deliver a broken game.

Megabyte Punch is the love-child of Mega Man and Super Smash Brothers, and does both parents proud.
I bought the game entirely on a whim and I am so glad I did as it has rapidly taken a place among my favorite games of all time. A little bit about where I'm coming from: I'm a 30-something that grew up on side-scrolling platformers like the original Mega Man series for NES as well as couch coop beat-em ups like Streets of Rage.  Very few games can scratch that itch these days, and this game manages to do that with an engaging adventure mode which has you working your way through various open ended stages and an arena mode with some of the most satisfying competitive play you'll find anywhere. Both modes can be played with between 1-4 players so grab your friends, a controller, a beer and be prepared to be entertained.

The combat is very much like Smash Brothers in that you don't just die after receiving a set amount of damage. Instead, the more damage you take makes it easier for you to be flung further and faster with each hit you take. Take a hit that launches you into a wall hard enough or off the stage and you blow up spectacularly. I cannot stress enough how satisfying it is to roundhouse kick an enemy through a wall and watch him break into bits on the rock behind it. This goes doubly so for launching your friend's character into orbit when they are sitting next to you on the couch and you can observe their reaction in real time!
The adventure mode's premise is that you are a digital being call a "Megac" born from something of a super computer called the Heartcore to protect your village. You quest through various large stages, each with multiple paths to the finish and a reasonable difficulty curve. Exploration is both highly encouraged and rewarded with goodies being hidden in unorthodox places that the keen observer (or just plain lucky) will find. As you destroy enemies there is a chance that they will drop one of their "parts" similar to how Mega Man can absorb defeated bosses powers but with a much higher degree of customization. As a Megac, you can take those parts and customize yourself on the fly creating various builds you can switch as the need arises. Your Megac is made up of a head, shoulders, core, hips, two arms and two legs. Each one of these can be customized making for characters that play wildly different from eachother. These parts can either buff a particular attribute of your Megac or provide a special ability. Bosses at the end of stages make for good challenges as well as dropping rare parts unique to them.
Multiplayer is an arena affair with all of your custom Megacs squaring off in a variety of floating platforms. All of the combat mechanics are the same, although certain parts become more useful in this setting than the adventure mode. A very skilled player will have no issues using any of the parts, however.
From a mechanical standpoint, the first time I booted up the game the controls felt a little "floaty." I realized that the reason for this is the game defaults to using an analog stick for movement which is different from my Mega Man/Smash Brothers muscle memory I have built up over the years by using the d-pad.  Having that much more throw in the control does take some getting used to and I suspect is the reason that some of these reviews say the platforming could use some work. Once you adapt to the difference or change your controls, you are fine.
For all that is great there are some criticisms I can level at the game. The elephant in the room is a lack of online multiplayer. At the time of development Team Reptile (who would later go on to make Lethal League) made the choice to forego online functionality as they weren't sure they could implement it to the standard the rest of the game was made. I'd love to see them revisit this title and add it now, as they most certainly have the expertise to do so. Also, there is the issue of unlocking parts. If you just buy this game now and sit down with your friends to play, you will have almost no parts to make your Megacs with because they are unlocked via the adventure mode. A "free vs." mode would have solved this issue entirely.
All in all, I can't recommend this game enough if you are okay with the caveats I have listed above. 9/10

A singleplayer MMO with lots of in-jokes (think RE:Zero).
This is a game about playing a game and all the MMO tropes are here (of course there is also some mystery about the character's background as she hasn't entered the game via the typical method).
The action is fast and fun (but circlestrafing and dodgerolling is always fun right?), the puzzles are rewarding and the levels have a lot of secret branching paths that are hidden in plain sight but require a bit of parkour to reach. The levels can be replayed at any time and you are free to explore the open world.
In fact, teleporting back to the start of the level and chaining together all of the enemies will boost your combat rating from D,C,B,A, all the way to S which means better item drops. As soon as you leave combat you get a short timer to start the next combat or you lose your rating. The rating pushes you to attack the next mobs even if they are harder and even if you're nearly dead and it can get really intense (as a death would put you back to the beginning).
There are even some elite mobs that will kill you in 2-3 hits that take a few mins to kill and are very reminiscent of Dark Souls bosses. The first one I found was a large dark blue hedgehog that spins to attack you (though he didn't have red shoes or white gloves).
The pixel art is really charming and the lighthearted music is amazing and varied. It definitely reminded me of classics such as Zelda and Alundra.

First time I heard about this game was somewhere in 2015. I played the demo and simply with that, I wanted to buy the game. But considering that the game is single player, is in early access AND it costs 20€, I was pretty sceptical about buying it. I mean, I had played the demo and I was confident that the quality of the game is amazing. It's just that I was afraid I'd be paying for a single player experience that'll get finished sometime in 2 or 3 years, at which time I'd already be bored with the game and not even bother playing the full version. So I decided to wait until it was out of early access... And considering that I already own the game and have played a few hours of it, you can probably tell that my impatience got the  better of me.
And what was the experience like? Well, it's as I assumed: a very fun action RPG with a colorful world and a cast of characters that you'd swear you've met and loved in any other MMORPG you've ever played... But as the game is in early access, the story leaves something to be desired. They ARE working on it, but know that the story is only added in little by little with some updates. It's not a bad thing, I mean you ARE getting the story and all. It's just that if you're planning on getting the game, know that you might have to wait a month or two or three just to get another piece of the story. It would be the only reason I wouldn't recommend the game yet, but the game itself is so much fun that I can't just not recommend it.
But that's not to say the story is bad. Absolutely not. It's just not finished, and seeing that this is a game in early access, that's to be expected. So if you want the full experience of CrossCode, my recommendation is that you play it when it comes out of early access for the full experience all at once. The problem with that is that if you don't have the patience to do that and you want to get this game, you'll probably go crazy because of the wait like I did.
On the other hand, you could jump on the development train and become involved! Buy and play the game, then report any bugs or typos or whatever to the devs and help them make CrossCode the masterpiece it deserves to be. Devstreams happen almost every week, so you can head over to Radical Fish Games Twitch channel on Sunday at 11am (PST) / 20:00 (CET) if you're interested in how the game is coming together.
All in all, CrossCode is a gem that, in my opinion, is on it's way to becoming a masterpiece. I know I haven't talked about the gameplay itself, but trust me when I say that it's fast, intense and extremely fun. The only thing I regret about buying CrossCode is that I bought it in a bundle for merely a fraction of CrossCode's original price. Gonna have to change that soonish: Going to wait until the sale on the game ends and buy it full price to support the devs.
It may still be in early access, but it's worth every penny of it's base asking price. I guarantee it.

-More Borderlands: The gameplay, atmosphere, and loot hunting goodness is pretty much identical to Borderlands 2, may or may not have come from laziness on the dev's part, but I loved BL2 so much I don't really care.
-Great New Playable Characters: The new "Vault Hunters" are fantastic and the addition of voice lines in response to NPC's dialog makes each of them feel much more unique, alive, and involved in the story than the playable characters in BL2 did.
-Creative skill trees: One of my favorite skill trees in BL2 was the siren's "harmony" tree, which was geared towards supporting your friends in co-op play. Most (if not all) of the playable characters in The Pre-Sequel have similar skill tree options that allow you to synergize with allies in co-op.
-Weak Story: I started to type up an in depth summary of this point, but it ended up being a 3 paragraph rant, so here's a brief summary instead: The main story of the game is filled with plot holes, contrived conflicts, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ portrayals of beloved characters, and uninteresting and abnoxious new characters. It reminds me a lot of the prequels to another popular sci-fi franchise...
-The Oxygen Mechanics: The double jumps are cool. The glides are cool. The "butt slams" are fantastic. But the fact that you constantly have to run around refilling your oxygen is annoying as hell. It's one of those terrible mechanics that doesn't make the game any more difficult (you only lose like 1% of your HP per second when you're out of O2), it just slows it down and makes it more tedious.
-Boring Locations: This is one that really killed the game for me. Some of the locations in BL2: Frozen Tundra, Deserts, Highlands, Volcanos. There was actually some interesting stuff going on there. Compare that to the locations in The Pre-Sequel: empty grey-blue expanse of moon, empty grey-blue expanse of moon with some lava, empty grey-blue expanse of moon with some glowing purple eridian stuff. I never realized I cared about the background in which I shot psychos in the face, but after about 8 zones that are slight variations of "abandoned factory on the moon", saying it gets a bit monotonous is an understatment.
This is one of those games where Steam's whole "yes or no" system of reviewing doesn't really work. Overall I'd say it's unfortunately one of the worst games in the Borderlands series, but is still worth playing. If you haven't played Borderlands 2, then
go buy that instead. If you're a fan of the Borderlands series and want more baddies to shoot and guns to loot, it's worth picking this up on sale.

tl;dr: There are too many things wrong here to recommend this.
Note: Don't be fooled by the time Steam shows for me playing this. I have played at least 20 hours of this.
I really, really wanted to like this game. Most of the things written I noticed just two missions into the game, but I kept on playing, hoping things would improve. They didn't.
It should be right up my alley: Turn-based, RPG touch, challenging.
For someone having played the hell out of games like XCOM, Battle Brothers, Temple of Elemental Evil and the like, this should be a no-brainer to enjoy.
But quite honestly I cannot enjoy this: it is too random, too unfair, lacking too many features and due to some crazy design decisions downright painful to play at times.
I am playing on hard as usual in most games, but honestly there is little difference here between the difficulties. All hard does is add few enemies to an encounter and decrease the gold you get on level up.
It isn't unusual for enemies to outnumber you 1.5 or 2 to 1)
As someone else said, your enemies have mass stun, fireballs and other mass damage spells, trolls that hit like a truck, area attacks, pushing attacks, summoning, enemies that have nothing but damaging throwables as they do not need to keep their soldiers alive during an encounter, ....
Meanwhile, your basic soldier can attack or block. And the latter only every 4 rounds. The only thing separating your main character from a normal soldier is a bit higher armor and a rally cry. That's it.
Your archer can shoot an arrow, your priest heal and bless, etc.
Comparing to what your enemies have, you might as well lead a band of children.
That is your starting situation, and
If you want any chance in the game later on, you CANNOT lose your units. Sure, you can resurrect them, but that imposes penalties on their stats. So what you get when reviving is worse than buying a new unit - yet you don't have enough gold to keep buying lots of new units. And there is no way to grind a bit to recover from losses as in Battle Brothers.
So you need to do anything to keep everyone alive. Which means buying health potions, which means your strangely limited potion slots (1!!!! per normal frontline soldier) are filled with things that do not really help you defeat your enemies.
The base hit chance in this game is 50%. I kid you not.
And then come all the negative modifiers like being cursed, out of stamina, low on morale, etc.
There are also positive modifiers, but good luck ever seeing a hit chance higher than 70-75% after some rounds of battle. Attacking from flanks is helpful - but downright impossible in most battles due to the enemy vastly outnumbering you on top of a better starting position to begin with.
It is painful to watch. Miss, miss, miss, hit, miss, miss, miss, miss, hit... Jesus! Have you ever met a person enjoying watching his units fail? I haven't. This is WAY worse than moments in XCOM.
The game also lacks an UNDO feature (at the very least for movement) and actions do not need to be confirmed.
If you are like me, extremely fast clicking in games in general, this game will force you to be patient in no nice manner.
I have lost count of the number of times I accidentally moved my still-selected last unit to some spot or attacked an enemy while I wanted to move next to it.
Here is
- or rather, the biggest letdown:
You cannot save during combat, only on the campaign map. Again, I'm not kidding.
I'm not against some sort of iron man mode for people who enjoy that. But here, every combat is in itself FORCED iron man mode.
Got to a good position after 5 rounds or so, wanting to save so that you can continue from there if RNG screws you badly? Nope.
Misclick in a tough fight that has just cost you more than half an hour of play time? Tough luck!
Adding all of these things together, you are left with an experience that is just thoroughly unenjoyable.
If the developer ever adds a saving feature to battles, I'd actually recommend this (though barely so, there are still all the other points).
But as long as that doesn't happen, I cannot in good conscience recommend the game.

A hardcore Turn-Based-Tactics game with average gameplay and a lot of flaws.
The plot is simple. Orcs are invading your country. Necromancers raise dead. You are commander of the small mercenary squad. You need to raise your power and save everyone.
There are 2 parts of the game: 1) Preparation menu where you can upgrade/hire troops, buy potions, change equipment and hire assistants. 2) Battle part where you need to eliminate your enemies in the Turn-Based Combat
Let's start from the battle. Your squad is about 7-16 units. You start with 7 at the first mission. Each unit has action points. Unit can move/attack/cast a spell. When AP endsyou should control another unit. There is an annoying battle system. Each unit has Accuracy and Evasion parameter. Chance of the hit equals 50% + (accuracy - evasion)*5% + other factors. In the game it appears that all units miss a lot. Sometimes it is like "Miss, miss, miss, hit, miss, miss, miss, miss, hit..." and etc. It's irritating often.
There are also a lot of other parameters (morale, stamina) and other mechanics (light, obstacle, swimming). Each unit has different abilities (passive usually) like Giant killer (+4 damage against huge monsters), regeneration, Heroic Cry (gives morale to allies), Vampiric strike and etc. There are a lot of spells like Heal, Massive Heal, Fireball, Smoke Screen, Ice Circle and etc.
So, actually the battle contains a lot of depth. So it could be really good. But I found Accuracy/Evasion mechanic is really a spoon of tar. I would prefer to see Critical strikes and 1 damage strikes instead of misses. Also, it increase the time of the battle and make it less dynamic.
When battle finishes all units get exp. When unit gets lvl up you can improve 1 of 3 skills for him (health, damage, stamina, morale and etc). At the 5 lvl an unit can gets new ability. If unit died in the battle you can resurrect him with a small constant stat reduction.
So the whole game is a big loop: 1) Battle 2) Resurrection/Hire phase 3) Upgrading and item picking 4) Read preview text on the global map 5) Battle again.
It could be a good game, but it cost 20 $. The game is not enough good for 20$

This has to be the... best tower defence game I've played.. ever.
The amount of options you have when it comes to upgrading skills, the way you can combine gems(gems are you towers, for anyone who hadn't figured that out), the talisman system and the way of how you unlock levels is awesome.
And hey, achievement collectors, get ready to collect 419 achievements.
In my personal opinion this game is completely fleshed out, the gameplay experience is great, no flaws, as far as I am concerned, after 15 hours of gameplay.
This games risk-reward system is amazing, you can bomb levels that are about to come with gems to enrage the level, increasing the HP, amount of monsters and amount of armour they have, but you gain mana(Mana is your 'money' in this game)+XP for it, do you want to bomb 2 levels for some mana+xp and risk loosing or do you want to keep it safe? You can even build strategies on some levels around this.
The game also has traits, traits are some things you can bump up for each level, for example you can make all the monsters have more armour(scales from 1 to 7), you can make it so you only receive your mana earned every 10 seconds while playing, making levels come faster, up to 50% faster, in return for a large XP bonus multiplier, the game also has 3 different difficulties(difficulties are tied to each level, the entire game is not hard if you set it to hard, you set each levels difficulty).
This game handles the risk-reward system very good, it's absolutely brilliant, I was very impressed by that.
The actual gameplay is well paced(yes, the game has fast forward options), it keeps you entertained and it's very fun and oh man, it is very addicting.
The game has a story but it's not really that entertaining, every now and then you unlock 1 or more pages of lore/story/whatever you want to call it, each page is about 30 words long, in my experience all they do is add to the dark and grim atmosphere of the game, I'm not invested in an actual story like I am when I'm playing Walking Dead(an extreme example but you get the point).
9/10, amazing game, an absolute must buy if you're into tower defence games, I strongly recommend it if you want to dip your feet in a tower defence game for the first time as well.

One of the top Tower Defense games available today.
It easily sits alongside Defense Grid and Prime World: Defenders as one of my favourite examples of the genre.
Initially it may seem too easy and feature out-dated graphics, but to ignore it because of this would be a HUGE mistake. This is probably the deepest / most complex Tower Defense game available and has 100s of hours of play available should you want to explore its modes fully.
With a HUGE variety of towers, skills, maps and a couple of fascinating and rewarding additional gameplay mehcanics this provides you with almost endless variety.
The particular benefit this game offers is the ability to upgrade. You upgrade your skills, the towers available, the gameplay modifiers you can use (which each have numerous levels), your talisman (which features 100s of "perk" combinations on more than 20 fragments which randomly drop during games, all of which can be, themselves, upgraded, and have a significant impact on gameplay). Additionally there are well over 100 levels which can be played at 3 difficulties and indeed a whole alternate game mode which significantly alters the challenge / experience.
This game represents rare quality and value for money. Suffice to say I eagerly await a sequel!

As I searched through the Steam Catalogue, I chanced upon this gem, CrossCode. It was probably the most positively reviewed game on Steam at that time, so I wanted to see what it was all about.
This game is fast-paced yet very smooth to play, I never felt that I was overwhelmed with the action presented to me but rather it felt just right, not too difficult and not too easy.
The cast of characters on display were all very likeable. Quirks like Lea's (The Main Character) inability to speak coherently and can only blurt out words or phrases at certain points along with her multitude of interesting faces that she makes, brings extra life to the characters.
The areas are also really beautifully represented but there are still some undeveloped areas due to being an Early-Access title. However, I don't regret buying this game as I feel that it was worth my money helping this developer.
What I did not really like was that it was rather confusing to find where the NPC where specifically. The game would tell you the general area but not the exact coordinates, this meant that you would spend time rather uneconomically by just running around trying to find this NPC.
Anyway, if you liked Secret of Mana and the rest of the Seiken Densetsu games or Illusion of Gaia, you would most certainly would want this in your library as it shares its gameplay but with a much more modern and faster feel.

This game has a lot going for it: a perfect free-to-play model, tight/responsive controls, a massive amount of freedom of movement, and there's something for every kind of player here, both casual and competitive. There are so many different weapon combinations that are fun and absolutely over-the-top, but they're rarely as good as the stock weapons you start with, with absolutely no additional parts added to them. This means if you know how the game works and you can aim, you barely even have to spend much of the ingame currency (which can only be gained by playing, so no pay to win here) to compete with other players.
The game has some balance issues, but the devs are extremely responsive and very involved and communicative with the community. I really enjoyed the game and a lesson it helped me realize. No matter what kind of art you focused on, ultimately you were at the mercy of your critics. Nobody will buy your art if it doesn't fit their tastes. And the tastes can be random yet specific (some just don't like the color pink). Even if you paint what you want, eventually you will be recognized into a niche and criticized for deviating from it. As a hobbyist artist outside of the game, it helped me realize that a serious art career is not for me. This game actually helped me feel a lot better about some decisions I've made in my life, which is a rare feat.
Anyway, the game. Painting is relaxing, though it can get tedious because you are forced into a niche (for me, minimalism was especially painful). Customers base their opinions of your art on their own tastes and statistics on your painting methods (such as number and "craziness" of colors used, brush size, stroke length, and speed of stroke). Speed of stroke appears to dictate the craft vs. expression line. The next level is determined by the colors and brush size you use. Then you keep at whatever you did in act 2 to complete the game.
A button on the screen to name your piece allows you to save a screenshot of just the canvas.
Overall a good little game. Would like a future update with more brushes and bigger canvases for Endless Mode.

Surprisingly entertaining and fairly fleshed out game, considering it was originally made for the 3ds. The story itself stands on its own, and could probably work even without any links to the other games. In fact, the only real big links to the other games are a couple of series name drops, and of course Chris and Jill, who return for this installment, but could easily be substituted with any new protagonists.
On that note, while at first kind of cringing at some of the new characters introduced, many of them grow on you as the game continues. I think that this could be in part to do with the fact that they are so heavily involved in the plot of the game, which is how it should work. A good comparison for this is Sheva from Resident evil 5. Sheva, apart from existing to allow a coop option, is given no real reason to be there, yeah Chris is her partner, but that's all, and that's a big reson why she is very forgettable. Parker (Jill's partner in this game), on the other hand, begins this whay as we are introduced to him, but as we see in flashbacks and in encounters with Raymond, he has a reason to be there, which makes him, as a character, a lot more interesting.
In terms of inventory, I myself prefer the organisational layout of the attaché case in RE4, but I consider this layout of limiting to 3 weapons on hand at any one time, not bad. The return of item chests is very welcome, and complements this otherwise, very restrictive inventory, by allowing items, such as rocket launchers and magnums to be put away until needed without having to wait until a chapter end.
Gameplay itself is very much the same as previous installments, however you can now shoot/reload while walking, which I found hard to get used to, just out of habit, but once gotten used to, it's incredibly useful. One thing, I never really got the hang of was dodging which seems useful, but also seems to only work sometimes, I don't know, I may just be doing it wrong. I will say though, that ally AI is still broken as hell. They fire at enemies, but they seem to make very little actual difference in combat, which is sad to say, considering that it worked better in previous games.
Enemywise, there weren't many types of enemies, but it didn't bother me because they each had a very different style. I was however, very disappointed in the boss battles within the game. They seemed very awkward and out of place, to the point that they didn't really need to exist.
Overall, I found the game very entertaining and suspenseful, with a few minor quirks, which can easily be overlooked. The game felt more "actiony" than classic games in the series, but I think it needs a certain amount of that to not make people feel too uncomfortable while playing, while still remaining within the survival horror genre.

Megabyte Punch is an intriguiging mix of a traditional 2D platformer and a four-player fighting game. In fact, it was described to me as Custom Robo meets Super Smash Brothers. I have not played the former, but I can tell you that Megabyte Punch postively smacks of the latter: Damage to players is calculated as an increasing percentage, and you do not die unless you are launched out of the arena or level: however, the higher your damage percentage, the further you get knocked by attacks, and unlike Smash, you can be exploded if you slam into a solid surface fast enough. Also like Smash, the game is horribly balanced, favoring setups that use cheap, powerful weapons and players with the response time of a goddamn hummingbird. Multiplayer is likely a blast for someone who enjoys such, as I did not. However, I found the campaign a mostly enjoyable experience, thanks to MP's excellent music, colorful graphics and simplistic, but eye-grabbing art style. There is considerable depth of character customization. The wall-jump mechanic is a bit odd, however- no actual use of the jump button is involved, you need only push away from the wall if you are contact with it. I've never seen this anywhere else and I found it more awkward then not. However, the game's greatest flaw is by far its difficulty. The campaign starts out easily enough but across a mere six or so levels, quickly ramps up to a ridiculous degree, aggrivated by an archaic lives system in which they only way to acquire more is to gather 64 bits, the game's coins. I was unable to beat the final boss and had grown weary of the game well before that point. I am sure there is someone out there who can and has beaten him. But regardless, there is enough about the game I like to give it a thumbs up, but be warned: non-fighting gamers may want to pass on it completely.

I'm sorry that I recommended this game about a year ago when it was on sale on the humble bundle store for about $1. I thought they had put more effort into the port than they did. But as it turns out it's just yet another bad port. Bad in a way that only japanese studios that regret their decision to take console exclusive deals can do.
Got it running by breaking physx for other games on my system that link to it. Only to see that the resolution is hardcoded to 1280x720. I was aware of dpfix. But even though it evidently loads the symbols just fine (as indicated by not segfaulting) it just sits forever eating my cycles. Likely caused by a recent update.
There are people on the forums trying to defend these incompetent developers.  They shouldn't. They're only further ruining Steam. Having a quirky game that likes to have a bit of fun despite itself is one thing (and is why I came to want it in the first place) but having a buggy piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥maintained by incompetent developers is another, and believe me they are incompetent.
The fact that libs that override d3d9 symbols exist in the first place is evidence of that. As the complexity of the problem goes up so does the complexity of the override libs. But ones like these -though written by undoubtedly competent people- merely provide basic features that the game should have in the first place. Like adding a second step that adjusts resolution based on values given in a config file.
I was able to fix the issue causing the game to just sit there eating cycles and have it running in my native resolution. The positive:
1) The battle system is well made: It is both complex and yet quite simple and easy to understand the rules - you get full understanding of the mechanics quite fast. There are not to many(compared to other games) spells and abilities, each one is unique and to the point, so no clones like we see in most games. I found all the abilities to be useful, used all of them depending on the situation. The lighting system is a great feature, it adds to the depth of your tactics and gives you another element to plan and utilise in your favor.
2) Light RPG element: Each character has one slot for an artifact\item, on leveling you have a choice of how to further develop the character - increasing it's stats in certain categories will affect the way that it will perform. So if you develop a Swordsman with mostley upgrades to strength, he will be a very heavy hitter but he would not hit as often and would run out of stamina faster.
3) Manageable RNG: By that I mean that RNG does have a significant effect, but if you know the game mechanics you can manage the RNG and make things go the way you planned. There are no critical hits, so damage is predictable and can be calculated. What will determine victory will be your tactics and not some RNG critical hit that will ruin everything.
4) Old school style of game: For me this is a plus, maybe it is my age(33), but I really enjoy the graphics and setting, it takes me back to titles that I enjoyed. It is like Lords of the Realm which meets Heroes of M&M and combines with Kings Bounty and Baldurs Gate.
5) You need to be creative: It is not wise to charge straight into the enemy, that will almost always get you killed. Quite a few of the battles really make you look for a creative solution, and go through several attempts before victory.
Examples:
Learning the use of fire - for lighting and for blocking enemy units. Changing terrain by digging a ford in front of your line so that the enemy will be in a disadvantage when they close in. Building a baricade at a crucial spot so the enemy has to bypass around it or break it.
At least one mission is impossible to pass without charging one group of enemies, and then holding the line against the rest. I really enjoyed that one, standing in one spot would have caused me to be overwhelmed on all sides. Well constructed level which I greatly appreciate. A game that makes you think ;)
6) Replayability: Warbanners is liniar, but it has quite a few choices along the way, these choices can change the game significantly. Beside that, it is important what types of characters will you add to your band of mercenaries, there are many combinations will be very intresti9ng to try in another playthrough.
The Negative:
1) The Plot is quite weak and very simple, also at times a bit confusing. It is difficult to understand which character is speaking while reading the text. But I found myself laughing a couple of times.
2) Outdated graphics: I simply love this old school style! But I realise that it is not appealing for everyone.
To sum up:
If you are looking for a good tactical turn based game, this is a great choice! For it's price it is a bargain!
I bought TW: Warhammer 2 and I find Warbanners to be much more intresting and appealing for me, at one third of the price.
My final verdict: 8/10

Champions and roles
Paladins provides various characters, called champions, for the players to choose during their multiplayer sessions. Each of these champions fall into one of the following categories: Front Line, Damage, Support and Flank. Being a team-based shooter, players must rely on strategy, character knowledge, coordination and teamwork in order to attain victory. Players may use VGS, along with text and voice chat to communicate. A good team will have a balanced choice of classes that will support each other during the game.
Front Line: Champions who serve as the anchor of the team, holding the front and protecting their allies. With high health pools and shielding capabilities, Front Line champions excel at blocking enemy fire and disrupting enemy objective captures.
Damage: Champions who possess reliable and consistent damage outputs or large burst damage potential. Their damage, coupled with average health pools and decent mobility, make Damage champions ideal for skirmishes and extended firefights.
Support: Champions with high utility and healing abilities, the backbone of any team. Due to their healing capabilities that keep their allies in the fight, Support champions are invaluable allies.
Flank: Champions who excel at traversing the battlefield and getting behind enemy lines, eliminating vulnerable key targets. While most Flank champions are relatively frail, having lower health pools than any other role, their excellent mobility and self-sustain provide them with the means of escape and survival.
There are 31 champions in Paladins, 6 of which are available from the start for new players to choose. Additionally, 4 champions are also temporarily accessible for free on a fortnightly rotation. Players can permanently acquire additional champions through purchases using in-game currency. More are slated for release in 2017.
Game Modes
There are different gameplay modes for Paladins:
Siege: The 'main' Paladins game mode, teams are tasked first to capture the map's central capture point and, if successful, push a payload that spawns from it to the enemy base. This mode is played in a best-of-seven format.
Payload: An attacking team is tasked with escorting a payload through an extended railroad track to push it as far as they can, or to the end goal, while a defending team thwarts their progress. A push is halted if the both teams engage in combat near the payload and it slowly moves backwards if no one on the attacking team is nearby to push it, though push progress the team has accumulated is not lost. Once time runs out or if the payload is pushed to the destination, teams switch attack/defense roles. The winner is determined by the team that pushes the payload the furthest, with the attacking team setting the bar in the first round. If the attacking team in the second round are able to push the payload the same distance as the first team, the second wins the game.
Survival: Teams try to outlast each other on a relatively small map with no respawning until the next round, all the while avoiding deathly fog that closes in from the outer edges of the map. The fog deals percentage-based damage of a champion's health and negates all healing while a champion is in it, foiling long term stall tactics. The fog starts at the edge of the map, which starts closing in after a short delay until it reaches the map's epicenter, where any surviving champion are forced to do battle. This mode is played in a best-of-six format. This game mode was removed in OB 52.
Co-op: A player versus environment game mode, a team of five face off against an AI-controlled team that possess extremely large health and high damaging attacks, as well as modified abilities. The objective in each PvE map vary from capturing an objective in a Siege game (where the mode is simplified so that only capturing the point is necessary) or a Survival game. This game mode was removed in OB 49.
Onslaught: Teams do battle over a large combat area in an attempt to take point control and earn points. Along with holding an uncontested presence on the control point, slaying enemy players also scores points for the team, akin to a team deathmatch. Killing an enemy scores the team 5 points, while holding control over the combat area earns the team 1 point per second. The first team to reach 400 points, or the team with the most points after 10 minutes, wins the game.
Test Maps: An additional game mode accessible in the casual section. Players can play untested maps that may be implemented into the game and give their rating for the map. The objective for test maps vary between Siege and Onslaught, and the maps available are rotated every major patch.
Competitive
The Competitive game mode is unlocked for players once they have unlocked 12 champions and reach a player profile level of 15. Competitive only features the Siege game mode. However, at the start of the match, players must choose their champions one by one. First one player chooses. Then, two players from the opposing team choose. Then two players from the team opposing the last choose. This continues until the last player (from the team opposing the one that has first pick) has a role. This challenges the teams to try and counter-build each other by specifically choosing certain champions. Competitive games also affects a player's Competitive rating.

~Genre: Action game with survival horror elements
~Number of players: 1-2
~Completion time: 8-30 hours
~Multiplayer cooperation mode
~Originally a Nintendo 3DS title
~Downloadable content: available
+Atmosphere:
offers a combination of survival horror elements and action sequences. Explore an abandoned ship, read memos of former events, examine corpses, solve puzzles along the way, but be ready to survive a relentless undead assault at any moment.
+That music made my day: The soundtrack, (mostly consisted of zombie growls, victim screams and background music) being atmospheric and experimental, transforms
into an unforgettable experience. Headphone use strongly recommended. The soundtrack on Youtube by Canal de Redblogij:

+Cast of characters: The original duet (Jill Valentine-Chris Redfield) has returned for a new dance with the undead. At the same time, some of the newest cast entries are quite interesting (Parker, Cadet, Jessica, etc.) and would definitely benefit future
titles with their appearance.
+Enemies: Instead of your ordinary, slow, rotting zombies,
features a wide array of enemies, each with its own strength and weaknesses. Since the title revolves around an aquatic environment, your opponents were designed accordingly. Their forms are some of the best the series has ever presented.
+Chapter separation:
is divided into chapters. Each chapter offers new challenges and gives the player the opportunity to control different characters. Before each new chapter a summary of the previous one is shown, thus preventing the players from forgetting what has happened, in case they decide to play the game sporadically.
+Scanning system: “Genesis” is a unique equipment which scans your surroundings for hidden ammo, herbs and items. Also, scanning enemies has its benefits.
+Inventory system:
demands clever use of herbs (only 5 can be carried at a time), bullets and grenades. Inventory is at first limited but can be expanded by finding certain inventory parts or weapon mods. Such limitation not only rewards the conservative and clever combatants but enhances the feeling of survival horror throughout the game.
+Raid mode: The highlight of the game and the main reason you will be spending hundreds of hours on
. Similar to the infamous
mode of previous
titles,
presents a new challenge: Enemies with special abilities and different levels swarm various locations from the single player campaign and the player must kill them all or advance to the end of the stage. As if the ordinary Hunter weren't enough, how about facing a Hunter boss or a sneaky Hunter baby with increased attack rating and tiny frame? Don't forget to spend your Battle points in the store after each raid for new weapons, mods and unlockable characters.
also features online or local cooperation for whole family entertainment!
+Difficulty levels: Three difficulty levels to master. Having played almost all
titles, I can assure you that
can be hard and punishing to reckless players (during boss fights, for instance). Completing the game on the hardest difficulty is a great achievement, especially for hardcore gamers.
+Weapon customization: Scattered around the map are special modification parts which can be attached to your weapons. Searching for them adds to the exploration and motivates the player to search remote or dangerous areas. The combinations are limitless and you can always change equipped mods at the iconic storage boxes from previous
games.
-Voice acting: It was always an issue with
titles but that doesn't mean it should be considered a tradition. Dear voice actors, show some enthusiasm during the recording sessions!
-Finishing/melee moves feel coarse and restricting. The dodging mechanism, albeit crucial for the latest parts of the game, seems deferred and difficult to master.
-Respect the elderly:
aged somewhat badly. In all honesty, I didn't get the feeling Capcom paid any attention to graphically upgrading the PC port.
-Downloadable content of minor (or cosmetic) value.
-The not so legendary Chris Redfield: The single player campaign lacks the cooperation mode of
and the AI controlled companions are rather weak.
±Comparison to Nintendo 3DS :Albeit close to its older brother, I found the online matching search in
cooperation faster than that of the 3DS version. Other than that, the two versions are almost identical.

I just wanted to give a heads up about the current situation of the game.
In other reviews I read about problems with the game that I did not encounter when playing the game over the last weeks. It might have been patched or maybe there is new information on how to get the game running.
It should be clear that this is by no means a perfect port, but I was able to complete it with only running into some minor problems.
Over the near 20hours of playing I experienced a total of 4 crashes, 2 of which where that DP.exe stopped working and 2 frozen screens that had me restart the PC. No framerate drop or other things that stopped me from playing.
When I first started the game it would always tell me that DP.exe did not work. The fix for that was to go into the Games folder: Steam/SteamApps/Common/Deadly Premonition The director's cut/redist
There you find the file: PhysX_SystemSoftware.msi
Right click Repair stopped the DP.exe from crashing and let me play the game. The error might occur again after some time when trying to start the game, so you might have to do this from time to time again when starting the game.
Apart from 2 times the error did not occur while actually playing the game.
I played the game under Windows 8.
If you bought the game a while ago and where unable to play it, maybe now is the time that it finally works.
Apart from these difficulties I really enjoyed the game.
The negative sites are the boring and repeatitive combat and some very annoying quick-time-events (especially when playing on keyboard).
For me the story, atmosphere and gerneral experience where worth getting through this. Therefore I recommend this game.

Heyyo,
"Do you feel it, Zach? My coffee warned me about it." Err... what? lol. Yep! This is a weird game... but weird in a good way. An oddly budget feeling, good way indeed. :P
I want to start this recommendation off with the major strength of this game and what will have you coming back despite the flawed gameplay and that is the story. You play as Fracis York Morgan, "But please, just call me York. That's what everyone calls me." Is the main character of the game who came to a small town to investigate a supernatural murder case and try to solve the mystery of why his most recent cases all have red seeds in them and where they are coming from.
The small town is filled with a pretty diverse set of characters and I think that’s the biggest strength in this game. It’s interesting to hear what they have to say and what kind of odd or oddly humorous things they have to say.
The gameplay, as stated earlier? Yep, it’s quite flawed haha. The controls feel a little clunky and the aiming takes a while to get used to and don’t flow as smoothly as for example Resident Evil 4 or 5.
The worst offender in the gameplay though? The vehicles. There is a small open town to drive around and the camera can give you motion sickness due to a bug that they never fixed in this port... For example, when you turn your car to the left? The camera pans slightly to the right and vise-versa. It messes with your brain and I found for the first few hours that yes, I was getting headaches or even a little nauseous as you’d expect the camera to pan in the same direction of the vehicle.
Second? The vehicles physics are some kind of weird mix between Mafia 1’s and those budget games you’d find on a rack at a gas station. Vehicles constantly clip in the ground when taking the exploratory paths, taking some corners too fast cause your vehicle to flip way too easily as if the weight of the vehicle is non-existent in this calculation and the engine sounds can sometimes be quite annoying.
So yeah… vehicles? Definitely the worst part of the game. They will annoy the crap out of you. In  the PS2 era this game came out? We had good arcade vehicle physics from the likes of GTA 3 as a prime example of how they should have gone about it. But? I don’t know the development cycle and I don’t know their budget (which feels VERY tight btw) so this may have been an area that they didn’t focus in… but at least they should have fixed the damn camera pan when they made this PC port. :P
Oh, one warning about this port? It can be quite unstable. As nice as it is you get bonus points for remembering to use phones (to manually save your game) there are times you will get screwed over especially during side-missions where the game will crash and cost you time if you don’t save… so it’s up to you if you wish to use manual or auto saving (toggled in the options menu).

Well, I liked Super Smash Bros. and Custom Robo, so naturally I loved this game. If you're a completionist you will easily find 40-50 hours trying to get all the parts. (I'm at 34 and still not 100%) It's a highly fun game to play.
The game plays exactly like Super Smash Bros, but with characters akin to the Custom Robo games. The customization is great, with all sorts of parts with different abilities or effects to mix and match. The story mode is engaging and challenging at the higher levels, with all sorts of hidden places to explore and find rare parts. There are even a few simple puzzles and riddles to follow.
That said, it could use a few things. Currently, there is no multiplayer, and that doesn't appear to be changing anytime soon. Also, you won't be able to set up interesting battles vs the AI. Aside from the story mode, you can either do tournament mode and fight the AI 1v1 8 times, or you can do battle mode and fight up to 4 players split-screen. There is no option to create a custom game with players vs AI, which is a shame since there are parts of the story mode that are actually 2v2, you and 1 AI vs 2 AI opponents, so the systems are there.
Despite this, I would recommend this game to any Super Smash Bros fans, especially those who also like customization such as that found in Custom Robo or other Mech games. There has been mention of the possibility of a sequel, however there is no word whether or not it's under development or not. Still, this version is worth a buy.

This is an interesting take on a novel and innovative concept. Further, it is well executed and fun to play.
My one complaint would be that the story and sellable art styles fork very drastically, and at each new act it is impossible to cater to the choice you didn't make. This means that if you chose one art style in act 1, you'll never be able to branch out and sell in a different art style in act 2 or 3. You must focus more and more on sub genres in order to pay the bills and finish the game. There are no crossover artists folks!
Singular complaint aside, I still had a wonderful time with the game. I worked hard on my art, ended up not able to sell any of it, and ended up starving and crying in to the barrel fire of canvas and paint I lit for warmth. Alone and forgotten. I felt a little cheated, as I thought my art was passible and some of it even good, given the limited tools available to create it. I shared it. Then I went to the community page to see what others had created. I'm no artist. I wouldn't go there until after you've played the game a bit. Don't get discouraged early. After you've had some time and uploaded your masterpieces, then look.
It also turns out to be a very great game for "hot seat" multiplayer, changing players each painting, and competing on who can sell for the most/quickest. It's not selling out, it's buying in.

Despite the limited toolset, I think the game is quite fun. It allowed me to enjoy making art without thinking too much. I just played for 2 hours for fun, but I see myself doing simple studies on here. It's quite motivating and rewarding for a novice artist. If you're a serious artist who prefer a lot of tools like Photoshop, you might get annoyed by the game for its limits, but at the same time, try challenging yourself using limited tools. It gets you to think another way.
Personally I'm not great with color, and this game kinda forces me to dive into it a little. I'm a little disappointed in the limited palets because I wanted to do a value study and color study. Nonetheless, the game gave me a good time. I ended up doing nudes with only browns half of the first act.

Fun and a good time killer, but extremely limited on tools. Way more than I would've thought, at least. Managed to sort of recreate a Bob Ross painting though, so that's always fun. I sincerely wish there was a thinner brush and/or more options with the colors/tools.
I was finally able to live out my dream of selling my drawings of poop and dongs (Sometimes even both!) to the French. 11/10 would sell poop and dong art again.
It was a cute little game. Depending on the customers, you need to decide on colors and shapes. It finished too fast though. I was expecting more. I'd give it 5/10
